lessons.title: Charge, current and static
lessons.teach: Charge comes in two signs: like charges repel and opposite charges attract. A neutral object is not empty; its positive and negative charge simply balance. The force between two charges falls with the square of distance, so doubling the gap quarters the force. Current is the rate charge passes a point: current equals charge divided by time, current in amps, charge in coulombs, time in seconds. Conventional current points the way positive charge would move, so electrons in a wire drift the opposite way. Electrostatic discharge, a quick jump of charge between objects at different potentials, can damage a chip even when you feel and see nothing. That is why you wear a grounded wrist strap before handling integrated circuits.
lessons.eli5: Think of a crowded shop. A neutral object is like the shop with exactly as many people coming as going: busy, not empty, but balanced. Charges are like people who push away anyone similar and pull toward anyone opposite. Current is how many people pass through the door each second, not how many are inside. And a static zap is like a sudden rush through a tiny doorway, enough to break a delicate door even if nobody noticed. So neutral means balanced, current is charge per second, conventional current follows positive charge, and unfelt static can still damage a chip.
lessons.deep: The lesson links four facts. Charge: like signs repel, opposite signs attract, and neutral means equal positive and negative, not zero charge. Force: by Coulomb's law it varies with one over the distance squared, so doubling the distance gives one quarter of the force and tripling gives one ninth. Current: formula first, current equals charge divided by time, amps from coulombs per second. Example: 9 millicoulombs passing in 3 milliseconds is 9 over 3, which is 3 amps, because the milli prefixes cancel; 9 millicoulombs in 3 seconds would be 3 milliamps. Direction: conventional current is the direction positive charge would move, so electrons drifting right mean conventional current to the left. Static: electrostatic discharge is a rapid charge transfer between objects at different potentials. The structures inside a chip are so small that a discharge you cannot feel can damage them, sometimes in a way that only shows later. The common misconception is that no sensation means no harm. That is why a properly worn and connected wrist strap keeps you at the bench's potential before you handle any integrated circuit. These ideas underpin every circuit calculation in the course.

lessons.title: Voltage compares two points
lessons.teach: A voltage always compares two points. V A B means the potential at A minus the potential at B; reverse the order and the sign flips. Ground is simply the node we choose to call zero volts. It is a reference, and the negative battery terminal is not automatically ground. Moving the reference changes the number given to each node, but every difference between two nodes stays the same. A voltmeter follows the same rule: its reading equals the red-probe potential minus the black-probe potential. Red on 7 volts and black on 2 volts reads plus 5 volts.
lessons.eli5: Think of heights on a hillside. You can only say a spot is 5 metres high once you pick where zero is, and if you say how much higher A is than B, swapping them just flips the sign. Voltage works the same way: V A B is A minus B, and ground is the zero you choose. Move the zero and every spot gets a new number, but the difference between any two spots stays the same. So a voltage always compares two points in order, ground is a choice, and a meter reads red minus black.
lessons.deep: Formula first: V A B equals potential at A minus potential at B, in volts, and V B A equals negative V A B. A voltmeter applies the same ordered subtraction: reading equals red-probe potential minus black-probe potential. Ground is the node chosen as zero; it is not automatically the negative battery terminal, and not automatically earth. Changing ground subtracts the same amount from every node, so every difference, and therefore every current, stays the same. Example: nodes at 9 volts, 4 volts and 0 volts with the 0 volt node as ground. Make the 4 volt node ground: the values become 5, 0 and minus 4 volts. The difference between the top and bottom is still 9 volts. Meter example: red on minus 1 volt and black on plus 3 volts reads minus 1 minus 3, which is minus 4 volts. Swapping the probes reads plus 4 volts. The common misconception is that a negative meter reading means a fault. It only means the red probe is on the lower point. Another is that the battery's negative terminal must be ground. It is ground only if you choose it. These rules apply to every node voltage and logic level measured in the lab.

lessons.title: Series drops and node voltage
lessons.teach: In a series circuit the same current flows through every resistor, and Kirchhoff's voltage law says the drops add up to the supply. Combine that with Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, voltage in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms, and the current is the supply voltage divided by the total resistance. Example: 12 volts across 2 kilohms on top and 4 kilohms at the bottom, in series. Total resistance is 6 kilohms, so the current is 2 milliamps. The drops are 4 volts and 8 volts, which add to 12. With the bottom of the 4 kilohm resistor grounded, the junction sits at 8 volts.
lessons.eli5: Think of a single path down a hill with two steep sections. Every walker passes along the whole path, so the same number of walkers per minute pass every point. The total drop from top to bottom is fixed, and the steeper section takes more of it. A series circuit is that path: the same current flows through every resistor, the drops add up to the supply, and the bigger resistor takes the bigger share. So current is the supply over the total resistance, and each drop is that current times its own resistance.
lessons.deep: Formula first: current equals supply voltage divided by total resistance, amps, volts and ohms; each drop equals current times its resistance; Kirchhoff's voltage law says the drops add up to the supply. The same current flows everywhere in a series loop because charge has nowhere else to go. Example: 9 volts across 2 kilohms on top and 1 kilohm at the bottom. Total resistance 3 kilohms, so current is 9 volts over 3 kilohms, 3 milliamps. Drops: 3 milliamps times 2 kilohms is 6 volts; 3 milliamps times 1 kilohm is 3 volts; 6 plus 3 is 9. With the bottom of the 1 kilohm resistor grounded, the junction voltage equals the lower resistor's drop, 3 volts. The divider shortcut gives the same: junction voltage equals supply times lower resistance over total, 9 times 1 over 3, which is 3 volts. Volts over kilohms gives milliamps, and milliamps times kilohms gives volts, which keeps the prefixes easy. The common misconception is that the junction voltage equals the top resistor's drop. It equals the drop across whatever lies between the junction and ground. These series drops are the basis of pull-up and pull-down inputs.

lessons.title: Prefixes and four-step calculations
lessons.teach: Engineering notation uses powers of ten in steps of three, written as prefixes, with the number kept between 1 and 999. Kilo is ten to the three, milli ten to the minus three, micro ten to the minus six. Moving to a smaller prefix makes the number a thousand times bigger: 0.025 millivolts is 25 microvolts. Letter case matters: small m is milli, capital M is mega. Every calculation uses four steps: name the quantity, write the formula, substitute values with units, give the answer with units. For example, Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, amps, volts, ohms: 4.7 volts over 4.7 kilohms is 1 milliamp. A result off by exactly a thousand points to a prefix slip.
lessons.eli5: Think of buying rope sold by the metre, the centimetre or the millimetre. The rope is the same length whichever unit you use; only the number on the label changes, getting bigger as the unit gets smaller. Prefixes work like that in steps of a thousand. And like a recipe card, every calculation shows what you are finding, the formula, the values with units, and the answer with a unit. So smaller unit means bigger number, keep the number between 1 and 999, and an answer off by exactly a thousand points to a prefix slip in the substitution.
lessons.deep: Formula first: new number equals old number times old prefix value over new prefix value. Kilo is ten to the three, milli ten to the minus three, micro ten to the minus six; neighbouring prefixes differ by one thousand. Example: 0.082 milliamps to microamps. Micro is one step smaller, so multiply by 1000: 82 microamps. Another: 0.0068 amps is 6.8 milliamps, which is engineering form because 6.8 lies between 1 and 999. Letter case: small m is milli, capital M is mega. Four-step example: find the current through 2.2 kilohms with 6.6 volts across it. Target: I. Formula: Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance. Substitution: 6.6 volts over 2.2 kilohms. Answer: 3 milliamps, since volts over kilohms gives milliamps. If someone typed 2.2 instead of 2200 ohms, they would get 3 amps, exactly a thousand times too big, and the four-step layout sends them straight to the substitution step. The common misconception is changing the prefix without changing the number, which silently changes the quantity by a factor of a thousand. These habits are used in every later calculation, including frequency and period.

lessons.title: Drawing IC pins and designators
lessons.teach: On a circuit drawing, each IC pin's number goes outside the body and its function goes inside. A horizontal pin has its number sitting just above the wire; a vertical pin has it beside the wire, so wires never run through the numbers. Every IC gets a designator, U1, U2, U3, with the part number, such as 74LS47, written below it. To find pin 1 on the real chip, hold it with the notch at the top; pin 1 is top left, and numbering runs down that side and back up the other. A bar over a pin name means the function is active low.
lessons.eli5: Think of house numbers and shop names on a street. The number goes on the kerb outside, where you can see it from the road; the shop's name goes on the sign inside. On a chip drawing, the pin number sits just outside the body, beside the wire, so wires never run through it, and the function goes inside. Each chip gets a unique name, U1, U2, with its part number below. A bar over a pin name means that job happens when the pin is LOW. So number outside, function inside, unique U label, and bar means active low.
lessons.deep: The conventions make every symbol traceable to one physical pin on one physical chip. The pin number sits outside the body: above a horizontal wire, beside a vertical one, so the connecting wire never covers it. The function, like V C C or A, sits inside. Each chip gets a designator, U followed by a number, unique on the drawing, with the part number such as 74 L S 47 directly below, in the same corner on every chip. On the real chip, hold the notch at the top; pin 1 is top left, numbers run down the left and back up the right. On a 16-pin chip, that puts pin 8 bottom left and pin 16 top right. A bar over a pin name means active low: the function is asserted by logic 0. Example: the 74 L S 47's lamp test pin, L T bar, normally sits HIGH; pulling it LOW lights every segment to check the display. The common misconception is that active low means a negative voltage. It only means LOW, logic 0, turns the function on. Another is that the pin number belongs on the wire. It belongs just off it. Together these rules let anyone build or troubleshoot your circuit from the drawing alone.

lessons.title: Gates drawn where they work
lessons.teach: A circuit drawing draws each gate where it does its job, not grouped inside a picture of the chip. The link to hardware is kept by labels. U1 names the package. A suffix letter, as in U1A or U1B, names which gate inside it. The part number sits below, and pin numbers go on the leads. A quad package has one supply pin and one ground pin, so its power connections are shown on exactly one of its gates, together with a decoupling capacitor from V C C to ground. Unused gates are still drawn, in a column at the edge, with inputs tied to plus 5 volts and outputs marked N C.
lessons.eli5: Think of a sports team list. On the field, each player stands where they play, not grouped by which bus they arrived on. But the list still records each player's team and shirt number. A circuit drawing places each gate where it works, and labels like U1A record which chip and which gate inside it. A quad chip shares one power connection, so power is drawn once. Spare players still sit on the bench, properly dressed. So gates are drawn by function, labels keep the hardware link, power appears once per package, and spare gates are tied off.
lessons.deep: The designator names the package, U1; the suffix names the gate inside, A to D for a quad; the part number below says what chip it is; and pin numbers on the leads say which pins are used. Example: U2C on a 74 L S 08 uses pins 9 and 10 as inputs and pin 8 as output. Because a quad package has one V C C pin and one ground pin, power is shown on exactly one of its gates, with a decoupling capacitor from V C C to ground. Drawing it four times would suggest four supplies. Unused gates are still powered, so they are drawn, usually in a spare column at the edge: inputs tied to plus 5 volts, outputs marked N C, no connection. Inputs are tied HIGH because a floating T T L input picks up noise, and a LOW input pushes current out of its input stage, while a HIGH draws very little. Outputs are left unconnected because tying a driven output to a rail makes it fight the rail. The common misconception is that unused outputs need tying like unused inputs. Inputs need a defined level; outputs already produce one. These conventions make a multi-chip drawing buildable by someone else.

lessons.title: Binary place values and fractions
lessons.teach: Binary uses only 0 and 1, and each place is worth twice the place to its right. From the right the weights are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. To convert to decimal, add the weights of the places holding a 1: one zero one one is 8 plus 2 plus 1, which is 11. Places to the right of the binary point keep halving: one half, one quarter, one eighth. So one zero one point zero one one is 4 plus 1 plus a quarter plus an eighth, which is 5.375. Never read binary fraction digits as if they were decimal.
lessons.eli5: Think of a set of measuring cups: 1 cup, 2 cups, 4 cups, 8 cups, each double the last, and also a half cup, a quarter cup and an eighth cup, each half the last. A binary number says which cups are filled: a 1 means use that cup, a 0 means skip it. Add up the filled cups and you have the value. So one zero one point one is the 4 cup, the 1 cup and the half cup, 5.5. So binary place values double to the left and halve to the right of the point, and the value is the sum of the places holding a 1.
lessons.deep: Formula first: value equals the sum of each bit times its place weight. Left of the point the weights are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, doubling; right of the point they are one half, one quarter, one eighth, halving. Because each bit is 0 or 1, you just add the weights where a 1 appears. Example: one one zero one is 8 plus 4 plus 1, which is 13. Example with a fraction: one one point zero one is 2 plus 1 plus a quarter, which is 3.25. And point one zero one is a half plus an eighth, which is 0.625. The rightmost whole-number bit is worth 1 and decides whether the number is odd or even. Leading zeros on the left and trailing zeros after the point add nothing. The common misconception is reading the fraction digits as decimal, so that point zero one would be one hundredth. In binary it is one quarter. Another is giving the first place after the point a weight of one tenth, out of decimal habit; in binary it is one half. Adding the weights back is also the check for every decimal-to-binary conversion in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Decimal to binary
lessons.teach: To convert decimal to binary, subtract the largest weight that fits and mark a 1 there, then carry on with what is left. For 43: 32 fits, leaving 11; 16 does not fit, so 0; 8 fits, leaving 3; 4 does not, so 0; 2 fits, leaving 1; and 1 fits. That gives one zero one zero one one. The other method is repeated division by two: write each remainder, then read them in reverse, last remainder first, because the first remainder is the ones bit. Always check by adding the weights back up.
lessons.eli5: Think of paying exactly 43 cents with one coin each of 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 cents. Take the biggest coin that fits, 32, leaving 11. The 16 is too big, skip it. Take the 8, leaving 3. Skip the 4. Take the 2 and then the 1. The coins taken are 1s and the skipped ones are 0s: one zero one zero one one. The other method, dividing by two, finds the bits from the smallest coin up, so you read it backwards. So decimal to binary means subtracting weights from the top, or dividing by two and reading remainders last to first.
lessons.deep: Method one: find the largest power of two not exceeding the number, write 1, subtract, and test each lower weight, writing 1 if it fits and 0 if not. Method two: divide by two repeatedly, recording each remainder, until the quotient is zero; read the remainders last to first. The reason for reading backwards: the first remainder says whether the number is odd, which is the ones bit, the least significant. Example by subtraction: 26. 16 fits, leaving 10; 8 fits, leaving 2; 4 does not; 2 fits, leaving 0; 1 does not. So one one zero one zero. Example by division: 26 over 2 is 13 remainder 0; 13 over 2 is 6 remainder 1; 6 over 2 is 3 remainder 0; 3 over 2 is 1 remainder 1; 1 over 2 is 0 remainder 1. Backwards: one one zero one zero, the same. Check: 16 plus 8 plus 2 is 26. The common misconception is reading the remainders in the order found, giving zero one zero one one, which is 11, not 26. Always add the weights back to check. Grouping these bits into octal and hex comes next.

lessons.title: Octal and hex groupings
lessons.teach: Octal is base eight, digits 0 to 7, place weights 1, 8, 64. Each octal digit is exactly three bits, so group binary in threes from the right: one one one, zero one one is 7 and 3, octal 73. Hexadecimal is base sixteen, using 0 to 9 then A to F for ten to fifteen. Each hex digit is four bits, a nibble, so group binary in fours: zero one one zero, one zero one one is 6 and B, hex 6B. For hex to decimal, the left digit counts sixteens: hex 2F is 2 times 16 plus 15, which is 47. For decimal to hex, count the sixteens, then write the remainder as one digit.
lessons.eli5: Think of counting marbles into small bags of eight, or bigger bags of sixteen. Octal counts in eights, so its digits only go 0 to 7. Hex counts in sixteens, so after 9 it needs letters, A to F, for ten to fifteen. Because eight is three binary places and sixteen is four, you convert by grouping bits: threes for octal, fours for hex, starting from the right. So octal digits are three bits each and hex digits are four bits each, and the left hex digit counts sixteens.
lessons.deep: Formula first: an octal number's value is each digit times 1, 8, 64 and so on; a hex number's value is each digit times 1, 16, 256 and so on. Eight is two cubed and sixteen is two to the fourth, so octal digits map to exactly three bits and hex digits to exactly four. Group from the right and pad the left with zeros. Example, binary one zero one one one zero. In threes: one zero one, one one zero, which is 5 and 6, octal 56. In fours: zero zero one zero, one one one zero, which is 2 and E, hex 2 E. Check both against decimal: 32 plus 8 plus 4 plus 2 is 46; octal 56 is 5 times 8 plus 6, which is 46; hex 2 E is 2 times 16 plus 14, which is 46. Decimal to hex: 75 is 4 sixteens, 64, with 11 left, and 11 is B, so hex 4 B. The common misconception is using 8 as an octal digit, or writing a remainder of 11 as two characters instead of the single digit B. Another is grouping from the left, which shifts every group. Hex is the shorthand used for A S C I I codes and memory addresses.

lessons.title: BCD: four bits per digit
lessons.teach: Binary coded decimal, or B C D, codes each decimal digit separately in four bits. So 59 in B C D is zero one zero one for the 5, then one zero zero one for the 9. That differs from pure binary, where 59 is one number, one one one zero one one. Only the groups zero zero zero zero to one zero zero one, 0 to 9, are valid; the six patterns for ten to fifteen are invalid in B C D. A three-digit display needs twelve B C D bits, four per digit.
lessons.eli5: Think of a row of separate scoreboards, one per digit, each showing only 0 to 9. That is B C D: each decimal digit gets its own four-bit scoreboard. So 59 is the 5 board, zero one zero one, next to the 9 board, one zero zero one. Pure binary is one big counter for the whole number, giving a different pattern. A board that shows ten to fifteen is broken, because no decimal digit is that big. So B C D codes each decimal digit in its own four bits, only 0 to 9 are valid, and a three-digit display needs twelve bits.
lessons.deep: B C D encodes each decimal digit independently as a four-bit binary number from zero zero zero zero to one zero zero one. Four bits could represent up to fifteen, but the six patterns for ten to fifteen are invalid in B C D. Example: 63. In B C D, the 6 is zero one one zero and the 3 is zero zero one one, eight bits. In pure binary, 63 is 32 plus 16 plus 8 plus 4 plus 2 plus 1, which is one one one one one one, six bits. Decoding: take each four-bit group alone. Zero one one one, zero zero one zero is 7 and 2, which is 72. If the same eight bits were read as pure binary, they would be 64 plus 32 plus 16 plus 2, which is 114. Displays handle one digit at a time, which is why B C D exists. The cost is extra bits: four per digit, so a three-digit display needs 3 times 4, which is 12 bits. The common misconception is that B C D is just binary with spacing. It is a different code once the number reaches 10. A group like one one zero zero, twelve, is invalid. A S C I I is the next code, for characters.

lessons.title: ASCII character codes
lessons.teach: A S C I I, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, gives each letter, digit, symbol and control character a seven-bit code, 128 codes in all, usually stored in a byte with a leading zero. Capital A is hex 41, and the capitals count up from there, so B is hex 42. Lowercase a is hex 61. The digit characters start at hex 30, so the character 5 is hex 35. That means the character 5 is not the number five: the code names a symbol to display, not a value to calculate with.
lessons.eli5: Think of numbered pigeonholes in a mailroom, each holding one kind of letter. Pigeonhole 41 holds capital A, 42 holds capital B, and so on. The number on the pigeonhole is just an address for the symbol, not a value to do maths with. A S C I I is that numbering system for characters, so computers can store and swap text. The character 5 lives in pigeonhole hex 35. So A S C I I gives each character a seven-bit code, and the code for a digit character is not the digit's value.
lessons.deep: A S C I I assigns each letter, digit, punctuation mark and control character a seven-bit code, two to the seven, which is 128 codes, usually stored in a byte with a leading zero. Systems need it because text must move between keyboards, memory, screens and other computers, and every device must agree which bit pattern means which character. The codes are ordered, so you can count from an anchor. Capital A is hex 41, so capital G, six letters later, is hex 47. Lowercase a is hex 61. Digit characters start at hex 30: the character 8 is hex 38. Example: the character 8, hex 38, is zero zero one one, one zero zero zero in binary, which is 56 as a number, not 8. To get the value from the character, subtract hex 30. The text 42 is stored as two bytes, hex 34 then hex 32, which is neither 42 in pure binary nor in B C D. The common misconception is that the code for the character 5 is binary five. It is hex 35. You do not need the whole table; you need the counting method and the distinction between a character and a value. Bits as states and flags come next.

lessons.title: Bits, states and status flags
lessons.teach: With n bits you get two to the n different patterns. As unsigned numbers they run from 0 up to two to the n, minus 1. Four bits give 16 patterns, 0 to 15. Six bits give 64 patterns, 0 to 63. To encode a number of states, pick the smallest n whose two to the n reaches it: 40 states need 6 bits, because 5 bits only give 32. Bits can also be status flags, where each bit position reports one condition. Then the pattern is a set of yes or no answers, read position by position, not a single number.
lessons.eli5: Think of light switches in a row. One switch gives 2 patterns, two give 4, three give 8: every switch you add doubles the patterns. If you number the patterns from zero, the last number is one less than the count. And sometimes the switches are not a number at all: each one just answers its own question, like porch light on, kitchen light on. So n bits give two to the n patterns, the largest unsigned value is two to the n minus one, and status bits are read one position at a time as yes or no flags.
lessons.deep: Formula first: states equal two to the n; largest unsigned value equals two to the n minus one. Each extra bit doubles the count because every existing pattern can be followed by a 0 or a 1. Example: 5 bits give 32 patterns, 0 to 31. To encode a number of states, pick the smallest n with two to the n at least that large: 20 states need 5 bits, because 4 bits give only 16. 100 states need 7 bits, since 6 give 64 and 7 give 128. Status flags: each bit position has its own meaning from a bit map. With the lesson's map, bit 3 over-temperature, bit 2 low level, bit 1 door open, bit 0 motor running, the status zero one one zero means low level and door open, with no over-temperature and the motor stopped. It does not mean a reading of six. The common misconception is the off-by-one: saying 6 bits reach 64. The largest value is 63, because zero uses one of the 64 patterns. Another is converting a status word to decimal and treating it as a measurement. Its meaning comes only from the bit map someone defined.

lessons.title: Gray code: one bit at a time
lessons.source: Assigned problems guide, Gray code handout
lessons.teach: In Gray code, neighbouring values differ in exactly one bit, unlike binary, where 3 to 4 flips three bits. To convert binary to Gray, copy the first bit; then each next Gray bit is the exclusive OR of that binary bit and the binary bit to its left, where same gives 0 and different gives 1. So binary one one zero zero becomes one zero one zero. To convert Gray back to binary, copy the first bit; then each Gray 1 flips the binary bit you just found, and each Gray 0 keeps it.
lessons.eli5: Think of a row of people holding cards to show a number. In ordinary binary, going from 3 to 4 means three people flip their cards at once, and since nobody flips at exactly the same instant, the row briefly shows nonsense. Gray code orders the patterns so that only one person flips for each step, so no wrong in-between number can appear. So in Gray code neighbouring values differ by exactly one bit, and conversion uses same gives 0, different gives 1.
lessons.deep: Binary to Gray: copy the first bit; each next Gray bit is the exclusive OR of that binary bit and the binary bit to its left, where exclusive OR gives 0 if they are the same and 1 if they differ. Example: binary zero one one one, which is 7. First Gray bit 0. Then 0 and 1 differ, 1. Then 1 and 1 same, 0. Then 1 and 1 same, 0. Gray is zero one zero zero. Gray to binary: copy the first bit, then for each next Gray bit, a 1 flips the binary bit just found and a 0 keeps it. From zero one zero zero: 0; Gray 1 flips to 1; Gray 0 keeps 1; Gray 0 keeps 1. Binary zero one one one, back to 7. Why one bit per step matters: in binary, 7 to 8 is zero one one one to one zero zero zero, all four bits changing, so a reader sampling mid-change could see any mix. In Gray, 7 is zero one zero zero and 8 is one one zero zero, one bit. The common misconception is reading a Gray word with binary place weights. Gray zero one zero zero is 7, not 4. Convert to binary first, then add the weights.

lessons.title: Analog versus digital
lessons.teach: An analog quantity varies smoothly and continuously, like temperature, wind speed or sound pressure. A digital quantity takes distinct steps, and in binary systems just two states, 0 and 1. To bring an analog signal into a computer you use an analog-to-digital converter, an A D C, which outputs a digital code. A digital-to-analog converter, a D A C, does the reverse, turning codes back into a smooth voltage, as a music player does before the speaker. Digital signals tolerate noise better, because a slightly noisy HIGH still reads as HIGH.
lessons.eli5: Think of a ramp versus a staircase. On a ramp you can stand at any height at all; that is analog, like temperature or wind speed. On a staircase you can only be on one step or another; that is digital, and binary has just two steps. Converting from ramp to staircase is like noting which step you are nearest: an A D C. Building a ramp from step readings is a D A C. So analog varies continuously, digital takes distinct states, an A D C turns analog into digital codes, and a D A C does the reverse.
lessons.deep: An analog quantity can take any value in a continuous range: temperature, wind speed, the pressure of a sound wave. A digital quantity takes distinct values, and in binary circuits two states, 0 and 1. The physical digital signal is still a voltage; the receiver decides whether it lies in the LOW range or the HIGH range. That decision gives noise tolerance. Example: if a receiver treats anything above 2 volts as HIGH, a 3.5 volt HIGH with 0.4 volts of noise, arriving anywhere from 3.1 to 3.9 volts, still reads HIGH, so the bit is exact; an analog value with the same noise would simply be 0.4 volts wrong. An analog-to-digital converter samples a voltage and outputs a digital code; its output is digital, never analog. A digital-to-analog converter takes codes and outputs a voltage, as a music player does before the speaker. The common misconception is that digital is noise-proof. Enough noise to push a signal into the wrong range still causes an error, and a HIGH need not be exactly 5 volts. Another is mixing up which converter does which job: the name reads from input to output. Clocks and waveforms, the time side of digital signals, come next.

lessons.title: Period and frequency
lessons.teach: A clock waveform repeats. Its period is the time for one full cycle, measured from one rising edge to the next rising edge. Frequency is the number of cycles per second. They are reciprocals: frequency equals one over period, frequency in hertz, period in seconds. Handy pairs: 1 kilohertz goes with 1 millisecond, and 1 megahertz goes with 1 microsecond. So 2 megahertz has a period of half a microsecond, and a 100 microsecond period means 10 kilohertz. An oscilloscope shows voltage on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis.
lessons.eli5: Think of a merry-go-round. The time for one full turn back to the same horse is the period. How many full turns happen each second is the frequency. If one turn takes a quarter of a second, it makes four turns each second. A clock signal is the same: period from one rising edge to the next, frequency in cycles per second. Speed it up and each turn takes less time. So frequency equals one over period, with 1 kilohertz pairing with 1 millisecond and 1 megahertz with 1 microsecond.
lessons.deep: Formula first: frequency equals one divided by period, frequency in hertz, period in seconds; equivalently, period equals one over frequency. The period is measured between matching points, such as rising edge to rising edge, because that is where the waveform repeats; the HIGH time alone is not the period. Example: a 5 megahertz clock has a period of one over 5 million seconds, 0.2 microseconds, which is 200 nanoseconds. A 250 microsecond period gives one over 250 times ten to the minus six, which is 4 kilohertz. The pairing check: megahertz times microseconds equals 1, so 5 megahertz times 0.2 microseconds is 1; kilohertz times milliseconds equals 1, so 4 kilohertz times 0.25 milliseconds, which is 250 microseconds, is 1. Doubling the frequency halves the period. On an oscilloscope, voltage is on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal, so the period is read as a horizontal distance between matching edges. The common misconception is that a higher frequency means a longer signal; it means shorter cycles. Another is measuring only the HIGH part of the waveform. Duty cycle, which uses the HIGH time, is a separate idea, covered next.

lessons.title: Duty cycle
lessons.teach: A pulse waveform spends part of each period HIGH and the rest LOW. The period is the HIGH time plus the LOW time. Duty cycle is the fraction of the period spent HIGH: duty cycle equals HIGH time divided by period, times 100 percent, with both times in the same unit. For example, HIGH for 20 microseconds out of an 80 microsecond period is 25 percent. Duty cycle and frequency are separate ideas: you can change how long the pulse stays HIGH without changing how often it repeats.
lessons.eli5: Think of a street light on a timer that repeats every hour. How often the cycle repeats is one idea. How much of each hour the light is on is another: it could be on for 15 minutes or 45 minutes of every hour, and it still repeats hourly. Duty cycle is the share of each cycle spent on. Fifteen minutes of every hour is 25 percent. So duty cycle is HIGH time divided by the whole period, as a percentage, and it can change without changing the frequency.
lessons.deep: Formula first: duty cycle equals HIGH time divided by period, times 100 percent, with both times in the same unit; period equals HIGH time plus LOW time; and frequency equals one over period, hertz and seconds. Duty cycle describes the shape of each cycle, while frequency describes how often cycles repeat, so they are independent. Example: HIGH for 6 microseconds and LOW for 24 microseconds. The period is 30 microseconds. Duty cycle is 6 over 30, which is 20 percent. Frequency is one over 30 microseconds, about 33.3 kilohertz. Keep the 30 microsecond period but make the HIGH time 15 microseconds: duty cycle becomes 50 percent, and the frequency is unchanged at about 33.3 kilohertz. The common misconception is dividing the HIGH time by the LOW time. Here that would give 6 over 24, which is 25 percent, wrong because the denominator must be the whole period. Another is using the HIGH time as the period when finding frequency, which would give one over 6 microseconds, about 167 kilohertz, five times too high. Always build the period from HIGH plus LOW first. Edges take a little time to rise and fall, but that transition time is not part of this calculation.

lessons.title: Serial versus parallel data
lessons.teach: Serial transmission sends one bit per clock period down a single line; Kleitz sends the least significant bit first. Parallel transmission uses one line per bit and sends a whole group in a single clock period. The time to send equals the number of clock periods used, times the period. Example: at 1 megahertz the period is 1 microsecond. Eight bits in serial take 8 microseconds; on an eight-bit parallel bus they take 1 microsecond. Parallel is faster in this model, but it needs more wires and circuitry.
lessons.eli5: Think of loading eight passengers onto a single-seat chairlift versus an eight-seat gondola. The chairlift takes eight trips, one passenger per trip; the gondola takes everyone in one trip, but it needs a much bigger and costlier machine. Serial data is the chairlift: one bit per clock period on one line. Parallel is the gondola: a whole group per clock period on many lines. So serial time is bits times the clock period, parallel time is groups times the period, and parallel is faster but costs more wires and circuitry.
lessons.deep: Formula first, ignoring start bits, parity and other overhead: serial time equals number of bits times clock period; parallel time equals number of groups times clock period; and clock period equals one over clock frequency. Example: four 8-bit numbers at 4 megahertz. The period is one over 4 million seconds, 0.25 microseconds. Serial: 32 bits times 0.25 microseconds is 8 microseconds. Parallel, eight lines: 4 groups times 0.25 microseconds is 1 microsecond. The ratio is 8, the number of lines, which is the expected speed-up in this model. The cost of parallel is more conductors, more connector pins and more circuitry. Bit order matters when reading a serial trace: Kleitz sends the least significant bit first, so the byte zero zero zero zero, zero one one one is sent in time as 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0. The common misconception is forgetting to convert the frequency to a period, or multiplying by the frequency instead of the period, which gives a meaningless number of microseconds. Another is reading the serial trace left to right as the binary number, which reverses the bits when the least significant bit is sent first. Both methods move the same data; they differ in time and hardware.

lessons.title: Poles and throws
lessons.teach: A mechanical switch is named by poles and throws. A pole is one independent path the switch controls; the instructor counts the pivot points of the moving contacts. A throw is a destination each pole can connect to. S P S T, single pole single throw, makes or breaks one path, and its open position is not a second throw. S P D T connects one common terminal to either of two destinations. A double-pole switch has two pivots moving together, shown by a dashed link, but their circuits stay separate. A stereo selector with three inputs needs D P 3 T.
lessons.eli5: Think of a train line with points that send a train to one of several platforms. Each separate line controlled by the switch is a pole, and each platform it can reach is a throw. A switch with two separate lines whose levers are tied together is double pole, but the trains on one line never cross to the other. Stopping a train is not a platform, so an open position is not a throw. So poles count independent paths, throws count destinations per pole, and a stereo selector needs two poles, one per channel.
lessons.deep: A pole is one independent electrical path with its own moving contact; the instructor counts these as pivots. A throw is one destination that contact can connect to. S P S T makes or breaks one path. S P D T connects a common terminal to either of two destinations. D P D T does that for two separate paths at once. The dashed link on a symbol means the poles move together mechanically; electrically their paths stay separate. Example: a selector that routes left and right audio channels together from one of five sources needs two poles, one per channel, and five throws, one per source: D P 5 T, with 10 destination terminals and 2 commons. A switch that turns two separate lamps on and off together is D P S T. Why open is not a throw: a throw is a destination, and the open position connects the pole to nothing. The common misconception is calling an S P S T switch double throw because it has two positions, open and closed. It has only one destination. Another is believing the dashed link joins the two circuits, which would mix the left and right channels. These names matter when ordering a switch or wiring a selector correctly the first time.

lessons.title: Relays: coil and contacts
lessons.teach: A relay is a switch worked by an electromagnet. Current through its coil pulls the contacts over. Normal means the coil is de-energized. Normally open, N O, contacts are open at rest and close when the coil is energized. Normally closed, N C, contacts are closed at rest and open when energized. A closed contact is an ideal short, with zero volts across it; an open contact carries no current but can have voltage across it. So N O contacts wired across the lower resistor of a divider short it when the coil is energized, pulling the output to zero volts.
lessons.eli5: Think of a gate on a spring that a magnet can pull. With the magnet off, the gate rests in its normal position. Turn the magnet on and it swings the gate the other way. A relay is a switch like that: current in the coil makes an electromagnet that pulls the contacts over. Normally open contacts close when energized; normally closed contacts open. Where the picture breaks: a relay is mechanical, so it is slow and can bounce. So normal means coil off, and energizing the coil moves every contact to its other state.
lessons.deep: Formula first for the divider: output equals supply times bottom resistance over total resistance, volts and ohms. With the coil de-energized, normally open contacts are open, and normally closed contacts are closed. Energizing the coil creates a magnetic field that pulls the armature, so normally open contacts close and normally closed contacts open. A closed contact is an ideal short, zero volts across it; an open contact passes no current but can hold a voltage. Example: 10 volts feeding 2 kilohms on top and 3 kilohms at the bottom, with normally open contacts across the bottom resistor. Coil off: contacts open, output is 10 times 3 over 5, which is 6 volts. Coil on: contacts closed, the bottom resistor is shorted, output 0 volts, and the top resistor carries 10 volts over 2 kilohms, which is 5 milliamps. With normally closed contacts instead, coil off gives 0 volts and coil on gives 6 volts. The common misconception is that the open contacts in the coil-off state have no voltage across them. They hold the full 6 volts of the divider output. Another is reading normally closed as usually closed in operation; it refers only to the de-energized coil.

lessons.title: Pull-ups, pull-downs and floating inputs
lessons.teach: A pull-up resistor runs from the supply to the output node, and a switch connects that node to ground. Switch open: no current, so the resistor drops nothing and the output sits at the supply, HIGH, while the open switch holds the full supply across it. Switch closed: the output is grounded, LOW, and the resistor limits current; current equals voltage over resistance, amps, volts, ohms, so 5 volts over 1 kilohm is 5 milliamps. A pull-down swaps the parts, so released is LOW and pressed is HIGH. With no resistor at all, an open switch leaves the input floating, with no defined level.
lessons.eli5: Think of a door on a spring hinge. With nobody touching it, the spring holds it in one definite position. Push it and it moves the other way; let go and it springs back. A pull-up resistor is a spring holding an input HIGH; pressing a button to ground overpowers it, making it LOW. A pull-down holds it LOW until a button connects it to the supply. Without any spring, the door just flaps in the wind: a floating input. So pull resistors give an input a defined level in both switch positions and limit the current when pressed.
lessons.deep: Formula first: Kirchhoff, supply equals resistor voltage plus switch voltage; Ohm, resistor voltage equals current times resistance. Pull-up with the button released: no current, so the resistor drops zero and the output equals the supply, HIGH, with the whole supply across the open switch. Pressed: the switch is a short, so the output is 0 volts, LOW, and the resistor carries supply over resistance. Example: 5 volts and a 2.2 kilohm pull-up. Released: 5 volts out. Pressed: 0 volts out, and the current is 5 volts over 2.2 kilohms, about 2.27 milliamps. Pull-down with a normally open button from 5 volts: released gives 0 volts, pressed gives 5 volts, with the same current through the resistor. So a pull-up makes a press active LOW, and a pull-down makes it active HIGH. Without any resistor, a switch from 5 volts to an input leaves the input floating when open: undefined, not zero. The common misconception is that zero current means zero voltage everywhere. That is true for the resistor, which has finite resistance, but the open switch carries no current and still holds the full 5 volts. Another is replacing the resistor with wire, which shorts the supply when pressed.

lessons.title: Diode bias and series circuits
lessons.teach: A diode passes conventional current from anode to cathode only; the bar on its symbol is the cathode. It is forward biased when the anode is more positive than the cathode, so judge by anode minus cathode, not either voltage alone. In the course model a conducting silicon diode holds about 0.7 volts, and a reverse-biased diode is open. Assume a state, then check. Five volts through a forward diode and 1 kilohm: the resistor gets 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, and Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, gives 4.3 milliamps. Reverse the diode and no current flows.
lessons.eli5: Think of a one-way door that needs a firm push before it opens. Push from the right side hard enough and it swings open; push from the wrong side and it stays shut, however hard you push. A diode is that door for current, from anode to cathode, and the firm push is about 0.7 volts for silicon. What matters is which side is pushing harder, anode minus cathode, not how high either side is. So a diode conducts when anode minus cathode reaches about 0.7 volts, and is an open circuit when reversed.
lessons.deep: Formula first: diode voltage equals anode minus cathode. In the course model, a conducting silicon diode holds 0.7 volts; a reverse-biased diode is open. In a series loop with the diode on, resistor voltage equals supply minus 0.7 volts, and current equals that over the resistance, amps, volts, ohms. Method: assume a state, solve, check. Example: 12 volts, a forward diode and 2 kilohms. Assume on: the resistor gets 12 minus 0.7, which is 11.3 volts, and the current is 11.3 volts over 2 kilohms, 5.65 milliamps. Positive current confirms on. Reverse the diode: assume off, zero current, so the resistor drops 0 volts and the diode holds the full 12 volts in reverse. Check: reverse voltage means off is consistent. Bias is judged by the difference: anode at 3 volts and cathode at 6 volts is minus 3 volts, reverse biased, even though both ends are positive. The common misconception is that a reversed diode has no voltage across it because no current flows. With zero current, Kirchhoff puts the whole supply across it. Another is forgetting the 0.7 volt drop, which here would give 6 milliamps instead of 5.65. The 0.7 volts is a model, not an exact value.

lessons.title: Diode AND and OR gates
lessons.teach: Diodes can make simple gates. In a diode AND, a resistor pulls the output up toward 5 volts, and each input connects through a diode with its cathode on the input. If any input goes to 0 volts, that diode conducts and clamps the output at 0.7 volts, a LOW. Only when all inputs are HIGH does the output stay HIGH. In a diode OR, a resistor pulls the output down to ground and each input drives an anode. Any input at 5 volts conducts and lifts the output to 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, a HIGH.
lessons.eli5: Think of a bucket kept topped up by a slow hose, with several drain holes plugged by corks. In a diode AND, the resistor is the slow hose keeping the output high. Each input LOW is a pulled cork: just one is enough to drain the output down near the bottom. In a diode OR, the output rests empty, and any one input HIGH is a tap that fills it. Where the picture breaks: a conducting diode leaves 0.7 volts, not exactly zero or full. So one LOW forces a diode AND LOW, and one HIGH forces a diode OR HIGH.
lessons.deep: Diode AND: a pull-up resistor to 5 volts, and a diode from the output to each input, cathode on the input. If every input is at 5 volts, no diode can be forward biased, so no current flows and the output stays high. If one input drops to 0 volts, its diode conducts, clamping the output at about 0.7 volts, LOW. The other diodes then have anode at 0.7 volts and cathode at 5 volts, so they are reverse biased. Current example with a 10 kilohm pull-up: 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, over 10 kilohms, 430 microamps into the LOW input. Diode OR: a pull-down resistor to ground, and a diode from each input to the output, anode on the input. One input at 5 volts makes the output 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, HIGH. Two inputs at 5 volts still give 4.3 volts, because the diodes are in parallel, not in series. The common misconception is that each extra conducting diode subtracts another 0.7 volts. Another is that the AND output with a LOW input is exactly 0 volts; the diode leaves 0.7 volts. That leftover 0.7 volts, and the drop of a HIGH to 4.3 volts, are why transistor gates replace diode gates.

lessons.title: Transistor switch and inverter
lessons.teach: A bipolar transistor has a base, a collector and an emitter. For an N P N switch, positive base drive through a base resistor turns it on: the collector-to-emitter path acts as a short, called saturation. No base current means cutoff, an open path. In the common-emitter inverter the input drives the base, the emitter is grounded, and a collector resistor pulls the collector up; the output is the collector. Input HIGH, transistor on, output LOW. Input LOW, transistor off, output HIGH. Base current equals input voltage minus 0.7, divided by base resistance, amps, volts, ohms.
lessons.eli5: Think of a light switch worked by a small lever. A little push on the lever closes a heavy-duty contact, letting a big current flow. A transistor's base is that lever, and its collector to emitter path is the contact. In the common-emitter inverter, a HIGH input pushes the lever, the contact closes, and the output is pulled down to ground, LOW. A LOW input leaves the contact open, and the collector resistor lifts the output to the supply, HIGH. So input HIGH gives transistor on and output LOW, and input LOW gives output HIGH.
lessons.deep: Formula first: base current equals input voltage minus 0.7 volts, divided by base resistance, amps, volts and ohms. A positive base drive turns an N P N on; with enough base current, the collector to emitter path is a short, saturation. With no base current it is open, cutoff. A negative base voltage would not turn it on. In the common-emitter inverter, the input feeds the base through a resistor, the emitter is grounded, and the output is taken at the collector, pulled up by a collector resistor. Example: a 5 volt input through 22 kilohms. Base current is 4.3 volts over 22 kilohms, about 195 microamps; the transistor saturates and the collector, with a 1 kilohm resistor from 5 volts, sits at 0 volts, carrying 5 milliamps. Input 0 volts: no base current, no collector current, the resistor drops nothing, and the output is 5 volts. The common misconception is that turning the transistor on makes the output HIGH. On connects the collector to ground, so the output goes LOW. Another is taking the base voltage to be the input voltage; the base sits at about 0.7 volts and the resistor takes the rest. Loading this output is the next lesson.

lessons.title: Loading the inverter output
lessons.teach: When the inverter's transistor is off, the output is not guaranteed to be the full supply. A load from the output to ground forms a divider with the collector resistor: output voltage equals supply times load resistance, over collector resistance plus load resistance, all in volts and ohms. With 5 volts, a 1 kilohm collector resistor and a 10 kilohm load, the output is about 4.55 volts; add more loads and it sags further. A small collector resistor helps the HIGH, but passes a large current when the transistor turns on. T T L's totem-pole output fixes this with an active pull-up transistor.
lessons.eli5: Think of a water tank feeding houses through one narrow pipe. With every tap closed, each house sees the tank's full pressure. Open taps, and water flows through the narrow pipe, so pressure at the houses drops; open more taps and it drops further. The collector resistor is the narrow pipe and the loads are the open taps. A totem-pole output replaces the narrow pipe with a pump that pushes actively. So when the inverter's transistor is off, the HIGH output sags under load by the divider rule, and an active pull-up fixes it.
lessons.deep: Formula first: output voltage equals supply times load resistance, divided by collector resistance plus load resistance, in volts and ohms. With the transistor off, the collector resistor and load form a series divider. Example: 5 volts, a 2 kilohm collector resistor and a 6 kilohm load. Output is 5 times 6 over 8, which is 3.75 volts. Add a second 6 kilohm load in parallel, making 3 kilohms in all, and the output falls to 5 times 3 over 5, which is 3 volts. A smaller collector resistor improves the HIGH, but when the transistor turns on, the full supply sits across it: with 200 ohms, the current is 5 volts over 200 ohms, 25 milliamps, wasted every time the output is LOW. T T L's totem-pole output avoids this trade-off. An upper transistor actively drives the output HIGH while the lower one is off, and the lower transistor pulls it LOW while the upper one is off, so there is no steady supply-to-ground current. The common misconception is that a HIGH output is always at the supply voltage. With a passive pull-up it depends on the load. Another is that two totem-pole outputs can be joined; one driving HIGH against one driving LOW creates a damaging current path.

lessons.title: TTL and the hex inverter
lessons.teach: T T L stands for transistor-transistor logic: gates built from bipolar transistors, diodes and resistors on one chip, running from a 5 volt supply. The simplest T T L function is the inverter, drawn as a triangle with a small bubble on its output. The 7404 is a hex inverter, and hex here means six, so the package holds six inverters. Inside each one are four transistors, two diodes and four resistors, ending in a totem-pole output stage. The symbol is the abstraction; the transistor circuit is what is really on the chip.
lessons.eli5: Think of a vending machine. From the outside you see a simple rule: coin in, snack out. Inside are motors, sensors and circuit boards you never look at. A logic symbol is the outside view; the chip holds the inside. T T L, transistor-transistor logic, builds its gates from bipolar transistors, diodes and resistors running on 5 volts. The inverter, a triangle with a bubble, has a rule of opposite in, opposite out. A 7404 is a hex inverter, holding six of them. So T T L gates are transistor circuits on a chip, and the symbol just states their rule.
lessons.deep: T T L stands for transistor-transistor logic: gates built from bipolar junction transistors, with diodes and resistors, on one chip, powered by a nominal 5 volt supply. The inverter's rule is output equals the complement of input. Inside one T T L inverter are four transistors, two diodes and four resistors, ending in a totem-pole output that actively drives both HIGH and LOW. The symbol, a triangle with a bubble, is an abstraction of all that. The 7404 is a hex inverter, hex meaning six, so it holds six inverters. Example of pin counting: six inverters need 6 inputs and 6 outputs, 12 pins, plus V C C on pin 14 and ground on pin 7, filling all 14 pins. A component count follows the same way: six inverters with four transistors each means 24 transistors in the package. The common misconception is that hex means hexadecimal, or sixteen. In part names, hex means six. Another is that the triangle shape itself means inversion; it is the bubble that marks inversion. Knowing the transistor circuit explains why T T L inputs behave as they do and why its outputs drive firmly, which the next lessons use.

lessons.title: Inside a TTL input
lessons.teach: The T T L input transistor has its base pulled toward 5 volts by a resistor. With the input LOW, current flows out through the base-emitter junction into the input pin, so the next stage stays off. With the input HIGH, that path is blocked, and the resistor's current flows instead through the base-collector junction into the next stage, turning it on. A protection diode sits on the input, anode at ground and cathode at the pin. At 0 or 5 volts it does not conduct. If ringing pulls the pin below about minus 0.7 volts, it conducts and clamps the pin there.
lessons.eli5: Think of a pipe that forks two ways, fed from a tank. One branch drains out through a door to the street, and the other turns a wheel inside the building. If the street door is open, the water rushes out there and the wheel stays still. Close the door and the water has to go through the wheel. A LOW T T L input is the open door: current flows out of the input pin. A HIGH input closes it, so current flows into the next stage and switches it on. So the input level steers the current, and a guard diode stops the pin going far below ground.
lessons.deep: The input transistor's base is fed from 5 volts through a resistor. Input LOW: the base-emitter junction conducts, the base sits about 0.7 volts above the pin, and the current flows out through the pin. That is not enough voltage to forward bias the base-collector junction and the next stage in series, so the next stage stays off. Input HIGH: the pin is as high as the supply, the base-emitter path cannot conduct, and the current goes through the forward-biased base-collector junction into the next stage, turning it on. Clamp diode, formula first: diode voltage equals anode minus cathode. With the anode at ground and the cathode at the pin, an input at 5 volts gives minus 5 volts, reverse biased; at 0 volts it gives zero, not conducting. Ringing that pulls the pin toward minus 1.5 volts makes the diode voltage plus 1.5 volts, so it conducts and holds the pin near minus 0.7 volts. The common misconception is that the input transistor is simply off when the input is HIGH. Its base-collector junction is conducting and steering current. Another is that the clamp also limits positive spikes; it only conducts for negative excursions, and only at limited current.

lessons.title: Unused inputs: tie them high
lessons.teach: An input left unconnected is floating. It picks up noise and its level is effectively random, causing failures that come and go and are hard to find. Every input must be driven or tied. For T T L, tie unused inputs HIGH, straight to plus 5 volts in this lab. Tying them LOW also works logically, but a LOW T T L input has to push current out of the input stage, up to about 0.4 milliamps each for the L S family, so the chip draws more supply current. A HIGH input draws very little. Unused outputs are different: leave them unconnected and mark them N C.
lessons.eli5: Think of a radio left on with no station tuned. It hisses and crackles randomly, and now and then blares out something. An unconnected gate input is like that: it picks up noise and its level wanders. Tying it to a fixed level is like tuning to a quiet, steady station. For T T L, tie it HIGH, because a LOW input actually leaks current out, like a dripping tap left open. Unused outputs are like speakers no one is listening to: just leave them unconnected. So tie unused T T L inputs HIGH, and mark unused outputs no connection.
lessons.deep: A floating input has nothing setting its voltage, so stored charge, leakage and coupling from nearby signals push it around. The gate may read it as either level or switch randomly, causing intermittent faults that are hard to find. Every input must be driven or tied. For T T L, both rails fix the noise, but they differ in current. A LOW input pushes current out of the input stage through the pin; a HIGH input draws only a tiny leakage current. Formula first: total current equals current per input times number of inputs. Example: six unused 74 L S inputs tied LOW, each pushing out up to 0.4 milliamps, could draw 6 times 0.4, which is 2.4 milliamps of extra supply current. Tied HIGH, at about 20 microamps each, six inputs take about 120 microamps. So tying HIGH wastes about a twentieth as much. Outputs follow a different rule: leave them unconnected and mark them N C, never tie them to a rail, because a driven output tied to a rail fights it. The common misconception is that an unconnected T T L input is safely HIGH. It is not dependable. Another is that tying to ground is safest because ground means off; for T T L it costs more current.

lessons.title: AND and OR gate ICs
lessons.teach: Gates come packaged in integrated circuits, usually 14-pin dual in-line packages. The 7408 holds four two-input AND gates, the 7432 four two-input OR gates, the 7411 three three-input AND gates, and the 7421 two four-input AND gates. On these 14-pin T T L parts, pin 14 is V C C, plus 5 volts, and pin 7 is ground. On the 7408, the first gate takes inputs on pins 1 and 2 and outputs on pin 3. Always check the exact datasheet before wiring, because not every chip uses the same arrangement.
lessons.eli5: Think of a four-flat apartment building with a single water main. The four flats are separate homes, but they share one supply coming in. A 7408 chip is that building: four separate two-input AND gates sharing one power pin and one ground pin. Other buildings hold different arrangements: the 7432 has four OR gates, the 7411 three three-input ANDs, and the 7421 two four-input ANDs. Where the picture breaks: each chip's gate pins can be laid out differently. So these 14-pin T T L chips use pin 14 for V C C and pin 7 for ground, but always check the datasheet.
lessons.deep: Gate chips package several gates sharing one power pair. In the 14-pin T T L parts here, pin 14 is V C C at plus 5 volts and pin 7 is ground. Counting pins shows why each chip holds what it does. The 7408: four gates times two inputs and one output is 12 signal pins, plus 2 power, 14. The 7432 is the same pattern with OR gates. The 7411: three three-input gates, 3 times 4, 12 signal pins. The 7421: two four-input gates, 2 times 5, 10 signal pins, so two pins are unused. On the 7408, gate one has inputs on pins 1 and 2 and its output on pin 3. Example: you need three two-input OR functions. One 7432 holds four, so it covers them, with one spare gate whose inputs are tied HIGH and output left unconnected. You need two four-input ANDs: one 7421. The common misconception is that every 14-pin gate chip has the same gate pins as the 7408. Power often matches; gate pins do not always, as the NOR chip in the next lesson shows. Another is powering only the gates you use; the one supply pair powers all gates in the package. Always wire from the exact datasheet.

lessons.title: NAND, NOR and inverter ICs
lessons.teach: The same 14-pin family includes the 7400, four two-input NAND gates; the 7402, four two-input NOR gates; and the 7404, six inverters. The 7410 holds three three-input NAND gates. C M O S versions exist too, such as the 4001 NOR. Power is still pin 14 and pin 7 on these T T L parts, but the gate pins are not all the same. On the 7402 NOR, the first gate's output is pin 1 and its inputs are pins 2 and 3, the reverse of the 7408. Always wire from the exact part's top-view pinout.
lessons.eli5: Think of two houses built from the same outside plan but with the rooms arranged differently inside. Walk into the second house from memory of the first and you end up in the wrong room. The 7400 NAND and the 7402 NOR look identical on the outside and share power on pins 14 and 7, but the 7402 puts its first gate's output on pin 1, where the 7408 has an input. So the inverting gate chips are the 7400 NAND, 7402 NOR, 7404 hex inverter and 7410 triple three-input NAND, and each must be wired from its own pinout.
lessons.deep: The inverting family: the 7400 holds four two-input NAND gates; the 7402 four two-input NOR gates; the 7404 six inverters; and the 7410 three three-input NAND gates. C M O S equivalents include the 4011 NAND and the 4001 NOR. Pin counting for the 7410: three gates with three inputs and one output each, 3 times 4, which is 12 signal pins, plus power on 14 and ground on 7. Gate layouts differ. On the 7408 AND and the 7400 NAND, gate one uses pins 1 and 2 as inputs and pin 3 as output. On the 7402 NOR, gate one's output is pin 1 and its inputs are pins 2 and 3. Example of the failure: wire a 7402 as if it were a 7408, with a switch on pin 1. Pin 1 is actually a NOR output, so the switch and the output both drive the same pin; when they disagree, a large current flows between them. Meanwhile pin 3, which you treat as the output, is really an input. The common misconception is that the part number's last digits only change the gate type, not the pins. They can change both. Another is confusing the 7404, six inverters, with a four-gate chip. Use the exact part's top-view pinout every time.

lessons.title: Input levels and CMOS
lessons.source: Quiz study pack, TTL input limits; Kleitz §2–11
lessons.teach: A logic input reads a voltage range, not an exact value. For the 74 L S 00 example in your notes, any input up to 0.8 volts is guaranteed LOW, and anything from 2.0 volts up is guaranteed HIGH. Between 0.8 and 2.0 volts nothing is guaranteed. These are input limits; outputs have their own separate guarantees. C M O S is the other main family, built from complementary M O S transistors, and it draws very little power while it is not switching. Floating C M O S inputs are especially troublesome, so they must be tied too.
lessons.eli5: Think of a line judge in tennis. A ball clearly inside the line is in; clearly outside is out; but the painted line itself is wide, and a ball landing on it gets no guaranteed call. A logic input judges voltage the same way: up to 0.8 volts is guaranteed LOW, from 2.0 volts up is guaranteed HIGH, and in between nothing is promised. C M O S is a second family of chips that uses very little power while not switching. So inputs read guaranteed ranges, and the band between them must be avoided.
lessons.deep: For the 74 L S 00 in the course notes, an input from 0 to 0.8 volts is guaranteed to read LOW, and from 2.0 volts up to the supply is guaranteed to read HIGH. Between them lies a band of 1.2 volts with no guarantee: the gate may read it either way, and two chips may disagree. Examples: 0.4 volts, guaranteed LOW; 2.7 volts, guaranteed HIGH; 1.4 volts, no guarantee. These are input limits only; outputs have separate guarantees for the levels they produce. C M O S, complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, is built from complementary M O S transistors. Its main advantage is very low power while not switching, though each switch still uses some energy. Thresholds and speeds depend on the exact part. Floating C M O S inputs are especially troublesome, so unused C M O S inputs must be tied too. The common misconception is that any voltage above half the supply, 2.5 volts, is the threshold for HIGH. For this T T L part the guaranteed HIGH starts at 2.0 volts, and the region below that, down to 0.8 volts, is undefined, not LOW. Another is that C M O S uses no power at all; it uses very little only while static.

lessons.title: AND and OR gates
lessons.teach: An AND gate outputs HIGH only when every input is HIGH; any LOW forces LOW. Its equation is X equals A and B, and it acts like switches in series. An OR gate outputs HIGH when at least one input is HIGH, and LOW only when all are LOW. Its equation uses a plus sign, but read it as or: in Boolean algebra, 1 or 1 is 1. It acts like switches in parallel. A truth table lists every input combination, and n inputs give two to the n rows. In an AND table only the all-ones row is 1; in an OR table only the all-zeros row is 0.
lessons.eli5: Think of a lamp wired through two switches. Put the switches one after the other, in series, and the lamp lights only when both are closed: that is AND. Put them side by side, in parallel, and either switch lights the lamp: that is OR. Where the picture breaks: a real gate gives a definite LOW voltage rather than just a broken path. A truth table lists every combination of switch positions. So AND is HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, OR is LOW only when all inputs are LOW, and n inputs give two to the n rows.
lessons.deep: Formula first: AND, X equals A B, read A and B; OR, X equals A plus B, read A or B; rows in a truth table equal two to the n, where n is the number of inputs. Each new input doubles the number of combinations, because every earlier combination now occurs with the new input at 0 and at 1. AND acts like multiplying 0s and 1s, so any 0 forces 0. OR is inclusive, so 1 or 1 is 1, never 2, and any 1 forces 1. Example: a four-input AND has two to the four, 16 rows, with a 1 only in row 1 1 1 1. A four-input OR has 16 rows, with a 0 only in row 0 0 0 0. Inputs 1, 1, 0, 1 give AND 0 and OR 1. The series and parallel switch pictures explain why: one open switch in series breaks the whole path, while one closed switch in parallel completes a path. The common misconception is that a gate with many inputs follows a majority vote. AND needs every input HIGH; OR needs only one. Another is reading the OR plus sign as arithmetic. The patterns, a single 1 for AND and a single 0 for OR, are the quickest way to recognise them in any table.

lessons.title: Reading timing charts
lessons.teach: A timing chart plots several signals against one shared time axis, the way a logic analyzer displays them. To find a gate's output, slice the chart vertically. Mark a boundary wherever any input changes, and in each interval read every input's level and apply the gate's rule. Example: A is HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds, and B is HIGH from 2 to 6 microseconds. An AND output is HIGH only where both overlap, from 2 to 4 microseconds. An OR output is HIGH wherever either one is HIGH, from 0 to 6 microseconds.
lessons.eli5: Think of a sheet of music for a band. Each line is one instrument over time. To know what the band plays at one moment, you read straight down through all the lines at that beat. A timing chart is the same: each trace is one signal, all sharing the same time axis. To find a gate's output, cut the chart into slices wherever any input changes, read every input in each slice, and apply the gate's rule. So a timing chart shows how signals relate over time, and you read it in vertical slices.
lessons.deep: A timing chart, as shown by a logic analyzer, plots several signals against one shared time axis. Its purpose is to show what each signal does over time and how signals line up, so a gate's output can be predicted or checked. Method: mark a boundary at every input change; in each interval the inputs are steady, so apply the gate rule once. Example: A HIGH from 1 to 5 microseconds, B HIGH from 3 to 7. Boundaries at 1, 3, 5 and 7. From 1 to 3: A 1, B 0. From 3 to 5: both 1. From 5 to 7: A 0, B 1. Outside those, both 0. So AND is HIGH from 3 to 5, 2 microseconds; OR is HIGH from 1 to 7, 6 microseconds; NAND is LOW only from 3 to 5; NOR is HIGH before 1 and after 7. In these ideal charts, outputs change exactly when inputs do; real gates add a short propagation delay. The common misconception is reading each trace on its own horizontally and trying to combine whole waveforms at once, which misses short overlaps and gaps. Another is forgetting a boundary, so an interval mixes two input combinations. Slicing at every change is what makes the method reliable.

lessons.title: Enable and disable
lessons.teach: A gate can let a signal through or block it. With an AND gate, hold the control input HIGH and the output copies the data signal: the gate is enabled. Hold the control LOW and the output is stuck LOW: disabled. That is how a clock is started and stopped: run equals enable and clock. An OR gate works the other way round: control LOW passes the signal, control HIGH forces the output HIGH. The value that takes over the output, 0 for AND and 1 for OR, is called the controlling value.
lessons.eli5: Think of a garden tap on a hose. Open the tap and whatever pressure arrives flows through; close it and nothing gets out, whatever happens upstream. An AND gate's control input is that tap. Control HIGH, the gate is enabled and the output copies the signal. Control LOW, the gate is disabled and the output is stuck LOW. An OR gate is the reverse: control LOW passes the signal, control HIGH sticks the output HIGH. Where the picture breaks: a disabled gate still outputs a definite level. So the controlling value, 0 for AND and 1 for OR, takes over the output.
lessons.deep: Formula first in words: for AND, 1 and A equals A, and 0 and A equals 0; for OR, 0 or A equals A, and 1 or A equals 1. The controlling value is the input value that alone decides the output: 0 for AND, 1 for OR. The other value, the non-controlling value, lets the output follow the data. A clock enable is the AND case: run equals enable and clock. Enable 1 gives run equal to the clock, so the circuit it drives steps along; enable 0 gives run equal to 0, so it freezes. Example: a 10 kilohertz clock gated by an enable held HIGH for 1 millisecond. The period is 0.1 milliseconds, so 10 pulses pass, then the output stays LOW. With an OR gate and its control held HIGH, the output is a steady HIGH: no pulses get through. The common misconception is that setting enable to 0 lets the clock through; for an AND gate, 0 is the controlling value, so it blocks. Another is that a disabled gate's output floats or disappears. It is a definite LOW for AND, a definite HIGH for OR. Changing enable while the clock is HIGH can cut a pulse short, so real clock gating needs care with timing.

lessons.title: Inverter, NAND and NOR
lessons.teach: An inverter complements its single input: 1 becomes 0, and 0 becomes 1. The small bubble on a symbol means inversion. A NAND gate is an AND with its output inverted, so its output is LOW only when every input is HIGH, and HIGH otherwise. A NOR gate is an OR with its output inverted, so its output is HIGH only when every input is LOW. Their equations put one bar over the whole AND or OR result: X equals A and B, all complemented. The bar covers the whole expression, not each variable separately.
lessons.eli5: Think of a contrary friend who always says the opposite of what they hear. Put that friend at the output of an AND gate and you get NAND: wherever AND says HIGH, NAND says LOW, and the other way round. Put the friend after OR and you get NOR. The bubble on a symbol is that contrary friend, and on its own, with one input, it is the inverter. So NAND is LOW only when every input is HIGH, NOR is HIGH only when every input is LOW, and the bar in the equation covers the whole result.
lessons.deep: Formula first: inverter, X equals A bar; NAND, X equals the complement of A B, one bar over the whole product; NOR, X equals the complement of A plus B, one bar over the whole sum; a three-input NOR is the complement of A plus B plus C. Evaluate in two steps: work out AND or OR, then invert. Examples: NAND with 1 and 1, AND is 1, so NAND is 0. NAND with 1 and 0, AND is 0, so NAND is 1. NOR with 0 and 0, OR is 0, so NOR is 1. NOR with 0 and 1, OR is 1, so NOR is 0. So NAND is HIGH unless every input is HIGH, and NOR is LOW unless every input is LOW. The scope of the bar matters: the complement of A B is not A bar times B bar. At A equals 1 and B equals 0, the complement of A B is 1, but A bar times B bar is 0 and 1, which is 0. They differ. The common misconception is putting a separate bar over each input instead of one over the whole result, which describes a different gate. The bubble means logical inversion, not a negative voltage. These inverting gates are the ones in the 7400, 7402 and 7404 chips.

lessons.title: Name the gate from its behaviour
lessons.teach: Each basic gate has a one-line rule. AND: HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH. OR: LOW only when all inputs are LOW. NAND: LOW only when all inputs are HIGH. NOR: HIGH only when all inputs are LOW. Inverter: the output is the opposite of its single input. Listen for two clues: which input row is the special one, and is the output there HIGH or LOW? Also, a NAND with one input held HIGH acts as an inverter for the other input, and so does a NOR with one input held LOW.
lessons.eli5: Think of identifying birds by one distinctive call. Each gate has one distinctive row in its truth table, either the all-HIGH row or the all-LOW row, where its output is the odd one out. AND says HIGH only for all HIGH. NAND says LOW only for all HIGH. OR says LOW only for all LOW. NOR says HIGH only for all LOW. And a NAND with one input held HIGH, or a NOR with one held LOW, just flips the other input, like an inverter. So name a gate by its special row and the output in that row.
lessons.deep: Two questions identify any basic gate: which input row is special, all HIGH or all LOW, and is the output in that row HIGH or LOW? All HIGH with output HIGH: AND. All HIGH with output LOW: NAND. All LOW with output LOW: OR. All LOW with output HIGH: NOR. Example: a three-input gate outputs 0 in every row except 0 0 0, where it outputs 1. Special row all LOW, output HIGH: NOR. Another: a gate outputs 1 in every row except 1 1, where it outputs 0. Special row all HIGH, output LOW: NAND. Using the non-controlling value: NAND with one input at 1 gives the complement of 1 and A, which is A bar, so the gate inverts A. NOR with one input at 0 gives the complement of 0 or A, which is also A bar. Feed a clock to the other input and the output is the clock turned upside down. The common misconception is mixing up NAND and NOR descriptions: LOW only when all are HIGH is NAND, not NOR. Another is thinking a NAND with one input HIGH passes the clock unchanged; the bubble inverts it. This identification skill is also how you check a chip on the bench.

lessons.title: Probe and pulser troubleshooting
lessons.teach: A logic probe touches a point and shows its level: HIGH, LOW, or pulsing. A logic pulser injects short pulses into a point so you can watch what the circuit does with them. To test one input of a gate with a pulser, hold the other input at the value that lets the signal through. For AND and NAND that means HIGH, since a LOW would lock the output. For OR and NOR that means LOW, since a HIGH would lock it. Then check that the output pulses. Before blaming the chip, check its supply, its actual input pins and its load.
lessons.eli5: Think of testing one string of fairy lights hidden among others. You plug in a test signal at one end and watch whether the far end blinks. But if another switch on the same circuit is off, nothing will blink no matter what, so you first make sure it is on. A pulser is the test signal and a logic probe is your eye. For AND and NAND, hold the other input HIGH so pulses can pass; for OR and NOR, hold it LOW. So test one input at a time with the other at its non-controlling value, and check supply and wiring before blaming the chip.
lessons.deep: A logic probe shows a node's state, HIGH, LOW or pulsing, depending on the instrument. A logic pulser injects short test pulses. The controlling value decides how to test: if the other input sits at the controlling value, it locks the output and the pulses cannot pass, so the test tells you nothing.
