lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §2–3
lessons.teach: The benches are shared, so the layout you sit down to was set up for someone with the other dominant hand. Put the iron stand on your dominant side, close to the work: a long reach means holding a hot iron over your own joint. Bring the cleaning pad forward, or every trip drags the iron across what you just built. Uncoil and separate the cords; coiling twists a cable along its axis, which is what kinks it. Fume extraction pulls the smoke from burning flux and melting solder away from your face, and the switches are ganged, so one switch runs them all. The solder is a lead and tin alloy, so wash your hands after soldering. The iron lives in its stand when not in your hand.
lessons.eli5: Think of getting into a car someone else just drove. You move the seat and mirrors to fit you before pulling out. A shared soldering bench is the same: the last person may have used the other hand. Put the iron stand on your dominant side, close to the work, and bring the cleaning pad forward, so the hot iron never stretches over your joint or drags across it. Uncoil the cords, because coiling twists a cable and leaves kinks. Run the fume extraction, and wash your hands after, since the solder has lead in it. Where the picture breaks: car seats do not burn you. So set the bench for your own hand before anything gets hot.
lessons.deep: Each layout rule follows the path of the hot iron. The stand goes on your dominant side, close to the work, because a long reach is a long time holding a hot iron over a joint you just made; right handed means stand on the right, left handed is the same layout mirrored. The cleaning pad comes forward, because you clean before every joint, and a pad behind the work means dragging the iron across what you built on every trip. Cords are uncoiled and separated: coiling twists a cable along its own axis, and that stored twist leaves permanent kinks. The fume extraction pulls away the smoke from burning flux and melting solder, and the switches are ganged, so one switch runs every station. The solder is a lead and tin alloy, and residue moves from your hands to your face, food and belongings later, which is why you wash your hands after soldering. The common misconception is that washing is pointless because nobody eats at the bench; the residue leaves on your hands. A worked example of the burn rule: a hot iron you touch by accident is most likely touched further down the barrel, not the tip, so the iron lives in its stand when it is not in your hand.

lessons.title: The combination tool and crimping
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §6
lessons.teach: Three hand tools carry most of the work: small needle-nose pliers, small wire cutters, and a combination crimping tool. The combination tool has several features. Serrated jaws at the tip grab and hold, but not tinned wire. Stripping holes are sized by wire gauge, so match the hole to the gauge. A shaping hole lets you form a loop by moving the wire around it progressively. Threaded screw holes restore a thread: run the screw in, cut the excess, and back it out. The crimp dies are colour coded red, yellow and blue to match insulated terminals, with a flat side and a round side, so the terminal goes in the correct way round. A crimp is a complete connection on its own; you do not solder it afterwards.
lessons.eli5: Think of a pocket multitool. Each blade only works for its own job. The combination crimping tool is like that. The serrated jaws grab and hold, but not tinned wire. The stripping holes are sized by wire gauge, so you match the hole to the wire. The crimp dies are coloured red, yellow and blue, and you match the die colour to the insulated terminal, put it in the right way round, and squeeze fully. Where the picture breaks: a multitool blade can be used again and again, but a crimp is made once. So a crimp is a complete connection on its own, and you do not solder it.
lessons.deep: Every feature of the combination tool works only when matched to its job. Serrated jaws grip by biting, which is fine for holding but damages the coating on tinned wire. Stripping holes are sized by gauge; the practice wire is twelve gauge and you will move to twenty two gauge, so the hole changes with the wire. The shaping hole forms a loop as you move the wire around it progressively. The threaded holes restore a thread: run the screw in, cut the excess, and back it out, and the thread is restored as the screw withdraws. The crimp dies are colour coded red, yellow and blue to match the insulated terminal's colour, and each has a flat side and a round side, so orientation matters. Production crimping uses large ratcheting tools, so the hand tool is a compromise that works when the terminal is seated properly and the handles are squeezed fully. A worked example: a blue terminal goes in the blue die, the right way round, with one full squeeze; the wrong die or a half squeeze is not a finished crimp. The common misconception is that a little solder flowed into a crimp makes it more secure. The rule is crimp or solder, never both.

lessons.title: Choosing pliers and cutters
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §2
lessons.teach: Two hand tools matter beyond the parts kit. First, needle-nose pliers whose jaws are flat and smooth, never serrated, because serrations cut through the coating on tinned wire and every mark is a corrosion site you made yourself. Second, a cutter. Flush cutters are spring loaded, the blades cross over, and they cut cleanly. Side cutters are the older squeeze and release design and tend to fold the wire as they cut. Either is acceptable; you do not need both, but the size matters. Do not lend your cutters. A borrowed pair came back with a semicircular notch bitten out of the blades because someone cut tungsten, which is far harder than the wire they are made for. A notched blade cannot be repaired.
lessons.eli5: Think of a good pair of fabric scissors. Lend them to someone who cuts wire with them and they come back nicked for good. Wire cutters are the same: they are made for soft wire, and a borrowed pair came back with a semicircular notch after someone cut tungsten, roughly ten times harder. So you make the cut for a classmate instead of lending. The pliers have their own rule: smooth, flat jaws, because serrated teeth cut through the tin on the wire. Where the picture breaks: scissors can sometimes be resharpened, but a notched cutter blade cannot be repaired. So keep tools for the material they were made for.
lessons.deep: Both tool rules come from what each tool does to the metal. Needle nose pliers form the wire, and their jaws touch it many times on a single joint; a hook joint alone needs a minimum of six turns. Serrated jaws cut through the tin coating at each grip, and every mark is a corrosion site you made yourself, so the jaws must be flat and smooth. Check them by eye before buying. For cutting, there are two designs. Flush cutters are spring loaded and their blades cross over to cut cleanly. Side cutters are the long-standing squeeze and release design and tend to fold the wire as they cut. Either is acceptable, you do not need both, and what matters is a cutter of the right size. Blade damage depends on the hardness of what is cut, not only its thickness. Tungsten, roughly ten times harder than the wire these cutters are made for, bit a permanent semicircular notch out of a borrowed pair, and a notched blade cannot be repaired. The common misconception is that if a wire fits between the jaws, the cutter can take it. Fitting is about size; damage is about hardness. These are the tools you will use to form and clip every hook joint and component lead in the second lab.

lessons.title: Reading the fillet and diagnosing
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §3
lessons.teach: A sound joint shows a concave fillet: the solder curves inward, meeting the wire and the pad at a shallow angle, pulled there by surface tension bonding to clean metal. You should not have to shape it or add extra solder to get it. If you kept adding solder to make it look right, the joint is wrong; reheat and redo both parts. Never paint solder over a bad joint. A convex, balled joint has not wetted, and neither has one that rolls under itself on one side. Both parts must be hot and both must be clean. Heat is the condition people check; cleanliness is the one that quietly fails. Heat also arrives unevenly: put the iron on the slow part and watch which way the solder flows.
lessons.eli5: Think of painting over a rusty patch on a car. It looks fine, but the paint is not really holding on. A sound joint shows a concave fillet that formed on its own once both parts were hot and clean. If you had to keep adding solder to make it look right, the bond underneath is not there, so you reheat and redo both parts. A convex ball, or an edge that rolls under itself, has not wetted. Where the picture breaks: rust spreads over time, while a bad joint simply never bonded. So the fillet shape tells you whether the joint is really bonded.
lessons.deep: Reading a joint is reading wetting. On clean, hot copper the solder wets, and surface tension pulls it into a concave fillet meeting the wire and the pad at a shallow angle. Where it cannot wet, surface tension pulls it into a convex ball instead. An edge that rolls under itself marks a region where nothing is bonded. Because the fillet forms on its own, needing extra solder to make it look right means a condition failed; reheat and redo both parts, and never paint solder over the top. Two conditions must both hold: both parts hot, and both parts clean of plastic, oxide and old solder. A worked example: a joint that was definitely hot enough still rolled under on one side. Heat was not the problem, so cleanliness was; clean and reflux that surface, then rework. Heat also arrives unevenly. Joining a light wire to a much heavier one, put the iron on the heavy, slow wire and let the light one come along, then watch which way the solder flows, because it flows toward the side that is really hot. The common misconception is that more heat or more seconds fixes any joint that will not take solder. More heat cannot fix dirty metal, and a fixed count of seconds tells you nothing; the solder does.

lessons.title: The hook joint and the insulation gap
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §4
lessons.teach: The joint is decided before the iron touches it. For a hook joint, hook the wire round the terminal, put your finger inside the loop, and wrap it tight, pushing each turn hard against the last, for a minimum of six turns. Clip the ends so nothing pokes out and bend the remainder in tight. Wrapping without a finger inside leaves the wire standing off the post with daylight between turns, and solder does not close a gap the forming left behind; it fills a tight wrap, it does not replace one. Between the end of the insulation and the start of the joint there is a deliberate gap whose length equals the diameter of that wire's own insulation. Measure it against the wire in your hand.
lessons.eli5: Think of winding thread onto a spool. Wound taut, each turn lies snug against the last; wound slack, the turns sit loose with gaps. A hook joint wrap is the same. Hook the wire round the terminal, keep a finger inside the loop, push each turn hard against the last, and make at least six turns. Where the picture breaks: thread is meant to unwind later, but this wrap is meant to stay. Solder bonds a tight wrap; it cannot close a gap the forming left. And the gap before the insulation is set by the wire itself: it equals that wire's own insulation diameter. So wrap tight first, then solder.
lessons.deep: The hook joint splits holding from bonding. The wrap holds: hook the wire round the terminal, put a finger inside the loop, and wrap tight, each turn pushed hard against the last, for a minimum of six turns. Clip the ends so nothing pokes out and bend the remainder in tight. Without the finger, the wire stands off the post and the turns spread, leaving daylight between them. Solder then wets and fills the tight wrap, but it does not close a gap, because the wire that should press against the post is not there to bond to. A worked way to see it: if two of six turns are tight and four stand off, you have two turns of hold, not six. The rule beside the hook is the insulation gap, stated as a formula in words: gap length equals the diameter of the insulation, both measured on the same wire. Because the reference is the wire itself, a wire with thicker insulation gets a longer gap, so you measure against the wire in your hand rather than to a fixed number. The common misconception is that a little extra solder can fill daylight in the wrap. It cannot; undo it and wrap again. These forming rules carry on to bus wire, stranded wire and turrets.

lessons.title: Pads, butt joints, strands and turrets
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §3–4
lessons.teach: A wire soldered onto a pad sits within the pad with nothing overhanging past it. Solder over the pad edge does not matter; covering the whole pad is not required. What matters is the concave fillet where wire meets pad. A butt joint is held only at the cut end faces of the metal, so it can look fine and still be the weakest thing on the board; that is why it is tested with a hard pull and discouraged for anything structural. Stranded wire is prepared in order: twist, tin, then form the loop. For a turret, tin the wire to the turret first, then attach it to the board, wrapping about three-quarters round. Do not linger, or you reflow the joint on its other side.
lessons.eli5: Think of a metal spoon left in a pot of hot soup. The handle gets hot too, because heat travels along the metal. A turret is like that spoon. Heat from your iron runs through the post, so if you sit on one joint too long, the joint on the other side melts again. That is why you tin the wire to the turret first, wrap about three quarters of the way round, and get in and out quickly. Where the picture breaks: soup heats a spoon slowly over minutes, but an iron on a small post works fast. Stranded wire, meanwhile, goes twist, tin, then loop. So on a turret, keep the heat short.
lessons.deep: Pads: the wire sits within the pad with nothing overhanging; solder over the edge does not matter, full coverage is not required, and the concave fillet where wire meets pad is what counts. Butt joints: two ends meet end to end, so the only bonded area is the cut end face of each wire, with no overlap and no wrap. As a worked comparison, a hook joint has at least six tight turns against its terminal, and a butt joint has one end face. That is why a butt joint is tested with a hard pull and discouraged for anything structural; it can pass a visual check and still be the weakest thing on the board. Stranded wire: twist, then tin, then form the loop, because tinning binds the strands so they bend as one and the loop holds its shape. Turrets: tin the wire to the turret first, then attach it to the board, wrapping about three quarters of the way round and cutting. Heat travels through the post, so lingering reflows the joint on the other side. Support the work with a third hand or a vise. The common misconception is that a joint that looks fine is strong; the butt joint shows geometry can hide the weakness.

lessons.title: The board: layers, mask and holes
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §5
lessons.teach: The common board material is FR4, a fibreglass substrate with copper bonded to it. Over the pads is a tin based finish that lets the tin oxidise instead of the copper, which is why a new board shows no bare copper. The green layer is solder mask: it covers everything not meant to be soldered, which makes machine soldering possible and prevents many bridges and shorts by hand. The white printing is silkscreen, the legend. The hole decides how many sides you solder. With unplated holes there is no copper in the hole, so each side is soldered separately; nothing carries between them. In a plated through hole copper lines the barrel, and wetting and capillary action carry solder up through it from the side you feed.
lessons.eli5: Touch a sugar cube to coffee and the coffee climbs into it by itself, against gravity. A plated through hole works like that. Its wall is lined with copper, so molten solder fed from one side is drawn up through the hole by wetting and capillary action. An unplated hole is bare fibreglass inside, so nothing draws the solder through, and each side is soldered separately. Where the picture breaks: the cube soaks up and dissolves, while the copper barrel stays put and just fills. So copper in the hole decides whether solder can travel through it.
lessons.deep: The board is layered. FR4 is fibreglass with copper bonded to it: fibreglass for structure, copper as conductor. The pads carry a tin based finish that oxidises instead of the copper, protecting it without thinning it, which is why a new board shows no bare copper. The green solder mask covers everything not meant to be soldered, so solder has nowhere to wet between pads; that makes machine soldering possible and prevents many bridges and shorts by hand. The white silkscreen is the printed legend. The hole decides how many sides you solder. With unplated holes there is no copper in the hole, so nothing connects the faces and each side is soldered separately. In a plated through hole, copper lines the barrel, with a thickness set by the board construction, and molten solder fed from the specified side is drawn through by wetting and capillary action. Gravity is barely involved; the fill would happen much the same upside down. You still check the fill, since sometimes the solder only reaches partway. A worked example of scale: multilayer boards bury conducting layers between FR4 sheets, and a board with eighteen layers is shown later in the course. The common misconception is that gravity carries solder through a plated hole. It is wetting and capillary action.

lessons.title: Lead forming and clipping
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §5
lessons.teach: There are three ways a component lead can sit in a hole. Straight through gives the least support and the part can fall out while you work. Fully clinched, bent flat along the pad, gives the most support and lowers the part's height, but it is the hardest to remove later. Set over to one side gives enough support to hold the part and is quick to undo, so it is the everyday choice. Whichever you use, check the clipped end. If you cut the lead after soldering, you can leave a bare copper end sticking out of the solder. If the lead was tinned before it went in, you are fine; if bare wire runs through, the cut end must finish covered.
lessons.eli5: Think of a nail driven through a board. Leave the point sticking straight out and the nail can work loose. Bend it over to one side and it holds, yet is easy to straighten. Hammer the point flat along the wood, which carpenters call clinching, and it holds hardest but is a fight to remove. Leads have the same three choices: straight through holds least, fully clinched holds most and sits lowest but is hardest to remove, and set over to one side holds enough and undoes easily, so it is the everyday choice. Where the picture breaks: a clipped lead must also end covered in solder. So choose the form by how much hold you need.
lessons.deep: Lead forming trades support against ease of removal. Straight through gives the least support: simple, but the part can fall out while you work. Fully clinched, the lead bent flat along the pad, gives the most support and lowers the part's height, but that same grip makes it the hardest to remove later. Set over to one side gives enough support to hold the part and is quick to undo, so it is the everyday choice. As a worked comparison of the three forms: ranked by support, clinched first, set over second, straight through third, and clinched is also the hardest to take out again. The second rule is the clipped end. Cutting the lead after soldering exposes a fresh end, and you can be left with bare copper sticking out of the solder. If the lead was tinned before it went in, that end is fine; if bare wire runs through, the cut end must finish covered. The common misconception is that clinching is always best because it is strongest. It also makes rework hardest, which is why setting the lead over is the everyday choice. These forms come back every time a lead goes through a hole on these boards.

lessons.title: Tip discipline every single time
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §6
lessons.teach: Inspect the tip every time it leaves the holder, not once at the start. A clean tip is bright and shiny. Oxide impairs wetting and heat transfer at the contact, so the routine is fixed: lift the iron and check the tip, wipe it every time without exception, and if a wipe does not clean it, add a little fresh solder and wipe again. Then go to the joint with a clean, hot iron. The test for a dead tip: put solder on it and watch. If it pulls away into a ball instead of spreading, there is oxide on the tip. Clean it properly; if that does not recover it, replace it. A plated tip is never filed. A tip in your hand goes dark while you are deciding.
lessons.eli5: Think of a greasy frying pan. Water splashed on it beads up instead of spreading. A dirty soldering tip does the same with solder. Touch solder to it, and if it pulls away into a ball instead of spreading, there is oxide on the tip. That oxide comes back within seconds, so the routine runs every time the iron leaves the holder: check the tip, wipe it, and if it is still dull, add a little fresh solder and wipe again. Where the picture breaks: you scrub a pan, but you never file a plated tip. So solder spreading on the tip is the sign it is clean.
lessons.deep: Oxide re-forms on a hot tip within seconds, and it impairs both wetting and heat transfer at the contact. That speed is why the check happens every time the iron leaves the holder rather than once a session. The routine is fixed: lift the iron and check the tip; wipe it, every time without exception; if the wipe does not clean it, add a little fresh solder and wipe again; then go to the joint with a clean, hot iron. The dead tip test reads surface tension directly. On clean metal, solder wets and spreads. On an oxide coating it cannot wet, so surface tension pulls it into a ball that pulls away. When you see that, clean the tip properly with tip cleaner, and if that does not recover it, replace it; a plated tip is never filed, because the file goes through the plating. A worked comparison: one check at the start of a session against oxide that returns in a few seconds means nearly every later joint starts with a dirty tip. The common misconception is that turning the station up burns the oxide off; the fix is cleaning, not heat. Another is that a clean tip stays clean. It goes dark while you are deciding.

items.q: True or false: a neutral object contains no electric charge at all.
items.right: Right, false. Neutral means balanced: equal positive and negative charge, so the net charge is zero, not that charge is absent.
items.wrong: Neutral does not mean empty. Every ordinary object is packed with positive nuclei and negative electrons. Neutral means those amounts balance, so the net charge is zero. Rubbing can transfer some electrons and upset the balance, which is how a balloon becomes charged. So the statement is false: a neutral object holds plenty of charge, just no net charge.
items.concept: Neutral means net charge zero: positive and negative charge are balanced, not absent.
items.hint: Think about what an atom contains even when it has no overall charge.

items.q: Twelve millicoulombs of charge pass a point in four milliseconds. What is the average current? Answer in amps.
items.right: Correct, 3 amps. Both quantities carry the milli prefix, so they cancel, leaving 12 over 4.
items.wrong: Use the definition: average current equals charge divided by time, current in amps, charge in coulombs, time in seconds. Here charge is 12 millicoulombs and time is 4 milliseconds. Both carry the milli prefix, so the prefixes cancel and you just divide 12 by 4. The average current is 3 amps. Multiplying instead gives charge times time, which is not a current.

slips.why: You multiplied charge by time. Current is charge divided by time, amps equal coulombs per second, so 12 millicoulombs over 4 milliseconds is 3 amps.
You converted only one quantity out of milli. Current equals charge over time: 0.012 coulombs over 0.004 seconds is 3 amps, because the two prefixes cancel.

items.concept: Average current equals charge divided by time; one amp is one coulomb per second.
items.hint: Divide charge by time. Notice both have the same prefix.

items.q: Two small charged objects are moved to twice their original separation. What happens to the force between them?
items.right: Yes, one quarter. Force depends on one over distance squared, so twice the distance gives one over four.
wrong: Halving would be true if force fell in simple proportion to distance. Coulomb's law says force equals a constant times the product of the charges, divided by distance squared; force in newtons, charge in coulombs, distance in metres. Because the distance is squared, doubling it divides the force by four.

Moving charges apart weakens their interaction; it never strengthens it. Coulomb's law puts distance squared in the denominator: force equals a constant times charge one times charge two, over distance squared. Doubling the distance makes the denominator four times larger, so the force falls to one quarter.

Distance matters strongly. Coulomb's law: force equals a constant times the product of the two charges, divided by the distance squared. The charges are unchanged, but the distance squared becomes four times larger, so the force becomes one quarter of what it was.
items.concept: Coulomb force falls with the square of distance: double the separation, one quarter the force.
items.hint: The distance in Coulomb's law is squared.

items.q: In a metal wire, electrons are drifting to the left. Which way does conventional current flow?
items.right: Right. Electrons are negative, so their leftward drift is a conventional current to the right.
wrong: That is the electron direction, not conventional current. Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would move. Electrons are negative, so their motion to the left is equivalent to positive charge moving to the right. Conventional current in this wire therefore flows to the right.

A steady drift in one direction gives one net current, not two. Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move. Negative electrons moving left count as positive charge moving right, so the conventional current flows to the right.

Electrons do carry charge, and their drift is exactly what makes current in a metal. Because they are negative, the conventional current, defined by positive charge motion, points opposite to them. Electrons drifting left means conventional current flows right.
items.concept: Conventional current follows positive charge; electron drift in metal is opposite to it.
items.hint: Electrons are negative. Flip their direction.

items.q: True or false: if you touched a chip and felt no shock and saw no spark, it cannot have been damaged by static discharge.
items.right: Correct, false. Damaging discharges can be far below what a person can feel or see.
items.wrong: Your senses are a poor E S D detector. Integrated circuits can be damaged by discharges far too small for you to feel or see. Feeling nothing proves only that the discharge was below your own sensing threshold. That is why the lab uses a grounded wrist strap and a protected work surface every time, rather than relying on whether you noticed anything.
items.concept: E S D can damage chips invisibly; wear the grounded wrist strap regardless of what you feel.
items.hint: Is your body a sensitive enough instrument to detect every harmful discharge?

items.q: Node A is at minus 3 volts and node B is at plus 2 volts. With the red probe on A and the black probe on B, what does the meter read? Answer in volts.
items.right: Yes, minus 5 volts. Red minus black is minus 3 minus 2, so A is 5 volts below B.
items.wrong: The meter reading equals red-probe potential minus black-probe potential, all in volts. Red is on A at minus 3 volts; black is on B at plus 2 volts. So the reading is minus 3 minus plus 2, which is minus 5 volts. The negative sign is real information: point A sits 5 volts below point B. Swapping the probes would read plus 5.

slips.why: Right size, wrong sign. The meter reads red minus black: minus 3 minus 2 is minus 5 volts. Plus 5 would be the reading with the probes swapped.
You added the two node voltages. A meter subtracts: red potential minus black potential. Minus 3 minus 2 gives minus 5 volts.

items.concept: A meter reads red-probe potential minus black-probe potential; a negative reading means red is lower.
items.hint: Compute red minus black, keeping both signs.

items.q: True or false: the negative terminal of a battery is automatically the circuit's ground.
items.right: Right, false. Ground is whichever node you choose as the zero-volt reference.
items.wrong: Ground is a choice, not a property of the negative terminal. It is whichever node we designate as zero volts. In the lecture's example, choosing the upper terminal as reference made it zero and the lower terminal minus 10 volts; the difference between them stayed 10 volts either way. Many circuits do ground the negative terminal, but that is a design decision, not automatic.
items.concept: Ground is a chosen reference node, not automatically the negative terminal or earth.
items.hint: Could you pick a different node to call zero?

items.q: You choose a different node as ground without changing any wiring. What stays the same?
items.right: Correct. Every node shifts by the same amount, so the differences between nodes stay the same.
wrong: Node voltages are each measured from ground, so when ground moves, their numbers shift. If the new reference was at 3 volts, every node voltage drops by 3. What survives is the difference between any two nodes, because the same 3 volts is subtracted from both and cancels.

The supply node is not special here. Every node voltage, including the supply's, is measured from the chosen reference, so all of them shift by the same amount when you move ground. Differences between nodes, and the currents, stay unchanged.

Something is preserved: differences. If you subtract the same reference value from every node, then V A minus V B is unchanged because the reference cancels. Currents are unchanged too, since the physical circuit is the same.
items.concept: Changing the reference shifts every node voltage equally; differences and currents are unchanged.
items.hint: If you subtract the same number from two values, what happens to their difference?

items.q: A 10 volt supply drives 1 kilohm and 4 kilohms in series. What is the current? Answer in milliamps.
items.right: Yes, 2 milliamps: ten volts over a total of 5 kilohms.
items.wrong: Series current comes from Ohm's law with the total resistance: current equals supply voltage divided by total resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Total resistance is 1 kilohm plus 4 kilohms, which is 5 kilohms. Ten volts divided by 5 kilohms is 2 milliamps. Using only one resistor ignores the other resistor sharing the voltage.

slips.why: You divided by only the 1 kilohm resistor. In series both resistors oppose the same current, so use the total: 10 volts over 5 kilohms is 2 milliamps.
You divided by only the 4 kilohm resistor. Series current equals supply voltage over total resistance: 10 volts over 5 kilohms gives 2 milliamps.

items.concept: Series current equals supply voltage divided by the sum of the resistances.
items.hint: Add the resistors first, then divide.

items.q: Same circuit: 10 volts, 1 kilohm on top, 4 kilohms at the bottom to ground. What is the voltage at the junction between them? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 8 volts. Two milliamps through 4 kilohms drops 8 volts, and that resistor's bottom is ground.
items.wrong: The junction voltage equals the drop across the bottom resistor, because its lower end is ground. Ohm's law: voltage equals current times resistance, volts, amps, ohms. The current is 2 milliamps, so the 4 kilohm resistor drops 2 milliamps times 4 kilohms, which is 8 volts. Check with Kirchhoff: the top resistor drops 2 volts, and 10 minus 2 is 8.

slips.why: Two volts is the drop across the top 1 kilohm resistor, not the junction voltage. The junction is measured from ground, so it equals the bottom resistor's drop: 2 milliamps times 4 kilohms is 8 volts.

items.concept: A node voltage is measured from ground; here it equals the bottom resistor's drop.
items.hint: Which resistor sits between the junction and ground?

items.q: Convert 0.047 milliamps to microamps. Answer in microamps.
items.right: Yes, 47 microamps. Going to the smaller prefix multiplies the number by a thousand.
items.wrong: One milliamp equals 1000 microamps, because milli is ten to the minus three and micro is ten to the minus six. Moving to the smaller unit, multiply the number by 1000. So 0.047 milliamps times 1000 is 47 microamps. Dividing by 1000 moves the wrong way and gives a value a million times too small.

slips.why: You shifted the decimal one place too many. One milliamp is 1000 microamps, so 0.047 times 1000 gives 47 microamps.

items.concept: Smaller prefix, bigger number: one milliamp is 1000 microamps.
items.hint: How many microamps are in one milliamp?

items.q: Which is the correct engineering-notation form of 0.00047 amps?
options: 4.7 times ten to the minus four amps
items.right: Right. 470 is between 1 and 999, and micro is ten to the minus six, a multiple of three.
wrong: The value 0.47 milliamps is equal, but it is not engineering notation, because the number must be at least 1 and under 1000. When the number falls below 1, step down one prefix and multiply by 1000: 0.47 milliamps becomes 470 microamps.

That is scientific notation, with one digit before the decimal and any exponent. Engineering notation requires the exponent to be a multiple of three, which lets you use a prefix. Ten to the minus six is micro, so the value is 470 microamps.

Forty-seven hundred microamps would be 4700 microamps, ten times too large, and it is not a standard form. Engineering notation keeps the number between 1 and 999 with a multiple-of-three prefix: 0.00047 amps is 470 microamps.
items.concept: Engineering notation: exponent a multiple of three, number at least 1 and less than 1000.
items.hint: Pick the prefix that puts the number between 1 and 999.

items.q: Your answer is exactly one thousand times too big, but the formula is right. Which of the four steps should you inspect first?
items.right: Yes. A factor of exactly one thousand is a prefix slip, and prefixes enter at the substitution step.
wrong: Naming the target catches finding the wrong quantity entirely, like a voltage instead of a current. A clean factor of one thousand points to prefixes instead. Milli, kilo and micro each differ by a thousand, so check step three, where values and units are substituted.

You already know the formula is right. A wrong formula usually gives an answer off by an irregular amount, not exactly a thousand. A factor of one thousand is the fingerprint of a prefix slip, which happens in step three, substitution with units.

Rounding changes the last digit or two, never the size by a factor of a thousand. That exact factor matches one prefix step, such as kilohms versus plain ohms. Go back to step three and check each substituted unit and prefix.
items.concept: Factor-of-1000 errors come from prefixes, so check the substitution step.
items.hint: Which engineering prefixes are a thousand apart?

items.q: Using Ohm's law, find the current when 4.7 volts is across 4.7 kilohms. Answer in milliamps.
items.right: Correct, 1 milliamp. Volts over kilohms gives milliamps directly.
items.wrong: Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Substitute 4.7 volts over 4.7 kilohms, which is 4700 ohms. That gives 0.001 amps, which is 1 milliamp. A handy shortcut: volts divided by kilohms comes out directly in milliamps.

slips.why: You treated 4.7 kilohms as 4.7 ohms, which gives one amp, a thousand milliamps. Kilo means times 1000, so 4.7 volts over 4700 ohms is 1 milliamp.

items.concept: Volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps.
items.hint: Current equals voltage over resistance; watch the kilo.

items.q: On a course circuit drawing, where does an IC's pin number go?
options: Inside the body, next to the function
Outside the body, near the pin's wire
Only in a separate pin table
Inside the body, in the corner
items.right: Right. Number outside the body, function inside.
wrong: Many datasheets print numbers inside the outline, but that is house style, not this course's circuit drawing standard. The rule is number outside, function inside. The number sits above a horizontal wire or beside a vertical one, so later wiring never runs through it.

A separate table makes the reader cross-reference. The circuit drawing itself should carry the pin numbers so every wire can be traced to a physical leg. Put each number outside the IC body next to its pin, with the function name inside.

Inside the body is for pin functions, such as A, B or V C C. Pin numbers belong outside the outline, above horizontal pins or beside vertical ones. Keeping the two separate makes the drawing readable and traceable.
items.concept: Pin number outside the IC body, pin function inside.
items.hint: Numbers and function names go on opposite sides of the outline.

items.q: True or false: a pin labelled L T with a bar over it performs its lamp-test job when that pin is held LOW.
items.right: Correct. A bar over the name means active low: the function happens at logic 0.
items.wrong: The bar marks an active-low signal. Active low means the function is asserted, switched on, when the pin sits at logic 0. So the lamp test happens when L T bar is held LOW, and the pin normally sits HIGH when you do not want a lamp test. A bar never means a negative voltage.
items.concept: An overbar on a pin name means active low: asserted when the pin is at logic 0.
items.hint: What does the bar tell you about which logic level activates the pin?

items.q: A 74LS08 quad AND package is used on your circuit drawing. On how many of its four gates do you show the V C C and ground connections?
options: Two, one for each supply pin
items.right: Right. One V C C pin and one ground pin per package, so power appears on exactly one gate.
wrong: Drawing power on all four suggests four separate supplies, wastes space and is more confusing. The package has one V C C pin and one ground pin shared by all four gates, so the convention is to show them once, on any one gate of that package.

Both supply pins belong to the same package and are shown together, not split across gates. The package's single V C C and single ground connection appear once, on one gate, with the decoupling capacitor beside them.
Power must appear, or the drawing cannot be built or traced. The rule is to show it exactly once per package, on one gate of your choice, often one of the unused gates.
items.concept: Show a package's power connections exactly once, on one of its gates.
items.hint: How many supply pins does the whole package have?

items.q: A gate on a circuit drawing is labelled U3B. What does the B tell you?
options: It is the second gate inside chip U3
It is the B input of the gate
It is a 74LS series B part
It is on page B of the drawing
items.right: Yes. U3 is the chip, and the suffix B picks the second gate inside it.
wrong: Input letters are signal names, not part of the designator. In U3B, the U3 identifies the physical chip and the suffix letter identifies which of its gates this is. A, B, C, D name the four gates of a quad package, so B is the second gate.
Family and series information lives in the part number, such as 74LS08, written below the designator. The suffix letter after U3 picks out a gate inside that package, and B means the second gate.
Page references are not part of a designator. U3 names the chip, and the suffix letter names a gate within it, A through D in a quad package. B is the second gate.
items.concept: A designator suffix letter identifies which gate inside the package is drawn.
items.hint: U3 names the package. What could a letter after it select?

items.q: True or false: the output of an unused gate must be tied to plus 5 volts, just like its unused inputs.
items.right: Correct, false. Leave the unused output unconnected and mark it N C.
items.wrong: Inputs and outputs have different jobs. An unused input must be tied, because a floating input picks up noise. An unused output can safely go nowhere; tying a driven output to a supply rail could fight the gate and damage it. On the circuit drawing you mark the unused output N C, for no connection, so the reader knows it is deliberate.
items.concept: Tie unused inputs; leave unused outputs unconnected and mark them N C.
items.hint: Does an output need a defined level from outside, or does it make its own?

items.q: Convert binary one zero one one to decimal.
items.right: Correct, 11. That is 8 plus 2 plus 1.
items.wrong: Write the weights under the bits, from the right: 1, 2, 4, 8. The pattern one zero one one has 1s in the 8, 2 and 1 places, and a 0 in the 4 place. Add the weights that hold a 1: 8 plus 2 plus 1 equals 11. Reading the bits as the decimal number one thousand and eleven confuses binary with decimal.

slips.why: You read the weights from the wrong end. The rightmost bit has weight 1. One zero one one has 1s in the 8, 2 and 1 places, giving 11. Thirteen would be one one zero one.

items.concept: Binary to decimal: add the place weights, 1, 2, 4, 8, where the bit is 1.
items.hint: The weights from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8.

items.q: Convert binary one zero one point zero one to decimal.
items.right: Correct, 5.25: 4 plus 1, plus one quarter.
items.wrong: Integer weights from the point leftward are 1, 2, 4, and fraction weights rightward are one half, then one quarter. One zero one gives 4 plus 1, which is 5. After the point, zero one means no half and one quarter. The total is 5.25. Reading point zero one as one hundredth treats the fraction as if it were decimal.

slips.why: You read the fraction as decimal. In binary the first place after the point is a half and the second is a quarter. Point zero one binary is one quarter, so the value is 5.25.
You gave the 1 the half weight. It sits in the second place after the point, worth one quarter. The value is 5.25.

items.concept: Binary fraction weights are one half, one quarter, one eighth, moving right.
items.hint: The first place after the point is a half; the second is a quarter.

items.q: In binary, what is the value of point one one?
items.right: Yes, one half plus one quarter is three quarters.
wrong: That reads the digits as decimal. In binary the first place after the point is worth one half and the second one quarter. Point one one is one half plus one quarter, which is three quarters, or 0.75.
One and a half would need a 1 before the point. Both digits here are after the point, worth one half and one quarter. Their sum is three quarters.
Three is binary one one without a point. After the binary point, weights halve instead of double: one half, then one quarter. Point one one equals three quarters.
items.concept: After the binary point, weights halve: a half, a quarter, an eighth.
items.hint: Add a half and a quarter.

items.q: Convert decimal 43 to binary. Say the bits one by one.
answer: one zero one zero one one
one oh one oh one one
items.right: Correct: 32 plus 8 plus 2 plus 1 is 43.
items.wrong: Subtract weights from the largest that fits. The weights are 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Forty-three minus 32 leaves 11, so the 32 bit is 1. Sixteen is too big: 0. Eight fits, leaving 3: 1. Four is too big: 0. Two fits, leaving 1: 1. One fits: 1. The result is one zero one zero one one. Check: 32 plus 8 plus 2 plus 1 is 43.
items.concept: Decimal to binary: subtract the largest weight that fits, mark 1, repeat with the remainder.
items.hint: Start with 32. What is left after subtracting it?

items.q: When converting decimal to binary by repeated division by two, how do you read the remainders?
options: First remainder is the most significant bit
Last remainder is the most significant bit
Only the even remainders are kept
items.right: Right. The first remainder is the ones bit, so read them in reverse: the last one is the M S B.
wrong: The first division by two tells you whether the number is odd or even, which is the ones place, the least significant bit. Each later division reveals a higher place, so the last remainder is the most significant bit. Read them in reverse, bottom to top.
Every remainder is kept; each one, zero or one, is a bit. The first remainder is the least significant bit and the last is the most significant bit, so read them in reverse order.
Adding remainders just counts the 1 bits and loses their positions. Each remainder is one bit of the answer. Read them in reverse: the last remainder is the most significant bit.
items.concept: Repeated division: the first remainder is the L S B; read the remainders bottom to top.
items.hint: Does the first division tell you about the ones place or the biggest place?

items.q: True or false: the digits allowed in octal are 0 through 8.
items.right: Right, false. Base eight uses 0 through 7.
items.wrong: Any base b uses digits from 0 up to b minus 1. Octal is base eight, so its digits run from 0 to 7, eight digits in all. After 7 the count rolls over to 10 in octal, meaning one eight and no ones. A digit 8 cannot exist in octal.
items.concept: Base b uses digits 0 to b minus 1; octal uses 0 through 7.
items.hint: How many digits does base eight need, starting from zero?

items.q: Convert binary one one one zero one one to octal. Say the octal digits as a number.
items.right: Correct, 73 octal: one one one is 7, and zero one one is 3.
items.wrong: Group the bits in threes from the right: one one one, then zero one one. Each group has weights 4, 2, 1. One one one is 4 plus 2 plus 1, which is 7. Zero one one is 2 plus 1, which is 3. So the octal number is 7 then 3, 73 octal. That equals 59 in decimal, but the question asked for octal.

slips.why: That is the decimal value. For octal, group the bits in threes from the right: one one one is 7 and zero one one is 3, so it is 73 octal.
You wrote the groups in reverse order. The left group, one one one, is the high octal digit 7; the right group gives 3. The answer is 73.

items.concept: Binary to octal: group bits in threes from the right; each group is one octal digit.
items.hint: Split into two groups of three bits.

items.q: Convert binary zero one one zero one zero one one to hexadecimal.
items.right: Correct, 6B: zero one one zero is 6, and one zero one one is eleven, which is B.
items.wrong: Split the eight bits into two nibbles: zero one one zero, and one zero one one. Each nibble has weights 8, 4, 2, 1. The first is 4 plus 2, which is 6. The second is 8 plus 2 plus 1, which is 11, and 11 in hex is the letter B. So the answer is 6B. Writing 6, 11 is wrong because each nibble must become a single hex digit.
items.concept: Binary to hex: group bits in fours from the right; each group is one hex digit, with 10 to 15 as A to F.
items.hint: Convert each group of four separately. What letter is eleven?

items.q: Convert hexadecimal 86 to decimal.
items.right: Yes, 134: eight sixteens is 128, plus 6.
items.wrong: Hex place weights are 1 and 16 for two digits. Hex 86 has 8 in the sixteens place and 6 in the ones place. Eight times 16 is 128, plus 6 is 134. Reading it as decimal eighty-six ignores that the left digit counts sixteens, not tens.

slips.why: You read hex 86 as decimal. The left hex digit counts sixteens: 8 times 16 is 128, plus 6 is 134.
You added the digits. Place value matters: the 8 is in the sixteens place, so it is worth 128. Add 6 to get 134.

items.concept: Two-digit hex to decimal: left digit times 16, plus the right digit.
items.hint: Eight times sixteen is 128.

items.q: Convert decimal 29 to hexadecimal.
items.right: Correct, 1D: one sixteen, plus 13, which is D.
items.wrong: Divide by 16. Twenty-nine contains one 16, with 13 left over. The sixteens digit is 1, and the ones digit is 13, which in hex is the letter D. So 29 is 1D. Saying one, thirteen puts a two-digit decimal number where a single hex digit must go.
items.concept: Decimal to hex: count the sixteens, then write the remainder as one digit from 0 to F.
items.hint: How many sixteens fit in 29, and what is left?

items.q: A B C D value is one zero zero one, one zero zero zero. What decimal number is it?
items.right: Correct, 98. One zero zero one is 9 and one zero zero zero is 8.
items.wrong: In B C D, decode each four-bit group on its own. One zero zero one is 8 plus 1, which is 9. One zero zero zero is 8. Put the digits side by side: 98. Treating all eight bits as one binary number gives 152, which ignores that B C D codes each digit separately.

slips.why: You decoded all eight bits as one binary number. B C D codes each decimal digit in its own four bits: one zero zero one is 9, one zero zero zero is 8, giving 98.

items.concept: Decode B C D one four-bit group at a time; each group is one decimal digit.
items.hint: Decode each group of four separately.

items.q: Write decimal 44 in B C D. Say all eight bits.
answer: zero one zero zero zero one zero zero
oh one oh oh oh one oh oh
items.right: Yes: each 4 is zero one zero zero.
items.wrong: B C D codes each decimal digit separately in four bits. The digit 4 is zero one zero zero. Forty-four has two 4s, so the code is zero one zero zero, zero one zero zero. Converting 44 as a whole binary number gives one zero one one zero zero, which is pure binary, not B C D.
items.concept: B C D: convert each decimal digit to its own four bits.
items.hint: What are the four bits for the digit 4?

items.q: How does B C D differ from ordinary binary?
options: It codes each decimal digit separately in four bits
It stores base ten digits directly
It uses three bits per digit
It can only represent numbers below ten
items.right: Right. Each decimal digit gets its own four-bit group.
wrong: B C D still uses only ones and zeros; no decimal digits appear in the bits. The decimal part of its name means each decimal digit gets its own four-bit binary group, rather than converting the whole number at once.
Three bits can only count to seven, which is octal's grouping. Decimal digits go up to nine, which needs four bits. So B C D uses four bits per decimal digit.

B C D can represent numbers of any size by adding more four-bit groups. A three-digit number simply uses three groups, twelve bits. The difference from binary is that each decimal digit is coded separately.
items.concept: B C D encodes each decimal digit separately in four bits; pure binary converts the whole number.
items.hint: Think about what the D in B C D stands for.

items.q: True or false: one one zero zero is a valid B C D digit group.
items.right: Correct, false. It is 12, and a B C D group only holds 0 to 9.
items.wrong: One one zero zero is 12. A B C D group stands for a single decimal digit, 0 to 9, so only zero zero zero zero through one zero zero one are valid. The six patterns for ten to fifteen never appear in correct B C D. Twelve would be written as two groups: zero zero zero one, then zero zero one zero.
items.concept: Valid B C D groups are 0000 to 1001; 1010 to 1111 are invalid.
items.hint: What decimal value is one one zero zero?

items.q: A three-digit voltmeter display receives B C D. How many data bits carry the three digits? Answer in bits.
items.right: Yes, 12 bits: four per digit, three digits.
items.wrong: B C D uses four bits for each decimal digit. A three-digit display shows three digits, so it needs three groups of four: 3 times 4 is 12 bits. For a reading of 120 volts, the code is zero zero zero one, zero zero one zero, zero zero zero zero. Pure binary would use fewer bits, but the display expects one group per digit.

slips.why: Seven bits is what pure binary needs to reach 120. B C D sends each decimal digit in its own four bits, so three digits need 12 bits.

items.concept: B C D needs four bits for every decimal digit displayed.
items.hint: Four bits per digit, times the number of digits.

items.q: Why do computer systems need the A S C I I code?
options: To represent letters and symbols as codes
To compress numbers into fewer bits
To convert decimal numbers into B C D
items.right: Right. A S C I I lets alphanumeric characters move into and out of a computer as bit patterns.
wrong: A S C I I does not speed arithmetic; arithmetic runs on pure binary numbers. A S C I I exists so text, meaning letters, digits, punctuation and controls, can be represented as bit patterns and moved between keyboards, computers and displays.

A S C I I usually needs more bits than pure binary for numbers, not fewer: the text 45 takes two bytes. Its job is representing characters, alphanumeric data, so they can go into and out of a computer.
B C D is its own separate code for decimal digits. A S C I I is a character code covering letters, digits and symbols, so that alphanumeric data can be entered, stored and displayed.
items.concept: A S C I I codes characters, letters, digits and symbols, as bit patterns.
items.hint: What kind of data is not a number?

items.q: Capital A is hex 41 in A S C I I. What is the hex code for capital E?
items.right: Correct, hex 45. E is four letters after A.
items.wrong: Capital letters are consecutive in A S C I I. A is hex 41, B is 42, C is 43, D is 44, and E is 45. Counting four places on from A gives 45. No hex letters appear in the code this early: I is hex 49, and the first code with a letter in it is J, hex 4 A.
items.concept: A S C I I capitals are consecutive, starting from hex 41 for A.
items.hint: Count up from 41: A, B, C, D, E.

items.q: True or false: the A S C I I code for the character 5 is the binary number five, zero zero zero zero zero one zero one.
items.right: Right, false. The character 5 is hex 35; a character code is not the number it shows.
items.wrong: A S C I I digit characters start at hex 30, so the character 5 is hex 35, which is zero zero one one, zero one zero one. The pattern for the number five, zero zero zero zero, zero one zero one, is a control code in A S C I I. A character is a symbol to display, not a numeric value.
items.concept: A S C I I digit characters are hex 30 to 39; the character is not its numeric value.
items.hint: Where do the digit characters start in A S C I I?

items.q: What is the largest unsigned value you can store in 6 bits? Answer as a decimal number.
items.right: Yes, 63. Six bits give 64 patterns, from 0 to 63.
items.wrong: With n bits there are two to the n patterns, and counting starts at 0, so the largest value is two to the n, minus 1. Two to the six is 64, so the largest six-bit value is 63, which is all six bits set: 32 plus 16 plus 8 plus 4 plus 2 plus 1. Sixty-four is the number of patterns, not the largest value.

slips.why: Sixty-four is how many patterns six bits give, but counting starts at zero, so the largest is 64 minus 1, which is 63.

items.concept: n bits give two to the n patterns; the largest unsigned value is two to the n, minus 1.
items.hint: Set all six bits to 1 and add the weights.

items.q: Four status bits, from bit 3 down to bit 0, mean over-temperature, low level, door open, motor running. The status is one zero one zero. Which conditions are present?
options: Only the value ten is reported
items.right: Right. Bits 3 and 1 are set: over-temperature and door open.
wrong: You read the bits from the wrong end. The leftmost bit is bit 3, over-temperature, and it is 1. Next is bit 2, low level, 0. Bit 1, door open, is 1. Bit 0, motor running, is 0. So over-temperature and door open are present.
As flags, the pattern is not a single value. Each bit answers its own yes or no question. Reading left to right from bit 3: over-temperature yes, low level no, door open yes, motor running no.
Only the first and third bits are 1. Bit 3, over-temperature, is 1; bit 2, low level, is 0; bit 1, door open, is 1; bit 0 is 0. So the conditions are over-temperature and door open.
items.concept: In a status word, each bit is its own flag; match each position with its meaning.
items.hint: Match each bit, left to right, with its condition.

items.q: Convert binary one one zero zero to Gray code. Say the four bits.
items.right: Correct. Copy 1; then 1 and 1 give 0, 1 and 0 give 1, 0 and 0 give 0.
items.wrong: Copy the first bit: 1. Then compare each neighbouring pair of the original binary bits, where same gives 0 and different gives 1. First pair, 1 and 1: same, 0. Second pair, 1 and 0: different, 1. Third pair, 0 and 0: same, 0. The Gray code is one zero one zero. Comparing against the new Gray bits instead of the original binary bits is the usual slip.
items.concept: Binary to Gray: copy the first bit, then exclusive OR each pair of neighbouring binary bits.
items.hint: Copy the first bit. Then ask: are the next two binary bits the same or different?

items.q: Convert Gray code one zero one zero back to binary. Say the four bits.
items.right: Yes. Copy 1; Gray 0 keeps it at 1; Gray 1 flips to 0; Gray 0 keeps 0.
items.wrong: Copy the first bit: binary starts with 1. Now walk right using the binary bit you just found. Gray bit 0 means keep: binary stays 1. Gray bit 1 means flip: binary becomes 0. Gray bit 0 means keep: 0. The result is one one zero zero. Comparing neighbouring Gray bits is the binary-to-Gray rule and gives the wrong answer here.
items.concept: Gray to binary: copy the first bit; each Gray 1 flips the previous binary bit, each Gray 0 keeps it.
items.hint: Copy the first bit, then let each Gray bit say keep or flip.

items.q: True or false: in Gray code, stepping from the value 3 to the value 4 changes three bits, just as in binary.
items.right: Correct, false. In three-bit Gray code, zero one zero goes to one one zero: one bit changes.
items.wrong: That is exactly what Gray code avoids. In binary, 3 to 4 is zero one one to one zero zero, three bits flipping at once. In three-bit Gray code, 3 is zero one zero and 4 is one one zero, so only one bit changes. Every adjacent step in Gray code changes exactly one bit.
items.concept: Adjacent Gray code values always differ in exactly one bit.
items.hint: What is the defining property of Gray code?

items.q: Is wind speed an analog or a digital quantity?
items.right: Right. Wind speed varies smoothly through every value, so it is analog.
wrong: Wind speed can be displayed digitally, but the quantity itself changes smoothly, passing through every value between, say, 10 and 11 kilometres per hour. That continuous variation is what analog means. A digital reading is only a stepped representation of it.

Units never decide analog or digital; kilometres per hour and metres per second describe the same smoothly varying quantity. Analog means continuously variable, and wind speed changes continuously, so it is analog.
items.concept: Analog quantities vary continuously; digital ones take distinct steps.
items.hint: Can wind speed take any value between two readings?

items.q: True or false: an analog-to-digital converter outputs an analog voltage.
items.right: Correct, false. An A D C outputs a digital code; a D A C outputs an analog voltage.
items.wrong: The name tells you the direction: analog to digital. An A D C takes an analog input, such as a sensor voltage, and outputs a digital code, a set of bits. The device that outputs an analog voltage is the D A C, the digital-to-analog converter.
items.concept: A D C: analog in, digital out. D A C: digital in, analog out.
items.hint: Read the name: analog to what?

items.q: A music player turns stored digital samples into a voltage for the speaker. Which process is that?
items.right: Yes. Digital samples in, smooth voltage out: a D A C.
wrong: Analog-to-digital goes the other way, turning a smooth signal like a microphone voltage into bits. Playing back music starts with stored bits and must produce a smooth voltage for the speaker, so it is digital-to-analog conversion, done by a D A C.
Parallel-to-serial changes how bits are sent, but the output is still bits. A speaker needs a continuously varying voltage, so the player uses a D A C, digital-to-analog conversion.
items.concept: Playback of stored digital audio uses a D A C.
items.hint: Which direction: from bits, or into bits?

items.q: A clock runs at 8 megahertz. What is the time from one rising edge to the next? Answer in nanoseconds.
items.right: Correct, 125 nanoseconds. One over 8 megahertz is 0.125 microseconds.
items.wrong: Period equals one over frequency, period in seconds, frequency in hertz. One over 8 megahertz is one eighth of a microsecond, which is 0.125 microseconds. One microsecond is 1000 nanoseconds, so the period is 125 nanoseconds. Rising edge to rising edge is exactly one period.

slips.why: You gave the frequency back. Period is the reciprocal: one over 8 megahertz is 125 nanoseconds.

items.concept: Period equals one over frequency; 1 megahertz pairs with 1 microsecond.
items.hint: One megahertz gives one microsecond. What does eight megahertz give?

items.q: A periodic waveform has a period of 50 nanoseconds. What is its frequency? Answer in megahertz.
items.right: Yes, 20 megahertz.
items.wrong: Frequency equals one over period, frequency in hertz, period in seconds. Fifty nanoseconds is 50 times ten to the minus nine seconds. One over that is 20 million hertz, which is 20 megahertz. Quick check: 1 microsecond gives 1 megahertz, and 50 nanoseconds is twenty times shorter, so the frequency is twenty times higher.

slips.why: You divided the wrong way. Frequency equals one over period: one over 50 nanoseconds is 20 megahertz, because 50 nanoseconds is one twentieth of a microsecond.
You slipped a factor of ten. Fifty nanoseconds is 0.05 microseconds, and one over 0.05 is 20, so the frequency is 20 megahertz.

items.concept: Frequency equals one over period; a shorter period means a higher frequency.
items.hint: How many 50-nanosecond periods fit into one microsecond?

items.q: A pulse is HIGH for 15 microseconds and LOW for 35 microseconds. What is its duty cycle? Answer in percent.
items.right: Correct, 30 percent: 15 out of a 50 microsecond period.
items.wrong: Duty cycle equals HIGH time divided by period, times 100 percent, both times in the same unit. The period is HIGH plus LOW: 15 plus 35 is 50 microseconds. Fifteen over 50 is 0.3, which is 30 percent. Dividing HIGH time by LOW time, 15 over 35, gives about 43 percent, which is not the definition.

slips.why: You divided HIGH time by LOW time. Duty cycle uses the whole period: 15 over 50 microseconds is 30 percent.
Seventy percent is the LOW fraction. Duty cycle is the HIGH fraction: 15 over 50 is 30 percent.

items.concept: Duty cycle equals HIGH time over the full period, times 100 percent.
items.hint: First add HIGH and LOW time to get the period.

items.q: Same pulse: HIGH 15 microseconds, LOW 35 microseconds. What is its frequency? Answer in kilohertz.
items.right: Yes, 20 kilohertz: one over 50 microseconds.
items.wrong: Frequency equals one over period, frequency in hertz, period in seconds. The period is the whole cycle, HIGH plus LOW, which is 50 microseconds. One over 50 microseconds is 20,000 hertz, which is 20 kilohertz. Using only the HIGH time, 15 microseconds, treats part of the cycle as if it were the whole period.

slips.why: You used the 15 microsecond HIGH time as the period. The period is the full cycle, 50 microseconds, so the frequency is 20 kilohertz.

items.concept: Period is the full cycle, HIGH plus LOW; frequency is one over that.
items.hint: What is the full cycle time?

items.q: How long does it take to send three 8-bit numbers in serial with a 5 megahertz clock, one bit per clock? Answer in microseconds.
items.right: Correct, 4.8 microseconds: 24 bits at 0.2 microseconds each.
items.wrong: First the period: period equals one over frequency, seconds and hertz. One over 5 megahertz is 0.2 microseconds. Serial sends one bit per period, and three 8-bit numbers are 24 bits. Time equals number of bits times period: 24 times 0.2 is 4.8 microseconds.

slips.why: That is the time for just one 8-bit number. There are three numbers, 24 bits in total, so 24 times 0.2 microseconds is 4.8 microseconds.
That is the parallel time, one clock per number. Serial sends one bit per clock: 24 bits times 0.2 microseconds is 4.8 microseconds.

items.concept: Serial time equals the number of bits times the clock period.
items.hint: Find the period of 5 megahertz first, then count the bits.

items.q: Which transmission method needs more conductors and circuitry?
items.right: Right. Parallel needs a line per bit, trading wiring for speed.
wrong: Serial is the economical one: a single data line, with bits sent one after another in time. Parallel gives each bit its own line so a whole word moves at once, which is why it needs more conductors and circuitry.
They differ. Serial sends bits one at a time on one line. Parallel sends all bits at once on separate lines, one per bit, so an 8-bit parallel link needs eight data lines instead of one.
items.concept: Parallel is faster in this model but needs one conductor per bit.
items.hint: Which method sends all bits at the same instant?

items.q: A selector switches the left and right audio channels together between four stereo inputs. What pole and throw designation is needed?
items.right: Correct, D P 4 T: two channels need two poles, and four inputs need four throws.
items.wrong: Count poles and throws separately. Poles are independent paths switched together: the left and right channels make two, so double pole. Throws are the destinations each pole can select: four stereo inputs, so four throws. The designation is D P 4 T. A single pole would switch only one channel.
items.concept: Poles count independent paths; throws count destinations per pole.
items.hint: How many channels, and how many inputs to choose between?

items.q: True or false: an S P S T switch has two throws, because it can be open or closed.
items.right: Correct, false. Open is not a destination, so S P S T has one throw.
items.wrong: Throws count the destinations a pole can connect to. An S P S T switch has one destination; the open position is just no connection, not a second destination. That is why it is single throw. A switch that picks between two destinations, S P D T, is double throw.
items.concept: The open position is not a throw; throws count connection destinations.
items.hint: Does the open position connect the pole to anything?

items.q: What happens to a relay's normally open contacts when its coil is energized?
items.right: Right. Normally open means open at rest; energizing the coil closes them.
wrong: Normally open contacts are already open at rest, with the coil off. Energizing the coil moves them away from their normal state, so they close and make a connection. It is the normally closed contacts that open when the coil is energized.
The whole purpose of the coil is to move the contacts. Energizing it pulls normally open contacts closed. If nothing changed, the relay could not switch anything.
Contacts do not have a polarity to reverse; they are either touching or apart. Normally open contacts close when the coil is energized, making a connection.
items.concept: N O contacts close when the coil is energized; N C contacts open.
items.hint: Normal describes the contacts with the coil off.

items.q: Twelve volts feeds 3 kilohms on top and 6 kilohms to ground. Relay N O contacts sit across the 6 kilohm resistor. With the coil off, what is the output across the 6 kilohms? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 8 volts. With the coil off the contacts are open, so it is a plain divider.
items.wrong: Coil off means the normally open contacts are open, so they do nothing and the circuit is a plain voltage divider. Output equals supply times bottom resistance over total resistance, all in volts and ohms: 12 times 6 kilohms over 9 kilohms, which is 8 volts. Zero volts is the energized case, when the contacts short the 6 kilohms.

slips.why: Zero volts is the output with the coil energized, when the closed contacts short the resistor. With the coil off the contacts are open, so the divider gives 12 times 6 over 9, which is 8 volts.
Four volts is the drop across the 3 kilohm top resistor. The output is across the 6 kilohm resistor: 12 times 6 over 9 is 8 volts.

items.concept: Divider output equals supply times bottom resistance over total resistance.
items.hint: Open contacts change nothing. Use the voltage divider.

items.q: Same circuit, but now the coil is energized. What is the output across the 6 kilohm resistor?
items.right: Yes, 0 volts. The closed contacts short the 6 kilohm resistor.
wrong: Eight volts is the de-energized case, when the contacts are open. Energizing the coil closes the normally open contacts, which short the 6 kilohm resistor. An ideal short has zero volts across it, so the output drops to 0 volts.

The output is across the shorted resistor, not at the top of the supply. Closed contacts make an ideal short across the 6 kilohms, forcing zero volts there. The full 12 volts now drops across the 3 kilohm resistor instead.
Four volts is the top resistor's share in the open case. Once the contacts close, the lower resistor is shorted, so the output is 0 volts and the whole 12 volts sits across the 3 kilohms.
items.concept: A closed contact is a short: zero volts across whatever it is connected across.
items.hint: What does a closed contact do to the resistor it sits across?

items.q: A 5 volt pull-up circuit uses a normally open pushbutton from output to ground. What is the output with the button released?
items.right: Right. Released means open: no current, no resistor drop, so the output is 5 volts.
wrong: LOW is the pressed state, when the closed button shorts the output to ground. Released, the normally open button is open, no current flows, the resistor drops nothing, and the output sits at the full 5 volts.

The pull-up is exactly what prevents floating. It gives the output a defined path to 5 volts when the switch is open. With no current there is no drop across the resistor, so the output is 5 volts, HIGH.

There is no divider here, just one resistor and an open switch. With the switch open, no current flows, so by Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, the resistor drops zero volts and the output is the full 5 volts.
items.concept: Pull-up with the switch open: no current, no drop, output at the supply.
items.hint: With no current through the resistor, how much voltage does it drop?

items.q: The same pull-up uses 5 volts and a 1 kilohm resistor. The button is pressed. How much current flows through the resistor? Answer in milliamps.
items.right: Correct, 5 milliamps: the full 5 volts across 1 kilohm.
items.wrong: Pressing the button shorts the output to ground, so the whole 5 volt supply appears across the resistor. Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance, amps, volts, ohms. Five volts over 1 kilohm is 5 milliamps. Zero current is the released case, when the switch is open.

slips.why: Zero current is the released state. When pressed, the switch connects the output to ground, putting the full 5 volts across 1 kilohm: 5 milliamps.

items.concept: Pressed pull-up: the full supply is across the resistor, so current equals supply over resistance.
items.hint: When pressed, what voltage is across the resistor?

items.q: True or false: an open switch carries no current, so the voltage across it must be zero.
items.right: Correct, false. In the pull-up, the open switch has the full 5 volts across it.
items.wrong: Zero current and zero voltage are separate facts. Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, only forces zero voltage across a resistor carrying zero current. An open switch has no finite resistance, so use Kirchhoff instead: in the pull-up, the resistor drops 0 volts, so the full 5 volts appears across the open switch.
items.concept: An open switch carries zero current but can have the full supply across it.
items.hint: Where does the supply voltage go if the resistor drops nothing?

items.q: A normally open button connects 5 volts to the output, and a resistor runs from the output to ground. What is the output when the button is pressed?
items.right: Right. Pressed connects the output to 5 volts; this pull-down makes a press active HIGH.
wrong: LOW is the released state, when the resistor holds the output at ground with no current. Pressing the button connects the output straight to 5 volts, so it goes HIGH. This is a pull-down, so a press is active HIGH.
The resistor to ground prevents floating in the released state, and pressing connects the output to 5 volts. Either way the output is defined. Pressed, it is 5 volts, HIGH.
The resistor sits between the output and ground, so it limits the current to 5 volts divided by its resistance. There is no direct short. The output is simply connected to 5 volts, HIGH.
items.concept: Pull-down: released gives LOW, pressed gives HIGH, so the press is active HIGH.
items.hint: Pressing the button connects the output to which rail?

items.q: A switch connects 5 volts to a logic input, with no other connection to that input. The switch is open. What is the input's level?
items.right: Right. Open switch, no other path: the input floats with no defined level.
wrong: With the switch open, nothing connects the input to ground, so there is no reason for it to sit at 0 volts. Stray charge, leakage and noise decide its voltage. That is a floating input. A pull-down resistor would give it a defined LOW.
The open switch disconnects the 5 volts, so nothing holds the input HIGH either. With no path to any reference, the input floats and its level is undefined. Add a pull-down resistor to define it.
Nothing sets 2.5 volts; there is no divider. With the switch open, the input connects to nothing, so it floats and noise decides its voltage. Floating never means a predictable value.
items.concept: An input with no path to a defined level floats; add a pull-up or pull-down.
items.hint: What connects the input to anything when the switch is open?

items.q: To forward bias a diode, how must the anode compare with the cathode?
items.right: Right. Anode more positive than cathode is forward bias.
wrong: An anode more negative than the cathode is reverse bias, which blocks current in the course model. Forward bias needs the anode more positive than the cathode, so conventional current can flow from anode to cathode.
Equal potentials give zero volts across the diode: no bias at all, so no current. Forward bias needs the anode more positive than the cathode, by about 0.7 volts for a silicon diode to conduct.
The anode's own voltage relative to ground does not decide bias. What matters is anode minus cathode. The anode must be more positive than the cathode for forward bias.
items.concept: Forward bias: anode more positive than cathode.
items.hint: Current flows from anode to cathode. Which end must be higher?

items.q: In the course model, about how many volts are across a conducting, forward-biased silicon diode?
items.right: Right, about 0.7 volts in the constant-drop model.
wrong: Point three volts is the old approximation for germanium diodes. This course uses silicon diodes, modelled with a constant forward drop of about 0.7 volts while conducting.
Zero volts is the ideal-diode model, which this course does not use for silicon calculations. Here a conducting silicon diode is modelled with about 0.7 volts from anode to cathode.

The full supply appears across a reverse-biased, open diode, not a conducting one. A forward-biased conducting silicon diode holds only about 0.7 volts; the rest of the supply drops across the resistor.
items.concept: Constant-drop model: a conducting silicon diode drops about 0.7 volts.
items.hint: It is less than one volt.

items.q: A 5 volt supply feeds a forward-biased silicon diode, then a 1 kilohm resistor to ground. What is the voltage across the resistor? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 4.3 volts: 5 minus the 0.7 volt diode drop.
items.wrong: Use Kirchhoff's voltage law: the supply equals the sum of the drops around the loop. The diode takes 0.7 volts, so the resistor gets 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts. Answering 5 volts forgets the diode drop; answering 0.7 volts confuses the diode's share with the resistor's.

slips.why: You forgot the diode's drop. A conducting silicon diode takes 0.7 volts, leaving 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, for the resistor.
Point seven volts is across the diode. The resistor gets the remainder: 5 minus 0.7 is 4.3 volts.

items.concept: Series diode circuit: the resistor voltage equals the supply minus 0.7 volts.
items.hint: Subtract the diode's drop from the supply.

items.q: In that circuit the diode is turned around, so it is reverse biased. What is the voltage across the resistor?
items.right: Right. The reversed diode is open, so zero current and zero resistor voltage.
wrong: 4.3 volts assumed the diode conducts. Reversed, it is an open circuit, so no current flows. By Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, and zero current gives zero volts across the resistor. The diode holds the whole 5 volts instead.
The full 5 volts is across the reversed diode, not the resistor. The open diode blocks current, so the resistor, carrying zero current, drops zero volts by Ohm's law.
Point seven volts appears only across a conducting silicon diode. A reverse-biased diode does not conduct, so current is zero and the resistor drops zero volts. The diode holds the full 5 volts.
items.concept: A reverse-biased diode is open: zero current, so series resistors drop nothing.
items.hint: How much current passes a reverse-biased diode?

items.q: In a diode AND gate with a pull-up to 5 volts, one input cathode is moved from 5 volts to 0 volts. What is the output voltage? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, about 0.7 volts: the grounded diode conducts and clamps the output.
items.wrong: The output node is the shared anodes, pulled up toward 5 volts. Once one cathode is at 0 volts, that diode is forward biased and conducts. A conducting silicon diode holds 0.7 volts from anode to cathode, so the output sits at 0 plus 0.7, which is 0.7 volts, a LOW. The other diodes turn off.

slips.why: The diode is not a perfect short in the course model. It conducts with 0.7 volts across it, so the output sits 0.7 volts above the grounded input.
4.3 volts is the diode OR result. In this AND network the grounded diode clamps the shared anodes 0.7 volts above ground: 0.7 volts.

items.concept: Diode AND: one LOW input clamps the output at 0.7 volts, a LOW.
