items.hint: The grounded diode conducts. How far above its cathode is its anode?

items.q: In a diode OR gate with a pull-down resistor, one input anode goes from 0 to 5 volts. What is the output voltage? Answer in volts.
items.right: Yes, 4.3 volts: 5 volts minus one diode drop.
items.wrong: The output is the shared cathodes, pulled down by the resistor. The input at 5 volts forward biases its diode, which conducts with 0.7 volts across it. Output equals input minus diode drop: 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, a HIGH. The other diodes, with 0 volt anodes, are reverse biased and stay off.

slips.why: You forgot the diode drop. The conducting diode takes 0.7 volts, so the output is 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts.
0.7 volts is the diode AND clamp. Here the conducting diode sits between the 5 volt input and the output, so the output is 5 minus 0.7: 4.3 volts.

items.concept: Diode OR: any HIGH input lifts the output to 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts.
items.hint: The output is one diode drop below the HIGH input.

items.q: A diode network outputs LOW if any input is LOW, and HIGH only if every input is HIGH. Which logic function is that?
items.right: Right, AND: HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH.
items.wrong: List the rule: any LOW input forces LOW, and all inputs HIGH gives HIGH. That is the AND function, HIGH only when every input is HIGH. OR would give HIGH when any input is HIGH, and would need all inputs LOW to output LOW, the opposite pattern.
items.concept: AND: output HIGH only when every input is HIGH.
items.hint: Which gate needs every input HIGH?

items.q: True or false: to turn on an N P N transistor switch, you apply a negative voltage to its base.
items.right: Correct, false. An N P N switch needs positive base drive.
items.wrong: An N P N transistor turns on when its base-emitter junction is forward biased, which means the base is driven positive relative to the emitter, by about 0.7 volts or more, through a base resistor. A negative base voltage reverse biases that junction, so the transistor stays in cutoff. P N P transistors use the opposite polarity.
items.concept: N P N turns on with positive base drive; the base-emitter junction must be forward biased.
items.hint: The base-emitter junction is a diode. Which way must it be biased?

items.q: When an N P N transistor switch is turned fully on, what does its collector-to-emitter path become?
items.right: Right. Saturation makes collector to emitter act like a closed switch.
wrong: Open is the cutoff state, with no base current. When base current flows and the transistor saturates, the collector-to-emitter path behaves like a closed switch, a short.
Point seven volts belongs to the base-to-emitter junction. In the course model, the collector-to-emitter path of a saturated transistor is treated as a short, with zero volts across it.
A reverse-biased diode blocks current, which describes the off state. Turned on, the collector-to-emitter path acts like a closed switch, a short, letting collector current flow.
items.concept: Saturated transistor: collector-emitter short. Cutoff: collector-emitter open.
items.hint: On means the switch is closed.

items.source: Lecture 05, worked N P N circuit
items.q: A 3.3 volt input drives an N P N base through 10 kilohms, emitter grounded. What is the base current? Answer in microamps.
items.right: Correct, 260 microamps: 2.6 volts across 10 kilohms.
items.wrong: The base-emitter junction takes 0.7 volts, so the base resistor has 3.3 minus 0.7, which is 2.6 volts. Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance, amps, volts, ohms. 2.6 volts over 10 kilohms is 0.26 milliamps, which is 260 microamps. Using 3.3 volts directly gives 330, forgetting the junction drop.

slips.why: You forgot the 0.7 volt base-emitter drop. The resistor has 3.3 minus 0.7, which is 2.6 volts, and 2.6 volts over 10 kilohms is 260 microamps.
0.26 is the base current in milliamps. In microamps it is 260: 2.6 volts over 10 kilohms.

items.concept: Base current equals input minus 0.7 volts, divided by the base resistance.
items.hint: Subtract the base-emitter drop first.

items.q: To use a common-emitter transistor as an inverter, where do the input and output connect?
options: Input to the base, output from the collector
Input to the collector, output from the base
Input to the emitter, output from the collector
Input to the base, output from the emitter
items.right: Right. Base in, collector out, emitter common to both.
wrong: The base is the control terminal, so the input belongs there, through a base resistor. The collector, with its pull-up resistor, is where the voltage swings between the supply and ground, so it is the output.
In common emitter, the emitter is shared, tied to ground as the reference. The input drives the base, and the output is taken at the collector.

The emitter is grounded in this circuit, so its voltage never changes; it cannot serve as the output. The input drives the base and the output comes from the collector, which is pulled up through the collector resistor.
items.concept: Common-emitter inverter: input to base, output at collector, emitter grounded.
items.hint: Common emitter: the emitter is shared. What is left for input and output?

items.q: True or false: in the common-emitter inverter, turning the transistor on makes the collector output HIGH.
items.right: Correct, false. On pulls the collector to ground: output LOW.
items.wrong: Turning the transistor on closes the collector-to-emitter path, connecting the collector to the grounded emitter. The collector resistor then drops the whole supply, and the output is 0 volts, LOW. That is why it inverts: input HIGH, transistor on, output LOW. The transistor's state and the output level are different ideas.
items.concept: In the inverter, transistor on means output LOW; transistor off means output HIGH.
items.hint: When the switch closes, what is the collector connected to?

items.q: An inverter's transistor is off. The collector resistor is 1 kilohm, the supply 5 volts, and the total load to ground is 1 kilohm. What is the output voltage? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 2.5 volts. Equal resistors split the 5 volts in half.
items.wrong: With the transistor off, the collector resistor and the load form a voltage divider. Output equals supply times load resistance over the total: 5 volts times 1 kilohm over 2 kilohms, which is 2.5 volts. Answering 5 volts assumes no load current, but the load draws current through the collector resistor, which drops voltage.

slips.why: Five volts is the unloaded output. The 1 kilohm load draws current through the collector resistor, forming a divider: 5 times 1 over 2 is 2.5 volts.

items.concept: Loaded HIGH output equals supply times load, over collector plus load resistance.
items.hint: It is a voltage divider of two equal resistors.

items.q: How does the T T L totem-pole output fix the problem of the single collector resistor?
options: An active transistor pulls the output up
A larger resistor limits the current
A diode clamps the output HIGH
The load is removed from the circuit
items.right: Right. The upper transistor actively drives HIGH, so no single resistor must compromise.
wrong: A larger collector resistor would cut the on-state current but make the HIGH output sag even more under load. That is the trade-off the totem pole escapes: it replaces the passive pull-up with a transistor that actively drives the output HIGH.

A clamp diode cannot supply load current to hold a HIGH. The totem pole uses two transistors in series: an upper one that actively drives the output HIGH and a lower one that pulls it LOW, one on while the other is off.

A gate must drive whatever loads are connected; removing them is not an option. The totem pole replaces the fixed collector resistor with an upper transistor that actively pulls the output up, giving strong HIGH drive without a big on-state current.
items.concept: Totem-pole output: one transistor actively pulls up, the other pulls down, one on at a time.
items.hint: What replaces the passive collector resistor?

items.q: What does T T L stand for?
items.right: Right: transistor-transistor logic, built from bipolar transistors.
wrong: There is no such family. T T L is transistor-transistor logic: bipolar transistors driving further transistor stages inside the chip, including the input stage and the totem-pole output.
The name is about what the gate is built from. T T L means transistor-transistor logic, logic made from bipolar junction transistors, running on 5 volts.
Threshold levels are a property of T T L inputs, not its name. T T L stands for transistor-transistor logic, a family built from bipolar transistors.
items.concept: T T L is transistor-transistor logic, a bipolar-transistor family on a 5 volt supply.
items.hint: Two of the three words are the same.

items.q: How many separate inverters are inside a 7404 hex inverter IC?
items.right: Right, six. Hex means six here.
wrong: In a part name, hex means six, from the Greek, not hexadecimal. The 7404 holds six inverters: six inputs and six outputs use twelve pins, and V C C and ground make fourteen.
Four gates is a quad package, such as the 7408 AND. The 7404 is a hex package: six inverters, each needing only one input and one output pin.
Eight inverters would need sixteen signal pins, more than a 14-pin package offers after its two power pins. Hex means six: the 7404 has six inverters.
items.concept: Hex in a part name means six; the 7404 holds six inverters.
items.hint: Hex is Greek for a number.

items.q: The T T L input clamp diode has its anode at ground and its cathode at the input. The input is at plus 5 volts. What is the diode's state?
items.right: Right. Anode minus cathode is minus 5 volts: reverse biased, not conducting.
wrong: Forward bias needs the anode above the cathode. Here the anode is at 0 volts and the cathode at 5 volts: anode minus cathode is minus 5 volts. That is reverse bias, so the diode is off. It only clamps when the input goes below about minus 0.7 volts.
Zero bias is the 0 volt input case, when anode and cathode are both at 0. At plus 5 volts, the anode is 5 volts below the cathode, which is reverse bias.
Breakdown needs a large reverse voltage beyond the diode's rating, not a normal logic HIGH. At plus 5 volts the diode is simply reverse biased: anode minus cathode is minus 5 volts.
items.concept: The input clamp diode is off for normal inputs and conducts only on negative undershoot.
items.hint: Compute anode minus cathode.

items.q: Ringing drives a T T L input toward minus 2 volts. In the 0.7 volt diode model, where does the clamp diode hold the pin? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, about minus 0.7 volts.
items.wrong: The clamp diode has its anode at ground, 0 volts, and its cathode on the input. Once the input goes more than 0.7 volts below ground, the diode is forward biased and conducts. A conducting diode holds 0.7 volts from anode to cathode, so the pin sits at 0 minus 0.7, which is minus 0.7 volts, instead of reaching minus 2.

slips.why: The sign matters. The diode's anode is at ground and the pin is its cathode, so the pin sits 0.7 volts below ground: minus 0.7 volts.
Minus 2 volts is where the ringing would go without the clamp. The diode conducts once the pin passes minus 0.7 volts and holds it there.

items.concept: The input clamp holds a negative-going input near minus 0.7 volts.
items.hint: The pin is the cathode, and the anode is at ground.

items.q: True or false: with a HIGH T T L input, current through the input transistor's base-collector junction turns on the next stage.
items.right: Correct. A HIGH input steers the base current through the base-collector junction into the next stage.
items.wrong: With the input HIGH, the base-emitter path out to the input pin cannot take the base resistor's current. That current flows instead through the forward-biased base-collector junction into the next stage, turning it on. This unusual base-to-collector conduction is the key to the T T L input, so the statement is true.
items.concept: T T L input HIGH: the base-collector junction conducts into the next stage.
items.hint: If current cannot leave through the input pin, where can it go?

items.q: Where should the unused inputs of a T T L gate be tied in this course, and why?
options: To plus 5 volts, for low standby current
To ground, for low standby current
Left open, since T T L reads open as HIGH
items.right: Right. Tie them to plus 5 volts: a defined level and low current.
wrong: Ground removes the noise problem, but a LOW T T L input has to push current out of the input stage, so each one tied low adds supply current. Tying unused inputs to plus 5 volts gives the low-current state.
An open T T L input may tend to read HIGH, but it is floating and picks up noise, causing intermittent faults. Every input must be driven or tied. The rule is to tie unused inputs to plus 5 volts.
Tying an input to the gate's own output creates feedback and can make the gate misbehave. The rule for unused inputs is a fixed tie to plus 5 volts, which is quiet and draws little current.
items.concept: Tie unused T T L inputs HIGH to plus 5 volts: no floating, low supply current.
items.hint: Which input level makes a T T L input pull less current?

items.q: Each 74 L S input tied LOW can push out up to 0.4 milliamps. What is the worst-case total for four unused inputs tied LOW? Answer in milliamps.
items.right: Correct, 1.6 milliamps, against only 80 microamps if they were tied HIGH.
items.wrong: Currents from separate inputs add: total current equals number of inputs times current per input, in milliamps. Four inputs times 0.4 milliamps is 1.6 milliamps. Tied HIGH, each would take at most 20 microamps, just 80 microamps for four. That difference is why unused T T L inputs are tied HIGH.

slips.why: That is one input. Four inputs each push up to 0.4 milliamps, so the total is 4 times 0.4, which is 1.6 milliamps.

items.concept: Tied-LOW T T L inputs each push out current, so the totals add up quickly.
items.hint: Multiply the per-input current by four.

items.q: Which pins of a 7408 AND IC connect to the power supply?
options: Pin 14 to plus 5 volts, pin 7 to ground
Pin 1 to plus 5 volts, pin 14 to ground
Pin 7 to plus 5 volts, pin 14 to ground
Pin 16 to plus 5 volts, pin 8 to ground
items.right: Right. Pin 14 is V C C at plus 5 volts; pin 7 is ground.
wrong: Pin 1 is the first gate's input on the 7408, not a supply pin. On standard 14-pin T T L gate packages, V C C, plus 5 volts, is pin 14, top right with the notch up, and ground is pin 7, bottom left.
You have the right pins but swapped. Pin 14 is V C C at plus 5 volts and pin 7 is ground. Reversing supply polarity can destroy the chip, so learn the order: 14 plus, 7 ground.
Pins 16 and 8 are the supply pins of a 16-pin package such as the 74LS47. The 7408 is a 14-pin package, powered with plus 5 volts on pin 14 and ground on pin 7.
items.concept: 14-pin T T L gate ICs: pin 14 is V C C, pin 7 is ground.
items.hint: The two corner pins diagonally opposite each other.

items.q: How many separate OR gates are inside a 7432 IC?
items.right: Correct, four: it is a quad two-input OR.
items.wrong: The 7432 is a quad two-input OR. Count the pins: 14 in total, minus 2 for power, leaves 12 signal pins. Each two-input gate uses three pins, two inputs and one output, so 12 divided by 3 gives four gates.

slips.why: Two is the gate count of the 7421, which has four-input gates. The 7432 uses two-input gates: 12 signal pins at three per gate makes four gates.
Six is the count for the 7404, whose inverters need only two pins each. Two-input OR gates need three pins each, so 12 signal pins give four gates.

items.concept: A 14-pin package of two-input gates holds four gates.
items.hint: Twelve signal pins, three pins per two-input gate.

items.q: What type of gate is inside the 7410 IC?
items.right: Right, NAND: three three-input NAND gates.
items.wrong: The 74 series numbers name functions: the 7400 is the two-input NAND and the 7410 is its three-input relative, a triple three-input NAND. Three gates of three inputs use 9 inputs and 3 outputs, which with power fills the 14 pins. Do not confuse it with the 7411, which is the three-input AND.
items.concept: The 7410 is a triple three-input NAND; the 7411 is the triple three-input AND.
items.hint: It is the three-input version of the 7400's gate.

items.q: Which part number is a T T L inverter IC?
items.right: Right, the 7404 hex inverter.
wrong: The 7408 is the quad two-input AND. The inverter, which complements a single input, is the 7404, a hex package with six inverters.
The 7432 is the quad two-input OR. The T T L inverter IC is the 7404, holding six inverters in one 14-pin package.
The 7402 is the quad two-input NOR. The T T L inverter IC is the 7404, the hex inverter with six inverters.
items.concept: 7400 NAND, 7402 NOR, 7404 inverter, 7408 AND, 7432 OR.
items.hint: It is the hex inverter.

items.source: Quiz study pack, TTL input limits
items.q: A 74 L S 00 input sits at 1.4 volts. How is it guaranteed to read?
items.right: Right. Between 0.8 and 2.0 volts, neither level is guaranteed.
wrong: Guaranteed LOW only reaches 0.8 volts for this part. At 1.4 volts the input is above that limit but below the 2.0 volt HIGH limit, in the band where neither level is guaranteed.
Guaranteed HIGH starts at 2.0 volts. At 1.4 volts the input is below that, and above the 0.8 volt LOW limit, so the reading is not guaranteed either way.
Floating means nothing is connected. This input is being driven to 1.4 volts; it is just in the undefined band between 0.8 and 2.0 volts, where neither LOW nor HIGH is guaranteed.
items.concept: 74 L S inputs: LOW guaranteed up to 0.8 volts, HIGH from 2.0 volts, undefined between.
items.hint: Compare 1.4 volts with 0.8 and 2.0.

items.q: What is a main advantage of the C M O S logic family?
options: Very low power when not switching
It is built from bipolar transistors
It is immune to static discharge
items.right: Right. C M O S draws very little power when it is not switching.
wrong: Every logic IC needs a supply; C M O S just draws very little current while it holds a steady state. Its switching still uses energy. That low static power is its main advantage.
Bipolar transistors are what T T L uses. C M O S uses complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, M O S, transistors, which use very little power when not switching.
C M O S is especially sensitive to static discharge, which is why the lab uses wrist straps. Its well-known advantage is very low static power consumption.
items.concept: C M O S uses complementary M O S transistors and has very low static power.
items.hint: Think about the power drawn while a gate just sits there.

items.q: True or false: all inputs to an AND gate must be HIGH for it to output HIGH.
items.right: Correct. AND is HIGH only when every input is HIGH.
items.wrong: That is the definition of AND. The output is HIGH only in the single case where every input is HIGH; any LOW input forces the output LOW. In a truth table, only the last row, all ones, gives a 1. So the statement is true.
items.concept: AND outputs HIGH only when every input is HIGH.
items.hint: Think of two switches in series.

items.q: How many different input combinations does the truth table of an eight-input AND gate have?
items.right: Correct, 256: two to the eighth.
items.wrong: Each input can be 0 or 1 independently, so the number of combinations is two to the power of the number of inputs. Two to the eighth is 256. Answering 16 treats it as 8 times 2; answering 8 counts the inputs, not the combinations.

slips.why: You multiplied 8 by 2. Each extra input doubles the combinations, so it is two to the eighth, which is 256.
Eight is the number of inputs. The number of combinations is two to the eighth, 256.

items.concept: A truth table with n inputs has two to the n rows.
items.hint: Each extra input doubles the number of rows.

items.q: What input condition makes the output of an OR gate LOW?
items.right: Right. OR is LOW only when every input is LOW.
wrong: One LOW input is not enough if another input is HIGH, since any HIGH input makes the OR output HIGH. The output is LOW only when every input is LOW.
All inputs HIGH gives a HIGH OR output, because OR is inclusive. The only way to get LOW is for every input to be LOW.
Exactly one HIGH input makes an OR output HIGH, not LOW. The single LOW case is when all inputs are LOW.
items.concept: OR outputs LOW only when every input is LOW.
items.hint: OR goes HIGH if anything is HIGH.

items.q: What is the purpose of a timing chart?
options: To show output changes as inputs change in time
To list every input combination once
To show the chip's pin connections
items.right: Right. It shows graphically how the output responds as the inputs change over time.
wrong: Listing each combination once is a truth table's job. A timing chart plots signals against time, so you can see when the output changes in response to the inputs as they change.
Pin connections belong to a pinout or circuit drawing. A timing chart shows signal levels against a shared time axis, revealing how outputs respond as inputs change.
The Boolean equation is the algebraic description. A timing chart is graphical: each signal's level plotted against time, so you can see output changes as inputs change.
items.concept: A timing chart shows every signal against one shared time axis.
items.hint: What is on a timing chart's horizontal axis?

items.q: A is HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds. B is HIGH from 2 to 6 microseconds. When is the two-input AND output HIGH?
items.right: Right. Both inputs are HIGH together only from 2 to 4 microseconds.
wrong: 0 to 6 microseconds is when either input is HIGH, which is the OR output. AND needs both HIGH at the same instant. Slice the time axis: both are HIGH only between 2 and 4 microseconds.
From 0 to 2 microseconds only A is HIGH; B has not risen yet. AND needs both. The overlap, where A and B are both HIGH, is 2 to 4 microseconds.
From 4 to 6 microseconds only B is HIGH, because A fell at 4. AND needs both inputs HIGH together, which happens from 2 to 4 microseconds.
items.concept: An AND output is HIGH only where all the inputs' HIGH times overlap.
items.hint: When are A and B both HIGH at once?

items.q: What level must one input of an AND gate be at so the signal on its other input passes to the output?
items.right: Right. A HIGH control input lets the other signal through an AND gate.
wrong: A LOW input controls an AND gate, forcing the output LOW regardless of the other input. That disables it. To pass the signal, hold the control HIGH: then the output equals the other input.
A floating input has no defined level, so the gate's behaviour becomes unpredictable. Enable an AND gate with a solid HIGH on the control input.
It matters completely. With the control LOW, AND is stuck LOW; with the control HIGH, the output follows the signal. HIGH enables an AND gate.
items.concept: AND enable: control HIGH passes the signal; control LOW forces LOW.
items.hint: One and A equals what?

items.q: A clock feeds one input of an OR gate. The other input is held HIGH. What does the output do?
items.right: Right. One or anything is one, so the output is stuck HIGH.
wrong: Copying the clock needs the OR control held LOW, because 0 or A equals A. With the control HIGH, 1 or anything is 1, so the output is stuck HIGH.
LOW is where an AND gate gets stuck when disabled. For OR, a HIGH control forces the output HIGH, because 1 or anything equals 1.
OR has no inversion. With a HIGH control, 1 or anything is 1, so the output stays HIGH. An inverted clock would need a NAND or NOR gate.
items.concept: OR disable: a HIGH control forces the output HIGH; a LOW control passes the signal.
items.hint: What is 1 or anything?

items.q: True or false: in a clock-enable circuit where run equals enable and clock, setting enable to 0 lets the clock pass through.
items.right: Correct, false. Enable at 0 forces the AND output LOW, stopping the clock.
items.wrong: With AND, a 0 on any input controls the gate: 0 and anything is 0. So enable at 0 holds the output LOW and stops the clock. Enable at 1 gives 1 and clock, which equals the clock, so it passes. The statement has it backwards.
items.concept: In run equals enable and clock, enable 1 passes the clock; enable 0 blocks it.
items.hint: What is 0 and anything?

items.q: How does a NAND gate differ from an AND gate?
items.right: Right. NAND is AND followed by an inverter on the output.
wrong: Inverting the inputs of an AND gives a different function, which by DeMorgan equals a NOR. NAND is AND followed by an inverter on the output: the bubble sits on the output.
NAND gates come with two, three, four or eight inputs, just like AND. The difference is the output: NAND is AND with its output inverted.
It is the other way round: the NAND symbol is an AND shape with a bubble added on the output. That bubble means the AND result is inverted.
items.concept: NAND is AND with its output inverted.
items.hint: Where does the bubble go on a NAND symbol?

items.q: A NAND gate's output is always HIGH unless what happens?
items.right: Right. NAND is LOW only when all inputs are HIGH.
wrong: All inputs LOW gives AND 0, which NAND inverts to 1, HIGH. NAND goes LOW only in the one case where AND goes HIGH: every input HIGH.
One HIGH input does not make AND HIGH, so NAND stays HIGH. NAND is LOW only when AND is HIGH, which needs every input HIGH.
Any LOW input makes AND LOW, so NAND is HIGH. The LOW output happens only when all inputs are HIGH.
items.concept: NAND output is LOW only when every input is HIGH.
items.hint: NAND is the opposite of AND. When is AND HIGH?

items.q: A two-input NAND gate has A equals 1 and B equals 0. Is the output HIGH or LOW?
items.right: Right, HIGH. A and B is 0, and NAND inverts it to 1.
items.wrong: Work in two steps. First the AND: 1 and 0 is 0, because not every input is HIGH. Then invert: NAND flips 0 to 1. So the output is HIGH. A NAND gate is LOW only when both of its inputs are 1.
items.concept: NAND: find the AND result, then invert it.
items.hint: AND first, then flip.

items.q: A two-input NOR gate has A equals 0 and B equals 1. Is the output HIGH or LOW?
items.right: Right, LOW. 0 or 1 is 1, and NOR inverts it to 0.
items.wrong: Two steps. First the OR: 0 or 1 is 1, because at least one input is HIGH. Then invert: NOR flips 1 to 0. So the output is LOW. A NOR gate is HIGH only when every one of its inputs is 0.
items.concept: NOR: find the OR result, then invert it.
items.hint: OR first, then flip.

items.q: Which is the Boolean equation for a three-input NOR gate?
options: X equals A or B or C, all complemented
X equals A bar or B bar or C bar
X equals A and B and C, all complemented
X equals A or B or C
items.right: Right. One bar over the whole OR of A, B and C.
wrong: Bars on each variable separately give a different function; by DeMorgan it equals a NAND of A, B and C. NOR places one bar over the entire OR: A or B or C, all complemented.
A bar over the AND is a three-input NAND. NOR is OR followed by inversion: X equals A or B or C, all complemented.
That is a plain three-input OR, with no inversion. NOR adds the inversion over the entire OR result: A or B or C, all complemented.
items.concept: NOR equation: one bar over the whole OR expression.
items.hint: NOR is an OR with its whole output inverted.

items.q: A two-input gate's output is LOW only when both inputs are HIGH. Which gate is it?
items.right: Right, NAND.
items.wrong: Find the special row. Only one combination, both inputs HIGH, gives a different output, and that output is LOW. AND has the same special row but outputs HIGH there. The inverted version, LOW only when all inputs are HIGH, is NAND.
items.concept: NAND: LOW only when all inputs are HIGH.
items.hint: It is the inverted version of the gate that needs all inputs HIGH.

items.q: A gate's output is HIGH only when every input is LOW. Which gate is it?
items.right: Right, NOR.
items.wrong: The special row is all inputs LOW, and there the output is HIGH. OR has the same special row but outputs LOW there, since OR is LOW only when all inputs are LOW. Invert that and you get NOR: HIGH only when every input is LOW.
items.concept: NOR: HIGH only when every input is LOW.
items.hint: It is the inverted version of OR.

items.source: Lecture 05, NAND with one input HIGH
items.q: One input of a NAND gate is held HIGH and a clock drives the other. What does the output do?
items.right: Right. One and clock is the clock, and NAND inverts it.
wrong: Copying the clock would be an AND with one input HIGH. NAND adds an inversion: 1 and clock equals clock, then NAND flips it, so the output is the inverted clock.
NAND is stuck HIGH when one input is LOW, because 0 and anything is 0, inverted to 1. With a HIGH control, the output depends on the clock: it is the clock inverted.
NAND never gets stuck LOW from one input alone; it goes LOW only when all inputs are HIGH. With one input HIGH, the output follows the inverse of the clock.
items.concept: A NAND with one input HIGH inverts the other input.
items.hint: Find 1 and clock, then invert.

items.q: You pulse one input of a 7408 AND gate. Where should the other input be held?
options: HIGH, so the pulses can pass
LOW, so the pulses can pass
items.right: Right. HIGH enables the AND, so the output follows the pulses.
wrong: LOW is the controlling value for AND: 0 and anything is 0, so the output would stay LOW and hide the pulses. Hold the other input HIGH; then the output equals the pulsed input.
Floating makes the result unpredictable, so the test proves nothing. Hold the other input at a solid HIGH so the AND output follows the pulses.
Feeding the output back would create a loop and confuse the test. Hold the other input HIGH, the non-controlling value for AND, so the output follows the pulser.
items.concept: Test a gate input by holding the other inputs at their non-controlling value.
items.hint: Which value on the other input lets an AND pass a signal?

items.q: True or false: when pulsing one input of an OR gate, you should hold the other input HIGH.
items.right: Correct, false. Hold it LOW, since a HIGH would lock the OR output HIGH.
items.wrong: A HIGH is the controlling value for OR: 1 or anything is 1, so the output would stay HIGH and the pulses could never appear. Hold the other input LOW instead. Then 0 or A equals A, and the output should follow the pulses if the gate works.
items.concept: For OR and NOR, hold the other test input LOW; for AND and NAND, hold it HIGH.
items.hint: What is 1 or anything?

items.q: A is HIGH from 1 to 6 microseconds, and B is HIGH from 3 to 8. Which expression is HIGH only from 1 to 3 microseconds?
items.right: Right. From 1 to 3, A is HIGH and B is LOW: A and B bar.
wrong: A and B is HIGH where both are HIGH, from 3 to 6 microseconds. From 1 to 3, B is still LOW, so you need its complement: A and B bar.
A bar and B is HIGH where A is LOW and B is HIGH, which is 6 to 8 microseconds. The window 1 to 3 has A HIGH and B LOW: A and B bar.
A or B is HIGH from 1 all the way to 8. The target window, 1 to 3, is exactly when A is HIGH and B is LOW, so use A and B bar.
items.concept: To make a window, AND the conditions true in it, inverting any signal that must be LOW.
items.hint: In the window, which signal is HIGH and which is LOW?

items.q: True or false: in this chapter, the Johnson shift counter is used as a repeating waveform generator.
items.right: Correct. Its outputs serve as repeating timed waveforms to combine with gates.
items.wrong: Kleitz uses the Johnson counter's outputs as ready-made timed waveforms. You combine them with gates to make pulses and windows at specific times. How the counter works inside comes in a much later chapter; here it is simply a repeating waveform generator. So the statement is true.
items.concept: The Johnson counter supplies repeating waveforms that gates combine into windows.
items.hint: What did the chapter need the counter's outputs for?

items.q: How many gates are needed to build X equals the group A or B, and-ed with C?
items.right: Correct, two: one OR for A or B, and one AND with C.
items.wrong: Count the operations. The group A or B needs one OR gate. Its result is then ANDed with C, needing one AND gate. That is 2 gates. Counting the letters, three, confuses inputs with gates.

slips.why: Three is the number of input variables. Gates count operations: one OR for A or B, then one AND with C, which is 2.

items.concept: Count gates by counting operations, not variables.
items.hint: How many operations appear in the expression?

items.q: A circuit's final output is wired back to one of its own inputs. What kind of logic is it?
items.right: Right. Feedback lets the output depend on history: sequential logic.
wrong: Combinational logic has no feedback: signals only flow from inputs toward the output, so the output depends only on present inputs. Feeding an output back lets the circuit depend on its own history, which makes it sequential.
Sum of products is a form of Boolean expression, not a type of circuit behaviour. A circuit with an output fed back to an input is sequential logic.
Inversion describes a gate's function, not whether the circuit has memory. Any feedback path from output to input makes the circuit sequential rather than combinational.
items.concept: Combinational: no feedback, output depends only on present inputs. Feedback makes it sequential.
items.hint: Can the output now depend on its own past?

items.q: Z equals the group A or C, and-ed with the complement of A and B. What is Z when A, B and C are all 1?
items.right: Right, 0. A and B is 1, so its complement is 0, which forces the final AND to 0.
items.wrong: Use intermediate values. D equals A and B: 1 and 1 is 1. F equals D complemented: 0. E equals A or C: 1. Z equals E and F: 1 and 0 is 0. The complement of A and B is what forces the result to zero; skipping the bar gives 1.
items.concept: Evaluate intermediate nodes in order before the final gate.
items.hint: Start with A and B, then complement it.

items.q: Which law turns B or the group D or E into the group B or D, or E?
items.right: Right. Same order, different grouping: associative.
wrong: Commutative changes the order of terms, such as B or D equals D or B. Here the order B, D, E stays the same; only the grouping moves. Changing grouping is the associative law.
Distributive spreads an AND across an OR, like A and the group B or C becoming A and B, or A and C. This example has only ORs and just regroups them: associative law.
DeMorgan deals with complements over groups. No bars appear here; the terms are simply regrouped, which is the associative law.
items.concept: Associative law: grouping does not matter within an all-AND or all-OR expression.
items.hint: Did the order change, or only the grouping?

items.q: Which law says C and A and B equals B and C and A?
items.right: Right. Only the order changed: commutative.
wrong: Associative is about grouping, where brackets move. Here the variables are rearranged into a different order, which is the commutative law.
Distributive involves an AND spread across an OR, as in A and the group B or C. There is no OR here at all; this is purely a reordering of three ANDed variables, which is the commutative law.
Absorption removes a redundant term, as in A or A and B equals A. Nothing is removed here; the variables are only reordered: commutative.
items.concept: Commutative law: the order of ANDed or ORed variables does not matter.
items.hint: What changed: the order or the grouping?

items.q: The lab needs a four-input AND, but the kit only has two-input ANDs. Which law makes A and B, and-ed with C and D, a valid substitute?
items.right: Right. Associative: regrouping ANDs gives the same result.
wrong: Commutative lets you reorder inputs but says nothing about splitting one gate into pairs. Regrouping A and B and C and D into two pairs joined by a third AND is the associative law.
DeMorgan converts between AND and OR forms with complements. No complements are involved here; you are just regrouping ANDs, which the associative law allows.
Absorption removes redundant terms. Building a four-input AND from three two-input gates relies on the associative law: grouping does not change an all-AND result.
items.concept: The associative law lets a wide AND or OR be built from smaller gates.
items.hint: You are changing the grouping of the ANDs.

items.q: True or false: an AND gate with one input tied to 1 always outputs the level on its other input.
items.right: Correct. A and 1 equals A.
items.wrong: Rule 2 says A and 1 equals A. Check both cases: if A is 0, 0 and 1 is 0; if A is 1, 1 and 1 is 1. The output matches A every time, so the gate simply passes its other input. That is why a HIGH enables an AND gate, and the statement is true.
items.concept: A and 1 equals A: tying an AND input HIGH passes the other input.
items.hint: Try A equals 0, then A equals 1.

items.q: True or false: an OR gate with one input tied to 1 always outputs the level on its other input.
items.right: Correct, false. A or 1 is always 1.
items.wrong: Rule 4 says A or 1 equals 1. Whatever A is, one input is already 1, so the OR output is 1. It does not follow the other input. Tying an OR input to 0 would pass the other input, because A or 0 equals A.
items.concept: A or 1 equals 1; A or 0 equals A.
items.hint: What is 0 or 1?

items.q: What does A or A bar always equal? Say zero, one, or A.
items.right: Right, 1. One of them is always 1.
items.wrong: A and A bar are always opposite, so exactly one of them is 1. OR outputs 1 if any input is 1, so A or A bar is always 1. The AND version, A and A bar, is always 0, since one of the two is always 0.
items.concept: A or A bar equals 1; A and A bar equals 0.
items.hint: A and its complement are always opposite.

items.q: Simplify B or the group B and C.
items.right: Right. Absorption: B or B and C equals B.
wrong: B or C comes from Kleitz's Rule 10, which needs B bar in the second term. Here the second term is B and C, with B uncomplemented. If B is 1 the result is 1; if B is 0 the result is 0. So it simplifies to B.
Test B equals 1, C equals 0: B or B and C gives 1, but B and C gives 0. They differ. By absorption, B or B and C equals B.
It is 1 only when B is 1. With B equal to 0, both terms are 0 and the result is 0. It always equals B, so the answer is B.
items.concept: Absorption: A or A and B equals A.
items.hint: What happens when B is 0? When B is 1?

items.q: Simplify A or the group A bar and B.
items.right: Right. Rule 10: A or A bar and B equals A or B.
wrong: That is absorption, which needs the second term to be A and B. Here it is A bar and B. Check A equals 0, B equals 1: the expression gives 0 or 1, which is 1, but A alone is 0. The correct result is A or B.
Test A equals 1, B equals 0: A or A bar and B gives 1, but B is 0. Rule 10 says A or A bar and B equals A or B.
Test A equals 1, B equals 0: the expression is 1, but A and B is 0. By Rule 10, A or A bar and B equals A or B.
items.concept: A or A bar and B equals A or B, not A.
items.hint: Try A equals 0. What is left?

items.q: True or false: X or the group X bar and Y simplifies to X, just like absorption.
items.right: Correct, false. It equals X or Y.
items.wrong: Check the case X equals 0 and Y equals 1. X bar and Y is 1 and 1, which is 1, so the expression is 1. But X is 0. One disagreeing case disproves it. The correct result is X or Y. Absorption only applies when the second term contains X itself, not its complement.
items.concept: X or X bar and Y equals X or Y; absorption needs X, not X bar.
items.hint: Try X equals 0 and Y equals 1.

items.q: By DeMorgan, the complement of A and B equals what?
items.right: Right. Break the bar, change AND to OR: A bar or B bar.
wrong: That inverts the variables but keeps the operator, the classic mistake. Test A equals 1, B equals 0: the complement of 1 and 0 is 1, but 0 and 1 is 0. DeMorgan says break the bar and change the operator: A bar or B bar.
Removing the bar without inverting anything changes the function. DeMorgan inverts each variable and flips the operator: the complement of A and B is A bar or B bar.
Only B is inverted here, and the operator is unchanged. DeMorgan inverts every variable under the bar and flips AND to OR: A bar or B bar.
items.concept: The complement of A and B equals A bar or B bar.
items.hint: Break the bar, change the operator.

items.q: By DeMorgan, the complement of A or B equals what?
items.right: Right. Break the bar, change OR to AND: A bar and B bar.
wrong: That keeps the OR. Test A equals 1, B equals 0: the complement of 1 or 0 is 0, but 0 or 1 is 1. The operator must flip: A bar and B bar.
The variables must be inverted as the bar breaks. The complement of A or B is A bar and B bar: both inverted, and OR changed to AND.
Only A is inverted and the operator is kept. DeMorgan inverts each variable and changes OR to AND: A bar and B bar.
items.concept: The complement of A or B equals A bar and B bar.
items.hint: Invert each variable and flip the operator.

items.q: True or false: the complement of X and Y equals X bar and Y bar.
items.right: Correct, false. The operator must flip: X bar or Y bar.
items.wrong: Test one case: X equals 1, Y equals 0. The left side is the complement of 1 and 0, which is the complement of 0, so 1. The right side is 0 and 1, which is 0. One disagreeing case disproves it. The correct form flips the operator: X bar or Y bar.
items.concept: DeMorgan always flips the operator; inverting only the variables is wrong.
items.hint: Try X equals 1 and Y equals 0.

items.q: Using DeMorgan, a NOR gate is equivalent to which gate with inverted inputs?
items.right: Right. The complement of A or B equals A bar and B bar: an AND with inverted inputs.
wrong: An OR with inverted inputs gives A bar or B bar, which by DeMorgan equals the complement of A and B, a NAND. NOR is the complement of A or B, which equals A bar and B bar: an AND with inverted inputs.
A NAND with inverted inputs gives the complement of A bar and B bar, which is A or B, a plain OR. NOR equals A bar and B bar: an AND with inverted inputs.
A NOR with inverted inputs gives the complement of A bar or B bar, which is A and B, an AND. NOR itself equals A bar and B bar: an AND gate with inverted inputs.
items.concept: NOR equals AND with inverted inputs; NAND equals OR with inverted inputs.
items.hint: Apply DeMorgan to A or B, all complemented.

items.q: Simplify X equals B and the group A or C, then or C.
items.right: Right: A and B, or C.
wrong: That swaps A and C, which is the answer to a different Kleitz example. Here, distribute B first: A and B, or B and C, or C. Factoring C from the last two gives C and the group B or 1, which is C. So the result is A and B, or C.
The C term does not disappear. After distributing, factor C from B and C, or C, giving C and the group B or 1, which is C. So X equals A and B, or C.
B or 1 is 1, but that 1 is ANDed with C, giving C, not 1. The result is A and B, or C. Ask which operator the 1 inherited: it came out of a product.
items.concept: Distribute, factor out the common variable, then use B or 1 equals 1 and C and 1 equals C.
items.hint: Distribute B, then factor C out of the last two terms.

items.q: True or false: after factoring, C and the group B or 1 simplifies to 1.
items.right: Correct, false. C and 1 equals C.
items.wrong: B or 1 is 1, but that 1 is ANDed with C, because it came out of the product C and the group. C and 1 equals C. The result would be 1 only if the operator were OR, as in C or 1. Always ask which operator the 1 inherited.
items.concept: After factoring, the bracket's 1 is ANDed with the factor: C and 1 equals C.
items.hint: Is the 1 ANDed or ORed with C?

items.q: Which form of Boolean equation is better suited for completing truth tables and timing charts?
items.right: Right. Each product term points to the rows where the output is 1.
wrong: Product of sums ANDs bracketed OR terms, which is awkward to read row by row. Kleitz notes sum of products is better for truth tables and timing charts: each product term marks exactly which input combinations give a 1.
Brackets make you evaluate inner groups first and slow truth-table work. Sum of products, product terms ORed together, is the form best suited to truth tables and timing charts.
items.concept: Sum of products suits truth tables: each product term marks the rows that give 1.
items.hint: Which form has no brackets?

items.q: True or false: A and B, and-ed with the group C or D, is already in sum-of-products form.
items.right: Correct, false. The bracket must be distributed first.
items.wrong: Sum of products allows only product terms ORed together, with no brackets. Here the OR of C and D sits inside a bracket that is ANDed with A and B. Distribute to reach sum of products: A and B and C, or A and B and D.
items.concept: Sum of products: product terms ORed together, with no brackets.
items.hint: Does the expression contain a bracket?

items.source: Lecture 09 §6, the slip caught in class
items.q: After DeMorgan, a term is C and A bar and B bar. A student rewrites it as A bar and C, or B bar and C. Is that valid?
options: No, it is one single product
items.right: Right. It is a single product; splitting it with an OR changes the function.
wrong: Distribution spreads an AND over an OR. Here everything is ANDed; there is no OR to distribute across. Test A equals 0, B equals 1, C equals 1: the original is 0, but the rewrite gives 1. It is one three-variable product.
DeMorgan applies to a bar over a group. No group bar remains here. C and A bar and B bar is already a single product term; splitting it with an OR changes the function.
Even with C equal to 1, the original is A bar and B bar, while the rewrite is A bar or B bar. Those differ when exactly one of A and B is 0. The term is one product and must stay that way.
items.concept: After DeMorgan, check whether a group is ANDed or ORed before distributing.
items.hint: Is there any OR in C and A bar and B bar?

items.q: Resistance is measured in ohms and capacitance in farads. What is the unit of inductance?
items.right: Yes, the henry. Resistance in ohms, capacitance in farads, inductance in henries.
items.wrong: Each element parameter has its own unit. Resistance, R, is in ohms. Capacitance, C, is in farads. Inductance, L, is in henries. Farads and henries are easy to swap: farads go with the capacitor, which stores energy in an electric field, and henries go with the coil, the inductor, which stores energy in a magnetic field. So the unit of inductance is the henry.
items.concept: Resistance in ohms, capacitance in farads, inductance in henries.
items.hint: It is named after the American scientist Joseph Henry.

items.q: True or false: an ideal capacitor holding a steady 5 volts across it carries zero current.
items.right: True. Capacitor current depends on how fast its voltage changes, and a steady voltage has zero rate of change.
items.wrong: The capacitor model says current equals capacitance times the rate of change of the capacitor voltage; current in amps, capacitance in farads, rate of change in volts per second. The trap is thinking a nonzero voltage must push a current. What matters is the change. Five volts that stays at five volts has zero rate of change, so the ideal current is zero. The statement is true.
items.concept: Ideal capacitor current follows the rate of change of its voltage: steady voltage, zero current.
items.hint: Think about the slope of the voltage, not its level.

items.q: A resistor must limit the current to 1.5 milliamps when 24 volts is across it. What resistance is needed? Answer in kilohms.
items.right: Correct, 16 kilohms. 24 volts over 1.5 milliamps, and volts over milliamps gives kilohms.
items.wrong: Use Ohm's law solved for resistance: resistance equals the voltage across the resistor divided by the current through it, resistance in ohms, voltage in volts, current in amps. Here that is 24 volts over 1.5 milliamps. Volts divided by milliamps gives kilohms, so you only need 24 divided by 1.5, which is 16. The resistor must be 16 kilohms.

slips.why: You multiplied voltage by current. Resistance equals voltage divided by current: 24 volts over 1.5 milliamps is 16 kilohms.
You divided current by voltage, which gives a conductance. Resistance is voltage over current: 24 divided by 1.5 is 16, and volts over milliamps is kilohms.

items.concept: Resistance equals voltage over current; volts over milliamps gives kilohms.
items.hint: Divide the voltage by the current.

items.q: On a graph of voltage against current for a resistor, the straight line passes through the origin and through 4 volts at 2 milliamps. What is the resistance? Answer in kilohms.
items.right: Right, 2 kilohms. The slope of a voltage-against-current line is the resistance.
items.wrong: With voltage on the vertical axis and current on the horizontal, the slope is resistance: resistance equals the change in voltage divided by the change in current, ohms from volts over amps. From the origin to the point, voltage rises 4 volts while current rises 2 milliamps. 4 volts over 2 milliamps is 2 kilohms, because volts over milliamps gives kilohms.

slips.why: You took current over voltage, which is the slope with the axes swapped, a conductance. With voltage up the side, slope is voltage over current: 4 volts over 2 milliamps is 2 kilohms.
You multiplied the two coordinates. Slope is rise over run: 4 volts divided by 2 milliamps, which is 2 kilohms.

items.concept: On a voltage-versus-current graph, the slope of a resistor's line is its resistance.
items.hint: Rise over run: change in volts over change in milliamps.

items.q: Two resistor lines are drawn on the same graph, voltage up the side and current along the bottom. Which line belongs to the larger resistance?
items.right: Yes. With voltage on the vertical axis, slope equals resistance, so the steeper line is the larger resistance.
wrong: The flatter line would be the larger resistance only if current were on the vertical axis, because then the slope is current over voltage, a conductance. Here voltage is vertical, so the slope equals change in voltage over change in current, which is resistance in ohms. A larger resistance needs more volts for each amp, so its line climbs faster: the steeper line.

Line length depends only on how far the axes were drawn, not on the resistor. What identifies the resistance is the slope: resistance equals change in voltage divided by change in current. With voltage up the side, a bigger resistance rises more volts per amp, so its line is steeper.

Different resistances cannot share a slope on these axes, because the slope is the resistance itself: change in voltage over change in current. Both lines pass through the origin, but the larger resistance rises more volts for each amp, so it is the steeper one.
items.concept: With voltage on the vertical axis, steeper means more resistance; swap the axes and the rule flips.
items.hint: Slope here is volts per amp.

items.q: In a copper wire, electrons are drifting to the left. Which way does the conventional current point?
options: Across the wire, at right angles
items.right: Right. Electrons are negative, so their leftward drift is a conventional current to the right.
wrong: That is the electron direction, not conventional current. Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would move. Electrons are negative, so electrons moving left carry charge the same way as positive charge moving right. The conventional current arrow therefore points right.

Current along a wire follows the wire. Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move, and negative electrons moving left count as positive charge moving right. So the conventional current points to the right, along the wire.

Electrons are the charge carriers in a metal, so their drift is exactly what makes the current. Because they are negative, the conventional current points opposite to them: electrons drifting left means conventional current to the right.
items.concept: Conventional current follows positive charge; electron drift in a metal runs the other way.
items.hint: Electrons are negative. Flip their direction.

items.q: True or false: in a steady single loop, a resistor uses up some of the current, so less current leaves it than enters.
items.right: Right, false. The same current enters and leaves; the resistor converts energy to heat, not charge.
items.wrong: Charge is conserved. In a steady loop, charge cannot pile up at a resistor, so the rate entering equals the rate leaving. Current is that rate: current equals charge divided by time, amps being coulombs per second. What the resistor removes is energy, turning electrical energy into heat. An ammeter before and after the resistor reads the same, so the statement is false.
items.concept: Resistors convert energy, not current; the same current enters and leaves.
items.hint: Where would the missing charge go?

items.q: A 6 volt source, a 2 kilohm resistor and a switch form one loop. The switch is open. What voltage appears across the open switch? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 6 volts. No current flows, so the resistor drops nothing and the whole source voltage sits across the gap.
items.wrong: The trap is thinking no current means no voltage. With the switch open, the current is zero. Ohm's law gives the resistor voltage: voltage equals current times resistance, volts from amps times ohms, so zero current gives zero volts across the resistor. Around the loop the drops must still add up to the 6 volt source, so the full 6 volts appears across the open switch.

slips.why: Zero is the current, not the voltage. The resistor drops current times resistance, which is zero, so the source's 6 volts must all appear across the open switch.
Splitting the voltage would need current through the resistor. With the switch open the current is zero, the resistor drops nothing, and all 6 volts is across the switch.

items.concept: An open path has zero current but can have the full source voltage across it.
items.hint: What does the resistor drop when no current flows?

items.q: True or false: if no current flows through an element, there can be no voltage across it.
items.right: Right, false. An open switch or a disconnected battery has voltage across it with zero current.
items.wrong: Voltage and current are different quantities. Voltage is energy per charge between two points; current is charge per second through a path. An open circuit forces the current to zero, yet the voltage across the gap can be large, as with a battery sitting on a shelf. Only for a resistor does Ohm's law tie them together: voltage equals current times resistance. So the statement is false.
items.concept: No current does not mean no voltage; an open circuit can hold the full source voltage.
items.hint: Think of a battery with nothing connected.

items.q: A meter measures a known 5.000 volt reference three times and reads 5.199, 5.200 and 5.201 volts. What best describes this meter?
items.right: Yes. The readings agree tightly with each other but all sit about 0.2 volts high.
wrong: The readings agree closely with each other, so they are precise. But accuracy compares them with the reference, and every reading is about 0.2 volts high. A consistent offset like that means precise but not accurate. Displaying many digits does not remove the bias.

Precision is judged by how well the readings agree with each other. A spread of only 2 millivolts is a tight cluster, so the meter is precise. It is the comparison with the 5.000 volt reference that fails: every reading is about 0.2 volts high. So it is precise but not accurate.

That reverses the two ideas. Precision is agreement among repeated readings, and these three agree within 2 millivolts, so they are precise. Accuracy is closeness to the true value, and all three sit about 0.2 volts above the 5.000 volt reference, so they are not accurate. Precise but not accurate points to a systematic offset.
items.concept: Precision is agreement among repeats; accuracy is closeness to the true value.
items.hint: Compare the readings with each other, then with the reference.

items.q: True or false: a meter that displays more digits is automatically more accurate.
items.right: Correct, false. More digits means finer resolution, not closer agreement with the true value.
items.wrong: Displayed digits describe resolution, the smallest change the meter can show. Accuracy is how close the reading is to the true value, and it depends on calibration, range and the meter's specification. A meter can display six digits and still carry the same offset in every reading. More digits help you see small changes, but they do not guarantee accuracy, so the statement is false.
items.concept: Resolution is not accuracy; extra digits do not remove a systematic error.
items.hint: Could a very detailed display still be wrong?

items.q: At a node, two currents enter: 3 amps and 2 amps. Two currents leave: one is 4 amps. What is the other leaving current? Answer in amps.
items.right: Right, 1 amp. 5 amps in must equal 5 amps out.
items.wrong: Kirchhoff's current law: the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving, all in amps. The entering currents add to 3 plus 2, which is 5 amps. The leaving currents must also total 5 amps. One of them is 4 amps, so the other is 5 minus 4, which is 1 amp.

slips.why: You added every current. Kirchhoff's current law balances entering against leaving: 3 plus 2 in equals 4 plus the unknown out, so the unknown is 1 amp.
5 amps is the total entering, not the missing branch. In equals out: 5 amps in, 4 amps already leaving, so the other leaving current is 1 amp.

items.concept: Kirchhoff's current law: current in equals current out at every node.
items.hint: Add what enters, then subtract what already leaves.

items.q: Measured at one node: 5.01 amps entering, 4.01 amps and 1.01 amps leaving. The signed sum is minus 10 milliamps. What is the best interpretation?
options: Ordinary measurement error; check meters and connections
Charge is being lost at the node
Kirchhoff's current law fails in real circuits
items.right: Right. A 10 milliamp leftover among readings of several amps is a measurement question, not a broken law.
wrong: A steady circuit cannot keep piling charge up at a node; that would break the balance of current in and current out. The 10 milliamp leftover comes from the readings, not from the node. Check meter uncertainty and connections rather than inventing stored charge.

Charge is conserved, and Kirchhoff's current law follows from that: total current in equals total current out, in amps. A 10 milliamp residual among readings of several amps is the size of ordinary meter uncertainty, contact effects, or readings taken at slightly different moments. Treat it as a reason to check, not as charge disappearing.

The law holds in real circuits as long as charge is not accumulating at the node. What does not balance perfectly is the set of readings, each with its own uncertainty. Current in equals current out; a small leftover of 10 milliamps points to the meters, the connections, or an unaccounted branch.
items.concept: A small KCL residual in measured data points to measurement limits, not a failure of the law.
items.hint: Is 10 milliamps big or small next to readings of several amps?

items.q: Which law says the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it? Say its name or abbreviation.
items.right: Yes, Kirchhoff's current law, KCL. It follows from conservation of charge.
items.wrong: That is Kirchhoff's current law, abbreviated KCL. Do not confuse it with Kirchhoff's voltage law, which says the directed voltages around a closed loop sum to zero. KCL is about currents at a node: current in equals current out, because charge cannot pile up at a junction in a steady circuit.
items.concept: KCL: at a node, current in equals current out. KVL: around a loop, directed voltages sum to zero.
items.hint: Kirchhoff's, then two words; the second word is current.

items.q: How many significant figures does the measurement 0.00470 amps have? That is zero point zero zero four seven zero. Answer with a plain number.
items.right: Correct, three: four, seven, and the final zero.
items.wrong: Leading zeros only place the decimal point, so the zeros before the four do not count. The four and the seven count. The final zero comes after the decimal point and after a nonzero digit, so somebody deliberately recorded it: it counts too. That gives three significant figures.

slips.why: You dropped the final zero. A trailing zero written after the decimal point records measured precision, so four, seven and that zero give three significant figures.
You counted the leading zeros. They only locate the decimal point. Only four, seven and the final zero count, giving three.

items.concept: Leading zeros never count; a trailing zero after the decimal point does.
items.hint: Start counting at the first nonzero digit.

items.q: A resistance is written as 1400 ohms, with no decimal point. How many significant figures does that show?
items.right: Right. Trailing zeros in a whole number might be measured or might just hold place value.
wrong: Four would be true only if both zeros were known to be measured. In a whole number with no decimal point, trailing zeros may just hold place value, so 1400 is ambiguous. Writing 1.400 kilohms would clearly show four significant figures.

Three is possible, but nothing in the writing says the first zero is measured and the second is not. Whole-number trailing zeros are ambiguous. To state three figures clearly, write 1.40 kilohms, or 1.40 times ten to the three ohms.

Two is one possible reading, but the writing does not say so. Trailing zeros in a whole number might be measured digits or might just hold place value. That is why 1400 on its own is ambiguous. To show three figures, write 1.40 kilohms, or 1.40 times ten to the three ohms.
items.concept: Trailing zeros in a whole number are ambiguous; use engineering notation to show the intended figures.
items.hint: Are those final zeros measured, or just placeholders?

items.q: Convert 0.08 milliseconds to microseconds. Answer in microseconds.
items.right: Right, 80 microseconds. One millisecond is 1000 microseconds.
items.wrong: One millisecond equals 1000 microseconds, because milli is ten to the minus three and micro is ten to the minus six, three powers of ten apart. Converting to the smaller unit makes the number bigger: 0.08 times 1000 is 80. So 0.08 milliseconds is 80 microseconds.

slips.why: You moved the decimal the wrong way. Microseconds are smaller units, so there are more of them: 0.08 milliseconds times 1000 is 80 microseconds.
You moved the decimal two places instead of three. Milli to micro is a factor of 1000: 0.08 times 1000 is 80 microseconds.

items.concept: Going to a smaller unit makes the number larger; milli to micro is times 1000.
items.hint: How many microseconds are in one millisecond?

items.q: A student writes 2 capital M ohms when he meant 2 milli-ohms. By what factor is his written value too large?
items.right: Yes. Mega is ten to the six and milli is ten to the minus three, a gap of ten to the nine.
wrong: A million is the gap between mega and plain ohms. Capital M, mega, is ten to the six; lowercase m, milli, is ten to the minus three. The ratio is ten to the six divided by ten to the minus three. Dividing powers of ten subtracts exponents: 6 minus minus 3 is 9. So the error is ten to the nine, a billion.

A thousand is a single prefix step, such as kilo to plain units. Mega is two steps above plain units and milli is one step below, and each step is a factor of 1000. Dividing, subtract exponents: 6 minus minus 3 is 9, so the error is ten to the nine, a billion.

Prefix letters are case-sensitive. Capital M is mega, ten to the six; lowercase m is milli, ten to the minus three. Mixing them up changes the value by ten to the six over ten to the minus three, which is ten to the nine, a factor of a billion.
items.concept: Capital M is mega, ten to the six; lowercase m is milli, ten to the minus three. They differ by a billion.
items.hint: Divide ten to the six by ten to the minus three.

items.q: Which SI prefix means ten to the minus nine?
items.right: Yes, nano. One nanosecond is ten to the minus nine seconds.
items.wrong: Walk down the prefix ladder in steps of three: milli is ten to the minus three, micro is ten to the minus six, nano is ten to the minus nine, and pico is ten to the minus twelve. So ten to the minus nine is nano, written with a lowercase n.
items.concept: Milli, micro, nano, pico: ten to the minus three, six, nine, twelve.
items.hint: It comes between micro and pico.

items.q: Multiply eight times ten to the minus three by four times ten to the five. Which is the result in engineering notation?
items.right: Correct. 8 times 4 is 32, minus 3 plus 5 is 2, and 32 times ten to the two is 3.2 times ten to the three.
wrong: When multiplying powers of ten you add the exponents, you do not multiply them, and the minus sign matters: minus 3 plus 5 is 2. With coefficients 8 times 4 giving 32, the product is 32 times ten to the two, or 3200, which is 3.2 times ten to the three in engineering notation.

The value is right but the form is not. Engineering notation needs an exponent that is a multiple of three. Multiply the coefficients, 8 times 4 is 32, and add the exponents, minus 3 plus 5 is 2, giving 32 times ten to the two, which is 3200. Rewritten with exponent three, that is 3.2 times ten to the three.

Multiply coefficients and add exponents: 8 times 4 is 32, and minus 3 plus 5 is 2, so 32 times ten to the two, which equals 3200. But 3.2 times ten to the two is only 320; the decimal moved without adjusting the exponent. In engineering form, 3200 is 3.2 times ten to the three.
items.concept: Multiply coefficients, add exponents, then shift to an exponent that is a multiple of three.
items.hint: 8 times 4, and minus 3 plus 5.

items.q: A neutral atom loses three electrons. What is its net charge?
options: It gains three protons' worth of mass
items.right: Right. Three protons are now unpaired, so the atom is a positive ion.
wrong: Losing electrons removes negative charge. The atom started neutral, with protons balancing electrons. Take away three negative charges and three protons are left unbalanced, so the net charge is positive: plus three elementary charges.

The protons are indeed unchanged, and that is exactly why the atom is no longer neutral. Neutral means protons equal electrons. With three electrons gone there are three more protons than electrons, so the net charge is plus three elementary charges.

Charge and mass are different properties. Losing three electrons changes the charge balance: three protons are now unpaired, so the net charge is plus three elementary charges. The mass barely changes, because electrons are very light.
items.concept: Losing electrons leaves a positive ion; the net charge equals the unpaired protons.
items.hint: Electrons are negative. What is left when you remove negatives?

items.q: Copper's 29 electrons sit in shells of 2, 8, 18, and one more. Why does that make copper a good conductor?
options: Its protons move along the wire
Its lone outer electron is loosely held
Its full inner shells carry current
items.right: Yes. That single, loosely held outer electron becomes a free carrier.
wrong: Protons sit in the nucleus, locked into the metal's lattice; they do not travel along a wire. Conduction in copper comes from its single loosely bound outer electron, which is easily freed and drifts when a field is applied.

Filled inner shells hold their electrons tightly, so those electrons do not drift through the metal. The useful feature is the lone electron in the outermost shell. It is loosely bound, easily freed, and becomes a mobile conduction electron. That is why copper conducts well.

Copper's outer shell is not empty; it holds exactly one electron, in a 2, 8, 18, 1 arrangement. That single, loosely held outer electron is easily freed to move through the metal, which is what makes copper a good conductor.
items.concept: Copper conducts well because its lone outer electron is loosely bound and becomes a free carrier.
items.hint: Think about the last number in 2, 8, 18, 1.

items.q: Two charges are moved apart from a separation r to twice that separation. What happens to the force between them?
items.right: Yes, one quarter. Force depends on one over distance squared, so twice the distance gives one over four.
wrong: Distance matters strongly. By Coulomb's law, force equals a constant times the product of the charges, divided by the distance squared. The charges are unchanged, but the distance squared is four times bigger, so the force becomes one quarter.

Halving would be true if force fell in simple proportion to distance. Coulomb's law says force equals a constant times the product of the charges, divided by the distance squared; force in newtons, charges in coulombs, distance in metres. Because distance is squared, doubling it makes the denominator four times bigger, so the force drops to one quarter.

Moving charges apart weakens the force; it never strengthens it. Coulomb's law puts distance squared in the denominator: force equals a constant times charge one times charge two, over distance squared. Twice the distance gives four times the denominator, so one quarter of the force.
items.concept: Coulomb force falls with distance squared: twice the distance, one quarter the force.
items.hint: The distance in Coulomb's law is squared.

items.q: An electric field points to the right. Which way is the force on an electron placed in it?
options: There is no force on it
items.right: Right. An electron is negative, so it is pushed opposite to the field.
wrong: The field direction is defined by the force on a positive test charge. The force on any charge equals its charge times the field: force in newtons, charge in coulombs, field in newtons per coulomb. An electron's charge is negative, so the product points opposite to the field: to the left.

Any charge in an electric field feels a force: force equals charge times field. An electron has negative charge, so it certainly feels a force; the negative sign only reverses the direction. With the field to the right, the electron is pushed to the left.

The force from an electric field lies along the field line, not across it. Force equals charge times field, so it is along the field for a positive charge and opposite for a negative one. The electron is negative, so it is pushed to the left.
items.concept: Field direction is the push on a positive charge; negative charges are pushed the opposite way.
items.hint: Force equals charge times field, and an electron's charge is negative.

items.q: 600 coulombs of charge pass through a wire in 4 minutes. What is the current? Answer in amps.
items.right: Correct, 2.5 amps. 4 minutes is 240 seconds, and 600 over 240 is 2.5.
items.wrong: Current equals charge divided by time, current in amps, charge in coulombs, time in seconds. The time must be in seconds: 4 minutes is 240 seconds. Then 600 coulombs divided by 240 seconds is 2.5 coulombs per second, which is 2.5 amps.

slips.why: You divided by 4 without converting minutes to seconds. Current is coulombs per second: 600 coulombs over 240 seconds is 2.5 amps.
You multiplied charge by time. Current is charge divided by time: 600 coulombs over 240 seconds is 2.5 amps.

items.concept: Current equals charge over time, with time in seconds.
items.hint: Change 4 minutes into seconds first.

items.q: A steady current of 2 milliamps flows in a conductor. How long does it take for 6 millicoulombs of charge to pass? Answer in seconds.
items.right: Right, 3 seconds. The milli prefixes cancel.
items.wrong: Rearrange the definition of current: time equals charge divided by current, time in seconds, charge in coulombs, current in amps. Here that is 6 millicoulombs over 2 milliamps. Both carry the milli prefix, so the prefixes cancel and you divide 6 by 2, giving 3 seconds.

slips.why: You multiplied charge by current. Time equals charge divided by current: 6 millicoulombs over 2 milliamps is 3 seconds.
You divided current by charge. Time equals charge over current: 6 divided by 2 is 3 seconds.

items.concept: Time equals charge divided by current; matching prefixes cancel.
items.hint: Charge over current.

items.q: A source transfers 24 joules of energy for every 2 coulombs of charge it moves. What is its voltage?
items.right: Correct, 12 volts, meaning 12 joules per coulomb.
wrong: 48 comes from multiplying. Voltage is energy per charge: voltage equals energy divided by charge, voltage in volts, energy in joules, charge in coulombs. So 24 joules over 2 coulombs is 12 joules per coulomb, which is 12 volts.
Adding energy and charge mixes two different quantities. Voltage equals energy divided by charge, volts being joules per coulomb. 24 joules divided by 2 coulombs is 12 volts.
That is charge divided by energy, upside down. Voltage is joules per coulomb: voltage equals energy over charge, 24 joules over 2 coulombs, which is 12 volts.
items.concept: Voltage equals energy over charge; one volt is one joule per coulomb.
items.hint: Joules per coulomb.

items.q: A uniform 2 kilohm resistor has 6 volts across it, and its lower end is the zero volt reference. Nothing is connected at its midpoint. What is the voltage at the midpoint?
items.right: Right, 3 volts. Each equal half drops half the total.
wrong: 6 volts is the top end. Treat the uniform resistor as two equal 1 kilohm halves in series. The current is voltage over total resistance, 6 volts over 2 kilohms, 3 milliamps. The lower half drops current times resistance, 3 milliamps times 1 kilohm, 3 volts. So the midpoint is at 3 volts.

Each half is 1 kilohm carrying the same 3 milliamps, found from current equals 6 volts over 2 kilohms. Each half drops current times resistance, 3 milliamps times 1 kilohm, which is 3 volts, not 1.5. The midpoint sits at 3 volts.

Zero volts is the bottom end, the reference. With steady current, voltage falls evenly along a uniform resistor. The lower half drops 3 milliamps times 1 kilohm, 3 volts, so the midpoint is 3 volts above the bottom.
items.concept: Along a uniform resistor with steady current, voltage falls evenly, so the midpoint is at half.
items.hint: Split it into two equal halves.

items.q: To measure the current through one resistor, how must the ammeter be connected?
options: Open the path and insert it in series
From one resistor lead to the reference
items.right: Right. The current has to flow through the ammeter, so it goes in series.
wrong: Across the resistor is how a voltmeter connects, because voltage is a difference between two points. Current flows through a path, so the meter must carry that current: open the path and insert the ammeter in series. An ammeter's low resistance placed across the resistor would bypass it instead.

An ammeter has very low resistance, ideally zero. Across the supply it becomes a near short circuit, drawing a large current that can damage the meter or the supply. To read current, open the path and insert the ammeter in series, so the circuit's own current flows through it.

Connecting from a resistor lead to the reference gives the meter a parallel path, and its low resistance could short out part of the circuit. Current must pass through the ammeter, so open the path at the resistor and insert the meter in series.
items.concept: Ammeter in series, through the path; voltmeter in parallel, across the element.
items.hint: The current has to flow through the meter.

items.q: True or false: an ideal voltmeter has infinite input resistance, so it draws no current from the circuit.
items.right: True. Drawing no current means it measures without disturbing the circuit.
items.wrong: A voltmeter sits across two points, adding a new parallel path. Ohm's law gives the current it draws: current equals voltage divided by the meter's resistance. For that current to be zero, the resistance must be infinite, and that is the ideal voltmeter. Real voltmeters have a very large but finite resistance, typically around 10 to 20 megohms for a digital meter. So the statement is true.
items.concept: Ideal voltmeter: infinite resistance, zero current. Ideal ammeter: zero resistance, zero voltage drop.
items.hint: What resistance would draw zero current?

items.q: A resistor's first three bands are brown, black, orange. What is its nominal value? Answer in kilohms.
items.right: Right, 10 kilohms: digits one and zero, times a thousand.
items.wrong: Read it as two digits and a multiplier: nominal resistance equals the two-digit number times ten to the multiplier power, in ohms. Brown is 1 and black is 0, giving 10. Orange as a multiplier means ten to the three, a thousand. So 10 times 1000 is 10,000 ohms, which is 10 kilohms.

slips.why: Brown, black, red would be 1 kilohm. Orange is the multiplier ten to the three: 10 times 1000 ohms is 10 kilohms.
Yellow would give 100 kilohms. Orange means times a thousand: 10 times 1000 ohms is 10 kilohms.

items.concept: Two digit bands, then a multiplier band that sets the power of ten.
items.hint: Brown is one, black is zero, orange means three zeros.

items.q: A resistor is marked yellow, violet, brown, silver. What is its nominal resistance?
items.right: Correct, 470 ohms, with a tolerance of plus or minus 10 percent.
wrong: 47 forgets the multiplier band. Nominal resistance equals the two-digit number times ten to the multiplier power. Yellow is 4 and violet 7, giving 47, and brown in the third position means times ten. So 47 times 10 is 470 ohms.
4.7 kilohms, 4700 ohms, would need a red multiplier, times a hundred. Brown in the multiplier position means times ten. Nominal resistance equals 47 times 10, which is 470 ohms.

That is far too large. Nominal resistance equals the two digits times the multiplier: yellow 4, violet 7, and a brown multiplier, times ten. 47 times 10 is 470 ohms. The silver band is the tolerance, not part of the value.
items.concept: Yellow 4, violet 7, brown multiplier times 10: 470 ohms.
items.hint: Two digits, then the brown band adds one zero.

items.q: A 10 kilohm resistor has a gold tolerance band. Which measured value lies outside its tolerance?
items.right: Yes. Gold is 5 percent, so the limits are 9.5 and 10.5 kilohms, and 10.6 is above the top.
wrong: 9.6 kilohms is inside, just above the lower limit. Gold means plus or minus 5 percent. The spread is 0.05 times 10 kilohms, which is 0.5 kilohms, so the band runs from 9.5 to 10.5 kilohms. Only 10.6 kilohms falls outside.

9.9 kilohms is close to nominal and well inside. The spread is tolerance times nominal, 5 percent of 10 kilohms, which is 0.5 kilohms, so anything from 9.5 to 10.5 kilohms passes. 10.6 kilohms is the one outside.

10.4 kilohms is inside. The allowed spread equals tolerance times nominal: 5 percent of 10 kilohms is 0.5 kilohms. So the limits are 10 minus 0.5, which is 9.5, and 10 plus 0.5, which is 10.5 kilohms. Only 10.6 kilohms is outside.
items.concept: Tolerance limits are nominal plus and minus tolerance times nominal.
items.hint: Gold is 5 percent. What is 5 percent of 10 kilohms?

items.q: A resistor marked 100 kilohms measures 98 kilohms. What is its percent deviation from nominal? Answer in percent.
items.right: Right, 2 percent, and it reads low.
