Internal resistance is not a real quantity
items.right: Right. An ohmmeter assumes an unpowered part; the live source breaks that assumption.
wrong: Internal resistance is usually small, often a fraction of an ohm. The real problem is the method. An ohmmeter pushes its own small test current and computes resistance as voltage over current. A live battery adds its own voltage, so the result is meaningless. Use the open-circuit and loaded readings instead.

Ohmmeters read low values too. The issue is that they supply their own test current and apply Ohm's law, resistance equals voltage over current. A live source's own voltage overwhelms that small test signal, so the reading means nothing. Infer the internal resistance from two terminal readings.

Internal resistance is real; it is why a battery's terminal voltage sags under load. It just cannot be measured directly, because the node inside is unreachable and an ohmmeter's test signal is swamped by the source voltage. Compare open-circuit and loaded readings.
items.concept: Measure internal resistance indirectly: open-circuit reading, loaded reading, then lost voltage over current.
items.hint: What does an ohmmeter assume about the part it measures?

items.q: In a written unit, what is the difference between lowercase k and uppercase K?
options: k is kilograms; K is kilo
k is kilo; K is kelvin
k is kelvin; K is kilo
items.right: Right. Lowercase k multiplies by 1000; uppercase K is the kelvin, a temperature unit.
wrong: SI symbols are case-sensitive. Lowercase k is kilo, a multiplier of 1000; uppercase K is kelvin, a temperature. Written carelessly, 20 kilograms could read as kelvin-grams, which is meaningless.
Lowercase k is only a prefix; on its own it is not a unit. It multiplies whatever unit follows by 1000, so kilograms is k plus g. Uppercase K is kelvin, a temperature unit.
That is backwards. Lowercase k is the prefix kilo, times 1000, as in kilohms. Uppercase K is the kelvin, the SI unit of temperature. So 20 kilohms, written with a lowercase k, is 20,000 ohms.
items.concept: Lowercase k: kilo, times 1000. Uppercase K: kelvin, temperature.
items.hint: One is a multiplier, the other a temperature.

items.q: Kilohms multiplied by milliamps gives which unit?
items.right: Right, volts. Kilo times milli is one.
items.wrong: Ohm's law: voltage equals current times resistance, volts from amps times ohms. Kilo is ten to the three and milli is ten to the minus three, so kilohms times milliamps multiplies by ten to the three times ten to the minus three, which is one. The prefixes cancel and you are left with plain volts. For example, 3 milliamps times 4 kilohms is 12 volts.
items.concept: Kilo times milli equals one, so kilohms times milliamps gives volts.
items.hint: Ten to the three times ten to the minus three.

items.q: Which statement defines two elements being in parallel?
options: They are the same distance apart everywhere
Both their ends share the same two nodes
They are drawn side by side
items.right: Right. Parallel is a statement about nodes, never about the picture.
wrong: Sharing a current is the series property, elements in series. Parallel elements share a voltage, because they connect across the same two nodes, and they generally carry different currents, each equal to that voltage over its own resistance.
Equal spacing is the geometry meaning of parallel, and it is the wrong one here. Electrically, parallel means both ends of each element connect to the same pair of nodes.

Side by side is a drawing position, not an electrical fact. Components placed side by side can be wired end to end, in series. Parallel means both ends of one element connect to the same pair of nodes as both ends of the other, which is why they share one voltage.
items.concept: Parallel: both ends on the same two nodes, so the same voltage.
items.hint: Think about nodes, not the drawing.

items.q: True or false: three resistors drawn side by side, evenly spaced, must be in parallel.
items.right: Right, false. The same drawing positions can be wired in series or in parallel.
items.wrong: Parallel is decided by connections: both ends of each element must land on the same two nodes. Three resistors in identical positions can be wired end to end, making one path in series, or across one pair of nodes, in parallel. Trace the nodes before deciding. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Series and parallel are electrical, never visual; trace the nodes.
items.hint: Could the same layout be wired end to end?

items.q: 10 volts is across a 1 kilohm resistor and a 2 kilohm resistor connected in parallel. What total current does the source supply? Answer in milliamps.
items.right: Correct, 15 milliamps: 10 through the 1 kilohm branch and 5 through the 2 kilohm branch.
items.wrong: Both branches see the full 10 volts, by elements in parallel. Ohm's law for each: current equals voltage over resistance, milliamps from volts over kilohms. 10 over 1 is 10 milliamps; 10 over 2 is 5 milliamps. The branch currents add to the total, 10 plus 5, which is 15 milliamps.

slips.why: You added the resistors as if in series. In parallel each branch has 10 volts: 10 plus 5 milliamps is 15 milliamps.
10 milliamps is only the 1 kilohm branch. Add the 2 kilohm branch's 5 milliamps: 15 milliamps.

items.concept: Parallel branch currents each equal V over R, and they add to the total.
items.hint: Find each branch current, then add.

items.q: In a parallel circuit, one branch's resistance is doubled while the voltage stays the same. What happens to that branch's current?
items.right: Right. Branch current equals voltage over resistance, so twice the resistance gives half the current.
wrong: Doubling resistance halves the current; it does not eliminate it. Branch current equals the shared voltage over that branch's resistance, in amps from volts over ohms. Current takes every path; a harder path carries less, not none.
Current and resistance are inversely related here. Branch current equals voltage divided by resistance, so with the voltage fixed, a resistance twice as large gives a current half as large.
The branch voltage is fixed, but its current depends on its resistance. Ohm's law gives branch current equals voltage over resistance, so doubling the resistance halves the current.
items.concept: Branch current is inversely proportional to branch resistance.
items.hint: Current equals voltage over resistance, with the voltage fixed.

items.q: A 3 ohm and a 6 ohm resistor are connected in parallel. What is their total resistance? Answer in ohms.
items.right: Correct, 2 ohms: 18 over 9, and less than the smaller resistor.
items.wrong: For two resistors, total resistance equals the product over the sum: R one times R two, over R one plus R two, in ohms. 3 times 6 is 18, and 3 plus 6 is 9, so 18 over 9 is 2 ohms. Check: 2 ohms is less than 3 ohms, the smallest resistor, as every parallel total must be.

slips.why: You added them as if in series. In parallel, use product over sum: 18 over 9 is 2 ohms.
0.5 is one over R total, in siemens. Flip it: one over 0.5 is 2 ohms.

items.concept: Two resistors in parallel: product over sum, and the result is below the smaller one.
items.hint: Multiply them, then divide by their sum.

items.q: Three 12 ohm resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
items.right: Right. Equal resistors in parallel: one value divided by how many, 12 over 3.
wrong: 36 ohms is the series total, 12 plus 12 plus 12. In parallel the total must be less than the smallest resistor. For equal resistors, total resistance equals one resistor's value divided by the number of them: 12 over 3, which is 4 ohms.

The parallel total can never equal one of the resistors; it must be smaller than the smallest. Each extra branch adds another path. For equal resistors, total equals R over N, the value over the count: 12 over 3 is 4 ohms.
6 ohms is what two 12 ohm resistors give. With three, the total is one value over the count: total resistance equals R over N, 12 over 3, which is 4 ohms.
items.concept: N equal resistors in parallel give R divided by N.
items.hint: Divide one value by how many there are.

items.q: A student adds one over 1 kilohm plus one over 2 kilohms, gets 1.5, and reports the total as 1.5 kilohms. What went wrong?
options: He did not take the reciprocal of the sum
He should have simply added 1 and 2 kilohms
He forgot to convert kilohms to ohms
items.right: Right. The sum is one over R total, so flip it: one over 1.5 millisiemens is about 667 ohms.
wrong: Adding the resistances directly is the series rule, and it would give 3 kilohms. For parallel, one over R total equals the sum of the reciprocals. The student's sum, 1.5, is one over R total, in millisiemens. Flip it once: R total is one over 1.5 millisiemens, about 667 ohms.

The kilohm units are consistent; that is not the problem. The reciprocal formula gives one over R total, not R total. The sum of 1 plus 0.5 is 1.5 per kilohm, so R total is one over 1.5 kilohms, about 667 ohms.
1.5 kilohms fails the parallel check at once: a parallel total must be less than the smallest resistor, 1 kilohm. The sum of reciprocals is one over R total, so it must be flipped: about 667 ohms.
items.concept: Sum the reciprocals, then flip once more: the formula gives one over R total.
items.hint: Is 1.5 kilohms smaller than 1 kilohm?

items.q: True or false: a meter across a genuine 1 kilohm and 2 kilohm parallel pair could correctly read 1.5 kilohms.
items.right: Right, false. A parallel total must be below the smallest resistor, 1 kilohm.
items.wrong: The bound catches this at once: a parallel combination is less than its smallest resistor. Product over sum gives 2 over 3 kilohms, about 667 ohms. A 1.5 kilohm reading means a wiring fault, perhaps the resistors are in series or something else is connected, or a meter problem. Find it before calculating further. The statement is false.
items.concept: Parallel total is always less than the smallest resistor; use that to catch errors.
items.hint: Compare 1.5 kilohms with the smaller resistor.

items.q: What is the conductance of a 2 kilohm resistor? Answer in millisiemens.
items.right: Right, 0.5 millisiemens. One over a kilohm is a millisiemens.
items.wrong: Conductance equals one over resistance: siemens from one over ohms. One over 2 kilohms: the reciprocal of kilo is milli, so this is one half of a millisiemens, 0.5 millisiemens. In plain units, one over 2000 ohms is 0.0005 siemens.

slips.why: 2 is the resistance in kilohms. Conductance is its reciprocal: one over 2 kilohms is 0.5 millisiemens.
500 is the value in microsiemens. Asked in millisiemens, one over 2 kilohms is 0.5 millisiemens, because kilo becomes milli.

items.concept: Conductance is one over resistance; one over kilohms gives millisiemens.
items.hint: One over 2, then kilo becomes milli.

items.q: What is the unit of conductance?
items.right: Yes, the siemens: one siemens is one over an ohm.
items.wrong: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, G equals one over R, and its unit is the siemens, symbol capital S. One siemens equals one per ohm. The name belongs to a person, so the unit keeps its final s in both singular and plural: one siemens, ten siemens.
items.concept: Conductance, G, is one over R, measured in siemens.
items.hint: Named after the German engineer Werner von Siemens.

items.q: True or false: for resistors in parallel, the total conductance is the sum of the individual conductances.
items.right: True. Conductances add in parallel, just as resistances add in series.
items.wrong: Each parallel branch carries current equal to the shared voltage times its conductance. Adding the branch currents gives total current equals voltage times the sum of the conductances, so total conductance is the sum: G total equals G one plus G two, in siemens. For example, a 3 ohm and a 6 ohm resistor give one third plus one sixth, one half siemens, which is 2 ohms. The statement is true.
items.concept: Resistances add in series; conductances add in parallel.
items.hint: Think of each branch as another path for current.

items.q: A motor draws 100 watts of electrical input and delivers 80 watts of mechanical output. What is its efficiency? Answer in percent.
items.right: Correct, 80 percent. The other 20 watts is lost, mostly as heat.
items.wrong: Efficiency equals useful output power over input power, times 100 for percent. The output is 80 watts and the input 100 watts, so 80 over 100 is 0.80, which is 80 percent. The 20 watt difference is the loss.

slips.why: 20 is the power lost, in watts. Efficiency is output over input: 80 over 100 is 80 percent.
You divided input by output. Efficiency is output over input, which can never exceed 100 percent: 80 percent.

items.concept: Efficiency is output over input; the difference is loss.
items.hint: Output divided by input.

items.q: An 80 percent efficient stage feeds a 90 percent efficient stage. What is the overall efficiency?
items.right: Right. Cascaded efficiencies multiply as decimals: 0.8 times 0.9 is 0.72.
wrong: Subtracting the percentages has no meaning here. For cascaded stages, total efficiency equals efficiency one times efficiency two, as decimals. 0.8 times 0.9 is 0.72, which is 72 percent.

Averaging the two gives 85 percent, but cascaded losses compound. Total efficiency equals the first efficiency times the second, as decimals. 0.8 times 0.9 is 0.72, so 72 percent. With 100 watts in, 80 watts leave the first stage and 72 watts leave the second.

Adding them gives more than 100 percent, which is impossible. For stages in cascade, total efficiency equals the product of the stage efficiencies as decimals: 0.8 times 0.9, which is 0.72, or 72 percent.
items.concept: Cascaded efficiencies multiply as decimals.
items.hint: Multiply 0.8 by 0.9.

items.q: What condition does a ground fault circuit interrupter respond to?
options: Outgoing and returning current not matching
Current rising above the breaker rating
Too much power used over a month
items.right: Right. It trips when some current returns by another path.
wrong: Excess current is what fuses and ordinary breakers respond to. A ground fault circuit interrupter watches for a different condition: the current going out on one conductor not matching the current returning on the other. That imbalance means current is leaking by another path, possibly through a person.

Voltage level is not what it senses. A ground fault circuit interrupter compares outgoing and returning current. If they differ, some current is taking another path to ground, and it disconnects the circuit.

Energy use over time is what the utility meter records. A ground fault circuit interrupter responds within moments to an imbalance between outgoing and returning current, which signals leakage by another path.
items.concept: Fuses and breakers: overcurrent. GFCI: outgoing and returning current imbalance.
items.hint: What does it compare?

items.q: An NTC thermistor warms up. What happens to its resistance?
items.right: Right. NTC means negative temperature coefficient: hotter, lower resistance.
wrong: A rising resistance with temperature is a positive temperature coefficient, like copper or a PTC thermistor. NTC stands for negative temperature coefficient, so its resistance falls as its temperature rises. That strong, deliberate change is what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.
A thermistor is built to change with temperature; that is its whole purpose. NTC means negative temperature coefficient: as it warms, its resistance falls, often steeply and not in a straight line.

Its resistance falls, but not to zero. An NTC thermistor has a negative temperature coefficient, so warming lowers its resistance smoothly over its range. Zero resistance would describe a superconductor, a different thing entirely.
items.concept: NTC thermistor: resistance falls as temperature rises.
items.hint: N stands for negative.

items.q: A surface-mount resistor is marked 4, 7, 2. What is its resistance?
items.right: Right. 47 followed by two zeros: 4700 ohms, 4.7 kilohms.
wrong: The three digits are not the value itself. The first two digits are significant, 47, and the third is the power of ten, here two zeros. So resistance equals 47 times ten to the two, 4700 ohms, which is 4.7 kilohms.
47 ohms would be marked 470: 47 times ten to the zero. With a final digit of 2, the resistance is 47 times ten to the two, 4700 ohms, which is 4.7 kilohms.
47 kilohms would be marked 473, three zeros. The final 2 means two zeros: 47 times ten to the two is 4700 ohms, or 4.7 kilohms.
items.concept: Three-digit code: two significant digits, then the number of zeros.
items.hint: The last digit says how many zeros to add.

items.q: True or false: the square root of 49 equals plus or minus 7.
items.right: Right, false. The radical symbol names the principal root only, so the square root of 49 is 7.
items.wrong: The plus or minus belongs to solving an equation, not to the radical symbol. The square root sign always names the principal root, the non-negative one, so the square root of 49 is 7 and nothing else. If instead you are solving x squared equals 49, you are asking for every number whose square is 49, and then both 7 and negative 7 qualify. Keep the two tasks apart: evaluate a root, one value; solve a squared equation, two values.
items.concept: The radical symbol gives one non-negative value; a squared equation can have two solutions.
items.hint: Is this evaluating a root, or solving an equation?

items.q: Solve x squared equals 49 over the real numbers. What is the complete solution?
options: x equals 7 or x equals negative 7
items.right: Correct. Both 7 and negative 7 square to 49, so an equation needs both.
wrong: You treated the equation like the radical symbol. The square root of 49 is indeed 7, but the equation x squared equals 49 asks for every number whose square is 49. Negative 7 times negative 7 is also 49, so the solution set has two members: 7 and negative 7.

You kept only the negative branch, perhaps thinking the positive root belongs to the radical alone. The equation asks for every number whose square is 49, and both 7 and negative 7 satisfy it. Write x equals plus or minus 7 when solving; write just 7 when evaluating the square root of 49.

There is a real solution because 49 is positive: real numbers square to non-negative results, and 49 is reachable. It would be an even root of a negative number that has no real value, for instance the square root of negative 49. Here x equals 7 or negative 7.
items.concept: Solving x squared equals a positive number gives two real solutions, plus and minus the root.
items.hint: How many numbers square to 49?

items.q: What is the cube root of negative 8?
items.right: Correct, negative 2, because negative 2 cubed is negative 8. Odd roots keep the sign.
wrong: Positive 2 cubed is positive 8, not negative 8. An odd root keeps the sign of its radicand, because an odd number of negative factors leaves one negative behind. Negative 2 times negative 2 is 4, times negative 2 again is negative 8. So the cube root of negative 8 is negative 2.

You applied the even-root rule to an odd root. It is even roots, square roots and fourth roots, that have no real value for a negative radicand, because an even number of negative factors always multiplies to a positive. A cube is odd: negative 2 cubed is negative 8, so the cube root of negative 8 is negative 2.

The plus or minus habit comes from solving x squared equals something, where two numbers share a square. A cube root is different: only one real number cubes to negative 8, and that is negative 2, since positive 2 cubes to positive 8. An odd root has exactly one real value.
items.concept: Odd roots keep the sign of the radicand; even roots of negatives have no real value.
items.hint: Which number, multiplied by itself three times, gives negative 8?

items.q: What is the square root of the quantity 36 plus 64? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, 10. Add first inside the root: 36 plus 64 is 100, and the root of 100 is 10.
items.wrong: The radical bar groups everything underneath it, so the addition happens first. Thirty-six plus 64 is 100, and the square root of 100 is 10. If you split the root over the plus sign you would get root 36 plus root 64, which is 6 plus 8, or 14, and 14 squared is 196, not 100. The product rule lets you split a root over multiplication, never over addition or subtraction.

slips.why: You took the root of each term separately: 6 plus 8. A root does not distribute over addition. Add first, 36 plus 64 is 100, then take the root, which is 10. Check: 14 squared is 196, not 100.

items.concept: A radical does not split over addition; add inside first, then take the root.
items.hint: Do the addition under the radical before anything else.

items.q: Simplify the square root of 72.
items.right: Correct. Seventy-two is 36 times 2, and root 36 is 6, so root 72 is 6 root 2.
wrong: That is a correct step but not fully simplified: 72 is 4 times 18, giving 2 root 18, but 18 still contains the square factor 9. Continue: root 18 is 3 root 2, so 2 root 18 becomes 6 root 2. Any square factor left inside means you are not done.

Seventy-two is 8 times 9, but 8 is not a perfect square, so pulling it out as a coefficient is not allowed. Only the root of a perfect square comes outside. Take root 9, which is 3, giving 3 root 8, then root 8 is 2 root 2, so the total is 6 root 2.

You pulled the whole 36 outside instead of its square root. Split 72 as 36 times 2, then the root of 36 is 6, and only that 6 comes out. Check by squaring: 36 root 2 squared would be 1296 times 2, far more than 72, while 6 root 2 squared is 36 times 2, which is 72.
items.concept: To simplify a square root, factor out the largest perfect square and take its root outside.
items.hint: Which perfect square divides 72?

items.q: Rearrange E equals m c squared to isolate m.
options: m equals c squared over E
m equals E over c squared
m equals E minus c squared
items.right: Correct. The whole factor c squared multiplies m, so divide both sides by c squared, with c not zero.
wrong: You inverted the fraction. Dividing both sides of E equals m c squared by c squared leaves E on top and c squared underneath. A quick check: if m were c squared over E, then m c squared would be c to the fourth over E, not E. The correct form is E over c squared.

You divided by c only once, which undoes a single factor of c and leaves m c on the right. The quantity multiplying m is the entire c squared, so both sides must be divided by c squared. Check by substituting back: E over c squared, times c squared, returns E.

You subtracted instead of divided. Subtraction undoes addition, but m is not added to c squared; it is multiplied by it. The inverse of multiplying by c squared is dividing by c squared, giving m equals E over c squared, with the restriction c not zero.
items.concept: Divide both sides by the entire factor multiplying the target, and state that it is nonzero.
items.hint: What is multiplying m, and what undoes multiplication?

items.q: To isolate t in v equals v nought plus a t, which operation comes first?
options: Subtract v nought from both sides
items.right: Correct. Peel off the outermost layer first: the added v nought, then divide by a.
wrong: Dividing first is possible but then every term must be divided, giving v over a equals v nought over a plus t, which is messier. Working outward from t, the formula multiplies by a and then adds v nought, so undo in reverse: subtract v nought first, then divide by a. That gives t equals v minus v nought, all over a.

Dividing by t would put the unknown in a denominator and take you further from isolating it. The target t is multiplied by a and then has v nought added. Reverse the construction: subtract v nought from both sides, then divide by a, giving t equals v minus v nought, all over a, with a not zero.

The a is not added to anything; it multiplies t. Subtracting it would not undo a multiplication. The term that is added is v nought, so subtract that first, leaving a t alone, then divide both sides by a.
items.concept: Undo operations in reverse order: remove what was added last before dividing out a factor.
items.hint: What was done to t last when the formula was built?

items.q: After rearranging P V equals n R T to T equals P V over n R, what restriction must be stated?
items.right: Correct. You divided by the product n R, so that product cannot be zero.
wrong: P ended up in the numerator, and a numerator is allowed to be zero. The restriction always attaches to what you divided by. Here both sides were divided by the whole product n R, so the condition is n R not zero.

Whether T is positive is a physics question about temperature, not an algebraic restriction from the rearrangement. The algebra only forbids dividing by zero, and you divided by n R, so the required statement is n R not zero.
V is a factor in the numerator, so it may be zero without breaking the formula. Restrictions come from divisors. Both sides were divided by n R, so n R must be nonzero.
items.concept: Every division in a rearrangement carries the restriction that the divisor is nonzero.
items.hint: What did you divide by?

items.q: What is the smallest number set that contains the square root of 49?
items.right: Correct. Root 49 simplifies to 7, a counting number, so it is natural and everything above.
wrong: You classified the symbol rather than the value. Root 2 is irrational, but root 49 is exactly 7 because 7 squared is 49. Always simplify first. Seven is a counting number, so its smallest set is the natural numbers.

Seven is an integer, but it is also a natural number, and the natural numbers are a smaller set inside the integers. The question asks for the smallest set, so the answer is natural. It is true that 7 is also whole, an integer, rational and real.

Seven is rational, since it can be written as 7 over 1, but it is also an integer and a natural number. Rational but not integer would describe something like one eighth. The smallest home for 7 is the naturals.
items.concept: Simplify first, then classify by value; the smallest set for 7 is the natural numbers.
items.hint: What does the square root of 49 simplify to?

items.q: To divide five sixths by ten ninths, what do you do?
options: Multiply six fifths by ten ninths
Multiply five sixths by ten ninths
Multiply five sixths by nine tenths
items.right: Correct. Invert the second fraction, the divisor, and multiply; the result reduces to three quarters.
wrong: You inverted the first fraction. The reciprocal goes on the divisor, the fraction you are dividing by, which is the second one. Five sixths stays as it is and ten ninths becomes nine tenths. The product is 45 over 60, which reduces to three quarters.

Dividing top by top and bottom by bottom is not the rule for dividing fractions. Division asks for a missing factor, and multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor supplies it. Keep five sixths, flip ten ninths to nine tenths, and multiply to get three quarters.

That is multiplication, not division. To divide by ten ninths you multiply by its reciprocal, nine tenths. Five sixths times nine tenths is 45 over 60, which is three quarters. Check: ten ninths times three quarters is 30 over 36, which is five sixths.
items.concept: To divide by a fraction, multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor, the second fraction.
items.hint: Which fraction gets flipped, the first or the second?

items.q: What is the reciprocal of negative three fifths?
items.right: Correct. Flip the fraction and keep the single negative sign; their product is 1.
wrong: You dropped the sign. A reciprocal must multiply the original to give positive 1, and negative three fifths times positive five thirds is negative 1. Keep the negative: negative three fifths times negative five thirds is positive 1.

You changed the sign but did not flip the fraction. The reciprocal of a number r is 1 over r, so the numerator and denominator swap. Negative three fifths becomes negative five thirds, and the two multiply to 1.

A number is not its own reciprocal unless it is 1 or negative 1. The reciprocal swaps numerator and denominator, giving negative five thirds. Check: negative three fifths times negative five thirds is 15 over 15, which is 1.
items.concept: The reciprocal of a fraction swaps top and bottom and keeps the sign; the product is 1.
items.hint: Reciprocal times original must equal 1.

items.q: What is minus 3 squared, written with no brackets around the minus 3? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, negative 9. The exponent applies to the 3 only; the minus sign waits outside.
items.wrong: Order of operations: powers before the leading negative sign. With no brackets, the base of the exponent is just 3, so 3 squared is 9 and the negative sign is applied afterwards, giving negative 9. To square negative 3 itself you must write brackets around negative 3, and then negative 3 times negative 3 is positive 9. Read the expression as the opposite of 3 squared.

slips.why: You squared negative 3, which needs brackets. Without brackets the exponent applies to the 3 alone, giving 9, and the leading minus sign then makes it negative 9.

items.concept: An exponent applies to the base immediately in front of it; a bare minus sign stays outside the power.
items.hint: Is the minus sign part of the base?

items.q: True or false: in the order of operations, multiplication is always done before division.
items.right: Right, false. Multiplication and division share one level and are done left to right.
items.wrong: The memory aids that list multiplication before division mislead many people. Multiplication and division have the same precedence, and so do addition and subtraction. Within a level you work left to right. So 12 divided by 2 times 3 is 6 times 3, which is 18, not 12 divided by 6. The real hierarchy is grouping symbols first, then powers and roots, then multiplication and division together, then addition and subtraction together.
items.concept: Multiplication and division share a level, worked left to right; so do addition and subtraction.
items.hint: Try 12 divided by 2 times 3 both ways.

items.q: True or false: in the fraction with the quantity x plus 3 on top and the quantity x plus 2 underneath, you may cancel the x from top and bottom to get 3 over 2.
items.right: Right, false. The x is a term inside a sum, not a factor, so nothing cancels.
items.wrong: Cancelling works because a common factor over itself equals 1. In x plus 3 over x plus 2, the x is added, not multiplied, so there is no common factor to form a 1. Test it: at x equals 1 the fraction is 4 over 3, which is not 3 over 2. Factor the whole numerator and the whole denominator first; only a factor shared by both can be cancelled.
items.concept: Only common factors cancel; terms inside a sum never do.
items.hint: Try x equals 1 in both versions.

items.q: Simplify x squared minus 9, all over x squared plus 5 x plus 6. Which values of x must be excluded?
options: x cannot be negative 2 or negative 3
items.right: Correct. The original denominator is x plus 2 times x plus 3, so both negative 2 and negative 3 are excluded.
wrong: The signs are reversed. The denominator factors as x plus 2 times x plus 3, and those factors are zero when x is negative 2 or negative 3, not positive 2 or 3. Set each factor to zero to find the excluded inputs.

You dropped the restriction that cancelled. The simplified form x minus 3 over x plus 2 only shows x not negative 2, but the original denominator also contained x plus 3, which is zero at x equals negative 3. Cancelling does not make the original defined there, so both exclusions stay.

You read the numerator's zeros as exclusions. A numerator may be zero; that just makes the fraction zero. Exclusions come from the denominator, x plus 2 times x plus 3, which vanishes at negative 2 and negative 3.
items.concept: Record excluded inputs from the original denominator before cancelling; they survive the cancellation.
items.hint: Factor the denominator and ask where each factor is zero.

items.q: True or false: a plus b, all squared, equals a squared plus b squared.
items.right: Right, false. The middle term 2 a b is missing; test with a equals b equals 1: 4 is not 2.
items.wrong: A power does not distribute over addition. Squaring a plus b means multiplying the whole bracket by itself, and every term multiplies every term: a squared, plus a b, plus b a, plus b squared. The two cross products combine into 2 a b. Test with a equals 1 and b equals 1: the left side is 2 squared, which is 4, while a squared plus b squared is 2. The correct identity is a squared plus 2 a b plus b squared.
items.concept: The square of a sum has a middle term: a squared plus 2 a b plus b squared.
items.hint: Try a equals 1 and b equals 1.

items.q: What is the first step in factoring 18 x squared minus 32?
options: Apply the difference of squares directly
items.right: Correct. Pull out the 2 first; 9 x squared minus 16 is then a clean difference of squares.
wrong: There is no middle term to split; the expression has only a squared term and a constant. Begin with the common factor 2, then recognise 9 x squared minus 16 as a difference of squares.

Eighteen and 32 are not perfect squares, so the pattern does not apply yet. Take out the common factor 2 first, leaving 9 x squared minus 16, and now both terms are squares: 3 x squared and 4 squared. The full factoring is 2 times 3 x minus 4 times 3 x plus 4.

The quadratic formula solves an equation; there is no equation here, just an expression to factor. Start the way the class always starts: remove the common factor 2, then factor the difference of squares that remains.
items.concept: Always remove a common factor first; it often exposes a difference of squares.
items.hint: What number divides both 18 and 32?

items.q: Nine x squared minus 25 is a special pattern. What is the pattern called?
items.right: Correct. Both terms are perfect squares with subtraction between them, so it factors as 3 x minus 5 times 3 x plus 5.
items.wrong: Read the structure: 9 x squared is 3 x squared, 25 is 5 squared, and there is a minus sign between them. That is a difference of squares, and it factors as a minus b times a plus b, here 3 x minus 5 times 3 x plus 5. Check by expanding: the outer and inner products, plus 15 x and minus 15 x, cancel, leaving 9 x squared minus 25. If the sign between them were plus, it would be a sum of squares and would not factor over the reals.
items.concept: Two perfect squares with a minus between them factor as conjugates.
items.hint: What are 9 x squared and 25 each the square of?

items.q: True or false: 9 x squared plus 25 can be factored as 3 x plus 5 times 3 x plus 5.
items.right: Right, false. That product expands to 9 x squared plus 30 x plus 25; a sum of squares does not factor over the reals.
items.wrong: Expand the proposed factoring and the mistake shows: 3 x plus 5, all squared, is 9 x squared plus 30 x plus 25, which has a middle term the original lacks. The conjugate pattern needs opposite signs so the middle terms cancel, and that produces a difference of squares, never a sum. Over the real numbers 9 x squared plus 25 has no factoring. Always check a factoring by expanding it.
items.concept: Only a difference of squares factors; a sum of squares does not, over the reals.
items.hint: Expand 3 x plus 5 times 3 x plus 5 and compare.

items.q: Factor x squared plus 9 x plus 20.
items.right: Correct. Four and 5 multiply to 20 and add to 9, the two conditions of the AC method.
wrong: The numbers are right but the signs are wrong. Negative 4 and negative 5 multiply to positive 20 but add to negative 9, which would factor x squared minus 9 x plus 20. The original middle term is positive, so both numbers are positive: x plus 4 times x plus 5.

Two and 10 multiply to 20 but add to 12, not 9. The AC method needs both conditions at once: product equal to a times c, which is 20, and sum equal to b, which is 9. The pair is 4 and 5. Check by expanding.

You copied the coefficients into the brackets. Expanding x plus 9 times x plus 20 gives x squared plus 29 x plus 180, nothing like the original. Find two numbers with product 20 and sum 9: they are 4 and 5.
items.concept: AC method: find two numbers whose product is a times c and whose sum is b.
items.hint: Which pair multiplies to 20 and adds to 9?

items.q: If a product of two factors equals zero, then at least one factor is zero. What is this rule called?
items.right: Correct. The zero-product rule is what turns a factored equation into two simple ones.
items.wrong: The rule is the zero-product rule: if A times B is zero, then A is zero or B is zero. It works because two nonzero real numbers always multiply to something nonzero. It is the whole reason we factor equations. Note the condition: the product must equal zero. If x minus 6 times x minus 2 equalled 5, you could not conclude anything about the individual factors, so you first move everything to one side to get zero.
items.concept: Zero-product rule: A times B equals zero means A is zero or B is zero.
items.hint: The name mentions both the product and the number it equals.

items.q: To solve x squared plus 3 x equals 10 by factoring, what must you do first?
options: Take the square root of both sides
Subtract 10 from both sides to get zero on one side
Factor the left side as x times x plus 3
items.right: Correct. The zero-product rule only works against zero; x squared plus 3 x minus 10 then factors as x plus 5 times x minus 2.
wrong: Dividing by x assumes x is not zero and leaves x plus 3 equals 10 over x, which is no easier. Put the equation in zero form instead, subtracting 10 from both sides, then factor and apply the zero-product rule.
Square roots undo a lone squared term, but here there is also a 3 x term, so the equation is not of that shape. Bring the 10 across to get zero on one side, then factor the trinomial.

Factoring the left side as x times x plus 3 is true but useless while the right side is 10. A product equal to 10 tells you nothing about each factor. Move the 10 over first: x squared plus 3 x minus 10 equals zero, then factor into x plus 5 times x minus 2.
items.concept: Get zero on one side before factoring; the zero-product rule needs a product equal to zero.
items.hint: What number must one side equal for the rule to apply?

items.q: True or false: to solve x times the quantity x minus 4 equals zero, it is fine to divide both sides by x first.
items.right: Right, false. Dividing by x discards the solution x equals zero; set each factor to zero instead.
items.wrong: Dividing by x is only legal when x is not zero, so the step quietly assumes away one of the answers. The equation is already a product equal to zero, so apply the zero-product rule directly: x equals zero, or x minus 4 equals zero, giving x equals zero or x equals 4. Check both in the original. The same trap returns later with trigonometric equations, where cancelling a common cosine loses a whole branch of solutions.
items.concept: Never divide by a factor that could be zero; factor and set each factor to zero.
items.hint: What value of x would you be forbidding by dividing?

items.q: Solve the quantity 2 x minus 5, times the quantity x minus 2, equals zero.
options: x equals negative five halves or negative 2
x equals five halves or x equals 2
items.right: Correct. Each factor set to zero gives 2 x equals 5, so x is five halves, or x equals 2.
wrong: The signs are reversed. Setting 2 x minus 5 to zero means 2 x equals positive 5, so x is positive five halves; setting x minus 2 to zero means x is positive 2. Moving a subtracted number across makes it positive.

You forgot to divide by the coefficient in the first factor. Two x minus 5 equals zero gives 2 x equals 5, so x is five halves, not 5. Check: 2 times 5 minus 5 is 5, not zero. The exact fraction five halves is a complete answer.

You dropped a solution. A product of two factors is zero when either factor is zero, so both must be solved. Two x minus 5 equals zero gives x equals five halves, and x minus 2 equals zero gives x equals 2.
items.concept: Set each factor equal to zero and solve; keep fractional solutions exact.
items.hint: Solve each bracket separately.

items.q: For a quadratic equation, the discriminant b squared minus 4 a c comes out negative. What does that tell you?
items.right: Correct. A negative discriminant needs the square root of a negative number, so no real solution exists.
wrong: One repeated solution happens when the discriminant is exactly zero, because plus or minus zero gives the same value twice. A negative discriminant puts a negative number under the square root, and that has no real value, so there are no real solutions.

Two distinct real solutions come from a positive discriminant, where plus and minus the root give two different numbers. A negative discriminant means the root is not real, so no real solutions at all.

The discriminant says nothing about whether the equation is quadratic; that is decided by a being nonzero. A negative discriminant means the square root in the formula is of a negative number, so there are no real solutions.
items.concept: Discriminant positive: two real roots; zero: one repeated; negative: no real roots.
items.hint: What happens when you try to square root a negative number?

items.q: What is the discriminant of x squared minus 6 x plus 9 equals zero? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, zero. Thirty-six minus 36 is zero, so there is one repeated real solution, x equals 3.
items.wrong: The discriminant is b squared minus 4 a c, where a is the coefficient of x squared, b the coefficient of x, and c the constant. Here a is 1, b is negative 6 and c is 9. Negative 6 squared is 36, and 4 times 1 times 9 is also 36, so the discriminant is zero. That means the plus or minus in the formula adds nothing and the equation has a single repeated solution, x equals 3. Indeed the left side is x minus 3, all squared.

slips.why: You added 4 a c instead of subtracting it. The discriminant is b squared minus 4 a c: 36 minus 36, which is zero, giving one repeated root.
It looks like you used negative 36 for b squared. A negative number squared is positive, so b squared is 36, and 36 minus 36 is zero.

items.concept: Discriminant equals b squared minus 4 a c; zero means one repeated real solution.
items.hint: Square b, then subtract 4 times a times c.

items.q: What is 2 cubed times 2 squared? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, 32. Same base, so add the exponents: 2 to the fifth is 32.
items.wrong: The product rule: a to the m times a to the n equals a to the m plus n, because you are counting factors of the base. Two cubed is three factors of 2 and 2 squared is two more, five factors in all, which is 2 to the fifth, or 32. You can also just compute: 8 times 4 is 32. Multiplying the exponents, 2 to the sixth or 64, is the rule for a power of a power, not for a product.

slips.why: You multiplied the exponents, which is the power-of-a-power rule. Multiplying same-base powers adds the exponents: 3 plus 2 is 5, and 2 to the fifth is 32.
You added the values, 8 plus 4. The question asks for the product, 8 times 4, which is 32; adding exponents is the shortcut for multiplying powers.

items.concept: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents.
items.hint: How many factors of 2 are there in total?

items.q: Simplify x cubed, all raised to the power 2.
items.right: Correct. A power of a power multiplies the exponents: 3 times 2 is 6.
wrong: You added the exponents, which is the rule for multiplying x cubed by x squared. Raising x cubed to the power 2 means x cubed times x cubed, six factors of x altogether, so the exponents multiply: x to the 6.
You may have cubed the exponent or confused the two numbers. The group x cubed is repeated twice, giving 3 times 2, which is 6 factors of x. The result is x to the 6.
Doubling the coefficient is what 2 times x cubed would do. The exponent 2 means the whole x cubed is multiplied by itself: x cubed times x cubed is x to the 6.
items.concept: A power of a power multiplies the exponents; a product of powers adds them.
items.hint: Write x cubed times x cubed and count the factors.

items.q: What is 2 to the power negative 3? Give the answer as a decimal.
items.right: Correct, one eighth, which is 0.125. A negative exponent means a reciprocal.
items.wrong: The negative-exponent rule: a to the minus n equals 1 over a to the n. So 2 to the minus 3 is 1 over 2 cubed, which is 1 over 8, or 0.125. The sign of the exponent tells you the factor belongs on the other side of a fraction bar; it never makes the result negative. Negative 8 would be the value of the different expression, negative 2 cubed.

slips.why: You made the value negative. A negative exponent means reciprocal, not negative: 2 to the minus 3 is 1 over 2 cubed, which is one eighth, or 0.125.
You took the reciprocal and also flipped the sign. Only the reciprocal is right: 1 over 8 is positive 0.125, because the base 2 is positive.

items.concept: A negative exponent means reciprocal: a to the minus n is 1 over a to the n.
items.hint: Where does a negative exponent move the factor?

items.q: Evaluate eight over 27, raised to the power two thirds.
items.right: Correct. Cube root first gives two thirds, then squaring gives four ninths.
wrong: Two thirds is the cube root, which is only the first step. The exponent two thirds means take the cube root and then square. Two thirds squared is four ninths.

Sixteen over 27 comes from treating the exponent as a multiplier: 2 times 8 is 16, with the 27 left alone. An exponent is not a multiplier, and it acts on the whole fraction. Two thirds means cube root, then square: the cube root of 8 over 27 is two thirds, and two thirds squared is four ninths.

Sixteen over 81 is four ninths squared, so the squaring happened twice. The denominator 3 of the exponent is the root index: the cube root of 8 over 27 is 2 over 3. The numerator 2 is the power, applied once: two thirds squared is four ninths.
items.concept: A fractional exponent m over n means the n-th root, then the m-th power.
items.hint: Take the cube root first, then square.

items.q: What is log base 2 of 8? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, 3. Two to the power 3 is 8.
items.wrong: Use the definition: log base b of x equals y means b to the y equals x, where b is the base, x is the argument and y is the exponent you are looking for. Ask the question in words: two to what power gives eight? Two squared is 4, two cubed is 8. So the exponent is 3, and log base 2 of 8 equals 3. A logarithm is never a division; 8 divided by 2 is 4, which is not the answer.

slips.why: You divided 8 by 2. A logarithm asks for an exponent, not a quotient: two to what power gives eight? Two cubed is 8, so the answer is 3.
You may have computed 2 times 8. The logarithm asks which exponent on 2 produces 8; that exponent is 3.

items.concept: Log base b of x is the exponent you put on b to get x.
items.hint: Two to what power gives eight?

items.q: What is log base 2 of 1 over 32? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, negative 5. Two to the minus 5 is 1 over 32.
items.wrong: The definition: log base b of x equals y means b to the y equals x. Ask, two to what power gives one thirty-second? Two to the fifth is 32, and a negative exponent means reciprocal, so two to the minus 5 is 1 over 32. The exponent is negative 5. Notice the argument, one thirty-second, is positive, as it must be; it is the answer, the exponent, that comes out negative. Any argument between 0 and 1 gives a negative log.

slips.why: You found the exponent for 32, not for 1 over 32. An argument less than 1 needs a negative exponent: two to the minus 5 is one thirty-second, so the answer is negative 5.
You negated the argument. The logarithm returns an exponent: which power of 2 gives 1 over 32? Two to the minus 5, so the answer is negative 5.

items.concept: An argument between 0 and 1 gives a negative logarithm; the exponent is negative, not the argument.
items.hint: Two to the fifth is 32. What power gives 1 over 32?

items.q: True or false: log base 10 of negative 100 is negative 2.
items.right: Right, false. Ten to any real power is positive, so a negative argument has no real logarithm.
items.wrong: Negative 2 is the log of one hundredth, since 10 to the minus 2 is 1 over 100. The argument of a real logarithm must be positive: ten to any real power is positive, so no exponent produces negative 100. The sign confusion goes the other way. Positive arguments smaller than 1 give negative logs; negative arguments give nothing at all. Check the domain, argument greater than zero, before evaluating.
items.concept: A logarithm's argument must be positive; a negative argument has no real log.
items.hint: Can 10 to a real power ever be negative?

items.q: Condense log 6 plus log 3 into a single logarithm.
items.right: Correct. Adding logs multiplies the arguments: 6 times 3 is 18.
wrong: A power inside the log corresponds to a multiplier outside, as in 3 log 6 equals log of 6 cubed. A plus between two logs is the product rule, giving log of 6 times 3, which is log 18.

You added the arguments. The product rule says adding logarithms multiplies the arguments, because adding exponents corresponds to multiplying powers. Log 6 plus log 3 is log of 6 times 3, which is log 18.
Log 2 would be log 6 minus log 3, the quotient rule. A plus sign between logs becomes multiplication inside: log 18.
items.concept: Product rule: log u plus log v equals log of u times v.
items.hint: Which operation inside matches addition outside?

items.q: Rewrite 3 log 5 as a single logarithm.
items.right: Correct. The multiplier becomes an exponent: 3 log 5 is log of 5 cubed, which is log 125.
wrong: You multiplied 3 by 5. The power rule says a coefficient in front of a log becomes an exponent on the argument: 3 log 5 is log of 5 to the third, and 5 cubed is 125.
The 3 is a coefficient, not a base. A base is written as a subscript below the log; a number in front multiplies the whole log. Three times log 5 equals log of 5 cubed, which is log 125.
You added 3 and 5. A coefficient outside a logarithm moves inside as an exponent: log of 5 cubed, which is log 125.
items.concept: Power rule: r times log u equals log of u to the r.
items.hint: Where does a coefficient in front of a log go?

items.q: True or false: log of the quantity u plus v equals log u plus log v.
items.right: Right, false. Test it in base 2: log of 16 plus 16 is 5, but log 16 plus log 16 is 8.
items.wrong: This is the false rule the class kept warning about. Adding logarithms matches multiplying arguments, so log u plus log v equals log of u times v, not u plus v. Test in base 2: log base 2 of 16 plus 16 is log base 2 of 32, which is 5, while log base 2 of 16 plus log base 2 of 16 is 4 plus 4, which is 8. Different numbers, so the statement is false. A sum inside a logarithm cannot be split by any rule.
items.concept: A log does not distribute over addition; only products, quotients and powers have rules.
items.hint: Try u equals 16 and v equals 16 in base 2.

items.q: What is 10 raised to the power log 5, where log means base 10? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, 5. Raising 10 to a base-10 log undoes the log and returns the argument.
items.wrong: Log 5 is, by definition, the exponent that turns 10 into 5. So putting that exponent back on 10 gives 5. In general, a to the log base a of x equals x for positive x, because the exponential and the logarithm of the same base are inverse operations. There is nothing to calculate: the answer is the argument, 5.

slips.why: You evaluated log 5 on its own, about 0.699, and stopped. The question raises 10 to that exponent, which returns the original argument, 5.
You may have replaced the exponent by zero. Log 5 is about 0.699, not zero, and 10 to that power is 5, because raising 10 to a base-10 log returns the argument.

items.concept: Base a raised to log base a of x returns x; the operations cancel.
items.hint: What is log 5, by definition? Put that exponent on 10.

items.q: Your calculator has only log and l n. How do you compute log base 7 of 20?
options: l n 7 divided by l n 20
l n 20 divided by l n 7
items.right: Correct. Change of base: argument's log on top, base's log underneath, same logarithm in both.
wrong: You put the base on top. The change-of-base formula is log base b of x equals l n x over l n b: the argument 20 goes on top and the base 7 goes underneath. A quick size check: 7 squared is 49, so log base 7 of 20 is between 1 and 2, and l n 20 over l n 7 is about 1.54, while the inverted fraction is about 0.65.
Subtraction inside a log is not a rule, and it is not how a different base is handled. Use change of base: l n 20 over l n 7.
Both parts of the fraction must use the same logarithm. Mixing l n on top with base-10 log underneath is not a change-of-base calculation. Use l n over l n, or log over log, but not one of each.
items.concept: Change of base: log base b of x equals l n x over l n b, argument on top.
items.hint: Which number is the argument and which is the base?

items.q: Log base 81 of 2401. Since 81 is 3 to the fourth and 2401 is 7 to the fourth, this equals what?
items.right: Correct. Change of base gives 4 l n 7 over 4 l n 3; the fours cancel, leaving log base 3 of 7.
wrong: Twenty-eight comes from multiplying 7 by 4, but the 4 is a common multiplier that cancels, not a factor of the argument. The result is log base 3 of 7.

You kept the 4 that should have cancelled. Writing the value as l n 2401 over l n 81 gives 4 l n 7 over 4 l n 3. The same multiplier 4 appears top and bottom, so it cancels completely, leaving l n 7 over l n 3, which is log base 3 of 7.

You inverted the result. The argument 2401 sits on top of the change-of-base fraction and the base 81 underneath, so after cancelling the fours you have l n 7 over l n 3, which is log base 3 of 7, not base 7 of 3.
items.concept: When base and argument are the same power, that power cancels in change of base.
items.hint: Write both as fourth powers and use the power rule top and bottom.

items.q: What is the domain of y equals log base 2 of the quantity x minus 2?
options: x greater than or equal to 2
items.right: Correct. The argument must be positive: x minus 2 greater than 0 means x greater than 2.
wrong: All real x is the domain of an exponential, not a logarithm. A log needs a positive argument, so x minus 2 must be greater than zero, giving x greater than 2.

You used the parent function's domain. Shifting right by 2 moves the boundary too. Solve argument greater than zero: x minus 2 greater than zero gives x greater than 2, and the vertical asymptote is now at x equals 2.
At x equals 2 the argument is zero, and log of zero is undefined; the graph approaches the asymptote there but never touches it. The inequality is strict: x greater than 2.
items.concept: Find a log's domain by solving argument greater than zero.
items.hint: What must the quantity inside the log be?

items.q: To solve 2 to the x equals 7, what is the first move?
options: Take a logarithm of both sides
items.right: Correct. Seven is not a whole power of 2, so log both sides and the power rule brings x down.
wrong: There are no logarithms in the equation yet, so there is nothing to condense. Introduce one by taking the log of both sides, then use the power rule.

Seven is not an integer power of 2, so no common base is available. That is exactly the signal for method four: take the log of both sides, giving x log 2 equals log 7, so x equals log 7 over log 2, about 2.807.
Dividing by 2 does not remove an exponent; 2 to the x over 2 is 2 to the x minus 1, which is no better. The unknown is in the exponent, and a logarithm is what brings it down.
items.concept: When the bases cannot be matched, take a log of both sides and use the power rule.
items.hint: Is 7 a power of 2?

items.q: To solve 3 to the power of the quantity 4 x plus 1, equals 27, what is the efficient first move?
options: Write 27 as 3 cubed and equate exponents
Take the natural log of both sides
items.right: Correct. Twenty-seven is 3 cubed, so 4 x plus 1 equals 3 and x is one half.
wrong: Dividing by 3 lowers the exponent by one but leaves the unknown up there. Recognise 27 as 3 cubed instead, then equate the exponents.
You cannot alter one exponent without changing the equation. Rewrite 27 as 3 cubed so both sides share the base, then set the exponents equal: 4 x plus 1 equals 3.

Taking logs would work but wastes effort, because 27 is a recognisable power of 3. Match the bases: 3 to the 4 x plus 1 equals 3 cubed, so 4 x plus 1 equals 3, giving x equals one half. Check: 4 times one half plus 1 is 3, and 3 cubed is 27.
items.concept: When both sides can be powers of one base, equate the exponents.
items.hint: Which power of 3 is 27?

items.q: Rewriting 8 to the power of the quantity x plus 2, as a power of 2, what exponent do you get on the 2?
items.right: Correct. Eight is 2 cubed, and a power of a power multiplies the whole exponent: 3 times x plus 2 is 3 x plus 6.
wrong: You added the 3 instead of multiplying. A power of a power multiplies exponents: 3 times x plus 2 gives 3 x plus 6.
You multiplied only the 2 by 3. The factor 3 applies to the whole bracket, x plus 2, giving 3 x plus 6.

This is the slip the class flagged. Two cubed raised to the x plus 2 multiplies the entire inner exponent by 3, not just the x. Three times the bracket x plus 2 is 3 x plus 6. Keep the bracket until you have expanded it.
items.concept: A power of a power multiplies the entire exponent; expand the bracket before equating.
items.hint: Eight is 2 cubed. Multiply the whole bracket by 3.

items.q: Before solving log x plus log of the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 1, what domain restriction applies?
options: x can be any real number
items.right: Correct. Both arguments must be positive; 2 x minus 1 greater than 0 is the tighter condition, x greater than one half.
wrong: A logarithm's argument must be positive, so real restrictions exist here. Both x and 2 x minus 1 must be positive, which together require x greater than one half.
You checked only the first argument. Both must be positive: x greater than 0 and 2 x minus 1 greater than 0. The second gives x greater than one half, which is stricter, so that is the domain.
One is the right-hand side of the equation, not a domain boundary. The restriction comes from the arguments: x greater than 0 and 2 x minus 1 greater than 0, so x greater than one half.
items.concept: Every log argument must be positive; the tightest condition is the domain.
items.hint: Set each argument greater than zero.

items.q: Solving log x plus log of the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 1 gives candidates five halves and negative 2. What is the actual solution? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, five halves. Negative 2 makes a log argument negative, so it is rejected.
items.wrong: The condensed equation, log of x times the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 1, becomes x times the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 10 by the definition of the log, and factoring gives 2 x minus 5 times x plus 2, so the candidates are five halves and negative 2. Test each in the original. Negative 2 would need the log of negative 2, which does not exist, so it is extraneous. Five halves works: log of 2.5 plus log of 4 is log 10, which is 1. The solution is 2.5.

slips.why: You kept the extraneous root. At x equals negative 2 both original arguments are negative, so the original equation is undefined there; only the condensed version accepts it. The solution is 2.5.
Ten is what x times the quantity 2 x minus 1 equals after changing the form, not the value of x. Solve the quadratic and reject negative 2: x equals 2.5.

items.concept: Reject any candidate that makes an original log argument non-positive.
items.hint: Which candidate makes a log argument negative?

items.q: Why can condensing two logarithms introduce an extraneous root?
options: Factoring always adds a false root
Logarithms of negatives are secretly allowed
The condensed equation has a wider domain than the original
The product rule is only approximately true
items.right: Correct. Two negative arguments multiply to a positive one, so the condensed form accepts values the original rejects.
wrong: Factoring is exact and adds nothing. The false root comes from the earlier step, condensing, which is defined on more inputs than the original pair of logarithms.
Real logarithms of negative numbers do not exist. That is precisely why the candidate is rejected: the condensed equation admitted a value the original arguments forbid.

The product rule is exactly true wherever both arguments are positive. The trouble is that where both are negative their product is positive, so the condensed log is defined there while the original two logs are not. The rewrite widened the domain, and the check catches it.
items.concept: A rewrite can enlarge the domain; test every candidate in the original equation.
items.hint: Where is log u plus log v equal to log of u v, and where is only the right side defined?

items.q: True or false: for 2 to the x equals 7, the exact solution is log 7 over log 2, and 2.807 is an approximation of it.
items.right: Right. The quotient of logs is the exact value; the decimal is rounded.
items.wrong: Taking the base-10 log of both sides gives x log 2 equals log 7, so x equals log 7 over log 2. That fraction is the exact answer, just as five halves is exact. Punching it into a calculator gives 2.80735 and so on, which is rounded to 2.807, an approximation. When a question asks for an exact answer and a decimal, give both, and do not present the rounded number as if it were exact. Sanity check: 2 cubed is 8, so x should be just under 3.
items.concept: The log expression is exact; a rounded decimal only approximates it.
items.hint: Which form has been rounded?

items.q: Richter magnitude is a base-10 logarithmic scale. Going from magnitude 5 to magnitude 7 multiplies the measured amplitude by how much?
items.right: Correct. Each whole point is a factor of 10, so two points is 10 squared, which is 100.
wrong: You subtracted the magnitudes. On a logarithmic scale a difference of two points is not a factor of two; each point multiplies the amplitude by 10, so two points multiply it by 10 times 10, which is 100.
Twenty mixes the two ideas, a difference of 2 and a factor of 10. Each step is a multiplication by 10, and two steps compound: 10 squared, which is 100.
Ten is the factor for one whole point. From 5 to 7 is two points, so the factor is 10 squared, which is 100.
items.concept: On a base-10 log scale, each unit step multiplies the quantity by 10; steps compound.
items.hint: How many points, and what does each point multiply by?

items.q: Simplify the square root of 216.
items.right: Correct. Two hundred sixteen is 36 times 6, and the root of 36 is 6.
wrong: You brought the whole perfect square outside instead of its root. Only the square root of 36, which is 6, comes out. Check: 6 root 6 squared is 36 times 6, which is 216, while 36 root 6 squared is far larger.

That is a valid first pass, since 216 is 4 times 54, but 54 still holds the square factor 9. Continue: root 54 is 3 root 6, so 2 root 54 becomes 6 root 6. Any square factor left inside means you are not finished.
You split 216 as 6 times 36 and pulled out the wrong part. Six is not a perfect square; 36 is. The root of 36 comes outside as 6, and the 6 stays inside: 6 root 6.
items.concept: Factor out a perfect square, take its root outside, and repeat until no square factor remains.
items.hint: Which perfect square divides 216?

items.q: Simplify the square root of 147. Say the answer as a number times a root.
items.right: Correct. The digits of 147 sum to 12, so it divides by 3: 147 is 49 times 3, giving 7 root 3.
items.wrong: Use the divisibility check the class taught: 1 plus 4 plus 7 is 12, a multiple of 3, so 147 divides by 3. That gives 147 equals 3 times 49, and 49 is 7 squared, a perfect square. So the root of 147 is root 49 times root 3, which is 7 root 3. Check by squaring back: 7 squared times 3 is 49 times 3, which is 147.
items.concept: Digit sum a multiple of 3 means divisible by 3; look for the perfect square that appears.
items.hint: Add the digits of 147. What does that tell you?

items.q: True or false: the square root of k squared equals k for every real number k.
items.right: Right, false. At k equals negative 3, the root of 9 is 3, not negative 3; the root of k squared is the absolute value of k.
items.wrong: A square root always returns a non-negative value, but k itself may be negative. Test k equals negative 3: k squared is 9, and the root of 9 is 3, which is not k. The correct identity is that the root of k squared equals the absolute value of k. You may drop the bars only when the question states that the variables are non-negative, which textbook exercise sets often do.
items.concept: The root of k squared is the absolute value of k, unless k is known to be non-negative.
items.hint: Try k equals negative 3.

items.q: Rationalize 1 over root 5.
items.right: Correct. Multiply top and bottom by root 5: root 5 over root 5 times root 5, and the denominator becomes 5.
wrong: You lost the radical from the numerator. Multiplying by root 5 over root 5 puts root 5 on top and root 5 times root 5, which is 5, on the bottom. The value is unchanged: about 0.447 either way, whereas 1 over 5 is 0.2.
That still has a radical in the denominator, so it is not rationalized. Multiply numerator and denominator by root 5: the top becomes root 5 and the bottom becomes 5.
Root 5 alone is about 2.24, but 1 over root 5 is about 0.447; you changed the value. Multiplying by a version of 1, root 5 over root 5, gives root 5 over 5.
items.concept: For a single square-root denominator, multiply top and bottom by that root.
items.hint: Multiply by root 5 over root 5.

items.q: To rationalize 1 over the quantity 2 minus root 3, you multiply top and bottom by 2 plus root 3. What is 2 plus root 3 called, relative to the denominator?
items.right: Correct. The conjugate flips the sign between the two terms, and the product is a difference of squares.
items.wrong: Two plus root 3 is the conjugate of 2 minus root 3: the same two terms with the sign between them flipped. Multiplying a two-term denominator by its conjugate uses the pattern a plus b times a minus b equals a squared minus b squared. The cross terms cancel and the root gets squared away: 2 squared minus root 3 squared is 4 minus 3, which is 1. That is why the class says two terms in the denominator means reach for the conjugate.
items.concept: A two-term denominator is cleared by multiplying by its conjugate.
items.hint: Same two terms, opposite sign in the middle.

items.q: What is the quantity 2 plus root 3, times the quantity 2 minus root 3? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, 1. Four minus 3: the cross terms cancel and root 3 squared is 3.
items.wrong: Use the conjugate pattern: a plus b times a minus b equals a squared minus b squared. Here a is 2 and b is root 3, so the product is 2 squared minus root 3 squared, which is 4 minus 3, which is 1. If you expand all four products you see it happen: 4, minus 2 root 3, plus 2 root 3, minus 3. The middle terms cancel exactly. That is why 1 over the quantity 2 minus root 3 rationalizes to just 2 plus root 3.

slips.why: You added the squares, 4 plus 3. Conjugates give a difference of squares, a squared minus b squared, so it is 4 minus 3, which is 1.
You subtracted in the wrong order. The first term squared comes first: 2 squared is 4, minus root 3 squared, which is 3, gives positive 1.

items.concept: Conjugates multiply to a squared minus b squared, which removes the radical.
items.hint: What are 2 squared and root 3 squared?

items.q: Rationalize 1 over the fourth root of 8. What do you multiply top and bottom by?
items.right: Correct. Eight is 2 cubed, one factor short of 2 to the fourth, so supply one more 2 under the fourth root.
wrong: Multiplying by a plain 2 over 2 changes nothing under the radical; the fourth root of 8 stays put. You need a fourth root of 2 to turn the radicand 2 cubed into 2 to the fourth.

This is the tempting wrong move. Multiplying gives the fourth root of 64, and 64 is 2 to the sixth, not a perfect fourth power, so the denominator is still irrational. Count factors: you have 2 cubed and want 2 to the fourth, so you need exactly one more 2, the fourth root of 2.
A square root will not complete a fourth power. The multiplier must be the same kind of root as the denominator, and it must supply what the radicand lacks: one more factor of 2 under a fourth root.
items.concept: For an n-th root, multiply by whatever completes a perfect n-th power under the radical.
items.hint: Eight is 2 cubed. How many more factors of 2 make a fourth power?

items.q: Simplify log base 5 of 50 by splitting the argument. Which is correct?
options: log base 5 of 25 times log base 5 of 2
log base 5 of 45 plus log base 5 of 5
items.right: Correct. Fifty is 25 times 2, so log base 5 of 50 is log base 5 of 25 plus log base 5 of 2, which is 2 plus log base 5 of 2.
wrong: You turned the 25 into a multiplier. Log base 5 of 25 is the number 2, and it is added, not multiplied: 2 plus log base 5 of 2.
The product rule turns multiplication inside into addition outside, not multiplication of two logs. Log base 5 of 25 times 2 is log base 5 of 25 plus log base 5 of 2, and log base 5 of 25 is 2.
You split 50 as a sum, 45 plus 5, but a log of a sum has no rule. Split it as a product instead: 25 times 2, giving 2 plus log base 5 of 2.
items.concept: Split a log argument into a perfect power times a leftover; the perfect power gives a whole number.
items.hint: Fifty is 25 times what, and what is log base 5 of 25?

items.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
items.q: What is one radian?
options: The central angle whose arc length equals the radius
The angle whose arc length equals the diameter
items.right: Correct. Wrap one radius along the rim and the angle it opens is one radian; 2 pi of them make a turn.
wrong: One radian is about 57.3 degrees, since 180 degrees is pi radians and 180 over pi is about 57.3. Ninety degrees is pi over 2 radians, roughly 1.57 radians.

That is a degree, a convention inherited from base-60 counting. A radian is defined from the circle itself: the angle whose arc is exactly one radius long. Since the circumference is 2 pi r, a full turn is 2 pi radians.
Using the diameter would give an angle of two radians. The definition uses the radius: one radius of arc opens one radian. That is why 2 pi radii wrap the full circle.
items.concept: One radian: arc length equal to the radius. A full turn is 2 pi radians.
items.hint: Bend one radius around the rim. How big is the angle?

items.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
items.q: How many radians are in one full turn? Say it in terms of pi.
items.right: Correct, 2 pi radians. The circumference is 2 pi times the radius, so 2 pi radii wrap the circle.
items.wrong: The circumference of a circle is 2 pi times the radius, and a radian is the angle opened by one radius of arc. So counting how many radii fit around the rim is counting how many radians make a full turn: 2 pi of them, about 6.28. Half a turn is pi radians, which is the 180 degrees you already know, and a quarter turn is pi over 2. Pi alone is only half a turn.
items.concept: Full turn: 2 pi radians, because circumference is 2 pi r.
items.hint: How many radii fit around the circumference?

items.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
items.q: True or false: the arc-length formula s equals r theta works when theta is in degrees.
items.right: Right, false. It is a radian-only formula; convert to radians first.
items.wrong: Arc length s equals r theta, with s and r in the same length unit and theta in radians, comes from the definition of a radian: each radian of angle lays one radius of arc along the rim. Test it. A full circle is 2 pi radians, and r times 2 pi is the circumference, correct. Substitute 360 for a full circle instead and you get 360 r, which is absurd. Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by pi over 180 before using the formula, never after.
items.concept: s equals r theta needs theta in radians; check it against the circumference.
items.hint: What does the formula give for a full circle if you put in 360?

items.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
items.q: Simplify 6 pi over 4.
items.right: Correct. Divide top and bottom by 2: 3 pi over 2, which is 270 degrees, three quarter turns.
wrong: That is a different angle, 120 degrees. Six steps of pi over 4 is six times 45 degrees, which is 270 degrees, and 270 degrees is 3 pi over 2.

This is the slip the class warned about. Dividing the numerator 6 pi by 2 leaves 3 pi, not pi. Reduce the fraction 6 over 4 to 3 over 2 and keep the pi: 3 pi over 2. Check in degrees: six steps of 45 is 270, and 3 pi over 2 is 270 degrees, while pi over 2 is only 90.
You halved the numerator but not the denominator. Both must be divided by the same number to keep the value: 6 over 4 becomes 3 over 2, so the angle is 3 pi over 2, which is 270 degrees.
items.concept: Reduce the fraction in front of pi; never just delete the number next to pi.
items.hint: Six steps of 45 degrees is how many degrees?

items.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
items.q: Convert pi over 6 radians to degrees. Answer in degrees.
items.right: Correct, 30 degrees. Pi is 180 degrees, so pi over 6 is 180 over 6.
items.wrong: Use the one relation that does all conversions: pi radians equals 180 degrees. To go from radians to degrees, multiply by 180 over pi. Pi over 6 times 180 over pi leaves 180 over 6, which is 30 degrees. That is also why the class counts in steps of pi over 6: each step is 30 degrees, so 2 pi over 6 is 60, 3 pi over 6 is 90, and so on around the circle.

slips.why: Forty-five degrees is pi over 4, the other counting step. Pi over 6 is 180 over 6, which is 30 degrees.
Sixty degrees is pi over 3, which is 2 pi over 6, two steps. One step of pi over 6 is 30 degrees.

items.concept: Pi radians is 180 degrees; divide 180 by the denominator for pi over n.
items.hint: What is 180 divided by 6?

items.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
items.q: Convert 210 degrees to radians.
items.right: Correct. Multiply by pi over 180: 210 over 180 reduces to 7 over 6, so 7 pi over 6.
wrong: Five pi over 6 is 150 degrees, the mirror angle in the second quadrant. Two hundred ten degrees is 30 past 180, so it is pi plus pi over 6, which is 7 pi over 6, in the third quadrant.
Seven pi over 4 is 315 degrees, seven steps of 45. Two hundred ten is seven steps of 30, so it is 7 pi over 6. Multiply 210 by pi over 180 and reduce: 7 pi over 6.
You forgot to divide by 180. Converting degrees to radians multiplies by pi over 180, so 210 times pi over 180 is 210 pi over 180, which reduces to 7 pi over 6.
items.concept: Degrees to radians: multiply by pi over 180 and reduce the fraction.
items.hint: How many steps of 30 degrees make 210?

items.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
items.q: In which quadrant does the angle 5 pi over 6 end? Answer one, two, three or four.
items.right: Correct, quadrant two. Five steps of 30 degrees is 150 degrees, between 90 and 180.
items.wrong: Count it: each step of pi over 6 is 30 degrees, so 5 pi over 6 is 150 degrees. Quadrant one runs from 0 to 90 degrees, quadrant two from 90 to 180, quadrant three from 180 to 270 and quadrant four from 270 to 360. One hundred fifty sits between 90 and 180, so the angle ends in quadrant two. Without converting: pi over 2 is 3 pi over 6 and pi is 6 pi over 6, and 5 pi over 6 lies between them.
items.concept: Pi over 2 to pi is the second quadrant; 5 pi over 6 sits just short of pi.
items.hint: Is 5 pi over 6 more or less than pi, and more or less than pi over 2?

items.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
items.q: Which angle is coterminal with negative pi over 4?
items.right: Correct. Add one full turn: negative pi over 4 plus 8 pi over 4 is 7 pi over 4. Same point on the rim.
wrong: Three pi over 4 is 135 degrees, in the second quadrant. Negative pi over 4 is a 45-degree clockwise turn, ending in the fourth quadrant. Adding a full turn of 2 pi, which is 8 pi over 4, gives 7 pi over 4.
Positive pi over 4 is the reflection of negative pi over 4 across the horizontal axis, not the same point. Coterminal angles differ by whole turns: negative pi over 4 plus 2 pi is 7 pi over 4.
Five pi over 4 is 225 degrees, in the third quadrant. Negative pi over 4 ends in the fourth quadrant, and adding 2 pi gives 7 pi over 4, which is 315 degrees.
items.concept: Coterminal angles differ by a whole number of full turns, 2 pi radians or 360 degrees.
items.hint: Add 2 pi, written as 8 pi over 4.

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: On the unit circle, the sine of an angle equals which coordinate of the point on the rim?
items.right: Correct. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, the hypotenuse is 1, and the opposite side is the vertical y.
wrong: The x coordinate is the adjacent side over a hypotenuse of 1, which is cosine. Sine is the opposite side, the vertical leg, which is the y coordinate.
The distance from the origin to the rim is the radius, always 1 on the unit circle. Sine is the height of the point, its y coordinate.
Y over x is tangent, opposite over adjacent. Sine alone is opposite over hypotenuse, and with hypotenuse 1 that is just y.
items.concept: On the unit circle: cosine is x, sine is y, tangent is y over x.
items.hint: Which leg of the dropped triangle is opposite the angle?

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: What is the exact value of cosine of 30 degrees?
items.right: Correct. In the 30 60 90 triangle the side adjacent to 30 is root 3 over 2, the longer leg.
wrong: Root 3 is tangent of 60, a ratio of legs, and it is bigger than 1. A sine or cosine on the unit circle is a coordinate and can never exceed 1. Cosine of 30 is root 3 over 2, about 0.866.

One half is sine of 30, the short leg opposite the 30-degree angle. Cosine of 30 is the adjacent leg, and the bigger side must face the bigger angle: the leg adjacent to 30 faces the 60, so it is the longer one, root 3 over 2. Check: one quarter plus three quarters is 1.

Root 2 over 2 belongs to the 45 45 90 triangle, where both legs are equal. Thirty degrees uses the 30 60 90 triangle, whose legs are one half and root 3 over 2, and cosine of 30 is the longer one, root 3 over 2.
items.concept: 30 60 90 triangle with hypotenuse 1: legs one half and root 3 over 2; cos 30 is root 3 over 2.
items.hint: Which leg touches the 30-degree angle, the long one or the short one?

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: What is the exact value of sine of 45 degrees?
items.right: Correct. Both legs of the 45 45 90 triangle are root 2 over 2, so sine and cosine of 45 are equal.
wrong: Root 3 over 2 is sine of 60, from the 30 60 90 triangle. The 45 45 90 triangle is half a square with two equal legs of root 2 over 2.
One is tangent of 45, opposite over adjacent with equal legs. Sine of 45 is a leg over the hypotenuse 1, which is root 2 over 2, about 0.707.

One half comes from the 30 60 90 triangle. At 45 degrees the two acute angles are equal, so the two legs are equal, each root 2 over 2. Check: root 2 over 2 squared is one half, and two halves make 1.
