items.concept: 45 45 90 triangle with hypotenuse 1: both legs root 2 over 2.
items.hint: Half a square: what do equal angles tell you about the legs?

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: What is the exact value of sine of 30 degrees?
items.right: Correct, one half. It is the short leg of the 30 60 90 triangle, opposite the 30-degree angle.
items.wrong: Sine is opposite over hypotenuse. In the 30 60 90 triangle nested in the unit circle, the hypotenuse is 1 and the side opposite the 30-degree angle is the short leg, one half, because the smaller angle faces the smaller side. So sine of 30 degrees is one half. Cosine of 60 degrees names the very same side from the other corner, so it is also one half. The longer leg, root 3 over 2, is cosine of 30 and sine of 60.
items.concept: Sine of 30 degrees is one half, the short leg; cosine of 60 is the same side.
items.hint: The smaller angle faces the smaller leg.

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: An angle ends in quadrant three. Which of sine, cosine and tangent is positive there?
items.right: Correct. Both x and y are negative in quadrant three, and a negative over a negative makes tangent positive.
wrong: Sine and cosine are both negative there, but tangent is their ratio: a negative over a negative is positive. Every quadrant has at least one positive function.
Sine is the y coordinate, and below the horizontal axis y is negative, so sine is negative in quadrant three. Tangent, y over x, is a negative over a negative and comes out positive.
Cosine is the x coordinate, and left of the vertical axis x is negative, so cosine is negative in quadrant three. It is tangent that turns positive, because both coordinates are negative.
items.concept: Quadrant three: sine and cosine negative, tangent positive.
items.hint: What are the signs of x and y below and to the left?

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: What is the exact value of cosine of 120 degrees?
items.right: Correct. The reference angle is 60, so the size is one half, and in quadrant two x is negative.
wrong: You have the size right but not the sign. One hundred twenty degrees is in quadrant two, where the x coordinate is negative, and cosine is x. So cosine of 120 is negative one half.
You used the sine value. The reference angle is 180 minus 120, which is 60 degrees, and cosine of 60 is one half, not root 3 over 2. With the quadrant-two sign, cosine of 120 is negative one half.
Root 3 over 2 is sine of 120, and it is positive because y is positive in quadrant two. Cosine of 120 uses cosine of the reference angle 60, one half, made negative: negative one half.
items.concept: Reference angle gives the size; the quadrant gives the sign.
items.hint: How far is 120 from 180, and is x positive or negative there?

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: For which angles is tangent undefined?
items.right: Correct. There the point is on the vertical axis, x is zero, and y over x has no value.
wrong: At 0 and 180 degrees the point is on the horizontal axis, where y is zero, so tangent is zero, not undefined. It is where x is zero, at 90 and 270, that y over x fails.
At 45 and 225 degrees the legs are equal, so tangent is exactly 1. Tangent fails only where the denominator x is zero: 90 and 270 degrees.

Tangent is y over x, and division by zero is undefined. At 90 and 270 degrees the point sits on the vertical axis with x equal to zero, so tangent has no value there. Sine and cosine are defined everywhere.
items.concept: Tangent is y over x, so it is undefined where x is zero: 90 and 270 degrees.
items.hint: Where on the circle is the x coordinate zero?

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: Give the negative angle between 0 and negative 360 that is coterminal with 298 degrees. Answer in degrees.
items.right: Correct, negative 62 degrees. Subtract one full turn: 298 minus 360.
items.wrong: Coterminal angles differ by whole turns of 360 degrees. Going counterclockwise 298 degrees ends in quadrant four, 62 degrees short of a full circle. Going clockwise to the same point takes 62 degrees, written as negative 62. Check: 298 minus 360 is negative 62. This is also why inverse tangent of tangent 298 returns negative 62, because that is the coterminal angle inside its band from negative 90 to 90.

slips.why: You found the size but not the direction. Clockwise angles are negative, so the coterminal angle is negative 62 degrees, which is 298 minus 360.
Negative 298 is a different point, 298 degrees clockwise, which lands in quadrant one. Subtract a whole turn instead: 298 minus 360 is negative 62.

items.concept: Subtract 360 degrees to find the coterminal angle measured clockwise.
items.hint: How far short of a full turn is 298?

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: True or false: 172 degrees and negative 8 degrees are coterminal because they have the same tangent.
items.right: Right, false. They differ by 180 degrees, half a turn, so they end at opposite points; tangent just repeats every 180.
items.wrong: Equal tangent is not the same as coterminal. Coterminal means differing by a whole number of full turns, 360 degrees. One hundred seventy-two minus negative 8 is 180, only half a turn, so the two angles end at opposite ends of one line through the centre. Both x and y flip sign there and y over x is unchanged, which is why the tangents match. To recover an angle in quadrant two from inverse tangent, add 180 to the calculator's answer.
items.concept: Coterminal means a difference of 360 degrees; same tangent only guarantees a difference of 180.
items.hint: What is 172 minus negative 8?

items.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
items.q: The inverse tangent key returns angles in which range?
items.right: Correct. That is why inverse tangent of a negative value comes back as a negative acute angle, like negative 62.
wrong: That band is a full turn wide, and tangent repeats every 180 degrees, so it would give two angles per value. Inverse tangent returns exactly one angle, between negative 90 and 90.
Zero to 180 is the band for inverse cosine. Inverse tangent uses negative 90 to 90, which is why tangent 298 came back as negative 62 rather than anything in quadrant two.
No inverse key returns a full turn of possibilities; each picks one angle from a half-turn band. Inverse tangent chooses between negative 90 and 90 degrees.
items.concept: Inverse tangent: negative 90 to 90; inverse cosine: 0 to 180; you supply the rest.
items.hint: Which band contains negative 62 but not 298?

items.q: Sine squared theta plus cosine squared theta equals 1. What kind of identity is this called?
items.right: Correct. It is Pythagoras applied to the triangle nested in the unit circle, where the hypotenuse is 1.
items.wrong: It is the Pythagorean identity. Pythagoras says a squared plus b squared equals c squared, with c the hypotenuse. Drop a vertical from a point on the unit circle: the horizontal leg is cosine theta, the vertical leg is sine theta, and the hypotenuse is the radius, 1. Substituting gives cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta equals 1 squared, which is 1. Dividing that through by cosine squared or sine squared gives the other two Pythagorean identities.
items.concept: The Pythagorean identity is Pythagoras with legs cosine and sine and hypotenuse 1.
items.hint: Which theorem relates the two legs and the hypotenuse of a right triangle?

items.q: In a proof you meet 1 minus sine squared x. What can it be replaced by?
items.right: Correct. Rearranging cosine squared plus sine squared equals 1 gives cosine squared equals 1 minus sine squared.
wrong: You dropped the square. The identity is between squares: cosine squared x plus sine squared x equals 1, so 1 minus sine squared x is cosine squared x, not cosine x. Test at 30 degrees: 1 minus one quarter is three quarters, which is cosine squared, while cosine is about 0.866.
Tangent squared appears in a different identity, 1 plus tangent squared equals secant squared, which comes from dividing by cosine squared. Here 1 minus sine squared is cosine squared.
The sign is wrong. From cosine squared plus sine squared equals 1, subtract sine squared from both sides: cosine squared equals positive 1 minus sine squared.
items.concept: 1 minus sine squared is cosine squared; 1 minus cosine squared is sine squared.
items.hint: Move sine squared to the other side of the first identity.

items.q: What does cosine squared theta mean?
options: Multiply the cosine of theta by two
Take the cosine of twice the angle theta
Take the cosine of theta, then square the result
Square the angle theta, then take the cosine
items.right: Correct. The square sits on the function's output: cosine squared of 30 degrees is root 3 over 2 squared, three quarters.
wrong: Squaring is not doubling. Cosine squared theta is cosine theta times cosine theta. At 30 degrees that is three quarters, whereas twice cosine 30 is about 1.73.
Cosine of 2 theta doubles the angle, which is not what the squared notation says. Cosine squared theta means the cosine of theta, multiplied by itself.
Cosine of theta squared would square the angle first, a completely different number. Cosine squared theta squares the cosine value: at 30 degrees, root 3 over 2 squared is three quarters.
items.concept: Cosine squared theta is the cosine of theta, squared; the exponent belongs to the output.
items.hint: Which is squared, the angle or the cosine value?

items.q: Which trig function is the reciprocal of cosine?
items.right: Correct, secant. Cosine already has the co prefix, so its reciprocal drops it.
items.wrong: Secant is 1 over cosine. The prefix rule helps: within each reciprocal pair exactly one name carries co, and cosine already has it, so its partner is plain secant. Cosecant, which sounds like it should go with cosine, is actually the reciprocal of sine. If you are ever unsure, go back to the sides: cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, so its reciprocal is hypotenuse over adjacent, which is secant.
items.concept: Secant is 1 over cosine; cosecant is 1 over sine; cotangent is 1 over tangent.
items.hint: Cosine already has the co. Does its reciprocal keep it?

items.q: Cotangent of theta equals which of these?
items.right: Correct. Cotangent is 1 over tangent, and tangent is sine over cosine, so flipping gives cosine over sine.
wrong: Sine over cosine is tangent itself, opposite over adjacent. Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent, so the fraction flips: cosine over sine, undefined where sine is zero.
One over cosine is secant. Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent, which is cosine over sine, undefined where sine is zero.
One over sine is cosecant. Cotangent is 1 over tangent, and since tangent is sine over cosine, cotangent is cosine over sine.
items.concept: Cotangent is cosine over sine, the reciprocal of tangent.
items.hint: Flip the fraction for tangent.

items.q: What is the exact value of secant of 60 degrees? Give a plain number.
items.right: Correct, 2. Cosine of 60 is one half, and secant is its reciprocal.
items.wrong: Secant is defined as 1 over cosine. Cosine of 60 degrees is one half, the short leg of the 30 60 90 triangle adjacent to the 60-degree angle. The reciprocal of one half is 2, so secant of 60 is 2. If you got a decimal near 1.15, you took 1 over sine of 60 instead; that is cosecant. The prefix rule reminds you: cosine's partner is secant, without the co.

slips.why: You took 1 over sine of 60, which is cosecant of 60, about 1.155. Secant is 1 over cosine, and cosine of 60 is one half, so secant of 60 is 2.
That is cosine of 60 itself. Secant is its reciprocal: 1 over one half is 2.

items.concept: Secant equals 1 over cosine; cosine 60 is one half, so secant 60 is 2.
items.hint: What is cosine of 60, and what is its reciprocal?

items.q: Where is cosecant undefined?
options: Where tangent is 1, at 45 and 225 degrees
Nowhere; cosecant is defined for every angle
Where sine is zero, at 0 and 180 degrees
Where cosine is zero, at 90 and 270 degrees
items.right: Correct. Cosecant is 1 over sine, and a fraction with a zero denominator has no value.
wrong: Tangent equal to 1 has nothing to do with it. Cosecant is a reciprocal of sine, so the only danger is sine being zero, at 0 and 180 degrees.
Every reciprocal inherits a restriction: cosecant is 1 over sine, and sine is zero at 0 and 180 degrees, so cosecant has no value there.
Cosine zero is where secant fails, since secant is 1 over cosine. Cosecant is 1 over sine, so it fails where sine is zero: on the horizontal axis, at 0 and 180 degrees.
items.concept: A reciprocal function is undefined wherever the function it inverts is zero.
items.hint: Cosecant is 1 over what?

items.q: What are the two rules the class gives for proving an identity?
options: Move everything to one side and set it equal to zero
Convert to sine and cosine, and change one side only
Substitute a test angle, then simplify both sides
items.right: Correct. Sine and cosine put everything in one language, and changing one side keeps the logic honest.
wrong: Setting to zero is the tactic for solving an equation, where you want particular angles. An identity is proved by rewriting one side, in sine and cosine, until it becomes the other side.

Cross-multiplying and squaring both sides treat the identity as an equation that is already true, which is what you are supposed to prove. Instead rewrite one side in sine and cosine and transform it until it matches the other.
Substituting an angle is a check, not a proof; it shows the two sides agree at one value, not at every value. A proof converts to sine and cosine and transforms one side into the other.
items.concept: Prove an identity by converting to sine and cosine and transforming one side only.
items.hint: Which two functions can everything be written in terms of?

items.q: True or false: when proving an identity, it is acceptable to multiply both sides by the same expression.
items.right: Right, false. Doing the same thing to both sides assumes they are equal, which is what you are trying to prove.
items.wrong: Operating on both sides is legitimate for an equation, because an equation asserts the sides are equal and you are hunting for the values that make it so. An identity proof is the reverse: the equality is the claim under test, so you may not use it. Multiplying both sides, squaring both, or cross-multiplying all start from the conclusion. Pick the messier side, rewrite it in sine and cosine, and transform it step by step until it reads exactly as the other side, which you never touch.
items.concept: In a proof, change one side only; both-sides moves assume the conclusion.
items.hint: What are you assuming when you do the same thing to both sides?

items.q: In a proof, the quantity 1 minus sine x, times the quantity 1 plus sine x, simplifies to what?
options: 1 minus sine squared x, and no further
items.right: Correct. Conjugates give a difference of squares, 1 minus sine squared x, and the first identity turns that into cosine squared x.
wrong: Two sine x is what you get from subtracting the two conjugate expressions, not multiplying them. Their product is 1 minus sine squared x, which is cosine squared x.

It is a difference of squares, so it does simplify: a minus b times a plus b is a squared minus b squared, here 1 minus sine squared x. Then the rearranged Pythagorean identity says 1 minus sine squared x is cosine squared x. Always take that second step.
The sign is wrong. Conjugates multiply to a difference of squares, 1 minus sine squared x, because the cross terms cancel. That equals cosine squared x.
items.concept: Conjugate factors multiply to 1 minus sine squared, which the identity turns into cosine squared.
items.hint: Difference of squares first, then the Pythagorean identity.

items.q: Solve sine x equals one half for x between 0 and 2 pi.
items.right: Correct. Reference angle pi over 6, sine positive in quadrants one and two: pi over 6 and pi minus pi over 6.
wrong: One angle is only half the story. Sine is the y coordinate, and the height one half occurs twice per turn, once on the right of the circle at pi over 6 and once on the left at 5 pi over 6. Both are needed.
Seven pi over 6 is in quadrant three, where sine is negative one half, not positive. The second angle with sine positive one half is the quadrant-two mirror, pi minus pi over 6, which is 5 pi over 6.
Pi over 3 has sine root 3 over 2, not one half. The reference angle for one half is pi over 6, since sine of 30 degrees is one half, giving pi over 6 and 5 pi over 6.
items.concept: Reference angle from the size, quadrants from the sign, two angles per turn for a value between the extremes.
items.hint: Where on the circle is the height one half?

items.q: Solve cosine x equals negative root 3 over 2 for x between 0 and 2 pi.
items.right: Correct. Reference angle pi over 6, and negative cosine puts the points in quadrants two and three.
wrong: You used the wrong reference angle. Cosine of pi over 3 is one half, not root 3 over 2. Root 3 over 2 belongs to pi over 6, and the negative sign moves you to quadrants two and three.

Those are the quadrant two and three angles for reference angle pi over 3, which would give cosine negative one half. For negative root 3 over 2 the reference angle is pi over 6, giving 5 pi over 6 and 7 pi over 6.

This is the commonest wrong answer: the reference angle used as if the number were positive. Those angles solve cosine x equals positive root 3 over 2. Cosine is the x coordinate, so a negative value means the left side of the circle, quadrants two and three: 5 pi over 6 and 7 pi over 6.
items.concept: Check the sign before the size: negative cosine means quadrants two and three.
items.hint: Which side of the circle has negative x?

items.q: True or false: for 2 cosine x plus root 3 equals 0, writing x equals 5 pi over 6 and x equals 7 pi over 6 is a complete answer.
items.right: Right, false. Those are two angles out of infinitely many; add 2 n pi, n any integer, to each.
items.wrong: The unit circle closes on itself, so an angle that works still works after any number of full turns, forwards or backwards. The two angles are correct, but the complete answer is x equals 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi or 7 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi, where n is any integer. Two answers out of infinity is essentially no answer; the general term is most of the answer. Only when a question restricts x to one turn do the bare angles suffice.
items.concept: A trig equation's solution is a family: base angle plus 2 n pi, n any integer.
items.hint: What happens if you add a full turn to a solution?

items.q: An equation reduces to sine x equals 2. What is the solution?
options: x equals inverse sine of 2 plus 2 n pi
items.right: Correct. Sine is a y coordinate on a circle of radius 1, so it never exceeds 1.
wrong: Two radians is an angle, and sine of 2 radians is about 0.91. The question asks which angle has sine 2, and no angle does, since sine lies between negative 1 and 1.
Inverse sine of 2 does not exist; a calculator returns an error. Sine cannot exceed 1, so the equation has no solution at all, which is a legitimate final answer.
Pi over 2 gives sine equal to 1, the largest sine ever gets. Nothing reaches 2, because sine is the height of a point on a circle of radius 1. The equation has no solution.
items.concept: Sine and cosine lie between negative 1 and 1; beyond that an equation has no solution.
items.hint: What is the largest value sine ever takes?

items.q: Solve cosine theta equals 0 in general.
options: theta equals pi over 2 plus 2 n pi only
theta equals pi over 2 plus n pi
items.right: Correct. Cosine is x, which is zero at the top and bottom of the circle, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2, half a turn apart.
wrong: That family captures pi over 2 but misses 3 pi over 2, the bottom of the circle, where cosine is also zero. The two points are half a turn apart, so one family with n pi covers both: pi over 2 plus n pi.
At theta equals 0 the cosine is 1, not 0. Cosine vanishes where the point sits on the vertical axis, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2, giving pi over 2 plus n pi.

Theta equals n pi is the answer to sine theta equals 0, the neighbouring fact and the slip recorded in class. Test theta equals pi: cosine of pi is negative 1, not 0. Cosine is the x coordinate, zero on the vertical axis at pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2, so theta equals pi over 2 plus n pi.
items.concept: Cosine is zero on the vertical axis: pi over 2 plus n pi. Sine is zero on the horizontal axis: n pi.
items.hint: Where on the circle is the x coordinate zero?

items.q: For 4 sine squared theta equals 3, the answer can be written pi over 3 plus n pi or 2 pi over 3 plus n pi. Why does n pi suffice instead of 2 n pi?
options: Sine repeats every pi, so half a turn is enough
Half the solutions were dropped to save space
The reference angle pi over 3 sets a period of pi
Only sine squared appears, so the opposite point also works
items.right: Correct. Adding pi flips the sign of sine, but squaring erases the sign, so the opposite point is also a solution.
wrong: Sine repeats every 2 pi, not every pi; it is tangent that repeats every pi. The n pi works here for a different reason: only sine squared appears, so sine and negative sine give the same value, and the point half a turn away is also a solution.

Nothing is dropped. Taking both square roots gives sine theta equals plus or minus root 3 over 2, four angles per turn, and the two n pi families list all four: pi over 3, 4 pi over 3, 2 pi over 3, 5 pi over 3. The equation is blind to the sign of sine, so half turns stay inside the solution set.

The reference angle does not set the step size. What matters is whether the equation can tell plus from minus. Here sine appears only squared, so a solution plus pi is still a solution, and n pi covers everything.
items.concept: Use n pi only when a solution plus pi is still a solution; test it rather than assume it.
items.hint: Does the equation notice the sign of sine?

items.q: For 2 cosine theta sine theta minus cosine theta equals 0, what is the right first move?
options: Divide both sides by cosine theta
Replace cosine theta with 1 minus sine theta
Take the square root of both sides
items.right: Correct. It becomes cosine theta times 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0, and the zero-product rule splits it into two easy equations.
wrong: Dividing by cosine theta silently assumes cosine theta is not zero, and cosine theta equals 0 is exactly one branch of the answer, theta equals pi over 2 plus n pi. Cancelling deletes it. Factor instead and set each factor to zero.

There is no identity that turns cosine into 1 minus sine; the Pythagorean identity relates the squares. And no conversion is needed here, because both terms already share the factor cosine theta. Factor it out.
Nothing is squared and alone here. The shape is a common factor in every term, so factor out cosine theta and apply the zero-product rule.
items.concept: Common factor in every term: factor and split; never divide by something that could be zero.
items.hint: What do both terms share?

items.q: True or false: dividing both sides of 2 cosine theta sine theta equals cosine theta by cosine theta loses solutions.
items.right: Right. It throws away every angle where cosine theta is zero, the whole branch pi over 2 plus n pi.
items.wrong: Division by cosine theta is only valid where cosine theta is not zero, so the step quietly excludes pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2, which do satisfy the original equation: at pi over 2 both sides are zero. The safe route is to bring everything to one side, factor out cosine theta, and use the zero-product rule, which keeps both branches: cosine theta equals 0, giving pi over 2 plus n pi, and sine theta equals one half. It is the same trap as dividing x times x minus 4 by x.
items.concept: Never divide an equation by a factor that could be zero; factor and split instead.
items.hint: Which angles make cosine theta zero, and do they satisfy the original?

items.q: What tactic fits 2 sine squared x minus 3 sine x plus 1 equals 0?
options: Substitute y for sine x and factor the quadratic
Take the square root of both sides
Divide every term by sine x
Replace sine squared x by 1 minus cosine squared x
items.right: Correct. It becomes 2 y squared minus 3 y plus 1, which factors as 2 y minus 1 times y minus 1, then undo the substitution.
wrong: Square roots only work when the squared function sits alone. Here there is also a first-power term, so the equation is a quadratic in disguise. Let y equal sine x, factor 2 y squared minus 3 y plus 1, and then return to sine x equals one half or sine x equals 1.

Dividing by sine x leaves a lone sine x and a 1 over sine x term, which is worse, and it assumes sine x is not zero. The shape is a squared term plus a first-power term plus a constant: substitute and factor.
Converting to cosine would introduce a cosine squared alongside a sine x, mixing two functions where you currently have one. The equation is already in sine alone; substitute y for sine x and factor.
items.concept: A squared and a first power of the same function: substitute, factor, then undo the substitution.
items.hint: Does it look like a quadratic if you rename sine x?

items.q: After substituting y for sine x, you get y equals one half or y equals 1. What comes next?
options: Add 2 n pi to one half and to 1
Take the inverse sine of x and add 2 n pi
Undo the substitution and solve each sine equation
Stop; y equals one half and y equals 1 are the answers
items.right: Correct. The question asked for x, so each y value becomes a trig equation to read off the circle.
wrong: One half and 1 are values of sine, not angles, so adding 2 n pi to them is meaningless. First return to sine x equals one half and sine x equals 1, then read the angles and attach 2 n pi to those.
Inverse sine applies to a value of sine, not to x. Write sine x equals one half and sine x equals 1, then find the angles on the unit circle: pi over 6, 5 pi over 6 and pi over 2, each plus 2 n pi.

Y was a temporary name for sine x, so y equals one half is not a solution of anything that was asked. Reverse the substitution: sine x equals one half gives pi over 6 and 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi, and sine x equals 1 gives pi over 2 plus 2 n pi.
items.concept: Every substitution must be reversed before the unit circle is consulted.
items.hint: What did y stand for?

items.q: An equation contains both cosine squared x and sine x. What is the first move?
options: Replace cosine squared x with 1 minus sine squared x
Replace sine x with 1 minus cosine x everywhere
Divide every term by cosine squared x first
Take the square root of both sides first
items.right: Correct. The Pythagorean identity turns it into an equation in sine alone, which you can then substitute and factor.
wrong: There is no identity linking sine x to 1 minus cosine x; the Pythagorean identity relates the squares. Convert the squared term instead: cosine squared x equals 1 minus sine squared x, leaving an equation in sine only.

Dividing by cosine squared would create tangent and secant terms and assumes cosine is not zero. The cleaner move is the identity: cosine squared x equals 1 minus sine squared x, so everything becomes sine.
With two different functions and a first-power term, a square root gets you nowhere. First reduce to one function with the Pythagorean identity, then substitute and factor.
items.concept: Mixed squares and first powers: use the Pythagorean identity to get one function, then substitute.
items.hint: Which identity rewrites cosine squared in terms of sine?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §4 Why the wire is not copper-coloured; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-e481f1086b39 (Why the wire is silver)
items.q: The practice wire is copper but looks silver on the reel. What has been done to it, and why?
options: It is aluminium wire, which is naturally silver in colour
Tin plated over it, to stop oxidation and keep it solderable
Solder mask sprayed on it, to insulate the conductor from shorts
items.right: Right. A thin tin coating over the copper. Tin takes the oxidation so the copper underneath stays clean and wets easily.
wrong: The colour fools you, but the conductor is copper. Only the surface is silver, because a thin layer of tin has been plated over it. Copper oxidises; tin takes that oxidation instead, so the wire stays clean and solderable.

Solder mask is a coating on circuit boards, not wire, and it is meant to keep solder off. The wire's silver coat does the opposite job: it keeps the copper surface clean so solder wets it easily. The coating is tin over copper, there to prevent oxidation.
items.concept: Tinned copper: a thin tin coat protects the copper from oxidation and keeps it easy to wet.
items.hint: Think about what happens to bare copper left in the air, and what a thin coat could prevent.

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-e481f1086b39 (Why the wire is silver)
items.q: True or false: because the wire is tin plated, the silver surface guarantees it is rated for a particular current.
items.right: Right, false. Plating protects the surface. Current rating depends on conductor size, insulation and operating conditions.
items.wrong: The tempting thought is that the coating preserves the copper, so the current rating is preserved too. But the tin only helps protect the surface and keep it solderable. How much current a wire can safely carry depends on the size of the copper, the insulation, the temperature and how it is installed. A silver surface tells you it is tinned; it does not certify a rating. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Tinning protects the surface; it does not set the wire's current rating.
items.hint: Separate what the coating does for the surface from what decides current capacity.

items.q: You grip tinned copper wire hard with sharp serrated plier jaws to form a hook. What is the risk?
options: The wire overheats and the insulation nearby is damaged by it
No real risk; serrations only matter on bare aluminium conductors
The teeth cut through the tin into the copper, inviting corrosion
items.right: Right. Serrations cut through the thin tin coat into the copper, and that bare spot is exactly where corrosion can start.
wrong: Pliers are a mechanical hazard here, not a thermal one. Nothing is hot when you form the wire. The problem is that sharp teeth bite through the thin tin coating into the copper, and a break in the coating is a place where the copper can corrode. Use smooth, flat jaws for tinned wire.

The risk is real on tinned copper. The coating exists to keep the copper sealed from the air, and sharp serrations cut straight through it. Every tooth mark is a small patch of bare copper that can corrode. Use smooth or fine jaws on tinned wire and keep the serrated ones for work where the surface does not matter.
items.concept: Serrated jaws cut through the tin coating; use smooth flat jaws on tinned wire.
items.hint: What is the coating for, and what do sharp teeth do to a thin coating?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §4 Solder and flux
items.q: What is the name of the agent in the core of the solder wire whose job is to remove oxide so the solder can wet the metal?
items.right: Correct, flux. It strips the oxide so the molten solder can bond to clean metal instead of sitting on top.
items.wrong: Inside the solder wire runs a core of flux. Oxide on a metal surface blocks solder from bonding, so flux chemically removes that oxide while the joint heats. That is what lets the solder wet the metal, spreading and bonding instead of balling up on top. Remember it as the cleaner that travels inside the solder.
items.concept: Flux is the oxide remover carried in the core of the solder wire.
items.hint: It travels inside the solder wire and cleans the metal as the joint heats.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §4 Solder and flux; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-7bbe793ba617 (When is core flux enough)
items.q: What is flux actually for in a solder joint?
options: Adding mechanical strength to the finished joint
Cooling the joint quickly so it sets hard
Removing oxide so the solder can wet the metal
items.right: Right. Flux strips oxide from the surfaces so the molten solder bonds to clean metal instead of sitting on top.
wrong: Strength comes from the mechanical forming and from solder wetting clean metal, not from flux. Flux is a cleaner. It removes the oxide that would stop the solder bonding. Once the joint is made, the flux has done its work and contributes nothing structural.
Flux has nothing to do with cooling. It acts while the joint is hot, chemically removing oxide so the solder can wet the metal. Think of it as clearing the surface, not setting the solder.
items.concept: Flux removes oxide; wetting needs clean metal, and flux provides it.
items.hint: Ask what stops solder from sticking to metal, and what flux does about it.

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-7bbe793ba617 (When is core flux enough)
items.q: True or false: on a surface that is already heavily oxidised, the flux inside the solder core is always enough by itself.
items.right: Right, false. Core flux may do the job on fresh tinned wire, but an oxidised surface needs cleaning and extra flux.
items.wrong: It is easy to assume the core flux handles any surface because it handles the practice wire. On fresh, clean, tinned wire it may be sufficient, and you know because the solder wets. On an already oxidised surface there is more oxide than that small amount of flux can clear. The solder then sits on top instead of bonding. Clean the surface and use approved extra flux. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Core flux may suffice on clean tinned wire; oxidised metal needs cleaning and extra flux.
items.hint: Compare a fresh tinned wire with an old dull one. Is there the same amount of oxide?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5 Two round wires barely touch; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-6bbfe89924ca (Two round wires)
items.q: True or false: two crossed round wires share heat freely with each other, because metal is touching metal.
items.right: Right, false. Two round surfaces meet at essentially one point, and almost no heat crosses a point.
items.wrong: Metal touching metal sounds like a good heat path, but what matters is contact area. Two round wires crossing meet at essentially a single point. Heat the top wire and very little of that heat reaches the bottom one. That is why solder can wet one wire and leave the other cold. The statement is false, and it is the reason the thermal bridge technique exists.
items.concept: Crossed round wires touch at a point; contact area, not contact itself, carries heat.
items.hint: Picture two round pencils crossed. How much of each surface is really touching?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5 Build a thermal bridge
items.q: A small amount of solder is placed deliberately where the iron meets the work, so heat flows into both wires at once. What is this technique called?
items.right: Correct, a thermal bridge. The molten solder spreads the contact so heat reaches both wires together.
items.wrong: The name is thermal bridge, or heat bridge. Two crossed wires barely touch, so heat does not cross from one to the other. A little solder at the iron and work contact bridges that gap thermally, spreading the contact and conducting heat into both wires at once. It is a deliberate step, done before the main solder is fed.
items.concept: The thermal bridge: a little solder at the iron contact that carries heat into both parts.
items.hint: It bridges a gap, but the gap it bridges is a heat gap, not an electrical one.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5 Build a thermal bridge; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-32ae96d40b92 (Build the bridge)
items.q: Where exactly does the small amount of solder for a thermal bridge go?
options: Anywhere on the workpiece near the joint
Only on the iron tip, kept away from the joint
Right where the iron tip touches the joint
items.right: Right. At the iron and work contact, so the molten solder spreads that contact and conducts heat into both wires.
wrong: Location is the whole technique. Solder somewhere nearby does not connect the iron to both wires thermally. The bridge has to form exactly where the tip meets the joint, so the molten solder widens that contact and carries heat into both parts at once.

Solder that stays on the tip away from the joint never touches the wires, so it cannot bridge anything. The bridge is molten solder at the point where the tip touches the work. There it spreads the contact and moves heat into both wires.
items.concept: The thermal bridge forms at the iron and work contact, nowhere else.
items.hint: The solder has to touch the iron and both wires at the same time. Where is that?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5 Why you feed from the far side; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-69c5ae193bd3 (Feed from the far side)
items.q: Why feed the solder to the side of the joint opposite the iron, instead of melting it on the tip?
options: It keeps the iron tip cleaner while you make the joint
It uses noticeably less solder than feeding it at the iron
Solder melting there proves the work is hot, not just the iron
items.right: Right. If the far side melts the solder, the joint has reached temperature. If not, wait; the work tells you when.
wrong: A cleaner tip is not the reason. The far side is a thermometer. When solder melts against the side away from the iron, you know the metal of the joint is hot enough to bond. Melting solder on the tip tells you only that the tip is hot.

Solder quantity is not the point. Feeding from the far side confirms that the work has reached temperature, because only a hot joint can melt solder on the side the iron is not touching. That is how you know it is time, instead of counting seconds.
items.concept: Far-side feeding proves the joint is hot; the work tells you when, not a stopwatch.
items.hint: Think of the solder as a thermometer. Which side of the joint would prove the metal is hot?

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-69c5ae193bd3 (Feed from the far side)
items.q: True or false: if the far side will not melt the solder, melting it on the iron and wiping it across the joint is an acceptable shortcut.
items.right: Right, false. A wipe-on blob sits on cold metal and never bonds. Keep the iron in place and let the heat go in.
items.wrong: The shortcut feels productive because the joint suddenly looks covered. But solder melted on the tip and wiped onto metal that has not reached temperature does not wet that metal. You get a blob that looks finished and was never bonded. If the far side will not melt the solder, the joint is not ready: leave the iron there and wait. So the statement is false.
items.concept: A wipe-on blob has never bonded; wait for the work to melt the solder.
items.hint: What does the far side not melting tell you about the metal underneath?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5 Two round wires barely touch
items.q: Solder has wetted one of two crossed wires but never bonded to the other, which stayed too cool. The joint looks finished but is not. What is this defect called?
items.right: Correct, a cold joint. Heat never reached the second wire, so the solder never bonded to it.
items.wrong: This is a cold joint: a joint where one part never got hot enough for the solder to wet it. On crossed round wires it happens when heat goes into one wire and cannot cross the point contact to the other. The solder wets the hot wire and lies against the cold one without bonding. It can look complete and still be weak and unreliable, which is what makes it dangerous.
items.concept: A cold joint: solder wetted one part but not the other because heat never arrived.
items.hint: The defect is named after what the second wire was when the solder touched it.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5 What a finished joint looks like; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-91662951aa20 (Name the curve)
items.q: On a finished joint there is a concave, feathered curve where the solder meets each wire. What is that feature called?
items.right: Correct, the fillet. Surface tension pulls wetted solder into that concave curve; you do not shape it yourself.
items.wrong: The concave curve where solder meets the metal is the fillet. It forms on its own when solder has wetted clean, hot metal: surface tension pulls the molten solder into a feathered, inward curve. A convex ball or a rolled edge means wetting did not happen. Not to be confused with the thermal bridge, which is a heating technique, or the wrap, which is the mechanical winding.
items.concept: The fillet is the concave curve of wetted solder, made by surface tension.
items.hint: It is the same word used for a curved inside corner in metalwork.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5 What a finished joint looks like; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-e459428c9094 (Which force wins)
items.q: What pulls the solder into the concave, feathered fillet on a small joint?
options: Gravity pulling the molten solder downward onto the joint
The angle at which you hold the iron against the joint
Surface tension acting on solder that has wetted the metal
items.right: Right. Surface tension, the same property that shapes a water droplet, pulls wetted solder into the curve.
wrong: Gravity is a much smaller influence at this scale, not literally absent, and it is not what makes the curve. The shape comes from surface tension acting on solder that has bonded to clean, hot metal. If the metal is not wetted, no orientation of the joint produces a fillet.

The iron angle affects how you work, not the shape of the finished solder. The fillet is made by surface tension pulling solder that has wetted the metal into a concave curve. You do not shape it; you create the conditions and it forms itself.
items.concept: Surface tension, not gravity or the iron, shapes the fillet once the solder wets.
items.hint: The guide compares it to the property that shapes a water droplet.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5 The stranded-wire test; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-63725fe75a6f (The stranded-wire test)
items.q: After soldering a stranded, tinned wire, what should you still be able to see, and what does a smooth featureless blob mean?
options: Bare copper strands poking out; a blob means it wetted well
Nothing but shiny solder; a blob means a strong joint
The individual strands; a blob means too much solder
items.right: Right. The solder should be a thin layer wetted into the strands. If it buries them, there is too much solder.
wrong: Bare copper poking out means an area that never got soldered at all, which is a different defect. The correct picture is strands visible through a thin layer of solder. A smooth blob means excess solder, not good wetting; it hides the evidence.

A shiny blob is not strength. Solder that buries the strands is simply too much solder, and it hides whether the strands were ever wetted. A sound joint shows the strand outlines through a thin, wetted layer.
items.concept: Strands visible through thin solder is right; a blob hiding them is too much.
items.hint: Which tells an inspector more: seeing the strands, or a smooth silver lump?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §3 Tip care; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-3af79da33ecc (Clean the tip)
items.q: What is the correct way to clean the tip in the brass wool, and why?
options: Wipe and roll it through the wool, shearing the oxide off
Stab it into the wool several times to knock the oxide loose
Rub it on a fine file until the metal is bright
items.right: Right. The wipe and roll shears the oxide off. Do it immediately before each joint, because the oxide re-forms in seconds.
wrong: Stabbing feels thorough but does not shear the oxide off, and it shortens the tip's life. The cleaning action is a wipe and roll as the tip comes out of the wool. Done right before each joint, it leaves a bright tinned surface that moves heat well.

Never file a tip. It is plated, and a file cuts straight through the plating, ruining it. A tip that will not take solder after proper cleaning is replaced, not resurfaced. Normal cleaning is a wipe and roll through brass wool.
items.concept: Wipe and roll through brass wool before every joint; never stab, never file.
items.hint: One motion cleans by shearing; the other just pokes. Which one drags the surface across the wool?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §3 Tip care; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-c6ce26530054 (Which face of the tip)
items.q: With a wedge tip, why do you place its flat face against the work rather than the rounded edge?
options: Contact area carries heat; the flat face touches far more surface
The flat face runs hotter than the rest of the tip
The rounded edge concentrates heat into one spot too strongly
items.right: Right. Heat moves through contact area. The flat face touches over an area; the rounded edge touches at a point and moves almost nothing.
wrong: The tip is one piece of metal at one temperature; the flat face is not hotter. What differs is contact area. The flat face touches the work over a surface, so heat flows in. The rounded edge touches at a point and transfers almost nothing.

That has it backwards. A point contact does not concentrate heat into the work; it barely transfers any, because so little surface is touching. The flat face moves more heat precisely because more area is in contact. Area, not temperature alone, carries heat.
items.concept: Contact area moves heat: flat face on the work, not the rounded edge.
items.hint: Two surfaces at the same temperature; one touches over an area, one at a point. Which moves more heat?

items.q: A joint is slow to heat. Which change should you make first, before touching the temperature setting?
options: Turn the station temperature up as hot as it will go
Hold the iron on the joint until it eventually looks right
Improve tip contact and tip choice, keeping dwell time short
items.right: Right. Use the approved bench setting and fix the contact. Good contact and short dwell time control the heat, not a higher number.
wrong: A hotter tip can move heat faster, but it also raises the damage risk and it does not guarantee less total heat in the component. Slow heating usually means poor contact: a dirty tip, the wrong face, the wrong size. Fix that first at the approved setting.

Dwell time is heat. Sitting on a joint that is not heating properly just pours heat into the surroundings and the component. The cure is better contact, a clean tip and the right tip shape, so the joint reaches temperature promptly at the approved setting.
items.concept: Fix contact and tip choice first; temperature alone does not guarantee less heat or less damage.
items.hint: What is more likely wrong on a slow joint: the number on the display, or how the tip is touching?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §3 The station; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-8922123c8d24 (Sleep mode)
items.q: The station drops into sleep mode when the iron is parked in its sensing stand. About how long after you lift the iron is it back at working temperature? Answer in seconds.
items.right: Correct, about five seconds. Sleep exists to extend tip life, so let it work rather than defeating it.
items.wrong: The stand senses when the iron is parked and the station drops the temperature to protect the tip. Lifting the iron brings it back to working temperature in about five seconds. That short recovery is why there is no reason to leave the iron out of the stand to keep it hot; doing so only wears the tip for nothing.

slips.why: Thirty seconds would be an annoying wait, and that is not what the station does. Recovery is about five seconds, which is why letting the iron sleep costs you nothing.
One second is faster than the station recovers. The stated figure is about five seconds, short but not instant.

items.concept: Sleep mode recovers in about five seconds; it exists to extend tip life.
items.hint: It is short enough that you would never notice the wait while positioning the work.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §3 Setting up for your own handedness; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-e3619500cce1 (Whose bench is this)
items.q: You sit down at a bench set up for someone with the opposite dominant hand. Where should the iron stand go?
options: On your dominant side, close to the work
Wherever the previous student left it
As far from the work as possible, for safety
items.right: Right. Close, on your own side, so you never reach a hot iron across your work and the trip to the stand is short.
wrong: Its position matters because the previous layout was built for the other hand. Left as is, you reach a hot iron across the joint every time. Move the stand to your dominant side, close to the work, so the iron's path is short and never crosses your work.

Distance is not safety here. A far stand means a long reach with a hot iron over your own joint every time you park it. Close and on your dominant side keeps the hot tip's path short and away from the work.
items.concept: Stand on your dominant side, close to the work; pad forward; cords uncoiled.
items.hint: Which layout keeps the hot tip's travel shortest and off your work?

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-a29751522345 (Why the fume extraction runs)
items.q: What does the bench fume extraction remove, and why does it matter that the switches are ganged?
options: Heat from the iron; each switch controls only its own station
Wire-cutting dust; ganging is only a wiring shortcut for the room
Solder and flux smoke; one switch turns on every station's extraction
items.right: Right. It pulls the smoke from burning flux and melting solder away from you, and one switch affects everyone on the circuit.
wrong: Extraction is not cooling. It removes the smoke given off as flux burns and solder melts, so you do not breathe it. And the switches are ganged: turning one on turns them all on, so what you do at your bench affects the whole room.

Wire cuttings are not smoke. The extraction targets the fumes from flux and solder. Ganging matters because a single switch controls every station on that circuit, so switching it changes the extraction for your classmates too.
items.concept: Extraction removes flux and solder smoke; the ganged switch runs every station.
items.hint: Think about what rises from the joint while you solder, and who else shares the switch.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §2 and §4 (hand-wash station; lead-tin solder); cf. Practice Q EFAB202-cd28e251f0df (Why wash your hands after soldering)
items.q: There is a hand-wash station in the soldering room and you are expected to use it after soldering. Which metal in the solder alloy makes that necessary?
items.right: Correct, lead. The solder is a lead and tin alloy, and residue on your hands can reach your face or food later.
items.wrong: The solder used in the lab is a lead and tin alloy. Lead is the reason for the hand wash: residue on your hands does not stay at the bench, it travels to your face, your food and your belongings. You are not eating in the lab, but you will touch your face and eat later, so wash after handling solder and before you leave. Flux and brass wool are not the concern here.
items.concept: Leaded solder: wash your hands after soldering, before food, face or leaving.
items.hint: The alloy has two metals. One of them is the reason for washing.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §6 Reading the combination tool; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-5e2864acb96b (Match the crimp die)
items.q: The combination tool's crimp dies are coloured red, yellow and blue. How do you choose the die?
options: Any die works, provided you squeeze the handles hard enough
Choose it by the colour of the wire's own insulation
Match the die colour to the insulated terminal's colour
items.right: Right. Die colour matches terminal colour, and the terminal goes in the correct way round against the flat and round sides.
wrong: Extra squeezing does not fix a die sized for a different terminal; it crushes or under-compresses it. Each colour matches a terminal colour and size range. Match the colours, seat the terminal the right way round, and squeeze fully.

The wire's insulation colour is unrelated. The colour code matches the die to the insulated terminal's colour, which is sized for a wire gauge range. Match die to terminal, then mind the flat side and round side orientation.
items.concept: Match crimp die colour to the terminal colour; orient the terminal correctly; squeeze fully.
items.hint: The colour code is on the die and on one other thing you are holding. Which?

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-5e2864acb96b (Match the crimp die)
items.q: True or false: after making a good crimp, you should flow a little solder into it for extra security.
items.right: Right, false. A crimp is a complete connection on its own. Crimp or solder, never both.
items.wrong: Adding solder feels like belt and braces, but a properly made crimp is a finished connection. The rule from the lab is crimp or solder, not both. The hand tool is a compromise compared with production ratcheting crimpers, and that is why seating the terminal properly and squeezing fully matters; solder afterwards is not the fix. So the statement is false.
items.concept: A crimp is complete by itself; it is not soldered afterwards.
items.hint: The lab rule was two words joined by or, not by and.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §6 Reading the combination tool
items.q: The combination tool has a row of stripping holes. What do you match a hole to before stripping a wire?
options: The length of insulation to remove
items.right: Right. The holes are sized by gauge. Practice wire was twelve gauge and you move to twenty-two gauge, so the hole changes.
wrong: Colour tells you nothing about conductor size. The stripping holes are sized by wire gauge so the blade cuts the insulation without nicking the copper. Pick the hole for the gauge in your hand: the practice wire is heavier than the twenty-two gauge you move to.
How much insulation you remove is set by where you place the wire, not by which hole. The hole is chosen by wire gauge so it cuts insulation cleanly without biting the conductor.
items.concept: Stripping holes are sized by wire gauge; match the hole to the wire.
items.hint: What property of the wire decides how big the hole must be?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §2 Cutters; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-2df491175614 (Flush versus side cutters)
items.q: What is the practical difference between flush cutters and side cutters?
options: Flush cutters cut cleanly; side cutters tend to fold the wire
They cut identically; only the price and the brand differ
Side cutters cut flat and clean; flush cutters fold the wire
items.right: Right. Flush cutters are spring loaded with blades that cross over and cut clean; side cutters tend to fold the wire.
wrong: The cut itself is different. Flush cutters, spring loaded with crossing blades, leave a clean cut. Side cutters, the older squeeze and release design, tend to fold the wire as they cut. Price is not the distinction the lab drew.

That is reversed. It is the flush cutter that leaves the clean, flat cut. The side cutter is the long-standing design and tends to fold the wire as the blades close. Either is acceptable for the course, but know which does what.
items.concept: Flush cutters cut clean; side cutters tend to fold the wire; either is acceptable.
items.hint: One design is spring loaded with blades that cross over. What kind of cut does that give?

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-2df491175614 (Flush versus side cutters)
items.q: True or false: for this course you need to own both flush cutters and side cutters.
items.right: Right, false. Either one is acceptable. What matters is having a cutter of the right size.
items.wrong: Because both were described, it is easy to think both are required. They are not. One cutter, either flush or side, is enough, provided it is the right size, the size that was passed around in class. Spend the money on one good pair rather than two cheap ones; the bargain sets were described as unusable. So the statement is false.
items.concept: One cutter, flush or side, of the right size, is enough.
items.hint: The lab was specific: either, not both.

items.q: Why should you not lend your wire cutters, and what do you do if a classmate genuinely needs a cut made?
options: They mostly get lost; lend them if they promise to return them
No real risk; lend them and remind the borrower to be careful
Hard wire can notch the blades for good; make the cut yourself
items.right: Right. A pair used on tungsten came back with a notch bitten out, and that cannot be repaired. Make the cut for them instead.
wrong: Loss is a minor worry next to the real one. Cutters are rated for soft wire; someone cutting tungsten, which is roughly ten times harder, leaves a semicircular notch that cannot be repaired. Keep the tool in your hand and make the cut for them.

There is a real risk, and a reminder does not prevent it. A borrowed pair came back notched because the borrower cut tungsten. A notched blade is ruined. If someone needs a cut, make it for them rather than handing the tool over.
items.concept: Cutters are ruined by wire beyond their rating; make the cut yourself instead of lending.
items.hint: Think about what a much harder metal does to a blade made for soft copper.

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-af21b392b8a2 (Diagnosing by how much solder you used)
items.q: You kept adding solder before the joint finally looked acceptable. What does that pattern tell you, and what do you do?
options: Suspect heat, cleanliness or wetting; reheat and redo both parts
Nothing; needing extra solder is normal on small practice joints
Paint a little more solder over the top to finish it neatly
items.right: Right. Extra solder was compensating for a joint that never wetted. Redo the whole joint rather than covering it.
wrong: It is not normal. A joint that wets properly pulls into a concave fillet without extra solder. Needing more and more means heat, cleanliness or wetting failed, and the solder was only hiding it. Stop, inspect both parts, clean, and rework.

Painting solder over the top covers the evidence and relies on a bond that is not there. The amount of solder you needed is the warning. Reheat and redo both parts of the joint so the solder actually wets the metal.
items.concept: If you had to add extra solder to make it look right, the joint is wrong; redo it.
items.hint: A good fillet forms by itself. What does needing to force it suggest?

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-20a63ed55fb1 (Hot but still failing)
items.q: A joint was definitely hot enough, yet the solder rolled under itself and lifted away on one side. What was wrong, and what do you do?
options: The iron must have been too cool; turn the temperature up
The solder was defective; keep adding until it stops rolling
That surface was not clean; clean and reflux it, then rework
items.right: Right. Hot is not sufficient. If the metal carries oxide or contamination, solder will not stick however much heat arrives.
wrong: Heat was adequate; that was given. Turning the temperature up attacks the wrong condition. The rolled-under region is a region where nothing was stuck, and the usual cause when heat was fine is a surface that was not clean. Clean it, reflux it, and redo the joint.

More solder on an unwetted surface just makes a bigger unwetted lump. Rolling under with adequate heat points first to contamination or oxide on that side. Clean and reflux the surface, then rework the whole joint.
items.concept: Both parts must be hot and clean; when heat was fine, suspect cleanliness.
items.hint: There are two conditions for wetting. One was satisfied. Which one is left?

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-04b8fce06c3a (Two wires, two heating rates)
items.q: You are joining a light wire to a much heavier one that heats slowly. Where does the iron go, and how do you confirm both are hot?
options: Light wire; count a fixed number of seconds before feeding
Split the heat evenly; check only the wire under the iron
Heavy slow wire; watch which side the solder flows toward
items.right: Right. Put the iron where the slow part is and let the fast one come along. The solder flows toward the side that is actually hot.
wrong: The light wire heats fast anyway. Putting the iron there leaves the heavy wire cold, and counting seconds tells you nothing about the work. Heat the slow part, and read the joint: solder flows toward the side that has reached temperature.

An even split ignores that the two have different thermal mass. Concentrate the iron on the heavy, slow wire and let the light one come along. Then watch which way the solder flows; that shows which side is actually hot, not just the one under the tip.
items.concept: Iron on the slow part; solder flows toward whichever side is truly hot.
items.hint: Which wire needs the help, and what does the solder do that tells you the truth?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §4 The hook joint; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-c06c37ff22ce (Wrapping a hook joint)
items.q: While wrapping a hook joint around a terminal, how do you keep the wrap tight?
options: Wrap loosely first, then tighten all the turns at the end
Use only the pliers and never let a finger touch the loop
Finger inside the loop, pushing each turn hard against the last
items.right: Right. A finger inside the loop pulls the wire onto the post so each turn sits hard against the previous one, with no gaps.
wrong: A loose wrap does not tighten afterwards; the turns stay standing off the post with gaps between them. Tightness is built turn by turn, with a finger inside the loop pushing each new turn hard against the last.

Pliers alone leave the wire standing off the post, and you finish with daylight between the turns. The technique is physical: finger inside the loop, wrap tight, each turn pressed against the previous one.
items.concept: Finger inside the loop, each turn pressed against the last, no gaps anywhere.
items.hint: What is inside the loop while you wrap, giving you something to pull against?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §4 The hook joint; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-c06c37ff22ce (Wrapping a hook joint)
items.q: What is the minimum number of turns for a hook joint wrap? Answer with a plain number.
items.right: Correct, a minimum of six turns, each pushed tight against the last, then the ends clipped and bent in.
items.wrong: The stated minimum is six turns. Fewer turns give less mechanical hold, and the mechanical wrap is what actually holds a hook joint; the solder only fills it. Six tight turns, no gaps, ends clipped so nothing pokes out and the remainder bent in tight.

slips.why: Three turns is half the stated minimum. The wrap is the mechanical hold, so the lab asks for at least six tight turns.
Two turns is far short. The requirement is a minimum of six turns, pressed tight against each other.

items.concept: Hook joint: at least six tight turns; the wrap holds, the solder fills.
items.hint: It is more than a handful and it is an even number.

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-a5f9397ff67f (Gaps in the wrap)
items.q: True or false: if you can see daylight between two turns of a hook wrap, solder added afterwards will fill the gap and make the joint sound.
items.right: Right, false. Solder fills a tight wrap; it does not close a gap the forming left. Undo the wrap and do it again.
items.wrong: It feels like solder should flow in and fill the gap. But the mechanical wrap is what holds the joint; solder bonds a wrap that is already tight. It cannot replace the missing contact, and a gap it bridges is not a mechanical hold. If you can see daylight in the wrap, undo it and re-form it tight before soldering. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Solder does not close a gap the forming left; re-wrap tight, then solder.
items.hint: Which does the holding: the wrap, or the solder?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §4 The gap at the insulation; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-d161bf1697e5 (The insulation gap)
items.q: On a hook terminal there is a deliberate gap between the end of the insulation and the start of the joint. How long is it?
options: Equal to the diameter of the bare conductor inside it
Equal to the diameter of that wire's own insulation
A fixed one millimetre, the same for every wire
items.right: Right. Measure the gap against the insulation on the same wire; that is what the specification is referenced to.
wrong: It is the insulation, not the conductor inside it, that sets the gap. The rule is gap length equals the diameter of the insulation on that same wire. Hold the wire next to the gap and compare.

There is no fixed number. The gap scales with the wire: its length equals the outside diameter of that wire's own insulation, so a heavier wire gets a bigger gap. Measure it against the wire in your hand.
items.concept: Insulation gap equals the diameter of that wire's own insulation.
items.hint: The reference is on the wire you are holding, not in a table.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §3 The pad; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-76840cbb81ff (Pad rules)
items.q: A wire is soldered onto a board pad. Which of these is actually required?
options: Solder must never extend past the edge of the pad
The pad must be completely covered over with solder
The wire sits within the pad, with nothing overhanging
items.right: Right. The wire stays on the pad, trimmed shorter if needed. Solder over the edge is fine, full coverage is not needed, the fillet is what counts.
wrong: Solder going over the pad edge does not matter. What the lab requires is that the wire itself sits on the pad with nothing running past it, and that a concave fillet forms where wire meets pad. Trim the wire shorter rather than let it overhang.

Fully covering the pad is not required. The requirements are that the wire lies within the pad boundary and that the wire-to-pad junction shows a concave fillet. How much of the pad is silver is not the criterion.
items.concept: Wire on the pad, nothing overhanging; the concave fillet is what matters.
items.hint: One of these is about the wire's position; the other two are about how much solder shows.

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-b9e38d372c2a (Testing a butt joint)
items.q: Why is a butt joint discouraged for anything structural, even when it is well made?
options: Solder cannot properly wet the cut end of a wire
It is held only at the cut end faces of the metal
It always looks visibly worse than other joints
items.right: Right. The contact area is just the end faces, with no mechanical interlock, so it can look fine and still be the weakest thing on the board.
wrong: Solder does wet the end face; that is how the joint is made at all. The problem is how little there is to hold: only the end faces touch, with no mechanical interlock. That is why it is tested by pulling hard, and why it is not used structurally.

That is the trap: a butt joint can pass a visual inspection. The weakness is not visible. It comes from geometry: the only contact is the cut end face of the metal, with no overlap and no wrap, so there is very little holding it.
items.concept: A butt joint is held only at the end faces; it can look fine and still be weak.
items.hint: How much metal is actually in contact when two wire ends meet end to end?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §4 Bus wire, stranded wire and turrets; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-7cb0a1b644f4 (Stranded wire)
items.q: Preparing stranded wire for a hook joint has three steps. In what order?
options: Tin, form the loop, then twist
Twist, tin, then form the loop
Form the loop, twist, then tin
items.right: Right. Twist the strands together, tin them so they behave as one wire, then form the loop, which now holds its shape.
wrong: Tinning loose, untwisted strands does not gather them into one conductor first. The order is twist to consolidate, tin to bind, then form the loop. Tinning first is what lets the bundle hold the loop's shape well.

Forming first leaves loose strands that hold the loop's shape poorly, and twisting after forming is awkward. Twist first to gather the strands, tin to bind them, then form; the tinned bundle bends like a single wire.
items.concept: Stranded wire: twist, tin, then form the loop, in that order.
items.hint: Which step turns many loose strands into something that bends like one wire?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §4 Bus wire, stranded wire and turrets; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-b74600be2af6 (Turrets)
items.q: True or false: for a turret terminal, you tin the wire to the turret first and then attach the turret to the board.
items.right: Right, true. Tin the wire to the turret, then mount it, wrapping about three-quarters of the way round. Get in and out quickly.
items.wrong: The order matters. Tin the wire to the turret first, then attach it to the board, wrapping about three-quarters of the way round before cutting. Turrets are a common source of trouble because heat travels through the post: if you sit on one joint too long, you reflow the joint on the other side. Work quickly and support the piece with a third hand or a vise. So the statement is true.
items.concept: Turret: tin wire to turret first, then attach; about three-quarters round; do not linger.
items.hint: Think about which is easier to do well while the turret is still loose in your hand.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §5 The material and the coatings; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-43c5a82cc12d (Solder mask and silkscreen)
items.q: What is the green coating on a circuit board called, the one that covers everything not meant to be soldered?
items.right: Correct, solder mask. It keeps solder off everything except the pads, which prevents bridges and shorts.
items.wrong: The green layer is the solder mask. It masks off every part of the copper that is not meant to receive solder, leaving only the pads exposed. That is what makes machine soldering possible, and it prevents a great many bridges and shorts in hand soldering too. The white printing on top is a different layer, the silkscreen legend.
items.concept: Solder mask covers everything not meant to be soldered; silkscreen is the printed legend.
items.hint: Its name says what it does: it masks the board from something.

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-2529dd74c993 (Why the board is not copper-coloured)
items.q: The pads on a new board are silver, not copper coloured. Why?
options: The pads are bare copper that looks silver under the lab lights
The pads are aluminium, not copper
A tin based finish protects the copper from oxidising
items.right: Right. Copper oxidises, so a tin coating over the pads oxidises instead, without thinning the copper. Same idea as tinned wire.
wrong: The colour is a real coating, not lighting. Copper oxidises, so a tin based solder finish is laid over the pads; it takes the oxidation instead and keeps the pads solderable. It is the same logic as the tinned practice wire.
The conductor is copper. What you see is a tin based finish over it, applied so the tin oxidises rather than the copper. That protects the pad without thinning the copper and keeps it easy to wet.
items.concept: Silver pads are copper under a protective tin based finish, like tinned wire.
items.hint: You met the same trick in Lab 1, on a different piece of copper.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §5 How many sides you solder; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-e3e441fcae37 (Solder an unplated hole)
items.q: A double-sided board has holes with no copper on the hole wall. A component lead passes through. How many sides do you solder?
options: Both sides, separately; nothing carries between them
Only the side where the component body sits
One side only; the solder wicks through on its own
items.right: Right. With no plating, there is bare fibreglass in the hole, so each face needs its own joint.
wrong: Soldering only the component side leaves the other face unconnected. Without copper in the hole, there is no path between the two faces except what you make. Each side gets its own solder joint.

Wicking through needs a plated barrel: copper for the solder to wet and capillary action to climb. An unplated hole is bare fibreglass, an insulator, so nothing carries through. Solder both sides separately.
items.concept: Unplated hole: no copper inside, so solder each side separately.
items.hint: What is on the wall of the hole, and can solder wet it?

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-9fe2717a81ed (Which side do you solder)
items.q: True or false: in a plated through hole, gravity is what carries the solder down through the hole to the far side.
items.right: Right, false. Wetting and capillary action pull solder up the copper barrel; gravity contributes very little at this scale.
items.wrong: Gravity sounds plausible because the solder is liquid. But the demonstrated process feeds from one side and the solder climbs the plated barrel, against or regardless of gravity, because it wets the copper and capillary action draws it along. That is also why feeding both sides of a plated hole is wasted heat. You still check that the required fill and fillets are present. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Capillary action and wetting fill a plated barrel; gravity is barely involved.
items.hint: Does a small solder fillet change shape when the joint is upside down?

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-39ee3753c1df (Choose a lead form)
items.q: True or false: the fully clinched lead, bent flat along the pad, is the everyday choice for holding a part while you solder.
items.right: Right, false. Clinching gives the most support but is hardest to undo. The everyday choice is setting the lead over to one side.
items.wrong: Clinching sounds best because it holds best, and it does. But it also makes the part hardest to remove later. For everyday work you only need enough support to stop the part falling out, and to be able to undo it easily: that is the lead set over to one side. Straight through is the least support of all. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Set over to one side is the everyday form; clinched is most support, hardest to remove.
items.hint: The everyday choice balances holding the part against being easy to undo.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §5 Lead forming
items.q: What is the name of the lead form where the lead is bent flat along the pad after it comes through the hole, giving the most support?
items.right: Correct, fully clinched. Most support and the lowest part height, but the hardest to remove later.
items.wrong: The lead bent flat along the pad is called clinched, or fully clinched. It gives the most mechanical support and also lowers the part's height, at the cost of being the hardest form to remove. Compare it with straight through, which gives the least support, and set over to one side, which gives enough and is easy to undo.
items.concept: Clinched: bent flat along the pad, most support, lowest height, hardest to remove.
items.hint: The word also describes a boxer holding on tight.

items.source: Practice Q EFAB202-39ee3753c1df (Choose a lead form)
items.q: You clip a component lead after soldering it. What must you check on the cut end?
options: Nothing; clipping the lead is what finishes the joint
That no bare copper end is left sticking out of the solder
That the lead is still long enough to grip with pliers
items.right: Right. Cutting after soldering can expose bare copper. A pre-tinned lead is fine; a bare wire running through must finish covered.
wrong: Clipping can create the defect rather than finish the joint. Cutting through a bare wire leaves an exposed copper end. Check every clipped end; if the lead was tinned before insertion you are fine, otherwise the end must be soldered over.

Length is not the concern once the joint is made; the point of clipping is to shorten it. What matters is the cut face: clipping can leave bare copper sticking out of the solder, and that end must finish covered.
items.concept: After clipping, make sure the cut end finishes covered by solder.
items.hint: What does a cutter expose when it goes through a wire that was not tinned?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §6 Tip discipline
items.q: You wipe the tip in the brass wool and it is still dull. What is the next step in the routine?
options: Go to the joint anyway; the core flux will clean the tip
Turn the station up so the oxide burns off
Add a little fresh solder to the tip, then wipe again
items.right: Right. Fresh solder re-tins the surface, and the second wipe takes the oxide with it. Then go to the joint clean and hot.
wrong: Flux cleans the work, not the tip, and a dull tip moves heat badly. The routine has a next step: add a little fresh solder to the tip and wipe again. Only a bright, tinned tip goes to the joint.

More heat does not remove oxide; it forms oxide faster. Stay at the approved setting. Add fresh solder to the tip, wipe again, and if the tip still will not take solder after proper cleaning, replace it.
items.concept: Check, wipe, and if still dull add fresh solder and wipe again, every time.
items.hint: The fix involves the same material you solder with.

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §6 The diagnostic for a dead tip; cf. Practice Q EFAB202-362d10294d76 (A tip that will not take solder)
items.q: You touch solder to the tip and it pulls away into a ball instead of spreading. What is happening, and what do you do?
options: The iron has lost its heat; wait until the station recovers
That spool of solder has gone bad; try a different spool
Oxide is blocking wetting; clean it properly, replace it if that fails
items.right: Right. Solder balling up is surface tension with no bond, which means an oxide coat on the tip. Clean it; if it will not recover, replace it.
wrong: A cold iron would not melt the solder at all. Here it melts but will not spread, which is a surface problem: oxide on the tip stops the solder wetting it. Clean the tip properly; if it still will not take solder, the tip is replaced.

The solder is fine; it is the tip's surface. Molten solder balling up instead of spreading means it cannot wet an oxidised tip. Use tip cleaner and clean it properly. If that does not recover it, replace the tip rather than filing it.
items.concept: Solder balling on the tip means oxide; clean properly, replace if it will not recover.
items.hint: It melted, so the heat is there. What would stop molten solder from spreading?

items.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection §6 Tip discipline
