items.q: True or false: checking and wiping the tip once at the start of a session is enough, because a clean tip stays clean.
items.right: Right, false. A tinned tip darkens within seconds. Check and wipe every time the iron leaves the holder.
items.wrong: A tip does not stay clean. Freshly cleaned and tinned, it goes from bright to dark in a few seconds as oxide re-forms, and a tip sitting in your hand goes dark while you are deciding. That is why the check and wipe happens every time the iron leaves the holder, immediately before the joint. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Oxide re-forms in seconds; check and wipe the tip every time it leaves the holder.
items.hint: How long does a bright tip stay bright?

lectures.title: Charge, voltage and circuit references
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 01 - Charge, Voltage and Circuit References.md; Kleitz Appendix F

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This first lecture sets up the language we will use for every circuit in the course. We will talk about charge, then about how to label a voltage and a current so that the signs mean something, then about ground as a chosen reference, and finally how to read a fully labelled circuit and a meter. If you hold on to one sentence, make it this one: voltage compares two points, current needs a reference direction, and ground chooses a zero. Everything else today is a consequence of those three ideas. None of it is hard arithmetic. The difficulty, if there is any, is in being careful about which point you are comparing with which, and in which order. Students who get confused about signs later on almost always skipped this step, so it is worth doing slowly now.
segments.expand: Explain why careful labelling of voltage direction and current direction prevents sign errors later, with a short example of a sign going wrong.
segments.eli5: Think of giving directions in a city. Saying the shop is three blocks away is useless until you say from where, and in which direction. Circuits are the same. A voltage is like the distance between two named spots, so you must say which spot you start from. A current is like traffic on a street, so you must first agree which way counts as forward. Ground is like choosing the town square as the starting point for every address. So: voltage compares two named points, current needs a chosen reference direction, and ground is the zero you pick for node voltages.
segments.deep: The three ideas exist because every electrical quantity in a circuit is relative. Voltage is a potential difference, so it only has a value once you say which point is subtracted from which; V A B means the potential at A minus the potential at B. Current is a signed rate of charge flow, so its sign only means something relative to an arrow you drew first. Ground is the node you agree to call zero, so node voltages depend on that choice while differences do not. Here is a sign going wrong. Suppose A sits 5 volts above B. One student writes V A B and gets plus 5 volts. Another writes V B A and gets minus 5 volts. Both are right for their labels. The error comes when someone computes V B A but reads it as if it were V A B, and then concludes B is higher. The common misconception is that a negative answer means a mistake. It does not; it means the real polarity or flow is opposite to the reference you chose. These habits carry straight into Kirchhoff's voltage law, meter readings, and later into logic levels, where a high or low is always a voltage measured from ground.

check.q: In the one sentence this lecture asks you to hold on to, voltage compares two points and current needs what?
check.again: The sentence has three parts. Voltage always compares two points, so it needs a pair of endpoints. Current needs a reference direction, an arrow you choose before you calculate, so that a positive or negative answer means something. And ground chooses a zero for node voltages. Notice that the current does not need ground and does not need a known value in advance. Think of a river gauge: you pick which way counts as downstream first, and only then can a reading of minus two metres per second tell you the water is flowing the other way.

segments.title: Charge and its two signs
segments.text: Electric charge is a property of matter, and it comes with two signs, positive and negative. You never see charge directly; you see its effects. Like signs repel, so positive pushes positive away and negative pushes negative away. Opposite signs attract. An electroscope's leaves spreading apart, a balloon clinging to a wall, and the spark when you touch a doorknob are all effects of charge. Here is a subtle point worth getting right early. A neutral object is not empty of charge. It holds enormous amounts of positive and negative charge that simply balance, so the net charge is zero. When you rub two materials together you do not create charge from nothing; you move some of it, usually electrons, from one object to the other. One ends up with a little extra negative charge and the other with a matching shortage. Also notice that attraction alone does not prove two objects carry opposite charges, because a charged object can attract a neutral one by rearranging the charge inside it.
segments.expand: Explain how a charged balloon attracts a neutral wall by polarization, and why repulsion is the more reliable sign of like charges.
segments.eli5: Think of a bank account that holds a huge amount of money and an equally huge debt. The balance reads zero, but the account is far from empty. A neutral object is like that: it holds enormous positive and negative charge that cancel. Rubbing two materials together is like transferring some money from one account to another. Nothing is created; one account goes a little negative and the other a little positive. Where the picture breaks: money does not push or pull on other money, but charges do, like repelling like and opposite attracting. So neutral means balanced charge, and charging an object means moving charge, usually electrons.
segments.deep: Charge is conserved: it is moved, never made. Rubbing a balloon on hair moves some electrons from one surface to the other, so one object gains a small negative excess and the other a matching positive shortage, and the totals still add to zero. The forces then follow two rules: like signs repel, opposite signs attract. A neutral wall can still be pulled by a charged balloon because of polarization. The balloon's charge pushes like charges in the wall surface slightly away and draws opposite charges slightly closer. Force falls off with distance, so the nearer opposite charges pull harder than the farther like charges push, and the net effect is attraction. That is why attraction is not proof of opposite charge: a charged object attracts both an oppositely charged object and a neutral one. Repulsion is the reliable test, because a neutral object is never repelled; only a like charge pushes back. The common misconception is that neutral means no charge at all. If that were true, polarization could not happen, because there would be nothing inside the wall to rearrange. This idea returns in Lecture 3 with Coulomb's law and with electrostatic discharge.

check.q: A neutral object contains no electric charge at all.
check.again: Neutral means balanced, not empty. A neutral object holds huge amounts of positive and negative charge that cancel, so its net charge is zero. Rubbing two objects together does not create charge; it moves some electrons from one to the other, leaving one slightly negative and the other with a matching shortage. Picture a bank account with a thousand dollars in and a thousand dollars out: the balance is zero, but there was plenty of money moving. That is also why a charged object can attract a neutral one: the charge inside the neutral object can shift a little, even though the total stays zero.

segments.title: Quantity versus unit
segments.text: Keep the name of a quantity separate from the name of its unit. Charge is the quantity, with the symbol capital Q, and it is measured in coulombs. Current is the quantity with the symbol capital I, measured in amperes, or amps. Voltage, also called potential difference, has the symbol capital V and is measured in volts. Current describes how fast charge moves past a point. Average current equals the charge that passes, divided by the time it takes: current in amps, charge in coulombs, time in seconds. So one amp is one coulomb passing every second. If 6 coulombs pass a point in 2 seconds, the average current is 6 divided by 2, which is 3 amps. A subscript, as in I one, just picks out a particular current in a particular part of the circuit. Getting into the habit of saying the quantity, the formula, and the unit together will make your calculations far easier to check later.
segments.expand: Give a second example of average current from charge and time using milli prefixes, and show how the prefixes cancel.
segments.eli5: Think of a shop counter. The number of customers who walk through the door is an amount, and you count it in people. How fast they come in is a rate, people per minute. Charge is the amount, counted in coulombs. Current is the rate, coulombs passing per second, and that unit has its own name, the amp. The name of the thing and the name of its unit stay separate, just as customers is not the same word as people per minute. So current equals charge divided by time, and one amp means one coulomb passing every second.
segments.deep: Formula first: average current equals charge divided by time, where current I is in amps, charge Q is in coulombs and time t is in seconds. The formula is really the definition of the amp: one coulomb crossing a point each second. It depends only on the charge that actually crosses the chosen point during the interval, not on how much charge sits in the wire. Example with milli prefixes: 6 millicoulombs pass a point in 2 milliseconds. Current is 6 millicoulombs over 2 milliseconds. Milli on top and milli on the bottom cancel, so the answer is 6 over 2, which is 3 amps, not 3 milliamps. If the prefixes differ, the answer changes: 6 millicoulombs in 2 seconds is 3 milliamps. The common misconception is that current and charge are the same thing, so a large current must mean a large amount of charge. A modest charge moved in a very short time is a large current, and a big charge moved slowly is a small current. Saying the quantity, the formula and the unit together is what catches these slips. The same habit drives the four-step calculation format in Lecture 2 and the charge and time problems in Lecture 3.

check.q: Six coulombs of charge pass a point in two seconds. What is the average current?
check.again: Average current equals charge passed divided by the time taken, with current in amps, charge in coulombs and time in seconds. So six coulombs over two seconds is three amps. One amp means one coulomb every second, so three coulombs each second is three amps. Multiplying six by two would give twelve, but current is a rate, so you divide the amount by the time. And the answer is in amps, not coulombs, because coulombs measure the amount of charge while amps measure how fast it moves. Another example: ten coulombs in five seconds is two amps.

segments.title: Labelling a voltage
segments.text: A voltage always compares two points, so it needs two endpoints and an order. The label V A B means the potential at A minus the potential at B. If V A B is plus 10 volts, then A is 10 volts higher than B. Reverse the order and the sign flips: V B A is minus 10 volts. That is not a different physical voltage, just the same comparison read the other way round. On a circuit you show this with a plus mark at the first point and a minus mark at the second. For a voltage source, a complete label has three parts: the polarity marks, a designator such as V one, and the value when you know it, such as 5 volts D C. In an analysis problem the value can be unknown, but you still name the source and mark its reference polarity. Those marks are a reference, not a claim. A positive answer means the plus-marked point really is higher; a negative answer means it is lower.
segments.expand: Work through what a negative calculated voltage means for the plus and minus reference marks, with a numeric example.
segments.eli5: Think of comparing the heights of two friends. Saying Anna minus Ben is ten centimetres tells you Anna is taller. Saying Ben minus Anna is minus ten centimetres says exactly the same thing from the other side. Nobody grew or shrank; only the order of comparison changed. A voltage label works the same way. V A B means A minus B, and the plus and minus marks on a drawing say which point comes first. So V B A is just V A B with its sign flipped, and a negative answer only means the plus-marked point is actually the lower one.
segments.deep: Formula first: V A B equals the potential at A minus the potential at B, both in volts. Swapping the order gives V B A, which equals negative V A B, because subtraction reverses sign when its order reverses. On a drawing the plus mark goes on the first point, A, and the minus mark on the second, B. Those marks are a reference you choose before calculating, not a statement of which side is really higher. Example: you mark a resistor plus on its left end and calculate its voltage as minus 3 volts. That says the left end is really 3 volts below the right end. You can leave the marks and keep the minus sign, or flip the marks and write plus 3 volts; both describe the same physical voltage. A complete source label adds a designator, such as V one, and a value when known, such as 5 volts D C. The common misconception is that a negative result means you set up the problem wrongly and must redo it. It is simply information about polarity relative to your marks. Kirchhoff's voltage law later in this lecture, and every meter reading, depend on keeping this order straight.

check.q: V A B is plus ten volts. What is V B A?
check.again: V A B means the potential at A minus the potential at B. If that is plus ten, A sits ten volts above B. V B A is the same two points read the other way, B minus A, so it is minus ten volts. Nothing physical changed; only the order of the subtraction flipped, and so did the sign. Think of two floors: if the third floor is ten metres above the first, then the first is ten metres below the third. Same gap, opposite sign. So swapping the subscripts always flips the sign, and it never gives zero unless the two points are at the same potential.

segments.title: Labelling a current
segments.text: Current also needs a reference. You draw an arrow, give it a name such as I one, and that arrow is your assumed direction. You do not need to know the real direction before you choose it. If the calculation comes out positive, the current really flows along the arrow. If it comes out negative, for example I one equals minus 5 milliamps, then 5 milliamps really flows the opposite way. The negative sign is not a mistake; it is information. Circuit arrows describe conventional current, which is the direction positive charge would move. In metal wires the charges that actually move are electrons, which are negative, so they drift opposite to the conventional arrow. That is fine, as long as you stick to one convention through a whole problem. This course, like both of your textbooks, uses conventional current, flowing out of the positive terminal of a source, through the external circuit, and back into the negative terminal.
segments.expand: Explain why a negative current answer is information rather than an error, and relate conventional current to electron drift in a metal wire.
segments.eli5: Think of a traffic counter on a two-way road. Before counting, you decide that cars going north count as positive. If the counter ends the hour at minus 50, the counter was not broken: 50 more cars went south than north. A current arrow is that decision. You choose it before you know the real direction, and a negative answer just says the flow went the other way. Where the picture breaks: in a wire the moving things, electrons, are negative, so the arrow describes where positive charge would go. So a negative current means the real conventional current flows against your arrow.
segments.deep: A current is a signed quantity measured against a reference arrow. If the calculation gives I one equals plus 5 milliamps, conventional current really flows along the arrow; if it gives minus 5 milliamps, the same 5 milliamps flows the opposite way. The method never needs you to guess the direction correctly, which is why you can draw arrows before solving. Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would move. In a metal wire the carriers are electrons, which are negative, so they drift opposite to the conventional arrow. Electrons moving left and positive charge moving right both carry charge the same net way, so both describe a conventional current to the right. Outside a source, conventional current leaves the positive terminal, passes through the external circuit, and returns to the negative terminal; electrons in the same wire drift from negative to positive. The common misconception is that conventional current is wrong because electrons go the other way. It is a convention, and every result comes out identical as long as you use one convention for the whole problem. This course and both textbooks use conventional current, and it returns in Lecture 3 and in every Ohm's law problem.

check.q: If a calculated current comes out negative, the arrow was drawn wrong and the answer is a mistake.
check.again: A negative current is information, not an error. The arrow you drew was only an assumed reference direction; you were never required to guess the real direction first. If I one comes out as minus five milliamps, five milliamps really flows opposite to the arrow. The calculation is correct and complete. Suppose you point an arrow into a battery's positive terminal and get a negative answer: that just tells you the current actually comes out of that terminal, as expected for conventional current. Keep the arrow, keep the sign, and read them together.

segments.title: Ground is a chosen zero
segments.text: Circuit ground is simply the node we decide to call zero volts. Think of surveying: heights only mean something once you pick a zero, like sea level. Node voltages are the same. Take a 10 volt source with upper terminal A and lower terminal B. If we call B ground, then A is plus 10 volts and B is zero. If we instead call A ground, then A is zero and B is minus 10 volts. In both cases A minus B is still 10 volts. So choosing a different zero changes the numbers given to individual nodes, but it does not change any voltage difference and it does not change any current, as long as the physical wiring stays the same. Mathematically, making a node the new reference subtracts its old voltage from every node, and that same amount cancels in every difference. One consequence: the negative terminal of a battery is not automatically ground. It is ground only if we choose it.
segments.expand: Show the subtraction argument for why voltage differences survive a change of reference, with three nodes.
segments.eli5: Think of measuring heights in a building. You could measure every floor from the street, or from the basement. If you switch from street to basement, every floor gets a bigger number, but the height between the second and fifth floors does not change at all. Ground is that chosen starting floor. Calling a node zero volts gives every other node a number, and moving that choice relabels every node by the same amount. So ground is a reference you pick: it changes node voltages, never the voltage difference between two nodes or any current.
segments.deep: Formula first: a node voltage V A is the potential at A minus the potential at the reference node. Changing the reference to a node R subtracts V R from every node voltage. The new value at A is V A minus V R, at B it is V B minus V R, and the difference is V A minus V R minus the quantity V B minus V R, which is still V A minus V B. The shift cancels. Example with three nodes: A at 10 volts, B at 4 volts, C at 0 volts with C as ground. Make B the new ground and subtract 4 volts from each: A becomes 6 volts, B becomes 0, C becomes minus 4 volts. A minus C was 10 volts and is still 6 minus negative 4, which is 10 volts. A minus B stays 6 volts. Because currents depend only on voltage differences across parts, they do not change either, as long as the wiring is the same. The common misconception is that the negative battery terminal must be ground. It is ground only if you choose it. This idea returns next with circuit common versus earth, and later whenever logic levels are measured from ground.

check.q: A ten volt source has upper terminal A and lower terminal B. If A is chosen as ground, what is the node voltage at B?
check.again: Ground is whichever node we choose to call zero. The source keeps A ten volts higher than B whatever we choose. Call B ground and A is plus ten. Call A ground instead, and A is zero, so B must be ten volts lower, which is minus ten volts. A minus B is still ten either way. Think of measuring heights from the roof instead of from the street: the roof becomes zero and the street becomes a negative height, but the building is just as tall. Moving ground relabels the nodes and never changes a difference or a current.

segments.title: Circuit common versus earth
segments.text: Two ideas often get mixed up. Circuit common, or reference ground, is the node chosen as zero volts in the circuit. Earth is a real physical connection into an earthing system, and protective earth is a conductor bonded to the metal parts of equipment so that a fault can trip a breaker. Choosing a reference is a mathematical decision; connecting to earth is a physical one. A battery-powered circuit can work perfectly well with no connection to earth at all. Be aware that many bench oscilloscopes tie their probe ground clip to protective earth, so that clip is not a free-floating zero you can clip anywhere. The same lecture used household mains as a time-varying example. For a sine wave, the peak voltage equals the square root of two times the R M S value, both in volts. A 120 volt R M S supply therefore peaks at about 1.414 times 120, roughly 170 volts. That relationship holds for sine waves, not for every possible waveform.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between R M S and peak for a sine wave, and why the square root of two appears.
segments.eli5: Think of sea level and your kitchen floor. When you measure the height of a table, you might use the kitchen floor as zero. That is just a choice you make. Sea level is a real, physical ocean, and it has nothing to do with your choice. Circuit common is like the kitchen floor: the node you decide to call zero volts. Earth is like the ocean: a real connection into the ground, used for safety. A battery circuit can use a kitchen-floor zero without ever touching the ocean. So circuit common is a chosen reference, while earth is a physical safety connection.
segments.deep: Choosing circuit common is a mathematical act; bonding to earth is a physical one. Protective earth ties the metal case of equipment into the earthing system so a fault drives a large current and trips a breaker. That is why a bench oscilloscope's probe ground clip, which is usually tied to protective earth, cannot be clipped to just any node: doing so physically connects that node to earth. The lecture also used mains as a time-varying example. Formula first: peak voltage equals the square root of two times the R M S voltage, both in volts. R M S stands for root mean square: square the waveform, average the squares, take the square root. For a sine wave this works out to the peak divided by the square root of two, about 0.707 of the peak. Example: 120 volts R M S times 1.414 is about 170 volts peak, more exactly 169.7 volts. The common misconception is that this factor applies to every waveform. It is specific to a sine wave; a waveform with a different shape has a different ratio, so the square root of two must not be applied blindly. The common versus earth distinction returns whenever an oscilloscope is used in the lab.

check.q: For a sine wave, a 120 volt R M S supply peaks at roughly what voltage?
check.again: For a sine wave, peak voltage equals the square root of two times the R M S voltage, both in volts. The square root of two is about 1.414, so 1.414 times 120 is about 170 volts. The R M S value is the effective value, the steady voltage that would deliver the same heating, and the true peak is higher than that. Dividing by 1.414 would give about 85 volts, but that goes the wrong way: peak is bigger than R M S, not smaller. A quick second example: a 10 volt R M S sine wave peaks at about 14.1 volts.

segments.title: Building a fully labelled circuit
segments.text: A circuit drawing shows electrical connections, not where parts sit on the bench. To make one you can analyse, work in this order. First, label the voltage source with its designator, polarity and value. Second, choose a current arrow and name it. Third, name each component, such as R one and R two, and name its voltage, V R one and V R two. Fourth, mark each resistor's polarity so that the assumed current enters its plus terminal. That rule is called the passive sign convention, and with it the resistor law is simply voltage equals current times resistance. Fifth, choose or follow ground if you need node voltages. There are two common layouts. One shows the source and the complete loop of wire. The other, a stem layout, shows a supply rail at the top and a common symbol at the bottom, with the return path implied. Repeated common symbols all mean the same connected node, not separate zeros.
segments.expand: Explain the passive sign convention and why the stem layout still represents a complete circuit through the supply.
segments.eli5: Think of a recipe card before you cook. You list the ingredients, name each bowl, and mark which bowl gets poured into which, before anything goes on the stove. A fully labelled circuit is that card. You name the source with its polarity and value, draw and name a current arrow, name each part and its voltage, and mark each resistor so the arrow enters its plus end. Then the arithmetic follows the card. Where the picture breaks: in a circuit the order matters for signs, not for timing. So a labelled circuit fixes every reference first, and then voltage equals current times resistance works without sign trouble.
segments.deep: The labelling order exists so that every sign in the later algebra has a defined meaning. The key step is the passive sign convention: mark each resistor so the assumed current enters its plus terminal. With that choice, Ohm's law is simply voltage equals current times resistance, voltage in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms, with no extra minus sign. If you marked a resistor the other way, the same physics would give V equals negative I R, which is where sign errors creep in. Example: 2 milliamps entering the plus end of a 3 kilohm resistor gives V R equals 2 milliamps times 3 kilohms, which is 6 volts, with the plus end higher. The stem layout draws a supply rail at the top and common symbols at the bottom with no visible return wire. It is still a complete loop, because every common symbol is the same node, and that node is the source's return terminal. The common misconception is that each ground symbol is a separate zero or a separate path to earth. They are one connected node. This order of labelling sets up the Kirchhoff loop in the next segment and the series circuits of Lecture 4.

check.q: With the passive sign convention, a resistor's plus mark goes at the terminal where the assumed current enters.
check.again: That is the passive sign convention. You choose the current arrow first, then put the plus mark on the resistor where the arrow goes in and the minus mark where it comes out. With the marks placed that way, the resistor law is simply voltage equals current times resistance, voltage in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms, with no extra minus sign to track. If your assumed current later comes out negative, the resistor voltage comes out negative too, and the two signs stay consistent. Set the marks before you calculate, and the algebra takes care of itself.

segments.title: Kirchhoff's voltage law and a worked example
segments.text: Kirchhoff's voltage law says that if you walk around any closed loop and add up the changes in potential, rises positive and drops negative, you get zero. You end where you started, at the same level. Take a 5 volt source driving two 1 kilohm resistors in series. Walking clockwise, the source is a rise of 5 volts and each resistor is a drop, so 5 minus V R one minus V R two equals zero. Now bring in Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance, with current in amps, voltage in volts and resistance in ohms. The total resistance is 2 kilohms, so the current is 5 volts divided by 2 kilohms, which is 2.5 milliamps. Each resistor then drops 2.5 milliamps times 1 kilohm, which is 2.5 volts. Check: 5 minus 2.5 minus 2.5 is zero. With the bottom grounded, the top node is at 5 volts and the midpoint is at 2.5 volts.
segments.expand: Repeat the Kirchhoff loop with unequal resistors, such as 1 kilohm and 4 kilohms on 10 volts, and show the check.
segments.eli5: Think of a hike that starts and ends at your car. You climb some hills and go down into some valleys, but when you get back to the car you are at exactly the height you started. Add every climb as positive and every descent as negative, and the total is zero. Kirchhoff's voltage law says the same about a loop in a circuit. The source is a climb, each resistor is a descent, and back at the start the total change is zero. So around any closed loop, the voltage rises minus the voltage drops add up to zero.
segments.deep: Formula first: the sum of voltage changes around any closed loop is zero, rises counted positive and drops negative. It holds because potential is a level each node has, so walking around a loop back to the start must return you to the same level. In a series loop, combine it with Ohm's law, current equals voltage divided by resistance, amps from volts over ohms. Example with unequal parts: 10 volts across 1 kilohm and 4 kilohms in series. Total resistance is 5 kilohms, so current is 10 volts over 5 kilohms, which is 2 milliamps. The 1 kilohm drops 2 milliamps times 1 kilohm, which is 2 volts. The 4 kilohm drops 2 milliamps times 4 kilohms, which is 8 volts. Check: 10 minus 2 minus 8 is zero. Notice that the larger resistor takes the larger share of the voltage, in proportion to its resistance. The common misconception is that the drops split equally, or that current gets used up along the loop. In a series loop the same current flows through every part; only the voltage is shared. This loop law is used again in Lecture 4 for series drops and node voltages, and later for switch and pull-up circuits.

check.q: A five volt source drives two one kilohm resistors in series. What current flows?
check.again: Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. In series the resistances add, so the loop sees one kilohm plus one kilohm, which is two kilohms. Five volts divided by two kilohms is 2.5 milliamps, because volts over kilohms come out in milliamps. Five milliamps would be the answer if only one resistor were in the loop, and that is the common slip: forgetting to add the second resistor. Check with Kirchhoff: each resistor drops 2.5 milliamps times one kilohm, 2.5 volts, and two drops of 2.5 make the full five volts.

segments.title: Component voltage versus node voltage
segments.text: Both are potential differences; the only question is which two points are compared. A component voltage, like V R one, compares the two terminals of that component. It needs no ground at all. A node voltage, like V A, compares node A with the chosen reference, so it only makes sense once ground is chosen. If R one joins node A to node B, with its plus mark at A, then V R one equals V A minus V B. If R two joins node B down to ground, then V R two equals V B minus zero, which is just V B. So a component voltage and a node voltage can have the same value when they compare the same pair of points. A voltmeter follows the same ordered subtraction: its reading is the red-probe potential minus the black-probe potential. With red on a node at minus 3 volts and black on a node at plus 2 volts, the meter reads minus 3 minus 2, which is minus 5 volts.
segments.expand: Give another meter-reading example and explain what swapping the probes does to the sign.
segments.eli5: Think of a staircase. The height of one step is measured from the bottom of that step to its top; you do not need to know where the ground floor is. That is a component voltage. The height of a particular step above the ground floor is a node voltage; it needs the ground floor chosen first. If a step sits right on the ground floor, its own height and its height above the floor are the same number. So a component voltage compares a part's two ends, a node voltage compares one point with ground, and a meter reads red minus black.
segments.deep: Formula first: for a resistor between node A and node B, with its plus mark at A, V R equals V A minus V B, all in volts. A node voltage V B is V B minus the reference, which is zero, so a component that sits between node B and ground has V R equal to V B. A voltmeter does the same ordered subtraction: reading equals red-probe potential minus black-probe potential. Example: red on a node at 7 volts, black on a node at 2 volts, the meter reads 7 minus 2, which is plus 5 volts. Swap the probes and it reads 2 minus 7, which is minus 5 volts. Nothing in the circuit changed; only the order of subtraction did. The lecture example, red at minus 3 volts and black at plus 2 volts, gives minus 3 minus 2, which is minus 5 volts. The common misconception is that a negative meter reading means the meter or circuit is faulty. It only means the red probe sits on the lower point. This ordered subtraction is used every time you measure a logic level, a supply rail, or a voltage drop in the lab.

check.q: The red probe is on a node at minus three volts and the black probe on a node at plus two volts. What does the meter read?
check.again: A voltmeter reads the red-probe potential minus the black-probe potential, in volts. Minus three minus plus two is minus five volts. It is an ordered subtraction, exactly like V A B, with red playing the part of A. A reading of minus one would come from adding the two numbers, and plus five from subtracting in the wrong order. Another example: red on plus four volts and black on plus nine volts reads four minus nine, which is minus five volts, even though both nodes are positive with respect to ground. The meter only ever cares about the difference.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Let us pull the lecture together into four ideas. First, charge has two signs; like charges repel, opposite charges attract, and neutral means balanced rather than empty. Second, every voltage compares two points in a stated order, so V A B is A minus B, and a meter reads red minus black. Third, every current needs a named arrow; a negative answer simply means the real current flows against the arrow, and arrows follow conventional current. Fourth, ground is a chosen zero. Moving it relabels every node but leaves every difference and every current unchanged, and it is not automatically the negative terminal or earth. With a fully labelled circuit, Kirchhoff's voltage law and Ohm's law then give you every current and voltage, and the signs will take care of themselves because you set up the references before you calculated.
segments.expand: Quiz the student with a short mixed question that uses reference direction, ground choice and a meter reading together.
segments.eli5: Think of setting up a board game before playing. You agree which way play goes around the table, who starts, and where the zero mark on the score track is. Once those are settled, the game runs itself. This lecture set up four agreements. Charge has two signs and neutral means balanced. A voltage compares two points in a stated order. A current needs a named arrow. Ground is a chosen zero. So once references are fixed, Kirchhoff's voltage law and Ohm's law give every voltage and current with the right sign.
segments.deep: The four ideas fit together because each one fixes a reference. Charge rules explain why forces and current exist at all: like signs repel, opposite signs attract, and neutral objects hold balanced charge. Voltage ordering, V A B equals A minus B, makes every potential difference unambiguous, and a meter applies the same rule as red minus black. Current arrows make a negative result meaningful: the real flow is against the arrow. Ground fixes node voltages, and moving it shifts every node by the same amount, so differences and currents stay the same. Here is a mixed example. A 9 volt source drives 1 kilohm on top and 2 kilohms below it, in series. Current is 9 volts over 3 kilohms, which is 3 milliamps. The drops are 3 volts and 6 volts. Ground the bottom, and the midpoint is at 6 volts. Move ground to the top, and the midpoint becomes minus 3 volts while the bottom becomes minus 9 volts, yet the 2 kilohm still drops 6 volts. The common misconception is treating these as four separate facts. They are one habit: set references first, calculate second. Lecture 2 builds the matching habit for numbers and units.

check.q: Moving the ground reference to a different node changes every voltage difference in the circuit.
check.again: Moving ground changes the individual node voltages but never a difference between two nodes, and never a current. Making a node the new reference subtracts that node's old voltage from every node in the circuit, and that same amount cancels out of every subtraction. Take two nodes at plus eight and plus three volts, a difference of five. Move ground so they become plus five and zero: still a difference of five. Ground is a chosen zero, like sea level for heights. Changing where you measure from does not make any mountain taller.

lectures.title: Engineering notation and careful calculation
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 02 - Lab Workflow and Engineering Notation.md; Kleitz §2-2 Examples 2-1, 2-2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture is about the tools you need to calculate cleanly: engineering notation with its prefixes, a four-step layout for every calculation, and the habits that let you find your own mistakes. We will finish by using prefixes on a digital clock, converting between frequency and period. None of this is glamorous, but a surprising number of wrong answers in electronics are not wrong physics at all. They are a prefix slipped by a factor of a thousand, or a number written without its unit. If you get fluent with prefixes now, every later topic gets easier, because you will be able to glance at an answer and know whether it is the right size.
segments.expand: Explain why prefix errors are the most common mistake in first-year electronics calculations, with an example.
segments.eli5: Think of a kitchen scale that reads in grams while the recipe is in kilograms. The baking chemistry can be perfect, but if you put in 500 kilograms of flour instead of 500 grams, the cake is ruined by a factor of a thousand. Electronics is the same. Most wrong answers are not wrong physics; they are a prefix slipped by a thousand, or a number with no unit. This lecture gives you the measuring habits: prefixes, a four-step layout, and checks. So fluency with prefixes and units is what lets you tell at a glance whether an answer is the right size.
segments.deep: Prefix errors dominate early electronics because component values span an enormous range. Resistors run from ohms to megohms, currents from microamps to amps, and clock periods from milliseconds to picoseconds. Each engineering prefix step is a factor of one thousand, so a single wrong prefix makes an answer a thousand, a million or a billion times off, while the method looks perfect. Example: Ohm's law, current equals voltage divided by resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Five volts across 1 kilohm is 5 volts over 1000 ohms, which is 5 milliamps. Read the resistor as 1 ohm by mistake and you get 5 amps, a thousand times too big, enough to suggest a component would burn. Read it as 1 megohm and you get 5 microamps, a thousand times too small. The common misconception is that a wrong answer means you misunderstood the physics. Often the physics was fine and step three, the substitution, slipped. That is why this lecture pairs prefixes with a four-step layout: when the result is off by exactly a thousand, you know where to look. These habits are used in every calculation from here on, including the clock frequency and period conversions at the end of this lecture.

check.q: This introduction says that many wrong answers in electronics are a prefix slipped by a factor of a thousand, not wrong physics.
check.again: The point of this lecture is that the physics is often understood while the bookkeeping fails. A kilo dropped in a substitution makes an answer a thousand times too big or too small, and a number written without its unit cannot be checked at all. Suppose someone divides five volts by 4.7 and writes 1.06 with no unit. Is that amps or milliamps? The resistor was 4.7 kilohms, so the honest answer is about 1.06 milliamps. Fluency with prefixes lets you glance at a result and know whether it is the right size, which catches these slips before they cost you a wrong answer or a burnt part.

segments.title: What engineering notation is
segments.text: Engineering notation writes a quantity using a power of ten whose exponent is a multiple of three: ten to the three, ten to the minus three, ten to the minus six, and so on. Each of those powers has a prefix name, so instead of writing the power you write the prefix in front of the unit. For a nonzero value, the number in front is kept at least 1 and less than 1000. That is the rule to hold on to. So 4700 ohms becomes 4.7 kilohms, and 0.00047 amps becomes 470 microamps, because 470 sits between 1 and 999. Note that the upper limit is less than 1000, so 999.5 millivolts is fine, but 1000 millivolts should become 1 volt. Scientific notation is different: it always puts one digit before the decimal point and allows any exponent. Engineering notation trades that for exponents you can say as prefixes, which is what engineers read on datasheets and meters.
segments.expand: Contrast scientific and engineering notation on two or three values, and explain why engineers prefer exponents in steps of three.
segments.eli5: Think of money in a country with only three-digit price tags. Instead of writing 4700 dollars, the shop writes 4.7 thousand, and instead of 0.00047 dollars it would write 470 millionths. The tag always shows a number from 1 up to just under 1000, and a word for the size. Engineering notation does exactly that with prefixes like kilo, milli and micro, each a step of one thousand. So in engineering notation the number in front stays between 1 and 999, and the prefix carries the power of ten in steps of three.
segments.deep: Formula first: a value is written as a number from 1 up to, but not including, 1000, times ten to a power that is a multiple of three, and that power is spoken as a prefix. Scientific notation instead keeps exactly one digit before the decimal point and allows any exponent. Compare three values. 4700 ohms is 4.7 times ten to the three in scientific notation, and in engineering notation it is also 4.7 kilohms. 0.00047 amps is 4.7 times ten to the minus four in scientific notation, but in engineering notation it is 470 times ten to the minus six, which is 470 microamps. 22000 hertz is 2.2 times ten to the four in scientific, but 22 kilohertz in engineering. The difference shows up whenever the scientific exponent is not a multiple of three. Engineers prefer steps of three because each step has a spoken prefix found on datasheets, meters and part markings, so the value can be read and said directly. The common misconception is that 0.47 kilohms is engineering notation because it has a prefix. The number must be at least 1, so it should be 470 ohms. These rules are used throughout this lecture and in every later calculation.

check.q: In engineering notation, the number written in front of the prefix is kept in which range?
options: At least one and less than a thousand
At least one and less than ten
Any range that the calculator gives
check.again: Engineering notation uses exponents that are multiples of three, and each of those exponents is spoken as a prefix. To make that work, the number in front is kept at least one and below one thousand. So 4700 ohms becomes 4.7 kilohms, and 0.00047 amps becomes 470 microamps. Keeping the number between one and ten is scientific notation, a different system that allows any exponent. And 1000 millivolts breaks the rule at the top, so it becomes one volt. A quick example: 0.0022 farads is 2.2 millifarads, with 2.2 sitting comfortably in the allowed range.

segments.title: The prefixes you need
segments.text: Here are the prefixes you will use constantly. Kilo, written with a small k, means ten to the three, or a thousand. Mega, a capital M, means ten to the six, a million. Giga, capital G, is ten to the nine. Going smaller, milli, a small m, is ten to the minus three, a thousandth. Micro, written with the Greek letter mu, is ten to the minus six, a millionth. Nano, a small n, is ten to the minus nine, and pico, a small p, is ten to the minus twelve. Each step is a factor of a thousand. Notice that the letter case matters. A small m is milli and a capital M is mega, and those differ by a factor of a billion. Mixing them up is not a small rounding slip; it wrecks the answer completely. So when you read a schematic value or a datasheet, read the case of the letter as carefully as the number itself.
segments.expand: Give memorable examples for each prefix from real components, such as kilohm resistors, microfarad capacitors and megahertz clocks.
segments.eli5: Think of a staircase where every step is a factor of a thousand. Going up from the base unit: kilo, then mega, then giga. Going down: milli, micro, nano, pico. Each stair is a thousand times bigger or smaller than its neighbour, like going from millimetres to metres to kilometres. The letters on the stairs are case sensitive: small m is milli, three steps down, capital M is mega, two steps up, and the gap between them is a billion. So each prefix names a power of ten in steps of three, and the case of the letter matters as much as the number.
segments.deep: Formula first: kilo is ten to the three, mega ten to the six, giga ten to the nine; milli is ten to the minus three, micro ten to the minus six, nano ten to the minus nine and pico ten to the minus twelve. The ratio between neighbours is always one thousand. Examples from real parts: a 4.7 kilohm resistor is 4700 ohms; a 1 megohm resistor, like the one in a wrist strap cord, is one million ohms; a 4 gigahertz processor clock completes four billion cycles each second; a 330 microamp current is 0.00033 amps. Small m against capital M: 1 milliohm is ten to the minus three ohms and 1 megohm is ten to the six ohms, so the ratio is ten to the nine, one billion. The common misconception is that letter case is cosmetic, like a capital at the start of a sentence. On a schematic or datasheet it is the difference between milli and mega. A related trap is micro, written with the Greek letter mu and often typed as a plain u, so 10 u A means 10 microamps. These prefixes are used next for converting values and later for clock frequencies and periods.

check.q: A small m and a capital M as prefixes differ by what factor?
check.again: Small m is milli, ten to the minus three, a thousandth. Capital M is mega, ten to the six, a million. From a thousandth up to a million is a factor of ten to the nine, a billion. That is why the case of the letter matters as much as the digits. Reading 2 megohms as 2 milliohms is not a rounding error; it is nine powers of ten. Neighbouring prefixes such as milli and micro differ by a thousand, and milli to kilo is a million, but milli to mega is the full billion. Read the case every time.

segments.title: Changing from one prefix to another
segments.text: Changing prefix never changes the quantity; it only changes how you express it. The rule of thumb: move to a smaller unit and the number gets bigger; move to a larger unit and the number gets smaller. Take 0.025 millivolts. One millivolt is 1000 microvolts, because milli is ten to the minus three and micro is ten to the minus six. So 0.025 millivolts times 1000 is 25 microvolts. That is the same voltage, now with a sensible number in front. Going the other way, 2700 ohms divided by 1000 is 2.7 kilohms. A classic mistake is to change the prefix without changing the number: writing 0.025 millivolts as 0.025 microvolts makes the value a thousand times too small. Another is reading 2.7 kilohms as 2.7 ohms. Whenever you switch prefixes, say to yourself, smaller unit, bigger number, and check that your number moved the right way by the right factor.
segments.expand: Walk through two more conversions, one to a smaller prefix and one to a larger prefix, and the check for each.
segments.eli5: Think of paying for something with coins instead of a bill. A ten-dollar bill becomes a thousand pennies. Same money, but because each penny is a smaller unit, you need a bigger count. Changing a prefix works the same way. Moving to a smaller unit, like millivolts to microvolts, makes the number bigger; moving to a larger unit makes it smaller. So 0.025 millivolts becomes 25 microvolts: smaller unit, bigger number, by a factor of a thousand per step, and the quantity itself never changes.
segments.deep: Formula first: when you change prefix, the new number equals the old number times the old prefix value divided by the new prefix value. From milli to micro, that is ten to the minus three over ten to the minus six, which is one thousand, so multiply by a thousand. Example toward a smaller prefix: 0.0033 amps to milliamps. Amps to milli is one step smaller, so multiply by 1000, giving 3.3 milliamps. Check: smaller unit, bigger number, and 3.3 is a sensible engineering figure. Example toward a larger prefix: 47000 ohms to kilohms. Kilo is one step larger, so divide by 1000, giving 47 kilohms. Check: larger unit, smaller number. Two steps at once multiply the factors: 2.2 megohms is 2200 kilohms, which is 2.2 million ohms. The common misconception is that you can swap the prefix and keep the digits, writing 0.025 millivolts as 0.025 microvolts. That silently divides the quantity by a thousand. Another is reading 2.7 kilohms as 2.7 ohms. Saying the rule aloud, smaller unit bigger number, catches both. This skill feeds the mental unit shortcuts and choosing a sensible prefix later in this lecture.

check.q: What is 0.025 millivolts expressed in microvolts?
check.again: Milli is ten to the minus three and micro is ten to the minus six, so one millivolt is one thousand microvolts. Moving to the smaller unit, microvolts, makes the number bigger by a thousand: 0.025 times 1000 is 25 microvolts. The value has not changed, only its expression. Writing 0.025 microvolts keeps the number and swaps the prefix, which silently shrinks the voltage a thousandfold. Another example: 0.0047 amps is 4.7 milliamps, because going from amps to milliamps multiplies the number by a thousand. Say it to yourself each time: smaller unit, bigger number.

segments.title: The four-step calculation format
segments.text: Every calculation should show four things. Step one names the quantity you are finding, such as I X. Step two writes the formula in symbols, such as I X equals V two divided by R three. Step three substitutes the values with their units. Step four gives the numerical answer with its unit. The steps can sit in one connected line; they do not need four separate paragraphs. The point is that someone reading your work, including you tomorrow, can see what you were finding, which relationship you used, and exactly which numbers and prefixes went in. Here is an example. A resistor of 2.7 kilohms has 4.76 volts peak to peak across it. The current, by Ohm's law, is voltage divided by resistance, amps from volts over ohms. So I X equals 4.76 volts peak to peak over 2.7 kilohms, which is about 1.76 milliamps peak to peak. Keep the peak to peak label on the answer too.
segments.expand: Show a second four-step calculation, and explain why the unit label such as peak to peak must travel with the answer.
segments.eli5: Think of a recipe card someone else will cook from. It says what dish you are making, which method you are using, exactly what goes in with amounts, and what comes out. A calculation laid out in four steps is that card. Step one names what you are finding, step two the formula, step three the numbers with their units, and step four the answer with its unit. Anyone, including you tomorrow, can then follow it or spot a wrong ingredient. So every calculation shows target, formula, substitution with units, and answer with units.
segments.deep: The four steps matter because each one isolates a different kind of mistake. Step one fixes the target, step two fixes the relationship, step three fixes the values and prefixes, step four fixes the arithmetic and the unit. Second example: find the current through a 4.7 kilohm resistor with 9 volts across it. Step one: the target is I R. Step two: Ohm's law, current equals voltage divided by resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Step three: I R equals 9 volts over 4.7 kilohms. Step four: about 1.91 milliamps. The unit label must travel with the answer because it says what kind of quantity it is. In the lecture example, 4.76 volts peak to peak gave 1.76 milliamps peak to peak. Drop the peak to peak label and a reader might assume a D C or R M S value, which for a sine wave differs from peak to peak by a factor of about 2.83. The common misconception is that the layout is just for marking and can be skipped if the answer is right. Without it, you cannot find your own error when it is wrong. The next segments build a mental unit check and a backtracking method on top of this format.

check.q: In the four-step calculation format, step three substitutes the values with their units into the formula.
check.again: The four steps are: name the quantity you want, write the formula in symbols, substitute the values with their units, and give the answer with its unit. Step three is the substitution line, and it is where prefixes go in, so it is where prefix mistakes live. For example: I X equals V two over R three, then 4.76 volts peak to peak over 2.7 kilohms, then about 1.76 milliamps peak to peak. All four can sit on one connected line. The habit is worth keeping because a reader, including you tomorrow, can see which numbers went in.

segments.title: A mental unit check
segments.text: A lovely shortcut falls out of the prefixes. Volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps, because dividing by ten to the three is the same as multiplying by ten to the minus three. So 4.76 volts over 2.7 kilohms comes out directly in milliamps, about 1.76. The same trick works the other way: milliamps times kilohms gives volts, because the ten to the minus three and the ten to the three cancel. Two milliamps through 4 kilohms drops 8 volts. You can also do it all in base units if you prefer: 4.76 divided by 2700 is about 0.00176 amps, which is 1.76 milliamps. Either way you get the same result. The point of the shortcut is speed and a sanity check. If your calculator says 1760 and you expected milliamps, you know immediately that a kilo went missing somewhere in step three.
segments.expand: Give more pairings like volts over kilohms equals milliamps, including microamps times kilohms, and show how to use them as sanity checks.
segments.eli5: Think of currency exchange where the rates are so simple you can do them in your head. Dividing by a thousand is the same as converting to a unit a thousand times smaller. So volts divided by kilohms comes out directly in milliamps, and milliamps times kilohms comes out directly in volts, because the thousand on top and the thousandth below cancel. You do not need to write the zeros. So pairing prefixes lets you predict the unit of the answer before you calculate, and a surprise in the number points to a missing prefix.
segments.deep: Formula first: Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, voltage in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms. Now track the powers of ten. Volts over kilohms is ten to the zero over ten to the three, which is ten to the minus three, so the answer is in milliamps. Milliamps times kilohms is ten to the minus three times ten to the three, which is ten to the zero, so the answer is in volts. Microamps times kilohms is ten to the minus six times ten to the three, which is ten to the minus three, so the answer is in millivolts. Volts over megohms gives microamps, and volts over milliamps gives kilohms. Example: 100 microamps through 4.7 kilohms. Microamps times kilohms gives millivolts, so 100 times 4.7 is 470 millivolts. Base-unit check: 0.0001 amps times 4700 ohms is 0.47 volts, the same. The common misconception is that the shortcut is an approximation. It is exact; it is only bookkeeping of the exponents. Its real value is as a sanity check: if you expect milliamps and the calculator shows 1760, you know a kilo was dropped in the substitution step. You will use these pairings in nearly every resistor calculation in the course.

check.q: Two milliamps flowing through four kilohms drops how many volts?
check.again: Ohm's law: voltage equals current times resistance, voltage in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms. The prefix shortcut is that milliamps times kilohms gives volts, because ten to the minus three times ten to the three cancels to one. So two milliamps times four kilohms is eight volts. In base units it is 0.002 amps times 4000 ohms, which is also eight volts. Dividing instead of multiplying would give 0.5, and forgetting the cancellation might tempt you to say millivolts. One more: three milliamps through two kilohms drops six volts.

segments.title: Finding your own mistakes
segments.text: The four steps are not only for the reader; they let you backtrack. If you found the wrong quantity altogether, look back at step one. If the relationship itself is wrong, say you used the total voltage instead of the voltage across one resistor, the problem is in step two. If the answer is off by a clean factor such as a thousand, the problem is almost certainly step three, a prefix or unit substituted wrongly, because each engineering prefix is a factor of a thousand from its neighbour. And if the formula and substitution are right but the number is still wrong, check step four, your calculator entry and rounding. A related habit: keep enough digits during the working and round only once, at the end, to the precision asked for. Rounding early and then multiplying can drift the last digit and make a correct method look wrong.
segments.expand: Give an example of a factor-of-one-thousand error and trace it back to the exact step where it happened.
segments.eli5: Think of baking a cake that comes out wrong. If you baked bread instead, you followed the wrong recipe. If it tastes odd, maybe the method was wrong. If it is exactly a thousand times too salty, someone read grams as kilograms. If everything was right but it burned, the oven was set wrong. The four calculation steps let you trace a bad answer the same way: target, formula, substitution, arithmetic. So a clean factor of a thousand points straight at the substitution step, where a prefix was used wrongly.
segments.deep: Each step can fail in its own recognisable way. A wrong target shows up as an answer of the wrong kind, such as a voltage when a current was asked. A wrong relationship, step two, gives an answer of the right kind but the wrong size by an untidy factor. A wrong prefix, step three, gives an answer off by exactly ten to the three, ten to the six or more, because every engineering prefix is a factor of a thousand from its neighbour. Example: find the current through 2.2 kilohms with 6.6 volts across it. Correct: current equals voltage over resistance, 6.6 volts over 2.2 kilohms, which is 3 milliamps. A student who enters 2.2 instead of 2200 gets 3 amps. The ratio between 3 amps and 3 milliamps is exactly one thousand, so the error is in step three: the kilo was dropped. Rounding is the other step-four trap. Keep full digits through the working and round once at the end. The common misconception is that rounding early only affects the last digit harmlessly. Multiplying a rounded value can shift that digit, making a correct method look wrong. This backtracking habit applies to every multi-step problem in the course.

check.q: Your answer is off by a clean factor of a thousand. Which step is the most likely culprit?
check.again: Each engineering prefix is a factor of a thousand from its neighbour, so a result that is exactly a thousand times too big or too small almost always means a prefix was substituted wrongly in step three. Step one errors give you the wrong quantity altogether, step two errors give a wrong relationship, and step four errors are calculator entry or rounding, which rarely land on a clean thousand. For instance, if you expected milliamps and got 1760, a kilo was probably dropped when a resistance went in as ohms instead of kilohms. Go straight to the substitution line and check the prefixes.

segments.title: Prefixes on a clock: period and frequency
segments.text: Here is where prefixes meet digital electronics directly. A digital clock repeats. Its period is the time for one complete cycle, from one rising edge to the next. Its frequency is how many cycles happen each second. They are reciprocals: frequency equals one over period, with frequency in hertz and period in seconds. Kleitz's first example has a period of 2 microseconds. One over 2 microseconds is 0.5 times ten to the six hertz, which is 0.5 megahertz, or 500 kilohertz. His second example goes the other way: a processor clock of 4 gigahertz has a period of one over 4 times ten to the nine seconds, which is 250 picoseconds. Two pairings are worth memorising, because they make these conversions almost instant: 1 kilohertz goes with 1 millisecond, and 1 megahertz goes with 1 microsecond. Double the frequency and the period halves.
segments.expand: Work one more frequency to period conversion in nanoseconds, and explain why rising edge to rising edge is one period.
segments.eli5: Think of a lighthouse beam that sweeps around. The time for one full sweep is the period. How many sweeps happen each second is the frequency. If one sweep takes a quarter of a second, there are four sweeps each second. A digital clock is the same: the period is the time from one rising edge to the next, and the frequency is how many such cycles fit into one second. Faster sweeps mean shorter periods. So frequency equals one over period, and 1 kilohertz pairs with 1 millisecond, 1 megahertz with 1 microsecond.
segments.deep: Formula first: frequency equals one divided by period, frequency in hertz, period in seconds; equally, period equals one divided by frequency. One hertz means one cycle per second. A period is measured from a rising edge to the next rising edge because that is where the waveform first repeats exactly; any matching point works, but rising edge to rising edge is the convention. Example in nanoseconds: a 50 megahertz clock. Period equals one over 50 times ten to the six hertz, which is 0.02 times ten to the minus six seconds, or 20 nanoseconds. Using the pairing shortcut, 1 megahertz goes with 1 microsecond, which is 1000 nanoseconds, and 50 times faster means 1000 over 50, which is 20 nanoseconds. From the lecture, 2 microseconds gives 500 kilohertz, and 4 gigahertz gives 250 picoseconds. The relationship depends only on the reciprocal, so doubling the frequency halves the period. The common misconception is that higher frequency means a longer or bigger signal. It means shorter cycles, packed more tightly in time. The same reciprocal returns with clock waveforms in Kleitz chapter one and with gate timing diagrams in chapter three.

check.q: A clock has a period of two microseconds. What is its frequency?
check.again: Frequency equals one over the period, with frequency in hertz and period in seconds. One over two microseconds is one over two times ten to the minus six, which is 0.5 times ten to the six hertz, that is 0.5 megahertz or 500 kilohertz. Two megahertz would be the answer for a period of half a microsecond, so watch for reciprocal slips. The anchor pairs help: one megahertz goes with one microsecond, so doubling the period to two microseconds halves the frequency to half a megahertz. Another example: a period of four milliseconds gives 250 hertz.

segments.title: Choosing a sensible prefix for an answer
segments.text: Once you have a number, pick the prefix that puts it between 1 and 999. A calculator might give 0.000877 amps. Move the decimal three places at a time: 0.877 milliamps is still below 1, so move again to 877 microamps. That is the engineering form. Similarly, 0.877 volts is better said as 877 millivolts. Do not overdo it in the other direction; 0.47 milliamps is a correct value but not engineering notation, because the number is below 1, so write 470 microamps. Finally, every final answer needs its unit. A bare number such as 1.76 tells the reader nothing, because it could be amps, milliamps or volts. In spoken work, say the unit every time, the way you are hearing it in this lecture. That habit will stop more errors than any clever technique.
segments.expand: Practise converting three calculator outputs into engineering notation and explain the move of three decimal places.
segments.eli5: Think of telling someone a distance. You would not say 0.0008 kilometres; you would say 80 centimetres. You pick the unit that makes the number easy to say. Engineering notation asks the same thing: shift the decimal three places at a time until the number sits between 1 and 999, and change the prefix each time you shift. So 0.000877 amps becomes 877 microamps, and 0.877 volts becomes 877 millivolts. Choose the prefix that puts the number between 1 and 999, and always say the unit.
segments.deep: Formula first: moving to the next smaller prefix multiplies the number by one thousand, which shifts the decimal point three places to the right. So repeat the shift until the number is at least 1 and below 1000. Practice one: 0.0033 amps. Shift once to 3.3 milliamps; it is between 1 and 999, so stop. Practice two: 0.000047 amps. Shift once to 0.047 milliamps, still below 1; shift again to 47 microamps. Practice three: 15000 ohms is too big, so shift the other way, three places left, to 15 kilohms. A value like 0.47 milliamps is correct but not in engineering form; it becomes 470 microamps. The common misconception is that any prefix is fine as long as the value is correct. It is still correct, but a number below 1 or above 999 is harder to read, harder to compare with a datasheet, and easier to misjudge by a factor of a thousand. A bare number without a unit is worse, because 1.76 could be amps, milliamps or volts. This habit applies to every final answer in every later lecture and lab.

check.q: A calculator shows 0.000877 amps. What is that in engineering form?
check.again: Move the decimal point three places at a time until the number sits between one and 999. Three places gives 0.877 milliamps, which is a correct value but still below one, so it is not yet engineering form. Three more places gives 877 microamps, and that is the answer. Getting 87.7 milliamps would mean moving only two places, which is not a prefix step. A parallel example: 0.000033 volts is 0.033 millivolts, still too small, so it becomes 33 microvolts. And always attach the unit, because 877 on its own tells nobody anything.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Four ideas from this lecture. One: engineering notation uses exponents in steps of three, written as prefixes, with the number kept between 1 and 999, and prefix letters are case sensitive, so small m is milli and capital M is mega. Two: changing prefix never changes the quantity; smaller unit means bigger number, by a factor of a thousand per step. Three: every calculation shows the target, the formula, the values with units, and the answer with its unit, and when something goes wrong a clean factor of a thousand points straight at the substitution step. Four: frequency and period are reciprocals, and the pairs 1 kilohertz with 1 millisecond and 1 megahertz with 1 microsecond let you convert in your head. Carry these habits into every lecture from here on.
segments.expand: Give the student a quick mixed drill: one prefix conversion, one Ohm's law answer in milliamps, and one frequency to period conversion.
segments.eli5: Think of a toolbox you open for every job. In it: a set of measuring cups that step by a thousand, called prefixes; a rule that swapping cups never changes how much flour you have; a four-line recipe card for every calculation; and a quick conversion chart linking how often something repeats with how long each repeat takes. With those tools out on the bench, every later problem gets easier. So prefixes, a four-step layout, and the frequency and period pairing are the habits to carry into every lecture.
segments.deep: The four ideas share one theme: keeping the size of a quantity under control. Engineering notation uses exponents in steps of three, written as prefixes, with the number from 1 to 999, and the letter case matters. Changing prefix never changes the quantity: smaller unit means bigger number, by one thousand per step. The four-step layout, target, formula, substitution with units, answer with units, lets you trace mistakes, and a clean factor of a thousand points at the substitution. Frequency equals one over period, hertz and seconds. A mixed drill: convert 0.0056 amps to 5.6 milliamps. Find the current through 2 kilohms with 8 volts across it: current equals voltage over resistance, so 8 volts over 2 kilohms is 4 milliamps, using volts over kilohms gives milliamps. Convert 10 kilohertz to its period: one over 10 times ten to the three hertz is 0.1 milliseconds, which is 100 microseconds. The common misconception is that these are only bookkeeping and the real content comes later. In practice most early errors are bookkeeping errors. These habits are used in the charge and current calculations of Lecture 3 and every circuit after.

check.q: One megahertz pairs with a period of one millisecond.
check.again: Frequency and period are reciprocals: frequency equals one over period, in hertz and seconds. One megahertz is a million cycles per second, so each cycle lasts a millionth of a second, which is one microsecond, not one millisecond. The two pairs to memorise are one kilohertz with one millisecond and one megahertz with one microsecond. A quick example: a ten megahertz clock has a period of 0.1 microseconds, or 100 nanoseconds, because ten times the frequency means a tenth of the period. Higher frequency always means a shorter period.

lectures.title: Charge, current and static discharge
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 03 - Charge, Current and ESD.md; Kleitz §9-5 (handling MOS devices, as cited)

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture connects three ideas: charge exerts force, moving charge is current, and a potential difference can drive that motion. Along the way we will see why a spark forms, why static electricity can quietly destroy an integrated circuit, how a wrist strap protects your chips, how to calculate current from charge and time, and which way current flows compared with the electrons. We will end with a short piece of history: why Volta's battery was such a big step beyond static electricity. Keep in mind the distinction we started last class: charge is an amount, current is a rate, and voltage is a difference between two points.
segments.expand: Summarise how charge, current and voltage relate, using the water tank and pipe comparison, and where the comparison breaks down.
segments.eli5: Think of a water tank on a hill feeding a pipe. The amount of water in the tank is like charge. How fast water flows past a point in the pipe is like current. The height difference between the tank and the outlet is like voltage, the push that can drive the flow. Where the comparison breaks: water flows because of gravity and can spill out of a broken pipe, while charge needs a complete circuit and has no up or down, and heights are always measured from somewhere chosen, just like voltage. So charge is an amount, current is a rate, and voltage is a difference between two points.
segments.deep: The three quantities are linked but not interchangeable. Charge, in coulombs, is an amount of electricity. Current, in amps, is the rate at which charge crosses a point: current equals charge divided by time, amps from coulombs per second. Voltage, in volts, is a potential difference between two points, the energy per unit charge available to push it. A voltage can exist with no current at all, as with a battery on a shelf, because current also needs a closed path. Example: 6 coulombs crossing a point in 3 seconds is 2 amps, regardless of whether the source is 1.5 volts or 9 volts; the voltage, along with the resistance in the path, decides how large that current would be, but the definition of current does not mention voltage. The water tank picture works for amount, rate and push, but breaks on two points. Water can flow out of an open pipe; charge cannot flow out of an open switch. And the tank picture suggests an absolute height, while voltage always compares two chosen points. The common misconception is that voltage is something that flows. It does not flow; charge flows, and voltage is the difference that drives it. This lecture builds on all three, ending with Volta's battery.

check.q: This introduction describes charge as a rate and current as an amount.
check.again: It is the other way round. Charge is an amount, a quantity of something, measured in coulombs. Current is a rate, how fast that charge passes a point, measured in amps, which is coulombs per second. Voltage is a difference between two points, measured in volts. Keeping those three roles straight is the whole foundation of this lecture. Picture water: the litres in a bucket are like charge, the litres per second through a hose are like current, and the pressure difference pushing the water along is like voltage.

segments.title: Attraction, repulsion and neutral objects
segments.text: Charge comes in two signs. Positive and positive repel; negative and negative repel; positive and negative attract. The labels positive and negative are a convention, but the forces are real and measurable. A neutral object has balanced positive and negative charge; it does not contain no charge. When solid objects become charged, it is usually electrons that move. Gain electrons and an object becomes more negative; lose them and it becomes more positive. Now the balloon. Rub a balloon so it picks up extra electrons, hold it near a neutral wall, and it sticks. The wall has not become positively charged. Instead the balloon's charge nudges the charges inside the wall surface, so the opposite charge sits slightly closer to the balloon than the like charge. The nearer charge wins, giving a net attraction. That is called polarization. So attraction alone does not prove the other object has the opposite charge. Repulsion is the clearer sign of like charges.
segments.expand: Explain polarization in more detail and why the nearer charges win because force depends on distance.
segments.eli5: Think of a magnet near a fridge door full of loose paper clips, except the clips can only shuffle slightly. Hold a negatively charged balloon near a neutral wall. Inside the wall surface, negative charge shuffles a tiny bit away and positive charge stays a tiny bit closer. The closer positive side is pulled more strongly than the farther negative side is pushed, so the wall attracts the balloon. Where the picture breaks: magnets work by a different force; this is purely electric. So a charged object can attract a neutral one by polarization, which is why only repulsion proves like charges.
segments.deep: Polarization works because electric force weakens with distance. When the charged balloon comes near, it does not add or remove charge from the wall. It shifts the balance inside the surface layer: like charges sit slightly farther from the balloon and opposite charges slightly closer. The total charge of the wall is still zero. But the opposite charges, being closer, feel a stronger attraction than the repulsion felt by the like charges farther away. Since force falls with the square of distance, even a small shift tips the balance toward attraction. Semi-quantitative example: if the nearer charge were at half the distance of the farther one, the force on it would be four times as strong per unit charge, so the pull clearly wins. The real shift is much smaller than that, but the direction of the effect is the same. The common misconception is that the wall must have become positive. It stays neutral overall; only its charge distribution changed. That is why a neutral object can be attracted by both a positive and a negative object, and why repulsion, which needs like charge on both, is the reliable test. Coulomb's law, next, makes the distance dependence exact.

check.q: A charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall. According to this segment, why?
options: The balloon gave up its charge
check.again: The wall stays neutral overall. The balloon's extra negative charge nudges the charges inside the wall's surface so that positive charge sits slightly nearer the balloon and negative charge slightly farther away. The nearer charge attracts more strongly than the farther charge repels, giving a net pull. That rearrangement is called polarization. This is why attraction alone does not prove two objects carry opposite charges; a charged object attracts neutral ones too. Repulsion is the clearer test, because only like charges repel. Try a charged comb near small bits of neutral paper: they jump to it for the same reason.

segments.title: Coulomb's law
segments.text: Charles Coulomb measured electrical forces in 1785 using a torsion balance, where a tiny force twists a suspended arm and the twist is calibrated. His result is Coulomb's law. The force between two point charges equals a constant k times the product of the two charges, divided by the distance between them squared. Force is in newtons, charge in coulombs, distance in metres, and k is about 8.99 times ten to the nine in newton metres squared per coulomb squared. The most useful part is the scaling.
