With a one kilohm resistor instead, the same 4.3 volts gives 4.3 milliamps.

segments.title: Two diodes in series
segments.text: With two diodes, each could be on or off, so there are four state combinations to consider. In a single series path, though, both diodes carry the same current, so one cannot conduct while the other blocks. That rules out the mixed cases quickly. Take 5 volts, a 3.3 kilohm resistor and two forward diodes. Assume both on: the resistor gets 5 minus 0.7 minus 0.7, which is 3.6 volts, and the current is 3.6 volts over 3.3 kilohms, about 1.09 milliamps. Now lower the supply to 1.5 volts. The two diodes take 1.4 volts, leaving only 0.1 volts for the resistor, so the current falls to about 30.3 microamps. And if the supply is below 1.4 volts, the formula would give a negative current. That does not mean current flows backwards through the diodes; it means the all-on assumption failed, and the path is off, with zero current.
segments.expand: Explain how to recognise a failed assumption from a negative current, and what the correct off-state solution looks like.
segments.eli5: Think of a road with two toll gates in a row, each charging the same fixed fee. A car must pass both or neither, because there is only one road. If you do not have enough money for both tolls, you do not get through at all. Two series diodes work like that: both conduct or neither does, and together they take 1.4 volts. With a 1.5 volt supply only 0.1 volts is left for the resistor, so the current is tiny. So two series diodes need more than 1.4 volts before any current flows, and the resistor gets the supply minus 1.4 volts.
segments.deep: Formula first: with both diodes on, Kirchhoff gives resistor voltage equals supply minus 0.7 minus 0.7, and current equals resistor voltage over resistance. In one series path, the same current flows through both diodes, so one cannot be on while the other is off; that removes two of the four state combinations immediately. Example from the lecture: 5 volts and 3.3 kilohms. The resistor gets 3.6 volts, and the current is 3.6 volts over 3.3 kilohms, about 1.09 milliamps. Lower the supply to 1.5 volts: the resistor gets only 0.1 volts, and the current falls to about 30.3 microamps. Lower it to 1.2 volts: the formula gives minus 0.2 volts over 3.3 kilohms, a negative current, about minus 60.6 microamps. That negative value is a contradiction, since a diode cannot conduct backward in this model, so the both-on assumption fails and the answer is zero current, with the diodes sharing the 1.2 volts between them. The common misconception is that a negative result means current flows backwards through the diodes. It means the assumed state was wrong. Assume, solve, check, applies to the transistor switch next.

check.q: Five volts, a 3.3 kilohm resistor and two forward silicon diodes in series, both on. What is the resistor voltage?
check.again: Each conducting diode takes 0.7 volts, so two in series take 1.4 volts. Kirchhoff's voltage law: five minus 0.7 minus 0.7 leaves 3.6 volts for the resistor. Ohm's law then gives 3.6 volts over 3.3 kilohms, about 1.09 milliamps, and a positive current confirms both diodes are on. Subtracting only one drop gives 4.3 volts, the single-diode answer. Both diodes carry the same current in a series path, so one cannot conduct while the other blocks. If the supply fell below 1.4 volts, the formula would go negative, meaning the all-on assumption fails and the path is simply off.

segments.title: The N P N transistor
segments.text: A bipolar junction transistor has three terminals: base, collector and emitter. The N P N type has its emitter arrow pointing outward. The key idea is control. A small current in the base circuit governs a larger current in the collector to emitter path, rather like a small valve operating a bigger one. The transistor does not create that energy; the collector supply does. With conventional currents flowing into the base and the collector and out of the emitter, Kirchhoff's current law says the emitter current equals the collector current plus the base current. Watch the subscripts on voltages too. V B E means base minus emitter, and V C E means collector minus emitter. Only when the emitter is grounded does V C E equal the collector's node voltage. In the classroom model, a fully on N P N has 0.7 volts from base to emitter and zero volts from collector to emitter, assuming the base drive is sufficient.
segments.expand: Explain why emitter current equals collector plus base current, and why the classroom switching model is a simplification.
segments.eli5: Think of a small tap that controls a big water valve. Turning the small tap a little lets a large flow through the main pipe, but the water in the main pipe comes from the main supply, not from your small tap. An N P N transistor works like that: a small base current controls a much larger collector to emitter current, and the energy comes from the collector supply. Both flows leave through the emitter. Where the picture breaks: this classroom model only uses fully on or fully off. So the emitter current equals the collector current plus the base current.
segments.deep: Formula first: Kirchhoff's current law at the transistor, emitter current equals collector current plus base current, all in amps, with conventional currents flowing in at the base and collector and out at the emitter. The emitter arrow points outward on an N P N, showing that direction. Voltage subscripts follow the ordered-subtraction rule: V B E means base potential minus emitter potential, and V C E means collector minus emitter. Only when the emitter sits at ground does V C E equal the collector's node voltage. Classroom on model: V B E equals 0.7 volts and V C E equals zero, provided the base drive is enough. Off model: no base current, no collector current. Example: a base current of 0.2 milliamps and a collector current of 4 milliamps give an emitter current of 4.2 milliamps. The common misconception is that the transistor amplifies by creating energy. The collector supply provides all the energy; the base only controls how much flows. Another trap is reading V C E as the collector voltage when the emitter is not grounded. The worked switch circuit next applies this model to a grounded-emitter transistor with two separate supplies.

check.q: V C E is always the same as the collector's node voltage.
check.again: V C E means collector minus emitter, a component voltage between two terminals. The collector's node voltage is collector minus ground. Those agree only when the emitter is tied to ground, so that the emitter potential is zero. If the emitter sits at two volts and the collector at five, V C E is three volts while the collector node voltage is five. The same subscript rule applies to V B E, base minus emitter. And by Kirchhoff's current law, with conventional currents into the base and collector and out of the emitter, the emitter current equals collector current plus base current.

segments.title: A worked transistor switch
segments.text: The emitter is grounded. A 3.3 volt input drives the base through a 10 kilohm resistor, and a separate 5 volt supply feeds the collector through 1.5 kilohms. Solve the base loop first. The base-emitter junction takes 0.7 volts, so the base resistor has 3.3 minus 0.7, which is 2.6 volts. Base current, by Ohm's law, is 2.6 volts over 10 kilohms, which is 260 microamps. Note that the 3.3 volt input is not the base voltage; the base sits at 0.7 volts and the resistor takes the difference. Now the collector loop, with the transistor fully on and zero volts from collector to emitter. The whole 5 volts is across the collector resistor, so the collector current is 5 volts over 1.5 kilohms, about 3.33 milliamps, and the output at the collector is 0 volts. The emitter current is the sum, about 3.59 milliamps. Set the input to 0 volts and everything switches off: no current, and the collector rises to 5 volts.
segments.expand: Recompute the transistor switch with a 5 volt input and a 1 kilohm collector resistor, and check both loops.
segments.eli5: Think of a doorbell that switches on a porch light through a separate circuit. Pressing the bell button uses a little effort, and that small push lets a separate, more powerful supply light the lamp. In the transistor switch, the 3.3 volt input pushes a small base current through 10 kilohms, and that turns on a separate collector path fed by 5 volts. When on, the collector is pulled to ground. Where the picture breaks: the transistor is electronic, with no moving parts. So the base loop sets the base current, and the collector loop, with the transistor fully on, sets the collector current.
segments.deep: Formula first: base current equals input voltage minus 0.7 volts, divided by the base resistance; collector current, fully on, equals collector supply minus zero, divided by the collector resistance; emitter current is their sum. Example from the lecture: 3.3 minus 0.7 is 2.6 volts, over 10 kilohms, gives 260 microamps of base current. The collector loop: 5 volts over 1.5 kilohms gives about 3.33 milliamps, and the output at the collector is 0 volts. Emitter current: 3.33 milliamps plus 0.26 milliamps, about 3.59 milliamps. Set the input to 0 volts: no base current, no collector current, the collector resistor drops nothing, and the output rises to 5 volts. Why solve the base loop first? It decides whether the transistor is on at all. The common misconception is that the base voltage equals the input voltage, 3.3 volts. The base-emitter junction holds the base at about 0.7 volts, and the base resistor takes the rest. Another trap is adding the input voltage into the collector loop. The two loops share only the emitter path. The next segment notices what this circuit does logically: it inverts.

check.q: A 3.3 volt input drives the base through ten kilohms, and the base-emitter junction takes 0.7 volts. What is the base current?
check.again: Solve the base loop first. The junction holds 0.7 volts, so the base resistor has 3.3 minus 0.7, which is 2.6 volts across it. Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance, amps from volts over ohms. So 2.6 volts over ten kilohms is 260 microamps. Using the full 3.3 volts would give 330 microamps, forgetting the junction drop; using 0.7 volts gives 70 microamps, mixing up which voltage is across the resistor. The input voltage is not the base voltage; the base sits at 0.7 and the resistor takes the difference. Separately, the collector loop gives about 3.33 milliamps.

segments.title: Why this circuit inverts
segments.text: Look at what that example did. Input 0 volts, transistor off, output 5 volts, HIGH. Input 3.3 volts, transistor on, output 0 volts, LOW. The output is the opposite of the input, so this common-emitter circuit is an inverter. The input goes to the base, the emitter is common, tied to ground, and the output is taken at the collector, which is pulled up by the collector resistor. Keep two ideas separate: the transistor's state and the output's logic level. Turning the transistor on pulls the output low. Kleitz adds one more warning in his section on T T L chips. When the transistor is off, the output is only at the full supply if nothing draws current from it. A load resistor to ground forms a divider with the collector resistor and pulls the high level down, which is why real logic chips use a stronger output stage.
segments.expand: Explain output loading on the inverter with a numeric divider example, and why a totem-pole output helps.
segments.eli5: Think of a light controlled by someone who does the opposite of what you ask. Ask for dark and they switch it on; ask for light and they switch it off. The common-emitter transistor is that contrary helper. A LOW input leaves the transistor off, so nothing pulls the collector down and the resistor holds the output HIGH. A HIGH input turns the transistor on, which pulls the output LOW. So turning the transistor on makes the output LOW: this circuit is an inverter, and its output is the opposite of its input.
segments.deep: Formula first: with the transistor off, no collector current flows, so the collector resistor drops zero and output equals the collector supply; with it on, V C E is zero and the output is 0 volts. Input LOW gives output HIGH; input HIGH gives output LOW, the definition of an inverter. Keep the transistor's state separate from the output's level: on means the switch conducts, which makes the output LOW. Kleitz's warning about loads: when the transistor is off, the output is at the full supply only if nothing draws current from it. Example: 5 volts, a 1.5 kilohm collector resistor, and a 1.5 kilohm load resistor from the output to ground. With the transistor off, the two resistors form a series divider, and the output is 5 volts times 1.5 over 3, which is 2.5 volts. The HIGH has sagged to half the supply, which may not be read as HIGH at all. The common misconception is that a transistor on means the output is on, or HIGH. In this circuit, on means LOW. The load-sagging problem is why real T T L chips use a stronger output stage, and the inverter symbol and its chip return in Lecture 6.

check.q: In the common-emitter circuit, turning the transistor on makes the output?
check.again: When the transistor is on, its collector to emitter path acts like a closed switch, pulling the collector down to about zero volts. The output is taken at the collector, so the output is LOW. When the input is zero, the transistor is off, no collector current flows, and the collector resistor pulls the output up to the supply, HIGH. Input HIGH gives output LOW and input LOW gives output HIGH, so the circuit is an inverter. Keep the transistor's state and the output's level as two separate ideas: on means LOW here. A load resistor to ground can pull that HIGH level down.

segments.title: From discrete parts to logic chips
segments.text: A logic chip packs many of these transistors and diodes together. T T L, transistor-transistor logic, is built from bipolar transistors like the N P N we just used. Before you wire any chip, orient the package. On a dual in-line package, find the notch or pin one marker; looking from the top, numbering runs down one side and back up the other. The exact part number and its datasheet decide which pins are power, ground, inputs and outputs, so never assume a pinout from the package shape alone. Next, give every input a defined level. An unconnected input floats, and its voltage can be pushed around by noise and coupling, so it is not a dependable HIGH or LOW. In the lab arrangement discussed, unused gate inputs are tied HIGH. Outputs are different: an unused output can be left unconnected, but a driven output must never be tied to a supply rail as if it were an input.
segments.expand: Explain why floating inputs misbehave and why inputs and outputs are treated differently when unused.
segments.eli5: Think of a row of light switches on a wall with no labels. Before you start flipping them, you find which one is the first, and you check the building plan to learn what each controls; you never guess from the plate's shape. A logic chip's pins are the same: find pin one at the notch, then count down one side and up the other, and read the datasheet for the exact part. And every switch must be set either on or off, never half way. So orient by the notch, trust only the datasheet, and give every input a defined level.
segments.deep: A dual in-line package numbers its pins in a fixed pattern: with the notch or pin one marker at the top and looking down on the chip, pin one is top left, numbering runs down the left side and continues up the right side. For a 14-pin chip, pin 7 is bottom left and pin 8 is bottom right, so pin 14 is top right, next to pin 1 across the notch. But the pattern only gives numbers; what each pin does depends on the part number, so the datasheet decides power, ground, inputs and outputs. Inputs need defined levels because an unconnected input floats. Its voltage is decided by noise and coupling, not by your design, so a gate may misread it or switch unpredictably. In the lab arrangement discussed, unused inputs are tied HIGH. Outputs differ: an unused output can be left unconnected, but an output that is driving must never be tied to a supply rail, because if it drives the opposite level it would force a large current between the output and the rail. The common misconception is that an unconnected input reads as zero. It is undefined. Unused input handling returns in Lecture 8 in detail.

check.q: In the lab arrangement discussed, unused gate inputs are tied HIGH.
check.again: An unconnected input floats, and its voltage can be pushed around by noise and coupling, so it is never a dependable HIGH or LOW. Every input therefore needs a defined level, and in the lab arrangement the unused ones are tied HIGH. Outputs are different: an unused output can simply be left unconnected, but a driven output must never be tied to a supply rail as though it were an input. And before wiring any chip, orient the package by its notch or pin one marker and read the exact part's datasheet, because the package shape alone does not tell you the pinout.

segments.title: Holding one gate input steady
segments.text: The class demonstration used a NAND gate, whose output is the inverse of the AND of its inputs. Hold one input HIGH and feed a clock to the other. One AND clock is just the clock, and the NAND inverts it, so the output is the clock turned upside down: clock LOW gives output HIGH, clock HIGH gives output LOW. This is a small case of what Kleitz calls enable and disable. With a plain AND gate, holding the control input HIGH lets the signal pass unchanged, because one and A equals A, while holding it LOW forces the output LOW, because zero and anything is zero. An OR gate works the other way: a LOW control passes the signal, and a HIGH control forces the output HIGH. The input value that takes over the output, zero for AND and one for OR, is called the controlling value.
segments.expand: Work through AND and OR enable with a clock, and explain how a run and stop control uses this idea.
segments.eli5: Think of a gatekeeper at a door. If the gatekeeper is told to let people through, whoever arrives walks in; if told to keep the door shut, nobody gets in, however many arrive. Holding one gate input fixed works like that. For an AND gate, a HIGH control lets the signal pass, and a LOW control blocks it, forcing the output LOW. For an OR gate, a LOW control passes the signal and a HIGH control forces the output HIGH. So the controlling value, zero for AND and one for OR, takes over the output whatever the other input does.
segments.deep: Formula first in words: for AND, one AND A equals A, and zero AND A equals zero; for OR, zero OR A equals A, and one OR A equals one. A NAND gate is AND followed by an inverter, so its output is the AND, complemented. Hold one NAND input HIGH and feed a clock to the other: one AND clock is the clock, and inverting gives the clock upside down. Clock HIGH gives output LOW; clock LOW gives output HIGH. Hold that NAND input LOW instead: zero AND clock is zero, inverted to one, so the output stays HIGH whatever the clock does; the clock is blocked. Example with an AND gate and a 1 kilohertz clock: control HIGH, the output is the same 1 kilohertz clock; control LOW, the output is a steady LOW. The common misconception is that a blocked gate outputs nothing, or floats. It outputs a definite level: LOW for a blocked AND, HIGH for a blocked OR or NAND. This is what Kleitz calls enable and disable, and it returns in chapter three with timing diagrams, where you trace an output while one input enables or disables a clock.

check.q: For an AND gate, which input value is the controlling value that takes over the output?
check.again: The controlling value is the input value that decides the output on its own. For AND, a zero on either input forces the output to zero, because zero and anything is zero, so zero is the controlling value. A one on the control input just passes the other signal through, since one and A equals A. For OR it is reversed: a one forces the output HIGH, while a zero passes the signal. That is why holding one NAND input HIGH with a clock on the other gives the clock inverted: the AND passes the clock and the bubble flips it.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: The main ideas from today. One: a diode is forward biased when anode minus cathode is positive; in our model it then holds 0.7 volts, and reverse biased it is open, so judge bias by the difference, never by one voltage alone. Two: solve device circuits by assuming a state, solving, and checking that the result supports the assumption; a negative forward current means the assumption failed. Three: an N P N transistor's base current, input minus 0.7 over the base resistor, switches its collector to emitter path, and in the common-emitter circuit that makes an inverter: transistor on, output LOW. Four: in logic chips, every input needs a defined level, and holding one gate input at a fixed value either passes a signal or blocks it.
segments.expand: Give a short diode question and a short transistor question, and discuss the typical mistake in each.
segments.eli5: Think of a set of locks and valves on a water system. A one-way valve opens only when pushed from the right side, and only past a small threshold. A small tap controls a big valve. And every pipe must end somewhere definite, or water sloshes randomly. Today's devices are those parts. A diode conducts one way with about 0.7 volts across it. A transistor's small base current controls its collector path, which makes an inverter. Logic inputs must be defined. So assume a state, solve, check, and never leave a logic input floating.
segments.deep: The common thread is modelling a switching device by its state and checking the state. Diode: bias is anode minus cathode; on means 0.7 volts across it and positive current; off means zero current and a voltage set by the circuit. N P N transistor: base current equals input minus 0.7 volts over the base resistance; fully on means zero collector to emitter voltage; emitter current is collector plus base current. Common emitter makes an inverter: transistor on, output LOW. A combined example: 5 volts through 2.2 kilohms and one forward diode gives 4.3 volts over 2.2 kilohms, about 1.95 milliamps. A 5 volt input through 10 kilohms into a transistor base gives 4.3 volts over 10 kilohms, 430 microamps of base current, turning it on and pulling the collector output to 0 volts. Logic chips need defined inputs, and holding one gate input at its controlling value blocks a signal, while the other value passes it. The common misconception is that a negative calculated current is a real backward current. It is a sign that the assumed state was wrong. Lecture 6 moves from these discrete parts to the transistor circuits inside T T L chips and how to draw them.

check.q: If the calculation gives a negative forward current, the diode is conducting backwards.
check.again: A negative forward current means the assumption that the diode is on has failed. The model diode cannot conduct backwards; reverse biased, it is an open circuit. So the right response is to reject the on assumption, treat the path as off, and set the current to zero. Suppose 1.2 volts drives two silicon diodes in series through a resistor: 1.2 minus 1.4 is negative, so the diodes are off and nothing flows. That is the assume, solve, check method at work. Judge bias by anode minus cathode, and let a failed check send you to the other state.

lectures.title: IC pinouts, schematics and TTL basics
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 06 - IC Pinouts, Schematics and Lab Standards.md; Kleitz §3-5, §2-9

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture moves us from discrete parts to integrated circuits. We will read a real datasheet pinout, for the 74 L S 47 decoder, a resistor array and a seven-segment display, and learn the professional conventions for putting a chip on a schematic: where pin numbers go, how to name each chip, and how active-low pins are marked. Then we look at why neat, flat wiring is an electrical issue, not only a tidy one. Finally we begin T T L itself: the transistor as a switch, the inverter, and the common gate chips such as the 7408. The theme is that a schematic is a set of instructions for someone who cannot ask you what you meant.
segments.expand: Explain why a schematic must be complete and unambiguous for someone else to build or troubleshoot from it.
segments.eli5: Think of leaving assembly instructions for flat-pack furniture with someone who cannot phone you. Every screw must be named, every hole numbered, and every step clear, because they cannot ask what you meant. A schematic with chips on it is those instructions. This lecture covers how to read a real chip's pinout, how to place a chip on a drawing so every pin is clear, why neat flat wiring matters electrically, and a first view of the transistors inside T T L chips. So a schematic must let a stranger build and troubleshoot the circuit without asking you anything.
segments.deep: A schematic is a contract between the designer and whoever builds, tests or repairs the circuit. Every convention in this lecture exists to remove guesswork. The pinout gives each pin's number and function from the manufacturer's datasheet. The drawing conventions, number outside the body, function inside, a U designator with the part number, and bars for active-low pins, make each symbol traceable to one physical pin on one physical chip. Flat wiring keeps the built circuit matching the drawing and reduces electrical coupling. Example of what goes wrong without it: a drawing shows a chip with no pin numbers on its power connections. The builder guesses pin 14 for supply because that worked on a 7408, but this is a 16-pin 74 L S 47, where supply is pin 16 and ground is pin 8. The chip does not work, and an hour is lost. The common misconception is that conventions are just neatness rules. Each one prevents a specific mistake by someone who does not share your memory of the design. The lecture then turns to T T L, building on the transistor switch of Lecture 5, and the common gate chips used in the lab.

check.q: According to this introduction, a schematic is a set of instructions for whom?
options: Someone who cannot ask what you meant
The manufacturer of every chip on it
The student who drew the circuit
check.again: The theme of the lecture is that a schematic must stand on its own. The person building, inspecting or repairing the board may never meet you, so every pin number, designator, part number and active-low mark has to be on the page. That is why the conventions matter: number outside, function inside, U designators with part numbers, consistent corners. Imagine handing your drawing to a technician in another city with no phone number attached. If they would have to guess anything, the schematic is not finished. The same rule explains why flat, traceable wiring is treated as an electrical matter.

segments.title: The three devices in this circuit
segments.text: The circuit discussed uses three devices. The 74 L S 47 is a B C D to seven-segment decoder and driver. It takes a four-bit binary coded decimal input and works out which of the seven segment lines to switch so that a digit appears. The seven-segment display is the digit itself: seven L E D bars, lettered a to g, plus a decimal point. The 330 ohm resistor array is a single package holding several 330 ohm resistors, one to limit the current in each segment. Using eight separate resistors would work electrically; the array is simply neater on a board. A little background explains why the resistors are there: the 47 is designed for common-anode displays, and its outputs pull low to light a segment. So current flows from the supply, through the display segment and its resistor, into the decoder's output. Without the resistor, that segment current would be far too large.
segments.expand: Explain how a B C D to seven-segment decoder decides which segments to light for a digit, using one digit as an example.
segments.eli5: Think of a scoreboard at a game. A computer decides which number to show, the board has light bars that form the digits, and each bar has its own fuse so a fault cannot burn it out. The 74 L S 47 is the computer: it turns a four-bit code into the right set of bars. The seven-segment display is the board, with bars a to g. The 330 ohm resistor array is the fuses, except resistors limit current all the time rather than breaking. So the decoder chooses the segments, the display shows them, and the resistors limit each segment's current.
segments.deep: The 74 L S 47 takes a four-bit binary coded decimal input, a digit from 0 to 9 in binary, and decides which of the seven segment lines to activate. Its outputs are designed for a common-anode display: all segment anodes share the supply, and a segment lights when the decoder pulls its cathode line LOW. So current flows from the supply, through the L E D segment, through its 330 ohm resistor, and into the decoder output. Without the resistor, nothing would limit that current except the L E D and the output transistor. Semi-quantitative example, with an assumed L E D drop of about 2 volts and a LOW output near 0 volts: the resistor would have about 3 volts across it. Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, gives 3 volts over 330 ohms, about 9 milliamps per segment, a safe level. Without the resistor the current would be far larger. The resistor array is simply several 330 ohm resistors in one package; separate resistors work identically. The common misconception is that the decoder supplies the current to light a segment. It sinks it: the supply provides the current and the decoder pulls it to ground. Reading these three parts' pinouts is the next step.

check.q: What does the 330 ohm resistor array do in the seven-segment display circuit?
options: Limits the current in each segment
Decodes the four-bit B C D input
Selects which digit the display shows
check.again: The array is one package holding several 330 ohm resistors, one for each segment line. Each resistor limits the current through its L E D segment. The decoding is done by the 74 L S 47, which takes the four-bit B C D input and decides which of the seven segments to switch on. The display is common anode, and the decoder's outputs pull low to light a segment, so current flows from the supply, through the segment and its resistor, into the decoder output. Without the resistor that current would be far too large. Eight separate resistors would work too; the array is just neater.

segments.title: Reading a pinout
segments.text: Doing a pinout means getting every pin's number and every pin's function onto the drawing, including the power pins, not only the ones you plan to wire. Take the datasheet from the manufacturer's own site, where the information is reliable. Pin 1 is marked on the package by a notch or a dimple, and sometimes a small dot. Hold the chip with the notch at the top: pin 1 is top left, numbering runs down that side and then back up the other. For the 74 L S 47 in its 16-pin package, the supply V C C is pin 16 and ground is pin 8. The binary inputs are capital A, B, C and D, on pins 7, 1, 2 and 6, while the lowercase letters a to g are the segment outputs. The display and the resistor array need the same care. The resistor array datasheet covers several internal arrangements, so read the one for your exact package.
segments.expand: Explain how to find pin 1 and count pins on a sixteen-pin package, and why the uppercase and lowercase letters matter.
segments.eli5: Think of house numbers on a street that loops around a block. Number one is at the corner by the park, numbers go down one side, then continue up the other side, so the highest number ends up opposite number one. A chip's pins follow that pattern, with the notch marking the park corner. Then a directory, the datasheet, tells you who lives at each number. Where the picture breaks: on a chip, the pattern never tells you what a pin does. So find pin one at the notch, count down and back up, and take every pin's function from the manufacturer's datasheet.
segments.deep: A pinout is every pin's number and function, including power and ground, not only the pins you plan to use. Numbering: with the notch at the top, viewed from above, pin 1 is top left, numbers run down the left and back up the right. On a 16-pin package, pin 8 is bottom left, pin 9 bottom right and pin 16 top right. Function comes only from the datasheet for the exact part, preferably from the manufacturer's own site. For the 74 L S 47, V C C is pin 16 and ground is pin 8, unlike the 14-pin gate chips with pin 14 and pin 7. The binary inputs, capital A, B, C and D, sit on pins 7, 1, 2 and 6, so they are not in order around the package, and the lowercase a to g are segment outputs. Mixing capital A with lowercase a would connect a binary input to a segment line. The common misconception is that the supply is always in the top-right and ground in the bottom-left corner. That is often true but must be checked for each part. A resistor array's datasheet also covers several internal arrangements, so read the one for your exact package before drawing it.

check.q: On the 74 L S 47 in its sixteen-pin package, which pin is the supply, V C C?
check.again: For the sixteen-pin 74 L S 47, V C C is pin sixteen and ground is pin eight. Pin fourteen is the supply on the fourteen-pin gate chips such as the 7408, so do not carry that over. Find pin one at the notch or dimple with the notch at the top: pin one is top left, numbering runs down that side and back up the other, so the highest number ends up top right. A pinout means every pin's number and function, including power pins, taken from the manufacturer's own datasheet. The binary inputs A, B, C and D sit on pins seven, one, two and six.

segments.title: Overbars mean active low
segments.text: Several 74 L S 47 pins carry names with a bar over them: L T, lamp test; B I or R B O, blanking in and ripple blanking out; and R B I, ripple blanking in. Spoken aloud you might say L T bar or L T not. The bar means the function is active low: it does its job when the pin is held at logic 0, not logic 1. So to run a lamp test, which lights every segment to check the display, you pull the L T pin LOW; in normal use it sits HIGH. Active low is simply a statement about which logic level asserts the function. It does not mean a negative voltage, and it does not change what HIGH and LOW mean physically. Many control pins in digital systems are active low, so learn to spot the bar and ask, what level turns this function on?
segments.expand: Give other examples of active-low control pins, and explain how a designer decides the idle level for such a pin.
segments.eli5: Think of a fire alarm wire in a building where the alarm sounds when the wire is cut, rather than when it is powered. The wire is normally live; dropping it to nothing triggers the action. An active-low pin works the same way: it sits HIGH in normal use, and pulling it LOW asserts its function. The bar over the name is the label telling you so. Where the picture breaks: LOW on a chip is a defined logic level, not a cut wire. So a bar over a pin name means the function happens at logic 0, without implying any negative voltage.
segments.deep: Active low is a statement about which logic level asserts a function. For a pin named with a bar, such as L T bar, the function happens when the pin is LOW, logic 0, and is inactive when HIGH. That is all it means. It does not mean a negative voltage, and HIGH and LOW keep their usual physical meaning. Example on the 74 L S 47: lamp test lights all seven segments so you can check the display. Its pin is L T bar, so in normal use it is held HIGH, and to test the lamp you pull it LOW. The blanking pins, B I bar or R B O bar, and R B I bar, are also active low, and in normal counting they are held HIGH or left as the datasheet allows. A similar idea appeared with the pull-up in Lecture 4: a pressed button gave LOW, so that press was active LOW. The common misconception is that the bar means the pin is an output, or that the pin should be tied to ground permanently. It only tells you which level does the job; grounding L T bar would light every segment all the time. Active-low marking on schematics, with bars and bubbles, returns in Lecture 8.

check.q: A bar over a pin name such as L T means the function is asserted by what?
check.again: The bar means active low: the pin does its job when it is held at logic zero. To run a lamp test on the 74 L S 47, you pull the L T pin LOW, and in normal use it sits HIGH. Active low says nothing about negative voltages, and it does not change what HIGH and LOW mean electrically; it only says which of the two levels turns the function on. Many control pins work this way, such as blanking inputs and resets. Whenever you see the bar, ask one question: what level asserts this?

segments.title: Number outside, function inside
segments.text: One rule governs every chip you place on a schematic: the pin number goes outside the body, and the pin function goes inside. On a horizontal pin, the number sits just above the wire; on a vertical pin, it sits beside the wire. The reason is practical. Every pin's wire has to run off somewhere once the drawing is finished. If the number sat on the line the wire will follow, the wire would end up passing straight through it. Keeping the number just off the wire leaves that path clear. Many manufacturers print numbers inside the outline on their own package drawings; that is their house style, not the schematic convention used here. The resistor array is the odd one out. It is an analog part with no functions to name, so you number all its pins outside and put a small resistor symbol inside between each connected pair.
segments.expand: Explain why the resistor array is drawn with resistor symbols inside its outline when digital chips are not.
segments.eli5: Think of street signs and building names. A street's house number goes on the kerb outside, where the road meets the building, while the business name is inside on the shop sign. Put the number in the middle of the road and the first car runs over it. On a schematic, the pin number sits just off the wire, outside the chip body, and the pin function is written inside. That keeps the path clear for the wire that will connect there. So pin numbers go outside the body, beside the wire, and pin functions go inside.
segments.deep: The rule is placement for readability once wires are added. On a horizontal pin, the number goes just above the wire; on a vertical pin, just beside it. If it sat on the line, the connecting wire would run straight through it, and a 1 could read as a 7 or vanish. Inside the body you write the function, such as V C C, G N D, A, or L T bar, so the reader sees both what the pin does and where it physically is. Example: a 74 L S 47 drawn with input A on its left side. Outside, above the wire, is the number 7; inside, next to the edge, is the letter A. The builder reads pin 7 for the breadboard and A for the logic. Manufacturers often print numbers inside their package outlines; that is their house style for package drawings, not the schematic convention for this course. The resistor array is the exception: it is analog, with no functions to name, so every pin number goes outside and a resistor symbol is drawn inside between each connected pair. The common misconception is that the convention is purely style. It directly prevents misread pin numbers. Designators and part numbers, next, complete each chip's label.

check.q: On a schematic, the pin number is written inside the chip body next to its function.
check.again: The convention is number outside, function inside. The pin function, such as V C C or input A, goes inside the body. The pin number goes outside, just above a horizontal pin's wire or beside a vertical one. The reason is practical: every pin's wire has to run off somewhere, and a number sitting on the wire's path would be crossed out by it. Manufacturers often print numbers inside their own package drawings, but that is their house style. The resistor array is the exception: it has no functions to name, so all its numbers go outside with a small resistor symbol between each pair.

segments.title: Designators and part numbers
segments.text: Each chip on a schematic needs a designator, a unique name for that physical part. Integrated circuits use the letter U: U1, U2, U3 and so on, not I C 1. Directly below the designator goes the part number, such as 74 L S 47 or 74 L S 193. That is a part number, not a value. Pick one corner of the chip outline for this label and use the same corner on every chip, because consistency is what lets a reader find labels quickly. The reason for all of this is traceability. Someone assembling, inspecting or troubleshooting a board must be able to match every symbol on the page to one physical part, without guessing which label belongs to which chip. A designator that is missing, duplicated or placed carelessly between two chips invites exactly the kind of mix-up that costs hours on the bench.
segments.expand: Explain how designators support assembly and troubleshooting, and what goes wrong when labels are ambiguous.
segments.eli5: Think of a hospital where every patient wears a wristband with a unique ID, and the chart says what treatment they get. If two patients had the same ID, or the wristband was missing, the wrong person might get the wrong medicine. A designator, like U1 or U2, is each chip's wristband: unique, and placed in the same corner every time. The part number below it, such as 74 L S 47, says what the chip is. So every chip gets a unique U designator with its part number below, placed consistently, so each symbol traces to one physical part.
segments.deep: A designator is a unique name for one physical part on the board. Integrated circuits use U, so U1, U2, U3, rather than I C 1. Resistors use R and so on. Directly below the designator goes the part number, such as 74 L S 193, which tells the builder which chip to fetch; it is not a value like 330 ohms. Consistency matters: pick one corner of the outline and use it for every chip so the eye learns where to look. The purpose is traceability, matching every symbol to exactly one physical object without guessing. Example of failure: a board has two 7408 chips, both labelled only with the part number. A fault is traced to the gate on pin 3 of the AND chip, but which one? Labelled U2 and U3, the answer is immediate. Duplicate designators are as bad as none: a parts list with two U2s cannot be built. The common misconception is that the part number is enough to identify a chip. Many identical chips can share a part number, so only the designator is unique. Clear labels, plus neat wiring, next, are what make troubleshooting a several-chip circuit possible.

check.q: What designator letter does an integrated circuit get on a schematic?
options: I C, as in I C 1
check.again: Integrated circuits are designated with the letter U: U1, U2, U3 and so on, not I C 1. Directly below the designator goes the part number, such as 74 L S 47, which names the kind of chip rather than a value. Put that label in the same corner of every chip outline so a reader finds it at once. The point is traceability: anyone assembling or troubleshooting the board must match every symbol on the page to exactly one physical part. A missing or duplicated designator invites the kind of mix-up that costs hours at the bench.

segments.title: Why wiring should lie flat
segments.text: Flat wiring, with every wire lying against the breadboard and no loops jumping over other wires or over chips, has an electrical reason. A loop of wire behaves like an antenna. Put two loops side by side, and a fast clock edge in one couples a spike into the other. The digital circuit then fails now and again, with glitches on a line, even though nothing in your logic is wrong. That kind of intermittent fault is among the hardest to find. The second reason is practical: a tangle of wires cannot be traced end to end, so it cannot be troubleshot. Wire cut to length and stripped so it lies flat keeps loop area small and keeps every connection visible. Once the circuits grow to several chips, this is what makes a fault a ten-minute job instead of an impossible one.
segments.expand: Explain how loop area relates to coupling between wires, and why fast edges make it worse.
segments.eli5: Think of two neighbours with big satellite dishes pointed at each other. Whatever one transmits, the other picks up. A loop of wire on a breadboard acts like a small antenna, and two loops side by side pass a sudden clock edge from one to the other as a stray spike. Wires lying flat with small loops are like dishes folded away. Where the picture breaks: these are not radio dishes, just wire loops, but the coupling effect is real. So flat wiring reduces glitches caused by coupling between loops and keeps every wire traceable.
segments.deep: A loop of wire behaves like a small antenna: a sudden change of current in one loop couples a brief voltage spike into a nearby loop, and the bigger and closer the loops, the stronger the coupling. A fast clock edge is the most sudden change on the board, so it couples most strongly. If the induced spike lands on a logic input at the wrong moment, it can be read as an extra edge or a wrong level, giving intermittent glitches with perfect logic. What it depends on: loop area, how close the loops are, and how fast the edges change. Lying wires flat against the breadboard, cut to length, keeps loop area small and loops apart. Semi-quantitative example: a jumper arching two centimetres above the board over a stretch of three centimetres encloses about six square centimetres; the same jumper lying flat encloses only a tiny sliver, so coupling drops sharply. The second reason is practical: a tangle cannot be traced end to end, so a fault cannot be found. The common misconception is that neat wiring is about appearance or marks. It is an electrical and troubleshooting issue, and intermittent faults from coupling are among the hardest to diagnose. This matters more as the circuits in later labs grow to several chips.

check.q: Why does this segment say a loop of wire on a breadboard is a problem?
options: It acts as an antenna and couples spikes
It adds resistance to the signal
It draws extra current from the supply
check.again: A loop of wire behaves like an antenna. Put two loops near each other, and a fast clock edge in one couples a spike into the other. The logic is right, yet the circuit glitches now and then, which is the hardest kind of fault to find. That is the electrical reason for flat wiring: wire cut to length and lying against the board keeps loop area small. The second reason is practical: a tangle cannot be traced end to end, so it cannot be troubleshot. A wire's resistance and supply current are not the issue here; coupling is.

segments.title: T T L transistors as switches
segments.text: T T L stands for transistor-transistor logic: logic built from bipolar junction transistors, dating from the nineteen sixties and still in use, running from a nominal 5 volt supply. For now we model the transistor's collector to emitter path as a plain switch. With base current flowing, the switch is closed; this is saturation, fully on. With zero base current, the switch is open; this is cutoff. The base-emitter junction behaves like a diode, needing about 0.7 volts before it conducts. So a 5 volt input through a base resistor pushes current into the base and turns the transistor on, while 0 volts gives no base current and turns it off. Treat any base current means fully on as a classroom simplification: real transistors also have an active region where they amplify, and real saturation needs enough base current for the load.
segments.expand: Explain saturation, cutoff and the active region, and why switching circuits avoid the active region.
segments.eli5: Think of a light switch operated by a tiny trickle of water: some flow, and a mechanism snaps the light fully on; no flow, and it snaps fully off. In T T L, a bipolar transistor's collector to emitter path is used as such a switch. Base current turns it fully on, called saturation; no base current turns it fully off, called cutoff. The base-emitter junction acts like a diode needing about 0.7 volts. Where the picture breaks: real transistors also have an in-between active region. So in this model, base current means closed, no base current means open.
segments.deep: Formula first: base current equals input voltage minus 0.7 volts, divided by the base resistance, amps, volts and ohms. If that is positive and large enough, the transistor saturates: collector to emitter is modelled as a closed switch. If the input is below 0.7 volts, no base current flows, and the transistor is in cutoff, an open switch. T T L, transistor-transistor logic, uses bipolar transistors inside, runs on a nominal 5 volt supply, and dates from the nineteen sixties. Example: 5 volts into a 10 kilohm base resistor gives 4.3 volts over 10 kilohms, 430 microamps of base current, turning the transistor on; 0 volts gives none, turning it off. What saturation really depends on is enough base current for the collector current the load demands; with too little, the transistor sits in the active region, where it amplifies rather than switches fully. The common misconception is that any base current at all guarantees fully on. The classroom model simplifies this, and it holds for the switching circuits here because they are designed with plenty of base drive. This switch picture supports the inverter and gate chips in the next segment.

check.q: With base current flowing, the transistor's switch is closed. What is that state called?
check.again: In the switch model, base current flowing means the collector to emitter path is closed, fully on, and that state is saturation. Zero base current means the path is open, and that is cutoff. The base-emitter junction acts like a diode needing about 0.7 volts, so a five volt input through a base resistor pushes current into the base and saturates the transistor, while zero volts gives no base current and cuts it off. The active region, where the transistor amplifies, is real, but the classroom model skips it: any base current is treated as fully on.

segments.title: The inverter and the gate chips
segments.text: The simplest logic function is the inverter: input LOW gives output HIGH, and input HIGH gives output LOW. It is drawn as a triangle with a small bubble on the output, and inside a real T T L inverter there are four transistors, two diodes and four resistors. The symbol is the abstraction; the transistor circuit is what is really on the chip. Kleitz's section on using logic chips introduces the common packages. The 7408 holds four two-input AND gates, the 7432 four two-input OR gates, the 7411 three three-input AND gates, and the 7421 two four-input AND gates. On these 14-pin T T L chips, pin 14 is V C C at plus 5 volts and pin 7 is ground. On the 7408, the first gate's inputs are pins 1 and 2 and its output is pin 3, and the other gates follow in the same pattern.
segments.expand: Walk through the 7408 pin arrangement for all four gates, and explain why the datasheet must be checked for other chips.
segments.eli5: Think of a car's steering wheel. You only see the wheel and know that turning left goes left; underneath are rods, gears and pumps you never look at. The inverter symbol, a triangle with a bubble, is the steering wheel: input LOW gives output HIGH, input HIGH gives LOW. Inside a real T T L inverter are four transistors, two diodes and four resistors doing the work. The gate chips package several such gates together. So the symbol shows the logic, the chip holds the circuit, and on 14-pin T T L gates pin 14 is plus 5 volts and pin 7 is ground.
segments.deep: The inverter is the simplest logic function: the output is the complement of the input. Its symbol is a triangle with a small bubble, and the bubble itself means inversion. A real T T L inverter uses several transistors, giving it the stronger output stage mentioned in Lecture 5, where the single-transistor inverter's HIGH sagged under load. Gate chips put several gates in one package sharing one power pair. Example counts: the 7408 holds four two-input AND gates, using 4 times 3, which is 12 signal pins, plus 2 power pins, filling all 14. The 7432 holds four two-input OR gates in the same pattern. The 7411 holds three three-input AND gates, 3 times 4, again 12 signal pins. The 7421 holds two four-input AND gates, 2 times 5, which is 10 signal pins, so two pins are unused. On the 7408, gate one uses pins 1 and 2 as inputs and pin 3 as output, and the others follow a similar pattern. The common misconception is that every 14-pin chip has the same gate pin layout. Power on 14 and 7 is common, but gate pins differ, so check the datasheet. Lecture 7 looks at T T L input behaviour and the gates themselves.

check.q: On a fourteen-pin T T L gate chip such as the 7408, which pin is ground?
check.again: On the fourteen-pin T T L gate chips, pin fourteen is V C C at plus five volts and pin seven is ground. That puts the supply top right and ground bottom left with the notch at the top. Pin eight is ground on the sixteen-pin 74 L S 47, a different package, so keep the two apart. On the 7408, the first gate's inputs are pins one and two and its output is pin three, with the other gates following the same pattern. The 7432 holds four OR gates, the 7411 three three-input ANDs, and the 7421 two four-input ANDs.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: The key ideas from today. First, a pinout means every pin's number and function, taken from the manufacturer's datasheet, with pin 1 at the notch, top left, counting down and back up. Second, on a schematic the number goes outside the body and the function inside, each chip gets a U designator with its part number below, and a bar over a pin name means active low. Third, flat wiring matters electrically, because loops act as antennas and couple glitches between signals. Fourth, T T L is built from bipolar transistors used as switches, saturated or cut off, and the common gate chips such as the 7408 put V C C on pin 14 and ground on pin 7.
segments.expand: Quiz the student on one pinout fact, one schematic convention and one T T L fact.
segments.eli5: Think of a well-kept workshop. Every tool has a labelled place, every drawer is numbered from the same corner, and cables are tied down flat so you can trace any of them by hand. Today's ideas are that workshop for circuits. A pinout gives every pin's number and function, from the notch. The drawing puts numbers outside, functions inside, a unique U label on every chip, and bars for active low. Wires lie flat. T T L chips are built from transistor switches. So clear conventions and flat wiring let anyone build and troubleshoot a multi-chip circuit.
segments.deep: The four ideas serve one aim: making the physical circuit match the drawing exactly. The pinout comes from the manufacturer's datasheet; pin 1 is at the notch, top left, counting down and back up, and power pins differ by part, 16 and 8 on the 74 L S 47, 14 and 7 on the 7408. On the schematic, the number sits outside the body beside the wire and the function inside; the designator, U1, U2, sits in a consistent corner with the part number below; a bar over a name means the function is asserted at logic 0. Flat wiring reduces loop area and so reduces coupled glitches, and makes every wire traceable. T T L uses bipolar transistors as switches: base current gives saturation, no base current gives cutoff, with a 0.7 volt base-emitter drop. Example tying them together: a lamp test on U1, a 74 L S 47, means pulling the L T bar pin, pin 3, LOW; on the drawing that pin shows the number 3 outside and L T with a bar inside. The common misconception is that conventions are optional once the circuit works. They are what lets the next person, or you later, find a fault. Lecture 7 continues with T T L input behaviour and Boolean gates.

check.q: Every chip on a schematic gets a U designator with its part number written below it.
check.again: Each chip is named U1, U2 and so on, with its part number, such as 74 L S 47, directly below the designator in a consistent corner. Together those tell a reader which physical part the symbol is and what kind of chip it is. Add the pin numbers outside the body and the functions inside, and a bar over a name for active low, and the drawing can be built by someone who cannot ask you questions. The recap's other points: flat wiring avoids antenna loops, and T T L transistors work as switches, saturated or cut off.

lectures.title: TTL inputs and Boolean gates
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 07 - TTL Inputs and Boolean Gates.md; Kleitz §3-1, §3-2, §3-3, §3-12

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Two ideas meet in this lecture. Underneath, we look inside a T T L input and see that an unusual junction, base to collector, is what actually turns the next stage on. Above that, we abstract the behaviour into gates you can describe in several equivalent ways: a symbol, a truth table and a Boolean equation. We will cover the AND and OR gates, gates with more than two inputs, how to read a timing diagram, and how an AND gate can start and stop a clock. Most of the course will live at the gate level, but it helps to see once how the transistor level supports it.
segments.expand: Explain why it is useful to understand one transistor-level circuit even though most work happens at the gate level.
segments.eli5: Think of a car. You can describe it as a set of gears, pistons and wires, or simply as something with a steering wheel and pedals that goes where you point it. Both descriptions are true; the second is the one you drive with. This lecture looks once under the bonnet of a T T L input, to see which junction actually switches the next stage, and then spends most of its time at the driver's level: gates described by symbols, truth tables and equations. So the transistor level explains how a gate works, and the gate level is where the logic design happens.
segments.deep: The lecture works at two levels of abstraction. At the transistor level, the T T L input transistor steers a base current either out through the input pin, when the input is LOW, or through its base-collector junction into the next stage, when the input is HIGH. That steering is what makes the gate's output depend on its input. At the gate level, the same behaviour is captured as a rule, such as output HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, and expressed three equivalent ways: a symbol, a truth table and a Boolean equation. Example of the link: for a two-input AND, the truth table has 2 to the 2, which is 4 rows, and only the row with both inputs 1 gives 1; the equation C equals A B and the AND symbol say exactly the same. Timing diagrams then apply the rule over time, column by column. The common misconception is that the gate level is a simplification that sometimes gives wrong answers. Within the rated operating conditions, the gate rule is exactly what the transistors deliver; the transistor level matters when inputs are left floating or driven outside normal levels. The rest of the course, including Boolean simplification in Lecture 9, lives at the gate level.

check.q: Inside a T T L input, which junction of the input transistor actually turns the next stage on?
check.again: The surprise in this lecture is that the input transistor is not used the normal way. Its base-to-collector junction, which is usually reverse biased, becomes forward biased when the input is HIGH, and current flows through it into the next stage to turn that stage on. The base-to-emitter junction is the path that matters when the input is LOW: current leaves through it into the input pin, and the next stage stays off. Above that transistor level, the rest of the lecture works with gates as symbols, truth tables and equations, which is where most of the course lives.

segments.title: N-type, P-type and junctions
segments.text: Silicon can be treated to carry charge in two ways. In N-type silicon the majority carriers are electrons. In P-type silicon the majority carriers are holes. A hole is a missing electron that behaves like a positive mobile carrier, but a piece of P-type silicon as a whole is still electrically neutral, not positively charged. Both types also have a few minority carriers. Where P and N meet, you get a P N junction, which is the diode you already know. An N P N transistor has two such junctions sharing the thin base region: base to emitter, and base to collector. The transistor is not just two separate diodes glued together, but it helps to know that either junction can be forward biased. That fact is the key to the T T L input, because the input stage uses the base-collector junction in an unusual way.
segments.expand: Explain what a hole is, and why a P-type sample is neutral overall even though holes act as positive carriers.
segments.eli5: Think of a car park. In one car park, the useful thing is a few spare cars that can drive around; that is N-type silicon, where spare electrons move. In another, the useful thing is a few empty spaces; as cars shuffle into a space, the empty space seems to move the other way. That moving gap is a hole, acting like a positive carrier. Both car parks are still neutral overall. Where the picture breaks: holes are not real particles, just missing electrons. So N-type carries charge mainly by electrons, P-type mainly by holes, and where they meet you get a P N junction, a diode.
segments.deep: Silicon is treated so that one kind of mobile carrier dominates. In N-type, the majority carriers are electrons; in P-type they are holes. A hole is a missing electron in the bonds of the crystal. When a neighbouring electron fills it, the hole appears to move in the opposite direction, so it behaves like a mobile positive charge. Both types also contain a few minority carriers of the other kind. The common misconception is that P-type silicon is positively charged. It is neutral overall: every hole is matched by a fixed charge in the crystal, so P means the majority carriers act positive, not that the material carries net charge. Where P meets N you get a P N junction, the diode of Lecture 5, conducting when the P side, the anode, is about 0.7 volts above the N side, the cathode. An N P N transistor has two junctions sharing a thin P base: base to emitter, and base to collector. Example: with the base at 0.7 volts and the collector at 0 volts, base minus collector is plus 0.7 volts, so the base-collector junction is forward biased. Normally only base-emitter is forward biased, but the T T L input relies on the base-collector junction conducting, as the next two segments show.

check.q: A piece of P-type silicon as a whole carries a positive charge.
check.again: P-type silicon is electrically neutral as a whole. Its majority carriers are holes, which behave like positive mobile charges, but the material's total charge still balances. Likewise N-type silicon, whose majority carriers are electrons, is neutral overall. The letters describe which carrier is free to move, not the net charge of the block. Where P and N meet you get a P N junction, the diode, and an N P N transistor has two such junctions sharing a thin base: base to emitter and base to collector. Either junction can be forward biased, which is what makes the T T L input work.

segments.title: Inside a T T L input: input LOW
segments.text: Take the input transistor of Kleitz's T T L inverter. A resistor from the 5 volt rail feeds its base, the emitter connects to the input pin, and the collector drives the next transistor. Suppose the input is at 0 volts. The resistor does not hold the base at 5 volts; with the base-emitter junction conducting, the base sits at about 0.7 volts. Kirchhoff's voltage law around that path says 5 volts minus the resistor voltage minus 0.7 volts minus the input voltage equals zero, so the resistor has 4.3 volts across it. Ohm's law then gives the base current, the resistor voltage divided by its resistance. If the resistor were 4.7 kilohms, that would be about 915 microamps. The important part is where that current goes: out through the base-emitter junction into the LOW input pin. So the next stage receives nothing and stays off.
segments.expand: Work the input-LOW current with a different base resistor value and explain where the current flows.
segments.eli5: Think of water from a tank on a hill flowing down to a fork in the pipe. One branch leads to a drain at the bottom of the hill; the other leads to a water wheel that powers the next machine. If the drain is open, nearly all the water rushes down the easy path to the drain and the wheel gets nothing. A LOW input is that open drain: the base current flows out through the input pin. Where the picture breaks: electric current does not need gravity, only a voltage difference. So with the input LOW, the current leaves through the input pin and the next stage stays off.
segments.deep: Formula first: Kirchhoff around the path from the 5 volt rail, through the base resistor, through the base-emitter junction to the input pin: 5 volts minus resistor voltage minus 0.7 volts minus input voltage equals zero. With the input at 0 volts, the resistor voltage is 4.3 volts, and Ohm's law gives the base current, resistor voltage over resistance. With the lecture's illustrative 4.7 kilohms, that is about 915 microamps. Why it goes that way: the base sits at about 0.7 volts because the base-emitter junction is conducting, and 0.7 volts is too low to forward bias the base-collector junction and the next transistor's base-emitter junction in series, which would need at least about 1.4 volts. So the easier path wins, and the next stage receives no current and stays off. Example with a different resistor: with 4 kilohms, the current would be 4.3 volts over 4 kilohms, about 1.08 milliamps, still out of the input pin. The common misconception is that the base sits at 5 volts because it is connected to the rail through a resistor. The resistor takes most of the supply. This outward current is also why unused T T L inputs are tied HIGH rather than LOW, in Lecture 8.

check.q: The T T L input pin is at zero volts. Where does the current from the base resistor go?
options: Back up to the five volt rail
check.again: With the input LOW, the base-emitter junction conducts, so the base sits about 0.7 volts above the input, not at five volts. Kirchhoff's voltage law: five volts minus the resistor voltage minus 0.7 volts minus zero equals zero, so the resistor has 4.3 volts across it. Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, gives about 915 microamps for a 4.7 kilohm resistor. That current flows out through the base-emitter junction and into the LOW input pin. Nothing reaches the next stage, so it stays off. This is also why a LOW input costs the driving source some current.

segments.title: Inside a T T L input: input HIGH
segments.text: Now put the input at 5 volts. The base-emitter path out through the input pin can no longer take the resistor's current, because the pin is as high as the supply. So the current finds the other route: through the forward-biased base-collector junction and into the next stage, turning that stage on. This is why simply saying the input transistor is off misses the real mechanism. The base-collector junction is conducting, which is not how a transistor is normally used, and that is the unusual behaviour that makes the T T L input work. Exact voltages depend on the full chip circuit, but the direction of the current tells the story. Input LOW, current leaves through the input pin and the next stage stays off. Input HIGH, current is steered into the next stage and turns it on.
segments.expand: Compare the current paths for input LOW and input HIGH, and explain why a LOW T T L input has to sink current.
segments.eli5: Think of the same water fork, but now the drain is blocked, because the drain is as high as the tank. Water can no longer go that way, so it all flows down the other branch and turns the water wheel, powering the next machine. A HIGH input is the blocked drain: the input pin is as high as the supply, so the base current cannot leave through it. Instead it flows through the base-collector junction into the next stage and turns it on. So with the input HIGH, current is steered into the next stage, and the next stage turns on.
segments.deep: When the input pin is at 5 volts, the base-emitter path out of the pin would need the base to be about 0.7 volts above the pin, at 5.7 volts, which is higher than the rail feeding the resistor. So that path cannot conduct. The resistor's current must take the other route: through the base-collector junction, which is now forward biased, and into the base of the next transistor, turning it on. The base now settles at the sum of the junction drops on that inward path, at least two drops, so 1.4 volts or more in the classroom model; the exact value depends on the full chip circuit. Semi-quantitative example, using the lecture's illustrative 4.7 kilohms and a base at 1.4 volts: the resistor would have 5 minus 1.4, which is 3.6 volts across it, about 766 microamps into the next stage, and a little less if more junctions are stacked. The direction is what matters. The common misconception is that the input transistor is simply off when the input is HIGH. Its base-collector junction is conducting, and that steering is the real mechanism. Input LOW sends current out of the pin; input HIGH sends it inward. The input clamp diode, next, handles a different situation: inputs pulled below ground by ringing.

check.q: Now the T T L input pin is at five volts. Where does the resistor's current flow?
options: Through base-collector into the next stage
Out through the input pin down to ground
Nowhere, because it simply stops flowing
check.again: With the pin as high as the supply, the base-emitter route out through the input can no longer carry the resistor's current. So the current takes the other route: through the forward-biased base-collector junction and into the next stage, turning it on. Saying the input transistor is off misses the mechanism; a junction is conducting, just an unusual one. The story is about direction. Input LOW, current leaves through the pin and the next stage is off. Input HIGH, current is steered inward and the next stage is on. Exact voltages depend on the whole chip, but the direction is what matters.

segments.title: The input clamp diode and ringing
segments.text: A protection diode sits on the T T L input pin with its anode at ground and its cathode at the pin. At 0 volts input, anode and cathode are both at zero, so it is not conducting. At 5 volts input, anode minus cathode is minus 5 volts, so it is reverse biased. So in normal use it does nothing. Its job appears on fast edges. A real voltage step can excite the small inductance and capacitance of the wiring, producing overshoot and ringing, where the voltage swings past its final value and oscillates briefly. If ringing pulls the input below ground by more than about 0.7 volts, the diode becomes forward biased and conducts, holding the pin near minus 0.7 volts instead of letting it swing further. That is an approximation at limited current; large currents can still cause damage. Short, organised wiring helps reduce the ringing in the first place.
segments.expand: Explain what causes ringing on a fast edge and how the clamp diode limits the negative swing.
segments.eli5: Think of a safety rail at the edge of a cliff path. When you walk normally, you never touch it. Only if you stumble toward the edge does it catch you and stop you going further. The clamp diode on a T T L input is that rail. At normal LOW and HIGH levels it is not conducting. But if ringing on a fast edge swings the input below ground by more than about 0.7 volts, it conducts and holds the pin there. Where the picture breaks: a big enough push can still break the rail. So the clamp diode is idle normally and limits negative undershoot only.
segments.deep: Formula first: diode voltage equals anode minus cathode. With the anode at ground and the cathode at the pin, the diode voltage is 0 minus the input voltage. At 0 volts input, that is zero: not conducting. At 5 volts input, it is minus 5 volts: reverse biased. It reaches the 0.7 volt conduction level only when the input falls to about minus 0.7 volts. Why the input might go negative: a fast step excites the small inductance and capacitance of the wiring, producing overshoot and ringing, where the voltage swings past its final level and oscillates briefly. Example: an input stepping from 5 volts down to 0 volts might ring down toward minus 1.5 volts. The diode conducts once the pin reaches about minus 0.7 volts, holding it near there instead of letting it reach minus 1.5. That is a model at limited current: the real clamp drop depends on current, and excessive current can still damage the input, so the device's input ratings still apply. The common misconception is that the clamp protects against any overvoltage, including high positive spikes. It only conducts for negative excursions. Short, organised wiring, from Lecture 6, reduces ringing in the first place.

check.q: The clamp diode on a T T L input conducts when the input is pulled where?
options: Above the five volt supply rail
check.again: The diode has its anode at ground and its cathode at the pin. At zero volts both ends match, and at five volts it is reverse biased, so in normal use it does nothing. A fast edge can excite the wiring's stray inductance and capacitance and cause ringing, where the voltage overshoots and oscillates. If ringing drags the pin below ground by more than about 0.7 volts, the diode becomes forward biased and conducts, holding the pin near minus 0.7 volts. That protection is approximate at limited current; large currents can still cause damage. Short, tidy wiring reduces the ringing in the first place.

segments.title: Four ways to describe a logic function
segments.text: Any logic function can be expressed four ways. One, a schematic symbol, the gate shape. Two, a truth table, listing every input combination with its output. Three, Boolean algebra, an equation. Four, a Karnaugh map, which comes in a later chapter, so we set it aside. The first three describe exactly the same thing, and moving fluently between them is most of what the Boolean part of this course asks for. A truth table is really a binary count. With n input variables, each independently 0 or 1, there are two to the n rows. Two variables give 4 rows, three give 8, and four give 16. Write the inputs out as a plain binary count, 0 0, 0 1, 1 0, 1 1, so that no row is missed and every table you make is in the same order.
segments.expand: Explain why n inputs give two to the n rows, and how counting in binary guarantees no row is missed.
segments.eli5: Think of a recipe described three ways: a photo of the finished dish, a full list of every ingredient combination and what you get, and a single written formula. All three describe the same dish. A logic function is the same: a symbol, a truth table and a Boolean equation all describe one behaviour, and you should move between them easily. The truth table lists every input combination by counting in binary, so no row is missed. So any logic function can be shown as a symbol, a truth table or an equation, and a table with n inputs has two to the n rows.
segments.deep: Formula first: number of rows equals two to the power n, where n is the number of input variables. Each input can be 0 or 1 independently, so each new input doubles the number of combinations. Two inputs give 4 rows, three give 8, four give 16, and five would give 32. Writing the inputs as a binary count, 0 0, 0 1, 1 0, 1 1, guarantees every combination appears exactly once and puts every table in the same order, so two tables can be compared row by row. Example for three inputs: the rows run from 0 0 0, which is zero, to 1 1 1, which is seven, eight rows in all. The symbol, truth table and equation are equivalent descriptions; a Karnaugh map is a fourth that belongs to a later chapter, so it is set aside here. The common misconception is that each extra input adds a fixed number of rows. It doubles them, which is why truth tables for many inputs become unmanageable by hand. The count also connects to the number systems of Kleitz chapter one: the row number is just the inputs read as a binary number. The AND and OR gates, next, each have a recognisable truth table pattern.

check.q: A truth table with three input variables has eight rows.
check.again: With n inputs, each independently zero or one, the table has two to the n rows. Three inputs give two to the three, which is eight. Two inputs give four rows and four inputs give sixteen. Write the inputs as a plain binary count, zero zero zero up to one one one, so no row is missed and every table is in the same order. The table, the gate symbol and the Boolean equation are three descriptions of one function, and the Karnaugh map, a fourth, comes later. A five-input function would need thirty-two rows.

segments.title: The AND gate
segments.text: For an AND gate, all inputs must be HIGH for the output to be HIGH. With two inputs, the truth table has a 1 only in the last row, where both are 1. The symbol has a flat back and a semicircular nose. The equation is C equals A B, and the AND operation is written like multiplication: A dot B, A and B in brackets side by side, or simply A B. One notation to avoid: do not write A times B with a cross, because a hand-written cross can look like a variable X and make the expression ambiguous. Kleitz also points out a switch analogy. Two switches in series with a lamp act like AND: the lamp lights only when both are closed. A pattern worth memorising: for an AND gate with any number of inputs, only one row of the truth table is 1, the row where every input is HIGH.
segments.expand: Explain the series-switch picture of AND, and give the truth table row by row for a three-input AND.
segments.eli5: Think of a bank vault that needs two keys turned at once by two different managers. If either key is missing, the door stays shut. Only when both keys are turned does it open. That is AND: the output is HIGH only when every input is HIGH. Kleitz uses two switches in series with a lamp: the lamp lights only if both switches are closed, because either open switch breaks the path. So for an AND gate, the output is 1 only in the truth table row where all inputs are 1, written C equals A B.
segments.deep: Formula first: C equals A AND B, written A dot B or simply A B, where each variable is 0 or 1. AND behaves like multiplication of 0s and 1s: any 0 makes the product 0, and only 1 times 1 gives 1. That is why the notation looks like multiplication. The truth table for two inputs: 0 0 gives 0, 0 1 gives 0, 1 0 gives 0, 1 1 gives 1. For any number of inputs, exactly one row out of two to the n is 1, the last one, where every input is HIGH. Example: a three-input AND has 8 rows and a 1 only in row 1 1 1. The symbol is a flat back with a round nose.
