Avoid writing A times B with a cross, because a hand-written cross can look like a variable X. The series-switch picture works for logic, but notice it describes switches, not voltages: in a real gate, a LOW output is a definite voltage near ground, not an open circuit. The common misconception is that AND outputs HIGH when most inputs are HIGH. A single LOW input forces LOW. This is also why 0 is AND's controlling value, used for gating a clock later in this lecture. OR, next, is the mirror image.

check.q: Two switches in series with a lamp behave like an OR gate.
check.again: Two switches in series act like an AND gate: the lamp lights only when both switches are closed, just as an AND output is HIGH only when every input is HIGH. The OR picture is two switches in parallel, where either one closing lights the lamp. For AND, the truth table has a single one, in the last row, where all inputs are one. Its equation is written like a product, C equals A B or A dot B, but avoid a cross for times because a handwritten cross looks like the variable X.

segments.title: The OR gate
segments.text: For an OR gate, any HIGH input makes the output HIGH. The output is LOW only when every input is LOW, so in the truth table only the first row, all zeros, gives 0. The symbol has a curved back and a pointed nose. The equation is C equals A plus B, and the plus sign plays the role of OR. Read it as or, not plus, because in Boolean algebra 1 or 1 is 1. There is no 2. OR is inclusive: both inputs HIGH still gives HIGH. The switch picture for OR is two switches in parallel: either one closing lights the lamp. So the two patterns to remember are mirror images. AND has a single 1, at the bottom of the table, when everything is HIGH. OR has a single 0, at the top of the table, when everything is LOW.
segments.expand: Explain why the OR plus sign should not be read as arithmetic addition, with the one or one example.
segments.eli5: Think of a house with a front door and a back door, each fitted with a doorbell wired to the same chime. If someone presses either button, or both, the chime sounds. Only when nobody presses anything is it silent. That is OR: any HIGH input gives a HIGH output, and the output is LOW only when every input is LOW. Kleitz's picture is two switches in parallel with a lamp: either closed switch lights it. So for an OR gate, the only 0 in the truth table is the all-zeros row, written C equals A plus B, read A or B.
segments.deep: Formula first: C equals A OR B, written A plus B, where the plus sign means OR, not addition. The truth table: 0 0 gives 0, 0 1 gives 1, 1 0 gives 1, 1 1 gives 1. Notice the last row: 1 or 1 is 1. There is no 2 in Boolean algebra, because each variable can only be 0 or 1. OR is inclusive: both inputs HIGH still gives HIGH, unlike the everyday or that sometimes means one but not both. For any number of inputs, exactly one row out of two to the n is 0, the first one, all zeros. Example: a four-input OR has 16 rows and a single 0, in row 0 0 0 0. The patterns mirror each other: AND has a single 1 at the bottom of the table; OR has a single 0 at the top. The parallel-switch picture shows why: any closed path lights the lamp. The common misconception is reading A plus B as arithmetic, so that 1 plus 1 gives 2, or as exclusive, so that 1 plus 1 gives 0. Both are wrong for OR. Because 1 forces OR's output HIGH, 1 is its controlling value, which matters for gating signals. Gates with more inputs, next, follow the same rules.

check.q: In Boolean algebra, what is one or one?
check.again: The plus sign in Boolean algebra means OR, not arithmetic addition. One or one is one, because an OR output is HIGH whenever at least one input is HIGH, and there is no such value as two. OR is inclusive, so both inputs HIGH still gives HIGH. In the truth table, the only zero is in the first row, where every input is zero. Picture two switches in parallel with a lamp: closing both does not make the lamp twice as lit; it is simply on. Read A plus B aloud as A or B to avoid slipping into arithmetic habits.

segments.title: Gates with more inputs
segments.text: Gates are not limited to two inputs. A three-input AND is written D equals A B C, a four-input AND E equals A B C D, and so on, and the rule does not change: every input HIGH for a HIGH output. The same goes for OR: any HIGH input gives HIGH. Three inputs are easy to show on a symbol, and a drafting template usually covers up to about three. Past that, a gate enlarged enough for seven or nine inputs looks ridiculous. The fix Kleitz shows is to keep the gate body its normal size and extend its input edge with a line, so all the extra input wires can land on it. The function is unchanged; it is still one AND or one OR, just with more inputs. And the truth table grows fast: an eight-input AND has two to the eight, which is 256 rows, with only the very last row giving 1.
segments.expand: Explain how the truth-table size grows with inputs, and why only one row is HIGH for any AND gate.
segments.eli5: Think of the bank vault again, but now it needs four keys from four managers instead of two. The rule has not changed: every key must be turned, or the door stays shut. A three-input or eight-input AND is the same rule with more inputs. OR with more inputs is the same too: any one doorbell rings the chime. Drawing a huge gate for many inputs looks silly, so the gate keeps its normal size and its input edge is extended with a line. So adding inputs never changes the gate's rule, only how many rows the truth table has.
segments.deep: Formula first: a three-input AND is D equals A B C, a four-input AND is E equals A B C D; the output is 1 only when every input is 1. An n-input OR is 1 whenever any input is 1. The rule does not change with n, but the truth table does: two to the n rows. For an eight-input AND, that is two to the eight, which is 256 rows, and exactly one of them, the last, gives 1. For an eight-input OR, exactly one row, the first, gives 0. Drawing convention from Kleitz: keep the gate body its normal size and extend its input edge with a line, so seven or nine input wires can land on it. The function is still a single AND or OR. Example: a five-input OR gate with inputs 0 0 0 1 0 outputs 1, because one input is HIGH. A five-input AND with 1 1 1 0 1 outputs 0, because one input is LOW. The common misconception is that a gate with many inputs needs most of them HIGH, like a vote. AND needs all of them; OR needs just one. Lecture 8 shows how to build a four-input AND from two-input gates when only two-input packages are available.

check.q: An eight-input AND gate's truth table has 256 rows. How many of them give a one?
check.again: However many inputs an AND gate has, its rule does not change: the output is one only when every input is one. That happens in exactly one row, the last one, where all eight inputs are HIGH. Every other row has at least one zero and gives zero. Eight inputs give two to the eight, which is 256 rows, so one row out of 256. For OR it is the mirror image: only the first row, all zeros, gives zero. On a symbol, extra inputs land on a line extending the gate's input edge rather than an enlarged gate body.

segments.title: Reading a timing diagram
segments.text: A logic analyzer has many leads that clip onto points around a circuit, and it displays a timing diagram: one trace per signal, all against the same time axis. The key skill is to read it vertically. Each trace, read horizontally, tells you one signal's history. To evaluate a gate, take a vertical slice at one instant, read every input's level in that column, and apply the gate's rule. Then move to the next column, placing a boundary wherever any input changes. For example, suppose A is HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds and B is HIGH from 2 to 6. An AND output is HIGH only where both are HIGH, from 2 to 4 microseconds. An OR output is HIGH wherever either is HIGH, from 0 to 6. For a three-input OR, the output is HIGH unless all three traces are LOW in the same column.
segments.expand: Work another two-input timing example, and explain why a boundary is needed at every input change.
segments.eli5: Think of a musical score for a band. Each line is one instrument, read left to right over time. To know what the whole band is playing at one moment, you read straight down through every line at that beat. A timing diagram is that score: each trace is one signal over time, and to find a gate's output you slice vertically at each instant, read every input's level, and apply the rule. Move the slice wherever any input changes. So read a timing diagram in vertical slices, applying the gate's rule to every input in that column.
segments.deep: A logic analyzer records many signals against one shared time axis, so the levels at any instant line up vertically. To evaluate a gate, mark a boundary wherever any input changes, then apply the rule to the column between boundaries. Between changes, nothing can change the output in this ideal model, so one evaluation per column is enough. Lecture example: A HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds, B HIGH from 2 to 6. Boundaries are at 2, 4 and 6. From 0 to 2, A is 1 and B is 0: AND gives 0, OR gives 1. From 2 to 4, both are 1: AND gives 1, OR gives 1. From 4 to 6, A is 0, B is 1: AND gives 0, OR gives 1. After 6, both are 0, and both outputs are 0. So AND is HIGH for 2 microseconds, from 2 to 4, and OR for 6 microseconds, from 0 to 6. The common misconception is reading each trace horizontally on its own and trying to combine whole waveforms at once. That misses short overlaps. This ideal model ignores gate delay; Kleitz chapter three adds propagation delay, which shifts output edges slightly later. The gated clock, next, is a timing diagram in action.

check.q: A is HIGH from zero to four microseconds and B is HIGH from two to six. When is the AND output HIGH?
check.again: Read the timing diagram in vertical slices. Put a boundary wherever any input changes: at two, four and six microseconds. From zero to two only A is HIGH; from two to four both are HIGH; from four to six only B is HIGH. AND needs both, so the output is HIGH only in the overlap, two to four. Zero to six is the OR output, HIGH wherever either input is HIGH. Zero to two is where A alone is HIGH, which AND rejects. For a three-input OR, the output is LOW only in a column where all three traces are LOW.

segments.title: The gated clock
segments.text: A state machine, a circuit that steps through a sequence of states, is usually driven by a clock that simply goes up and down, up and down. Suppose you want a run and stop control. Feed the clock and an enable line into an AND gate, so run equals enable and clock. With enable at 1, one and zero is zero and one and one is one, so the output copies the clock and the machine runs. With enable at 0, zero and anything is zero, so the output stays LOW and the machine freezes in its current state. The enable line can come from a toggle switch with a pull-up. The same idea works with an OR gate, but reversed: a LOW control passes the clock, and a HIGH control holds the output HIGH. One real world caution: if enable changes while the clock is HIGH, you can get a shortened pulse, so real clock gating needs careful timing.
segments.expand: Explain why changing the enable during a HIGH clock can produce a short pulse, and how the OR version differs.
segments.eli5: Think of a conveyor belt that only moves when a worker holds down a run button. The motor is always turning, but the belt only moves while the button is held. A gated clock is the same. The clock always ticks, and an AND gate passes it through only while the enable line is HIGH. Release enable and the output sits LOW, so the machine it drives freezes where it is. Where the picture breaks: changing enable at the wrong instant can chop a clock pulse short. So run equals enable AND clock: enable 1 passes the clock, enable 0 blocks it.
segments.deep: Formula first: run equals enable AND clock. With enable equal to 1, run equals 1 AND clock, which is the clock itself, so the state machine receives every pulse and steps through its sequence. With enable equal to 0, run equals 0 AND clock, which is 0, so no rising edges arrive and the machine stays in its present state. The OR version is the reverse: run equals control OR clock, where a LOW control passes the clock and a HIGH control holds the output HIGH. Example: a 1 kilohertz clock, with enable HIGH for 5 milliseconds. Each period is 1 millisecond, so 5 complete pulses pass, and then the output stays LOW. The enable line can come from a toggle switch with a pull-up, from Lecture 4. The caution: if enable drops while the clock is HIGH, the output falls early, giving a shortened pulse, which a state machine may or may not respond to. The common misconception is that a blocked AND gate outputs nothing, or floats. It outputs a definite LOW. Lecture 5 introduced the same enable and disable idea with a NAND gate; in Kleitz chapter three it is analysed with timing diagrams.

check.q: The clock and an enable line feed an AND gate. With enable at zero, what does the output do?
check.again: Run equals enable and clock. With enable at one, one and zero is zero and one and one is one, so the output copies the clock and the state machine steps along. With enable at zero, zero and anything is zero, so the output sits LOW and the machine freezes where it is. An OR gate does the reverse: a LOW control passes the clock and a HIGH control holds the output HIGH. One caution: changing enable while the clock is HIGH can produce a shortened pulse, so real clock gating needs care about timing.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Let us gather the main ideas. First, inside a T T L input, a LOW input draws the base current out through the input pin, while a HIGH input steers it through the base-collector junction to turn on the next stage. Second, the clamp diode on the input is idle at normal levels and conducts only when ringing drives the pin below about minus 0.7 volts. Third, a logic function can be a symbol, a truth table or an equation, and a truth table with n inputs has two to the n rows, written as a binary count. Fourth, AND is HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, OR is LOW only when all inputs are LOW, and an enable input on an AND gate lets a clock through or blocks it. Read timing diagrams in vertical slices.
segments.expand: Give the student a quick timing-diagram question and a gate-rule question to check these ideas.
segments.eli5: Think of a city seen from two heights. From the street, you see pipes and junctions steering water one way or another; from a plane, you just see neighbourhoods and roads following simple rules. Inside a T T L input, a LOW sends current out of the pin and a HIGH steers it into the next stage, with a clamp diode guarding against ringing below ground. From above, gates follow rules: AND HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, OR LOW only when all are LOW, read on timing diagrams in vertical slices. So the transistor level explains the gates, and the gate rules are what you design with.
segments.deep: The lecture connects mechanism and abstraction. Mechanism: in a T T L input, with the input LOW, the base current, about supply minus 0.7 volts over the base resistor, leaves through the input pin; with the input HIGH, it flows through the base-collector junction to the next stage. The clamp diode, anode at ground and cathode at the pin, conducts only if the pin falls to about minus 0.7 volts. Abstraction: a function is a symbol, a truth table or an equation; a table has two to the n rows, written as a binary count. AND has a single 1 in its last row; OR has a single 0 in its first row; extra inputs do not change those rules. Example: three inputs at 1 0 1. A three-input AND gives 0, a three-input OR gives 1, and the table for either has 8 rows. Timing diagrams are evaluated column by column, and an enable line on an AND gate passes a clock when HIGH and blocks it when LOW. The common misconception is that the transistor level and gate level might disagree. Within normal operating levels they agree exactly. Lecture 8 turns to drawing these gates on schematics and handling unused inputs.

check.q: To evaluate a gate from a timing diagram, you take vertical slices and apply the gate's rule in each one.
check.again: Each trace read left to right tells one signal's history, but to evaluate a gate you read vertically. Mark a boundary wherever any input changes, take one column at a time, read every input's level in that column, and apply the gate rule to get the output for that interval. Then move to the next column. For example, if A is HIGH from one to five microseconds and B from three to seven, an AND output is HIGH only from three to five, while an OR output is HIGH from one to seven. This is the recap's last point and the core skill for timing questions.

lectures.title: Schematic conventions and unused gates
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 08 - Schematic Conventions and Unused Gates.md; Kleitz §3-11, §5-2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture is about keeping two things apart: a schematic describes function, and the package describes hardware. We will see why gates are drawn individually rather than inside a picture of the chip, how designators, gate suffixes, part numbers and pin numbers keep the link to real silicon, why power is shown once per package, and what to do with the gates and inputs you do not use. We also meet the NAND, NOR and inverter chips, and we finish with the Boolean law that lets you build a four-input AND from two-input gates. None of these conventions is decoration: each one makes a board buildable by someone else and troubleshootable by you.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between describing function and describing hardware, and why a schematic should do the first.
segments.eli5: Think of a theatre program and a seating chart. The program tells you what happens in the play, scene by scene. The seating chart tells you where each person physically sits. You would not mix the two on one page. A schematic is the program: it shows what the circuit does, one gate at a time. The package is the seating chart: which physical chip and pin each gate uses. Labels link the two. So a schematic describes function, the package describes hardware, and the labels on each gate carry the connection between them.
segments.deep: The lecture keeps function and hardware separate but linked. Function goes on the schematic: each gate drawn where it does its job. Hardware is recorded in labels: the designator names the chip, the suffix names the gate inside it, the part number names the chip type, and the pin numbers name the physical pins. Power appears once per package, with its decoupling capacitor. Unused gates are handled deliberately: inputs tied to plus 5 volts, outputs marked no connection. Example: an AND function used in two places on a sheet can be drawn as U1A near one part of the circuit and U1B near another, both from the same 7408, without any box drawn around them. The builder still knows they share one chip, because both say U1. The common misconception is that conventions are decoration or local habits. Each one prevents a specific error: a wrong pin, a missing supply, a floating input, or a fight between an output and a rail. The lecture ends with the associative law, which turns the design question of building a four-input AND from two-input gates into an exact Boolean identity, leading into Boolean algebra in Lecture 9.

check.q: This introduction says a schematic describes function. What describes the hardware?
check.again: The theme is to keep two things apart. The schematic shows what the circuit does, gate by gate, wherever each gate does its work. The package, the physical chip with its numbered pins, is hardware. The link between the two is carried by labels: designator, gate suffix, part number and pin numbers. Power is shown once per package, unused inputs are tied, and unused outputs are marked. Truth tables and equations are other ways of describing the function, not the hardware. Think of a recipe versus the pots and pans: the schematic is the recipe, the package is the cookware.

segments.title: Pictorial versus schematic
segments.text: The instinctive way to show a logic chip is to show the chip: a rectangle, fourteen numbered pins around its edge, and the gates placed inside. That is a pictorial, and it does not belong on a schematic. On a schematic you place one gate at a time, in the part of the circuit where that gate does its work, not grouped inside a box representing the plastic package. A pictorial answers where the chip is; a schematic answers what the circuit does. The connection to the physical part is not lost. It moves into the labels on each gate, which we cover next. These are industry practices, not a local habit. The back of the textbook shows gates labelled in exactly this way, and you will see the same conventions in published schematics for programmable logic devices.
segments.expand: Give an example of how a pictorial becomes confusing in a larger circuit, compared with a proper schematic.
segments.eli5: Think of a map of bus routes versus a photo of the bus depot. The photo shows where every bus is parked, side by side. The route map shows where each bus goes and what it connects, with no attention to where it parks. A pictorial of a chip is the depot photo: every gate shown inside the package outline. A schematic is the route map: each gate drawn where it does its job in the circuit. Labels on each gate still say which bus and which depot slot. So a schematic places each gate by function, not inside a picture of the chip.
segments.deep: A pictorial shows physical arrangement: the package rectangle, fourteen numbered pins and the gates inside. That answers where the chip is, but it forces every gate in a package to sit together, even when the gates do unrelated jobs in different parts of the circuit, so signal paths must loop back and forth across the page. A schematic answers what the circuit does. Each gate is placed in the signal flow where it works, so the logic reads from inputs to outputs. The physical link is kept by labels on each gate: designator, suffix, part number and pin numbers. Example: a circuit uses one 7408 gate near the inputs and another near the outputs. On a pictorial, both must be drawn inside the same box, with long wires crossing the sheet. On a schematic, U1A sits near the inputs and U1B near the outputs, with short wires and no confusion. The common misconception is that drawing the chip outline is more accurate. It is accurate about placement but hides the function, and the labels already carry all the placement information. These are industry practices, matching the gate labelling at the back of Kleitz and published schematics for programmable logic devices. The labels themselves come next.

check.q: On a proper schematic, the gates are drawn grouped inside a box that represents the chip package.
check.again: That drawing is a pictorial, and it does not belong on a schematic. A schematic places one gate at a time, in the part of the circuit where that gate does its job, not inside a rectangle with fourteen numbered pins. The pictorial answers where the chip is; the schematic answers what the circuit does. The link to the physical part is not lost: it moves into the labels on each gate, the designator, suffix, part number and pin numbers. The back of the textbook and published schematics for programmable logic use exactly this convention.

segments.title: Designator, suffix, part number, pins
segments.text: Four labels attach to each gate, and each answers a different question. The designator, such as U1, says which physical chip. The gate suffix, as in U1A or U1B, says which gate inside that chip; a quad package has gates A, B, C and D. The part number, such as 74 L S 08, written below the designator, says what kind of chip it is. The pin numbers on the leads say which physical pins you used. You choose the numbering: with five chips, which one is U1 is up to you, and within a quad package you may use any gate for any job. The only requirement is that the drawing records the choice. Then a technician reading U1A, 74 L S 08, pin 1 can say: that is pin 1 of the 74 L S 08 labelled U1 on this board. The suffix and the pins are both needed, because each tells you something the other does not.
segments.expand: Explain why the gate suffix and the pin numbers are not redundant, with an example of what is lost if one is missing.
segments.eli5: Think of a postal address: building, apartment, the kind of building, and which door. Each part answers a different question, and leaving one out can send a letter astray. A gate's labels work the same way. The designator, U1, is the building: which physical chip. The suffix, A to D, is the apartment: which gate inside. The part number, 74 L S 08, is the kind of building. The pin numbers are the doors you actually use. So designator, suffix, part number and pin numbers together trace every gate on the drawing to exact pins on one physical chip.
segments.deep: Each label answers one question. Designator: which physical chip on the board, such as U1. Suffix: which gate inside that chip, A, B, C or D for a quad package, written U1A. Part number: what kind of chip, such as 74 L S 08, written below the designator. Pin numbers: which physical pins this gate uses. The designer chooses the assignments, which chip is U1 and which gate is used for which job, and the drawing records those choices. Example: U1B, 74 L S 08, with pins 4 and 5 as inputs and pin 6 as output. A technician goes to the chip labelled U1, confirms it is a 74 L S 08, and probes pin 6 for the output. Why both suffix and pins? The suffix groups the pins into one gate, so you know pins 4, 5 and 6 belong together; the pins tell you exactly where to probe. Without pins, the technician must look up the pinout; without the suffix, they may not know which pins form one gate. The common misconception is that the part number identifies the chip. Two chips on one board can both be 74 L S 08; only the designator is unique. Power connections, next, are shown once per package.

check.q: In the label U1B, what does the letter B tell you?
options: Which physical chip on the board
check.again: Four labels attach to each gate. The designator, U1, says which physical chip. The suffix, A, B, C or D, says which of the four gates inside that quad package you used. The part number below, such as 74 L S 08, says what kind of chip it is. The pin numbers on the leads say which physical pins carry the signals. You choose which chip is U1 and which gate does which job; the drawing just has to record the choice. Then a technician reading U1A, 74 L S 08, pin one knows exactly where to put the probe.

segments.title: Power once per package
segments.text: A quad gate package has one V C C pin and one ground pin, shared by all four gates. So the convention is to show the power connections on exactly one gate of each package; which gate is your choice. The other three are drawn with no power lines at all. Two reasons. First, traceability: a technician can find a package's supply connection in one place. Second, space and clarity: repeating V C C and ground on all four gates clutters the page and reads as though there were four separate supplies. Alongside the power connection goes the decoupling capacitor. Every chip gets a capacitor from V C C to ground, shown with its power connection. On the board, the class demonstration placed these capacitors across the power and ground rails beside the chips; running a supply wire over the top of the package also works but wastes a row of holes.
segments.expand: Explain what a decoupling capacitor does for a logic chip and why it sits close to the supply pins.
segments.eli5: Think of an apartment building with four flats but one main water connection from the street. On the plumbing plan, you show the main connection once, at the building, not four times. A quad gate chip is that building: four gates sharing one V C C pin and one ground pin. So on the schematic, the power connection is drawn on just one gate of each package, and the decoupling capacitor goes with it. Drawing it four times would suggest four separate supplies. So power and its capacitor are shown once per package, on any one gate.
segments.deep: A quad package has a single V C C pin and a single ground pin serving all four gates internally. Showing power on one gate per package records that connection exactly once, so a technician can find it in one place, and avoids implying four separate supplies or cluttering the page. Which gate carries it is the designer's choice. For example, on a 7408 labelled U1, the drawing might show U1A with pin 14 to plus 5 volts and pin 7 to ground, and U1B, U1C and U1D with no power lines at all. The decoupling capacitor, one per chip from V C C to ground, is drawn alongside that connection. On the breadboard, the class demonstration placed it across the power and ground rails beside the chip; a wire running over the package also works but wastes a row of holes. The common misconception is that a gate drawn without power lines is unpowered. Every gate in the package is powered through the shared pins; the drawing shows it once. Another is that a quad package needs four supply connections on the board. Only one pair of pins exists. Spare gates, next, are still powered even when unused, which is why their inputs must be handled.

check.q: The V C C and ground connections are drawn on every gate of a quad package.
check.again: A quad package has one V C C pin and one ground pin shared by all four gates, so the power connection is shown on exactly one gate of each package, whichever you choose, and the other three are drawn with no power lines at all. Two reasons: a technician can find the package's supply in one place, and repeating it four times clutters the page and reads as four separate supplies. The decoupling capacitor from V C C to ground is drawn with that same power connection, and on the board it sits across the rails beside the chip.

segments.title: Unused inputs: tie them HIGH
segments.text: Use two gates of a quad package and two are left over, still on the board and still powered. Their inputs must not be left unconnected. A floating input picks up noise, and its logic level becomes effectively random, causing failures that come and go and are very hard to find. So every input must be driven or tied. For T T L there are two choices, and both cure the noise, but they differ in current. Tied to ground, a T T L input is LOW, and a LOW input must push current out of its input stage, which is the input-LOW current path you met last lecture. Tied to plus 5 volts, the input is HIGH and draws very little. So the rule is: tie unused inputs to plus 5 volts. For a 74 L S input, a LOW can push out up to about 0.4 milliamps, so four inputs tied LOW could cost 1.6 milliamps, against about 80 microamps tied HIGH.
segments.expand: Connect the tie-high rule to the T T L input circuit from Lecture 07 and compute the current difference for several inputs.
segments.eli5: Think of a spare radio left switched on in a cupboard with no station tuned in. It picks up static, crackles randomly, and might suddenly blare. A floating gate input is that radio: it picks up noise, and its level wanders. So unused inputs must be tied to something definite. Tying them HIGH is like turning the radio to a quiet fixed station. Where the picture breaks: the choice between HIGH and LOW is about current. So for T T L, tie unused inputs to plus 5 volts, because a LOW input pushes out current and a HIGH one draws very little.
segments.deep: Unused gates in a package are still powered, so their inputs still respond to whatever voltage they see. A floating T T L input is undefined: noise and coupling push it around, and the gate may switch at random, causing intermittent faults. Tying the input to either rail fixes the noise; the difference is current. Recall Lecture 7: with a T T L input LOW, the input-stage base current flows out through the input pin. With it HIGH, that path is blocked and the pin draws only a small leakage current. Formula first: total current equals current per input times number of inputs. For a 74 L S input, LOW can push out up to about 0.4 milliamps, so four inputs tied LOW could cost 4 times 0.4, which is 1.6 milliamps. Tied HIGH, the lecture's figure of about 80 microamps for four inputs is 20 microamps each. So tying HIGH wastes about one-twentieth as much. The common misconception is that tying to ground is safest because ground means off. For T T L inputs, ground is the more power-hungry choice. Another is that an unconnected T T L input is a reliable HIGH. Its level is not dependable, so tie it. Outputs, next, follow a different rule.

check.q: What should be done with the inputs of an unused T T L gate?
options: Tie them to plus five volts
Tie them to the ground rail
check.again: A floating input picks up noise and its level becomes effectively random, causing faults that come and go. So every input must be driven or tied. Both HIGH and LOW cure the noise, but they cost different current. A LOW T T L input has to push current out of its input stage, up to about 0.4 milliamps for a 74 L S input, so four inputs tied LOW could cost 1.6 milliamps. A HIGH input draws very little, about 80 microamps for four. So the rule is: tie unused inputs to plus five volts.

segments.title: Unused outputs and the spare-gate column
segments.text: Outputs are different from inputs. An unused output can safely go nowhere; it causes no harm. On the schematic, mark it N C, for no connection, so the reader knows the loose end is deliberate rather than an unfinished drawing. Never tie a driven output to a supply rail as if it were an input, because the gate would be fighting the rail. A neat way to show spare gates is to stack them in a column at the edge of the sheet, out of the way of the working circuit. One plus 5 volt line can then serve every tied input in the column. The spares can come from different packages. Each still needs its designator and suffix, its pin numbers, N C on its output and its inputs tied to plus 5 volts. And a common trick: show each package's power connection on one of its unused gates, so the working circuit stays clear.
segments.expand: Describe how a column of unused gates from two different packages would be labelled completely.
segments.eli5: Think of a garden hose tap you are not using. Leaving the tap's spout free is fine; nothing bad happens. But jamming its spout into another running pipe would make the two fight. An unused gate output is like that free spout: it can be left unconnected, marked N C so readers know it was deliberate. Never tie a driven output to a supply rail. Unused inputs, by contrast, get tied to plus 5 volts. So unused outputs go nowhere and are marked no connection, while spare gates are stacked neatly at the edge of the sheet.
segments.deep: An output drives a level of its own. Left unconnected, it has nothing to drive and does no harm. Tied to a rail, it is forced to hold the rail's level, and whenever the gate wants the opposite level it fights the rail, drawing excessive current that can heat or damage the output. So unused outputs are left unconnected and marked N C, for no connection, telling the reader the loose end is deliberate. The spare-gate column puts all unused gates at the edge of the sheet. One plus 5 volt line runs down the column, tying every spare input, and each spare still carries its designator with suffix, pin numbers, and N C on its output. Example: a design uses three gates of U1, a 7408, and one gate of U2, a 7432. The column holds U1D and U2B, U2C and U2D, four spare gates with eight inputs tied to plus 5 volts and four outputs marked N C. A useful trick: show each package's power on one of its spare gates, keeping the working circuit clear. The common misconception is that unused outputs need tying like inputs. Inputs need a defined level; outputs already provide one. Labels for Alpha board signals come next.

check.q: How is an unused gate output shown on the schematic?
check.again: Outputs are different from inputs. An unused output can safely go nowhere; it causes no harm. Mark it N C, for no connection, so a reader knows the loose end is deliberate rather than an unfinished drawing. Never tie a driven output to a supply rail as if it were an input, because the gate would fight the rail. Spare gates are neatly stacked in a column at the sheet's edge, each with its designator and suffix, pin numbers, N C on the output and inputs tied to plus five volts, and often carrying the package's power connection.

segments.title: Alpha board labels and indicators
segments.text: Where your circuit meets the Alpha board, the drawing must say which board signal is used. An input that arrives from one of the board's logic outputs, the toggle switches, is labelled with that output's name, for example L O 3. Without it, a reader knows a signal arrives but not from where. An output that goes to one of the board's logic indicator lights is drawn as a rectangular indicator symbol with the indicator's name inside. That symbol has one pointed end, and the point carries information: it points in the direction of signal flow. On an output it points away from the gate. Official schematics for programmable logic devices use the same shape. Connection dots matter too: a dot marks where wires actually join, and a missing dot leaves the reader unsure whether two crossing wires connect.
segments.expand: Explain how signal-flow arrows and connection dots remove ambiguity on a schematic.
segments.eli5: Think of a train map that marks where lines leave the city, with signs naming the connecting town and an arrow showing which way the trains go. Without the sign, you would know a track leaves the map but not where to. On a schematic, an input from the Alpha board's toggle switches is labelled with the switch output's name, such as L O 3, and an output to a board light gets a pointed indicator symbol naming that light, pointing in the direction of signal flow. So every off-sheet connection is named, and the indicator's point shows signal direction.
segments.deep: These labels close the gap between the drawing and the lab board. An input labelled L O 3 tells the builder exactly which logic output on the board drives that wire; without it, the signal's origin is a guess. An output going to an indicator light is drawn as a rectangular symbol with one pointed end and the light's name inside. The point carries information: it shows the direction of signal flow, so on an output it points away from the gate, toward the light. Connection dots carry information too: a dot marks a real junction where wires join. Where two wires cross with no dot, the reader cannot be sure whether they connect. Example: a gated clock design has its enable labelled L O 1, its output going to an indicator symbol pointing right, labelled with that light's name, and a dot where the clock line branches to two gates. The builder wires L O 1, finds the light, and connects both gates to the clock. The common misconception is that the pointed shape is just decoration. It encodes direction, matching the official schematics for programmable logic devices. The inverting gate chips, next, need equal care with their pinouts.

check.q: The indicator symbol for an Alpha board light has one pointed end. Which way does the point go?
options: In the direction of signal flow
Toward the chip that drives it
check.again: The rectangular indicator symbol carries the light's name inside, and its pointed end points in the direction of signal flow. On an output it points away from the gate, toward the indicator. Official schematics for programmable logic devices use the same shape. Inputs from the board's toggle switches are labelled with the switch output's name, such as L O 3, so a reader knows where a signal comes from. And connection dots matter: a dot marks where wires really join, and a missing dot leaves the reader unsure whether two crossing wires connect.

segments.title: NAND, NOR and inverter chips
segments.text: Kleitz's second section on using logic chips adds the inverting gates. The 7400 holds four two-input NAND gates, the 7402 four two-input NOR gates, and the 7404 six inverters, which is why it is called a hex inverter. The 7410 holds three three-input NAND gates. There are C M O S equivalents too, such as the 4001 NOR and the 4011 NAND. On these 14-pin T T L parts, V C C is still pin 14 and ground pin 7, but the gate pins are not all arranged the same way. On the 7408 AND, the first gate's inputs are pins 1 and 2 and its output is pin 3. On the 7402 NOR, the first gate's output is pin 1 and its inputs are pins 2 and 3. Wiring a 7402 from memory of the 7408 would connect an output to a driven input. Always use the exact part's top-view pinout.
segments.expand: Explain the danger of assuming all gate chips share one pinout, using the 7402 and 7408 as the example.
segments.eli5: Think of two apartment buildings with the same outside shape and the same front door, but different layouts inside. In one, the kitchen is first on the left; in the other, the bedroom is. Walk in from memory of the first building and you end up in the wrong room. The 7408 and the 7402 are like that. Both have power on pins 14 and 7, but the 7402 puts its first gate's output on pin 1, where the 7408 has an input. So always use the exact part's top-view pinout, even when the packages look identical.
segments.deep: The inverting gate chips fill out the T T L family. The 7400 holds four two-input NAND gates, the 7402 four two-input NOR gates, the 7404 six inverters, which is why it is called a hex inverter, and the 7410 three three-input NAND gates. C M O S equivalents include the 4011 NAND and 4001 NOR. Pin counting: a 7404 has six inverters, each needing one input and one output, 6 times 2, which is 12 signal pins, plus 2 for power, filling all 14. Power is still pin 14 and ground pin 7 on these 14-pin T T L parts, but the gate pins differ. On the 7408, gate one has inputs on pins 1 and 2 and its output on pin 3. On the 7402, gate one has its output on pin 1 and its inputs on pins 2 and 3. Wire a 7402 as if it were a 7408 and you drive pin 1 from a switch while the NOR output is also driving it: an output fighting a driven signal. The common misconception is that all quad two-input gate chips share a pinout. Same package and power pins, different gate layout. Always check the specific datasheet. The associative law, next, helps when the right gate size is not in the kit.

check.q: On the 7402 NOR chip, which pin is the first gate's output?
check.again: The 7402 does not follow the 7408's pattern. On the 7408 AND, the first gate's inputs are pins one and two and its output is pin three. On the 7402 NOR, the first gate's output is pin one and its inputs are pins two and three. Wiring a 7402 from memory of the 7408 would connect an output to a driven input. V C C is still pin fourteen and ground pin seven on both. The 7400 holds four NANDs and the 7404 six inverters, the hex inverter. Always work from the exact part's top-view pinout.

segments.title: A four-input AND from two-input gates
segments.text: The lab circuit needs a four-input AND gate, but the parts kit has none. The reasoning tool is a Boolean law. AND is associative, meaning the grouping of an all-AND expression does not change its result. So A and B and C and D equals the group A and B, and-ed with the group C and D. That identity is exact, not an approximation, and it is what makes building a wide AND from narrower gates legitimate. Its partner, the commutative law, says the order does not matter either: A and B equals B and A. Both laws hold for OR as well. These come from Kleitz's section on Boolean laws, which we will use heavily for simplification. Working out how many two-input gates you need, which package they come from, and how to label them is the design task, using everything else in this lecture.
segments.expand: Explain the associative and commutative laws with small truth-table checks, and how many two-input gates a four-input AND needs.
segments.eli5: Think of checking that four friends all agree. You can ask the first two whether they both agree, ask the other two whether they both agree, and then check that both pairs said yes. Grouping them into pairs does not change the final answer: everyone agrees only if all four do. That is the associative law for AND. It lets you build a four-input AND from two-input gates: AND A with B, AND C with D, then AND the two results. So A and B and C and D equals the quantity A B, and-ed with the quantity C D, exactly.
segments.deep: Formula first: associative law, A B C D equals the quantity A B times the quantity C D, where times means AND; equally, the quantity A B, times C, times D. It is exact because AND outputs 1 only if every input is 1, and grouping does not change whether every input is 1. The commutative law adds that order does not matter: A B equals B A. Both laws hold for OR too. Design example: a four-input AND from two-input gates needs three gates: one for A B, one for C D, and one to AND those results. A 7408 holds four, so one package does it: U1A, U1B and U1C, with U1D as a spare whose inputs are tied to plus 5 volts and whose output is marked N C. Check one row: A B C D equals 1 1 0 1. A B is 1, C D is 0, and 1 AND 0 is 0, matching a single four-input AND. The common misconception is that the law works for any mix of gates, such as grouping inside a NAND. It does not hold for NAND or NOR. Lecture 9 uses these laws heavily for simplification.

check.q: Which Boolean law justifies building a four-input AND from two-input AND gates?
check.again: AND is associative: the grouping of an all-AND expression does not change its result. So A and B and C and D equals the group A and B, and-ed with the group C and D. That identity is exact, which is what makes two-input gates a legitimate substitute when the kit has no four-input gate. The commutative law is its partner and says order does not matter, A and B equals B and A, but it is grouping, not order, that the four-input build relies on. Both laws also hold for OR. For example, two-input ANDs also build a three-input AND: A and B, then and C.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: The key ideas from this lecture. First, a schematic shows each gate where it works, not inside a picture of the chip; the link to hardware is carried by the designator, the gate suffix, the part number and the pin numbers. Second, power and the decoupling capacitor appear once per package, on one gate. Third, unused T T L inputs are tied to plus 5 volts, because a LOW input pushes out current and a floating one picks up noise, while unused outputs are left unconnected and marked N C. Fourth, the 7400, 7402 and 7404 give NAND, NOR and inverters, but their pinouts differ from the 7408, so always check. Fifth, the associative law lets a four-input AND be built from two-input gates.
segments.expand: Ask the student to label a spare gate fully and to explain the tie-high rule in their own words.
segments.eli5: Think of an orchestra's sheet music. It shows each instrument's part where it plays, not where each musician sits; the program lists who plays which part. Today's conventions are the same. A schematic draws gates where they work, and labels say which chip, gate and pins. Power is noted once per package. Spare players still need instructions: unused inputs are tied HIGH and unused outputs marked no connection. Chips that look alike can be laid out differently inside. So function goes on the drawing, hardware goes in the labels, and every unused input is tied.
segments.deep: Five ideas summarise the lecture. First, gates are drawn by function; the designator, suffix, part number and pin numbers carry the hardware link. Second, power and the decoupling capacitor appear once per package. Third, unused T T L inputs are tied to plus 5 volts because a LOW input pushes current out, up to about 0.4 milliamps each for 74 L S, while unused outputs are left unconnected and marked N C. Fourth, the 7400 NAND, 7402 NOR and 7404 hex inverter share power pins 14 and 7 with the 7408, but their gate pins differ. Fifth, the associative law lets wide gates be built from narrow ones. Combined example: build a three-input AND from a 7408. A B uses U1A, and that result with C uses U1B, two gates. U1C and U1D go in the spare column with inputs tied HIGH and outputs N C, and U1's power is shown on U1C. The common misconception is that unused parts of a chip can simply be ignored. They are powered and must be handled. Lecture 9 builds on the associative and commutative laws with the full set of Boolean laws.

check.q: A LOW input on a T T L gate pushes current out, which is one reason unused inputs are tied to plus five volts.
check.again: A T T L input held LOW must push current out of its input stage, the input-LOW current path from the previous lecture, up to about 0.4 milliamps for a 74 L S input. A HIGH input draws only a few tens of microamps. Both stop the input floating, but HIGH is cheaper in current, so unused inputs go to plus five volts. The recap's other points: gates are drawn where they work with designator, suffix, part number and pins carrying the link to hardware; power appears once per package; outputs left unconnected are marked N C; and the 7402 pinout differs from the 7408.

lectures.title: Boolean algebra and simplification
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 09 - Boolean Algebra and Simplification to SOP.md; Kleitz §5-1, §5-2, §5-3, §5-5, §5-8

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: A schematic, a Boolean expression and a truth table are three spellings of one logic function, and the algebra is the only one of the three you can simplify. That is the theme of this lecture. We will define combinational logic, see why gate delays can cause glitches, read a circuit into algebra using intermediate variables, fill a truth table column by column, and then learn the laws that simplify expressions: the identities, absorption, and DeMorgan's theorem. We finish by cooking expressions down to a sum of products. The individual laws are easy; the skill is choosing which one to use next, and that only comes with practice.
segments.expand: Explain why algebra is the representation used for simplification, rather than the truth table or schematic.
segments.eli5: Think of one message written three ways: spoken aloud, in shorthand, and as a long formal letter. All three say the same thing, but only the shorthand can be edited quickly to cut the waffle. A logic function is the same. The schematic, the truth table and the Boolean expression all describe one function, but only the algebra can be simplified. This lecture teaches how to read a circuit into algebra, check it with a truth table, and use the laws to shorten it. So algebra is the representation you simplify, and the truth table is how you check you kept the same function.
segments.deep: Simplification matters because fewer gates and fewer inputs mean fewer chips, less wiring and fewer places for faults. The three representations are equivalent: any one can be built from another. But only the Boolean expression can be manipulated step by step with laws that are guaranteed to keep the function unchanged. The truth table is the referee: every simplified version must give exactly the same output in every row. Example of what is gained: the textbook circuit X equals B and the group A or C, then or C, uses three gates. After simplification it becomes A and B, or C, two gates, and both versions give 1 in exactly the same five of the eight rows. The lecture's path: combinational logic and delays, intermediate variables to read a circuit, filling a truth table column by column, then the laws, the identities, the structural laws, absorption and DeMorgan's theorem, and finally simplifying to a sum of products. The common misconception is that simplifying is about memorising laws. The laws are short; the skill is choosing which to apply next, which comes from practice. The truth table always lets you check whether a step was legal.

check.q: Of a schematic, a Boolean expression and a truth table, which one can you actually simplify?
check.again: All three are spellings of the same logic function, but only the algebra has rules for making it shorter. A truth table is fixed; it just lists every input combination with its output. A schematic can be redrawn, but you only know a smaller one is correct because the algebra says so. The lecture's plan: define combinational logic, read a circuit into algebra with intermediate variables, fill a truth table by columns, then apply the identities, absorption and DeMorgan's theorem to reduce an expression to a sum of products. The laws are easy; choosing which one to apply next takes practice.

segments.title: Combinational logic and delay
segments.text: A circuit is combinational when information flows one way, from inputs to output, and no output is fed back to an input. Its output then depends only on the present inputs, which is why a truth table describes it completely. Feed an output back and you have sequential logic, which can depend on its own history; that comes later. Real gates are fast but not instant; each has a small propagation delay. Delay alone is harmless. The trouble starts when two paths from the same input pass through different numbers of gates. A change then reaches a later gate by one route before the other, which is a race, and while it runs, the output can briefly show a wrong value called a glitch. It can be a nanosecond wide and still cause failures downstream. For now we treat gates as infinitely fast, get the logic right, and deal with races later.
segments.expand: Walk through the lecture's glitch example, holding B at 1 and C at 0 while A rises, and explain why the truth table cannot predict it.
segments.eli5: Think of two runners carrying the same news from a starting line by different routes, one short and one long. The person at the finish, waiting for both, briefly hears only the first runner and may act on half the story before the second arrives. Two signal paths through different numbers of gates are those runners. While one arrives early, the output can show a brief wrong value, a glitch. A combinational circuit has no feedback, so once both arrive, its output depends only on the present inputs. So combinational logic is fully described by a truth table, while unequal path delays can still cause brief glitches.
segments.deep: A circuit is combinational when signals flow only from inputs to output, with no output fed back. Then the output is a function of the present inputs only, and a truth table describes it completely. Feedback creates sequential logic, which can remember, and that comes later in the course. Every real gate has a propagation delay, the time between an input change and the resulting output change. A uniform delay only shifts the output later. A race happens when one input reaches a later gate by two paths with different numbers of gates. Example: input A goes to a final AND gate directly and also through an inverter, so the gate sees A and A bar. Logically, A and A bar is always 0. But if the inverter takes 10 nanoseconds, then for 10 nanoseconds after A rises, both inputs read 1, and the output pulses HIGH: a 10 nanosecond glitch. A circuit downstream that responds to edges might count it. The common misconception is that a correct truth table means a glitch-free circuit. The truth table describes the settled outputs, not the transitions between them. For now gates are treated as instant, so the logic can be got right first, and races are handled later.

check.q: Two paths from one input pass through different numbers of gates. The brief wrong output that can result is called what?
check.again: Every real gate has a small propagation delay. When a change reaches a later gate by one route before another, the paths race, and while the race runs the output can briefly show a wrong value. That short wrong pulse is a glitch, perhaps a nanosecond wide, but enough to upset circuits downstream. Feedback is a different thing: an output wired back to an input, which makes the circuit sequential, so it depends on its history. Combinational logic has no feedback, so a truth table describes it completely. For now, treat gates as infinitely fast and get the logic right first.

segments.title: Intermediate variables
segments.text: To read a circuit into algebra, do not write the growing expression beside each gate on the drawing. It runs out of room and it breeds mistakes. Instead, give every internal node its own letter. In the class circuit the inputs are A, B and C, the output is Z, and the internal nodes are D, E and F. Then write one small equation per gate. D equals A and B. F equals D inverted. E equals A or C. Z equals E and F. Substitute only at the end, which gives Z equals the group A or C, and-ed with the complement of A and B. One more habit from class: read the plus sign as or and the dot as and, not as plus and times. They are written with arithmetic symbols because they distribute like arithmetic, but reading them as arithmetic tempts you into rules that do not hold.
segments.expand: Evaluate the class circuit for one input combination using the intermediate variables in order.
segments.eli5: Think of following a recipe with several sub-steps. Rather than writing one enormous sentence describing the final dish, you label the intermediate bowls: bowl D holds the creamed butter and sugar, bowl E the dry mix, and so on. Each step is short and easy to check, and you combine the bowls at the end. Intermediate variables do the same for a circuit. Every internal node gets a letter, each gate gets one small equation, and you substitute only at the end. So name every internal node, write one equation per gate, and combine them last.
segments.deep: The method breaks one large reading task into several one-gate tasks. Each internal node gets a letter, so each gate's equation involves only its own inputs and output, and each equation can be checked against the gate's rule on its own. For the class circuit: D equals A and B; F equals D, complemented; E equals A or C; Z equals E and F. Substitute F first, then D: Z equals the group A or C, and-ed with the complement of the group A and B. Check one row: A equals 1, B equals 0, C equals 0. D is 0, F is 1, E is 1, so Z is 1. The substituted expression gives 1 or 0, which is 1, and the complement of 1 and 0, which is the complement of 0, which is 1; 1 and 1 is 1. They match. Writing growing expressions beside each gate instead runs out of room, and a bracket dropped early spreads through every later gate. Read the plus sign as or and the dot as and. The common misconception is that the symbols are arithmetic, tempting you to write X plus X as 2 X. In Boolean algebra, X or X is X. The intermediate columns also give the order for filling the truth table, next.

check.q: In the class circuit, D equals A and B, and F equals D inverted. So F equals what?
check.again: Intermediate variables mean one small equation per gate. D is A and B. F is D with a bar over it, so F is the complement of the whole product A and B, the bar covering both letters. It is not A and B, which is D itself, and it is not A or B, which is a different gate. The other nodes: E equals A or C, and Z equals E and F. Substituting only at the end gives Z equals the group A or C, and-ed with the complement of A and B. Read plus as or and dot as and.

segments.title: Filling the truth table
segments.text: Three inputs give two to the three, which is 8 rows. List A, B and C as a plain binary count from 0 0 0 up to 1 1 1. Then fill one intermediate column at a time, in the order the signals are produced, rather than working along each row. Go down the D column looking only at A and B: D is 1 only in the two rows where A and B are both 1. Then F, which is just D flipped. Then E from A and C: it is 0 only where both are 0. Only then fill Z from E and F. Working in columns turns one hard eight-row problem into four easy ones, and a mistake stays in one place instead of spreading along a row. For this circuit, Z comes out 1 in four rows: 0 0 1, 0 1 1, 1 0 0 and 1 0 1. That list is what any simplified version of the circuit must reproduce exactly.
segments.expand: Fill the class circuit's truth table aloud column by column and confirm which rows give Z equal to 1.
segments.eli5: Think of marking an exam with eight students and four questions. You could mark each student's whole paper before moving to the next, or mark question one for everyone, then question two for everyone. Marking by question is faster and more consistent, because you only think about one question's rule at a time. Filling a truth table column by column is the same: fill D for all eight rows, then F, then E, then Z. Each column follows one simple gate rule. So fill truth tables one intermediate column at a time, in the order the signals are produced.
segments.deep: Formula first: rows equal two to the n, with n the number of inputs; three inputs give 8 rows, listed as a binary count from 0 0 0 to 1 1 1. D equals A and B: 1 only in rows 1 1 0 and 1 1 1. F equals D complemented: 0 in those two rows, 1 in the other six. E equals A or C: 0 only where A and C are both 0, rows 0 0 0 and 0 1 0. Z equals E and F: 1 where E is 1 and F is 1. Checking every row: 0 0 1 gives E 1, F 1, so Z 1; 0 1 1 gives Z 1; 1 0 0 gives Z 1; 1 0 1 gives Z 1; rows 1 1 0 and 1 1 1 have F equal to 0, so Z 0; and rows 0 0 0 and 0 1 0 have E equal to 0, so Z 0. So Z is 1 in exactly four rows. The common misconception is that working along each row is faster. It mixes four rules at once, and a slip spreads along the row. This four-row list is the standard any simplified expression must reproduce, and the laws, next, are how to simplify.

check.q: For the class circuit, the output Z is one in exactly four of the eight rows.
check.again: Three inputs give eight rows, listed as a binary count. Filling column by column, D is one only where A and B are both one; F is D flipped; E is zero only where A and C are both zero; and Z is E and F. Z comes out one in four rows: zero zero one, zero one one, one zero zero and one zero one. That list is the fingerprint of the function, and any simplified circuit must reproduce it exactly. Working in columns turns one hard eight-row job into four easy ones and keeps any mistake in one place.

segments.title: The single-variable identities
segments.text: The operators behave like arithmetic, with exceptions, and the exceptions are the point. X and 0 is 0: nothing ANDed with false is true. X and 1 is X. X and X is X, not X squared, because there are no powers here. X and X bar is 0, since one of them is always 0. For OR: X or 0 is X. X or 1 is 1: anything ORed with something always true is true. X or X is X, not 2 X. X or X bar is 1. And X double bar is X; bars cancel in pairs, so an even number of bars leaves X and an odd number leaves X bar. Watch the pair that catches everyone: X and 1 is X, but X or 1 is 1. The same 1 has opposite effects because 1 is the identity for AND, while 0 is the identity for OR. When in doubt, prove it with a truth table: one variable needs only two rows.
segments.expand: Prove X or 1 equals 1 and X and 1 equals X with two-row truth tables, and explain the identity element idea.
segments.eli5: Think of AND as a strict security guard and OR as a generous host. The guard lets you in only if every check passes: any 0, any failed check, and the answer is 0; a 1 just means that check passed, so the result depends on the rest. The host lets you in if any invitation is valid: any 1 means yes, and a 0 just means that invitation was missing. So X and 0 is 0, X and 1 is X, X or 1 is 1, X or 0 is X. Repeating yourself adds nothing: X and X is X, X or X is X, and a pair of bars cancels.
segments.deep: Each identity can be proved with a two-row truth table, X equal to 0 and X equal to 1. X and 0: both rows give 0. X and 1: rows give 0 and 1, which is X. X and X: 0 and 0 is 0, 1 and 1 is 1, so X; there are no powers, so never X squared. X and X bar: one of them is always 0, so 0. X or 0 gives X. X or 1 gives 1 in both rows. X or X gives X, never 2 X. X or X bar gives 1, because one of them is always 1. X with two bars is X, since each bar flips the value and two flips return it. Example: the group A or A bar, and-ed with B, is 1 and B, which is B. The pair X and 1 equals X, X or 1 equals 1 traps everyone because the same 1 behaves oppositely. The reason: 1 is the identity for AND, leaving X unchanged, while 0 is the identity for OR. The common misconception is borrowing arithmetic, where 1 plus anything is never just 1. Boolean OR is not addition. These identities finish every simplification, including the worked example in segment ten.

check.q: What does X or one simplify to?
check.again: Anything ORed with something always true is true, so X or one is one. Compare X and one, which is X, because one is the identity for AND, while zero is the identity for OR: X or zero is X. That pair catches everyone because the same one behaves differently with the two operators. The rest of the single-variable identities: X and zero is zero, X and X is X, not X squared, X and X bar is zero, X or X is X, X or X bar is one, and a double bar cancels. When unsure, a two-row truth table settles it.

segments.title: Commutative, associative, distributive
segments.text: The structural laws let you rearrange. Commutative: order does not matter, X and Y equals Y and X, and the same for OR. That is a fact about these operations, not a general rule; putting on socks and then shoes does not commute. Associative: grouping does not matter, so X and the group Y and Z equals the group X and Y, and-ed with Z. Distributive: X and the group Y or Z equals X and Y, or X and Z. That is the same expansion you know from ordinary algebra, and it is the move you will use most. Even more useful is running it backwards: spotting a common factor and pulling it out. For example, A and B, or A and C, can be written as A and the group B or C. Factoring is often what makes terms collapse, as we will see in the worked example.
segments.expand: Give an example of factoring a common variable out of two product terms and explain why it helps simplification.
segments.eli5: Think of packing a shopping bag. Whether you put in apples then bread, or bread then apples, you end up with the same bag; that is commutative. Whether you pack apples and bread into a small bag first and then add milk, or bread and milk first, the shopping is the same; that is associative. Distributive is like saying a sandwich with ham or cheese is the same as a ham sandwich or a cheese sandwich. Where the picture breaks: some everyday actions do depend on order, like socks then shoes. So order and grouping do not change AND or OR, and AND distributes over OR.
segments.deep: Formula first in words. Commutative: X and Y equals Y and X; X or Y equals Y or X. Associative: X and the group Y and Z equals the group X and Y, and-ed with Z; the same for OR. Distributive: X and the group Y or Z equals X and Y, or X and Z. These hold because each side gives the same output in every truth table row, not because they look like arithmetic. Run the distributive law backwards and it becomes factoring: A B or A C equals A and the group B or C. Example: A B or A B bar. Factor A: A and the group B or B bar. B or B bar is 1, and A and 1 is A. So A B or A B bar equals A. Check a row: A equals 1, B equals 0 gives 0 or 1, which is 1, and A is 1. Factoring often reveals a group that collapses to 1 or to a single variable. The common misconception is that any rule from arithmetic carries over. Commutative, associative and this distributive law do; others, like X and X equals X squared, do not. The worked example in segment ten uses distributing and then factoring in exactly this way.

check.q: A and B, or A and C, can be factored into what?
options: A and the group B or C
A or the group B and C
check.again: This is the distributive law run backwards. Forwards, X and the group Y or Z equals X and Y, or X and Z. Spotting the common factor A in both products and pulling it out gives A and the group B or C. The bracket keeps the OR of B and C together, and it is ANDed with A. Check with A equals one, B equals zero, C equals one: the original is zero or one, which is one; the factored form is one and one, also one. Factoring is often the move that makes terms collapse in a simplification.

segments.title: Absorption, and the look-alike
segments.text: Two rules make expressions dramatically shorter. Absorption: X or the group X and Y equals X. Prove it by cases. If X is 1, the whole thing is 1. If X is 0, then X and Y is 0 too, so the whole thing is 0. Either way it equals X, whatever Y does. Its partner is X and the group X or Y, which also equals X. Now the near twin that gives a different answer: X or the group X bar and Y equals X or Y, not X. Check by cases. If X is 1, both sides are 1. If X is 0, the left side becomes X bar and Y, which is just Y, and the right side is Y. So the result is X or Y. This was the question set aside to ponder in class. If you wrote X in your notes, correct it. Changing X to X bar inside the second term changes the answer completely.
segments.expand: Prove both rules by cases again with a different letter, and give an example of each inside a larger expression.
segments.eli5: Think of a club where you get in if you are a member, or if you are a member who brought a friend. The second condition adds nothing; members get in anyway, so the rule is just: members. That is absorption, X or X Y equals X. Now change the rule: you get in if you are a member, or if you are not a member but brought a friend. Now the second condition admits new people, non-members with a friend, so the rule becomes members or anyone with a friend: X or Y. So X or X Y is X, but X or X bar Y is X or Y.
segments.deep: Formula first: absorption, X or X Y equals X, and its partner X and the group X or Y equals X. Proof by cases: if X is 1, X or anything is 1, which is X; if X is 0, X Y is 0, so the result is 0, which is X. Y never matters. The look-alike: X or X bar Y equals X or Y. Cases: if X is 1, both sides are 1. If X is 0, X bar is 1, so the left side is Y, and the right side is 0 or Y, which is Y. They agree in all cases. Example: A or A B C simplifies to A by absorption, since A B C contains A as a factor. But A or A bar B C simplifies to A or B C, by the look-alike. The common misconception, and the one set aside in class, is that X or X bar Y also equals X. Testing X equal to 0, Y equal to 1 gives 1 on the left, but X gives 0. One bar changes everything. Both rules shorten expressions in the sum of products work that follows.

check.q: What does X or the group X bar and Y simplify to?
check.again: Prove it by cases. If X is one, the whole expression is one, and X or Y is also one. If X is zero, X bar is one, so the second term becomes Y, and the whole thing is Y, which matches X or Y. So the answer is X or Y. The look-alike is absorption: X or the group X and Y equals X, because when X is zero the second term is zero too. Changing X to X bar inside the second term changes the answer completely. If your notes say X, correct them.

segments.title: DeMorgan's theorem
segments.text: DeMorgan's theorem is how you get a bar off a bracket. The complement of X and Y equals X bar or Y bar. The complement of X or Y equals X bar and Y bar. The reliable way to apply it is mechanical. Write the operator explicitly, so the bar has three things to land on. When it lands on the first variable, that variable inverts. When it lands on the operator, AND becomes OR, or OR becomes AND. When it lands on the second variable, that inverts too. The common trap is inverting both variables but leaving the operator alone. One counterexample kills it. Take X equals 1 and Y equals 0. The complement of 1 and 0 is the complement of 0, which is 1. But 0 and 1 is 0. They disagree, so the operator must flip. DeMorgan matters because until the bar is off, you cannot distribute, factor or combine anything inside it.
segments.expand: Apply DeMorgan to a three-variable expression and explain the break the bar, change the operator shortcut.
segments.eli5: Think of the sign on a ride: you may not ride if you are both under ten and alone. Turn that around to who is allowed: you may ride if you are not under ten, or not alone. The not spread to each condition, and both turned into or. That is DeMorgan's theorem. The complement of X and Y is X bar or Y bar, and the complement of X or Y is X bar and Y bar. Where the picture breaks: everyday language is loose, while Boolean algebra is exact. So breaking a bar flips each variable and also flips the operator.
segments.deep: Formula first: the complement of X and Y equals X bar or Y bar; the complement of X or Y equals X bar and Y bar. Proof by truth table: the complement of X and Y is 0 only when X and Y are both 1. X bar or Y bar is 0 only when X bar and Y bar are both 0, which also means X and Y are both 1. The two columns match in all four rows. The mechanical method: write the operator explicitly; as the bar breaks, it lands on three things: the first variable inverts, the operator flips, the second variable inverts. Example: the complement of A or B bar becomes A bar and B double bar, which is A bar and B. The common trap is inverting the variables without flipping the operator. With X equals 1 and Y equals 0, the complement of 1 and 0 is 1, but 0 and 1 is 0, so the operator must flip. Until the bar is broken, nothing inside can be distributed or factored, which is why DeMorgan usually comes first in the four-variable example later.

check.q: By DeMorgan's theorem, the complement of X and Y equals what?
check.again: DeMorgan gets a bar off a bracket by doing three things: invert the first variable, flip the operator, invert the second variable. So the complement of X and Y is X bar or Y bar, and the complement of X or Y is X bar and Y bar. The common trap is inverting both variables but leaving the operator alone. Test it with X equals one and Y equals zero: the complement of one and zero is the complement of zero, which is one, but zero and one is zero, so the operator must flip. Until the bar is gone you cannot distribute or factor inside.

segments.title: Sum of products
segments.text: A product is a set of variables ANDed together, such as A and B, or A bar and B bar and C. A single variable, such as C, counts as a product of one. A sum of products ORs such terms together and contains nothing else: no brackets, and no bar over anything larger than a single variable. Why aim for that form? Because it drops straight into a truth table. Each product term tells you exactly which rows give a 1. And a function read back out of a truth table comes out as a sum of products again, so it is the common meeting point between representations. A warning, though: sum of products is a shape, not a guarantee of being minimal. An expression can be a perfectly good sum of products and still reduce further. What you actually want is the minimum sum of products.
segments.expand: Give examples of expressions that are and are not in sum-of-products form, and explain why each fails or passes.
segments.eli5: Think of a menu of set meals. Each set meal is a combination that must all come together, like soup and bread and tea. The menu is a list of such combinations, and you are happy if any one of them is served. A sum of products is that menu: each product term is a set meal of variables ANDed together, and the terms are ORed, so any one being true makes the output 1. No brackets and no bar over more than one variable. So a sum of products is product terms ORed together, and each term names the truth table rows that give 1.
segments.deep: Formula first in words: a product is variables or complemented variables ANDed, such as A B, or A bar B bar C, or just C; a sum of products ORs such products, with no brackets and no bar over more than a single variable. Why it is useful: each product term is 1 exactly in the rows where all its variables match, so the 1s in the truth table can be read straight off. Example: A B or C. The term A B gives 1 in rows 1 1 0 and 1 1 1. The term C gives 1 in rows 0 0 1, 0 1 1, 1 0 1 and 1 1 1. Together, counting row 1 1 1 once, that is five rows with output 1. Going the other way, reading a function from a truth table also yields a sum of products, so the form is the meeting point between representations. The common misconception is that any sum of products is already minimal. A B or A B bar is a sum of products, yet it reduces to A by factoring. The target is the minimum sum of products: fewest terms, fewest variables. The textbook worked example, next, gets there step by step.

check.q: An expression written as a sum of products is guaranteed to be the minimal form.
check.again: Sum of products is a shape, not a guarantee. It means product terms, variables ANDed together, joined by OR, with no brackets and no bar over anything bigger than a single variable. An expression can have that shape and still shrink further. For instance, A and B, or A and B bar, is a sum of products, yet it reduces to just A. What you actually want is the minimum sum of products. The form is valuable because it drops straight into a truth table, each product naming the rows that give a one, and reading a table back out produces a sum of products again.

segments.title: Worked example from the textbook
segments.text: Read straight off Kleitz's circuit: X equals B and the group A or C, then or C. Step one, distribute B: A and B, or B and C, or C. Step two, factor C out of the last two terms: A and B, or C and the group B or 1. Step three, B or 1 is 1. Step four, that 1 is ANDed with C, and C and 1 is C. So X equals A and B, or C. This is the step that tripped the room. Half the class said C and half said 1. The way to settle it is to ask which operator the 1 inherited. It came out of a product, C and the bracket, so it is C and 1, which is C. Had it been C or 1, the answer would have been 1. The result, A and B, or C, is a sum of products and cannot be reduced further.
segments.expand: Work Kleitz's second example, the group A or B, and-ed with B and C, then or A, step by step.
segments.eli5: Think of a shop offering a discount if you buy a coat, or if you buy a coat and also a hat. Since buying a coat alone is already enough, the extra condition about the hat changes nothing. In the worked example, after distributing, C appears alone and also in a term with B. Factor C out and you get C and the group B or 1. B or 1 is always true, so that group is 1, and C and 1 is just C. So the hat term vanishes, and X equals A and B, or C. Keep track of which operator the 1 meets: C and 1 is C, not 1.
segments.deep: Formula first: start with X equals B and the group A or C, then or C. Distribute: A B or B C or C. Factor C from the last two: A B or C and the group B or 1. Identity: B or 1 is 1. Identity: C and 1 is C. Result: X equals A B or C. The deciding question is which operator the 1 inherited: it sits inside a product with C, so the identity C and 1 equals C applies.
