segments.expand: Work the loaded-output divider with different values and explain the collector resistor trade-off.
segments.eli5: Think of a water tank feeding a house through a narrow pipe. With all taps closed, the pressure at the house equals the tank's. Open a tap and water flows through the narrow pipe, and the pressure at the house drops. Open many taps and it drops further. The collector resistor is the narrow pipe, and each load connected to the output is an open tap. Where the picture breaks: voltage, not pressure, is shared by the resistors. So when the transistor is off, the output HIGH equals the supply times load over collector plus load, and heavier loading pulls it lower.
segments.deep: Formula first: output voltage equals supply times load resistance, divided by collector resistance plus load resistance, in volts and ohms. With the transistor off, the collector resistor and the load form a series divider from the supply to ground. Example: 5 volts, a 1 kilohm collector resistor and a 4.7 kilohm load. The output is 5 times 4.7 over 5.7, about 4.12 volts. Kleitz's Example 2-13 with a 10 kilohm load gives about 4.55 volts, and loading down to 1 kilohm gives 2.5 volts, which may no longer read as HIGH. Shrinking the collector resistor raises the loaded HIGH, but when the transistor turns on, the full supply sits across it. Formula: power equals voltage squared over resistance, watts, volts and ohms. With 100 ohms: current is 5 volts over 100 ohms, 50 milliamps, and power is 25 over 100, which is 0.25 watts, wasted every time the output is LOW. The common misconception is that the HIGH level is a fixed property of the gate. With a passive pull-up, it depends on the load. A single resistor cannot give both a strong HIGH and a low LOW-state current, which is why T T L uses the totem pole, next.

check.q: Five volt supply, one kilohm collector resistor, transistor off, ten kilohm load to ground. The output is about?
check.again: With the transistor off, the load and the collector resistor form a divider. Output equals the supply times the load resistance divided by the collector resistance plus the load resistance, in volts and ohms: five times ten over eleven is about 4.55 volts. The full five volts would need no load at all. If more loads bring the total down to one kilohm, the output falls to five times one over two, which is 2.5 volts. Shrinking the collector resistor helps the HIGH level but wastes power when the transistor is on: 100 ohms at five volts carries 50 milliamps and dissipates a quarter of a watt.

segments.title: The totem-pole output
segments.text: T T L chips escape that trade-off with a totem-pole output. Instead of a fixed collector resistor, it uses two transistors stacked one above the other. In a settled HIGH state, the upper transistor actively drives the output up; in a settled LOW state, the lower transistor pulls it down. One is on while the other is off, so there is no steady path straight from supply to ground. That gives far better drive than a passive pull-up. T T L itself, transistor-transistor logic, is built from bipolar transistors, diodes and resistors on one chip. The 7404 hex inverter holds six such inverters. Two cautions. The output current still has datasheet limits. And two ordinary totem-pole outputs must never be wired together, because one could be driving HIGH while the other drives LOW, fighting each other.
segments.expand: Explain how the two transistors in a totem pole share the job, and why two such outputs must not be connected.
segments.eli5: Think of a door with two people: one whose job is to push it open, and one whose job is to pull it shut. They never both push at once; whoever is on duty does the job firmly. A totem-pole output is that pair. The upper transistor actively drives the output HIGH, and the lower one actively pulls it LOW, one on while the other is off. That beats a lazy spring, the collector resistor. Where the picture breaks: two such doors wired together would fight. So the totem pole drives both levels firmly without a steady supply-to-ground current.
segments.deep: In the settled HIGH state, the upper transistor conducts and drives the output toward the supply, while the lower one is off. In the settled LOW state, the lower one conducts and pulls the output to ground, while the upper one is off. Because one is always off in a settled state, there is no steady path from supply to ground, unlike a small collector resistor, which wastes current whenever the output is LOW. Compare the single-resistor inverter: to keep a 1 kilohm load above about 4 volts, Kleitz's divider formula needs a collector resistor of 250 ohms or less, since 5 times 1 over 1.25 is 4 volts; then the LOW state wastes 5 volts over 250 ohms, 20 milliamps. The totem pole avoids that trade-off. T T L chips, like the 7404 hex inverter with six inverters, use this stage. Two cautions. The output current still has datasheet limits. And two totem-pole outputs must never be tied together: if one drives HIGH while the other drives LOW, the upper transistor of one connects through the lower transistor of the other, a low-resistance path from supply to ground. The common misconception is that a totem pole can drive any load. It drives better, not unlimited.

check.q: Two ordinary totem-pole outputs can be wired together to get more drive.
check.again: They must never be wired together. A totem-pole output has an upper transistor that actively drives HIGH and a lower one that pulls LOW, with one on while the other is off. If two such outputs are joined and one drives HIGH while the other drives LOW, they fight each other through a low-resistance path. The totem pole exists to escape the passive pull-up's trade-off, giving strong drive in both directions with no steady path from supply to ground. Its output current still has datasheet limits. The 7404 hex inverter holds six inverters built this way.

segments.title: C M O S, input levels and packages
segments.text: The other main family is C M O S, complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, built from complementary M O S transistors. Its big advantage is very low power while it is not switching, though switching still uses energy, and its speed and thresholds depend on the exact part. Whatever the family, an input reads voltage ranges, not exact values. For the 74 L S 00, an input up to 0.8 volts is guaranteed LOW and one from 2.0 volts up is guaranteed HIGH; between those, nothing is guaranteed. Those are input limits, separate from what an output guarantees. Packages matter too. A dual in-line package, D I P, has two rows of leads that go through holes in the board. Surface-mount devices sit on pads on the board's surface and are much smaller and lighter. The same logic function can come in either, with different pinouts, so check the exact package's datasheet.
segments.expand: Explain why an input voltage between the two guaranteed limits is a problem, and what floating C M O S inputs can do.
segments.eli5: Think of a referee judging whether a ball is in or out. There is a clear in zone and a clear out zone, with a painted line that has some width. A ball landing on the wide line is a doubtful call. A logic input is that referee: below 0.8 volts is clearly LOW, above 2.0 volts is clearly HIGH, and in between there is no guaranteed call. C M O S is a second family of chips, using very little power while not switching. So inputs read voltage ranges, and the same logic function may come in different families and packages with different pinouts.
segments.deep: Inputs are specified by guaranteed ranges. For the 74 L S 00, an input from 0 up to 0.8 volts is guaranteed LOW, and from 2.0 volts up to the supply is guaranteed HIGH. Example: 0.5 volts is a guaranteed LOW; 3.2 volts is a guaranteed HIGH; 1.5 volts sits between the limits, so the datasheet promises nothing, and the gate might read it either way or differently from chip to chip. These are input limits, separate from the levels an output guarantees to produce, and a well-designed output sits safely inside the input ranges so a little noise does not move it into the undefined band. C M O S, complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, uses complementary M O S transistors. Its advantage is very low power while not switching, though switching still uses energy, and its thresholds and speed depend on the exact part. Packages: a D I P has two rows of through-hole leads; surface-mount devices sit on pads and are much smaller. The same logic function, such as a quad NAND, can come in either package, with different pin counts or arrangements. The common misconception is that any voltage above half the supply is HIGH. Only the datasheet ranges are guaranteed, and the undefined band between them is to be avoided.

check.q: For a 74 L S 00 input, from what voltage upward is a HIGH guaranteed?
check.again: An input reads voltage ranges, not exact values. For the 74 L S 00, anything up to 0.8 volts is guaranteed LOW, and anything from 2.0 volts up is guaranteed HIGH. Between 0.8 and 2.0 nothing is guaranteed. Those are input limits, separate from what an output guarantees. HIGH does not have to be exactly five volts. C M O S is the other main family, built from complementary M O S transistors, with very low power when not switching and thresholds that depend on the part. Packages differ too: through-hole D I P versus much smaller surface-mount, each with its own pinout.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from Chapter 2. One: frequency equals one over period, measured edge to matching edge, and duty cycle is the HIGH fraction of the period. Two: serial sends one bit per clock on one line, parallel a whole group per clock on many lines, so parallel is faster but costs wiring. Three: a closed switch has no voltage and an open one no current; a relay coil moves every contact from its normal state. Four: a conducting silicon diode drops about 0.7 volts and a reversed one is open; diodes can form simple AND and OR networks. Five: the common-emitter transistor inverts, loading pulls its HIGH level down, and T T L's totem pole fixes that with active pull-up and pull-down.
segments.expand: Ask one timing question, one switch question and one transistor question, and discuss each typical mistake.
segments.eli5: Think of learning a sport in layers. First, the rhythm of play: how long each round lasts and how much of it is active. Then, how the ball is passed: one player at a time or many at once. Then the equipment: switches, a remote-controlled switch, one-way gates, and a powered helper that flips signals over. Chapter 2 is those layers for digital signals. So the five ideas are period and duty cycle, serial and parallel, switches and relays, diode models and networks, and the transistor inverter with its totem-pole improvement.
segments.deep: The chapter ties timing to devices. Waveforms: frequency equals one over period; duty cycle equals HIGH time over period, times 100 percent. Data: serial time equals bits times period, parallel time equals groups times period. Switches: closed means zero volts, open means zero current; relay contacts are named for the de-energized coil. Diodes: about 0.7 volts when conducting, open when reversed; diode AND and OR networks show how one input can control an output. Transistors: base current switches the collector path; the common-emitter circuit inverts; a passive pull-up's HIGH sags under load by the divider rule; the totem pole drives both levels actively. Combined example: a 1 megahertz clock with 25 percent duty is HIGH for 0.25 microseconds of each 1 microsecond period. Fed into an inverter, the output is HIGH for 0.75 microseconds, a 75 percent duty cycle at the same 1 megahertz. Sending one 8-bit byte serially on that clock takes 8 microseconds. The common misconception is treating these as separate facts. Each device is modelled by state and solved with Kirchhoff and Ohm, and each waveform by period. Kleitz chapter three builds gates, timing diagrams and noise margins on this.

check.q: An ideal closed switch has no voltage across it, and an ideal open switch has no current through it.
check.again: A closed switch is a zero-resistance path, a short, so there is no voltage across it even though current flows. An open switch is a break, so no current flows, but it can have voltage across it. That is the recap's third idea, together with the relay whose coil moves every contact from its normal state. The others: frequency equals one over period, measured edge to matching edge, and duty cycle is the HIGH fraction; serial sends one bit per clock and parallel a whole group; a conducting silicon diode drops about 0.7 volts; and the common-emitter transistor inverts, with the totem pole fixing loading.

lectures.title: Logic gates, timing and troubleshooting
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Textbook/DIGI 210 - Chapter 03 - Logic Gates and Timing.md; Kleitz §3-1 to §3-12

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture covers Kleitz Chapter 3, the basic logic gates. We cover AND, OR, the inverter, NAND and NOR, each as a rule, a truth table and an equation. Then we use gates over time with timing diagrams, see how one input can enable or disable a signal, and build waveform windows. Finally we move to the bench: gate chips and their pins, and how to troubleshoot with a logic probe and pulser. The idea running through it all is that a gate turns a rule into a circuit, and a wrong output can come from the gate, its wiring, its supply or its load.
segments.expand: Explain why each gate can be described by a rule, a truth table and an equation, and how to move between them.
segments.eli5: Think of a set of house rules turned into machines. One rule says the door opens only if everyone agrees; another says it opens if anyone asks. A gate is a rule built as a circuit. This chapter covers the five basic rules, AND, OR, inverter, NAND and NOR, then watches them working over time on timing diagrams, uses them to let signals through or block them, and finally takes them to the bench with chips, a probe and a pulser. So a gate turns a rule into a circuit, and a wrong output can come from the gate, its wiring, its supply or its load.
segments.deep: The chapter moves from rule to circuit to fault finding. Each gate is defined three equivalent ways: a one-sentence rule, a truth table with two to the n rows, and an equation. Timing diagrams apply the rule interval by interval over time, and real gates add propagation delay. A control input holding its non-controlling value passes a signal, while its controlling value forces the output, which is how clocks are enabled and windows are carved. On the bench, the same rule tells you what to expect at each pin. Example linking all three: a 7400 NAND with inputs 1 and 1 should output 0. If the probe shows HIGH at the output pin, the rule says something is wrong, but not what. The supply at pin 14 may be missing, an input may actually be floating rather than HIGH, the output may be shorted to a HIGH node, or the chip may be faulty. The common misconception is that a wrong output means a bad chip. Most faults are wiring, supply or loading problems, and swapping chips first wastes time. The chapter's troubleshooting method, predict, measure in signal-flow order, find the first disagreement, uses everything before it. Boolean algebra in Lecture 9 then simplifies the gate networks built here.

check.q: According to this introduction, a wrong gate output can come from the gate, its wiring, its supply or its load.
check.again: A gate turns a rule into a circuit, but the circuit lives on a real board. When the output is wrong, the gate itself is only one suspect. The wiring can have an open or a short, the chip may not be getting its supply, or the next stage or an indicator may be loading or shorting the output. That is why troubleshooting checks the supply at the chip, the real input levels and the load before declaring a chip faulty. The chapter covers AND, OR, inverter, NAND and NOR, timing diagrams, enable and disable, waveform windows, gate chips and pins, and the probe and pulser.

segments.title: AND and OR
segments.text: An AND gate outputs HIGH only when every input is HIGH; any LOW forces a LOW. Its equation is X equals A and B, written like a product. An OR gate outputs HIGH when at least one input is HIGH; it is LOW only when every input is LOW. Its equation is X equals A or B, written with a plus sign but meaning OR, so 1 or 1 is 1. OR is inclusive: both HIGH still gives HIGH. Kleitz uses switches to picture them. Two switches in series with a lamp act as AND, since both must close. Two switches in parallel act as OR, since either one closing lights the lamp. For any number of inputs, the AND truth table has a single 1, in the all-HIGH row, and the OR table has a single 0, in the all-LOW row. With n inputs there are two to the n rows, so an eight-input AND table has 256 rows.
segments.expand: Walk through the three-input AND and OR truth tables and point out the single special row in each.
segments.eli5: Think of two light switches controlling one lamp. Wired one after the other in series, both must be on for the lamp to light; that is AND. Wired side by side in parallel, either one lights the lamp; that is OR. Where the picture breaks: a real gate outputs a definite LOW voltage rather than simply breaking a path. AND gives a HIGH only when every input is HIGH; OR gives a LOW only when every input is LOW. So the AND truth table has a single 1, in the all-HIGH row, and the OR table a single 0, in the all-LOW row.
segments.deep: Formula first: AND, X equals A B, read A and B; OR, X equals A plus B, read A or B. Each variable is 0 or 1. AND acts like multiplying 0s and 1s, so any 0 gives 0. OR is inclusive, so 1 or 1 is 1, and any 1 gives 1. Number of truth table rows equals two to the n. For three inputs that is 8 rows: AND is 1 only in row 1 1 1; OR is 0 only in row 0 0 0. Example: inputs 1, 0, 1. Three-input AND gives 0, because of the single 0. Three-input OR gives 1, because at least one input is 1. An eight-input AND has two to the eight, 256 rows, with one 1. The switch pictures explain the patterns: in series, any open switch breaks the path, so AND needs all closed; in parallel, any closed switch completes a path, so OR needs only one. The common misconception is reading the plus as arithmetic, giving 1 plus 1 equals 2, or as exclusive or, giving 0. Neither is OR. Another is thinking an AND with most inputs HIGH outputs HIGH. One LOW forces LOW. NAND and NOR, next, add an inverting bubble to these two gates.

check.q: In which row of its truth table is an OR gate's output LOW?
options: Every row with one LOW input
check.again: An OR gate outputs HIGH when at least one input is HIGH, so it is LOW only when every input is LOW, the first row of the table. The AND gate is the mirror image: HIGH only in the all-HIGH row, the last one. Both patterns hold for any number of inputs, and with n inputs there are two to the n rows, so an eight-input AND table has 256 rows with a single one. The switch pictures: series switches for AND, parallel switches for OR. The OR equation uses a plus sign that means or, so one or one is one.

segments.title: Inverter, NAND and NOR
segments.text: The inverter complements its one input: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1. The small circle, or bubble, on a symbol means inversion. Put a bubble on the output of an AND and you get NAND, which is AND followed by an inverter. Its output is LOW only when every input is HIGH, and HIGH otherwise. Put a bubble on an OR and you get NOR: HIGH only when every input is LOW. The equations place one bar over the whole result: NAND is A and B, all complemented, and a three-input NOR is A or B or C, all complemented. The scope of the bar matters. A and B, all complemented, is not the same as A bar and B, where only A is inverted. To evaluate a NAND or NOR, work in two steps: find the AND or OR, then flip it. A NAND with inputs 1 and 0 gives AND 0, flipped to HIGH.
segments.expand: Evaluate NAND and NOR for all four two-input rows, and explain why the bar's scope matters.
segments.eli5: Think of a contrary assistant who always reports the opposite of what they are told. Put that assistant after an AND gate and you get NAND: whatever AND would say, NAND says the reverse. After an OR gate, you get NOR. The small circle on a symbol, the bubble, is that assistant. Where the picture breaks: the bar in the equation covers the whole result, not one input. So NAND is LOW only when all inputs are HIGH, NOR is HIGH only when all inputs are LOW, and you evaluate them by finding AND or OR first, then flipping.
segments.deep: Formula first: inverter, X equals A bar; NAND, X equals the complement of A B, one bar over the whole product; NOR, X equals the complement of A plus B, one bar over the whole sum. Two-step evaluation: compute the AND or OR, then invert. Example, three-input NAND with inputs 1, 1, 0: the AND is 0, so the NAND is 1. With 1, 1, 1: AND is 1, NAND is 0. Three-input NOR with 0, 0, 1: the OR is 1, so the NOR is 0; only 0, 0, 0 gives NOR 1. Scope of the bar matters. The complement of A B is not A bar B: at A equal to 0 and B equal to 0, the complement of A B is 1, while A bar B is 1 and 0, which is 0. The common misconception is placing the bar on each input instead of the whole result, which gives a different gate. A bar times B bar is actually NOR, by DeMorgan in Lecture 9. The bubble means logical inversion, never a negative voltage. Recognising gates from a description comes next.

check.q: A two-input NAND gate has inputs one and zero. What is its output?
check.again: Work in two steps: find the AND, then flip it. One and zero is zero, and flipping zero gives one, HIGH. NAND is LOW only when every input is HIGH, and HIGH otherwise. NOR is OR followed by an inverter, HIGH only when every input is LOW. The equations put one bar over the whole result, and the scope of the bar matters: A and B, all complemented, is not the same as A bar and B, where only A is inverted. Another example: a NOR with inputs zero and one gives OR one, flipped to LOW.

segments.title: Naming a gate from its behaviour
segments.text: Each gate can be recognised from one sentence. AND: HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH. OR: LOW only when all inputs are LOW. NAND: LOW only when all inputs are HIGH. NOR: HIGH only when all inputs are LOW. Inverter: the opposite of its single input. So when someone describes behaviour, ask two questions: which input row is the special one, all HIGH or all LOW, and is the output in that row HIGH or LOW? Kleitz also shows the rectangular I E E E and I E C symbols, where an ampersand inside the box marks AND, a greater-than-or-equal-to-one mark indicates OR, a 1 marks the inverter, and an inversion mark on the output turns AND into NAND or OR into NOR. Remember that a bubble or inversion mark means logical inversion, not a negative voltage.
segments.expand: Give three behaviour descriptions and identify the gate for each, explaining the two-question method.
segments.eli5: Think of describing a person by the one thing that makes them stand out. For gates, each one has a single special row in its truth table. AND is the one that says HIGH only when everyone says HIGH. OR says LOW only when everyone says LOW. NAND says LOW only when everyone says HIGH. NOR says HIGH only when everyone says LOW. The inverter just says the opposite. So to name a gate from its behaviour, ask which row is special, all HIGH or all LOW, and whether its output there is HIGH or LOW.
segments.deep: The four multi-input gates each have one special row, with an output different from all the other rows. AND: special row all HIGH, output HIGH. NAND: special row all HIGH, output LOW. OR: special row all LOW, output LOW. NOR: special row all LOW, output HIGH. Two questions identify any of them: which row is special, and what is the output in it? Example: a three-input gate gives 1 in every row except 0 0 0, where it gives 0. The special row is all LOW, and its output is LOW, so the gate is OR. Another: a gate gives 0 in every row except 0 0, where it gives 1. Special row all LOW, output HIGH: NOR. The rectangular I E E E and I E C symbols carry the same information as text: an ampersand means AND, a greater-than-or-equal-to-one mark means OR, since at least one input must be 1, a 1 marks a single-input buffer or inverter, and an inversion mark on the output makes NAND or NOR. The common misconception is that NAND means HIGH only when all inputs are LOW. That describes NOR. NAND is LOW only when all are HIGH, and HIGH in every other row. Timing analysis, next, applies these rules over time.

check.q: Which gate is HIGH only when all of its inputs are LOW?
check.again: Each gate has a one-sentence signature. AND: HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH. OR: LOW only when all inputs are LOW. NAND: LOW only when all inputs are HIGH. NOR: HIGH only when all inputs are LOW. Ask two questions: which row is special, all HIGH or all LOW, and is the output in that row HIGH or LOW? All LOW with a HIGH output is NOR. OR is LOW in that same row, and NAND cares about the all-HIGH row. Kleitz also shows the rectangular symbols, where an ampersand marks AND, and a bubble means logical inversion, not a negative voltage.

segments.title: Timing analysis
segments.text: A timing diagram puts every signal on one shared time axis. To find a gate's output, mark a boundary at every point where any input changes, read the stable input combination in each interval, and apply the gate rule to find the output across that interval. Take A HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds and B HIGH from 2 to 6. The AND output follows the overlap: HIGH from 2 to 4. The OR output is HIGH from 0 to 6, and a NOR output is HIGH only in the gaps where both are LOW. These ideal diagrams assume zero delay. Real gates have propagation delay: t P L H is the delay for the output going LOW to HIGH, and t P H L for the output going HIGH to LOW. The letters describe the output transition, even for an inverter where the input moves the other way. And a gate's delay is not the clock period.
segments.expand: Work a timing example with a NOR gate interval by interval, and explain what the two propagation delays describe.
segments.eli5: Think of a row of people passing a message, each pausing a moment before passing it on. The final listener hears the message, but slightly late. A real gate is like that: its output changes a few nanoseconds after its input. Ideal timing diagrams ignore the pause and just apply the gate rule in each interval between input changes. With the pause included, every output edge shifts a little later. So find a gate's output by slicing the diagram at every input change, and remember real outputs lag by the propagation delay, t P L H for rising outputs and t P H L for falling ones.
segments.deep: Formula first in words: in each interval between input changes, output equals the gate rule applied to the input levels in that interval. Example: A HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds, B HIGH from 2 to 6. Boundaries at 2, 4 and 6. AND is HIGH from 2 to 4; OR from 0 to 6; NOR is HIGH where both are LOW, after 6 and before 0; NAND is LOW only from 2 to 4. Propagation delay: t P L H is the delay before the output goes from LOW to HIGH, and t P H L before it goes from HIGH to LOW. The names describe the output, not the input. For an inverter, a rising input causes a falling output, so the relevant delay is t P H L. Semi-quantitative example: if an inverter has t P H L of 10 nanoseconds, an input rising at 100 nanoseconds gives an output falling at 110 nanoseconds. The common misconception is confusing propagation delay with the clock period. A gate's delay is how late it responds; the period is how often the clock repeats. Unequal delays on two paths are what produce the glitches mentioned in Lecture 9. Enable and disable, next, uses one input to control another.

check.q: What does the propagation delay t P H L describe?
options: The output going from HIGH to LOW
The input going from HIGH to LOW
The length of the clock period
check.again: The letters in t P H L and t P L H describe the output transition. t P H L is the delay for the output to go from HIGH to LOW after the input change that causes it, and t P L H is for the output going LOW to HIGH. That holds even for an inverter, where the input moves the other way. A gate's delay is a few nanoseconds and is not the clock period. Ideal timing diagrams assume zero delay: mark a boundary at every input change and apply the gate rule in each interval.

segments.title: Enable and disable
segments.text: A second input can let a signal through, block it, or invert it. Call the data A and the control E. For AND, E at 1 passes A and E at 0 forces 0. For OR, E at 0 passes A and E at 1 forces 1. For NAND, E at 1 passes A inverted and E at 0 forces 1. For NOR, E at 0 passes A inverted and E at 1 forces 0. The value that takes over the output, 0 for AND and NAND, 1 for OR and NOR, is the controlling value. A clock enable uses exactly this: the output equals the clock ANDed with enable, passing the clock when enable is 1 and holding the output LOW when enable is 0. Two related terms. Active HIGH means a function is asserted by a HIGH; active LOW means it is asserted by a LOW, such as a reset that acts when its pin is LOW.
segments.expand: Explain the controlling-value idea for all four gates, and why changing enable during a HIGH clock can cut a pulse short.
segments.eli5: Think of a TV remote with a mute button. With mute off, the sound passes through to the speakers; with mute on, the speakers stay silent whatever the show does. A control input on a gate is that mute button. For AND, control 1 passes the signal and control 0 forces 0. For OR, control 0 passes and control 1 forces 1. NAND and NOR do the same, but pass the signal inverted. Where the picture breaks: a forced output is a definite level, not silence. So the controlling value takes over the output, and the other value lets the signal through.
segments.deep: Formula first in words: AND, 1 and A is A, 0 and A is 0. OR, 0 or A is A, 1 or A is 1. NAND, the complement of 1 and A is A bar, and the complement of 0 and A is 1. NOR, the complement of 0 or A is A bar, and the complement of 1 or A is 0. The controlling value, 0 for AND and NAND, 1 for OR and NOR, decides the output alone. The non-controlling value makes the output depend on the data. Example: a 500 kilohertz clock into a NOR gate with control E. With E at 0, the output is the clock inverted, still 500 kilohertz. With E at 1, the output is held at 0. A clock enable built from AND: output equals clock and enable. Enable 1 passes it; enable 0 holds LOW. Active HIGH means a function is asserted by a HIGH; active LOW means asserted by a LOW, like a reset pin that clears when pulled LOW. The common misconception is that a disabled gate outputs nothing. It always outputs a definite level, and which level depends on the gate: LOW for AND and NOR, HIGH for OR and NAND. This idea is also the basis of the pulser test later in the lecture.

check.q: For a NOR gate, which control value takes over the output?
check.again: The controlling value is the input value that forces the output regardless of the other input. For OR and NOR that value is one: an OR with a one input is forced HIGH, and a NOR with a one input is forced LOW. For AND and NAND the controlling value is zero. The non-controlling value lets the data through: for NOR, a zero control passes the data inverted. A clock enable uses an AND, passing the clock when enable is one and holding LOW when it is zero. Active HIGH means asserted by a HIGH, active LOW by a LOW.

segments.title: When an input cannot be inferred
segments.text: Sometimes you know a gate's output and one input, and must work out the other. For X equals A and B, if A is 1 and X is 0, then B must be 0. But if A is 0 and X is 0, B could be either, because A alone already forces the output LOW. In that situation B is a don't care: its value does not change the result. Kleitz marks such intervals on timing diagrams with diagonal hash marks. Be careful not to confuse this with hardware. A don't care is a statement about a truth table condition; it is never permission to leave a physical input floating. A real input must always be driven or tied to a defined level, even if its value happens not to matter for the logic at that moment.
segments.expand: Work a don't care example with an OR gate and explain the difference between a don't care and a floating input.
segments.eli5: Think of a vote that needs everyone's yes. If one person has already said no, the result is no, and you cannot tell from the result how the others voted; their votes did not matter. In an AND gate, if one input is 0 and the output is 0, the other input could be either value. That input is a don't care for that moment. Where the picture breaks: a real input wire still must be connected to something. So a don't care means the value does not change the result, never that a physical input may be left floating.
segments.deep: Working backward from an output: for X equals A and B, if A is 1, then X equals B, so X reveals B exactly. If A is 0, then X is 0 regardless, so B cannot be inferred. Its value does not affect the output, so it is a don't care in that condition. Kleitz shows such intervals on timing diagrams with diagonal hash marks. Example with OR: X equals A or B. If A is 0 and X is 1, then B must be 1. If A is 1 and X is 1, B is a don't care, because A's 1 is the controlling value and forces the output. The rule: an input can be inferred only while every other input holds its non-controlling value. The common misconception is that a don't care input can be left unconnected in hardware. A floating T T L input picks up noise and its level becomes undefined, and when the other input changes to its non-controlling value, that floating input suddenly matters. Don't care is a statement about the truth table at that moment, never permission to leave a wire unconnected. Physical inputs are always driven or tied, as Lecture 8 required. Waveform windows, next, use known inputs to carve precise intervals.

check.q: X equals A and B. You know A is zero and X is zero. What can you say about B?
check.again: When A is zero, the AND output is zero whatever B does, so B could be either value and you cannot infer it. That is a don't care, marked on Kleitz's timing diagrams with diagonal hash marks. Contrast the case where A is one and X is zero: then B must be zero, because only B could have pulled the output down. A don't care is a statement about the logic, never permission to leave a physical input floating. A real input must always be driven or tied, even when its value happens not to matter at that moment.

segments.title: Making waveform windows
segments.text: Gates can carve precise windows out of timed signals. Kleitz uses the outputs of a Johnson shift counter as a ready supply of repeating waveforms; how the counter works inside comes much later. Suppose A is HIGH from 1 to 6 microseconds and B is HIGH from 3 to 8, in a repeating frame. We want an output HIGH only from 1 to 3 microseconds. In that interval A is HIGH and B is LOW, so the output is A and B bar: invert B, then AND. If you want the same window but LOW inside and HIGH elsewhere, complement the whole result with a NAND after the inverter. To pass clock pulses only inside the window, AND the clock in too: clock and A and B bar. Without the clock, the window is a steady level, not a series of pulses.
segments.expand: Design another window from the same two waveforms, such as HIGH only from 6 to 8 microseconds.
segments.eli5: Think of a stencil. Two overlapping shapes can be combined to leave exactly the area you want: keep where the first shape is, but not where the second shape is. Gates do that with time intervals. If A is HIGH from 1 to 6 microseconds and B from 3 to 8, then A and not B is HIGH exactly where A is on and B is off, from 1 to 3. Add the clock as a third AND input and only the clock pulses inside that window get through. So gates combine timed signals to cut out precise windows.
segments.deep: Formula first in words: window equals A and B bar, where A must be HIGH and B LOW inside the window. To design a window, find which level each signal has inside it and outside it, then AND the signals with the right ones inverted. Example: A HIGH from 0 to 5 microseconds, B HIGH from 2 to 7, repeating. A and B bar is HIGH where A is 1 and B is 0, from 0 to 2 microseconds. A bar and B is HIGH from 5 to 7. A and B is HIGH from 2 to 5. Lecture example: A from 1 to 6 and B from 3 to 8 gives A and B bar from 1 to 3. For an active-LOW window, LOW inside and HIGH outside, use NAND instead: the complement of A and B bar. To get pulses instead of a level, AND in the clock: clock and A and B bar passes only the clock pulses inside the window. Kleitz uses a Johnson counter's outputs as handy repeating waveforms; how the counter works comes much later, so treat them simply as given signals. The common misconception is using A and B for a window where B must be LOW, which gives the overlap instead. Gate chips, next, bring these designs to the breadboard.

check.q: A is HIGH from one to six microseconds and B from three to eight. Which expression is HIGH only from one to three?
check.again: Look at what is true in the wanted window. From one to three microseconds, A is already HIGH but B has not yet gone HIGH, so A is HIGH and B is LOW. Invert B, then AND with A: A and B bar. Plain A and B would give the overlap, three to six. A bar and B would give six to eight, where B is HIGH after A has dropped. For the same window inverted, LOW inside and HIGH elsewhere, use a NAND after the inverter. To pass clock pulses only inside the window, AND the clock in as well.

segments.title: Gate chips and pins
segments.text: A logic diagram, an electrical family and a physical package are three separate pieces of information. A part number such as S N 74 L S 08 N names a manufacturer's low-power Schottky T T L AND chip in a plastic D I P. The common base numbers: 7400 NAND, 7402 NOR, 7404 inverter, 7408 AND, 7432 OR, 7411 three-input AND, 7421 four-input AND. On the 14-pin 74 L S 08, pin 14 is V C C and pin 7 is ground. Gate 1 takes inputs on pins 1 and 2 with output on pin 3, and the others use 4 and 5 to 6, 9 and 10 to 8, and 12 and 13 to 11. That is a top view, counting down the left and up the right. The 74 L S 02 NOR differs: its first gate outputs on pin 1 from inputs 2 and 3. So always use the exact part's pinout, and remember the output's drive comes from the chip's supply, not from its inputs.
segments.expand: Walk through the 7408 pin assignments for all four gates and explain why the 7402 must not be wired the same way.
segments.eli5: Think of a product code on a box of cereal. It tells you the brand, the recipe, and the box size, three separate facts packed into one label. A chip part number does the same. S N 74 L S 08 N says the maker, the family, low-power Schottky T T L, the function, quad AND, and the package, plastic D I P. Then the pinout tells you where each gate's pins are. Where the picture breaks: chips that look identical can have different pin layouts inside. So a part number names family, function and package, and the exact pinout must always come from that part's datasheet.
segments.deep: A part number such as S N 74 L S 08 N combines three independent facts: manufacturer prefix S N, the logic family L S, low-power Schottky T T L, the function 08, a quad two-input AND, and the package suffix N, a plastic D I P. Base numbers to know: 7400 NAND, 7402 NOR, 7404 inverter, 7408 AND, 7432 OR, 7411 three-input AND, 7421 four-input AND. 74 L S 08 pinout, top view: V C C on 14, ground on 7; gates on pins 1 and 2 to 3, 4 and 5 to 6, 9 and 10 to 8, 12 and 13 to 11. Example check: four gates times three signal pins is 12, plus two power pins, 14. On the 74 L S 02 NOR, gate one has its output on pin 1 and inputs on pins 2 and 3, so wiring it as an 08 would drive a switch into its output. The output's current comes from the chip's own supply through pin 14, not from its inputs, so a chip with a missing supply cannot drive its outputs properly, even with correct input levels. The common misconception is that same-size chips share pinouts. Power pins often match; gate pins often do not. Troubleshooting, next, uses these pin facts at the bench.

check.q: On the 74 L S 08, gate one's inputs are on pins one and two. Its output is on which pin?
check.again: On the fourteen-pin 74 L S 08, the four AND gates use pins one and two to three, four and five to six, nine and ten to eight, and twelve and thirteen to eleven, with V C C on pin fourteen and ground on pin seven. That is the top view, counting down the left side and up the right. The 74 L S 02 NOR differs: its first gate outputs on pin one from inputs on pins two and three. A part number such as S N 74 L S 08 N also names the manufacturer, the family and the package.

segments.title: Troubleshooting with probe and pulser
segments.text: A logic probe touches a point and shows its state: HIGH, LOW or pulsing, depending on the instrument. A logic pulser injects a controlled test stimulus. To test one input of a gate with the pulser, hold the other input at its non-controlling value so the pulses can pass: HIGH for AND and NAND, LOW for OR and NOR. Then watch the output with the probe. An open is a broken connection, such as a lifted pin or cracked track; a short is an unintended connection, such as a solder bridge. In a larger circuit, predict each intermediate node, measure at the actual pins in signal-flow order, and find the first disagreement. Before declaring a chip faulty, check its supply at the chip, its real input levels, and whether the next stage or an indicator is loading or shorting its output. One passing test does not prove the whole truth table.
segments.expand: Walk through troubleshooting a NAND whose output reads LOW with inputs 0 and 1, including checking the load.
segments.eli5: Think of checking a garden hose with a kink somewhere along it. You turn on the tap and walk along the hose from the tap end, checking the flow at each point, until you find the first spot where water stops. Everything before that point is fine; the fault is just after it. Troubleshooting a gate circuit works the same way. Predict what each node should do, measure at the actual pins in signal-flow order, and find the first point where reality disagrees. So the first disagreement, found in order, locates the fault.
segments.deep: The method is predict, measure, compare, in signal-flow order. A logic probe shows a node's state, HIGH, LOW or pulsing, depending on the instrument. A logic pulser injects test pulses. To test one input of a gate, hold the other input at its non-controlling value so the gate passes the pulses: HIGH for AND and NAND, LOW for OR and NOR. Example: testing a 7408 gate on pins 1, 2 and 3. Hold pin 2 HIGH, pulse pin 1, and probe pin 3. A pulsing output is correct. A steady LOW at pin 3 suggests a problem: check V C C at pin 14 and ground at pin 7 at the chip itself, check pin 2 really is HIGH rather than floating, and check whether pin 3 is shorted to ground by a solder bridge or loaded down by the next stage. An open, like a lifted pin, breaks a connection; a short, like a solder bridge, makes an unintended one. Only then suspect the chip. The common misconception is that one passing test proves the gate works. It proves one path for one input condition, not the whole truth table. Note also that a pulser should never be forced against an output that is already being driven.

check.q: To pulse one input of an OR gate with a logic pulser, you hold the other input LOW.
check.again: The other input must sit at its non-controlling value so the pulses can pass through. For OR and NOR that is LOW, since a HIGH would force the output and hide the pulses. For AND and NAND the other input is held HIGH. Then watch the output with the logic probe, which shows HIGH, LOW or pulsing. In a bigger circuit, predict each intermediate node, measure at the actual pins in signal-flow order, and find the first disagreement. Before blaming a chip, check its supply at the chip, its real input levels, and whether its output is being loaded or shorted.

segments.title: Evaluating a small gate network
segments.text: When several gates connect, evaluate the intermediate nodes in order rather than jumping to the final gate. Suppose P equals A and B, Q equals C inverted, and X equals P or Q. For A equals 0, B equals 1 and C equals 0: P is 0 and 1, which is 0; Q is the inverse of 0, which is 1; and X is 0 or 1, which is 1. Writing each intermediate value stops you from applying the final gate's rule to the wrong signals. You can also translate the network into one equation, X equals A and B, or C bar. That equation is the bridge to the next topic, Boolean algebra, where the laws let you simplify such expressions so that the same function needs fewer gates.
segments.expand: Evaluate the same network for all input combinations where X equals 0, and explain why they are the only ones.
segments.eli5: Think of following a recipe with several bowls. You mix bowl P, prepare bowl Q, and only then combine them in the final dish. Jumping straight to the final step with the raw ingredients gives the wrong result. Evaluating a gate network is the same: work out each intermediate node, P and Q, then apply the final gate to those values, not to the raw inputs. So evaluate gate networks node by node in signal order, and the network can also be written as one equation, which Boolean algebra later simplifies.
segments.deep: Formula first: P equals A and B; Q equals C bar; X equals P or Q, so X equals A B or C bar. Evaluating node by node prevents applying the final gate's rule to the wrong signals. Example: A equals 1, B equals 1, C equals 1. P is 1 and 1, which is 1; Q is the inverse of 1, which is 0; X is 1 or 0, which is 1. Another: A equals 1, B equals 0, C equals 1. P is 0; Q is 0; X is 0. Lecture example: A 0, B 1, C 0 gives P 0, Q 1, X 1. Over all eight rows, X is 1 whenever C is 0, four rows, and also in row 1 1 1, giving five rows in all. That five-row list is what any simplified version must reproduce. The common misconception is treating the network as a single gate, for example applying OR directly to A, B and C, which would give 1 for the 1 0 1 row instead of the correct 0. Writing the intermediate values guards against that. The one-equation form, A B or C bar, is already a sum of products, and Boolean algebra in Lecture 9 shows how to reduce larger expressions like it.

check.q: P equals A and B, Q equals C inverted, and X equals P or Q. With A zero, B one and C zero, what is X?
check.again: Evaluate the intermediate nodes in order rather than jumping to the final gate. P is A and B, zero and one, which is zero. Q is C inverted, the inverse of zero, which is one. X is P or Q, zero or one, which is one. Writing each intermediate value keeps you from applying the final rule to the wrong signals. The whole network is one equation, X equals A and B, or C bar, and that equation is the bridge to Boolean algebra, where laws let you simplify so the same function needs fewer gates.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from Chapter 3. One: AND is HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, OR is LOW only when all inputs are LOW, and NAND and NOR are those with the output inverted. Two: in a timing diagram, divide at every input change and apply the rule in each interval; ideal diagrams ignore delay, and t P L H and t P H L describe the output's transitions. Three: a control input with the non-controlling value passes a signal, and with the controlling value forces the output. Four: gate chips such as the 7408 put V C C on pin 14 and ground on pin 7, but check each pinout, since the 7402 differs. Five: troubleshoot by predicting, measuring in signal-flow order and finding the first disagreement.
segments.expand: Ask one gate identification question, one enable question and one troubleshooting question.
segments.eli5: Think of learning a new board game. First, the rules for each piece. Then, how play unfolds turn by turn. Then, special moves that let one piece block or release another. Then, the physical board and pieces. And finally, how to find out who made a wrong move. Chapter 3 is that sequence for gates: the five gate rules, timing diagrams, enable and disable, chips and pinouts, and troubleshooting. So gates turn rules into circuits, and a careful, ordered check of each node finds what went wrong.
segments.deep: Five connected ideas. Gate rules: AND HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, OR LOW only when all are LOW, NAND and NOR inverted, inverter opposite. Timing: slice at every input change and apply the rule; real outputs lag by t P L H or t P H L, named for the output's transition. Control: the non-controlling value passes a signal, the controlling value forces the output. Chips: the 74 L S 08 has power on 14 and ground on 7, gates 1 and 2 to 3 and so on, but the 74 L S 02 differs. Troubleshooting: predict, measure in signal-flow order, find the first disagreement, and check supply, inputs and loading before blaming the chip. A combined example: a NAND clock gate with enable at 1 passes the clock inverted; with enable at 0, the output is held HIGH. If the probe shows the output held HIGH even with enable at 1, first check that enable really reaches the input pin at a HIGH level, then check the clock arrives, then the supply at pin 14. The common misconception is jumping to replacing the chip. Most faults are wiring, supply or level problems. Lecture 9 takes these gate networks into Boolean algebra for simplification.

check.q: To troubleshoot a gate circuit, predict each node, measure in signal-flow order and stop at the first disagreement.
check.again: That is the chapter's troubleshooting method: work out what every intermediate node should be, then measure at the actual pins in the order the signal flows, and the first place where prediction and measurement disagree is where the fault lives. One passing test does not prove the whole truth table. The recap's other ideas: AND is HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, OR is LOW only when all are LOW, and NAND and NOR invert those; timing diagrams are read interval by interval; a non-controlling control value passes a signal; and the 7408 puts V C C on pin fourteen and ground on pin seven, but the 7402 differs.

lectures.title: Component models and measurement
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 01 - Component Models and Measurement.md; Boylestad §1.5, §1.7, §2.2, §2.4, §4.2, §4.3, §4.7, §6.8; §10.3, §10.10, §11.3, §11.4 at model level only

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This first lecture builds the habit that runs through the whole course: connect a physical component, the relationship between its voltage and current, a labelled diagram, and a calculation you can check. We will meet three ideal element models, the resistor, the capacitor and the inductor. We will look at Ohm's law as an equation and as a graph, and at what a rate of change means without any heavy calculus. Then we turn to charge and the direction of conventional current, the difference between an open path and a closed one, and finally what makes a measured number trustworthy: precision, accuracy, resolution and significant figures. If you keep one sentence from today, keep this one: every quantity needs a unit, and every voltage and current needs a clear reference, or the number means nothing.
segments.expand: Explain why pairing a component, its voltage-current relationship, a diagram and a calculation catches mistakes that any one of them alone would miss.

check.q: According to this lecture's opening, what does every voltage and every current need before the number means anything?
options: A clear reference and a unit
A calculator check and a graph
A colour code and a symbol
check.again: The one sentence to keep from the opening is this: a quantity is meaningless without a unit, and a voltage or current is meaningless without a reference. Saying six is not a measurement; six volts is. Saying six volts across the resistor, with the plus end named, is a complete statement. The same goes for current: three milliamps needs an arrow saying which way it flows through which element. The lecture ties a component, its voltage-current relationship, a labelled diagram and a calculation together, and the unit and the reference are what make those four agree.

segments.title: Three ideal element models
segments.text: An element model is an idealized description of how a component behaves. The resistor has resistance, R, measured in ohms. The capacitor has capacitance, C, measured in farads. The inductor has inductance, L, measured in henries. Each model links the voltage across the element to the current through it. For the resistor, voltage equals current times resistance. For the capacitor, current equals capacitance times the rate of change of its voltage. For the inductor, voltage equals inductance times the rate of change of its current. The subscripts in names like v sub R tell you which element a quantity belongs to, and a lowercase v or i reminds you the quantity might change with time. Real parts are never perfectly ideal; a real resistor has a little inductance, and a real coil has resistance in its wire. The model is a useful description, not the whole truth.
segments.expand: Compare the three relationships side by side, and explain what an unwanted, or parasitic, resistance or capacitance means in a real part.

check.q: In the ideal capacitor model, the voltage across the capacitor equals its capacitance times the rate of change of its current.
check.again: That is the inductor's rule with the names swapped. The capacitor model says current equals capacitance times the rate of change of voltage: current in amps, capacitance in farads, rate of change of voltage in volts per second. The inductor is the mirror image: voltage equals inductance times the rate of change of current, in volts, henries and amps per second. A quick way to keep them straight: the capacitor responds to changing voltage, the inductor responds to changing current. And the resistor is the simple one, voltage equals current times resistance, with no rate of change at all.

segments.title: Ohm's law in three forms
segments.text: For an ideal resistor carrying steady current, Ohm's law says the voltage across the resistor equals the current through it times its resistance: volts equal amps times ohms. Rearranged, current equals voltage divided by resistance, and resistance equals voltage divided by current. The critical detail is that the voltage and the current belong to the same resistor: the voltage across it and the current through it. Here is the class example. A 2 kilohm resistor has 6 volts across it. Current equals 6 volts over 2 kilohms. Notice a handy pairing: volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps, so the answer is simply 6 over 2, which is 3 milliamps. If your calculator shows 0.003 amps, that is the same current, written in engineering form as 3.00 milliamps. And remember that dividing needs a nonzero denominator: the point of zero volts and zero current alone cannot tell you a resistance.
segments.expand: Work a second example that uses a different prefix pair, such as volts over megohms giving microamps.

check.q: A 2 kilohm resistor has 6 volts across it. What current flows through it?
check.again: Ohm's law rearranged: current equals voltage divided by resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Six volts over two thousand ohms is 0.003 amps. The shortcut is that volts divided by kilohms comes out directly in milliamps, so six over two is three milliamps. Twelve would come from multiplying instead of dividing, and three amps forgets the kilo. Try another one: 9 volts across a 3 kilohm resistor gives nine over three, which is 3 milliamps again. The voltage and current must belong to the same resistor for this to work.

segments.title: The graph is the same law
segments.text: Plot a fixed resistor with current along the horizontal axis and voltage up the vertical axis, and you get a straight line through the origin. The slope of that line, the change in voltage divided by the change in current, is the resistance. So a larger resistance gives a steeper line on these axes. For the 2 kilohm resistor, 1 milliamp goes with 2 volts, 2 milliamps with 4 volts, 3 milliamps with 6 volts; the slope is 2 volts per milliamp, which is 2 kilohms, not 2 ohms, because of the milli on the axis. Swap the axes, putting current up the side, and the slope becomes current over voltage, which is the conductance, one over the resistance. Then the larger resistance is the flatter line. A curved characteristic, like a diode's, cannot be described by one fixed resistance across its whole range.
segments.expand: Explain how to read the prefixes on a graph's axes before computing a slope, with an example of the factor-of-a-thousand error.

check.q: Plot a resistor with current along the horizontal axis and voltage up the vertical axis. The slope of the line represents what?
check.again: Slope is rise over run. With voltage as the rise and current as the run, slope equals change in voltage divided by change in current, which is exactly resistance: volts over amps gives ohms. That is why a bigger resistance draws a steeper line on these axes. For example, a 4 kilohm resistor climbs 4 volts for every extra milliamp, twice as steep as the 2 kilohm line. Only if you swap the axes, current up the side, does the slope become current over voltage, the conductance, and then the larger resistance is the flatter line.

segments.title: Rate of change, without heavy calculus
segments.text: A rate of change is a slope: how much a quantity changes divided by the time the change took. For a straight segment of a graph, that is just the change over the elapsed time. The capacitor model says its current equals its capacitance times the rate of change of its voltage. The class example: a 1 microfarad capacitor whose voltage rises steadily from 0 to 2 volts in 2 milliseconds. The rate of change is 2 volts over 2 milliseconds, 1 volt per millisecond. Multiply by 1 microfarad and you get 1 milliamp while the voltage is rising. Once the voltage stops changing, the rate of change is zero, so the ideal capacitor current is zero, even though the voltage is still 2 volts. That is the key idea: a nonzero level can have zero slope. A capacitor holding a steady voltage carries no ideal current.
segments.expand: Walk through how the capacitor current would look while the voltage rises, holds, then falls, and why it goes negative when the voltage falls.

check.q: A 1 microfarad capacitor holding a steady 2 volts still carries the 1 milliamp of ideal current it had while charging.
check.again: The capacitor rule is current equals capacitance times the rate of change of voltage, current in amps, capacitance in farads, rate of change in volts per second. Once the voltage stops changing, its rate of change is zero, and anything times zero is zero. So the ideal current is zero while the voltage sits at a steady 2 volts. The 1 milliamp existed only during the rise, when the voltage was climbing at 1 volt per millisecond. The lesson is that a level and a slope are different things: a nonzero voltage can have zero slope, and it is the slope that sets the capacitor current.

segments.title: The inductor is the mirror image
segments.text: The inductor swaps the roles. Its voltage equals its inductance times the rate of change of its current: volts equal henries times amps per second. The class example: a 2 millihenry inductor whose current rises steadily from 0 to 3 milliamps in 3 milliseconds. The rate of change is 3 milliamps over 3 milliseconds, 1 amp per second. Multiply by 2 millihenries and the voltage is 2 millivolts while the current is rising. Once the current holds steady, its rate of change is zero and the ideal inductor voltage is zero, even though a current is still flowing. A real coil also has resistance in its winding, so a real steady current would still show a small resistive drop. For now, what you need is the pattern: capacitor current follows changing voltage, inductor voltage follows changing current.
segments.expand: Explain why an ideal inductor with steady current behaves like a plain wire, and what the winding resistance adds in a real one.

check.q: A 2 millihenry inductor's current rises steadily at 1 amp per second. What voltage appears across it while the current rises?
check.again: The inductor rule: voltage equals inductance times the rate of change of current, voltage in volts, inductance in henries, rate of change in amps per second. Two millihenries is 0.002 henries, and 0.002 times 1 amp per second is 0.002 volts, which is 2 millivolts. Two volts forgets the milli on the inductance. As a second example, a 5 millihenry coil with current rising at 2 amps per second shows 10 millivolts. When the current stops rising, the slope is zero and the ideal voltage drops to zero even though current still flows.

segments.title: Charge and conventional current
segments.text: Electric charge comes in two signs. Like signs repel and opposite signs attract. Current is the flow of charge, and by convention its direction is the way positive charge would move. That is conventional current, and it is what every arrow in this course means. In a metal wire, though, the charges that actually move are electrons, which are negative, so they drift the opposite way to the conventional current arrow. Both descriptions are correct; just pick the conventional one and use it consistently. One more point that saves a lot of confusion: electrons are already present throughout the wire, and a load does not use them up. In a steady single loop, the same current enters and leaves every part. What a resistor converts is energy, into heat, not charge.
segments.expand: Give an everyday picture of why the same current enters and leaves a resistor, and what actually is being used up.

check.q: In a metal wire, which way do the electrons actually drift compared with the conventional current arrow?
check.again: Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would move, and every arrow in this course uses that convention. But the movers in a metal are electrons, which are negative, so they drift against the arrow. Both pictures describe the same physical flow; the course simply commits to the conventional one so that every arrow means one thing. Picture a battery driving a lamp: the conventional current arrow leaves the positive terminal and goes round to the negative terminal, while the electrons creep the other way round the loop. Neither is used up; the lamp converts energy, not charge.

segments.title: Open paths and closed paths
segments.text: Closed means the conducting path is complete; open means it is broken somewhere. A closed ideal switch has zero volts across it, because it is just a piece of ideal wire. An open switch carries zero current, because there is no path. But an open switch can still have a voltage across it. The class example: a 6 volt supply, a 2 kilohm resistor and a switch in one loop. Closed, the current is 6 volts over 2 kilohms, 3 milliamps, and the switch drops nothing. Open, the current is zero, so the resistor drops current times resistance, which is zero, and the whole 6 volts appears across the switch gap. No current and no voltage are different statements. A fuse fits the same picture: intact, it is a closed low-resistance path; blown, it is an open, deliberately broken path.
segments.expand: Explain why you cannot find the open-circuit voltage by multiplying zero current by infinite resistance, and what to reason with instead.

check.q: In the 6 volt, 2 kilohm loop with the switch open, what voltage appears across the switch?
check.again: An open switch carries no current, but it can still have a voltage across it. With no current, the resistor's drop is current times resistance, zero times 2 kilohms, which is zero. The supply still pushes 6 volts round the loop, and the only place left for that voltage is the gap in the switch, so the switch shows the full 6 volts. Closed, the picture flips: the switch is ideal wire with zero volts across it, and the resistor takes all 6 volts with 3 milliamps flowing. Zero current and zero voltage are separate claims; check each on its own.

segments.title: Precision, accuracy and resolution
segments.text: A meter display is a measurement result, not a guarantee. Three words describe how good it is. Precision is how closely repeated readings agree with one another. Accuracy is how close a reading is to the accepted true value. Resolution is the smallest change the instrument can display. These are independent. Picture a meter that reads a known 5.000 volt reference as 5.199, 5.200 and 5.201 volts. Those readings are tightly clustered, so the meter is precise, but every one sits about 0.2 volts high, so it is not accurate. That pattern points to a systematic offset. More digits on the display improve resolution, which lets you see smaller changes, but they do not remove a bias. When the last digits flicker, the stable digits, the meter's specification and the conditions decide what you can honestly report.
segments.expand: Describe how you would test whether a meter has a systematic offset, and why averaging more readings does not fix one.

check.q: A meter reads a known 5.000 volt reference as 5.199, 5.200 and 5.201 volts. How would you describe that meter?
check.again: Precision asks whether repeated readings agree with each other; accuracy asks whether they agree with the true value. Readings of 5.199, 5.200 and 5.201 are within two thousandths of one another, so the meter is very precise. But all three sit about 0.2 volts above the real 5.000, so it is not accurate; there is a steady offset. Think of arrows landing in a tight cluster off to one side of the bullseye. Resolution is a third, separate idea: the smallest change the display can show. Extra digits improve resolution but do nothing about a bias.

segments.title: Comparing sizes and counting figures
segments.text: Before judging whether a difference matters, put both quantities in the same unit. One millivolt compared with one kilovolt: a millivolt is ten to the minus three volts and a kilovolt is ten to the three volts, so the ratio is ten to the minus six, one millionth. Small, perhaps negligible for some jobs, but not zero. Significant figures tell the reader how precisely a number is known. Leading zeros only locate the decimal point, so 0.00420 volts has three significant figures: four, two and the final zero. Zeros between nonzero digits count, so 2.005 kilohms has four. A whole number like 1000 ohms is ambiguous; writing 1.00 kilohms says three figures clearly. Engineering notation uses powers of ten in steps of three to match the prefixes: 0.00420 volts is 4.20 times ten to the minus three volts, which is 4.20 millivolts.
segments.expand: Give more examples of zeros that do and do not count, and explain why a prefix change never changes the number of significant figures.

check.q: How many significant figures are in 0.00420 volts?
check.again: Leading zeros only tell you where the decimal point sits, so none of the zeros before the 4 count. The 4 and the 2 count, and the final zero counts too, because someone chose to record it; it says the value is known to that place. That makes three significant figures. In engineering notation the same value is 4.20 times ten to the minus three volts, or 4.20 millivolts, and there the three figures are plain to see. Compare 2.005 kilohms: the zeros sit between nonzero digits, so they count, giving four figures.

segments.title: Recap of lecture one
segments.text: Here are the ideas to carry forward. First, three ideal elements: a resistor, where voltage equals current times resistance; a capacitor, whose current follows the rate of change of its voltage; and an inductor, whose voltage follows the rate of change of its current. Steady voltage means zero ideal capacitor current; steady current means zero ideal inductor voltage. Second, Ohm's law in any of its three forms, always with the voltage across and the current through the same resistor, and its graph, where the slope of voltage against current is the resistance. Third, conventional current follows positive charge, electrons drift the other way, and resistors convert energy, not current. Fourth, open means zero current but not necessarily zero voltage. Fifth, precision, accuracy and resolution are different questions, and extra digits are not extra truth.
segments.expand: Quiz me quickly on one example from each of the five recap points.

check.q: The recap says an open path means zero current, and therefore also zero voltage across the break.
check.again: Open means the path is broken, so no current can flow. It does not mean the voltage is zero. In the example from this lecture, opening the switch in a 6 volt loop stopped the current, and the resistor drop went to zero, but the entire 6 volts then appeared across the switch gap. Zero current and zero voltage are two different statements that must be checked separately. The other recap points hold up the same way: steady voltage gives zero ideal capacitor current, steady current gives zero ideal inductor voltage, and extra display digits are not extra truth.

lectures.title: Measurement, charge, current and voltage
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 02 - Measurement, Charge, Current and Voltage.md; Boylestad §1.5 to §1.8, §2.2 to §2.4, §2.8, §2.10, §5.7, §6.5, §10.2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture two ties four ideas together. Charge is conserved. Current describes how quickly charge moves. Voltage describes energy per charge. And measurement lets us test those ideas, provided we report numbers honestly. We start with Kirchhoff's current law, which is charge conservation at a junction. Then we tighten up significant figures, engineering notation and the SI prefixes. After that we look inside the atom, see why copper conducts, and meet the electric field and Coulomb's law. Finally we define current as charge per time and voltage as energy per charge, and end with a uniform resistor whose midpoint sits at half the voltage. Keep an ear out for units throughout: coulombs, amps, volts, joules and newtons each measure something different.
segments.expand: Explain how charge, current and voltage relate, using a single simple circuit as the example.

check.q: This lecture's opening defines voltage as which of these?
check.again: The opening names four ideas: charge is conserved, current is how quickly charge moves, voltage is energy per charge, and measurement tests them. So current is the charge per time, in coulombs per second, which are amps. Voltage is the energy per charge, in joules per coulomb, which are volts. Force per charge is the electric field, in newtons per coulomb. A helpful picture: a 9 volt battery gives each coulomb of charge 9 joules of energy to spend around the loop, however fast or slowly that charge moves.

segments.title: Kirchhoff's current law
segments.text: Kirchhoff's current law comes straight from conservation of charge. In a steady circuit, charge cannot keep piling up at a junction, so the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it. You can state it two ways. Count entering currents as positive and leaving currents as negative, and the signed sum is zero. Or put the entering currents on one side and the leaving currents on the other, as plain sizes. Just do not mix the two descriptions in one equation. The class example: 5 amps enters a node, and 4 amps and 1 amp leave. Five minus four minus one is zero, so the node balances. If two currents enter, 3 amps and 2 amps, and one of two leaving currents is 4 amps, the other must be 1 amp.
segments.expand: Work a node with four branches, choosing a sign convention first, and show how an unknown current's sign reveals its true direction.

check.q: Currents of 3 amps and 2 amps enter a node. One leaving current is 4 amps. What is the other leaving current?
check.again: Kirchhoff's current law: the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it, because charge cannot pile up there. Entering: 3 plus 2 is 5 amps. Leaving: 4 amps plus the unknown. For the two sides to match, the unknown must be 5 minus 4, which is 1 amp. Five amps would be the whole incoming total, and nine adds everything together instead of balancing. Another quick one: if 7 amps enters and 2 amps and 3 amps leave, a third leaving current of 2 amps completes the balance.

segments.title: When measured currents do not balance
segments.text: Now the same node with real meter readings: 5.01 amps entering, and 4.01 amps and 1.01 amps leaving. The signed sum is 5.01 minus 4.01 minus 1.01, which is minus 0.01 amps, minus 10 milliamps. Has charge conservation failed? No. The negative sign simply says the displayed outgoing total is 10 milliamps more than the displayed incoming total. That is the size of ordinary meter uncertainty, contact effects, or readings taken at slightly different moments, or perhaps a branch you did not account for. The right response is to investigate, not to discard the law, and certainly not to round the readings selectively until they balance. Keep the measured values as they were recorded and explain the residual. The zero-sum node equation assumes charge is not accumulating at the node, which holds for the steady circuits in this course.
segments.expand: List the checks you would make, in order, when measured currents at a node leave a residual.

check.q: Measured currents at a node show 10 milliamps more leaving than entering. What did the lecture say to do?
options: Round the readings until they balance
check.again: Real meter readings of 5.01 amps in, 4.01 and 1.01 amps out, leave a signed sum of minus 0.01 amps. That small leftover does not overturn Kirchhoff's current law; it is the size of ordinary meter uncertainty, contact resistance, readings taken at different moments, or a branch that was missed. The honest response is to keep the readings exactly as recorded, state the residual, and look for its cause. Adjusting or selectively rounding numbers so the sum comes out to zero would be hiding information, not fixing anything.

segments.title: Significant figures are not decimal places
segments.text: Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a reported value. Nonzero digits count. Zeros between them count. Leading zeros never count, because they only place the decimal point. A trailing zero after the decimal point does count, because someone deliberately recorded it. So 0.004070 has four significant figures, 4, 0, 7 and the final 0, and 1.000 has four. A whole number like 1400 is ambiguous. Scientific notation removes the doubt: 1.40 times ten to the three has three figures, and 1.400 times ten to the three has four. Carry extra digits while you calculate and round once, at the end. The course reports calculated final answers to three significant figures in engineering notation, but that formatting rule does not make a measurement more accurate than it really is.
segments.expand: Explain why rounding intermediate results causes errors, using a two-step calculation as the example.

check.q: How many significant figures does 0.004070 have?
check.again: Work through the digits. The leading zeros before the 4 only place the decimal point, so they never count. The 4 counts. The zero between the 4 and the 7 counts, because zeros between nonzero digits are meaningful. The 7 counts. And the final zero after the decimal point counts, because it was deliberately recorded. That gives four: 4, 0, 7, 0. Three would be the answer if you dropped the trailing zero, and six would be the answer if you counted the leading zeros. Remember also to carry extra digits while calculating and round once at the end.

segments.title: Engineering notation and SI prefixes
segments.text: Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 up to 10 times a power of ten. Engineering notation allows a coefficient from 1 up to 1000 but restricts the power to multiples of three, so that it lines up with an SI prefix. Climbing the ladder: tera, ten to the twelve; giga, nine; mega, six; kilo, three. Going down: milli, ten to the minus three; micro, minus six; nano, minus nine; pico, minus twelve; femto, minus fifteen. The symbols are case-sensitive: capital M is mega and lowercase m is milli, a factor of a billion apart. The class example: 0.000047026 amps. One microamp is ten to the minus six amps, so this is 47.026 microamps, which rounds to 47.0 microamps at three figures. The zero after the 47 is what keeps the third figure.
segments.expand: Practise converting a few awkward values into engineering notation, including one that rounds across a prefix boundary.

check.q: Express 0.000047026 amps to three significant figures in engineering notation.
check.again: Engineering notation uses a power of ten that is a multiple of three, so the coefficient lines up with a prefix. One microamp is ten to the minus six amps. Counting the places, 0.000047026 amps is 47.026 times ten to the minus six amps, so 47.026 microamps. Rounded to three figures that is 47.0 microamps, and the zero is kept on purpose to show the third figure. Milliamps would be a thousand times too big, and nanoamps a thousand times too small. Another example: 0.0033 amps is 3.30 milliamps.

segments.title: Compare in the same unit
segments.text: Prefixes make comparison easy, but only after both values use the same unit. The class example compares 2.40 milliamps with 8.00 microamps. Comparing the bare numbers, 2.40 against 8.00, would suggest the second is larger. Convert first: 2.40 milliamps is 2400 microamps, and 2400 over 8 is 300. So the milliamp current is three hundred times larger. The same discipline applies to powers of ten. When you multiply, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents: eight times ten to the minus three times four times ten to the five is 32 times ten to the two, which is 3.2 times ten to the three in engineering form. When you add, first match the exponents. Changing a prefix changes the number you write, never the physical quantity it describes.
segments.expand: Explain the exponent rules for multiplying, dividing and raising a power of ten to a power, with a quick example of each.

check.q: The lecture compared 2.40 milliamps with 8.00 microamps. How many times larger is the milliamp current?
check.again: Never compare bare numbers with different prefixes. Put both in the same unit first. One milliamp is a thousand microamps, so 2.40 milliamps is 2400 microamps. Then 2400 divided by 8.00 is 300. So the milliamp current is three hundred times the microamp current, even though 2.40 looks smaller than 8.00 on the page. As another example, 5 milliamps against 50 microamps: 5000 over 50 is 100 times. Changing a prefix only changes how the number is written; the physical current is unchanged.

segments.title: Atoms, charge and why copper conducts
segments.text: In the simple atomic model, protons in the nucleus carry positive charge, neutrons carry none, and electrons outside the nucleus carry negative charge.
