A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Remove electrons and it becomes a positive ion; add electrons and it becomes negative. The size of one electron's charge is about 1.602 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs, so one coulomb is about 6.24 times ten to the eighteen electrons' worth of charge. Copper has 29 electrons, arranged in the shell model as 2, 8, 18 and 1. That single outer electron is loosely held, and in the metal it becomes delocalized, free to drift when a field is applied. Silver conducts a little better than copper, while gold is valued for resisting corrosion, not for conducting better.
segments.expand: Explain what a delocalized electron is and why a metal stays neutral overall while carrying current.

check.q: Copper conducts well because its single outer electron is loosely held and becomes free to drift in the metal.
check.again: Copper has 29 electrons in shells of 2, 8, 18 and 1. That lone outer electron is far from the nucleus and weakly bound, so in the solid metal it is not tied to any one atom. It becomes delocalized, shared across the whole piece of copper, and a small electric field is enough to make those free electrons drift. That drifting is the current. Silver conducts slightly better than copper for the same reason, while gold is prized for resisting corrosion, not for being a better conductor than copper.

segments.title: Electric fields and Coulomb's law
segments.text: Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges: force equals a constant times the product of the charges, divided by the distance between them squared. Force is in newtons, charge in coulombs, distance in metres, and the constant is about 8.99 times ten to the nine. Like signs repel; opposite signs attract. Double either charge and the force doubles. Double the distance and the force falls to one quarter, because distance is squared. The electric field describes the force a small positive test charge would feel, per unit of its charge: field equals force over charge, in newtons per coulomb, which is the same as volts per metre. The field points away from positive charges and toward negative ones. A positive charge is pushed along the field; a negative charge, such as an electron, is pushed the opposite way.
segments.expand: Explain why we divide by the test charge to define a field, and why the test charge must be small.

check.q: If the distance between two point charges is doubled, the Coulomb force between them becomes what?
check.again: Coulomb's law: force equals a constant times the product of the two charges, divided by the distance squared, with force in newtons, charge in coulombs and distance in metres. Because the distance is squared, doubling it multiplies the denominator by four, so the force drops to one quarter. Halving the distance would make the force four times bigger. Doubling one charge, on the other hand, simply doubles the force, since the charges appear in the product without any squaring. So charge scales the force directly, but distance works on it through the square.

segments.title: Current is charge per time
segments.text: Average current is the charge that crosses a chosen surface divided by the time it took: current in amps, charge in coulombs, time in seconds. One amp is one coulomb per second, so amps already mean per second; amps per second would be a rate of change of current, a different quantity. In a metal external circuit, conventional current leaves the battery's positive terminal and electrons drift from its negative terminal. Why does a lamp light the instant you close a switch, when electron drift is slow? Because charges are already present everywhere in the wire, and the electrical disturbance travels through the circuit far faster than any electron drifts, like a wave passing along water that only moves locally. Three instruments came up: the multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance; the oscilloscope shows voltage against time; the function generator supplies a test signal.
segments.expand: Explain drift velocity versus signal speed with a second analogy, and why a resistor does not use up current.

check.q: Since one amp is one coulomb per second, the lecture said amps per second means the same thing as amps.
check.again: Current is charge divided by time: amps equal coulombs per second. So the per second is already built into the amp. Amps per second would be a current that changes by so many amps every second, a rate of change of current, which is what the inductor rule uses, not a current itself. Keep the two apart: a steady 3 amps means 3 coulombs cross the surface every second; 3 amps per second means the current is climbing, reaching 3 amps after one second, 6 after two. The lamp lights instantly because the disturbance travels fast, not because electrons rush.

segments.title: Voltage is energy per charge
segments.text: Voltage is a difference in electric potential between two points. The voltage from A to B equals the potential at A minus the potential at B, and one volt is one joule per coulomb. So a voltage is neither a force nor an energy by itself: it is energy per unit charge, and the energy transferred depends on how much charge moves. Now a useful example. Take a uniform resistor with constant material and cross-section, so its resistance is proportional to length. Put 6 volts across a 2 kilohm uniform resistor, with the lower end as the zero volt reference. Treat it as two equal 1 kilohm halves. The current is 6 volts over 2 kilohms, 3 milliamps. The lower half drops 3 milliamps times 1 kilohm, 3 volts, so the midpoint sits at 3 volts, provided nothing is connected there.
segments.expand: Explain why the midpoint rule fails if the resistor is not uniform or if a load is connected at the midpoint.

check.q: A uniform 2 kilohm resistor has 6 volts across it, lower end at zero. With nothing else connected, what is the midpoint voltage?
check.again: A uniform resistor has resistance in proportion to length, so its midpoint splits it into two equal 1 kilohm halves. Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance, in amps, volts and ohms; 6 volts over 2 kilohms is 3 milliamps through the whole thing. The lower half then drops current times resistance, 3 milliamps times 1 kilohm, which is 3 volts. Measured from the zero volt lower end, the midpoint sits at 3 volts, half the total. Move the tap to a quarter of the way up and it reads a quarter of 6 volts, 1.5 volts.

segments.title: Meters connect differently
segments.text: Voltage is a difference between two points, so a voltmeter connects across the element, in parallel with it, reading the red probe's potential minus the black probe's. Current passes through a path, so an ammeter must be inserted in series: open the path and let the current flow through the meter. The ideal voltmeter draws no current, which means infinite resistance; the ideal ammeter has zero resistance and drops no voltage. Those are the instruments' ideal limits, and real meters come close enough for most work. One safety point follows directly: an ammeter's low resistance must never be placed straight across a supply, where it acts almost like a short circuit.
segments.expand: Explain what happens, step by step, if an ammeter is mistakenly connected across a supply.

check.q: To measure a current, the ammeter is inserted in series so the current passes through it.
check.again: Current is a flow through a path, so the meter has to be part of that path: open the circuit and let the current pass through the ammeter. The ideal ammeter has zero resistance, so it drops no voltage and does not disturb the current. A voltmeter is the opposite case: voltage is a difference between two points, so the voltmeter goes across the element, in parallel, and ideally draws no current. Because an ammeter is nearly a short circuit, placing it straight across a supply is exactly what must never be done.

segments.title: Recap of lecture two
segments.text: Five ideas from lecture two. One: Kirchhoff's current law, current in equals current out at a node, because charge is conserved; a small residual in measured data is a measurement question. Two: significant figures count meaningful digits, leading zeros never count, and you round once at the end. Three: engineering notation uses powers of ten in steps of three to match the prefixes, and capital M and lowercase m are a billion apart. Four: charge is measured in coulombs; like charges repel, and Coulomb force falls with distance squared; a field is force per charge. Five: current is charge per time, one amp being one coulomb per second, and voltage is energy per charge, one volt being one joule per coulomb, always between two points.
segments.expand: Quiz me on the units: which quantity is measured in coulombs, amps, volts, joules and newtons per coulomb?

check.q: The recap says capital M for mega and lowercase m for milli differ by a factor of a thousand.
check.again: Mega is ten to the six and milli is ten to the minus three. The gap between them is ten to the nine, a factor of a billion, not a thousand. Reading 4.7 megohms as 4.7 milliohms would be wrong by nine powers of ten. A thousand is the step between neighbouring prefixes, milli to plain units, or kilo to mega. The recap's other points stand: current in equals current out at a node, leading zeros never count as significant figures, Coulomb force falls with distance squared, one amp is one coulomb per second, and one volt is one joule per coulomb.

lectures.title: Components, measurements and circuit nodes
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Labs/ELTR 238 - Lab 01 - Components, Measurements and Circuit Nodes.md; Boylestad §1.7, §3.5, §3.6, §3.8, §5.9, §5.13; §10.4 markings only

segments.title: What this lab session covers
segments.text: This lab connects four things: a part in your hand, its schematic symbol, its measured value, and its place in a circuit. We will recognise the three basic passive elements, read prefixes and capacitor markings, understand the three terminals of a potentiometer, decode the resistor colour code and its tolerance, measure resistance properly with a bench multimeter, compare measured and nominal values, and finally read node voltages and carry a schematic onto a connection board by its nodes. Only the technical skills are covered here; your own readings are what belong in your own records.
segments.expand: Explain why translating between a physical part, its symbol and its measured value is the core skill of bench work.

check.q: This lab's opening says a potentiometer has how many terminals?
check.again: A potentiometer has three terminals: the two fixed ends of its resistive track and a movable wiper that slides along the track. That is why it can act as an adjustable divider rather than just an adjustable resistor. The lab lists this among the skills it builds: recognising the three passive elements, reading prefixes and capacitor markings, understanding the pot's three terminals, decoding the resistor colour code, measuring resistance properly, comparing measured with nominal values, and moving a schematic onto a connection board node by node.

segments.title: Three basic passive elements
segments.text: The resistor, capacitor and inductor are the three basic passive elements. A resistor relates voltage and current and dissipates energy as heat. A capacitor stores energy in an electric field associated with separated charge; an inductor, usually a coil, stores energy in a magnetic field associated with its current. Ideal capacitors and inductors give stored energy back; none of the three generates energy. A fixed resistor has no polarity, so reversing it changes nothing. For a fixed voltage across a resistor, current equals voltage over resistance, so doubling the resistance halves the current: 10 volts across 10 kilohms gives 1 milliamp, and across 20 kilohms gives 500 microamps. That is why resistors are used to limit current, though a resistor alone does not fix one current regardless of the circuit.
segments.expand: Explain what passive means, and why it does not mean a component only works in unpowered circuits.

check.q: 10 volts is placed across a 20 kilohm resistor. What current flows?
check.again: Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Ten volts over twenty thousand ohms is 0.0005 amps, which is 0.5 milliamps or 500 microamps. The quick version: volts over kilohms gives milliamps, ten over twenty is a half. Compare the 10 kilohm case, which gave 1 milliamp; doubling the resistance halved the current, which is the whole reason resistors are used to limit current. But a resistor alone does not fix one current for all circuits; the voltage across it matters just as much.

segments.title: Prefixes and capacitor markings
segments.text: Read the prefix as part of the unit. Capital M is mega; lowercase m is milli; lowercase k is kilo. A label may print u F when the micro symbol is unavailable. In engineering notation, 0.000047 farads is 47 microfarads, and 0.0033 henries is 3.3 millihenries. The class capacitor was marked 47 microfarads and 50 volts. The 47 microfarads is its nominal capacitance. The 50 volts is its voltage rating, the most it should ever have across it, not the voltage it holds and not a voltage it produces. Its actual voltage depends on the circuit. It was a polarized electrolytic, so orientation matters: in the course symbol the curved plate is negative, and on the body a stripe marks the negative lead. Reverse voltage or overvoltage can damage it.
segments.expand: Explain how to identify an electrolytic capacitor's negative lead, and why a longer lead is an unreliable clue once leads are trimmed.

check.q: A capacitor is marked 47 microfarads and 50 volts. What does the 50 volts mean?
check.again: The two numbers on the capacitor answer two different questions. Forty seven microfarads is its nominal capacitance, how much it stores per volt. Fifty volts is a limit: the most that should ever be applied across it. It is not a voltage the part creates, and it is not a voltage the part sits at; the actual voltage depends entirely on the circuit it is in, and could be 3 volts or 20 volts. Go past the rating, or connect an electrolytic backwards against its negative stripe, and the part can be damaged.

segments.title: The potentiometer's three terminals
segments.text: A potentiometer has a resistive track with two fixed ends and a movable wiper. In the lab the ends were called A and B and the wiper C. The end-to-end resistance stays about constant; for a 10 kilohm pot it is 10 kilohms. Moving the wiper splits the track into two segments that always add up to that total, so as one grows, the other shrinks. At the midpoint, each is 5 kilohms. Over the full travel, each segment can range from about zero to the full 10 kilohms, not just half of it. If the track measures 10.0 kilohms and one segment reads 3.20 kilohms, the other segment should be about 6.8 kilohms. Always identify the wiper from the part's pinout rather than guessing from which pin is in the middle.
segments.expand: Explain how to find which pin is the wiper using only an ohmmeter.

check.q: A 10 kilohm pot's track measures 10.0 kilohms and one segment reads 3.20 kilohms. The other segment should be about what?
check.again: The wiper divides the track into two pieces, and those two pieces always add up to the end-to-end resistance. So the second segment is the total minus the first: 10.0 minus 3.20 is 6.8 kilohms. Adding them would give more resistance than the whole track, which is impossible, and 3.2 would only be right at the exact midpoint where both halves are 5 kilohms. Turn the knob further and one piece shrinks toward zero while the other grows toward the full 10 kilohms. Identify the wiper from the pinout, not from its position.

segments.title: Decoding a four-band resistor
segments.text: On a four-band resistor, bands one and two are digits, band three is the multiplier, and band four is tolerance. The digit colours run black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9. The nominal value is the two-digit number times ten to the multiplier's power. Brown, black, red is 10 times a hundred, 1 kilohm. Brown, black, orange is 10 times a thousand, 10 kilohms. Brown, black, yellow is 100 kilohms. Only the third band changed, and each step is a factor of ten, which is why similar-looking parts must be kept sorted. A gold fourth band means plus or minus 5 percent, silver 10 percent, and no band 20 percent. As multipliers, gold means times one tenth and silver times one hundredth.
segments.expand: Walk through reading a five-band precision resistor and how it differs from a four-band one.

check.q: A four-band resistor reads brown, black, orange. What is its nominal value?
check.again: Bands one and two are digits, band three is the multiplier. Brown is 1 and black is 0, giving the two-digit number 10. Orange is 3, so the multiplier is ten to the three, a thousand. Ten times a thousand is ten thousand ohms, 10 kilohms. Change only the third band and the value jumps by a factor of ten each step: red would make it 1 kilohm, yellow 100 kilohms. That is why parts that look almost alike must be kept sorted. The fourth band gives tolerance: gold 5 percent, silver 10 percent, none 20 percent.

segments.title: Measuring resistance with the bench meter
segments.text: Resistance is measured on an unpowered, isolated part. The meter supplies its own small test current, so outside voltage ruins the reading. Use the two-wire resistance function, with the red lead in the volts-and-ohms input and the black lead in its low terminal, not the sense pair or the current jack. Choose autorange or a suitable manual range. Clip onto metal, not insulation, wait for a steady display, and read the prefix as carefully as the digits: ohms, kilohms and megohms are different scales. An overload message such as OVLD is a prompt, not a value. A 3.3 kilohm resistor on a 1 kilohm range overloads; so can an open connection. Holding both metal ends with your fingers puts your body in parallel and makes the reading low.
segments.expand: Explain why touching both leads lowers a resistance reading, using the idea of two paths in parallel.

check.q: Holding both metal ends of a resistor with your fingers while measuring it makes the reading come out high.
check.again: Your body is a conductor, a rather poor one, but when your fingers bridge both leads it forms a second path in parallel with the resistor. Two paths side by side always let more current through than either alone, so the meter sees less total resistance, and the reading comes out low, not high. For a large value like 1 megohm the error can be big. Hold the part by its body or use clips, keep it unpowered and isolated, clip to bare metal, read the prefix, and treat an overload message as a prompt to check range and contacts.

segments.title: Nominal, tolerance and measured value
segments.text: Keep three ideas apart. The nominal value is what the marking says. The tolerance is the permitted manufacturing spread. The measured value is what the instrument reports. The allowed spread is the tolerance times the nominal value. For 3.3 kilohms at 5 percent, the spread is 165 ohms, so the part may be anywhere from 3.135 to 3.465 kilohms. Percent deviation equals the difference between measured and nominal, divided by nominal, times 100. The class reading of 3.286 kilohms differs from 3.3 by 14 ohms, which is about 0.424 percent, low but inside a 5 percent band. A 98 kilohm reading on a 100 kilohm part is 2 percent low; it is not a 10 kilohm resistor, so check the multiplier band before assuming a wrong part.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between a component's tolerance and the meter's own measurement uncertainty.

check.q: For a 3.3 kilohm resistor at 5 percent tolerance, the allowed spread either side of the nominal value is what?
check.again: The allowed spread equals the tolerance times the nominal value. Five percent is 0.05, and 0.05 times 3300 ohms is 165 ohms. So the part may measure anywhere from 3300 minus 165, which is 3135 ohms, up to 3300 plus 165, which is 3465 ohms. Thirty three ohms would be one percent, and 330 ohms would be ten percent, the silver band. Percent deviation of a reading is the difference from nominal, over nominal, times 100; a reading of 3.286 kilohms is 14 ohms low, about 0.42 percent, well inside the band.

segments.title: Drawing symbols in the course's language
segments.text: The course resistor symbol is the zigzag with three peaks and three troughs. A voltage source is a circle with plus and minus marks. A cell is a long and a short plate, with the long plate positive; several pairs make a battery. A current source is a circle with an arrow. A circle marked V or A is a voltmeter or ammeter. A triangle at a node marks the local zero volt reference, while three decreasing bars mean an actual earth connection, which is a different thing. Label each resistor with its name and value, each voltage with a polarity, and each current with a named arrow. The plus and minus beside a resistor are your chosen voltage reference, not a property of the part; with current entering the plus terminal, the resistor's voltage equals current times resistance.
segments.expand: Explain why a circuit can work without any earth connection, and what the reference triangle is really for.

check.q: In the course's symbols, a triangle at a node marks the local zero volt reference, while three decreasing bars mean an actual earth connection.
check.again: The triangle at a node says: measure voltages from here; this is my chosen zero. It is a bookkeeping choice, not a physical connection. The three decreasing bars mean something different, an actual earth connection to the ground. A circle with an arrow is a current source, and a circle with plus and minus is a voltage source. On your own drawings label each resistor with a name and value, give each voltage a plus and minus, and give each current a named arrow. Those marks are your references; with current entering the plus end, the resistor voltage is current times resistance.

segments.title: Node voltages and differences
segments.text: A node is every point joined by ideal wire, with no component in between; bends in a wire do not create new nodes. Name nodes with lowercase letters. A single subscript, V sub A, means the voltage at node A with respect to the marked reference. A double subscript, V sub A B, means the voltage at A with respect to B, which equals V sub A minus V sub B; the first letter is the red probe and the second the black. The class example had node A at 10 volts, node B at 5 volts, and node C as the zero volt reference. So the voltage across R one, V sub A B, is 5 volts; across R two, V sub B C, is 5 volts; and V sub A C is 10 volts. Swap the probes and V sub B A reads minus 5 volts. The circuit did not change.
segments.expand: Work the same three-node circuit with the reference moved to node A, and show which numbers change.

check.q: Node A is at 10 volts and node B at 5 volts, both relative to the reference. What is V sub B A?
check.again: A double subscript reads first minus second: V sub B A is the voltage at B minus the voltage at A, with B on the red probe and A on the black. Five minus ten is minus 5 volts. The circuit is identical to the case where V sub A B is plus 5 volts; only the probe order changed, and the sign flipped to say so. Adding the two node voltages has no meaning here. Another example: if node D is at 2 volts and node E at 8 volts, V sub D E is minus 6 volts and V sub E D is plus 6.

segments.title: Building the circuit by its nodes
segments.text: The last task put two resistors in series between the supply's positive and negative connections. The skill is to preserve the nodes, whatever the physical layout looks like. Node A joins the supply's positive terminal and one lead of R one. Node B joins R one's other lead and one lead of R two. Node C joins R two's other lead and the supply's negative terminal, the local zero volt reference. First learn which holes on the board share a metal connection; physical closeness means nothing. Give each node its own group, place each resistor so its two leads land in two different groups, and check every connection against the node list. If both leads of a resistor share one group, that resistor is bypassed. Red conventionally goes to the positive supply and black to the return.
segments.expand: Explain a systematic way to check a finished board against a schematic, node by node.

check.q: If both leads of a resistor land in the same connection group on the board, that resistor is bypassed.
check.again: A connection group is one node: every hole in it is joined by metal. If a resistor's two leads sit in the same group, the wire joins its ends directly, so the current takes the wire and the resistor does nothing. It is shorted out. That is why you build node by node: node A gets the supply positive and one end of R one; node B gets the other end of R one and one end of R two; node C gets the far end of R two and the supply return. Each resistor must bridge two different groups, and physical closeness on the board means nothing.

segments.title: Recap of lab one
segments.text: Five points from lab one. One: the resistor dissipates energy, while ideal capacitors and inductors store it; a capacitor's voltage marking is a maximum rating, and an electrolytic's curved plate is negative. Two: a potentiometer's two segments always add up to the end-to-end resistance, and each can span nearly the whole range. Three: four-band resistors read digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance, and the allowed spread is tolerance times nominal. Four: measure resistance unpowered and isolated, read the prefix, and treat an overload message as a prompt to check range and contacts. Five: nodes are defined by connections, V sub A B means A minus B, and a board is built node by node, never by appearance.
segments.expand: Give me a quick colour-code drill: say three bands and I will name the value.

check.q: In the recap, what does the double subscript V sub A B mean?
options: Voltage at A minus voltage at B
Voltage at B minus voltage at A
Voltage at A plus voltage at B
check.again: The first letter is the point you are measuring, the second is the point you measure from, so V sub A B equals V sub A minus V sub B, red probe on A and black on B. Reverse the letters and the sign reverses. The recap's other points: the resistor dissipates energy while ideal capacitors and inductors store it; the capacitor voltage marking is a maximum; a pot's two segments add to the track total; four-band resistors read digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance; and resistance is measured on an unpowered, isolated part.

lectures.title: Fields, resistance and meters
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 03 - Fields, Resistance and Meters.md; Boylestad §2.2, §2.5, §2.10, §3.2 to §3.5, §3.8, §3.13, §4.2, §4.4, §5.3, §6.8, §7.8, §10.2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture three shifts from single points to relationships across a whole circuit. A field relates a charge to the force it would feel. A voltage relates two points. A current describes charge passing through a path. A resistance links the voltage across an element to the current through it. We start with field versus force, then diodes, light and solar cells. Next comes resistance as a quantity versus the resistor as a component, and how to place meters correctly. Then we think in complete circuits, look at real wire, gauge and temperature, resistor construction and power ratings, and finish with the potentiometer as an adjustable voltage divider. Three distinctions run through it all: field versus force, across versus through, and property versus component.
segments.expand: Explain the three distinctions, field versus force, across versus through, property versus component, with one example each.

check.q: The opening names three distinctions that run through this lecture. Which pair is one of them?
check.again: The three distinctions are field versus force, across versus through, and property versus component. A field describes the environment and a force is what a particular charge feels in it. Voltage is measured across two points, while current flows through a path, which is why the two meters connect differently. And resistance is a property, a quantity in ohms, while a resistor is a manufactured component chosen to have that property. Keep those three pairs in mind and the rest of the lecture, from diodes and solar cells to wire gauge and the potentiometer, hangs on them.

segments.title: Field versus force
segments.text: Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges: a constant times the product of the charges, over the distance squared. Mass does not appear; electric force depends on charge. Now divide that force by the test charge it acts on, and you get the field produced by the source charge at that spot, in newtons per coulomb. The field describes the electrical environment; the force is what a particular charge experiences in it: force equals charge times field. The class example: a plus 20 nanocoulomb source, and a point 300 millimetres away. The field there is about 2 kilonewtons per coulomb, pointing away from the positive source. Place a minus 3 nanocoulomb charge there and the force is 3 nanocoulombs times 2000, 6 micronewtons, pointing toward the source, opposite the field, because the charge is negative.
segments.expand: Explain why a field still exists at a point after the test charge is removed, and why field strength falls with distance squared.

check.q: A minus 3 nanocoulomb charge sits where a positive source makes a field of 2 kilonewtons per coulomb. What force does it feel?
check.again: Force equals charge times field: force in newtons, charge in coulombs, field in newtons per coulomb. Three nanocoulombs is 3 times ten to the minus nine coulombs, and 2 kilonewtons per coulomb is 2000. Multiply: 6 times ten to the minus six newtons, which is 6 micronewtons. The field from a positive source points away from it, but this test charge is negative, so its force points the opposite way, back toward the source. Millinewtons would be a thousand times too big. A positive 3 nanocoulomb charge there would feel the same 6 micronewtons pushed away.

segments.title: Diodes, and arrows that mean light
segments.text: Conventional current is a sign convention: it points the way positive charge would move. An ordinary diode strongly favours one direction. Its forward conventional current flows from the anode to the cathode, and the cathode is the bar on the symbol. Treating a diode as a perfect one-way switch is only an approximation; real diodes leak a little and can break down in reverse. Watch the extra arrows on diode symbols. Arrows pointing in, on a photodiode, mean incident light, not current. Arrows pointing out, on a light-emitting diode, mean emitted light. Light itself is electrically neutral; photons bring energy that can free carriers in the junction, and those carriers make a measurable current. The light must reach the device's sensitive region, and the response depends on wavelength.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between a photodiode used as a sensor and a photovoltaic cell used as a source.

check.q: On a photodiode symbol, the small arrows pointing in toward the diode mean what?
check.again: Arrows on a diode symbol come in two kinds. The diode's own triangle shows the forward conventional current direction, anode to cathode, with the cathode being the bar. The extra little arrows are about light, not current. Pointing in, on a photodiode, they mean light arriving at the junction. Pointing out, on a light-emitting diode, they mean light leaving. Light carries no charge; photons deliver energy that frees carriers in the junction, and those carriers produce the measurable current. The light has to reach the sensitive region, and the response depends on wavelength.

segments.title: The solar cell's internal resistances
segments.text: A photovoltaic cell delivers electrical energy from light. With nothing connected it can show an open-circuit voltage; connect a load and it delivers current, with the light supplying the energy. A useful model draws the light-generated current dividing three ways: some through the junction diode, some leaking through an internal shunt resistance, and the rest out to the load. The output current also passes through an internal series resistance, which drops voltage equal to current times resistance. So the design goal is a large internal shunt resistance, so little current leaks away inside, and a small internal series resistance, so little voltage is lost. Do not confuse a small internal series resistance with making the external load as small as possible; those are different resistors doing different jobs.
segments.expand: Explain what happens to a solar cell's output if its shunt resistance becomes small, say through damage.

check.q: For a good solar cell, the lecture wants the internal shunt resistance to be small so that little voltage is lost.
check.again: In the model, the light-generated current has three ways to go: through the junction diode, through the internal shunt resistance, or out to the load. Any current through the shunt is wasted inside the cell, so you want that shunt resistance large, letting almost nothing leak. The internal series resistance is the other one: the output current passes through it and drops voltage equal to current times resistance, so it should be small. Notice these are two different internal resistors with opposite goals, and neither is the external load, which is a separate choice altogether.

segments.title: The load chooses the operating point
segments.text: A solar cell is neither an ideal voltage source nor an ideal current source across all loads. Its output depends on the illumination, the temperature and the load. Delivered power equals the load voltage times the current. At open circuit, the current is zero, so delivered power is zero, even though a voltage is present. At a short circuit, the voltage is zero, so delivered power is again zero, even though current flows. Useful maximum power lies at an operating point somewhere between those two extremes. That is why a panel's rated output only makes sense with its stated test conditions, and why a voltmeter reading on an unloaded panel tells you nothing about its maximum power. The same idea, power equals voltage times current, will follow us through every circuit.
segments.expand: Explain why the maximum power point lies between open circuit and short circuit, using power equals voltage times current.

check.q: At open circuit a solar cell shows its full voltage, so that is where it delivers the most power.
check.again: Power delivered equals voltage times current, power in watts, voltage in volts, current in amps. At open circuit the voltage may be at its highest, but no current flows, and anything times zero is zero watts. At short circuit the current is large but the voltage is zero, again zero watts. The useful maximum power sits at a load somewhere between the two extremes. For example, a cell giving 0.5 volts at 2 amps into a suitable load delivers 1 watt, while the same cell unloaded delivers nothing. So a voltmeter on an unloaded panel says nothing about its power.

segments.title: Resistance, resistors, and labels
segments.text: Resistance is a physical quantity, R, in ohms. A resistor is a manufactured component made to provide a chosen resistance. Wires, contacts and semiconductors have resistance too, without being resistors. For a resistor under steady conditions, voltage equals current times resistance; current equals voltage over resistance; and resistance equals voltage over current, as long as the current is not zero. The voltage is across that resistor, and the current is through that same resistor. A diode is not a fixed resistor: its voltage-to-current ratio changes with operating conditions. Fully label every resistor: its name and value, its voltage with a plus and minus reference, and its current with a named arrow. When the current arrow enters the plus terminal, voltage equals current times resistance and positive power means the resistor absorbs energy.
segments.expand: Explain why careful subscripts on voltage and current prevent the most common Ohm's law mistake.

check.q: Which statement matches the lecture's distinction between resistance and a resistor?
options: Resistance is a quantity; a resistor is a component
Resistance is a component; a resistor is a quantity
The two words mean exactly the same thing
check.again: Resistance, R, is a physical quantity measured in ohms, and many things have it: wires, switch contacts, semiconductor junctions, your own body. A resistor is a manufactured part built to provide a chosen, steady resistance. So a diode has resistance in the sense of a voltage-to-current ratio, but it is not a resistor, because that ratio shifts with operating conditions. For a resistor, voltage equals current times resistance, using the voltage across and the current through that same part, and label it fully: name, value, plus and minus for the voltage, and a named current arrow.

segments.title: Meters: through and across
segments.text: To measure current, the current must pass through the ammeter, so power off, open the path, and insert the meter in series, with conventional current entering the red current input and leaving the common terminal for a positive reading. Choose the right jack and range. To measure voltage, connect the voltmeter across the two terminals you care about; it reads the red probe's potential minus the common's. The ideal ammeter has zero resistance; the ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance. Never put a current input across a supply. The worked example: an ideal 6 volt supply across a 1 ohm resistor. Current equals 6 volts over 1 ohm, 6 amps, and the resistor would dissipate 6 volts times 6 amps, 36 watts. Check: 6 amps times 1 ohm returns 6 volts. The answer is a current in amps, not a resistance in ohms.
segments.expand: Explain what a burden voltage is and why a real ammeter always has some.

check.q: An ideal 6 volt supply is placed across a 1 ohm resistor. What current flows, and what power does the resistor dissipate?
check.again: Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance, in amps, volts and ohms. Six volts over one ohm is 6 amps; the answer is a current, not the number 6 in ohms. Then power equals voltage times current, watts from volts times amps: 6 times 6 is 36 watts, a lot of heat for a small part. Check by going back: 6 amps times 1 ohm gives 6 volts. To measure that current you would break the loop and put the ammeter in series, current entering the red input; to measure the voltage you put the voltmeter across the resistor.

segments.title: Thinking in complete circuits
segments.text: In a single loop, moving an ideal ammeter from before a resistor to after it changes nothing: it still reads the same current. The resistor does not let a large current in and a smaller one out; it converts energy to heat, not charge. If a current mismatch ever shows up in a steady circuit, look for another path, charge storage or a measurement error. An ideal wire has zero resistance, so it drops no voltage even when carrying current, and its two ends are the same node. Break that wire and the loop current becomes zero, while a voltage may appear across the gap. Now put two equal 1 kilohm resistors in series across 6 volts. The total is 2 kilohms, the current 3 milliamps, each resistor drops 3 volts, and taking the bottom as reference, the nodes sit at 6, 3 and 0 volts.
segments.expand: Explain why a voltage reading changes when you move the probes, while the current in a single loop does not.

check.q: Two equal 1 kilohm resistors are in series across 6 volts. Taking the bottom as reference, the middle node sits at what voltage?
check.again: Series resistances add, so the loop sees 2 kilohms. Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance; 6 volts over 2 kilohms is 3 milliamps, the same through both resistors, because a resistor converts energy, not current. Each resistor then drops current times resistance, 3 milliamps times 1 kilohm, 3 volts. Starting from 6 volts at the top, one drop of 3 volts lands the middle node at 3 volts, and the second drop reaches 0 at the bottom. With 3 kilohms and 1 kilohm instead, the middle node would sit at 1.5 volts.

segments.title: Real wire: gauge and geometry
segments.text: American Wire Gauge numbers run backwards to thickness: a smaller gauge number is a thicker wire, so 12 gauge is thicker than 14, which is thicker than 22. For a uniform conductor, resistance equals resistivity times length divided by cross-sectional area: ohms from ohm-metres times metres over square metres. So doubling the length doubles the resistance; doubling the area halves it; and because area goes with the square of diameter, doubling the diameter cuts resistance to a quarter. Real wire always has some resistance. Calling it negligible means its effect is small for the job at hand, not that it vanishes; at high current or long length, the wire's own drop, current times wire resistance, can matter. Gauge alone does not set a safe current; that depends on insulation, installation and temperature too.
segments.expand: Work a quick scaling example: the same wire made three times as long and twice the diameter.

check.q: If a wire's diameter is doubled, keeping the same length and material, its resistance becomes what?
check.again: Resistance equals resistivity times length divided by cross-sectional area: ohms from ohm-metres times metres over square metres. Area depends on the square of the diameter, so doubling the diameter makes the area four times larger, and the resistance drops to a quarter. Halving would be the answer if area went up only in proportion to diameter, which it does not. Doubling the length, by contrast, doubles the resistance. Remember also that gauge numbers run backwards: 12 gauge is thicker than 22 gauge, so it has lower resistance per metre.

segments.title: Temperature changes resistance
segments.text: Copper and most ordinary metals have a positive temperature coefficient: their resistance rises as they warm. Some semiconductor devices have a negative coefficient over a useful range, and special alloys are made to change very little. Over a limited range, a straight-line approximation works: the new resistance equals the reference resistance times one plus the coefficient times the temperature change. Use the change in temperature, not the final temperature. A specification such as 100 parts per million per degree means 100 millionths per degree, not 100 percent. This matters in operation, because current heats a component, the heat changes its resistance, and that changes the current. Do not stretch a short-range straight-line model over huge temperature ranges.
segments.expand: Work a small example: a 10 kilohm resistor at 100 parts per million per degree, warmed by 40 degrees.

check.q: In the straight-line model, the new resistance equals the reference resistance times one plus the coefficient times the final temperature.
check.again: The formula uses the change in temperature, not the final temperature: new resistance equals reference resistance times one plus the coefficient times the temperature change, resistance in ohms, coefficient in per degree, temperature change in degrees. Suppose a copper winding of 100 ohms at 20 degrees with a coefficient of 0.004 per degree warms to 70 degrees. The change is 50 degrees, so the resistance is 100 times one plus 0.2, which is 120 ohms. Using 70 instead of 50 would wrongly give 128 ohms. Copper has a positive coefficient; some semiconductors are negative, and special alloys barely change.

segments.title: Construction and power ratings
segments.text: Resistors come as composition, film, wirewound, surface-mount parts and networks, each suited to different needs. Size hints at scale, but the ratings come from the marking or data sheet; a resistor's value in ohms says nothing about the heat it can handle. The worked example: a resistor with 5 volts across it carrying 2 amps. Power equals voltage times current, 5 times 2, 10 watts, which is 10 joules of heat every second. Its resistance is 5 over 2, 2.5 ohms, and current squared times resistance, 4 times 2.5, confirms 10 watts. A quarter-watt resistor of exactly the right 2.5 ohms would still be unsuitable, because it cannot shed 10 watts. Value, power rating and voltage rating are separate specifications, and at high temperatures the allowed power may need derating.
segments.expand: Explain what derating means and why a resistor's allowed power falls as the surrounding temperature rises.

check.q: A resistor has 5 volts across it and carries 2 amps. How much power does it dissipate?
check.again: Power equals voltage times current: power in watts, voltage in volts, current in amps. Five times two is 10 watts, which means 10 joules of heat every second. You can confirm it another way: resistance equals voltage over current, 5 over 2, 2.5 ohms, and power equals current squared times resistance, 4 times 2.5, again 10 watts. The number 2.5 is the resistance, not the power. A quarter-watt part of exactly 2.5 ohms would overheat badly, because value, power rating and voltage rating are separate specifications, read from the marking or data sheet.

segments.title: The potentiometer as a divider
segments.text: A potentiometer has track ends and a wiper; the two segments always add to the end-to-end resistance. Put 10 volts across the ends, with the bottom end at zero volts. For an unloaded wiper, the output equals the supply times the lower segment's resistance over the whole track. At 50 percent of the track, the output is 5 volts; at 75 percent, 7.5 volts; at 1 percent, 100 millivolts. With a 10 kilohm track, the track current is 10 volts over 10 kilohms, 1 milliamp, and 1 milliamp through a 5 kilohm lower half confirms 5 volts. That simple fraction assumes nothing draws current from the wiper. Connect a load from wiper to bottom and it sits in parallel with the lower segment, making that part smaller, so the output falls below the unloaded value.
segments.expand: Show how much a 10 kilohm load pulls down the midpoint output of a 10 kilohm pot on 10 volts.

check.q: Ten volts sits across a 10 kilohm potentiometer with its bottom end at zero. The unloaded wiper at 75 percent of the track gives what?
check.again: With nothing drawing current from the wiper, the output equals the supply voltage times the lower segment's resistance over the whole track. Seventy five percent of the way up means the lower segment is 7.5 kilohms out of 10, and 10 volts times 7.5 over 10 is 7.5 volts. Check it with current: 10 volts over 10 kilohms is 1 milliamp through the track, and 1 milliamp times 7.5 kilohms is 7.5 volts. At 25 percent it would be 2.5 volts. Connect a load from wiper to bottom and the output falls, because the load sits in parallel with the lower segment.

segments.title: Recap of lecture three
segments.text: Five ideas from lecture three. One: the field describes the environment, and force equals charge times field, with negative charges pushed opposite the field. Two: diode forward current runs from anode to cathode, and a solar cell delivers useful power only between open circuit and short circuit, ideally with a large shunt and small series internal resistance. Three: resistance is a quantity and a resistor is a component; use the voltage across and the current through the same one, and meter current through, voltage across. Four: resistance grows with length, shrinks with area, and for copper rises with temperature; smaller gauge numbers are thicker wires. Five: a resistor's power rating is separate from its value, and a potentiometer divides voltage by its segment fraction until a load pulls the output down.
segments.expand: Give me one quick question on each recap point.

check.q: The recap says a smaller wire gauge number means a thinner wire.
check.again: American Wire Gauge runs the opposite way from what the numbers suggest: a smaller gauge number is a thicker wire. Twelve gauge is thicker than 14, and both are far thicker than 22. Thicker means more cross-sectional area, and resistance equals resistivity times length over area, so the lower gauge number has less resistance per metre. The recap's other points: force equals charge times field; diode forward current runs anode to cathode; use the voltage across and current through the same resistor; copper resistance rises with temperature; and power rating is separate from value.

lectures.title: Series circuits and meter loading
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 04 - Series Circuits and Meter Loading.md; Boylestad §4.4, §5.2, §5.3, §5.6, §5.7, §5.9, §5.12, §6.3, §6.5, §6.9

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture four is about the series circuit and the instruments we use on it. The central sentence is this: one series path has one current, but its elements can have different voltage drops. We will define series by connections, see why a resistor does not use up current, add series resistances and voltage drops, and check with Kirchhoff's voltage law. Then we look at voltage along a uniform resistor, at how real ammeters and voltmeters change the circuit they measure, at a first look at current splitting between parallel branches, and finally at choosing references so that signs mean something. By the end, a negative answer should feel like information, not a mistake.
segments.expand: Explain in your own words why one path means one current, but not one voltage.

check.q: The opening gives the lecture's central sentence about a series path. What is it?
options: One current, but different voltage drops
Same current and same drop everywhere
check.again: In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same charge per second passes through every element, and the current is the same throughout. But each element has its own voltage drop, set by its own resistance: a bigger resistor drops more of the supply. Picture 1, 2 and 3 ohm resistors carrying one amp: they drop 1, 2 and 3 volts. The lecture builds on that sentence to add series resistances, check with Kirchhoff's voltage law, and then look at how real meters disturb the circuit and why a negative answer is information.

segments.title: Series is an electrical connection
segments.text: Components are in series when they lie on one path and the junctions between them have no other current-carrying branch. Then the same charge per second passes through each one, so the current through every series element is the same. That is about connectivity, not the drawing. Resistors drawn side by side can be in series if they are wired end to end; parts drawn in a neat column need not be in series if another branch joins at their junction. Read the connections actively: start at one terminal, follow the wire through each component, and finish at the other. A bend adds nothing. The series rule even applies to unlike parts, such as a resistor and a capacitor on one path: their voltage laws differ, but their current is common.
segments.expand: Give an example of a circuit that looks like a series chain in the drawing but is not, because of a hidden junction.

check.q: Components drawn in a neat column are always in series with one another.
check.again: Series is about connectivity, not the picture. Two parts are in series when they sit on one path and the junction between them has no other current-carrying branch. Then the same current must flow through both. Parts drawn side by side can still be in series if they are wired end to end, and parts drawn in a tidy column are not in series if a third wire joins their junction. Test it by tracing: start at one terminal, follow the wire through each component, and see if you reach the other terminal without a fork. Even a resistor and a capacitor share one current when in series.

segments.title: Same current, but not unchanging current
segments.text: An ammeter reads the current through its own position. If it reads 2 amps somewhere in an unbranched series loop, the series rule lets you infer 2 amps everywhere in that loop. If later readings disagree, check the wiring, the supply, the connections and the meter before doubting charge conservation. Be careful with one idea, though. The same current everywhere in one circuit does not mean the current can never change. Compare the circuit before and after you change a resistor, and the current can be quite different. With a fixed supply, increasing the total resistance decreases the current through every series part at once; decreasing it increases the current everywhere. Inside the wire, a changed current mostly means the electrons drift at a changed rate.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between comparing points in one unchanged circuit and comparing a circuit before and after a change.

check.q: With a fixed supply, increasing the total resistance of a series loop decreases the current through every series part at once.
check.again: Ohm's law for the whole loop: current equals supply voltage over total resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Raise the total and the one shared current falls, and since it is the same current everywhere, every part feels the drop together. Twelve volts across 4 kilohms gives 3 milliamps; add 2 kilohms more and 12 over 6 gives 2 milliamps everywhere. The same current everywhere is a statement about one circuit at one time. It never means the current can never change; compare before and after, and it can be quite different.

segments.title: Adding series resistance and drops
segments.text: For resistors in series, the total resistance is the sum: 10, 20 and 30 ohms make 60 ohms. Replacing the chain with that total keeps the same behaviour at the outer terminals. The worked model: a 6 volt supply with 1, 2 and 3 ohm resistors in series. The total is 6 ohms, so the current is 6 volts over 6 ohms, 1 amp, through every resistor. Now Ohm's law on each resistor separately: voltage equals current times that resistor. The drops are 1, 2 and 3 volts. Kirchhoff's voltage law checks the loop: plus 6 minus 1 minus 2 minus 3 is zero. Different resistances, different drops, one current. A common slip is using the supply voltage for one resistor's drop just because it is the most visible number; use the voltage across that resistor.
segments.expand: Work a series circuit where the answer comes out in milliamps, such as 12 volts across 1, 2 and 3 kilohms.

check.q: A 6 volt supply drives 1, 2 and 3 ohm resistors in series. What voltage is across the 2 ohm resistor?
check.again: First the total: series resistances add, 1 plus 2 plus 3 is 6 ohms. Then Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance, 6 volts over 6 ohms, 1 amp through every resistor. Now apply Ohm's law to the 2 ohm resistor alone: voltage equals current times resistance, 1 amp times 2 ohms, 2 volts. The 1 ohm drops 1 volt and the 3 ohm drops 3 volts. Kirchhoff's voltage law checks it: 6 minus 1 minus 2 minus 3 is zero. Using the full 6 volts for one resistor is the common slip; each resistor gets only its own share.

segments.title: Node voltages and the voltage gradient
segments.text: In the 6 volt chain, with the return node as zero volts, the successive nodes sit at 6, 5, 3 and 0 volts. A node voltage compares one node with the reference; a component voltage compares its own two terminals. Along a uniform resistor the voltage falls steadily. Picture a uniform 100 ohm resistor as ten equal 10 ohm sections carrying 2 amps. Each section drops 2 amps times 10 ohms, 20 volts; two sections drop 40 volts; all ten drop 200 volts. A voltmeter across one section reads one section's drop, and across two reads their sum. The general idea is the voltage divider: in series, drops are proportional to resistance. With 45 volts across 2, 5 and 8 kilohms, the 8 kilohm resistor takes 8 fifteenths of 45, which is 24 volts.
segments.expand: Explain the voltage divider rule as a shortcut, and show it gives the same answer as finding the current first.

check.q: 45 volts is across 2, 5 and 8 kilohm resistors in series. What voltage does the 8 kilohm resistor take?
check.again: In series, the drops are proportional to the resistances, because the same current flows through each. That is the voltage divider: a resistor's drop equals the total voltage times its resistance over the sum of the resistances. The sum is 2 plus 5 plus 8, 15 kilohms, so the 8 kilohm resistor takes 8 fifteenths of 45 volts, which is 24 volts. The 5 kilohm takes 15 volts and the 2 kilohm takes 6, and 24 plus 15 plus 6 returns 45. Checking with current: 45 over 15 kilohms is 3 milliamps, times 8 kilohms is 24 volts.

segments.title: Real meters join the circuit
segments.text: The ideal ammeter has zero resistance and the ideal voltmeter infinite resistance. Real ones do not. Insert a real ammeter with 1 ohm of internal resistance into the 6 volt, 6 ohm circuit. The loop now totals 7 ohms, so the current is 6 over 7, about 857 milliamps, instead of 1 amp. The meter correctly reports the current in the modified circuit, but the circuit has changed by about 14 percent. The meter's own drop, current times its resistance, about 857 millivolts, is called its burden voltage. The 1 ohm figure is illustrative; real ammeter resistance depends on the meter and range, and on the current jack's limits. The lesson is that inserting an instrument can change what you are trying to measure.
segments.expand: Explain how to estimate whether an ammeter's resistance matters for a particular circuit.

check.q: A real ammeter with 1 ohm of resistance is inserted into the 6 volt, 6 ohm loop. What does it read?
check.again: A real ammeter is not zero ohms; its resistance joins the series chain. The loop now totals 6 plus 1, 7 ohms, and Ohm's law gives current equals 6 volts over 7 ohms, about 0.857 amps or 857 milliamps. The meter reports that current faithfully, but it is the current of the changed circuit, about 14 percent below the 1 amp that flowed before. The meter's own drop, current times its resistance, about 857 millivolts, is its burden voltage. The 1 ohm figure is just an illustration; real values depend on the meter and its range.

segments.title: Voltmeter loading
segments.text: A real voltmeter adds its input resistance as a new branch in parallel with whatever it measures. Place a 20 megohm voltmeter across the 2 ohm resistor reading about 2 volts. It draws about 2 volts over 20 megohms, 100 nanoamps, which is tiny next to the circuit's 1 amp, so the reading still rounds to 2.00 volts. Small does not mean infinite, though. In a circuit built from resistors in the megohm range, the same meter becomes a significant parallel path. The parallel combination of the resistor and the meter is smaller than the resistor alone, so the measured node drops. The meter then displays the voltage of the loaded circuit, which can be well below the unloaded value.
segments.expand: Work a loading example with two equal high-value resistors and a meter of the same resistance.

check.q: A 20 megohm voltmeter placed across a 2 ohm resistor carrying 1 amp causes a large loading error.
check.again: A voltmeter adds its input resistance as a parallel branch. Across roughly 2 volts, a 20 megohm meter draws 2 over 20 million, about 100 nanoamps. Next to the circuit's 1 amp that is negligible, so the reading still shows 2.00 volts. The same meter in a circuit made of megohm resistors is a different story: then its branch is comparable to the resistors, the parallel combination is noticeably smaller than the resistor alone, and the node voltage sags. The meter displays the loaded circuit's voltage, which can be well below the unloaded value.

segments.title: Current takes every branch
segments.text: Path of least resistance is an unreliable slogan. Two finite resistances in parallel have the same voltage across them, so both conduct; the smaller resistance simply takes more. With a 1 ohm and a 2 ohm branch, each branch current is the shared voltage over its resistance, so the 1 ohm branch carries twice the current of the 2 ohm branch. If the total is 5 amps, the split is about 3.33 and 1.67 amps, which add back to exactly 5, and both branches see about 3.33 volts. This preview explains voltmeter loading too: once a meter is connected across a resistor, the current arriving equals the resistor's current plus the meter's current, and you cannot keep applying the single-path rule through both branches separately.
segments.expand: Work a split of 6 amps between 1 ohm and 2 ohms, and check both branch voltages agree.

check.q: A 1 ohm branch and a 2 ohm branch share 5 amps in parallel. Roughly how does the current divide?
check.again: Both branches have the same voltage across them, so each carries current equal to that voltage over its own resistance. The 1 ohm branch therefore takes twice what the 2 ohm branch takes. Two parts plus one part make three parts of 5 amps: two thirds is about 3.33 amps in the 1 ohm branch and one third is about 1.67 amps in the 2 ohm branch, and the shared voltage is about 3.33 volts. Path of least resistance is a poor slogan: the smaller resistance takes more, but every finite branch conducts some. An equal split only happens with equal resistances.

segments.title: Choose references before reading signs
segments.text: A voltage is an ordered comparison: V sub A B equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B, and V sub B A is its negative. An ideal 1.5 volt cell reads plus 1.5 with red on its positive terminal and minus 1.5 with the probes swapped. The reference changed, not the cell. For a resistor, place the plus sign where your chosen current arrow enters; then voltage equals current times resistance. Suppose you choose current from A to B through 2 kilohms, with A at 1 volt and B at 5 volts. Current equals A minus B over R: minus 4 volts over 2 kilohms, minus 2 milliamps. That negative sign is information: the real current is 2 milliamps from B to A. It is not negative resistance and not a failed calculation.
segments.expand: Explain what changes if you reverse only the current arrow but keep the voltage polarity marks.

check.q: Current is defined from A to B through 2 kilohms, with A at 1 volt and B at 5 volts. What does the calculation give?
check.again: With the arrow chosen from A to B, the resistor's voltage is V sub A B, the voltage at A minus the voltage at B: 1 minus 5 is minus 4 volts. Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance, minus 4 volts over 2 kilohms, minus 2 milliamps. The minus sign is information, not an error: the real current is 2 milliamps flowing from B to A, the higher potential to the lower. The resistance stays a positive 2 kilohms. It is just like reading an ideal 1.5 volt cell as minus 1.5 with the probes swapped; the reference changed, not the circuit.

segments.title: Entering positive is a bookkeeping choice
segments.text: For node bookkeeping you may count currents entering a node as positive and leaving as negative; then Kirchhoff's current law says the algebraic sum is zero. You may choose the opposite, as long as you stay consistent. At a two-terminal element in steady operation, currents defined into each terminal sum to zero, which does not mean the series current changes size across the element. A supplying battery drives current out of its positive terminal, so a current defined into that terminal comes out negative. With several supplies in one circuit, choose provisional arrows and solve. The supplies and connections decide the real directions, and any negative answer simply tells you which arrow points the other way.
segments.expand: Work a small example with a provisional arrow that turns out backwards, and show the sign telling you so.

check.q: If you count currents entering a node as positive, a current defined into a supplying battery's positive terminal comes out negative.
check.again: A supplying battery pushes conventional current out of its positive terminal. If your bookkeeping defines a current as going into that terminal, the actual flow is opposite to your arrow, so the number you get is negative. That is not a fault; it says the arrow points the wrong way. The sign convention itself is a free choice, entering positive or leaving positive, as long as you use one rule throughout an equation. With several supplies, draw provisional arrows, solve, and let any negative results tell you which arrows to mentally reverse.

segments.title: Recap of lecture four
segments.text: Five ideas from lecture four. One: series is decided by connections: one path, no side branches, so one current through every element. Two: series resistances add, the current is supply voltage over the total, each resistor drops current times its own resistance, and Kirchhoff's voltage law says the drops add up to the supply; drops are proportional to resistance. Three: raising any series resistance lowers the one current everywhere. Four: real ammeters add series resistance and real voltmeters add a parallel branch, so meters can load the circuit, badly so in high-resistance circuits. Five: current takes every parallel branch, and a negative result means the real direction is opposite your reference arrow.
segments.expand: Quiz me with a three-resistor series circuit: total, current, and one drop.

check.q: In the recap, a negative current result means what?
options: The real direction is opposite your arrow
check.again: A negative answer is information about direction. You chose a reference arrow before solving; the minus sign says the real current flows the other way, and that is all. Resistance stays positive, and the arithmetic was fine. The recap's other points: series is decided by connections, giving one current through every element; series resistances add, each resistor drops current times its own resistance, and the drops are proportional to resistance; raising any series resistance lowers the shared current; and real meters load the circuit, ammeters by adding series resistance, voltmeters by adding a parallel branch.

lectures.title: Breadboard nodes and measurement reporting
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Labs/ELTR 238 - Lab 02 - Breadboard Nodes and Measurement Reporting.md; Boylestad §1.5, §3.6, §3.8, §4.2, §5.13, §6.12

segments.title: What this lab session covers
segments.text: This lab session has three threads. Know what is connected, know what you measured, and show what your answer means. First we map a breadboard's connections, because a correct circuit depends on electrical nodes, not on how neat the layout looks. Then we measure resistors and compare them with their colour codes and tolerance. Finally we report numbers well: counting significant figures, rounding to three figures, the arithmetic rules for sums and products, what a half digit on a meter display means, and the four-part way to set out any calculation. Only the technical skills are covered here.
segments.expand: Explain why the same skill, tracing what is truly connected, applies both to breadboards and to schematics.

check.q: This lab's opening says a correct circuit depends on what?
check.again: The three threads of the lab are: know what is connected, know what you measured, and show what your answer means. The first thread is about nodes. A circuit is correct when every component bridges the right pair of electrical nodes, whatever the layout looks like; a tidy board can still be wrong and a messy one can be right. The other threads cover measuring resistors against their colour codes and tolerance, and reporting numbers properly: significant figures, rounding to three figures, the rules for sums and products, the meter's half digit, and the four-part layout of a calculation.

segments.title: Map the board before placing parts
segments.text: A node is a set of points joined by conductor, all at one potential in the ideal-wire model. On a breadboard, several separate-looking holes belong to one node when a metal strip joins them underneath. A break in the strip makes separate groups unless you add a wire across it. Do not turn one demonstration into a rule like every row or every column is connected on every board. Boards differ, and some have split rails. Trace the actual board's groups, including cuts. Two holes right next to each other, but separated by a cut, are two different nodes. Proximity never proves continuity.
segments.expand: Explain how to find out, with a meter and no power, which holes on an unfamiliar board are connected.

check.q: Two breadboard holes right next to each other, but separated by a cut in the strip, are two different nodes.
check.again: A node is everything joined by conductor, all at one potential in the ideal-wire model. On a breadboard the joining is done by metal strips under the holes, and a cut in a strip ends the node right there. Holes on either side of the cut may be millimetres apart yet electrically unrelated until you bridge them with a wire. Proximity never proves continuity. Do not turn one board into a general rule either; boards differ, some have split power rails, so trace each board's actual groups, including any cuts, before placing parts.

segments.title: From drawing to board
segments.text: A reliable translation has four steps. Name the schematic's nodes. Find a matching board group for each node. Place each component between its two required nodes, checking both leads, not just where the body sits. Then check every intended connection and every intended separation. A neat-looking layout can still be wrong. If both leads of a resistor go into the same connected group, the board bypasses it. Both ends sit at the same voltage, so the resistor has zero volts across it and, by Ohm's law, carries no current. That is completely different from placing it across two distinct nodes. An unintended wire can also merge two nodes that should stay separate.
segments.expand: Describe the symptoms you would measure on a circuit where one resistor has been accidentally bypassed.

check.q: Both leads of a resistor are pushed into the same connected group on the board. What happens to that resistor?
options: It is bypassed and carries no current
It sees the full supply voltage
check.again: One connected group is one node, so both ends of the resistor sit at the same potential. The voltage across it is zero, and by Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, zero volts over any resistance is zero current. The board's metal strip has shorted it out; the circuit behaves as if the resistor were not there. That is why the four-step translation checks both leads of every part, not just where the body sits, and then verifies every intended connection and every intended separation. A stray wire merging two nodes causes the same kind of error.

segments.title: Checking connections safely
segments.text: With power disconnected and any stored energy safely discharged, a continuity or resistance measurement can confirm an uncertain connection. A continuity beeper only tells you the resistance is below that meter's threshold; a beep is not a precise resistance value. Resistance measurements are always made on unpowered components, isolated from other paths when necessary, because an in-circuit reading can include those other paths. Use the meter's resistance function with the volts-and-ohms input, never the current jack. Split rails are real features of some boards, so verify them rather than trusting appearance.
segments.expand: Explain why an in-circuit resistance reading can come out lower than the resistor's true value.

check.q: A continuity beep from the meter tells you the exact resistance of the connection.
check.again: The beeper only says the resistance is below that meter's threshold, which might be a few ohms or tens of ohms depending on the instrument. It confirms a path exists; it does not give a value. If you need the number, use the resistance function, with power disconnected, stored energy discharged, and the part isolated when necessary, since an in-circuit reading can include other paths in parallel. Use the volts-and-ohms input, never the current jack. And verify things like split rails by measuring them, rather than trusting how the board looks.

segments.title: Comparing a resistor with its bands
segments.text: The bench task was to choose two resistors, measure each, and compare with the colour code. Agreement means within tolerance, not identical digits. Take brown, black, red, gold. Brown 1, black 0, red means times a hundred: 1000 ohms, 1.00 kilohm, with gold tolerance of plus or minus 5 percent. The allowed interval runs from 1.00 times 0.95, which is 0.950 kilohms, to 1.00 times 1.05, which is 1.05 kilohms. A reading of 0.987 kilohms gives a signed deviation of 0.987 minus 1.00, over 1.00, times 100, which is minus 1.30 percent: low, but inside the band. A reading near a boundary needs the meter's own accuracy before any firm verdict. Never adjust a reading to match what you expected.
segments.expand: Work the tolerance interval for a 4.7 kilohm, 10 percent resistor, and decide whether 5.1 kilohms passes.

check.q: A brown, black, red, gold resistor measures 0.987 kilohms. What is its signed percent deviation from nominal?
check.again: Brown, black, red is 10 times a hundred, 1000 ohms or 1.00 kilohm, and gold means plus or minus 5 percent, an allowed band from 0.950 to 1.05 kilohms. Percent deviation equals measured minus nominal, over nominal, times 100. That is 0.987 minus 1.00, which is minus 0.013, over 1.00, times 100: minus 1.30 percent. The sign is negative because the reading is low. It is comfortably inside the 5 percent band, so the resistor agrees with its bands. Agreement means within tolerance, never identical digits, and a reading is recorded as it is, not adjusted.

segments.title: Counting significant figures again
segments.text: Significant figures communicate the meaningful digits of a value; they are not decimal places and not the number of characters on a display. Nonzero digits count: 317 has three. Zeros between significant digits count: 301 has three. Leading zeros never count: 0.00407 has three. A final zero after a significant digit in a decimal records precision: 2.040 has four. A whole number like 8000 is ambiguous as written. Note the trap in 0.004070: the first two zeros after the decimal point are still leading zeros, so the significant digits are 4, 0, 7 and 0, four in all. When precision matters for a whole number, use scientific notation: 8 times ten to the three has one figure, while 8.00 times ten to the three has three.
segments.expand: Give me five numbers to classify, including one tricky leading-zero case, and explain each.

check.q: How many significant figures does 2.040 have?
check.again: Count from the first nonzero digit. The 2 counts, the zero between 2 and 4 counts because it sits between significant digits, the 4 counts, and the final zero after the decimal point counts because it records precision; someone deliberately recorded it. That makes four. Three would be right for 2.04, and two for 2.0. Leading zeros are the ones that never count: 0.00407 has three. And a whole number like 8000 is ambiguous as written, so use scientific notation when it matters: 8.00 times ten to the three has three figures.

segments.title: Reporting to three significant figures
segments.text: The lab asks for requested measurements reported to three significant figures, while you keep the original displayed readings in your raw record so the step is traceable. Some examples. 2.046 kilohms: keep 2, 0 and 4; the next digit, 6, rounds the 4 up, giving 2.05 kilohms. 0.004070 volts: the leading zeros do not count, so three figures is 0.00407 volts, or 4.07 millivolts. 12.96 volts: rounding carries into the next place, giving 13.0 volts, and that final zero is what shows three figures. Keep working digits until the end; rounding an intermediate result and reusing it can shift the final answer. And never add digits the instrument did not provide.
segments.expand: Explain why 13.0 and 13 are different reports of the same reading.

check.q: Report 12.96 volts to three significant figures.
check.again: Three figures from 12.96 means keeping 1, 2 and 9, then looking at the 6. Six rounds the 9 up, which carries into the 2, giving 13.0. The final zero is not decoration: it is the third significant figure, and it tells the reader the value is known to the tenths place. Plain 13 would claim only two figures, and 12.9 ignores the rounding carry. Keep the original displayed reading in your raw record so the step is traceable, carry working digits to the end, and never add digits the instrument never gave you.

segments.title: Sums, products and precision
segments.text: The rule depends on the operation. For addition and subtraction, put the quantities in the same unit, then the least precise decimal place limits the answer. 12.34 volts plus 1.2 volts is 13.54, but the 1.2 volt reading is only known to tenths, so report 13.5 volts. For multiplication and division, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures among the measured inputs. The current through a 2.40 kilohm resistor with 7.20 volts across it is 7.20 over 2.40, 3.00 milliamps: both inputs have three figures, and volts over kilohms gives milliamps. Exact counts and defined conversions do not limit the figures the way measured values do.
segments.expand: Work a subtraction example where the answer keeps fewer figures than either input.

check.q: 12.34 volts plus 1.2 volts should be reported as what?
check.again: For addition and subtraction the rule is about decimal places, not significant figures. Put both quantities in the same unit, then the least precise decimal place limits the result. The 1.2 volt reading is known only to tenths, so although the arithmetic gives 13.54, the sum can only honestly be stated to tenths: 13.5 volts. Multiplication and division follow a different rule, the fewest significant figures among the measured inputs: 7.20 volts over 2.40 kilohms gives 3.00 milliamps, three figures in, three figures out. Exact counts and defined conversions never limit the figures.

segments.title: The half digit on the meter
segments.text: In the five and a half digit description used in class, five positions can each show 0 through 9, while the leading position is restricted to 0 or 1. So there are six visible positions, and the half describes the restricted leading one. It is a display convention. It is not five and a half significant figures, and it is not an accuracy guarantee. Keep three ideas apart. Resolution is the smallest change the selected range can display. Accuracy is how close the reading is to the true value, within the instrument's specification. Reported precision is the digits you choose to keep. More display digits can reveal small changes without making the reading any closer to the truth.
segments.expand: Explain how changing a meter's range changes its resolution.

check.q: In a five and a half digit meter, what does the half refer to?
options: A leading position limited to 0 or 1
Half a significant figure of accuracy
A rounding of the last digit
check.again: The half is a display convention.
