Five positions can show any digit from 0 to 9, and one extra leading position can show only 0 or 1, so there are six visible positions and the restricted one is called the half. It is not five and a half significant figures and it promises nothing about accuracy. Keep three ideas separate: resolution is the smallest change the range can display; accuracy is how close the reading is to the truth, within the specification; reported precision is the digits you decide to keep. More digits can reveal small changes without bringing the reading closer to the truth.

segments.title: Four parts of every calculation
segments.text: Setting out a calculation in four parts makes it checkable. First, name the quantity you are finding. Second, write the formula with named quantities. Third, substitute the values with their units. Fourth, state the result with its unit and suitable rounding. For example: target, the current through R one. Formula, by Ohm's law, the current through R one equals the voltage across R one over R one. Substitution, 6.00 volts over 2.00 kilohms. Result, 3.00 milliamps. Then check: a few volts over a few kilohms should give milliamps. The subscripts keep every quantity attached to the same component, and they stop you from dropping the supply voltage into a formula that needs one resistor's voltage.
segments.expand: Walk through the four parts for finding a resistor's power, and point out the check at the end.

check.q: What is the second of the four parts of a well set out calculation?
check.again: The four parts run: name the quantity you are finding; write the formula with named quantities; substitute the values with their units; state the result with its unit and sensible rounding. Take the voltage across R two. Formula: by Ohm's law, the voltage across R two equals the current through R two times R two. Substitution: 2.00 milliamps times 4.70 kilohms. Result: 9.40 volts. Then sanity check, milliamps times kilohms gives volts. The subscripts keep each quantity tied to its own component, which stops you dropping the supply voltage into a formula that needs one resistor's voltage.

segments.title: Recap of lab two
segments.text: Five points from lab two. One: a node is whatever is joined by conductor; closeness means nothing, and cuts create separate groups. Two: a component with both leads in one connected group is bypassed, with zero volts across it. Three: compare measured resistance with nominal using the tolerance interval, and keep real readings as they are. Four: count significant figures from the first nonzero digit, round once to three figures, and keep a final zero that shows precision; sums follow decimal places, products follow significant figures. Five: a half digit is a display feature, not accuracy, and every calculation reads as quantity, formula, substitution, result.
segments.expand: Give me three numbers to round to three significant figures, one of which carries.

check.q: The recap says sums follow decimal places while products follow significant figures.
check.again: When adding or subtracting, the answer can only be as precise as the least precise decimal place among the inputs: 12.34 plus 1.2 is reported as 13.5. When multiplying or dividing, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures among the measured inputs: 7.20 over 2.40 gives 3.00. The recap's other points: a node is whatever is joined by conductor, and cuts make separate groups; a part with both leads in one group is bypassed with zero volts across it; compare a measurement with its tolerance interval and keep readings as recorded; and a half digit is a display feature, not accuracy.

lectures.title: Series rules, Ohm's law and power
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 05 - Series Rules, Ohm's Law and Power.md; Boylestad §4.2 to §4.5, §5.2 to §5.4, §5.7, §5.8

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture five is built on one idea: a number means something only when you can name the rule that produced it. We fix a small set of rules you are allowed to cite, the element container and its three truths, then E I C, E I S, E I P, O L, R I S and K V L. We examine why Ohm's law is written with subscripts, how series resistors add, and how power differs from energy. Then we derive three faces of the power formula, compare a linear graph with a square law, and solve real circuits by gathering, targeting, working and checking. We finish with sign conventions for sources and power, and a first taste of the proportional divider and Kirchhoff's voltage law.
segments.expand: Explain why naming the rule beside each step helps you, not just the reader.

check.q: What single idea does the opening say lecture five is built on?
options: A number means something only with its rule
Every circuit has exactly one current
Power and energy are the same thing
check.again: The theme is justification: every number in your working should come with the name of the rule that produced it. That is why the lecture fixes a short list of rules you are allowed to cite, the element container truths and then E I C, E I S, E I P, O L, R I S and K V L. Citing the rule makes the work readable to someone else and, more importantly, makes you confirm that the rule really applies, for instance that Ohm's law is being used with a voltage across and a current through the same resistor.

segments.title: The element container and its truths
segments.text: An element container is any two-terminal box. Inside there might be one part or a whole sub-circuit; from outside it connects through just two terminals. For elements on a single unbranched path, three truths hold. Truth one: the same current flows through every element, so measuring it anywhere on the path tells you it everywhere. Truth two: the element voltages add up to the container's terminal voltage. Truth three: the elements can be reordered, provided each keeps its own orientation. Use them as a self-check. If your working shows two different currents on one path, or element voltages that do not add to the terminal voltage, an earlier step is wrong: go back rather than carry on. A two-terminal box can hide internal branches, so check the path really is unbranched.
segments.expand: Give an example of a two-terminal box whose inside is not all in series, and explain why the truths then fail.

check.q: For elements on one unbranched path, truth two of the element container says what?
options: Element voltages add to the terminal voltage
Element currents add to the terminal current
check.again: An element container is any two-terminal box, and for elements on a single unbranched path inside it, three truths hold. Truth one: the same current flows through every element. Truth two: the element voltages add up to the voltage across the container's terminals. Truth three: elements may be reordered as long as each keeps its own orientation. Adding resistances is a separate resistor-only rule, and currents adding is a parallel-node idea, not a series truth. Use the truths as a check: if your working shows two different currents on one path, an earlier step is wrong.

segments.title: Reorder, but never reverse
segments.text: Truth three lets you move a component along a series path. It does not let you turn it around. If an element is drawn with its plus on the left, it must still have its plus on the left after you move it. Reordering leaves the current and every element's voltage unchanged; reversing an element changes the circuit, because it flips that element's polarity in the loop. So in a chain of a source, a capacitor, an inductor and a resistor, you may swap the inductor and the resistor freely, but you may not flip the capacitor. One more caution: taking an element out of its series position changes its connections. It is not automatically in parallel with something just because it has left the chain; recheck which two nodes its ends touch.
segments.expand: Explain why reversing a source in a series loop changes the current, using the loop's rises and drops.

check.q: Truth three lets you swap the positions of two series elements, and also lets you turn one of them around.
check.again: Reordering is allowed; reversing is not. Sliding an element to a different spot on the series path changes nothing, because the same current still passes through it in the same direction and every element voltage stays as it was. Flipping an element end for end reverses its polarity in the loop, which is a different circuit. In a chain of a source, a capacitor, an inductor and a resistor, the inductor and resistor can trade places, but the capacitor must keep its plus where it was. And lifting an element out of the chain changes its connections, so recheck which two nodes it touches.

segments.title: Cite a rule at every step
segments.text: Here is the fixed rule set, worth memorising rather than looking up. E I C, elements in container: the three truths. E I S, elements in series: the same current through every series element. E I P, elements in parallel: the same voltage across every element connected to the same two nodes. O L, Ohm's law: resistance equals the voltage across a resistor over the current through it, rearranged as needed. R I S, resistors in series: the total is the sum of the resistances. K V L, Kirchhoff's voltage law: the directed voltages around a closed path sum to zero. Write the abbreviation beside each line of working. It tells a reader why you did what you did, and, more usefully, it keeps you honest, because writing O L forces you to confirm you have a voltage across and a current through the same element.
segments.expand: Quiz me on the six abbreviations, one at a time, asking what each states.

check.q: In the rule set, what does E I P state?
options: Same voltage across elements on the same two nodes
Same current through every element in series
The sum of directed voltages around a loop is zero
check.again: E I P is elements in parallel: anything connected between the same two nodes has the same voltage across it. Its partner E I S, elements in series, says the same current flows through every element on one path. O L is Ohm's law, resistance equals the voltage across a resistor over the current through it. R I S, resistors in series, says the total is the sum. K V L says the directed voltages around a closed path sum to zero. And E I C is the container with its three truths. Writing the abbreviation beside each line keeps you honest about which rule you used.

segments.title: Ohm's law lives on subscripts
segments.text: The course writes Ohm's law with subscripts: resistance equals the voltage across R divided by the current through R; equivalently, voltage across R equals current through R times R, and current through R equals voltage across R over R. The subscripts are the content, not decoration. Many books write just V over I and leave you to guess which voltage and which current; in a circuit with several parts, that guess is exactly where mistakes start. A good habit: picture the meters, even with no bench in front of you. Current through means an ammeter inserted in series. Voltage across means a voltmeter with red on one end and black on the other. That picture fixes both the value and the sign. You may point a current arrow either way; if it opposes the real flow, the answer is simply negative.
segments.expand: Explain how picturing the meter connections tells you the sign of a reading before you calculate it.

check.q: The subscripts in the course's version of Ohm's law are decoration, and plain V over I means exactly the same thing.
check.again: In a circuit with several parts there are many voltages and many currents, and Ohm's law only works when you pair the voltage across a particular resistor with the current through that same resistor. The subscripts carry exactly that pairing; plain V over I leaves you guessing, and the guess is where errors begin. A useful mental picture: voltage across means a voltmeter with red on one end of the resistor and black on the other, and current through means an ammeter inserted in series with it. If your chosen current arrow opposes the real flow, the answer simply comes out negative.

segments.title: Resistors in series add
segments.text: Resistors in series: the total resistance equals R one plus R two plus and so on, up to however many resistors are on the path. Either the written-out form or the summation form is fine. This is the rule that turns a chain into something Ohm's law can handle. Reduce the chain to one equivalent resistance, find the path current, then return to the individual resistors for their voltages. Keep one distinction firmly in mind. The container truths, same current and voltages adding, apply to any elements in series: resistors, capacitors, inductors, or unknowns. Adding the values themselves is special to resistors. Capacitors in series do not add that way. So R I S is a resistor rule, and E I S is the general one.
segments.expand: Explain why adding values works for resistors in series, starting from the same current and adding voltages.

check.q: Because elements in series share one current, capacitors in series also add their values the way resistors do.
check.again: Keep the general rule apart from the resistor rule. E I S, the same current through every series element, and the container truths, voltages adding to the terminal voltage, apply to anything in series: resistors, capacitors, inductors or unknown boxes. But adding the values themselves, R I S, is a fact about resistors only: 1 ohm plus 2 ohm plus 3 ohm is 6 ohms. Capacitors in series do not combine that way, so do not carry the resistor habit across. The reduce-and-return routine is: sum the resistors, find the path current, then go back to each resistor for its own voltage.

segments.title: Power is a rate, energy is the total
segments.text: Power and energy belong to every physical system, not just electricity. Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts, where one watt is one joule per second, named for James Watt. Energy is power accumulated over time: energy equals power times time, joules from watts times seconds, or kilowatt-hours from kilowatts times hours. A household meter makes the difference concrete: how fast it turns shows the power you are drawing right now, and what the bill charges for is the accumulated energy. A 1500 watt heater that has used 12 kilowatt-hours has been running for 12 divided by 1.5, which is 8 hours. A kilowatt-hour is an amount of energy, never a power.
segments.expand: Work two quick energy examples, one in joules and one in kilowatt-hours, and explain why the units differ.

check.q: A 1500 watt heater has used 12 kilowatt-hours. How long has it been running?
check.again: Energy equals power times time: energy in kilowatt-hours, power in kilowatts, time in hours, or joules from watts times seconds. Rearranged, time equals energy over power. Fifteen hundred watts is 1.5 kilowatts, and 12 kilowatt-hours divided by 1.5 kilowatts is 8 hours. Eighteen would come from multiplying, and 12 from forgetting the power entirely. Power is a rate, how fast energy moves, in watts, one joule per second; energy is the total delivered. The spinning meter shows power right now; the bill charges for accumulated energy. A kilowatt-hour is always an amount of energy.

segments.title: Three faces of one formula
segments.text: Start from the power dissipated in a resistor: power equals the voltage across it times the current through it. Substitute Ohm's law for the current, voltage over resistance, and you get power equals voltage squared over resistance. Substitute Ohm's law for the voltage instead, current times resistance, and you get power equals current squared times resistance. All three are the same law; pick the face that uses the two quantities you already have, so you are not calculating a third quantity just to reach a remembered formula. Resistors dissipate energy, mostly as heat; you will feel that on a fingertip one day. Ideal capacitors and inductors store energy and give it back without heating. An ideal source has no resistance and does not warm; a real battery is modelled as an ideal source plus a small internal resistance, and that resistance is what gets warm.
segments.expand: Explain which power face is quickest when you know only the current and the resistance, and why.

check.q: Substituting Ohm's law for the current in power equals voltage times current gives which formula?
options: Power equals voltage squared over resistance
Power equals current squared times resistance
check.again: Start with power equals voltage times current, watts from volts times amps. Ohm's law says current equals voltage over resistance, so replace the current: voltage times voltage over resistance, which is voltage squared over resistance. Replacing the voltage instead, with current times resistance, gives current squared times resistance. All three are one law; choose the face that uses the two quantities you already hold. For example, 12 volts across 6 ohms: 144 over 6 is 24 watts, with no need to find the current first. Resistors turn that power into heat; ideal sources and ideal storage elements do not warm up.

segments.title: A straight line and a square law
segments.text: Plot current against voltage for a fixed resistance and you get a straight line through the origin, with a slope of one over R. A graph like that is called linear, and much of electronics is modelled as linear over a working range; that is a good approximation, not a law of nature. Power is different. Power equals voltage squared over resistance, so at fixed resistance power follows a square law: double the voltage and the power becomes four times as large, not twice. A resistor dissipating 24 watts at 12 volts dissipates 96 watts at 24 volts. Both graphs pass through the origin, because no voltage means no current and no power. The square law is why a small increase in voltage can overheat a part that was comfortably within its rating.
segments.expand: Explain what happens to power when the voltage is halved, and when the current is tripled at fixed resistance.

check.q: A resistor dissipates 24 watts at 12 volts. At 24 volts, with the same resistance, it dissipates what?
check.again: Power equals voltage squared over resistance, watts from volts squared over ohms, so at fixed resistance power follows a square law. Doubling the voltage multiplies the power by two squared, four, so 24 watts becomes 96 watts. Forty eight would be the answer if power grew in simple proportion, which is how current behaves, not power. Check it directly: 24 watts at 12 volts means 144 over R is 24, so R is 6 ohms; at 24 volts, 576 over 6 is 96 watts. That square law is why a modest voltage increase can push a part past its rating.

segments.title: Gather, target, work, check
segments.text: The routine is the same every time. Gather what you know and label every given. Identify the one quantity you actually need. Do the work, justifying each step with a named rule. Box the answer and, where a second route exists, check with it. Worked example one: a 10 volt source across a single 5 ohm resistor. By E I P, the resistor has the full 10 volts. By O L, its current is 10 over 5, 2 amps. Its power is 10 volts times 2 amps, 20 watts, and both other faces agree: 100 over 5 and 2 squared times 5. Worked example two: a 12 volt source, an ammeter reading 4 amps, and an unknown resistor. By E I S the resistor carries 4 amps, and by O L its resistance is 12 over 4, 3 ohms. Do not solve more than you were asked.
segments.expand: Work a backward problem where the total resistance and two resistors are known, and name each rule used.

check.q: A 12 volt source, an ammeter reading 4 amps and an unknown resistor form one loop. What is the resistance?
check.again: Gather: 12 volts, 4 amps, one loop. Target: the resistance. Work: by E I S, the resistor carries the same 4 amps the ammeter reads, and by E I P it has the full 12 volts across it. Then O L, resistance equals voltage across over current through, 12 volts over 4 amps, 3 ohms. Forty eight would be voltage times current, which is power in watts, and 8 is a subtraction that means nothing here. Check: 4 amps times 3 ohms gives back 12 volts. And stop there; the question asked only for the resistance.

segments.title: What a negative number is telling you
segments.text: Once arrows and polarities are drawn, the algebra can return negative values, and the course fixes the conventions. A current referenced into a source's positive terminal is negative; referenced out of it, positive. Power into the circuit is negative; power leaving the circuit is positive. Add up all the powers in a closed circuit and the total is zero. So if a loop carries 2 amps and you happened to point the source's arrow into its positive terminal, the source current comes out as minus 2 amps; the physical current did not reverse, your reference did. The zero sum of powers is conservation of energy written in those signs, and in a series circuit it means the source's power equals the sum of the resistors' powers. Choose a convention and hold it for the whole problem.
segments.expand: Work the power bookkeeping for a 12 volt source driving 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms in series.

check.q: With the course's conventions, a current referenced into a source's positive terminal comes out negative, and all powers in a closed circuit sum to zero.
check.again: A source drives current out of its positive terminal, so an arrow pointing into that terminal opposes the real flow and the value comes out negative. The physical current has not reversed; only your reference points the other way. For power, the course counts power entering the circuit as negative and power leaving as positive, so the powers of every element in a closed circuit add to zero. That zero is conservation of energy: in a series circuit, the source supplies exactly what the resistors dissipate. Pick one convention at the start and hold it for the whole problem.

segments.title: The proportional divider, and exact values
segments.text: Put a 1 ohm and a 2 ohm resistor in series across 10 volts. One current flows through both, by E I S, so their voltages are proportional to their resistances: the 2 ohm resistor drops twice as much as the 1 ohm. By K V L the two drops add to 10 volts. Two equations, two unknowns: twice the first drop plus the first drop is 10, so the first drop is ten thirds of a volt, about 3.33, and the second is twenty thirds, about 6.67. Ten thirds and twenty thirds are exact and add to exactly 10. Rounded early to 3.3 and 6.6, they add to 9.9, leaving a false 0.1 volt gap that is not in the circuit. Carry full precision through the working and round only the final answer.
segments.expand: Show the same divider solved current-first, and confirm both routes give identical exact values.

check.q: A 1 ohm and a 2 ohm resistor are in series across 10 volts. What exact voltage is across the 1 ohm resistor?
check.again: By E I S one current flows through both, so by Ohm's law their voltages are proportional to their resistances: the 2 ohm resistor drops twice what the 1 ohm does. By K V L the two drops add to 10 volts. Call the 1 ohm drop x; then x plus 2x is 10, so x is ten thirds of a volt, about 3.33, and the 2 ohm resistor takes twenty thirds, about 6.67. Five volts would only be right for equal resistors. Keep the exact fractions in the working: ten thirds and twenty thirds add to exactly 10, whereas 3.3 and 6.6 add to a false 9.9.

segments.title: Recap of lecture five
segments.text: Five ideas from lecture five. One: on an unbranched path, the element container truths hold: same current, voltages adding to the terminal voltage, and reordering without reversing. Two: cite a rule for every step: E I C, E I S, E I P, O L, R I S, K V L, and know what each states. Three: Ohm's law lives on subscripts, voltage across and current through the same resistor, and resistors in series add, a rule for resistors only. Four: power is a rate and energy is power times time; power equals V I, I squared R, or V squared over R, and it follows a square law. Five: with consistent signs, a current into a source's positive terminal is negative and all powers sum to zero; carry exact values and round once.
segments.expand: Run a rapid rule drill: name each abbreviation and state its rule.

check.q: The recap says resistors in series add. Which kinds of elements does that adding rule apply to?
check.again: The container truths, same current and voltages adding to the terminal voltage, hold for any elements on an unbranched path. Adding the values, R I S, is special to resistors; capacitors do not combine that way. The recap's other points: reorder without reversing; cite a rule for every step; Ohm's law lives on subscripts, voltage across and current through the same resistor; power is a rate and energy is power times time, with power equal to V I, I squared R or V squared over R, a square law; and a current into a source's positive terminal is negative, while all powers sum to zero.

lectures.title: Series analysis, KVL and node notation
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 06 - Series Analysis, KVL and Node Notation.md; Boylestad §5.2, §5.3, §5.6, §5.7, §5.9, §5.10

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture six starts from one sentence: a voltage is never a property of one point. It is a difference between two, and every notation today exists to say which two. We reduce a series chain to find its current, then return to the original drawing for each voltage. We check answers by two independent routes. We state Kirchhoff's voltage law in its two forms and walk a loop consistently, in calculation and with a meter. Then we define a node and learn two ways of naming voltages: the double subscript, which names both points, and the single subscript, which needs a marked reference node.
segments.expand: Explain why a voltage always needs two points, using a meter with one probe left unconnected as the example.

check.q: The opening sentence of this lecture says a voltage is a property of a single point.
check.again: The opening says the opposite: a voltage is never a property of one point. It is always a difference between two points, and the whole point of today's notation is to say which two. The double subscript names both points outright, V sub A B being the voltage at A minus the voltage at B. The single subscript names only one point and leans on a marked reference node for the other. The lecture also reduces a series chain to find its current, returns to the original drawing for each voltage, checks by two routes, and states Kirchhoff's voltage law in two forms.

segments.title: Reduce the chain, then solve it
segments.text: To find each resistor's voltage you first need the current, and to find the current you first need the total resistance. The worked example: a 10 volt source with a 1 ohm and a 2 ohm resistor in series. By R I S, the total is 3 ohms. By O L, the current is 10 volts over 3 ohms, ten thirds of an amp, about 3.33 amps, and by E I S that flows through both resistors. Now Ohm's law on R one: ten thirds of an amp times 1 ohm is ten thirds of a volt, about 3.33 volts. Then K V L gives R two's voltage: 10 minus ten thirds is twenty thirds, about 6.67 volts. Watch the units while working fast: 10 volts divided by 3 ohms gives amps, not ohms. Writing the unit on every line is the cheapest error check you have.
segments.expand: Work the same method on 12 volts across 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms, keeping units on every line.

check.q: A 10 volt source drives a 1 ohm and a 2 ohm resistor in series. What current flows?
check.again: First reduce: by R I S the total resistance is 1 plus 2, 3 ohms. Then O L for the whole loop: current equals voltage over resistance, 10 volts over 3 ohms, ten thirds of an amp, about 3.33 amps. Watch the units: volts divided by ohms gives amps, not ohms. Ten amps would ignore the 2 ohm resistor, and 30 comes from multiplying instead of dividing. By E I S that same current flows through both resistors, so R one drops ten thirds of a volt and R two, by K V L, takes the remaining twenty thirds, about 6.67 volts.

segments.title: The equivalent is an analysis device
segments.text: Replacing the 1 ohm and 2 ohm resistors by a single 3 ohm resistor reproduces the source voltage and the current at the two outer terminals. That is all the reduction promises. Inside the equivalent, the node between the original resistors no longer exists, so you cannot read R one's voltage from the reduced drawing. Reduce to get the current; then go back to the original circuit for the element voltages. The equivalent resistor is a calculation tool, not a claim about the hardware. This idea returns constantly: every time you simplify a network, ask which points still exist in the simplified version and which have been absorbed.
segments.expand: Explain what information is kept and what is lost when a series chain is replaced by its total.

check.q: Once the 1 ohm and 2 ohm resistors are replaced by a single 3 ohm equivalent, you can read R one's voltage from the reduced drawing.
check.again: The equivalent resistor only promises to reproduce what happens at the two outer terminals: the same source voltage and the same current. The node that sat between the original two resistors has been absorbed; it no longer exists in the reduced picture, so nothing in that picture can tell you R one's own voltage. The routine is reduce to get the current, then return to the original circuit and apply Ohm's law to each resistor. Whenever you simplify a network, ask which points survive in the simplified version and which have been swallowed.

segments.title: Carry the digits
segments.text: Ten thirds is a repeating decimal. Round it to 3.33 and then multiply, and the rounding error travels into every later step and can grow across a long problem. Keep full precision inside the calculation and round once, at the answer. On a calculator, store an intermediate value in memory rather than retyping a rounded one. A spreadsheet carries the digits automatically, which is one reason building a circuit calculation in a spreadsheet is a useful exercise. Remember the difference between exact and approximate: ten thirds of a volt is exact; 3.33 volts is its three significant figure approximation, and that is what you report at the end.
segments.expand: Show a two-step calculation where early rounding changes the third significant figure of the answer.

check.q: What does the lecture advise about a repeating value like ten thirds during a calculation?
options: Keep full precision and round once at the end
Round to a whole number for safety
check.again: Rounding an intermediate value and then reusing it plants an error that travels into every later step and can grow over a long problem. So carry the exact value, ten thirds, or the full calculator display, and round only the final answer. On a calculator, store the intermediate result in memory rather than retyping a rounded version; a spreadsheet carries the digits for you. Keep exact and approximate apart: ten thirds of a volt is exact, and 3.33 volts is its three significant figure approximation, which is what you report at the end.

segments.title: Two routes, one answer
segments.text: Almost every quantity in these circuits can be reached two ways; use one for the answer and the other as a check. In the worked example, R two's voltage came from K V L: the source minus R one's drop. The independent route is Ohm's law on R two directly: ten thirds of an amp times 2 ohms is twenty thirds of a volt, the same 6.67 volts. The two routes agree, so the current and both element voltages are consistent. If two routes ever disagree, one or both contain a mistake, and knowing that is worth more than a single unchecked answer. At the same time, calculate only what the question needs; if only one voltage is asked for, there is no reason to work out every power in the circuit.
segments.expand: Explain which second route you would use to check a series current, and why it is independent.

check.q: R two's voltage came from K V L. What independent route did the lecture use to check it?
options: Ohm's law on R two directly
check.again: Most quantities in these circuits can be reached two different ways, and the second way makes a check. K V L gave R two's voltage as the source minus R one's drop, 10 minus ten thirds, twenty thirds of a volt. The independent route is Ohm's law on R two itself: voltage equals current through it times its resistance, ten thirds of an amp times 2 ohms, again twenty thirds, about 6.67 volts. Agreement means the current and both element voltages hang together. Disagreement means a mistake somewhere, which is worth knowing. But only calculate what the question asks for.

segments.title: Kirchhoff's voltage law, said two ways
segments.text: There are two standard statements, and they are the same law. Form one: the sum of the directed voltages around a closed path is zero. Form two: the sum of the voltage rises equals the sum of the voltage drops. The word directed carries the content. Some terms in form one must be negative, or the sum could never be zero, and directed says the sign comes from the direction you travel through each element. Leaving that word out is the commonest way to state the law wrongly. Form two avoids negative terms by putting rises on one side and drops on the other. Either works if you are consistent. For the worked circuit, form two reads 10 volts equals ten thirds plus twenty thirds, exactly. And note the spelling: Kirchhoff has two h's, one in each half of the name.
segments.expand: State both forms of KVL for a loop with two sources and two resistors.

check.q: In form one of Kirchhoff's voltage law, which word carries the sign information?
check.again: Form one says the sum of the directed voltages around a closed path is zero. Directed is the word that matters: it says each voltage takes its sign from the direction you travel through the element. Without it the statement is wrong, because a sum of plain positive drops could never come to zero. Form two sidesteps negative terms: the sum of the rises equals the sum of the drops. For the worked circuit, 10 volts equals ten thirds plus twenty thirds. Both forms are one law; just be consistent. And Kirchhoff is spelled with two h's.

segments.title: Walk the loop consistently
segments.text: To apply form one, pick a starting point and a direction, and travel all the way round. At each element, the sign of its voltage comes from which terminal you enter: enter at plus, add plus V; enter at minus, add minus V. Walking the example loop with the current, starting from the source's negative terminal, you enter the source at minus, so minus 10; then R one at plus, plus 3.33; then R two at plus, plus 6.67. The sum is zero. Walk it the other way and every term flips sign, and the sum is still zero. Reversing the direction of travel cannot change the physics; it only changes the bookkeeping. The law always holds. If your numbers do not close the loop, there is an arithmetic or sign error somewhere.
segments.expand: Walk a loop containing a second source that opposes the first, and show the signs at each element.

check.q: Walking a loop for form one, what sets the sign you write for an element's voltage?
options: Which terminal you enter, plus or minus
Whether the element is a source or resistor
check.again: Pick a start and a direction, then travel all the way round. At each element, enter at its plus terminal and write plus V; enter at its minus terminal and write minus V. In the example, starting at the source's negative end and moving with the current, you enter the source at minus, so minus 10; then R one at plus, plus 3.33; then R two at plus, plus 6.67; total zero. Reverse the direction and every sign flips, and the total is still zero. If your loop does not close to zero, look for an arithmetic or sign error.

segments.title: The same discipline at the bench
segments.text: Measuring around a loop works exactly the same way, with the meter leads playing the part of the direction of travel. If you put the red probe at the far end of one element and then swap the probes on the next, your readings will not add to zero, and the circuit will not be at fault. Keep the probe orientation consistent all the way round. If you do swap them for one reading, negate that reading before you add. A sign convention you have physically performed is one you stop getting wrong in calculations, so this is worth practising with a real meter whenever you can.
segments.expand: Describe how to measure around a three-resistor loop so the readings sum to zero, probe by probe.

check.q: If you swap the meter probes for one reading while going round a loop, you must negate that reading before adding it.
check.again: At the bench, the meter leads play the part of the direction of travel. Keep the same probe orientation all the way round the loop and the readings add to zero, just as in the calculation. Swap red and black for one element and that reading comes out with the opposite sign; the circuit is fine, your bookkeeping just changed. Either avoid swapping, or flip the sign of that one reading before you add. Doing this physically with a real meter is the best way to stop getting sign conventions wrong in calculations.

segments.title: Nodes and the double subscript
segments.text: A node is a region of one voltage: every point joined by ideal wire. A length of wire, a bend, a stretch of circuit board track are all one node, because no voltage develops across an ideal conductor. Label nodes with lowercase letters, a, b, c, d. Then V sub A B means red probe on node A and black probe on node B, and it equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B. The order of the subscripts is the probe placement, which is why the notation is unambiguous: V sub B A equals minus V sub A B. Swapping probes negates the reading without changing the voltage itself. A single letter alone cannot mean anything, because one point is not a measurement. With A at plus 20 and B at minus 15 volts, V sub A B is 20 minus minus 15, which is 35 volts.
segments.expand: Work three double-subscript examples, including one with a negative node voltage.

check.q: Node A is at plus 20 volts and node B at minus 15 volts. What is V sub A B?
check.again: V sub A B means red probe on A, black on B, and equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B. Twenty minus minus fifteen is 20 plus 15, which is 35 volts. Five volts is what you get by forgetting that B is negative. Minus 35 would be V sub B A, the probes swapped. The subscript order is the probe placement, which is what makes the notation unambiguous. A node is a region of one voltage, everything joined by ideal wire, and one point alone is not a measurement; you always need two.

segments.title: Reading a chain with double subscripts
segments.text: A 10 volt source drives three resistors dropping 7 volts, 2 volts and 1 volt. Nodes a, b, c and d run along the chain, with a at the source's positive terminal. V sub A B is the first drop, 7 volts. V sub A C spans the first two, 7 plus 2, 9 volts. V sub A D spans all three, 10 volts. Is Kirchhoff's voltage law satisfied? 7 plus 2 plus 1 is 10, and V sub A D is the source voltage, so yes. In fact V sub A D never needed adding up: K V L already guaranteed it. The same bookkeeping works backwards: if V sub A B is 5 volts and B is 4 volts above ground, A must be 9 volts above ground.
segments.expand: Ask me for V sub B D and V sub D A in the same chain and explain the signs.

check.q: Resistors along a chain drop 7, 2 and 1 volts, with nodes a, b, c, d in order. What is V sub A C?
check.again: V sub A C is the voltage from node a down to node c, so it spans everything between them: the first drop, 7 volts across R one, plus the second, 2 volts across R two, which is 9 volts. V sub A B alone is 7 volts, and V sub A D, spanning all three drops, is 7 plus 2 plus 1, 10 volts, which matches the source and is exactly what K V L guarantees. The bookkeeping works backwards too: if V sub A B is 5 volts and node b sits 4 volts above ground, node a must be 9 volts above ground.

segments.title: The single subscript needs a reference
segments.text: A single subscript, V sub B, names only the red probe's node. The black probe is understood to sit on a reference node, and that node must be marked on the diagram before the notation means anything. A downward-pointing triangle marks the local zero volt common used for measurements; a variant with a number inside serves circuits with more than one common. The three-bar symbol means earth, which is a different idea. People say ground loosely for both, which is exactly why the symbol on the page matters more than the word. If no reference is drawn, you cannot use single subscripts; use double subscripts instead, which are always available. On a floating circuit you may nominate a reference for your own working, but say where you put it.
segments.expand: Explain why a circuit can have a local common without any earth connection.

check.q: A single subscript like V sub B can be used even when no reference node is marked on the diagram.
check.again: A single subscript names only the red probe's node. The black probe is understood to sit on the reference node, so if no reference is marked the notation means nothing. Mark it first: the downward triangle is the local zero volt common, a numbered variant serves circuits with several commons, and the three-bar symbol means earth, a different idea. If no reference is drawn, fall back on double subscripts, which always work because they name both points. On a floating circuit you may nominate a reference for your own working, as long as you say where it is.

segments.title: The same chain, reference at node b
segments.text: Place the reference at node b and read every node. Node a is 7 volts above b across R one, so it is plus 7 volts. Node b is the reference, zero. Node c is 2 volts below b across R two, so minus 2 volts. Node d is a further 1 volt below, minus 3 volts. Check against the double subscript result: a minus d is 7 minus minus 3, which is 10 volts, matching V sub A D. The reference is arbitrary: move it to node a and every single-subscript number shifts by minus 7 volts, while every difference stays identical. In practice it usually goes on the negative side of the supply. Choose it once, at the start, and never move it partway through a set of measurements, or half your numbers will be rebased.
segments.expand: Redo the node voltages with the reference at node d, and check one difference against the first set.

check.q: With the reference at node b, node c is 2 volts below b and node d a further 1 volt below. What is V sub D?
check.again: Single subscripts are measured from the reference, so V sub B is zero. Going down the chain, node c is 2 volts below b, so V sub C is minus 2. Node d is another 1 volt lower, so V sub D is minus 2 minus 1, minus 3 volts. Node a, 7 volts above b, is plus 7. Check with a double subscript: V sub A D is 7 minus minus 3, which is 10 volts, the source voltage. Move the reference to node a and every single-subscript value shifts by minus 7, but every difference stays the same. Choose the reference once and leave it.

segments.title: Recap of lecture six
segments.text: Five ideas from lecture six. One: reduce a series chain with R I S to find the current by O L, then return to the original drawing for each element's voltage; the equivalent loses the inner nodes. Two: check by a second route, and carry exact values until the final rounding. Three: Kirchhoff's voltage law, the directed voltages around a closed path sum to zero, or rises equal drops; the sign comes from the terminal you enter. Four: a node is one voltage region, and V sub A B is red on A, black on B, equal to A minus B, with V sub B A its negative. Five: single subscripts need a marked reference node; moving it shifts every node voltage but no difference.
segments.expand: Give me a quick loop to walk and a chain to label with both notations.

check.q: The recap says that moving the reference node changes what?
options: Every node voltage, but no difference
Every difference, but no node voltage
Nothing at all in the numbers
check.again: Single-subscript node voltages are measured from the reference, so moving the reference shifts all of them by the same amount. Differences between nodes, the double-subscript voltages, are untouched, because the shift cancels when you subtract. The recap's other points: reduce a series chain with R I S, find the current with O L, then return to the original drawing for each voltage, since the equivalent loses the inner nodes; check by a second route and carry exact values to the end; K V L means directed voltages sum to zero around a loop; and V sub A B equals A minus B.

lectures.title: Sources, internal resistance and loading
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 07 - Sources, Internal Resistance and Meter Loading.md; Boylestad §2.5, §2.6, §5.2, §5.5, §5.11, §5.12, §6.9; §8.2 current source definition only

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture seven rests on one sentence: a real source is a circuit, not a number. We model a real source as an ideal source in series with a resistance, and that hidden resistor is why the terminal voltage sags the moment current is drawn. Once the resistor is drawn, the sag becomes an ordinary series calculation. We restate the toolkit, stress that series and parallel are electrical rather than visual, meet voltage and current sources and their symbols, read a source's label correctly, compare cells and batteries, and then work the loading calculation all the way through, including the open-circuit case and a method for inferring the internal resistance.
segments.expand: Explain why modelling a battery as an ideal source plus a resistor makes its behaviour predictable.

check.q: How does this lecture model a real source?
options: An ideal source in series with a resistance
An ideal source in parallel with a resistance
An ideal source with a fixed current
check.again: The one sentence is: a real source is a circuit, not a number. The model is an ideal voltage source with a resistor in series with it, hidden inside the same package. That hidden resistor is why the terminal voltage sags as soon as current is drawn: the current flows through it and drops current times resistance before reaching the terminals. Once the resistor is drawn, the sag is an ordinary series calculation with the rules you already have. The lecture works that calculation through, including the open-circuit case and how to infer the internal resistance.

segments.title: The toolkit, restated
segments.text: Nothing new here; this is the rule set everything today is built on. Resistors in series: the total is the sum. Elements in series: the same current through every element. Ohm's law: voltage across equals current through times resistance, in any of its forms. Kirchhoff's voltage law: the directed voltages around a closed path sum to zero. And one shortcut, the voltage divider rule, which reaches an element's voltage in one step without finding the current first: that element's voltage equals the total voltage times its resistance over the total resistance. The divider rule is not new physics. Ohm's law plus Kirchhoff's voltage law always give the same answer; the rule is just quicker. Use whichever you can justify, and be able to name the one you used.
segments.expand: Show the voltage divider rule derived from Ohm's law and KVL in three short lines.

check.q: According to the toolkit restatement, what is the voltage divider rule?
options: A shortcut for Ohm's law plus K V L
A new law separate from Ohm's law
A rule that only applies to sources
check.again: The divider rule says an element's voltage equals the total voltage times that element's resistance over the total series resistance. It reaches the answer in one step without finding the current first, but it is not new physics. Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's voltage law give the same result: the current is the total voltage over the total resistance, and the element's voltage is that current times its own resistance, which is the same fraction. For example, 12 volts across 1 kilohm and 3 kilohms puts 9 volts on the 3 kilohm resistor either way. Use whichever rule you can name.

segments.title: Series and parallel are electrical
segments.text: Series and parallel describe how elements are connected electrically, not how they are arranged on the page or on the board. On a printed circuit board, components often sit side by side in neat rows because that uses space well, and they can still be electrically in series with one another. That is why node reasoning matters more than the picture. Trace what is joined to what, and never read the topology off the physical positions. The habit pays off immediately in this lecture, because a source's internal resistance is in series with the load even though you cannot see it at all.
segments.expand: Describe a board layout where parts look parallel but are in series, and how you would prove it with a meter.

check.q: Components placed side by side in neat rows on a circuit board cannot be electrically in series.
check.again: Series and parallel describe electrical connections, not layout. On a printed circuit board, parts are set out in rows because that packs them efficiently, and a row of parts can be wired end to end so that they are in series, or wired between the same two nodes so that they are in parallel, or neither. You find out by tracing what is joined to what, never by looking at positions. This lecture depends on that habit immediately, because a source's internal resistance is in series with the load and is completely invisible from the outside.

segments.title: Voltage sources and current sources
segments.text: An ideal voltage source fixes its terminal voltage, whatever current is drawn. An ideal current source fixes its current, whatever voltage that requires; by Ohm's law, the voltage is then set by the load. Either kind has both a voltage and a current at its terminals, and real sources have operating limits. A bench supply can do both jobs: in constant-voltage mode it holds the set voltage while the load current stays below the limit; if the load demands more, it switches to constant-current mode and adjusts its voltage to hold the limit, within its capability. The symbols: in a cell, the long plate is positive, and several cells make a battery; a circular voltage source carries polarity marks; a circular current source carries an arrow.
segments.expand: Explain what a bench supply does when a load tries to draw more than its current limit.

check.q: What does an ideal current source hold fixed?
options: Its current, whatever voltage that requires
Its voltage, whatever current is drawn
Both its voltage and its current
check.again: An ideal current source fixes the current through itself, and by Ohm's law the voltage across it is then whatever the load needs: 2 amps through 5 ohms means 10 volts, through 50 ohms means 100 volts. An ideal voltage source is the mirror image: it fixes the terminal voltage and lets the load decide the current. Neither fixes both. A bench supply can play either part: in constant-voltage mode it holds the set voltage until the load asks for more than the current limit, then it switches to constant-current mode and lowers its voltage to hold that limit.

segments.title: Reading a source's label
segments.text: A source's label carries two numbers, and one is routinely misread. Call the terminals A and B. The voltage, V sub A B, regardless of current draw, is the definition of an ideal constant-voltage source: what we would like to buy and cannot. The current on the label is the maximum current that can be drawn. It is a boundary, not a requirement. The source does not push that current out; the load decides how much flows. Disconnect the load and the source is driving an infinite resistance, so by Ohm's law the current is zero, whatever the label says. This was named in class as the single commonest misunderstanding about source specifications. Overdraw a source, on the other hand, and it heats up, which is its own problem.
segments.expand: Explain how much current a 5 volt, 2 amp supply delivers into a 1 kilohm load, and why.

check.q: The current printed on a source's label is the current it always pushes out, regardless of the load.
check.again: The label's current is a maximum: the most you may draw before the source overheats or leaves its rating. It is a boundary, not a delivery. The load decides how much current actually flows. Connect a large resistance and only a small current flows; disconnect the load entirely and the source is driving an infinite resistance, so by Ohm's law the current is zero, whatever the label says. This was called the commonest misunderstanding about source specifications. The label's voltage, V sub A B regardless of current, describes the ideal constant-voltage source we would like but cannot buy.

segments.title: Nominal voltage, cells and batteries
segments.text: Nominal voltage is a representative label, not an exact loaded value or a guaranteed minimum. Terminal voltage depends on chemistry, state of charge, temperature, load and age. A fresh nominal 1.5 volt alkaline cell can read above 1.5 volts on a nearly unloaded voltmeter. A cell is one electrochemical unit; in the traditional vocabulary, a battery is a group of cells, though everyday usage calls a single packaged cell a battery too. Cells connected series-aiding add their voltages, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, and every cell in the chain carries the same current, by elements in series, which is why one current, I sub S, describes the whole source. Four 1.5 volt cells in series give 6 volts. Typical nominal values are about 2 volts for lead-acid, 1.5 for alkaline, and 3.6 to 3.7 for many lithium-ion cells.
segments.expand: Explain why a battery pack might combine cells in series and also in parallel.

check.q: Four nominal 1.5 volt cells are connected series-aiding. What is the total nominal voltage?
check.again: Series-aiding cells add their voltages, by Kirchhoff's voltage law: four times 1.5 is 6 volts. And by elements in series, every cell carries the same current, which is why one current, I sub S, describes the whole source. Remember that nominal is a representative label, not a guaranteed loaded value: a fresh alkaline cell can read above 1.5 volts nearly unloaded, and terminal voltage shifts with chemistry, charge state, temperature, load and age. Typical nominal values are about 2 volts for lead-acid, 1.5 for alkaline, and 3.6 to 3.7 for many lithium-ion cells.

segments.title: Capacity in ampere-hours
segments.text: A battery's capacity is usually stated in ampere-hours, which is a measure of charge: one ampere-hour is 3600 coulombs. The ideal run time equals the capacity divided by the load current, hours from ampere-hours over amps. A 72 ampere-hour battery supplying a steady 1.8 amps could ideally last 40 hours; a 2 ampere-hour battery at a quarter of an amp, 8 hours. Treat these as estimates. Real capacity depends on the discharge rate, the temperature, the age, and the cutoff voltage the device needs, and a discharge curve for the actual cell tells the real story. Ampere-hours also are not energy; to estimate watt-hours you multiply by the voltage.
segments.expand: Explain why drawing a battery down faster usually gives less than its rated ampere-hours.

check.q: A 72 ampere-hour battery supplies a steady 1.8 amps. What is the ideal run time?
check.again: Run time equals capacity divided by load current: hours from ampere-hours over amps. Seventy two over 1.8 is 40 hours. Multiplying instead gives about 130, which has no meaning here, and 72 hours ignores the current. Ampere-hours measure charge, one ampere-hour being 3600 coulombs, and they are not energy; multiply by the voltage to estimate watt-hours. Treat the result as an estimate, because real capacity depends on discharge rate, temperature, age and the cutoff voltage the device needs. A 2 ampere-hour battery at a quarter of an amp gives 8 hours the same way.

segments.title: Internal resistance, and the node inside
segments.text: Every real source has internal resistance. Nobody installed it; it is distributed through the plates, electrolyte and connections, and a single series resistor is an approximation over the range being studied. You can show it as a note beside the symbol, or show it explicitly as a series resistor, with a box around the ideal source and the resistor together to show that the box is the physical component. The names R sub S, R internal and R series all mean the same thing. Label the nodes: A between the ideal source and its resistor, B at the positive terminal, C at the negative terminal. Node A is not measurable. It sits inside the source; a flashlight cell gives you two terminals and nothing else. Every measurement you can actually make is V sub B C, across the terminals.
segments.expand: Explain why internal resistance must be inferred rather than probed directly.

check.q: In the internal resistance model, node A between the ideal source and its resistor can be reached with a probe at the terminals.
check.again: A real cell offers exactly two terminals, B and C. The internal resistance is not a separate part somebody installed; it is spread through the plates, electrolyte and connections, and the single series resistor is an approximation. So the node between the ideal source and that resistor is a feature of the model, not a place you can touch with a probe. Every measurement you can actually make is V sub B C, across the terminals, after the internal drop has already been taken. R sub S, R internal and R series are all names for the same resistor.

segments.title: Kilo, kelvin, and prefix arithmetic
segments.text: Lowercase k means kilo, the multiplier one thousand. Uppercase K means kelvin, a temperature. Write them so they cannot be confused; a quick fix is to print the letter even in the middle of cursive. Twenty kilograms is twenty thousand grams, while twenty capital K g would mean kelvin-grams, which is nonsense. Kelvin and Celsius share the same step size, so a change of one degree Celsius is a change of one kelvin; they differ only by an offset of about 273, with zero kelvin at absolute zero. Degrees Celsius take a degree sign; kelvins do not. And a piece of prefix arithmetic to practise in your head: kilo times milli is one, so kilohms times milliamps gives volts, and volts over kilohms gives milliamps.
segments.expand: Drill me on prefix products: kilohms times microamps, megohms times microamps, and volts over megohms.

check.q: What is the difference between lowercase k and uppercase K in this course?
check.again: Lowercase k is the prefix kilo, one thousand. Uppercase K is the kelvin, the unit of temperature. Twenty kilograms is twenty thousand grams; twenty capital K g would be kelvin-grams, which means nothing. Print the letter clearly so the two cannot be confused. Kelvin and Celsius share the same step size, differing by an offset of about 273, and kelvins take no degree sign. The prefix arithmetic worth holding in your head: kilo times milli is one, so kilohms times milliamps gives volts, and volts over kilohms gives milliamps.

segments.title: Loading, worked all the way through
segments.text: Take an ideal 10 volt source with 10 ohms of internal resistance, driving a 1 kilohm load. First the ideal case for comparison: with no internal resistance, the load sees 10 volts and the current is 10 volts over 1 kilohm, 10 milliamps. Now the real case. By R I S the loop total is 10 plus 1000, 1010 ohms. By O L the current is 10 volts over 1010 ohms, about 9.90 milliamps, and by E I S the same through both. The terminal voltage, across the load, is that current times 1 kilohm, about 9.90 volts. The internal resistor drops the current times 10 ohms, about 99 millivolts. K V L checks: the two add to 10 volts. The loading cost about 0.1 volts and 100 microamps; negligible for many jobs, and knowing when is the point of calculating it.
segments.expand: Repeat the loading calculation with a 100 ohm load and compare how much voltage is lost.

check.q: A 10 volt source with 10 ohms internal resistance drives a 1 kilohm load. What is the terminal voltage?
check.again: By R I S the loop total is 10 plus 1000, 1010 ohms. By O L the current is 10 volts over 1010 ohms, about 9.90 milliamps, and by E I S it flows through both resistors. The terminal voltage is the load's voltage: 9.90 milliamps times 1 kilohm, about 9.90 volts. The internal resistor takes the rest, 9.90 milliamps times 10 ohms, about 99 millivolts, and K V L confirms the two add to 10. Exactly 10 volts would be the ideal source with no internal resistance. The loading cost about a tenth of a volt here; calculating it tells you whether that matters.

segments.title: Open circuit is not zero voltage
segments.text: Now remove the load entirely, leaving the terminals open. The load is replaced by an infinite resistance, not a zero one. So the loop total is infinite, and by Ohm's law the current is zero. By E I S the internal resistor carries that zero current, so it drops zero times 10 ohms, zero volts. By K V L, the terminal voltage is the source voltage minus zero: the full 10 volts. This was named in class as a classic beginner's mistake. No current is not the same as no voltage. It is also why an unloaded 1.5 volt cell can read 1.6 volts: with no load, there is no internal drop left to subtract, so the meter sees the full chemical voltage.
segments.expand: Explain what a high-resistance voltmeter shows across an unloaded source, and why it is almost an open circuit.

check.q: The load is removed from the 10 volt, 10 ohm internal resistance source. What appears across the open terminals?
check.again: An open circuit is an infinite resistance, not a zero one. By Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, and dividing by infinity gives zero current. With zero current, the internal resistor drops zero times 10 ohms, zero volts, so by K V L the terminal voltage is the source voltage minus nothing: the full 10 volts. Zero volts is the classic beginner's mistake, confusing no current with no voltage. This is also why an unloaded 1.5 volt cell can read 1.6 volts: with nothing drawing current, there is no internal drop to subtract from the chemical voltage.

segments.title: Measuring the internal resistance
segments.text: An ohmmeter is the wrong tool. It measures resistance by pushing its own small known current through the part and applying Ohm's law; across a live source, the source's own voltage swamps that measurement, and the reading means nothing. The method that works is the loading experiment, run deliberately. First, read the open-circuit terminal voltage; with no current, that is the ideal source voltage. Second, connect a load resistor roughly equal to the internal resistance and read the terminal voltage again. Third, infer the internal resistance: the lost voltage divided by the load current. For the 10 volt, 10 ohm source with a 10 ohm load, the current is 10 over 20, 0.5 amps, and the terminal voltage 5 volts, exactly half: the lost 5 volts over 0.5 amps returns 10 ohms.
segments.expand: Explain why a load roughly equal to the internal resistance makes the drop large enough to measure well.

check.q: Why is an ohmmeter the wrong tool for measuring a source's internal resistance?
options: The source's own voltage swamps the meter's test current
The internal resistance is too small to register
check.again: An ohmmeter pushes a small known current through the part and applies Ohm's law to what it sees. Across a live source, the source's own voltage overwhelms that tiny test signal, and the number displayed means nothing. Instead run the loading experiment on purpose. Read the open-circuit terminal voltage, which is the ideal source voltage since no current flows. Connect a load near the internal resistance and read again. Internal resistance equals the lost voltage over the load current. For the 10 volt, 10 ohm source with a 10 ohm load: 0.5 amps, 5 volts at the terminals, and 5 over 0.5 returns 10 ohms.

segments.title: Recap of lecture seven
segments.text: Five ideas from lecture seven. One: series and parallel are electrical, not visual, and the voltage divider rule is a shortcut for Ohm's law plus K V L. Two: an ideal voltage source fixes voltage, an ideal current source fixes current; a label's current is a maximum, and with nothing connected no current flows. Three: nominal voltage is a label; series-aiding cells add, and run time is ampere-hours over amps. Four: a real source is an ideal source plus internal resistance, the inside node is unreachable, and the terminal voltage sags by current times internal resistance, while an open circuit shows the full voltage. Five: infer the internal resistance from open and loaded readings, never with an ohmmeter; and write k and K so they cannot be confused.
segments.expand: Give me an internal resistance problem with two readings to solve in my head.

check.q: The recap says an open circuit across a real source shows the full source voltage at its terminals.
check.again: With nothing connected, no current flows, so the internal resistance drops nothing and the terminals show the ideal source voltage. Connect a load and the terminal voltage sags by current times internal resistance. The recap's other points: series and parallel are electrical, not visual, and the divider rule is a shortcut for Ohm's law plus K V L; an ideal voltage source fixes voltage and an ideal current source fixes current; a label's current is a maximum; series-aiding cells add and run time is ampere-hours over amps; infer internal resistance from open and loaded readings, never with an ohmmeter.

lectures.title: Parallel circuits, branch currents and conductance
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 08 - Parallel Circuits, Branch Currents and Conductance.md; Boylestad §3.7, §6.2, §6.3, §6.5 (named only), §6.6 (inverse proportion only)

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture eight introduces parallel circuits, and it starts from one statement: parallel is about nodes, not about the picture. Two elements are in parallel when both ends of one touch the same two nodes as both ends of the other. That single fact produces everything else: one shared voltage, a separate current in each branch, a total resistance smaller than any single resistor, and a total conductance that simply adds. We will ask what a voltage is relative to, name branch currents, see why current does not only take the easy road, redraw awkward circuits onto their nodes, derive the parallel resistance formula, and meet conductance in siemens. Series does the mirror image of all this, which is why the two are taught together.
segments.expand: Explain the mirror-image relationship between series and parallel in two sentences.

check.q: This lecture's opening definition: two elements are in parallel when what is true?
options: Both ends of each touch the same two nodes
They are drawn side by side on the page
The same current passes through each of them
check.again: Parallel is about nodes, not the picture. Two elements are in parallel when one element's two ends sit on exactly the same pair of nodes as the other element's two ends. Everything else follows from that: they share one voltage, each carries its own branch current, the combined resistance comes out smaller than any single resistor, and conductances simply add. Sharing a current is the series property, the mirror image. The lecture goes on to name branch currents, show that current takes every path, redraw awkward circuits onto their nodes, derive the parallel formula and introduce siemens.

segments.title: Parallel is electrical, never visual
segments.text: In geometry, two lines are parallel when the distance between them is the same everywhere. That is the meaning most people bring into the room, and it is the wrong one here. Electrically, two elements are in parallel when both of their ends connect to the same pair of nodes. Nothing about position, orientation or spacing is part of the definition. Place three resistors side by side, evenly spaced, and they look parallel; connect them end to end and they are in series, in exactly the same drawing positions. On printed circuit boards, parts sit in neat rows because that uses space well, not because they are in parallel. Redrawing someone else's schematic to understand it is a normal professional habit, not an admission of confusion.
segments.expand: Describe how to decide, from connections alone, whether two resistors on a board are in parallel.

check.q: Three resistors placed side by side and evenly spaced are electrically in parallel because of that arrangement.
check.again: The geometric meaning of parallel, lines that stay the same distance apart, is the wrong one for circuits. Electrically, elements are in parallel only when both ends of each connect to the same two nodes. Three resistors in a neat row can be wired end to end and be in series, in exactly those positions. Circuit boards put parts in rows to save space, not to declare a connection. So trace what is joined to what, and feel free to redraw a schematic to make the nodes obvious; professionals do it all the time.

segments.title: The same voltage, relative to what?
segments.text: Parallel elements share one voltage, but that is only half a statement until you say what the voltage is measured against. There is no such thing as a voltage at a point. When someone says the voltage here is 10 volts, the first question is, relative to what? The meter makes this concrete: put the red probe on a point and leave the black probe in mid-air, and the number displayed is meaningless. The black probe is the relative to what. Now pick any reference and measure along the top conductor of a parallel group: the same number everywhere. Move the reference and every number shifts together, but they still agree with each other. The reference changes the values; it never changes the fact that they are equal.
segments.expand: Explain why the equality of parallel voltages does not depend on the choice of reference.

check.q: The segment says there is no such thing as a voltage at a single point.
check.again: There is no such thing as a voltage at a single point. A voltage is a difference, so a number is meaningless until you know the second point. The meter makes it concrete: red probe on the point, black probe waving in the air, and the display means nothing; the black probe is the relative to what. Pick any reference and measure along the top conductor of a parallel group, and every point reads the same. Move the reference and all the readings shift together, still equal. The reference changes the values, never the fact that they match.

segments.title: Keep the signs consistent
segments.text: Put three voltmeters across three parallel elements. Connect two of them the same way round and the third backwards, and the equality seems to break: the first two agree, and the third reads the negative of them. Nothing electrical changed. The magnitude is identical; only that meter's reference direction flipped. Measuring every element the same way round gives three equal positive readings; measuring every one the other way gives three equal negatives, which is equally correct. Measuring one backwards by accident gives an inconsistent set, and the mistake looks like a circuit fault instead of a probe fault. And whatever else is connected, a battery, a bench supply, or a larger circuit, the voltages across the parallel elements remain equal: that property belongs to the connection, not the source.
segments.expand: Describe how you would spot a reversed probe among several parallel voltage readings.

check.q: Three voltmeters sit across three parallel elements; one is connected backwards. What does that meter show?
options: The same size, with a negative sign
A reading of exactly zero volts
A completely different size of reading
check.again: Parallel elements share one voltage, so all three meters see the same magnitude. The backwards meter has its red and black swapped, so its reference direction is reversed and it reads the negative of the other two. Nothing electrical changed; only the probe orientation did. Measure all three the same way round and you get three equal positives; all the other way round, three equal negatives, equally correct. One accidental swap produces an inconsistent set that looks like a circuit fault but is a probe fault. The equal-voltage property belongs to the connection, whatever source drives it.

segments.title: Branches and branch currents
segments.text: Each parallel path is a branch. Give each branch its own current name, I one, I two, I three; some people name the current after the element instead, I sub R one and so on. Either works if you keep to it. Here is the whole contrast in one sentence: parallel elements have the same voltage and, in general, different currents; series elements have the same current and, in general, different voltages. Within one branch, every element carries the same current, because a branch is itself an unbranched series path, elements in series, which is why one symbol per branch is enough.
segments.expand: Give an example of a branch containing two resistors in series, and explain how its current is found.

check.q: Which statement is the contrast this segment gives in one sentence?
options: Parallel: same voltage, different currents; series: same current, different voltages
Parallel: same current, different voltages; series: same voltage, different currents
Parallel and series both share one current
check.again: Parallel elements sit on the same two nodes, so they share one voltage, and each branch draws its own current according to its own resistance. Series elements sit on one path, so they share one current, and each drops its own voltage. Each parallel path is a branch, named I one, I two, I three, or after its element, I sub R one and so on; pick one scheme and keep it. Within one branch every element carries the branch current, because the branch itself is an unbranched series path, which is why one current symbol per branch is enough.

segments.title: Current does not take the easy road
segments.text: Current follows the path of least resistance is the commonest wrong sentence in electronics. Current follows every available path; a harder path simply carries less. For branches sharing one voltage, Ohm's law gives each branch current directly: branch current equals the shared voltage divided by that branch's resistance. So a branch's share is inversely proportional to its resistance, or, equivalently, directly proportional to its conductance. Double a branch's resistance and it carries half the current, not none. The split was described in class as being in proportion to the path resistance, and the direction of that proportion is what matters: more resistance means less current.
segments.expand: Work the split in a branch pair of 1 kilohm and 3 kilohms across 6 volts.

check.q: In a parallel group, doubling one branch's resistance halves that branch's current rather than stopping it.
check.again: Current takes every available path; a harder path just carries less. With one shared voltage across the branches, Ohm's law gives each branch current as that voltage over the branch's own resistance, amps from volts over ohms. So the share is inversely proportional to resistance: twice the resistance, half the current, never zero. Ten volts across 1 kilohm gives 10 milliamps; across 2 kilohms, 5 milliamps. Path of least resistance is the commonest wrong sentence in electronics. The direction of the proportion is what to remember: more resistance means less current, not no current.

segments.title: Branch currents add to the total
segments.text: What flows into a node must flow out of it, so the branch currents add up to the total current supplied: total current equals I one plus I two plus and so on. That is Kirchhoff's current law, named here and developed further in the next class. Now the class's worked circuit: 10 volts across a 1 kilohm and a 2 kilohm resistor in parallel. Both see the full 10 volts, because they share both nodes. The 1 kilohm branch carries 10 volts over 1 kilohm, 10 milliamps; the 2 kilohm branch carries 10 over 2, 5 milliamps. The total is 15 milliamps. Kilohms and milliamps work together again: volts over kilohms gives milliamps directly. And notice the ratio: the resistance doubled, so the current halved.
segments.expand: Work the same circuit at 6 volts and check that the branch currents still add to the total.

check.q: 10 volts is across a 1 kilohm and a 2 kilohm resistor in parallel. What is the total current supplied?
check.again: Both resistors touch both nodes, so each sees the full 10 volts. Ohm's law per branch: current equals voltage over resistance, and volts over kilohms gives milliamps directly. The 1 kilohm branch carries 10 milliamps and the 2 kilohm branch carries 5 milliamps. Kirchhoff's current law says the branch currents add to what the source supplies: 10 plus 5 is 15 milliamps. Ten milliamps is just one branch, and 3.33 would be the series answer, 10 volts over 3 kilohms. Notice the ratio: the resistance doubled from one branch to the other, and the current halved.

segments.title: Redrawing a circuit onto its nodes
segments.text: Given a circuit drawn awkwardly, with one resistor sideways and another upside down, the reliable method is mechanical. Pick a node and call it A; trace every conductor joined to it, through corners and junctions, along any length of wire. All of that is node A. Do the same for a second node, B. Then ask of each element: is one end on A and the other on B? Every element that answers yes is in parallel with the others. Redraw with A as the top rail and B as the bottom rail and hang each element between them. Orientation does not matter: a resistor upside down or rotated is unchanged if its ends land on the same nodes. The bench check: a voltmeter between two points of the same node reads zero. And always classify deliberately: series, parallel, or neither.
segments.expand: Walk me through classifying three resistors where two are parallel and the third is in series with the pair.

check.q: When redrawing an awkward circuit, what is the bench check that two points belong to the same node?
options: A voltmeter between them reads zero
An ammeter between them reads zero
A voltmeter between them reads the supply
check.again: A node is everything joined by conductor, so no voltage develops between any two points of it: a voltmeter between them reads zero. The redrawing method is mechanical. Name a node A and trace every wire joined to it, through corners and junctions; that whole region is A. Do the same for B. Then ask of each element whether one end is on A and the other on B. Every element that answers yes hangs between the A rail and the B rail, in parallel, no matter how it was drawn or rotated. And always classify deliberately: series, parallel, or neither.

segments.title: The bounds that catch mistakes
segments.text: Before any formula, learn the two bounds, because they are your error check. A series total is the sum, so it is greater than the largest resistor.
