A parallel total must be less than the smallest resistor in the group. The parallel bound catches mistakes instantly. One kilohm in parallel with two kilohms cannot measure 1.5 kilohms; that is larger than 1 kilohm, so something is wrong with the wiring or the meter, and there is no point calculating further until it is found. Perhaps the resistors are really in series, or something else is connected across them. Likewise, a series string that measures less than its largest resistor is telling you about a fault.
segments.expand: Explain why adding a parallel branch always lowers the total resistance, using the idea of an extra path.

check.q: One kilohm in parallel with 2 kilohms measures 1.5 kilohms. What does the segment say that tells you?
options: A fault; it must be below 1 kilohm
Fine; parallel totals sit between the two values
Fine; parallel totals are the sum of both
check.again: A parallel combination must be less than the smallest resistor in the group, because adding a branch gives current another way through. So 1 kilohm in parallel with anything must come out below 1 kilohm. A reading of 1.5 kilohms is impossible for that connection; perhaps the resistors are actually in series, something else is connected across them, or the meter is misused. Find the fault before calculating further. The series bound is the mirror image: the sum is greater than the largest resistor, so a series string reading less than its biggest part is also announcing a fault.

segments.title: Deriving the parallel formula
segments.text: Drive a parallel pair with a source; call the shared voltage V and the total current I. The equivalent resistance is defined by Ohm's law: V equals I times R total. By Kirchhoff's current law, I equals I one plus I two. By Ohm's law on each branch, I one is V over R one and I two is V over R two, with the same V across both. So I equals V over R one plus V over R two. Factor out V, divide both sides by V, and you get I over V equals one over R one plus one over R two. But I over V is one over R total. So one over R total equals one over R one plus one over R two. The step that does the work is factoring out V, legitimate only because the voltage really is common. And keep the reciprocal on the left: dropping it is the commonest slip, and it fails the less-than-smallest check at once.
segments.expand: Extend the derivation to three branches and show where each step comes from.

check.q: In deriving the parallel formula, which step does the real work, and why is it allowed?
options: Factoring out V, because the voltage is shared
Adding the resistances, because they are in series
Dividing by I, because the current is shared
check.again: Start with Kirchhoff's current law: I equals I one plus I two. Ohm's law on each branch gives I one as V over R one and I two as V over R two, the same V because both branches share the nodes. So I equals V over R one plus V over R two. Because V really is common, you may factor it out and divide both sides by it, leaving I over V equals one over R one plus one over R two. Since I over V is one over R total, the formula follows. Keep the reciprocal on the left; dropping it fails the bound check at once.

segments.title: Product over sum, and equal resistors
segments.text: For exactly two resistors, put the reciprocals over a common denominator and flip, and you get the shortcut: R total equals R one times R two, divided by R one plus R two. For 3 ohms and 6 ohms, that is 18 over 9, 2 ohms, below the smaller resistor as it must be. Product over sum is for two resistors only. Writing three resistors' product over their sum is wrong; either apply the shortcut twice, combining two and then the result with the third, or use the reciprocal form, which is why the reciprocal form is the one worth memorising. In a spreadsheet, the reciprocal form simply grows as resistors are added. For equal resistors there is an even quicker route: one value divided by how many there are, so three 12 ohm resistors in parallel make 4 ohms.
segments.expand: Combine 2, 3 and 6 kilohms in parallel two different ways and confirm the results match.

check.q: Three 12 ohm resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
check.again: For equal resistors in parallel, the total equals one value divided by how many there are: 12 ohms over 3 is 4 ohms, comfortably below the 12 ohm bound. Thirty six is the series total, and 6 would be two of them, not three. For two unequal resistors, product over sum works: 3 ohms and 6 ohms give 18 over 9, 2 ohms. But product over sum is for exactly two; for three or more, either apply it twice or use the reciprocal form, one over R total equals the sum of the reciprocals, which is the version worth memorising.

segments.title: Conductance, the easier way round
segments.text: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance: G equals one over R. Its unit is the siemens, symbol capital S. The unit is named after a person, so the symbol is a capital S while the name is written in lowercase, and it is siemens in both singular and plural. Asked whether a component is a resistor or a conductor, the honest answer is yes: it is one object, and resistance, the opposition to current, and conductance, the readiness to allow it, are two descriptions of the same property. The reciprocal of a kilohm is a millisiemens, so 2 kilohms is 0.5 millisiemens. Rewrite the parallel result with conductance and it becomes simple: in parallel, conductances add. Resistances add in series; conductances add in parallel.
segments.expand: Show how thinking in conductance makes a three-branch parallel total quicker to find.

check.q: What is the conductance of a 2 kilohm resistor?
check.again: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance: G equals one over R, in siemens, symbol capital S. The reciprocal of a kilohm is a millisiemens, so 2 kilohms gives one half of a millisiemens, 0.5 millisiemens. Two millisiemens would be the reciprocal of 500 ohms, and 0.5 siemens the reciprocal of 2 ohms. Resistance and conductance are two descriptions of one property: opposition to current and readiness to allow it. The payoff is the parallel rule in its simplest form: conductances add in parallel, just as resistances add in series.

segments.title: The worked circuit, both ways
segments.text: Back to 10 volts across 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms. The branch currents were 10 and 5 milliamps, 15 in total. The equivalent resistance by product over sum is 1 times 2 over 1 plus 2 kilohms, two thirds of a kilohm, about 667 ohms. By conductance, 1 millisiemens plus 0.5 millisiemens is 1.5 millisiemens, and one over that is again about 667 ohms. Two thousand over three ohms is exact; 667 ohms is the three-figure answer. Two checks, every time. First, 10 volts over two thirds of a kilohm gives 15 milliamps, matching the total. Second, 667 ohms is below 1 kilohm, the smaller resistor. An added study example: 12 volts across 2, 3 and 6 kilohms. The conductances are one half, one third and one sixth of a millisiemens, adding to exactly 1, so the total is 1 kilohm and the current 12 milliamps.
segments.expand: Check the three-branch example by adding the branch currents: 6, 4 and 2 milliamps.

check.q: 12 volts is across 2, 3 and 6 kilohm resistors in parallel. What total current flows?
check.again: Conductances add in parallel, and the reciprocal of a kilohm is a millisiemens. Two kilohms gives one half, 3 kilohms one third, 6 kilohms one sixth of a millisiemens, and one half plus one third plus one sixth is exactly 1 millisiemens, so the total resistance is 1 kilohm. Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance, 12 volts over 1 kilohm, 12 milliamps. Six would be only the 2 kilohm branch. Check it branch by branch: 6 plus 4 plus 2 milliamps is 12. And the check on the bound: 1 kilohm is below 2 kilohms, the smallest resistor.

segments.title: Recap of lecture eight
segments.text: Five ideas from lecture eight. One: parallel means both ends on the same two nodes; it is never about how the parts look, and a voltage is always relative to something. Two: parallel elements share one voltage and carry their own currents, each equal to that voltage over the branch resistance; current takes every path, and double the resistance means half the current. Three: branch currents add to the total, by Kirchhoff's current law. Four: one over R total is the sum of the reciprocals; product over sum is for two resistors only; equal resistors give R over N; and the total must be below the smallest resistor. Five: conductance is one over R, in siemens, and conductances add in parallel.
segments.expand: Give me two parallel pairs to combine in my head, one equal and one unequal.

check.q: The recap says product over sum works for any number of resistors in parallel.
check.again: Product over sum is a shortcut for exactly two resistors: R one times R two over R one plus R two. With three resistors, their product over their sum is simply wrong. Either apply the two-resistor shortcut twice, or use the general form: one over R total equals the sum of the reciprocals. Equal resistors have their own shortcut, one value over how many. The recap's other points: parallel means both ends on the same two nodes; parallel elements share one voltage and carry their own currents; branch currents add by Kirchhoff's current law; the total must be below the smallest resistor; and conductances add in parallel.

lectures.title: Units, notation and significant figures
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Textbook/ELTR 238 - Chapter 01 - Units and Engineering Notation - Study Pack.md; quiz study pack; Boylestad §1.3 to §1.9, §1.12

segments.title: What this chapter covers
segments.text: Chapter one of Boylestad is about the numbers themselves, before any circuit appears. A physical quantity is a number with a unit, and a correct piece of arithmetic can still give a wrong physical answer if the units are mishandled. The chapter covers units and unit systems, significant figures and rounding, powers of ten and their rules, scientific and engineering notation with the SI prefixes, converting between prefixes and between unit systems, and using a calculator or software with your judgement switched on. These habits run through every calculation in the course, so they are worth making automatic.
segments.expand: Explain why a correct calculation can still produce a wrong physical answer, with a unit example.

check.q: The opening says a correct piece of arithmetic can still give a wrong physical answer if the units are mishandled.
check.again: A physical quantity is a number together with a unit, and the arithmetic only describes the world when the units are handled properly. Divide 6 volts by 2 kilohms and write 3 amps, and the digits are fine while the answer is wrong by a factor of a thousand. That is why chapter one comes before any circuit: it covers unit systems, significant figures and rounding, powers of ten, scientific and engineering notation with the SI prefixes, converting between prefixes and systems, and using a calculator with your judgement switched on. The aim is to make those habits automatic.

segments.title: Quantities, units and systems
segments.text: A quantity is a number with a unit; drop the unit and the problem changes. The SI system is built on base units such as the metre, the kilogram, the second and the ampere, and electrical units such as the volt, the ohm and the watt are derived from them. You will also see the older names M K S, for metre, kilogram, second, and C G S, for centimetre, gram, second. Before substituting values into any equation, make the units compatible. A unit conversion changes the number but never the physical quantity: 0.24 metres is 24 centimetres, the same length described in a smaller unit, so it needs a bigger number.
segments.expand: Explain why using a smaller unit always needs a larger number for the same quantity.

check.q: 0.24 metres is converted to centimetres. What does the segment say happens to the number?
options: It gets bigger, because the unit got smaller
It gets smaller, because the unit got smaller
It stays the same, because the length is the same
check.again: A conversion changes the number, never the physical quantity. Describing the same length in a smaller unit takes more of those units, so 0.24 metres becomes 24 centimetres: a smaller unit, a bigger number. Going the other way, to a larger unit, the number shrinks. The SI system builds everything from base units like the metre, kilogram, second and ampere, with the volt, ohm and watt derived from them; you may also meet the older names M K S and C G S. Before substituting into any equation, make the units compatible.

segments.title: Significant figures and exact numbers
segments.text: Measurements have limited precision, and significant figures communicate it. Writing 22.1 says you know the tenths; writing 22.10 claims you also know the hundredths. The textbook treats quantities stated in its problems as exact, while laboratory measurements are approximate. The counting rules are the ones from class: nonzero digits count, zeros between them count, leading zeros never count, and a trailing zero after the decimal point counts. So 0.004070 has four significant figures, while 8000 on its own is ambiguous; write 8.00 times ten to the three to show three. Exact counts and defined conversions, such as 1000 metres in a kilometre, never limit the figures of a result.
segments.expand: Give three examples of exact numbers that never limit significant figures, and explain why.

check.q: Which of these does the segment say never limits the significant figures of a result?
check.again: Defined conversions, like 1000 metres in a kilometre, and exact counts, like three resistors, are not measurements; they have no uncertainty, so they place no limit on the figures of an answer. Measurements are what limit precision, and the textbook treats the values in its problems as exact while laboratory readings are approximate. The counting rules: nonzero digits count, zeros between them count, leading zeros never count, and a trailing zero after the decimal point counts. So 0.004070 has four figures, and 8000 alone is ambiguous; write 8.00 times ten to the three to show three.

segments.title: Rounding when you combine numbers
segments.text: How many figures a result keeps depends on the operation. For addition and subtraction, first put the quantities in the same unit; then the least precise decimal place limits the answer. For example, 2.36 milliamps plus 410 microamps is 2.36 plus 0.410 milliamps, which is 2.770, reported as 2.77 milliamps if the second reading is good to the thousandths of a milliamp. For multiplication and division, the result ordinarily keeps the fewest significant figures found among the measured inputs. In every case, keep the intermediate digits and round only the final answer. A calculator showing ten digits does not improve the measurements it was given.
segments.expand: Work an addition where one reading limits the result to fewer decimal places than the other.

check.q: In a multiplication or division of measured values, how many significant figures does the result ordinarily keep?
check.again: For products and quotients, the result is only as good as the least precise measured input, so it keeps the fewest significant figures found among them: 7.2 volts over 2.40 kilohms gives 3.0 milliamps, two figures, because 7.2 has only two. Addition and subtraction follow a different rule, the least precise decimal place after putting everything in the same unit: 2.36 milliamps plus 410 microamps is 2.36 plus 0.410, which is 2.77 milliamps. In every case, keep the intermediate digits and round once at the end. Ten digits on a calculator do not improve the measurements it was given.

segments.title: Powers of ten and their rules
segments.text: Powers of ten make very large and very small quantities manageable, and each operation has its own exponent rule. To multiply, add the exponents: ten to the three times ten to the three is ten to the six. To divide, subtract them. To raise a power to a power, multiply them: ten to the three, cubed, is ten to the nine. Notice that those two examples differ, and mixing them up is a common error. Addition is different again: you cannot add exponents across a sum. First match the exponents, then add the coefficients: 3.2 times ten to the three plus 4.8 times ten to the two becomes 3.2 plus 0.48, times ten to the three, which is 3.68 times ten to the three.
segments.expand: Work one example each of multiplying, dividing, and raising a power of ten to a power.

check.q: Ten to the three, cubed, is what?
check.again: Raising a power to a power means multiplying the exponents: three times three is nine, so ten to the three cubed is ten to the nine, a billion. Ten to the six would be the answer to a different question, ten to the three times ten to the three, where you add the exponents. Mixing those two up is a common error. Division subtracts exponents. Addition follows none of these: match the exponents first. 3.2 times ten to the three plus 4.8 times ten to the two is 3.2 plus 0.48, times ten to the three, which is 3.68 times ten to the three.

segments.title: Scientific and engineering notation
segments.text: Both notations write a number as a coefficient times a power of ten. Scientific notation keeps the coefficient from 1 up to 10. Engineering notation lets the coefficient run from 1 up to just under 1000 but restricts the exponent to multiples of three, so each power lines up with an SI prefix: giga, ten to the nine; mega, six; kilo, three; then milli, micro, nano and pico for minus three, six, nine and twelve. Capital M and lowercase m differ by a factor of a billion, so capitalization matters. For example, 0.0000470 amps is 4.70 times ten to the minus five amps in scientific form, and 47.0 microamps in engineering form. The same three figures appear in every version.
segments.expand: Convert 0.000674 and 50,420 into both scientific and engineering notation.

check.q: In engineering notation, the coefficient may run over what range?
check.again: Scientific notation keeps the coefficient between 1 and 10, so the exponent can be anything. Engineering notation instead pins the exponent to a multiple of three, matching the SI prefixes, and to make that possible the coefficient is allowed to run from 1 up to just under 1000. Take 0.0000470 amps: scientific form is 4.70 times ten to the minus five; engineering form is 47.0 times ten to the minus six, which is 47.0 microamps. The same three figures survive in every version. Capital M and lowercase m differ by a factor of a billion, so capitalization matters.

segments.title: Converting between prefixes
segments.text: When you change the prefix, you must make a compensating change in the number. Move to a larger unit and the number gets smaller; move to a smaller unit and the number gets larger. For example, 20 kilohertz is 0.02 megahertz, a larger unit and a smaller number. Going the other way, 0.08 milliseconds is 80 microseconds, because each millisecond holds 1000 microseconds. Likewise 2.40 milliseconds is 2400 microseconds. A quick check keeps you safe: after converting, ask whether the number moved in the right direction for the size of the new unit. If you went to a bigger unit and the number grew, something is backwards.
segments.expand: Give me four prefix conversions to do in my head, mixing larger and smaller target units.

check.q: Convert 0.08 milliseconds to microseconds.
check.again: Each millisecond holds 1000 microseconds, so moving to the smaller unit multiplies the number by 1000: 0.08 times 1000 is 80 microseconds. The direction check confirms it: you went to a smaller unit, so the number should grow, and 80 is bigger than 0.08. Eight microseconds would be a factor of ten out. The reverse case: 20 kilohertz is 0.02 megahertz, a larger unit and a smaller number. After every conversion, ask whether the number moved the right way for the size of the new unit; if it went to a bigger unit and grew, something is backwards.

segments.title: Conversion factors
segments.text: A conversion factor is a ratio of two equal quantities, so it equals one, and multiplying by it changes the units without changing the quantity. To convert 1.5 minutes to seconds, multiply by 60 seconds per minute: 90 seconds. Arrange the factor so the unwanted unit cancels. For areas, the whole conversion is squared: 2.50 square millimetres is 2.50 times ten to the minus three, squared, square metres, which is 2.50 times ten to the minus six square metres. For volumes, cube it. Forgetting to square the factor for an area is a classic error, and it will matter in Chapter 3 when wire cross-sections appear in resistance calculations.
segments.expand: Explain why an area conversion needs the length factor squared, with a square-centimetre example.

check.q: 2.50 square millimetres is converted to square metres. What is it?
options: 2.50 times ten to the minus six
2.50 times ten to the minus three
2.50 times ten to the minus nine
check.again: A conversion factor is a ratio of two equal quantities, so it equals one and changes only the units. A millimetre is ten to the minus three metres, but an area is length times length, so the whole factor gets squared: ten to the minus three, squared, is ten to the minus six. So 2.50 square millimetres is 2.50 times ten to the minus six square metres. Forgetting to square the factor gives minus three, a thousand times too big, and that error matters in chapter three where wire cross-sections enter the resistance formula. For a volume, cube the factor.

segments.title: Rounding off
segments.text: Rounding reduces the reported digits to a chosen precision. Check the digit just after the last one you want to keep. If it is 5 or more, round the kept digit up; if it is less than 5, leave it alone. To tenths, 14.6026 becomes 14.6, because the next digit is 0. To hundredths, 56.0420 becomes 56.04. Rounding can carry: 12.96 to three significant figures becomes 13.0, and that final zero must stay to show three figures. Truncating, simply chopping digits off, is not rounding and biases results low. Round once, at the end of a calculation, and keep the unrounded values in memory while you work, so small rounding errors do not pile up across several steps.
segments.expand: Round 1046.06 to tenths, hundredths and three significant figures, explaining each.

check.q: Round 56.0420 to the nearest hundredth.
check.again: Check the digit right after the place you are keeping. Keeping hundredths means keeping the 4; the next digit is 2, which is less than 5, so the 4 stays: 56.04. Rounding up to 56.05 would need a 5 or more in the thousandths place. Rounding can carry: 12.96 to three significant figures becomes 13.0, and that final zero must stay. Simply chopping digits off is truncating, not rounding, and it biases results low. Do the rounding once, at the end, and keep unrounded values in the calculator while you work so small errors do not pile up.

segments.title: Calculators and software need judgement
segments.text: The chapter closes with tools. A calculator follows the order of operations exactly as you key it, so brackets must enclose the whole numerator and the whole denominator of a fraction, or you will compute something else entirely. Before trusting any result, estimate its size: a few volts over a few kilohms should come out in milliamps, not amps. Computer analysis and simulation packages are powerful, but they calculate only what the model and your inputs describe. A simulation is a calculation under a model, not proof that a real circuit was wired correctly. Understanding the underlying principles is what lets you spot a wrong input or an unreasonable answer.
segments.expand: Give an example of a missing bracket that silently changes a calculator result.

check.q: The chapter says a simulation result proves that the real circuit was wired correctly.
check.again: A simulation calculates what the model and your inputs describe, nothing more. If the model is wrong, or the values keyed in are wrong, the output is wrong, and it says nothing about whether the physical circuit on the bench matches the drawing. The same judgement applies to a calculator: it follows the order of operations exactly as keyed, so brackets must enclose a whole numerator and a whole denominator, and before trusting any result you should estimate its size; a few volts over a few kilohms should come out in milliamps. Understanding the principles is what lets you catch a bad input.

segments.title: Recap of chapter one
segments.text: Five points from chapter one. One: a quantity is a number with a unit, and units must be compatible before you calculate. Two: significant figures show precision; leading zeros never count, trailing decimal zeros do, and exact numbers never limit a result. Three: sums round to the least precise decimal place, products to the fewest significant figures, and you round only at the end. Four: multiply powers of ten by adding exponents, raise a power by multiplying them, and match exponents before adding. Five: engineering notation uses exponents in steps of three to match the prefixes, and changing a prefix needs a compensating change in the number.
segments.expand: Quiz me on one example from each of the five points.

check.q: The recap says you should round at every step of a calculation to keep the numbers tidy.
check.again: The recap says the opposite: round only at the end. Rounding an intermediate value and reusing it plants an error that can grow through the later steps. Keep the digits, or store the value in memory, and report the final answer to the right precision. The other recap points: a quantity is a number with a unit, and units must be compatible before calculating; leading zeros never count and trailing decimal zeros do; sums round to the least precise decimal place and products to the fewest significant figures; multiply powers of ten by adding exponents and raise a power by multiplying them; and engineering notation matches the prefixes.

lectures.title: Voltage and current
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Textbook/ELTR 238 - Chapter 02 - Voltage and Current - Study Pack.md; quiz study pack; Boylestad §2.2 to §2.10

segments.title: What this chapter covers
segments.text: Chapter two sets out the two quantities everything else is built on: voltage and current. It starts inside the atom, to explain why some materials conduct, then defines voltage as energy per charge and current as charge per time. It surveys the sources that maintain a voltage, explains battery capacity in ampere-hours, compares conductors, insulators and semiconductors, and finishes with how ammeters and voltmeters must be connected. Keep one distinction sharp throughout: voltage concerns energy per charge between two points, and current concerns charge passing per second through a path.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between voltage and current in one sentence each, with units.

check.q: The opening asks you to keep one distinction sharp. Which is it?
options: Voltage is energy per charge; current is charge per time
Voltage is charge per time; current is energy per charge
Voltage and current are both forms of energy
check.again: Chapter two is built on two quantities. Voltage is the energy per unit charge between two points, in joules per coulomb, which are volts. Current is the amount of charge passing through a path each second, in coulombs per second, which are amps. One is about energy between two places; the other is about flow through one place. The chapter reaches them by starting inside the atom to explain conduction, then surveys sources that maintain a voltage, battery capacity in ampere-hours, conductors, insulators and semiconductors, and finally how meters are connected.

segments.title: Atoms, ions and shells
segments.text: Protons carry positive charge and sit in the nucleus with neutral neutrons; electrons carry negative charge around it. The atomic number counts protons, and a neutral atom has as many electrons. Losing electrons makes a positive ion; gaining them makes a negative ion; the proton count does not change. Charge is conserved when it moves between objects. In the shell model, the maximum occupancy of shell n is 2 n squared: 2, 8, 18 and 32 for the first four shells, a capacity limit rather than a strict filling order. Copper has 29 electrons arranged 2, 8, 18 and 1, and that single loosely held outer electron is the start of the story of why copper conducts so well.
segments.expand: Explain how an atom that loses three electrons ends up with a net charge of plus three elementary charges.

check.q: In the shell model, what is the maximum number of electrons in shell number three?
check.again: The capacity of shell n is 2 n squared. For the third shell, n is 3, 3 squared is 9, and 2 times 9 is 18. The first four shells hold at most 2, 8, 18 and 32. That is a capacity limit, not a strict filling order. Copper has 29 electrons arranged 2, 8, 18 and 1, so its single outer electron is loosely held, which begins the story of why copper conducts. Remember also that an ion forms by losing or gaining electrons; the proton count never changes, and charge is conserved when it moves between objects.

segments.title: Coulomb's law
segments.text: For two point charges, Coulomb's law gives the size of the force: a constant, about 8.99 times ten to the nine, times the product of the charges, divided by the distance squared, with force in newtons, charge in coulombs and distance in metres. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract; distance only changes how strong the force is, not which way it acts. Because distance is squared, doubling the separation cuts the force to a quarter, and tripling it cuts the force to one ninth. Plot force against distance and the curve drops steeply, not in a straight line, which is the signature of a squared term in the denominator.
segments.expand: Explain what happens to the force if both charges double and the distance also doubles.

check.q: The separation between two point charges is tripled. The Coulomb force becomes what?
check.again: Coulomb's law: force equals a constant, about 8.99 times ten to the nine, times the product of the charges, divided by the distance squared, with force in newtons, charge in coulombs and distance in metres. Because distance is squared, tripling it multiplies the denominator by nine, so the force is one ninth of what it was. One third would be right only if force fell in simple proportion to distance, which it does not. Doubling the distance gives one quarter. Distance only sets the strength; like charges still repel and unlike charges still attract.

segments.title: Voltage is energy per charge
segments.text: Voltage is a potential difference: the energy change per unit charge between two points. Voltage equals energy divided by charge, so one volt is one joule per coulomb, and 12 volts means 12 joules for every coulomb moved. That is 12 joules per coulomb, not 12 coulombs and not 12 amps. The measurement order matters: V sub A B equals the potential at A minus the potential at B. If A is at 3 volts and B at 8 volts from the same reference, V sub A B is minus 5 volts, which just means the polarity is opposite to the order you chose. An open switch can have a voltage across it with no current at all, and a voltage always exists between two points.
segments.expand: Work an energy example: how much energy moves 8 millicoulombs across 60 volts?

check.q: Point A is at 3 volts and point B at 8 volts from the same reference. What is V sub A B?
check.again: V sub A B equals the potential at A minus the potential at B: 3 minus 8 is minus 5 volts. The negative sign means the real polarity is opposite to the order you named, B is the higher point. Plus 5 would be V sub B A. Voltage is energy per charge between two points: one volt is one joule per coulomb, so 12 volts means every coulomb moved gains or loses 12 joules. It is not a current and not a charge. And a voltage can exist with no current at all, as across an open switch.

segments.title: Current is charge per time
segments.text: Current is the rate at which net charge crosses a surface: current equals charge divided by time, amps from coulombs per second. For a steady current, charge equals current times time. For example, 90 millicoulombs passing in 3 seconds is 30 milliamps. In the external metal circuit of a discharging battery, conventional current runs from the positive terminal, through the load, to the negative terminal, while net electron drift runs the other way. Random thermal motion alone gives no net current; the drift is small and superimposed on it. Direct current means current in one direction, not necessarily perfectly constant in size.
segments.expand: Explain why electrons are already everywhere in the wire, and why a signal does not wait for one to cross the circuit.

check.q: 90 millicoulombs of charge pass a point in 3 seconds. What is the current?
check.again: Current equals charge divided by time: amps from coulombs per second. Ninety millicoulombs over 3 seconds is 30 millicoulombs per second, which is 30 milliamps. Multiplying gives 270, which is not a current, and 3 milliamps is a slip of a factor of ten. For a steady current the relation runs backwards too: charge equals current times time, so 30 milliamps for 3 seconds moves 90 millicoulombs. In the external circuit of a battery, conventional current runs from the positive terminal through the load to the negative terminal, while net electron drift runs the other way.

segments.title: Sources of voltage
segments.text: A source converts some form of energy to maintain a potential difference; the external circuit then decides the current, within the source's limits. Primary cells run on a chemical reaction and are not designed to recharge. Secondary cells use a reversible process and are designed to be recharged with the right method. Fuel cells need a continuing supply of reactants. Photovoltaic cells convert light. Generators convert mechanical input. Regulated supplies condition electrical energy from another supply. On a cell symbol, the long line is positive. The energy a source supplies per coulomb is called its E M F, measured in volts despite the old name electromotive force. Series-aiding cells add: two 1.5 volt flashlight cells give 3 volts.
segments.expand: Compare a primary cell, a secondary cell and a fuel cell in terms of where their energy comes from.

check.q: A secondary cell is designed to be recharged, while a primary cell is not.
check.again: A primary cell runs on a chemical reaction that is not designed to be reversed; when it is spent, it is done. A secondary cell uses a reversible process and is meant to be recharged, with the right method for its chemistry. Neither word says anything about voltage. Other sources: fuel cells need a continuing supply of reactants, photovoltaic cells convert light, generators convert mechanical input, and regulated supplies condition electrical energy from another supply. On a cell symbol the long line is positive, the energy supplied per coulomb is the E M F in volts, and two 1.5 volt cells series-aiding give 3 volts.

segments.title: Ampere-hour capacity
segments.text: A battery's capacity in ampere-hours measures charge; one ampere-hour is 3600 coulombs. The ideal run time is the capacity divided by a constant load current: hours from ampere-hours over amps. A 2.0 ampere-hour battery at a steady 0.25 amps gives about 8 hours; a 1.20 ampere-hour battery at 60 milliamps gives about 20 hours. These estimates assume the full rated capacity is usable at that current. Real capacity depends on discharge rate, temperature, age and the cutoff voltage, which discharge curves show. And capacity is charge, not energy: a 12 volt, 2 ampere-hour battery represents roughly 24 watt-hours, not 24 watts.
segments.expand: Explain why a battery delivers fewer ampere-hours in freezing weather or at high current.

check.q: A 1.20 ampere-hour battery supplies a steady 60 milliamps. What is the ideal run time?
check.again: Run time equals capacity divided by load current, hours from ampere-hours over amps. Sixty milliamps is 0.060 amps, and 1.20 over 0.060 is 20 hours. Seventy two would come from multiplying 1.2 by 60, and 2 hours drops a factor of ten. The estimate assumes the full rated capacity is usable at that current; real capacity depends on discharge rate, temperature, age and cutoff voltage. And ampere-hours are charge, one ampere-hour being 3600 coulombs, not energy: a 12 volt, 2 ampere-hour battery represents about 24 watt-hours, never 24 watts.

segments.title: Conductors, insulators, semiconductors
segments.text: Conductors readily support current because they have many mobile carriers; copper wiring is the everyday example. Insulators have very low conductivity under their intended conditions, like a wire's plastic jacket, but a strong enough field can make an insulator break down and conduct; its breakdown strength tells you how much voltage a given thickness can withstand. Semiconductors sit between the two, and their conductivity can be controlled by doping, temperature, light or fields. In semiconductors, current can be carried by electrons and by holes, which are electron vacancies that behave like mobile positive carriers. Silicon and germanium each have four valence electrons.
segments.expand: Explain what a hole is and why it behaves like a positive charge carrier.

check.q: An insulator can never conduct, no matter how strong the electric field across it becomes.
check.again: An insulator has very low conductivity under its intended conditions, like the plastic jacket on a wire, but push the field high enough and it breaks down and conducts. Its breakdown strength says how much voltage a given thickness can withstand. Conductors, such as copper, have many mobile carriers. Semiconductors sit between, with conductivity controlled by doping, temperature, light or fields; silicon and germanium each have four valence electrons, and current in them can be carried by electrons and by holes, vacancies that behave like mobile positive carriers.

segments.title: Connecting ammeters and voltmeters
segments.text: A voltmeter connects across the two points of interest, in parallel, and its reading is the red lead's potential minus the black lead's. Ideally its resistance is infinite, so it draws no current. An ammeter is inserted in series with the branch, so the branch current passes through it; ideally its resistance is zero. Real voltmeters take a little current and real ammeters drop a little voltage, called burden voltage. Never connect a current-mode meter straight across a supply: it can act as a short circuit. For current measurement, switch off, insert the meter in the correct fused input, then energize. An analog meter reads the fraction of full scale times the range: six tenths of full scale on a 5 volt range is 3 volts.
segments.expand: Walk through the safe sequence for measuring a branch current and then switching back to voltage.

check.q: An analog voltmeter needle sits at six tenths of full scale on the 5 volt range. What is the reading?
check.again: An analog meter reads the fraction of full scale times the selected range: six tenths of 5 volts is 3 volts. The fraction alone, 0.6, is not a voltage until you multiply by the range. The connection rules from the same segment: a voltmeter goes across the two points, in parallel, reading red minus black, ideally with infinite resistance; an ammeter goes in series so the branch current passes through it, ideally with zero resistance. Real ammeters drop a small burden voltage. Never place a current-mode meter across a supply, and for current, switch off, insert the meter in the fused input, then energize.

segments.title: Sources in everyday equipment
segments.text: A flashlight is the simplest complete circuit: two 1.5 volt cells in series aiding give 3 volts, a switch completes or breaks the path, and the bulb is the load. With the switch open there is voltage across it but no current; closed, current flows and the bulb lights. A plug-in D C supply converts the wall's alternating supply into a steady D C output within its ratings, and its label gives a voltage and a maximum current, not a current it forces out. A charger must suit the cell chemistry; matching the voltage alone is not enough. When a circuit behaves oddly, check the source first: its polarity, its actual terminal voltage, and whether its path is complete.
segments.expand: Walk through the flashlight circuit with the switch open and closed, stating the current and the switch voltage.

check.q: In the flashlight circuit with the switch open, there is a voltage across the switch but no current.
check.again: Two 1.5 volt cells in series aiding give 3 volts, the switch completes or breaks the path, and the bulb is the load. With the switch open there is no complete path, so no current flows and the bulb is dark, yet the full source voltage sits across the open switch contacts. Close the switch and current flows and the bulb lights. The same segment notes that a plug-in D C supply's label gives a voltage and a maximum current, not a current it forces out, and that when a circuit misbehaves you check the source first: polarity, actual terminal voltage, and a complete path.

segments.title: Recap of chapter two
segments.text: Five points from chapter two. One: atoms hold protons, neutrons and electrons; losing electrons makes a positive ion, and copper's lone outer electron makes it a good conductor. Two: Coulomb force is proportional to the product of the charges and falls with distance squared. Three: voltage is energy per charge, one volt being one joule per coulomb, always between two points; current is charge per time, one amp being one coulomb per second, with conventional current opposite electron drift. Four: sources convert energy; capacity in ampere-hours gives run time as ampere-hours over amps. Five: voltmeters go across, ammeters go in series, and never put an ammeter across a supply.
segments.expand: Quiz me on units: coulombs, amps, volts, joules and ampere-hours.

check.q: According to the recap, which direction does conventional current run compared with electron drift?
options: The same way as electron drift
At right angles to electron drift
check.again: Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move, and in the external circuit of a battery it runs from the positive terminal through the load to the negative terminal. Electrons carry negative charge, so their net drift is the other way. Both describe one flow. The recap's other points: losing electrons makes a positive ion and copper's lone outer electron makes it a good conductor; Coulomb force goes with the product of the charges and falls with distance squared; one volt is one joule per coulomb and one amp is one coulomb per second; and voltmeters go across while ammeters go in series.

lectures.title: Resistance
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Textbook/ELTR 238 - Chapter 03 - Resistance and Resistor Selection - Study Pack.md; quiz study pack; Boylestad §3.2 to §3.8, §3.12, §3.13

segments.title: What this chapter covers
segments.text: Chapter three asks what sets the resistance of a wire or a component. Material and geometry come first: longer means more resistance, thicker means less. Temperature changes resistance too. Then the chapter turns to practical resistors: types, ratings, potentiometers, colour codes, standard values and surface-mount markings. It introduces conductance, the reciprocal of resistance, explains how an ohmmeter must be used, and ends with devices whose resistance is designed to change, such as thermistors and light-dependent cells. Keep one distinction clear from the start: resistance belongs to a particular object, while resistivity belongs to its material.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between resistance and resistivity using two copper wires of different lengths.

check.q: Resistivity belongs to the material, while resistance belongs to a particular object.
check.again: Resistivity is a property of the material itself: copper has one value, aluminium another, whatever shape the piece is. Resistance belongs to a particular object and depends on the material and the geometry: longer means more resistance, thicker means less, and temperature changes it too. That is the chapter's starting point, before it moves on to practical resistors, their types and ratings, potentiometers, colour codes, standard values and surface-mount markings, then conductance as the reciprocal of resistance, the correct use of an ohmmeter, and devices built to change resistance such as thermistors.

segments.title: Material and geometry
segments.text: For a uniform conductor, resistance equals resistivity times length divided by cross-sectional area: ohms from ohm-metres times metres over square metres. The model assumes uniform material, uniform cross-section and a stated temperature. Scaling is often faster than recalculating. Double the length and resistance doubles. Double the area and it halves. Area goes with diameter squared, so double the diameter and resistance drops to a quarter; double both length and diameter and it halves. Reduce the area to a quarter while doubling the length, and resistance rises by a factor of eight: a 0.2 ohm wire becomes 1.6 ohms. Use one consistent unit system for resistivity, length and area.
segments.expand: Work a scaling problem where the length triples and the diameter halves.

check.q: A wire's length is doubled and its cross-sectional area is cut to a quarter. Its resistance changes by what factor?
check.again: Resistance equals resistivity times length divided by area: ohms from ohm-metres times metres over square metres. Doubling the length doubles the resistance. Cutting the area to a quarter multiplies it by four. Together, two times four is eight, so a 0.2 ohm wire becomes 1.6 ohms. Remember that area goes with diameter squared, so doubling the diameter alone drops resistance to a quarter, and doubling both length and diameter halves it. The model assumes uniform material and cross-section at a stated temperature, and one consistent unit system throughout.

segments.title: Circular mils and wire tables
segments.text: American wire tables use the circular mil for area. A mil is one thousandth of an inch, and a circular mil is the area of a circle one mil across, so a round wire's area in circular mils is simply its diameter in mils, squared: a 50 mil wire has 2500 circular mils. That definition already accounts for the circle, so do not multiply by pi over four again. For stranded wire, add the strands' areas. In the wire tables, a higher gauge number means a thinner wire and more resistance per length. Multiply the table's resistance per length by the actual length, and remember a circuit needs a conductor out and a conductor back, so both lengths count. A resistance table alone does not tell you how much current a wire may safely carry.
segments.expand: Explain why a two-wire run needs double the one-way length in a wire-resistance calculation.

check.q: A round wire is 50 mils in diameter. What is its area in circular mils?
check.again: A circular mil is the area of a circle one mil across, and a mil is a thousandth of an inch. That definition already has the circle built in, so the area of a round wire in circular mils is just its diameter in mils, squared: 50 squared is 2500 circular mils. Multiplying by pi over four again, which gives about 1963, is the classic double-counting error. For stranded wire, add the strands' areas. In the wire tables a higher gauge number is a thinner wire with more resistance per length, and a circuit needs conductor out and back, so both lengths count.

segments.title: Temperature effects
segments.text: Most metals, copper included, have a positive temperature coefficient near room temperature: resistance rises as they warm. Over a limited range, a straight-line model works: the new resistance equals the reference resistance times one plus the coefficient times the temperature change. For example, 100 ohms at 20 degrees with a coefficient of 0.004 per degree, warmed to 70 degrees, changes by 50 degrees: 100 times one plus 0.2, which is 120 ohms. Use the change in temperature, not the final temperature. A coefficient in parts per million per degree gives the fractional change directly: 100 parts per million over a 40 degree rise is 0.4 percent. The book's inferred absolute temperature is just where the extrapolated line would hit zero, not absolute zero.
segments.expand: Work the resistance of a 10 ohm copper wire warmed from 20 to 60 degrees at 0.00393 per degree.

check.q: A 100 ohm copper resistor at 20 degrees, coefficient 0.004 per degree, warms to 70 degrees. What is its resistance?
check.again: The straight-line model: new resistance equals reference resistance times one plus the coefficient times the temperature change, with resistance in ohms, the coefficient in per degree and the change in degrees. The change is 70 minus 20, 50 degrees. 0.004 times 50 is 0.2, so the resistance is 100 times 1.2, which is 120 ohms. Using the final temperature of 70 instead of the change gives the wrong 128 ohms. A coefficient in parts per million works the same way: 100 parts per million over a 40 degree rise is a 0.4 percent change.

segments.title: Types and specifications of resistors
segments.text: A practical resistor has several independent specifications. The nominal resistance is the marked target value. The tolerance is the permitted initial deviation from it. The temperature coefficient describes drift with temperature. The power rating is the dissipation it can handle under stated mounting and temperature conditions. And the working voltage rating limits the voltage applied. Film resistors use a resistive film; wirewound resistors use resistance wire, and construction affects power handling, precision, noise and high-frequency behaviour. Within one product family a larger body often means more power handling, but size and colour alone never identify the value or all the ratings; check the data sheet.
segments.expand: Explain why two resistors with the same resistance can have very different power ratings.

check.q: The segment says a resistor's body size and colour are enough to identify its value and all of its ratings.
check.again: A practical resistor has several independent specifications: nominal resistance, tolerance, temperature coefficient, power rating under stated mounting and temperature conditions, and working voltage rating. Within one product family a larger body often handles more power, but size and colour never tell you the value or the full set of ratings; the data sheet does. Construction matters too: film resistors use a resistive film, wirewound resistors use resistance wire, and the choice affects power handling, precision, noise and high-frequency behaviour. Treat each specification as a separate question.

segments.title: Potentiometers and rheostats
segments.text: A potentiometer has two track ends and a wiper. Ideally, its end-to-end resistance stays fixed while the two wiper-to-end resistances vary and always add to that total. A 10 kilohm pot with 3 kilohms between one end and the wiper has 7 kilohms on the other side. Using all three terminals gives a voltage divider: across 5 volts, the unloaded voltage across the 3 kilohm section is 5 volts times 3 over 10, 1.5 volts. Using just the wiper and one end gives a two-terminal variable resistance, called a rheostat connection. A connected load can change the divider's output, and terminal locations must be identified from the device, not assumed from appearance.
segments.expand: Explain how to wire a potentiometer as a rheostat and what happens at each end of its travel.

check.q: A 10 kilohm pot has 5 volts across its ends. The unloaded voltage across a 3 kilohm section is what?
check.again: With all three terminals in use, the pot is a voltage divider: the unloaded voltage across a section equals the total voltage times that section's resistance over the whole track. Five volts times 3 over 10 is 1.5 volts, and the other 7 kilohm section takes the remaining 3.5 volts. The two wiper-to-end resistances always add to the end-to-end total: 3 plus 7 is 10 kilohms. Using only the wiper and one end gives a two-terminal variable resistance, the rheostat connection. A connected load can pull the divider output down, and terminals must be identified from the device.

segments.title: Colour codes and tolerance
segments.text: A four-band resistor reads digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance; a five-band one reads three digits, then multiplier, then tolerance. The digit colours run black 0 through white 9, with brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7 and grey 8. Gold as a multiplier means times one tenth and silver times one hundredth; as tolerance, gold is 5 percent, silver 10 percent, brown 1 percent, red 2 percent, and no band 20 percent. Brown, black, orange, gold is 10 kilohms plus or minus 5 percent, so anything from 9.5 to 10.5 kilohms is in tolerance. Red, violet, orange, gold is 27 kilohms, allowed from about 25.65 to 28.35 kilohms.
segments.expand: Drill me on three colour codes, one with a gold multiplier band.

check.q: A resistor reads red, violet, orange, gold. What is its nominal value and tolerance?
check.again: Four bands read digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Red is 2, violet is 7, so the digits give 27. Orange as a multiplier is ten to the three, so 27 thousand ohms, 27 kilohms. Gold as a tolerance is 5 percent, which allows anything from about 25.65 to 28.35 kilohms. Silver would be 10 percent, brown 1 percent, red 2 percent, and no band 20 percent. A red multiplier would have made it 2.7 kilohms. As multipliers, gold means times one tenth and silver times one hundredth. Five-band parts read three digits, then multiplier, then tolerance.

segments.title: Standard values and surface-mount codes
segments.text: Resistors are made in preferred-value series that repeat every decade. The E12 series is 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68 and 82, times powers of ten; E24 offers more choices per decade for tighter tolerances. The series name does not replace a part's stated tolerance. Surface-mount resistors often carry a three-digit code: the first two digits are significant and the third is the power of ten. So 472 means 47 times ten to the two, 4.7 kilohms, while 470 means 47 ohms, and 473 would be 47 kilohms. Some manufacturers use a letter and digit scheme instead, which needs its own lookup table.
segments.expand: Decode three surface-mount codes, including one ending in zero.

check.q: A surface-mount resistor is marked 472. What is its value?
check.again: In the three-digit code the first two digits are significant and the third is the power of ten. So 472 is 47 times ten to the two, 4700 ohms, which is 4.7 kilohms. Reading the three digits as a plain number, 472 ohms, is the common mistake. By the same rule 470 is 47 ohms and 473 is 47 kilohms. Some makers use a letter and digit scheme that needs its own table. Resistors also come in preferred series: E12 is 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68 and 82 times powers of ten, and E24 offers more values per decade.

segments.title: Conductance and the ohmmeter
segments.text: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance: G equals one over R, in siemens, where one siemens is one per ohm. For a 2 kilohm resistor, G is one over 2000 ohms, 0.0005 siemens, which is 0.5 millisiemens: the reciprocal of a kilohm is a millisiemens. An ohmmeter measures resistance by applying its own test signal, so the circuit must be de-energized, stored energy discharged, and the resistor isolated by lifting at least one lead if other paths could affect the reading. An O L display can mean an open path or a value beyond the range. A continuity beep only means the resistance is below the meter's threshold. Never apply an ohmmeter to a live circuit.
segments.expand: Explain how an ohmmeter can check whether a fuse is intact or blown.

check.q: An ohmmeter may be applied to a live circuit as long as the voltage is low.
check.again: Never apply an ohmmeter to a live circuit. The meter measures resistance by sending its own small test signal through the part and applying Ohm's law; any outside voltage corrupts the reading and can damage the meter. De-energize the circuit, discharge stored energy, and lift at least one lead of the resistor so parallel paths cannot affect the result. An O L display can mean an open path or a value beyond the range, and a continuity beep only means the resistance is below the meter's threshold. Conductance is one over resistance in siemens: a 2 kilohm resistor is 0.5 millisiemens.

segments.title: Devices whose resistance changes
segments.text: Some devices are built to change resistance. An N T C thermistor's resistance falls as its temperature rises; a P T C thermistor's rises over its intended range; both can respond strongly and non-linearly, and self-heating can disturb a reading. A photoconductive cell, or light-dependent resistor, usually falls in resistance as the light on it increases; it changes resistance, whereas a photovoltaic cell generates electrical output. A varistor is strongly non-linear with voltage and is used to clamp surges within its ratings. A superconductor has zero D C resistance below its critical conditions, a distinct physical state, not the end of a copper wire's straight-line temperature model.
segments.expand: Explain how a thermistor could be used to sense temperature in a simple divider.

check.q: As an N T C thermistor gets hotter, what happens to its resistance?
check.again: N T C stands for negative temperature coefficient: resistance goes down as temperature goes up, often strongly and non-linearly. A P T C thermistor does the reverse over its intended range. Because measuring current warms the device, self-heating can disturb a reading. A photoconductive cell, or light-dependent resistor, usually drops in resistance as light increases; it changes resistance, unlike a photovoltaic cell, which generates output. A varistor is strongly non-linear with voltage and clamps surges. A superconductor has zero D C resistance below its critical conditions, a distinct physical state, not copper's straight line extended to nothing.

segments.title: Recap of chapter three
segments.text: Five points from chapter three. One: resistance equals resistivity times length over area, so it scales up with length and down with area, and a higher gauge number is a thinner wire. Two: copper's resistance rises with temperature, and a straight-line coefficient model works over a limited range using the temperature change. Three: nominal value, tolerance, temperature coefficient, power rating and voltage rating are separate specifications; colour bands and codes give the value and tolerance, and potentiometer segments add to the total. Four: conductance is one over resistance, in siemens, and ohmmeters are for unpowered, isolated parts only. Five: thermistors and light-dependent cells are designed to change resistance.
segments.expand: Give me a quick question on each of the five points.

check.q: The recap says a higher wire gauge number means a thinner wire.
check.again: In the wire tables the gauge numbers run backwards to size: a higher number is a thinner wire, with less cross-sectional area and therefore more resistance per length, since resistance equals resistivity times length over area. The recap's other points: copper's resistance rises with temperature, modelled over a limited range with the temperature change, not the final temperature; nominal value, tolerance, temperature coefficient, power rating and voltage rating are separate specifications, with colour bands giving value and tolerance; conductance is one over resistance in siemens; ohmmeters are for unpowered, isolated parts; and thermistors are designed to change resistance.

lectures.title: Ohm's law, power and energy
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Textbook/ELTR 238 - Chapter 04 - Ohm's Law, Power and Energy - Study Pack.md; quiz study pack; Boylestad §4.1 to §4.7

segments.title: What this chapter covers
segments.text: Chapter four connects voltage, current and resistance through Ohm's law, and then asks what that means for energy. We cover Ohm's law and its rearrangements, reading its graph, power as the rate of energy transfer and its sign, the three power formulas for a resistor and what they say about ratings, energy over time and its cost, efficiency, and the protective devices that keep circuits safe. Unless stated otherwise, the examples use steady D C and ideal connections. Throughout, keep asking two questions: which element does each quantity belong to, and what is held fixed when something changes?
segments.expand: Explain why asking what stays fixed is essential when predicting how power changes.

check.q: The opening says to keep asking two questions throughout. One is which element each quantity belongs to. What is the other?
options: What is held fixed when something changes
How many significant figures to keep
check.again: Chapter four links voltage, current and resistance through Ohm's law and then asks what that means for energy: rearranging Ohm's law, reading its graph, power as the rate of energy transfer with its sign, the three power formulas and ratings, energy over time and its cost, efficiency, and protective devices. Two questions guard every step. First, which element does this voltage or current belong to, so you never pair a supply voltage with the wrong resistor. Second, what stays fixed when something changes, because doubling the resistance halves the power at fixed voltage but doubles it at fixed current.

segments.title: Applying Ohm's law
segments.text: For a resistor, with the current reference entering the terminal marked plus, voltage equals current times resistance, current equals voltage over resistance, and resistance equals voltage over current. Use the voltage across that resistor and the current through it; a supply voltage can only be used directly when it is the same as the resistor's voltage. A 4.7 kilohm resistor with 12 volts across it carries 12 over 4.7, about 2.55 milliamps, because volts over kilohms gives milliamps. At fixed resistance, doubling the voltage doubles the current; at fixed voltage, doubling the resistance halves it. A starter motor of only 40 milliohms on a 12 volt battery draws 12 over 0.04, a startling 300 amps.
segments.expand: Work three quick Ohm's law problems, one solving for each of voltage, current and resistance.

check.q: A 4.7 kilohm resistor has 12 volts across it. What current does it carry?
check.again: Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance, current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Twelve volts over 4700 ohms is about 0.00255 amps. The shortcut: volts over kilohms gives milliamps directly, so 12 over 4.7 is about 2.55 milliamps. Fifty six would come from multiplying, and amps forgets the kilo. Compare the starter motor: 12 volts across only 40 milliohms, 12 over 0.04, draws 300 amps. At fixed resistance, doubling the voltage doubles the current; at fixed voltage, doubling the resistance halves it.

segments.title: Open circuits and short circuits
segments.text: Ohm's law also explains the two extreme loads. An ideal open circuit is an infinite resistance: current equals voltage over infinity, which is zero, even though the full voltage can appear across the gap. A short circuit is a very small resistance: current equals voltage over a tiny number, which is large, limited only by the source and whatever resistance remains in the path. The 40 milliohm starter motor drawing 300 amps from 12 volts is close to that territory. An ideal voltage source with an ideal zero-resistance short would demand an infinite current, a sign the ideal model has been pushed past its limits; in reality, the source's internal resistance and the wiring set the current.
segments.expand: Explain why shorting a car battery with a metal spanner is dangerous, using Ohm's law.

check.q: An ideal voltage source across an ideal zero-resistance short would demand an infinite current.
check.again: Ohm's law says current equals voltage over resistance, and dividing a fixed voltage by zero resistance gives no finite answer, so the ideal model breaks down; that infinite current is a signal you have pushed the model past its limits. In reality the source's internal resistance and the wiring resistance set the current, which is still dangerously large. The other extreme is the open circuit: an infinite resistance gives zero current even though the full voltage can appear across the gap. The 40 milliohm starter motor drawing 300 amps from 12 volts is near short-circuit territory.

segments.title: Reading the Ohm's law graph
segments.text: With voltage on the vertical axis and current on the horizontal, an ohmic resistor gives a straight line through the origin, and its slope, change in voltage over change in current, is the resistance; a greater resistance is a steeper line. Swap the axes and the slope becomes conductance, so a greater resistance is then a shallower line. Always check the axes and their prefixes. A line through 2 milliamps at 4 volts and 5 milliamps at 10 volts has a slope of 6 volts over 3 milliamps, which is 2 kilohms. For a non-linear device, the ratio of voltage to current at one operating point and the local slope near that point are different numbers, so one constant resistance cannot describe it.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between the static resistance and the local slope of a diode's curve.

check.q: A resistor's line passes through 2 milliamps at 4 volts and 5 milliamps at 10 volts. What is its resistance?
check.again: With voltage on the vertical axis and current on the horizontal, the slope is the change in voltage over the change in current, and that slope is the resistance: ohms from volts over amps. From the first point to the second, the voltage rises by 6 volts while the current rises by 3 milliamps. Six volts over 3 milliamps is 2 volts per milliamp, which is 2 kilohms, because of the milli on the current axis; 2 ohms forgets the prefix. Always read the axes and their prefixes first. Swap the axes and the slope becomes conductance, so a bigger resistance is a shallower line.

segments.title: Power and its sign
segments.text: Power is the rate of energy transfer: energy over time, one watt being one joule per second. Combining voltage as energy per charge with current as charge per time gives power equals voltage times current for steady D C. Signs record the direction of transfer. With the current reference entering the positive terminal, positive power means the element absorbs energy and negative means it delivers. A 12 volt source delivering 2 amps out of its positive terminal delivers 24 watts, so its absorbed power is minus 24 watts, and the load absorbs plus 24 watts. A negative absorbed power is not a negative amount of heating; it means the element is supplying energy.
segments.expand: Work the power bookkeeping for a source and one resistor, and show the powers sum to zero.

check.q: A 12 volt source delivers 2 amps out of its positive terminal. What is its absorbed power?
check.again: Power equals voltage times current, watts from volts times amps: 12 times 2 is 24 watts. The sign records direction. With the current reference entering the positive terminal, positive power means absorbing energy and negative means delivering it. The source pushes current out of its positive terminal, so its absorbed power is minus 24 watts, and the load absorbs plus 24 watts. Minus 24 does not mean negative heating; it means the source is supplying 24 joules every second. Power is the rate of energy transfer, one watt being one joule per second.

segments.title: Three power formulas and ratings
segments.text: For a resistor, power equals V times I, which equals I squared times R, which equals V squared over R. Choose the form that uses what you know. A 1 kilohm resistor across 12 volts dissipates 12 squared over 1000, 144 milliwatts. An eighth of a watt part, 125 milliwatts, is not enough; a quarter watt part passes this nominal check, though a real choice also considers temperature derating, tolerance, supply variation and working voltage. A resistor must satisfy both its power limit and its voltage limit. And a supply rated 12 volts, 2 amps can provide up to 24 watts; it does not force every load to draw 2 amps.
segments.expand: Work the maximum voltage allowed across a 100 ohm, quarter watt resistor.

check.q: A 1 kilohm resistor sits across 12 volts. Is an eighth of a watt part enough?
check.again: Power equals voltage squared over resistance, watts from volts squared over ohms: 12 squared is 144, over 1000 is 0.144 watts, 144 milliwatts. An eighth of a watt is 125 milliwatts, less than that, so it fails; a quarter watt part passes this nominal check, though a real choice also allows for temperature derating, tolerance, supply variation and working voltage. The other two faces, V times I and I squared R, give the same 144 milliwatts. A resistor has to satisfy both its power limit and its voltage limit, and a 12 volt, 2 amp supply can give up to 24 watts without forcing any load to draw 2 amps.

segments.title: Scaling needs a fixed condition
segments.text: Before predicting how power changes, name what stays fixed. Double the voltage across a fixed resistance and the power becomes four times as large, because power equals voltage squared over resistance. Double the current through a fixed resistance and power again quadruples, from current squared times resistance. Double the resistance at a fixed voltage and power halves. Double the resistance at a fixed current and power doubles. These answers look contradictory until you notice the fixed quantity differs. It is also why a small rise in supply voltage can push a resistor past its rating: the square law amplifies the change.
segments.expand: Explain why doubling resistance halves power in one case but doubles it in another.

check.q: The resistance is doubled while the current through it is held fixed. What happens to the power?
check.again: Name what is fixed before predicting. With the current fixed, use power equals current squared times resistance: the current squared does not change, the resistance doubles, so the power doubles. With the voltage fixed instead, power equals voltage squared over resistance, and doubling the resistance halves the power. Quadrupling happens when you double the voltage at fixed resistance, or double the current at fixed resistance, because of the square. The answers only look contradictory until you notice which quantity was held still, and that square law is why a small supply rise can overrun a rating.

segments.title: Energy and its cost
segments.text: For constant power, energy equals power times time. Watts times seconds give joules; watts times hours give watt-hours; kilowatts times hours give kilowatt-hours. One watt-hour is 3600 joules, and one kilowatt-hour is 3.6 million joules. A kilowatt-hour is energy; a kilowatt per hour would be something else entirely. A 40 watt device running for 3 hours uses 120 watt-hours, which is 0.120 kilowatt-hours. A 750 watt heater running 2 hours a day for 30 days uses 0.75 times 2 times 30, 45 kilowatt-hours; at 15 cents per kilowatt-hour, the energy charge is 6.75 dollars. If a thermostat cycles the heater, use its actual on-time.
segments.expand: Work how long a 1500 watt heater can run on 12 kilowatt-hours, and on 3 kilowatt-hours.

check.q: A 40 watt device runs for 3 hours. How much energy does it use?
check.again: Energy equals power times time: watts times hours give watt-hours, watts times seconds give joules, kilowatts times hours give kilowatt-hours. Forty watts times 3 hours is 120 watt-hours, which is 0.120 kilowatt-hours or 432 thousand joules, since one watt-hour is 3600 joules. Watts alone are a rate, not an amount, so 120 watts is the wrong kind of quantity. A kilowatt-hour is energy; a kilowatt per hour would be something else. The heater example: 750 watts for 2 hours a day over 30 days is 45 kilowatt-hours, which at 15 cents each costs 6.75 dollars.

segments.title: Efficiency
segments.text: At steady operation, input power equals useful output power plus losses. Efficiency is useful output over input, as a decimal, or times 100 for percent. A motor taking 100 watts electrically and delivering 80 watts mechanically is 80 percent efficient, with 20 watts of loss; that loss is energy turned into unwanted forms, not destroyed. For stages in cascade, each feeding the next, the overall efficiency is the product of the stage efficiencies as decimals: an 80 percent stage then a 90 percent stage give 0.8 times 0.9, 72 percent. Averaging or multiplying the percentages as whole numbers gives nonsense. Mechanical horsepower is about 746 watts, so a 1 horsepower motor at 80 percent needs about 933 watts in.
segments.expand: Work a three-stage cascade and find the power lost at each stage for a 100 watt input.

check.q: An 80 percent efficient stage feeds a 90 percent efficient stage. What is the overall efficiency?
check.again: Efficiency is useful output over input, as a decimal or times 100 for percent. For stages in cascade, the overall efficiency is the product of the stage efficiencies as decimals: 0.8 times 0.9 is 0.72, so 72 percent. Averaging the percentages to 85 or adding them to 170 gives nonsense; nothing can exceed 100 percent. Losses are energy turned into unwanted forms, not destroyed: a motor taking 100 watts and delivering 80 watts mechanically loses 20 watts as heat. One horsepower is about 746 watts, so a 1 horsepower motor at 80 percent needs about 933 watts in.

segments.title: Fuses, breakers and GFCIs
segments.text: Protective devices answer specific conditions. A fuse responds to excessive current for a duration set by its time-current characteristic; its element melts open, and after the fault is fixed it is replaced with the correct rating. A conventional circuit breaker responds to overcurrent, thermally or magnetically, and can be reset. A ground fault circuit interrupter responds to something different: an imbalance between the outgoing and returning current, meaning some current is returning by another path. It can react to leakage far smaller than a breaker's trip level. None of these holds current exactly at its printed rating, and fitting a higher-rated fuse is never a fix for a fault.
segments.expand: Explain why a GFCI can trip on a small leakage that would never trip an ordinary breaker.

check.q: A ground fault circuit interrupter responds to an imbalance between outgoing and returning current, not simply to overcurrent.
check.again: A fuse and a conventional breaker both answer overcurrent: the fuse's element melts open on a time-current characteristic and is replaced, while the breaker trips thermally or magnetically and can be reset. A ground fault circuit interrupter watches something different: whether the current going out equals the current coming back. If some current is returning by another path, perhaps through a person, the two differ, and the GFCI opens on a leakage far smaller than any breaker's trip level. None of these devices holds current exactly at its rating, and a bigger fuse is never a fix for a fault.

segments.title: Recap of chapter four
segments.text: Five points from chapter four. One: Ohm's law ties the voltage across and the current through the same resistor, and volts over kilohms gives milliamps. Two: on a voltage-against-current graph, slope is resistance; swap the axes and it is conductance. Three: power equals V I, I squared R, or V squared over R; signs show absorption or delivery, and a part's power rating must exceed its dissipation. Four: energy is power times time, and a kilowatt-hour is energy. Five: efficiency is output over input, cascaded efficiencies multiply, fuses and breakers respond to overcurrent, and a GFCI responds to current imbalance.
segments.expand: Quiz me on one problem from each of the five points.

check.q: The recap says a kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.
check.again: A kilowatt-hour is energy: a kilowatt of power sustained for one hour, which is 3.6 million joules. Power is the rate, in watts; energy is power times time. The recap's other points: Ohm's law pairs the voltage across and the current through the same resistor, with volts over kilohms giving milliamps; on a voltage-against-current graph the slope is resistance and swapping the axes gives conductance; power is V I, I squared R or V squared over R, with signs showing absorption or delivery and ratings that must exceed the dissipation; efficiency is output over input and cascades multiply; fuses and breakers answer overcurrent and a GFCI answers imbalance.

lectures.title: Series dc circuits
lectures.source: Boylestad §5.2 to §5.13 as cited by Lectures 02 to 07 and Labs 01 to 02

segments.title: What this chapter covers
segments.text: Chapter five is the series circuit, taught across lectures four to seven. We will define series elements and add their resistances, solve a series circuit for its current and every drop, check that the source's power equals the power dissipated, combine sources in series, apply Kirchhoff's voltage law, and use the voltage divider rule. We will also see why series elements may be interchanged, how single- and double-subscript notation names voltages, why the choice of ground matters, how a source's internal resistance affects its terminal voltage, how meters load a series circuit, and how breadboards implement it.
segments.expand: Explain what makes elements series, and why that single fact produces the rest of the chapter.

check.q: The chapter's opening says that after solving a series circuit, the source's power is checked against what?
options: The total power dissipated by the resistors
The total resistance of the whole chain
The voltage across the largest resistor
check.again: In any resistive circuit the power the source delivers must equal the power the resistors turn into heat, so the chapter lists that comparison as the check on a solved series circuit. Power in each resistor is current squared times resistance, watts from amps squared times ohms, and the source delivers its voltage times the one series current. Take 6 volts across 1 ohm and 2 ohms: the current is 2 amps, the resistors dissipate 4 watts and 8 watts, 12 watts together, and the source supplies 6 times 2, also 12 watts. If the two totals disagree, a drop or the current is wrong.

segments.title: Series resistors
segments.text: Two elements are in series if they share exactly one terminal and nothing else connects at that shared point, so one current passes through both. For series resistors, the total resistance is the sum, and it is what the source sees. For N equal resistors, the total is N times one of them. You can also work backwards: if a three-resistor chain totals 12 kilohms and two of the resistors are 4 and 6 kilohms, the third is 12 minus 10, 2 kilohms. Remember the drawing can mislead; resistors that look side by side are in series if they are joined end to end with nothing else at the joints.
segments.expand: Work a chain of three equal resistors plus one different one, and give the total.
