check.q: A three-resistor series chain totals 12 kilohms. Two of the resistors are 4 and 6 kilohms. What is the third?
check.again: Series resistances add, so the total is the sum of all three. Working backwards, the third resistor is the total minus the known two: 12 minus 4 minus 6 is 2 kilohms. Ten would be the sum of the two known ones, and 22 adds everything. Two elements are in series when they share exactly one terminal with nothing else connected there, so one current passes through both; the drawing can mislead, and side-by-side resistors joined end to end are in series. For N equal resistors, the total is N times one of them.

segments.title: Solving a series circuit
segments.text: The method: find the total resistance, then the source current as the source voltage over the total, then each drop as that current times each resistor. Take a 20 volt source with 2 ohm, 1 ohm and 5 ohm resistors. The total is 8 ohms, so the current is 20 over 8, 2.5 amps, the same through every element. The drops are 2.5 times 2, which is 5 volts; 2.5 times 1, which is 2.5 volts; and 2.5 times 5, which is 12.5 volts. They add up to 20 volts, as they must. With a single source, conventional current leaves the source's positive terminal, and each resistor's plus end is where the current enters it. Change any resistor and the one current changes everywhere.
segments.expand: Explain how to find the direction and polarity of every drop in a single-source series circuit.

check.q: A 20 volt source drives 2, 1 and 5 ohm resistors in series. What is the voltage across the 5 ohm resistor?
check.again: Method: total resistance, then current, then each drop. The total is 2 plus 1 plus 5, 8 ohms. Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance, 20 over 8, 2.5 amps, the same through every element. Each drop is that current times its resistor: 2.5 times 5 is 12.5 volts, with 5 volts on the 2 ohm and 2.5 volts on the 1 ohm. The three add to 20, as they must. Twenty volts would wrongly give the supply voltage to one resistor, and 4 is the supply over the resistor count, which has no meaning. Each resistor's plus end is where the current enters.

segments.title: Power in a series circuit
segments.text: In any resistive circuit, the power delivered by the source equals the total power dissipated by the resistors. Check it on the 20 volt example. The source delivers 20 volts times 2.5 amps, 50 watts. The resistors dissipate current squared times resistance: 2.5 squared is 6.25, so 6.25 times 2 is 12.5 watts, 6.25 times 1 is 6.25 watts, and 6.25 times 5 is 31.25 watts. The sum is 50 watts. In series, the largest resistor dissipates the most power, because the current is common and power equals current squared times resistance. That also tells you which part needs the highest power rating.
segments.expand: Explain why, in series, the largest resistor gets the most power, but in parallel the smallest does.

check.q: In a series circuit the largest resistor dissipates the most power.
check.again: Power in a resistor equals current squared times resistance, watts from amps squared times ohms. In series the current is common to every resistor, so the power is in direct proportion to the resistance: the biggest resistor heats the most, and it is the one that needs the highest power rating. In the 20 volt example with 2.5 amps, 2.5 squared is 6.25, giving 12.5 watts in the 2 ohm, 6.25 watts in the 1 ohm and 31.25 watts in the 5 ohm resistor, 50 watts in all, which equals the source's 20 volts times 2.5 amps. Source power always equals the total dissipated.

segments.title: Voltage sources in series
segments.text: Voltage sources in series can be combined into one equivalent source. Sources aiding each other, each positive terminal joined to the next one's negative terminal, simply add: two 1.5 volt cells make 3 volts, and four make 6 volts. That follows from Kirchhoff's voltage law, and by elements in series, every cell carries the same current. A source connected the other way round opposes the rest, and its voltage subtracts in the loop. Whichever way they face, walk the loop with consistent signs and the net source voltage falls out of the bookkeeping.
segments.expand: Work the net voltage of a 9 volt and a 3 volt source connected in series, first aiding and then opposing.

check.q: A source in a series chain is connected the opposite way round to the others. What happens to its voltage in the loop?
check.again: Sources aiding each other, each positive terminal joined to the next one's negative, add up: two 1.5 volt cells make 3 volts and four make 6. That is Kirchhoff's voltage law at work, and by elements in series every cell carries the same current. A source facing the other way opposes the rest and its voltage subtracts: three aiding 1.5 volt cells plus one reversed give 4.5 minus 1.5, 3 volts net. Whichever way they face, walk the loop with consistent signs and the net source voltage falls out of the bookkeeping.

segments.title: Kirchhoff's voltage law
segments.text: Kirchhoff's voltage law says the algebraic sum of the voltage rises and drops around any closed path is zero, or equivalently, the rises equal the drops. What matters is the polarity you meet as you travel, not whether the element is a source or a resistor: a drop across a source is still a drop. Walk clockwise around a loop with a 16 volt source, and known drops of 4 volts and 9 volts, and the remaining drop must be 16 minus 4 minus 9, which is 3 volts. You can also apply the law to part of a circuit, around any closed path, to find one unknown voltage without solving the whole circuit.
segments.expand: Apply KVL to a loop containing two sources, one of which is met as a drop.

check.q: A loop has a 16 volt source and known drops of 4 volts and 9 volts. What is the remaining drop?
check.again: Kirchhoff's voltage law: the algebraic sum of the rises and drops around any closed path is zero, or equivalently the rises equal the drops. The source supplies a 16 volt rise, so the drops must total 16. Two of them account for 4 plus 9, 13 volts, leaving 16 minus 13, 3 volts for the third. Thirteen is the subtotal, not the answer, and 29 adds everything together. What matters is the polarity you meet as you travel, not what kind of element it is; a drop across a source is still a drop. The law works on any closed path, even part of a circuit.

segments.title: The voltage divider rule
segments.text: In a series circuit, the voltage divides in proportion to resistance: the larger the resistor, the larger its share. The ratio rule says the ratio of two drops equals the ratio of their resistances. The voltage divider rule says the voltage across one resistor equals the total voltage times that resistance over the total resistance. With 45 volts across 2, 5 and 8 kilohms, the total is 15 kilohms; the 2 kilohm resistor takes 45 times 2 over 15, 6 volts, and the 8 kilohm resistor takes 45 times 8 over 15, 24 volts. The rule reaches a voltage in one step without the current, and it gives exactly what Ohm's law plus Kirchhoff's voltage law would give.
segments.expand: Use the divider rule on a 1 ohm and a 2 ohm pair across 9 volts, and check with the current method.

check.q: 45 volts is across 2, 5 and 8 kilohm resistors in series. What does the 2 kilohm resistor take?
check.again: The voltage divider rule: the voltage across one resistor equals the total voltage times that resistance over the total resistance. The total is 2 plus 5 plus 8, 15 kilohms, so the 2 kilohm resistor takes 45 times 2 over 15, which is 6 volts. The 5 kilohm takes 15 volts and the 8 kilohm takes 24, and 6 plus 15 plus 24 returns 45. The larger the resistor, the larger its share, and the ratio of two drops equals the ratio of their resistances. The rule skips the current, but gives exactly what Ohm's law plus Kirchhoff's voltage law would.

segments.title: Interchanging series elements
segments.text: The elements of a series circuit can be interchanged without changing the total resistance, the current, or any element's voltage. Redrawing a circuit with its sources grouped together and its resistors grouped together often makes it easier to solve. The catch is orientation. Moving an element along the path is fine; turning it around is not, because that reverses its polarity in the loop and changes the circuit. So reorder freely, but carry each element's plus and minus with it. This is exactly the third truth of the element container from lecture five.
segments.expand: Show how regrouping a loop with two sources and three resistors simplifies it.

check.q: Series elements may be moved along the path freely, as long as each keeps its own plus and minus orientation.
check.again: Interchanging the elements of a series circuit changes nothing: the total resistance, the one current and every element's voltage all stay the same, which is why grouping the sources together and the resistors together often makes a circuit easier to solve. The one catch is orientation. Sliding an element to a new position is fine; turning it around reverses its polarity in the loop, which is a different circuit. So reorder freely, but carry each element's plus and minus with it. This is exactly the third truth of the element container from lecture five.

segments.title: Single and double subscripts
segments.text: Double-subscript notation names both points: V sub A B is the voltage at A with respect to B, equal to the voltage at A minus the voltage at B. Single-subscript notation names one point and measures it from ground, the reference. So if A is at 16 volts and B at 20 volts, V sub A B is minus 4 volts: B is the higher point. If V sub A B is 5 volts and B sits at 4 volts, A is at 9 volts. And if A is at plus 20 volts and B at minus 15 volts, V sub A B is 20 minus minus 15, 35 volts, like a bank balance going from plus 20 to owing 15. Careful sign handling with negative node voltages is the whole skill.
segments.expand: Work three examples of finding a node voltage from a double-subscript voltage and a known node.

check.q: Point A is at 16 volts and point B at 20 volts. What is V sub A B?
check.again: V sub A B is the voltage at A with respect to B, which is the voltage at A minus the voltage at B: 16 minus 20 is minus 4 volts, meaning B is the higher point. Plus 4 would be V sub B A. Single-subscript voltages are measured from ground, the reference. The same bookkeeping runs both ways: if V sub A B is 5 volts and B is at 4 volts, A is at 9 volts. With negatives, A at plus 20 and B at minus 15 gives 20 minus minus 15, 35 volts, like a bank balance going from plus 20 to owing 15.

segments.title: Ground connection awareness
segments.text: Ground is the reference from which single-subscript voltages are measured, and its symbol on a schematic tells you where the zero is. Moving the ground point to a different node changes every single-subscript voltage by the same amount, but it cannot change any voltage between two nodes, because the shift cancels in the subtraction. In practice the reference usually sits on the negative side of the supply. Integrated circuits and systems often mark their supply and ground connections as single-subscript voltages; the same rule applies. Pick the reference first, and do not move it partway through a problem.
segments.expand: Explain why moving ground changes node voltages but never a voltage across a component.

check.q: The ground point is moved to a different node. What changes?
options: Every node voltage, by the same amount
check.again: Ground is the reference for single-subscript voltages, so moving it shifts every node voltage by one common amount. A voltage between two nodes is a difference, and the shift cancels in the subtraction, so double-subscript voltages are untouched. If every node moves up by 5 volts, V sub A B is still A minus B. In practice the reference usually sits on the negative side of the supply, and integrated circuits mark supply and ground pins as single-subscript voltages under the same rule. Choose the reference first and do not move it partway through.

segments.title: Internal resistance and regulation
segments.text: An ideal supply holds its terminal voltage for any load. A real one behaves as an ideal source in series with an internal resistance, so its terminal voltage falls as the load current rises. With no load, there is no current and no internal drop, so the terminals show the full source voltage. Under load, the lost voltage divided by the load current gives the internal resistance: a battery reading 12 volts unloaded and 10 volts with a 5 ohm load carries 2 amps and loses 2 volts, so its internal resistance is 1 ohm. Voltage regulation expresses the same sag as a percentage: the no-load voltage minus the full-load voltage, over the full-load voltage, times 100. Here, 2 over 10, 20 percent. An ideal supply has zero regulation.
segments.expand: Explain why a smaller voltage regulation figure means a better supply.

check.q: A battery reads 12 volts unloaded and 10 volts with a 5 ohm load. What is its internal resistance?
check.again: Under load, internal resistance equals the lost voltage divided by the load current. The load current is the terminal voltage over the load: 10 volts over 5 ohms, 2 amps. The lost voltage is 12 minus 10, 2 volts. Two volts over 2 amps is 1 ohm. Two ohms is the lost voltage mistaken for a resistance, and 5 ohms is the load itself. With no load there is no current and no internal drop, so the terminals show the full 12 volts. Voltage regulation states the same sag as a percentage: no-load minus full-load, over full-load, times 100, here 2 over 10, 20 percent.

segments.title: Loading effects of instruments
segments.text: An ammeter inserted in a series circuit adds its own internal resistance to the loop. In most circuits that resistance is small next to the others and the effect is negligible, but in a low-resistance circuit it is not. A 12 volt supply across 5 ohms carries 2.4 amps; insert an ammeter with 1 ohm of resistance and the loop becomes 6 ohms, so the meter reads 2 amps. The meter correctly measures the modified circuit, and the difference is its loading effect. Its own voltage drop, current times its resistance, is its burden voltage. Knowing a meter's internal resistance lets you judge when its loading matters.
segments.expand: Work how small an ammeter's resistance must be to change a 10 ohm circuit's current by under 1 percent.

check.q: A 12 volt supply across 5 ohms has an ammeter of 1 ohm inserted. What does the meter read?
check.again: Without the meter, Ohm's law gives 12 volts over 5 ohms, 2.4 amps. Inserting the ammeter adds its 1 ohm to the loop, so the total is 6 ohms and the current becomes 12 over 6, 2 amps. The meter reads 2 amps correctly for the circuit it is now part of; the difference from 2.4 is its loading effect. Its own drop, 2 amps times 1 ohm, 2 volts, is the burden voltage. In most circuits the meter's resistance is small next to the others and this is negligible, but in a low-resistance loop like this one it is not.

segments.title: Protoboards
segments.text: A protoboard, or breadboard, lets you build a circuit without soldering. Its holes are connected in groups by metal strips underneath, typically short strips on each side of a central channel and long rails along the edges, but boards differ, so learn the actual pattern. Holes in one group are one node. To build a series circuit, each component must bridge two different groups, with each shared node being one group. Two holes separated by the central channel or a cut are separate nodes until you add a wire. A resistor with both leads in the same group is shorted out.
segments.expand: Describe how a three-resistor series chain is laid out across breadboard groups, node by node.

check.q: On a protoboard, two holes on opposite sides of the central channel are connected unless you cut the strip.
check.again: It is the other way round: the central channel separates the two sides, so holes across it are different nodes until you add a wire between them. Typically short strips run on each side of the channel and long rails run along the edges, but boards differ, so learn the actual pattern. Holes in one group are one node. To build a series circuit each component must bridge two different groups, with each shared node being one group. A resistor with both leads in the same group is shorted out. A cut in a strip also separates nodes.

segments.title: Recap of chapter five
segments.text: Five points from chapter five. One: series elements share one current; series resistances add; the current is the source voltage over the total, and each drop is that current times its resistance. Two: the source's power equals the sum of the resistor powers, and aiding sources add. Three: Kirchhoff's voltage law, rises equal drops around any closed path; the voltage divider rule gives a drop as the total voltage times its resistance over the total. Four: series elements can be interchanged but not reversed; V sub A B is A minus B, and moving ground shifts node voltages but not differences. Five: real sources sag by current times internal resistance, and meters load the circuits they measure.
segments.expand: Give me a complete series problem to solve in my head: total, current, two drops and a KVL check.

check.q: According to the recap, moving ground shifts what?
check.again: Ground is only the reference for single-subscript voltages, so moving it adds the same offset to every node voltage while every voltage between two nodes stays as it was. The recap's other points: series elements share one current, series resistances add, the current is the source voltage over the total and each drop is that current times its resistance; source power equals the sum of the resistor powers and aiding sources add; rises equal drops around any closed path, and the divider rule gives a drop as the total times its resistance over the total; and real sources sag by current times internal resistance.

lectures.title: Parallel circuits, as far as Lecture 08
lectures.source: Boylestad §6.2, §6.3, §6.5, §6.8, §6.9, §6.12 and the inverse-proportion idea of §6.6, only as taught in Lectures 01 to 08 and Lab 02

segments.title: What this chapter covers, so far
segments.text: This lecture covers the parts of Boylestad's parallel-circuits chapter that class has reached. We define parallel elements and find their total resistance, including the reciprocal formula, the two-resistor shortcut and equal resistors, and we use conductance. We look at a parallel circuit's shared voltage and its branch currents, and at Kirchhoff's current law, which says those currents add to the total. We note how current divides inversely with resistance, revisit open circuits, and see how a voltmeter loads a circuit as a parallel branch. Later parts of the chapter wait for later classes.
segments.expand: Explain the one fact about parallel elements that everything else in this lecture follows from.

check.q: This chapter lecture says a voltmeter loads a circuit in what way?
check.again: A voltmeter connects across the element it measures, so its internal resistance becomes one more branch in parallel with that element. That lowers the combination's resistance and can drop the measured voltage, which is why voltmeter loading belongs in the parallel chapter. The lecture covers the parts of the chapter reached so far: the definition of parallel elements, total resistance by the reciprocal formula, the two-resistor shortcut and equal resistors, conductance, the shared voltage and branch currents, Kirchhoff's current law, inverse current division, open circuits and this loading effect.

segments.title: Parallel elements
segments.text: Two elements, branches or networks are in parallel if they have two points in common. That is the whole definition; the way they are drawn is irrelevant. The same three resistors can be drawn stacked, side by side, or at odd angles, and still be one parallel combination, as long as each connects across the same two nodes. And resistors in neat identical positions can just as easily be wired end to end, in series. The practical routine: identify the two nodes, trace every conductor joined to each, and check that both ends of each element land on the pair. Then redraw the group between two rails if it helps.
segments.expand: Walk through identifying the two common points in an awkwardly drawn three-resistor circuit.

check.q: Two elements are in parallel when they have two points in common, regardless of how they are drawn.
check.again: Two elements, branches or networks are in parallel when they share two points, that is, both ends of each land on the same pair of nodes. Nothing about the drawing enters the definition. The same three resistors can be stacked, side by side or at odd angles and still be one parallel group, while three in neat identical positions can be wired end to end and be in series. The routine is: identify the two nodes, trace every conductor joined to each, check that both ends of every element land on the pair, and redraw between two rails if it helps.

segments.title: Total parallel resistance
segments.text: For parallel resistors, one over the total resistance equals the sum of one over each resistance. The total is always less than the smallest resistor, which is your instant error check, and adding another branch always lowers it. For two resistors, the product over the sum is the shortcut: 3 ohms and 6 ohms give 18 over 9, 2 ohms. For N equal resistors, divide one value by N: three 12 ohm resistors give 4 ohms. For three unequal resistors, apply product over sum twice: 1 ohm and 4 ohms give 4 over 5, 0.8 ohms, and 0.8 ohms with 5 ohms gives 4 over 5.8, about 0.69 ohms. And never forget the final flip in the reciprocal form.
segments.expand: Combine 2, 3 and 6 ohms in parallel using the reciprocal form, then check with product over sum twice.

check.q: 1 ohm, 4 ohms and 5 ohms are in parallel. Using product over sum twice, what is the total?
check.again: Product over sum handles two resistors at a time. First 1 ohm and 4 ohms: 1 times 4 over 1 plus 4 is 4 over 5, 0.8 ohms. Then 0.8 ohms with 5 ohms: 0.8 times 5 over 0.8 plus 5 is 4 over 5.8, about 0.69 ohms. Stopping at 0.8 leaves out the third resistor, and 2.2 is not below the smallest resistor, so the bound rejects it at once. The general rule is one over the total equals the sum of the reciprocals, with a final flip. For N equal resistors, divide one value by N: three 12 ohm resistors give 4 ohms.

segments.title: Conductance in parallel
segments.text: Conductance, G, is one over resistance, measured in siemens. For parallel elements, the total conductance is simply the sum of the branch conductances, just as series resistances add. The 3 ohm and 6 ohm pair: 3 ohms is one third of a siemens and 6 ohms is one sixth; together they make one half siemens, and one over one half is 2 ohms, matching the product over sum result. The branch with the smallest resistance has the largest conductance and dominates the total. In a spreadsheet or in your head, adding conductances is often the quickest route to a parallel total.
segments.expand: Explain which branch dominates a parallel total, and why, using conductance.

check.q: 3 ohms and 6 ohms are in parallel. What is their total conductance?
check.again: Conductance G is one over resistance, in siemens. Three ohms is one third of a siemens, 6 ohms is one sixth, and in parallel conductances simply add: one third plus one sixth is one half siemens. Flip it and the total resistance is 2 ohms, matching product over sum, 18 over 9. Nine siemens would be adding the resistances and calling them conductances, and one ninth is the reciprocal of that. The smallest resistance has the largest conductance and dominates the total. Adding conductances is often the quickest route to a parallel answer, in your head or a spreadsheet.

segments.title: The parallel circuit
segments.text: Connect a source across parallel elements and the voltage across every parallel element is the same: here, the source voltage. The source current equals the source voltage over the total resistance, and each branch current equals that same voltage over its own resistance. With 10 volts across 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms, the branches carry 10 milliamps and 5 milliamps. The total resistance is about 667 ohms, and 10 volts over 667 ohms gives the same 15 milliamps as adding the branches. That agreement is the check. Unlike series, where one current flows and the voltages differ, here one voltage appears and the currents differ.
segments.expand: Work a three-branch parallel circuit and check the source current two ways.

check.q: 10 volts is across 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms in parallel. What current flows in the 2 kilohm branch?
check.again: Every parallel element has the same voltage, here the source's 10 volts. Each branch current is that voltage over its own resistance: volts over kilohms gives milliamps, so the 2 kilohm branch carries 10 over 2, 5 milliamps, and the 1 kilohm branch carries 10 milliamps. Fifteen is the total, not one branch. The check is that the total by branches, 15 milliamps, agrees with the source voltage over the total resistance, 10 volts over about 667 ohms. Series and parallel are mirror images: one current and different voltages, versus one voltage and different currents.

segments.title: Kirchhoff's current law
segments.text: Kirchhoff's current law says the sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving it. It is conservation of charge: in a steady circuit, charge cannot build up at a node. At the top of a parallel group, the source current splits into the branch currents, and at the bottom they recombine. So the branch currents add up to the source current. To find an unknown current at a node, balance what enters against what leaves: with 3 amps and 2 amps entering and 4 amps leaving by one path, 1 amp must leave by the other. Work one node at a time, starting where there is only one unknown.
segments.expand: Work a two-node example where the second node can only be solved after the first.

check.q: Kirchhoff's current law is a statement of conservation of charge: in a steady circuit, charge cannot build up at a node.
check.again: Because charge is conserved and does not pile up at a junction in a steady circuit, whatever enters a node must leave it: the sum of the currents entering equals the sum leaving. At the top of a parallel group the source current splits into the branch currents, and at the bottom they recombine, so the branch currents add to the source current. To find an unknown, balance the node: with 3 amps and 2 amps entering and 4 amps leaving by one path, 1 amp leaves by the other. Work one node at a time, starting where only one current is unknown.

segments.title: How the current divides
segments.text: For parallel branches, the current divides in inverse proportion to resistance: the smaller resistance takes the larger share. Two equal branches split the current equally. A branch with twice the resistance of another carries half its current, so with 1 ohm and 2 ohm branches sharing 6 amps, the split is 4 amps and 2 amps. None of the branches carries zero just for being harder; current takes every available path. When one resistance is far larger than the others, its share is small, and that is the grain of truth in the path-of-least-resistance slogan, but only a grain.
segments.expand: Work the split of 9 milliamps between 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms.

check.q: A 1 ohm branch and a 2 ohm branch share 6 amps. How does the current split?
check.again: Current divides in inverse proportion to resistance: the branch with twice the resistance carries half the current. So the 1 ohm branch carries twice what the 2 ohm branch carries; two parts plus one part make three parts of 6 amps, giving 4 amps in the 1 ohm branch and 2 amps in the 2 ohm branch. Equal splitting only happens for equal branches. And no finite branch carries zero just for being harder; current takes every available path. When one resistance is far larger than the others its share is small, which is the only grain of truth in the least-resistance slogan.

segments.title: Open circuits
segments.text: An open circuit is two isolated terminals with no connection between them. The current through an open circuit is always zero, but the voltage across it can be anything the rest of the circuit establishes. A battery with nothing connected, or an open switch in a series loop, has its full voltage across the gap with no current flowing. The opposite idea, a short circuit, is a very low resistance connection: the voltage across it is zero, but it can carry whatever current the rest of the circuit allows, which is why an accidental short across a supply is dangerous.
segments.expand: Explain why an open switch in a series loop has the full supply voltage across it.

check.q: Which pair correctly describes an ideal open circuit?
check.again: An open circuit is two isolated terminals with nothing joining them, so no current can flow through it, ever. But the rest of the circuit can put whatever voltage it likes across the gap: a battery with nothing connected, or an open switch in a series loop, shows its full voltage across the opening with no current. The short circuit is the mirror image, a very low resistance connection with zero volts across it that can carry whatever current the rest of the circuit allows, which is why an accidental short across a supply is dangerous.

segments.title: Voltmeter loading effects
segments.text: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with what it measures, so its internal resistance forms a new branch. The parallel combination of the meter and the resistor is lower than the resistor alone, so the measured voltage can drop. With a typical digital meter of about 10 megohms, the effect is negligible across small resistors. It matters in high resistance circuits. With 12 volts across two 1 megohm resistors in series and a 1 megohm meter across the lower one, the lower part becomes 0.5 megohms, and the meter reads a third of 12, 4 volts, instead of 6. A higher meter resistance always means less loading.
segments.expand: Explain how you could tell, from two readings with different meters, that loading is affecting a measurement.

check.q: 12 volts is across two 1 megohm resistors in series, and a 1 megohm voltmeter is placed across the lower one. What does it read?
check.again: The meter's 1 megohm sits in parallel with the lower 1 megohm resistor, and two equal resistors in parallel give half: 0.5 megohms. The chain is now 1 megohm above 0.5 megohms, 1.5 megohms in all, so the divider gives the lower part 12 volts times 0.5 over 1.5, which is 4 volts, instead of the unloaded 6 volts. That drop is the loading effect. A typical digital meter of about 10 megohms would barely disturb small resistors, but in high resistance circuits like this one it matters, and a higher meter resistance always means less loading.

segments.title: Protoboards for parallel networks
segments.text: On a protoboard, a parallel network is easy to see in terms of nodes: every element in the group has one lead in the first node's group of holes and the other lead in the second node's group. The long rails along the edges are convenient for this, since each rail is one node. Check that each element truly bridges both nodes. An element with both leads in one group is bypassed, with zero volts across it. A quick unpowered resistance check across the two nodes should read below the smallest resistor, exactly the parallel bound from lecture eight.
segments.expand: Describe how to lay out three resistors in parallel on a breadboard and check them before powering up.

check.q: An unpowered resistance check across the two nodes of a parallel group should read below the smallest resistor in the group.
check.again: A parallel total is always less than the smallest branch, because each extra branch gives current another way through. So a resistance reading across the two nodes of a correctly built parallel group must come out below the smallest resistor; a higher reading means a branch is missing or something is miswired. On the protoboard, every element in the group has one lead in the first node's group of holes and the other in the second's, and the long edge rails are handy since each rail is one node. An element with both leads in one group is bypassed, with zero volts across it.

segments.title: Recap of chapter six so far
segments.text: Five points so far. One: parallel elements have two points in common, whatever the drawing looks like. Two: one over the total resistance is the sum of the reciprocals; the total is below the smallest resistor; product over sum is for two resistors, and N equal resistors give R over N. Three: conductances add in parallel. Four: every parallel element has the same voltage, each branch current is that voltage over its resistance, and by Kirchhoff's current law the branch currents add to the source current; current divides inversely with resistance. Five: an open circuit has zero current but can hold voltage, and a voltmeter loads a circuit as an extra parallel branch.
segments.expand: Give me two parallel combinations and a branch current to find in my head.

check.q: According to the recap, in a parallel circuit the current divides how?
check.again: Every parallel element has the same voltage, and each branch current is that voltage over its own resistance, so the smaller resistance takes the larger share: the division is inverse to resistance. Equal shares happen only for equal branches. The recap's other points: parallel elements have two points in common whatever the drawing looks like; one over the total is the sum of the reciprocals, the total is below the smallest resistor, product over sum is for two resistors, and N equal resistors give R over N; conductances add in parallel; branch currents add to the source current; and an open circuit has zero current but can hold voltage.

lectures.title: Roots and rearranging formulas
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 01 - Roots and Rearranging Formulas.md; Washington §1.3, §1.6, §1.10, §1.11

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This first lecture is about two skills that support everything else in the course: simplifying a number without changing its value, and rearranging an equation without changing its solutions. A root reverses a power, and inverse operations uncover a target variable. In both jobs the routine is the same: identify the structure, use a rule that is actually valid, and check that the result still represents the original problem. We will start with what a root means and why the square root symbol names only one value, then simplify radicals by pulling out perfect squares, then talk about exact versus approximate answers, and finish with rearranging formulas by undoing operations in reverse order. None of it needs heavy arithmetic. What it needs is care about which rule applies, and the habit of checking.
segments.expand: Give a one-sentence preview of why roots and rearranging both come down to identify, apply a valid rule, check.

check.q: According to this lecture, what does a root do?
check.again: A root is the undo button for a power. Squaring turns 5 into 25, so the square root turns 25 back into 5. Cubing turns 2 into 8, so the cube root turns 8 back into 2. A root never reverses an addition; subtraction does that. And a root is not doubling or halving; it asks which number, raised to the power named by the index, gives back the number inside. That is why the lecture pairs roots with rearranging: both are about undoing an operation to recover what you started with.

segments.title: A root reverses a power
segments.text: Because 2 squared is 4, the square root of 4 is 2. That is all a root is: the reverse of a power. In the general n-th root of a, the small number n tucked into the radical sign is the index, and it tells you which power is being reversed. The number inside is the radicand. When no index is written, the root is a square root, index 2. So the fourth root of 16 is 2, because 2 to the fourth is 16. The cube root of 27 is 3, because 3 cubed is 27. Keep the vocabulary straight, because later lessons on radicals and on fractional exponents lean on it: index outside, radicand inside, and the answer is the number that, raised to the index, gives back the radicand. Checking a root is always the same move: raise your answer to the index and see whether the radicand comes back.
segments.expand: Explain index and radicand with one more example, such as the fifth root of 32, and how to check it.

check.q: In the fourth root of 16, what is the small number 4 called?
check.again: Two names live in every root. The index is the small number tucked into the radical sign, and it says which power is being undone. The radicand is the number sitting inside, the thing you are taking the root of. In the fourth root of 16, the index is 4 and the radicand is 16, and the answer is 2 because 2 to the fourth is 16. With the cube root of 125, the index is 3, the radicand is 125, and the answer is 5. No index written means index 2, a square root.

segments.title: One value, or two solutions
segments.text: Here is the distinction the class insists on. The square root symbol names exactly one value, called the principal root, and it is never negative. So the square root of 49 is 7, full stop, not plus or minus 7. Solving the equation x squared equals 49 is a different task. An equation asks for every permitted value that makes it true, and both 7 and negative 7 square to 49, so the solution is x equals 7 or x equals negative 7. You write plus or minus when solving; you write just 7 when evaluating the radical. One consequence that matters later: the square root of x squared is the absolute value of x, not x itself. Try x equals negative 7. Squaring gives 49, and the principal root of 49 is 7, which is the absolute value of negative 7. Squaring erases the sign, and the radical symbol only ever gives back the non-negative one.
segments.expand: Contrast evaluating a root with solving a squared equation using a second pair of numbers, and explain why root of x squared is absolute x.

check.q: Evaluated as a radical, the square root of 49 is plus or minus 7.
check.again: The radical symbol names one value only, the principal root, and it is never negative. So the square root of 49 is 7, and the square root of 100 is 10, not plus or minus 10. The plus or minus appears only when you solve an equation: x squared equals 100 has two solutions, 10 and negative 10, because both square to 100. Keep the two jobs separate. Evaluating a radical gives one non-negative number; solving a squared equation lists every value that works. The same idea gives the square root of x squared equals the absolute value of x.

segments.title: Even roots and odd roots
segments.text: Why do even and odd roots behave differently with negative numbers? Think about the factors. Negative 2 squared is negative 2 times negative 2, which is positive 4: an even number of negative factors pairs off and the result is positive. Negative 2 cubed is 4 times negative 2, which is negative 8: an odd number leaves one negative factor unpaired. So an even root, square root or fourth root, of a negative radicand has no real value, because no real number raised to an even power comes out negative. The fourth root of negative 16 is not a real number. An odd root keeps the sign of its radicand: the cube root of negative 8 is negative 2, and the cube root of positive 8 is positive 2. Saying no real value is not saying the notation is meaningless; it only says that within the real numbers there is no answer. A larger number system is previewed at the end of the lecture, but the core work stays with real numbers.
segments.expand: Give the reasoning again with fourth powers: why negative 3 to the fourth is positive 81, so the fourth root of negative 81 is not real.

check.q: What is the cube root of negative 8?
check.again: An odd root keeps the sign of its radicand. Negative 2 cubed is negative 2 times negative 2 times negative 2: the first two factors make positive 4, and the third makes negative 8. So the cube root of negative 8 is negative 2, a perfectly real number. It is even roots that fail on negatives: no real number squared is negative, so the square root of negative 9 has no real value. Rule of thumb: count the negative factors. An odd count leaves one unpaired negative, an even count pairs them all off, so only odd roots can take a negative radicand.

segments.title: Simplifying a radical
segments.text: To simplify a square root, pull out a perfect-square factor without changing the value. The perfect squares worth knowing on sight are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121 and 144. The rule that allows the split is: for non-negative a and b, the square root of a times b equals the square root of a times the square root of b. Take the square root of 72. Seventy-two is 36 times 2, and 36 is a perfect square. So root 72 equals root 36 times root 2, which is 6 root 2. The 6 comes outside, the 2 stays inside. Check it by squaring: 6 root 2 squared is 36 times 2, which is 72. You do not have to spot the largest square straight away. If you used 4 instead, you would get 2 root 18, and 18 still contains 9, so root 18 is 3 root 2 and the total is again 6 root 2. Stopping at 2 root 18 is exact but not fully simplified, because a square factor is still hiding inside.
segments.expand: Simplify root 75 and root 48 step by step, showing a two-pass route for 48.

check.q: Fully simplified, what is the square root of 72?
check.again: To simplify a square root, find a perfect-square factor and pull its root outside. The rule: root of a times b equals root a times root b for non-negative a and b. Seventy-two is 36 times 2, and 36 is a perfect square with root 6, so root 72 is 6 root 2. If you only spot the factor 4 you get 2 root 18, which is equal but not finished, since 18 still hides the square 9. Another example: root 50 is root of 25 times 2, which is 5 root 2. Check by squaring: 5 root 2 squared is 25 times 2, which is 50.

segments.title: Roots do not split over addition
segments.text: The product rule tempts people into inventing a sum rule, and there is none. A radical does not distribute across addition or subtraction. Compare two expressions. The square root of the quantity 36 plus 64 is one square root: add first, 36 plus 64 is 100, and the root of 100 is 10. The square root of 36 plus the square root of 64 is two roots: 6 plus 8, which is 14. Different numbers. You can see the failure by squaring the wrong answer: 14 squared is 196, not 100. So the radical bar acts as a grouping symbol. Whatever is under it gets evaluated by the normal order of operations first, and only then do you look for perfect-square factors. Do not turn an addition into a multiplication just to use a convenient rule. When you catch yourself splitting a root over a plus sign, stop, compute the inside, and start again.
segments.expand: Show one more counterexample, root of 9 plus 16 versus root 9 plus root 16, and connect it to the radical bar as a grouping symbol.

check.q: The square root of the quantity 36 plus 64 equals the square root of 36 plus the square root of 64.
check.again: A root splits over multiplication but never over addition or subtraction. The radical bar is a grouping symbol, so add first: 36 plus 64 is 100, and root 100 is 10. Splitting instead gives 6 plus 8, which is 14, a different number. A smaller example shows the same failure: the square root of the quantity 9 plus 16 is root 25, which is 5, while root 9 plus root 16 is 3 plus 4, which is 7. Whenever a plus or minus sits under a root, compute the inside completely before looking for perfect-square factors.

segments.title: Exact and approximate answers
segments.text: An exact answer preserves the full mathematical value. A rounded decimal replaces it with a nearby value. So 6 root 2 is exact and 8.49 is an approximation to two decimal places. Use the word equals between equal values and approximately equals when you have rounded: root 72 equals 6 root 2, approximately 8.49. Keep the exact form unless a decimal is requested, and when a decimal is requested, follow the precision the question asks for. Round once, at the end; several small roundings in the middle can add up to a wrong final digit. Two more points. A decimal is not automatically approximate: 0.25 is exactly one quarter. The question is whether the value has been rounded, not whether it has a decimal point. And in an application, the measurement precision of the data also limits what the result can honestly claim. A worked example from class: t equals 0.25 times the square root of h, with h equal to 900. The root of 900 is 30, so t is 0.25 times 30, which is 7.5, exactly.
segments.expand: Explain why rounding intermediate values can accumulate error, with a short numeric illustration.

check.q: A number with a decimal point, like 0.25, is automatically an approximation.
check.again: What makes an answer approximate is rounding, not the decimal point. The decimal 0.25 is exactly one quarter, and 0.5 is exactly one half, so both are exact. On the other hand 8.49 as a stand-in for 6 root 2 is an approximation, because digits were cut off. Say equals between equal values and approximately equals after rounding. Keep the exact form, like 6 root 2 or 7.5, unless a decimal is asked for, and then round once at the very end so that small roundings in the middle cannot pile up into a wrong final digit.

segments.title: Rearranging by undoing operations
segments.text: A formula relates quantities, and rearranging it means isolating a different target. The method is inverse operations, applied to both sides. Adding is undone by subtracting, multiplying by dividing, and the reverse. Nothing changes sign just by crossing the equals sign; that phrase is shorthand for a balanced operation on both sides. Take E equals m c squared and isolate m. The whole factor c squared multiplies m, so divide both sides by c squared: m equals E over c squared, with c not zero. Dividing by only c would leave m c, not m. The same idea handles E equals I R, giving I equals E over R, and P V equals n R T, giving T equals P V over n R, where the entire product n R divides. Check a rearrangement by substituting back: E over c squared, times c squared, is E. And every division carries a restriction, the divisor cannot be zero. That restriction is part of the answer, not a footnote.
segments.expand: Rearrange E equals I R for R and P V equals n R T for n, stating each restriction.

check.q: Solving E equals m c squared for m gives what?
options: m equals E over c squared
m equals E times c squared
check.again: Rearranging means undoing whatever was done to the target, on both sides. In E equals m c squared, the whole factor c squared multiplies m, so the undo is dividing both sides by c squared: m equals E over c squared, with c not zero. Dividing by only c would leave m c on the right, not m alone. Check by substituting back: E over c squared, times c squared, returns E. Same pattern with P equals I squared R solved for R: divide both sides by I squared, giving R equals P over I squared, I not zero.

segments.title: Two operations, reverse order
segments.text: When the target has two things done to it, undo them in the reverse order of construction. In v equals v nought plus a t, look outward from t. First t was multiplied by a, then v nought was added. So to solve for t, subtract v nought from both sides first, then divide by a: t equals v minus v nought, all over a, with a not zero. The fraction bar groups the whole difference; it is not v minus v nought over a with only the second term divided. Dividing first is possible, but then every term must be divided, which is messier. With v equal to 23, v nought equal to 5 and a equal to 3, that gives 18 over 3, which is 6, and the check is 5 plus 3 times 6 equals 23. What if a were zero? Then the division is invalid and you go back to the original: v equals v nought, which either holds for every t or for none. A restriction is part of the solution.
segments.expand: Walk through the reverse-order idea with a formula of the shape y equals m x plus b solved for x, then discuss the m equals zero case.

check.q: To solve v equals v nought plus a t for t, which operation comes first?
options: Subtract v nought from both sides
Divide only the t term by a
check.again: Undo operations in the reverse order they were built. Looking outward from t: first t was multiplied by a, then v nought was added on. Reversing that, the addition is undone first, so subtract v nought from both sides, then divide by a. The result is t equals the quantity v minus v nought, all over a, with a not zero; the fraction bar covers the whole difference. Try v equal to 20, v nought equal to 8 and a equal to 4: 20 minus 8 is 12, over 4 is 3, and the check is 8 plus 4 times 3 equals 20.

segments.title: Nested brackets, outside inward
segments.text: When the target sits inside brackets inside a multiplier, peel the layers from the outside inward. The class example is V equals V nought times the quantity 1 plus B times the quantity T minus T nought, solved for T. The outermost operation is the multiplier V nought acting on the whole bracket, so divide both sides by V nought. Next, the 1 is added, so subtract 1. Then B multiplies the inner bracket, so divide by B. Finally T nought is subtracted from T, so add T nought. The result is T equals T nought plus the quantity V over V nought minus 1, all over B, which tidies to T nought plus V minus V nought, over B V nought. Order matters: subtracting 1 from V at the start would not remove the inner 1, because that 1 is still inside a bracket multiplied by V nought. Check by substituting back into the original; the added T nought cancels in T minus T nought and the right side collapses to V. Restrictions: V nought and B are both nonzero.
segments.expand: Describe the forward chain of operations applied to T and the reverse chain that undoes it, one operation per step.

check.q: In V equals V nought times the quantity 1 plus B times the quantity T minus T nought, what is undone first when solving for T?
options: Divide both sides by V nought
check.again: Peel the layers from the outside inward. The outermost thing acting on the bracket is the multiplier V nought, so the first move is dividing both sides by V nought. Only then is the 1 exposed, so subtract 1; then B multiplies the inner bracket, so divide by B; finally add T nought. Subtracting 1 first would be wrong because that 1 is still wrapped inside a bracket that V nought multiplies. Think of unwrapping a parcel: the outer layer comes off before the inner one, and each layer is removed from both sides of the equation.

segments.title: Before you accept an answer
segments.text: The class closes with a checklist, and it is worth hearing in full because it is the same checklist for the rest of the course. Is the requested variable alone, preferably on the left? Does every division have a nonzero denominator, and have you said so? Do the brackets and fraction bars group the terms you intended? Does a radical answer have the right sign, and does it reproduce its radicand when raised to the index? Does any numerical solution satisfy the original equation, including its domain restrictions, not just the last line you wrote? Do the sign, the units and the requested precision fit the application? A rearranged formula solves a whole family of problems, so it is worth getting right once and reusing. Keep the letters until the target is isolated, then substitute numbers and units.
segments.expand: Explain why checking in the original equation, rather than a later line, catches lost restrictions and invalid divisions.

check.q: The checklist says to substitute numbers before the target variable is isolated.
check.again: The advice is the other way round: keep the letters until the target stands alone, then substitute the numbers and units. A rearranged formula solves a whole family of problems, so isolating the letter once and reusing it beats redoing arithmetic every time. For example, isolate r in C equals 2 pi r first, getting r equals C over 2 pi, and only then drop in a circumference. The rest of the checklist asks whether every divisor is nonzero, whether brackets group what you meant, whether radical answers have the right sign, and whether the solution satisfies the original equation.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas to keep. One: a root reverses a power, and the radical symbol names one non-negative value; solving a squared equation gives two. Two: even roots of negatives have no real value, odd roots keep the sign. Three: simplify a square root by pulling out perfect-square factors, since a root splits over a product, but never over a sum; compute under the radical bar first. Four: exact forms like 6 root 2 are complete answers, and a rounded decimal is only an approximation, so round once at the end. Five: rearrange a formula by undoing operations in reverse order on both sides, keep every nonzero restriction, and check by substituting back into the original.
segments.expand: Pick the one idea from this lecture most likely to be tested and give a fresh example of it.

check.q: According to the recap, a root splits over which operation?
options: Both a product and a sum
check.again: The recap's third idea: a root splits over a product, never over a sum. Root of 4 times 25 is root 4 times root 25, which is 2 times 5, and root 100 confirms it as 10. But root of 9 plus 16 is root 25, which is 5, while root 9 plus root 16 is 7, so splitting over a plus sign gives a wrong number. Compute under the radical bar first, then pull out perfect-square factors. The other recap ideas: a radical names one non-negative value, even roots of negatives are not real, exact forms are complete answers, and rearrange by undoing in reverse order.

lectures.title: Number sets, fractions and signs
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 02 - Number Sets, Fractions and Signs.md; Washington §1.1, §1.2, §1.4, §6.2, §6.3, §6.5 to §6.7

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: The idea that connects this whole lecture is: change the form without changing the value. Multiplying by a carefully chosen form of 1 creates equivalent fractions, converts units, and explains why common factors cancel. Parentheses and denominator restrictions tell you when each step is legal. We will classify numbers into their sets, look at repeating decimals and absolute value, then do fraction arithmetic the way the class does it, by finding ones. After that come reciprocals, a return to radicals, factoring before cancelling in algebraic fractions, and finally signed numbers and the order of operations, including the trap of a minus sign in front of a power. Every piece is elementary on its own. The value is in doing each one correctly under time pressure.
segments.expand: Explain in two sentences what multiplying by a form of one means and why it never changes a value.

check.q: This lecture's connecting idea is to multiply by a carefully chosen form of which number?
check.again: Multiplying by 1 never changes a value, and a form of 1 can look like 4 over 4, 60 seconds over 1 minute, or x over x. That single trick builds equivalent fractions, converts units, and explains cancelling. For instance, to write two thirds in twelfths, multiply by 4 over 4 and get 8 twelfths, the same amount renamed. Multiplying by zero would destroy the value, and multiplying by ten would change it tenfold. The lecture's promise is that fractions, units, cancelling and signs all come back to changing the form while keeping the value.

segments.title: The number sets
segments.text: Classify a number by its value, not by how it is written, so simplify first. The natural numbers are the counting numbers, 1, 2, 3 and so on; this course starts them at 1. Add zero and you have the whole numbers. Add the negatives and you have the integers. The rational numbers are every ratio of integers with a nonzero denominator, which includes every integer, since 7 is 7 over 1. The irrational numbers are the reals that are not ratios: root 2, root 3, pi, e, the golden ratio. Rationals and irrationals together make the real numbers, all the points on the number line, and the complex numbers sit beyond that. The sets nest: natural inside whole inside integer inside rational inside real inside complex. So the square root of 49 is 7, and 7 is natural, whole, an integer, rational and real. Negative root 16 is negative 4, an integer. Pi over 4 is irrational. A classification question may have several correct memberships; the smallest set is the most specific answer.
segments.expand: Classify 0, negative 13, 0.125 and root 2, naming the smallest set and the larger sets each also belongs to.

check.q: Negative root 16 simplifies to negative 4. Which is the most specific set it belongs to?
check.again: Classify by the simplified value. Negative root 16 is negative 4. The natural numbers start at 1 and the whole numbers add zero, so neither includes a negative. The integers are the first set that does, so integer is the most specific answer; negative 4 is also rational and real, since every set nests inside the next. Compare root 25, which is 5: natural, whole, integer, rational and real. And root 5 cannot be written as a ratio of integers, so it is irrational, while still real. Simplify first, then find the smallest set that fits.

segments.title: Repeating decimals and absolute value
segments.text: A rational number's decimal either terminates, like one eighth equals 0.125, or eventually repeats, like one third equals 0.333 repeating or one sixth equals 0.1 6 repeating. An irrational decimal neither terminates nor repeats. A famous example is 2.101001000100001 and so on, with ever longer runs of zeros; it follows a rule but never settles into a repeating block. Be careful: any finite display is rational, since it is an integer over a power of 10. Only the infinite continuation makes the number irrational. A neat consequence: 0.999 repeating equals 1, because one third is 0.333 repeating, and three times that is 1. There is no gap. Absolute value is distance from zero, never negative. The absolute value of negative 13 is 13, of 7 is 7, of 0 is 0. Evaluate inside the bars before taking the distance: the absolute value of 3 minus 8 is the absolute value of negative 5, which is 5.
segments.expand: Explain why 0.999 repeating equals 1 using the one-third argument, and why 0.999 with three nines is less than 1.

check.q: The number 0.999 repeating equals 1.
check.again: There is no gap between 0.999 repeating and 1. One third is 0.333 repeating; multiply both by 3 and you get 1 on one side and 0.999 repeating on the other, so they are the same number. Any finite string of nines, like 0.999, is slightly less than 1, but the infinite repetition closes the gap completely. This sits with the segment's other points: a rational number's decimal either stops or repeats, an irrational one does neither, and absolute value is distance from zero, so the absolute value of 2 minus 9 is 7.

segments.title: Multiplying by one
segments.text: The multiplication identity says anything times 1 is itself, and a useful form of 1 can look nothing like the digit 1: 9 over 9, a thousand over a thousand, pi over pi, x over x for nonzero x, the quantity x plus 2 over itself for x not negative 2. The instructor calls this the big one idea. To make an equivalent fraction, multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number: three fifths times 12 over 12 is 36 sixtieths, same value, renamed in sixtieths. Reducing runs the process backwards: 38 over 24 is 2 times 19 over 2 times 12, and the 2 over 2 is a 1, leaving 19 over 12. That is what cancelling really is, and the class wants you to say finding ones rather than just crossing things out. Unit conversion is the same move: 60 seconds over 1 minute equals 1, so 2.5 minutes times 60 seconds per minute is 150 seconds, with the minutes cancelling. One thing you can never do is divide by zero. One over zero, zero over zero, and the quantity x plus 2 over itself at x equals negative 2 are all undefined, and infinity is not a value you may substitute.
segments.expand: Show a unit conversion where the factor must be flipped the other way round, and explain how to choose the orientation.

check.q: Reducing 38 over 24 to 19 over 12 works by removing which form of one?
check.again: Reducing a fraction means finding a form of 1 hiding inside it. Thirty-eight is 2 times 19 and 24 is 2 times 12, so the fraction is 2 over 2 times 19 over 12, and 2 over 2 is simply 1. Take it away and 19 over 12 is left, same value, smaller numbers. That is what crossing out really does, which is why the class says finding ones. Another example: 45 over 60 is 15 over 15 times 3 over 4, so it reduces to three quarters. The same move runs forwards to make equivalent fractions and to convert units.

segments.title: Adding, subtracting and multiplying fractions
segments.text: The denominator names the size of the parts; the numerator counts them. To add or subtract, the parts must be the same size, so first match the denominators using forms of 1. Three fifths plus seven twelfths: multiply the first by 12 over 12 and the second by 5 over 5, giving 36 sixtieths plus 35 sixtieths, which is 71 sixtieths. The exact answer is 71 over 60, about 1.183. The product of the denominators always works, but the least common denominator keeps numbers smaller: for 4 and 6, use 12 rather than 24. Five sixths minus one quarter is 10 twelfths minus 3 twelfths, which is 7 twelfths. Multiplication is simpler: multiply tops and multiply bottoms, and reduce common factors before multiplying large numbers. Negative five eighths times 12 over 25: the 5 pairs with the 25 and the 4 in 12 pairs with the 8, leaving negative 3 over 10. The single negative sign stays with the result.
segments.expand: Add two fractions with denominators 4 and 6 using the least common denominator, and explain why 12 beats 24.

check.q: What is three fifths plus seven twelfths?
check.again: You can only add pieces of the same size, so the denominators must match before adding. Fifths and twelfths both fit into sixtieths: three fifths times 12 over 12 is 36 sixtieths, and seven twelfths times 5 over 5 is 35 sixtieths. Now add the counts: 36 plus 35 is 71, so the sum is 71 over 60. Adding tops and bottoms separately, 10 over 17, is wrong because it ignores piece size. Smaller example: one half plus one third is 3 sixths plus 2 sixths, which is 5 sixths.

segments.title: Division and reciprocals
segments.text: To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. The first fraction stays put; the second fraction, the divisor, is inverted. Five sixths divided by ten ninths is five sixths times nine tenths, which is 45 sixtieths, which reduces to three quarters. Why does it work? Division asks for a missing factor: which number k makes ten ninths times k equal five sixths? Multiplying both sides by nine tenths turns the coefficient of k into 1. Check by reversing: ten ninths times three quarters is 30 over 36, which is five sixths. The reciprocal of a nonzero number r is 1 over r, and their product is 1. The reciprocal of 8 is one eighth. The reciprocal of negative three fifths is negative five thirds; the sign stays. For a mixed number like one and three quarters, convert to seven quarters first, then flip to four sevenths. Zero has no reciprocal, since nothing times zero gives 1. An algebraic reciprocal needs both restrictions: the reciprocal of A plus B over C is C over A plus B, with C not zero and A plus B not zero.
segments.expand: Explain the missing-factor view of division with another example, and why zero can have no reciprocal.

check.q: To divide by a fraction, you invert the first fraction and multiply.
check.again: It is the second fraction, the divisor, that gets flipped; the first fraction stays exactly as it is. Two thirds divided by four fifths becomes two thirds times five quarters, which is 10 twelfths, reducing to five sixths. Flipping the first fraction instead would give a different, wrong number. The reason it works: dividing by four fifths asks what number times four fifths gives two thirds, and multiplying by five quarters turns that coefficient into 1. The reciprocal of a number r is 1 over r, the sign stays, and zero has no reciprocal.

segments.title: Radicals and the calculator
segments.text: The radical ideas from Lecture 1 came back with a calculator emphasis. Root 72 is root 36 times root 2, which is 6 root 2, about 8.485. Like radicals combine like terms: 3 root 5 minus 2 root 5 is root 5. Unlike radicals, and radicals of sums, do not combine: the root of 9 plus 49 is root 58, not 3 plus 7. On a calculator with linear entry, the radical bar is a grouping symbol, so open the root group before the 3 squared and close it after the 7 squared; closing early describes a different expression. A plus or minus symbol means two evaluations. For 5 plus or minus the root of 25 minus 9, all over 2, simplify the shared root first: root 16 is 4. Then 5 plus 4 over 2 is nine halves and 5 minus 4 over 2 is one half. Group the whole numerator before dividing by 2. Read the calculation before pressing enter: identify the complete base of every power, the complete radicand, and the complete numerator and denominator, then reproduce those groups with brackets.
segments.expand: Describe the two calculator entries that differ only in where the square-root bracket closes, and what each one computes.

check.q: Five plus or minus the root of the quantity 25 minus 9, all over 2, gives which two values?
check.again: A plus or minus sign means two separate evaluations, and the radical bar and the fraction bar are both grouping symbols. First finish the radicand: 25 minus 9 is 16, and root 16 is 4. Then the whole numerator is 5 plus 4, which is 9, or 5 minus 4, which is 1, and each of those is divided by 2: nine halves and one half. Forgetting the division gives 9 and 1. On a calculator, close the root bracket after the 9 and bracket the whole numerator before dividing, or the machine evaluates a different expression.

segments.title: Factor before you cancel
segments.text: Expanding turns a product into a sum; factoring reverses it. Before simplifying an algebraic fraction, factor the numerator and denominator completely and record the excluded inputs. Take x squared minus 9 over x squared plus 5 x plus 6. The numerator is a difference of squares: x plus 3 times x minus 3. The denominator factors by finding two numbers with product 6 and sum 5, which are 2 and 3, so it is x plus 2 times x plus 3. Before cancelling, record x not equal to negative 2 and x not equal to negative 3. Now the x plus 3 over x plus 3 is a form of 1, and the fraction simplifies to x minus 3 over x plus 2, with both restrictions kept. Cancelling is valid on the original domain; it does not make the original expression defined at negative 3. Graphically, the cancelled factor leaves a hole at x equals negative 3, at height 6, while the surviving denominator factor gives a vertical asymptote at x equals negative 2. And never cancel terms: in the quantity x plus 3 over the quantity x plus 2, the x is part of a sum, not a factor, so nothing cancels.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between a hole and a vertical asymptote in terms of which factor cancelled and which stayed.

check.q: After cancelling, the quantity x squared minus 9, over the quantity x squared plus 5 x plus 6, becomes what, restrictions kept?
options: x minus 3, all over x plus 2
x plus 3, all over x plus 2
x minus 3, all over x minus 2
check.again: Factor both parts fully before cancelling anything. The top is a difference of squares, x plus 3 times x minus 3. The bottom needs two numbers with product 6 and sum 5, so 2 and 3, giving x plus 2 times x plus 3. Record x not equal to negative 2 and not equal to negative 3, then the x plus 3 over x plus 3 is a form of 1 and disappears, leaving x minus 3 over x plus 2. Only whole factors cancel, never single terms inside a sum, so nothing further cancels in the result.

segments.title: Signed numbers
segments.text: In negative 7 the sign marks a number below zero. In 5 minus 7 the sign is the operation of subtraction. Rewrite subtraction as adding the opposite: a minus b is a plus negative b. On the number line, 24 plus negative 3 moves left to 21; negative 7 plus 12 moves right to 5; 5 minus 9 moves left to negative 4; 3 minus negative 8 moves right by 8 to 11. So negative 7 plus 12 minus 9 is 5 minus 9, which is negative 4. For multiplication and division, same signs give positive and different signs give negative: negative 3 times negative 4 is 12, and negative 18 divided by 3 is negative 6. Why is a negative times a negative positive? Distribution has to stay consistent. Since 3 plus negative 3 is zero, negative 2 times that sum is zero. Distributing gives negative 6 plus negative 2 times negative 3 equals zero, so negative 2 times negative 3 must be positive 6.
segments.expand: Give the distribution argument for negative times negative once more with different numbers.

check.q: A negative number times a negative number gives a negative result.
check.again: Same signs multiply or divide to a positive result; different signs give a negative one. So negative 4 times negative 5 is positive 20, while negative 4 times 5 is negative 20, and negative 20 divided by negative 4 is positive 5. The lecture's reason is consistency with distribution: since 5 plus negative 5 is zero, negative 3 times that sum must be zero; the first part gives negative 15, so negative 3 times negative 5 has to be positive 15 to bring the total back to zero.

segments.title: Order of operations and the sign trap
segments.text: The order: grouping symbols first, including fraction bars and radical bars; then powers and roots; then multiplication and division from left to right; then addition and subtraction from left to right. Multiplication does not automatically beat division; they share a level, and so do addition and subtraction. Negative 18 over 3 minus 5 is negative 6 minus 5, which is negative 11. Four minus the quantity 3 minus negative 8 is 4 minus 11, which is negative 7. Now the trap. An exponent applies only to the base immediately in front of it. Minus 3 squared, with no brackets, is the negative of 3 squared, which is negative 9. Brackets around negative 3, then squared, is negative 3 times negative 3, which is positive 9. For an odd exponent the two agree: minus 2 cubed and negative 2 in brackets cubed are both negative 8. Finally, a denominator is a group: negative 12 over the product negative 2 times 3 is negative 12 over negative 6, which is 2, whereas negative 12 over negative 2, then times 3, is 18. Group the whole denominator before dividing.
segments.expand: Contrast minus 2 to the fourth with negative 2 in brackets to the fourth, and explain which is which.

check.q: With no brackets, what is minus 3 squared?
check.again: An exponent attaches only to the base directly in front of it. In minus 3 squared with no brackets, the base is 3, so the power is 9 and the minus sign is applied afterwards: negative 9. Put brackets around negative 3 and then square, and the base is negative 3, giving negative 3 times negative 3, which is positive 9. Same story with minus 5 squared: negative 25 without brackets, positive 25 with them. For odd powers the two readings agree, since minus 2 cubed and negative 2 in brackets cubed are both negative 8.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Here are the ideas to carry out of this lecture. Classify a number by its simplified value, and remember the sets nest: natural, whole, integer, rational, real. Rational decimals terminate or repeat; irrational ones do neither. Change form without changing value by multiplying by a form of 1: that builds common denominators, reduces fractions by finding ones, and converts units. To divide by a fraction, multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor; zero has no reciprocal, and nothing may be divided by zero. Factor an algebraic fraction completely, record the excluded inputs, then cancel factors, never terms. Subtracting is adding the opposite, same signs multiply to positive, and an exponent belongs only to the base right in front of it, so minus 3 squared is negative 9. Group the whole denominator or radicand before you do anything else.
segments.expand: Choose the two ideas here most often confused with each other and explain how to tell them apart.

check.q: The recap says you may cancel terms as well as factors in an algebraic fraction.
check.again: Only factors cancel, never terms. A factor is something multiplied; a term is something added or subtracted. In the quantity x plus 4 over the quantity x plus 1, the x is part of a sum on both levels, so nothing cancels. In 3 x over 3, the 3 is a factor on top and bottom, so it does cancel, leaving x. That is why the recap insists on factoring completely first: x squared minus 4 over x plus 2 factors to x plus 2 times x minus 2 over x plus 2, and now a whole factor cancels, giving x minus 2 with x not negative 2.

lectures.title: Factoring, equations and exponents
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 03 - Factoring, Equations and Exponents.md; Washington §1.8, §6.1 to §6.3, §7.1, §7.3, §1.4, §11.1, §11.2, §13.2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Algebra moves between equivalent forms. Expanding reveals individual terms; factoring reveals multiplication; a zero product reveals solutions. That is the spine of this lecture. We expand brackets carefully, including the special products. We factor in a fixed order: common factor, difference of squares, then the AC method for trinomials. We solve equations with the zero-product rule, and we see when to reach for the quadratic formula and what the discriminant predicts. We rearrange a formula where the target appears with a squared term nearby, work a word problem where the algebra gives two roots but the situation accepts one, and finish with the exponent laws, a mental-arithmetic trick that uses the same algebra, and a first look at logarithms as the inverse of exponentiation. Use it in three passes: understand what each operation does, work the example without its last line, then try a new question.
segments.expand: Summarise the three verbs expand, factor and solve, and what each one reveals.

check.q: This lecture factors in a fixed order: common factor, difference of squares, then the AC method.
check.again: The lecture keeps one order for factoring so nothing gets missed. First pull out any common factor, like the 3 in 3 x squared minus 12. Next, look for a difference of squares: x squared minus 4 becomes x plus 2 times x minus 2. Only then reach for the AC method on a trinomial. The order matters because taking the common factor out first makes the remaining bracket smaller and easier to recognise. The lecture then uses factoring for the zero-product rule, brings in the quadratic formula for stubborn cases, and ends with exponent laws.

segments.title: Expanding and the special products
segments.text: An expression is built from terms separated by plus and minus, and a coefficient multiplies a variable part: in negative 6 x the coefficient is negative 6. Like terms share the same variable powers: 7 x plus 4 x is 11 x, but x squared and x cannot combine. The distributive law multiplies every term inside the bracket: 5 times x minus 3 is 5 x minus 15, and negative 2 times 3 x plus 7 is negative 6 x minus 14, with the sign kept attached to the multiplier. Two brackets: every term times every term, so x plus 4 times x plus 7 is x squared plus 11 x plus 28. Three patterns to know on sight: a plus b all squared is a squared plus 2 a b plus b squared; a minus b all squared is a squared minus 2 a b plus b squared, last term positive; and a plus b times a minus b is a squared minus b squared, the middle terms cancelling. So 3 x minus 2 all squared is 9 x squared minus 12 x plus 4, and x plus 6 times x minus 6 is x squared minus 36. The warning: a power does not distribute over addition. A plus b squared is not a squared plus b squared.
segments.expand: Expand 2 x plus 5 all squared and 2 x plus 5 times 2 x minus 5, naming the pattern each time.

check.q: What is 3 x minus 2, all squared?
check.again: The pattern for a minus b, all squared, is a squared minus 2 a b plus b squared, with the last term positive because a negative times a negative is positive. Here a is 3 x and b is 2: a squared is 9 x squared, 2 a b is 12 x with a minus sign, and b squared is positive 4. So the result is 9 x squared minus 12 x plus 4. A power never distributes over a sum, so there is always a middle term. Check with x equal to 1: both sides give 1.

segments.title: Factor in a sensible order
segments.text: Factoring reverses expanding, and the order matters. Step one, always: check for a common factor. Eight x plus 20 is 4 times 2 x plus 5. Twelve x squared minus 18 x is 6 x times 2 x minus 3. Take out the greatest common number and every shared variable factor, then look inside the bracket for more. Step two: recognise a difference of squares, a squared minus b squared equals a minus b times a plus b. Both terms must be squares with subtraction between them: 9 x squared minus 25 is 3 x minus 5 times 3 x plus 5. Expanding it back, the plus 15 x and minus 15 x cancel, which is why opposite signs are essential. A sum of squares, 9 x squared plus 25, does not factor over the reals. The two steps combine: 18 x squared minus 32 is 2 times 9 x squared minus 16, which is 2 times 3 x minus 4 times 3 x plus 4. Factoring is an identity, true for every x; it produces no values of x unless there is also an equation.
segments.expand: Factor 50 x squared minus 8 completely, saying which step applies at each stage.

check.q: A sum of squares like 9 x squared plus 25 factors over the reals.
check.again: A difference of squares factors; a sum of squares does not, at least not with real numbers. Nine x squared minus 25 is 3 x minus 5 times 3 x plus 5, and expanding shows why the subtraction is essential: the cross terms plus 15 x and minus 15 x cancel. With a plus sign between the squares there is no pair of real factors whose cross terms vanish. Remember the order too: common factor first, so 2 x squared minus 50 is 2 times x squared minus 25, which is 2 times x minus 5 times x plus 5.

segments.title: The AC method for trinomials
segments.text: A quadratic has the form a x squared plus b x plus c with a not zero. To factor it, find two numbers m and n whose product is a times c and whose sum is b, split the middle term into m x plus n x, and factor by grouping. For x squared plus 9 x plus 20, the product is 20 and the sum is 9, so choose 4 and 5, giving x plus 4 times x plus 5. For x squared minus 11 x plus 24, both numbers must be negative: negative 3 and negative 8 multiply to positive 24 and add to negative 11, giving x minus 3 times x minus 8. When the leading coefficient is not 1, the method still works. For 2 x squared plus 7 x plus 3, the product a c is 6 and the sum is 7, so 6 and 1: split into 2 x squared plus 6 x plus x plus 3, group as 2 x times x plus 3 plus 1 times x plus 3, and factor the bracket to get 2 x plus 1 times x plus 3.
