Check by expanding. If no integer pair exists, the quadratic may not factor over the integers, and for an equation the quadratic formula is the general tool.
segments.expand: Factor 3 x squared plus 10 x plus 8 with the AC method, showing the split and the grouping.

check.q: For x squared minus 11 x plus 24, which two numbers does the AC method use?
check.again: The AC method wants two numbers whose product is a times c and whose sum is b. Here a is 1 and c is 24, so the product is positive 24, and the sum must be negative 11. A positive product with a negative sum means both numbers are negative: negative 3 times negative 8 is 24, and negative 3 plus negative 8 is negative 11. So the trinomial is x minus 3 times x minus 8. Using 3 and 8 would give a middle term of plus 11 x instead. Expanding is always the check.

segments.title: The zero-product rule
segments.text: An expression like x minus 6 times x minus 2 is not an equation until it equals something, and for the zero-product rule that something must be zero. The rule: if A times B is zero, then A is zero or B is zero, and there is no third possibility, because two nonzero real numbers cannot multiply to zero. So x minus 6 times x minus 2 equals zero gives x equals 6 or x equals 2. Fractional solutions are complete answers: 2 x minus 5 times x minus 2 equals zero gives x equals five halves or x equals 2. Put the equation in zero form first: for x squared plus 3 x equals 10, subtract 10 to get x squared plus 3 x minus 10 equals zero, which factors as x plus 5 times x minus 2, so x is negative 5 or 2. One more caution. In x times x minus 4 equals zero, do not divide by x. That assumes x is not zero and loses the solution x equals zero. Set each factor to zero instead, and check every proposed solution in the original equation, not in a later line.
segments.expand: Explain why a product equal to 5 tells you nothing about the factors, using a numeric example.

check.q: The zero-product rule can be used when a product equals any number, not only zero.
check.again: The rule works only against zero, because zero is the one number two nonzero factors can never make. If A times B equals zero, then A is zero or B is zero. If A times B equals 12, the factors could be 3 and 4, 2 and 6, or countless other pairs, so nothing follows about either one. That is why an equation like x times the quantity x plus 1 equals 12 must first be expanded and rearranged to zero form, x squared plus x minus 12 equals zero, and then factored as x plus 4 times x minus 3.

segments.title: Rearranging with a squared term nearby
segments.text: The formula d equals v t plus one half a t squared uses d for displacement, v for initial velocity, a for constant acceleration and t for time. To solve for v, treat one half a t squared as a whole added quantity: subtract it from both sides, then divide by t. That gives v equals d over t minus a t over 2, with t not zero. Why does the last term simplify? Because t squared over t is t. The restriction belongs to the rearranged formula: at t equals zero the original relation says d is zero and cannot determine v. A formula solves a whole family of problems, so keep the letters until the target is isolated, then substitute numbers and units. If instead you wanted t, notice it appears both to the first and second power, so a single chain of undoing is not enough; that is a quadratic in t and needs the next tool.
segments.expand: Rearrange d equals v t plus one half a t squared for a, stating the restriction.

check.q: Solving d equals v t plus one half a t squared for v gives what?
options: v equals d over t minus a t over 2
v equals d over t minus a t squared
v equals d minus a t over 2
check.again: Treat one half a t squared as a single added quantity. Subtract it from both sides: v t equals d minus one half a t squared. Then divide everything by t: v equals d over t minus a t over 2, since t squared over t is just t, with t not zero. Leaving t squared in the last term forgets that division. Check with d equal to 20, a equal to 2 and t equal to 4: 20 over 4 minus 8 over 2 is 5 minus 4, so v is 1, and 4 plus one half times 2 times 16 is 20.

segments.title: The quadratic formula and the discriminant
segments.text: When factoring is hard, write the equation in standard form, a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero with a not zero, and use the formula: x equals negative b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4 a c, all over 2 a. The whole numerator is divided by 2 a, and every coefficient keeps its sign. For 2 x squared plus 4 x minus 3 equals zero, no integer pair has product negative 6 and sum 4, so use the formula with a equal to 2, b equal to 4 and c equal to negative 3. The discriminant b squared minus 4 a c is 16 plus 24, which is 40, so x equals negative 4 plus or minus root 40, over 4, which simplifies to negative 2 plus or minus root 10, over 2. The discriminant predicts the outcome: positive means two distinct real solutions, zero means one repeated real solution, negative means no real solutions. Applying the formula to time in d equals v t plus one half a t squared gives t equals negative v plus or minus the root of v squared plus 2 a d, all over a, and for elapsed time you keep the non-negative root.
segments.expand: Compute the discriminant of x squared plus 2 x plus 5 and of x squared minus 6 x plus 9 and say what each predicts.

check.q: In the quadratic formula, what does a negative discriminant predict?
check.again: The discriminant is b squared minus 4 a c, the part under the square root in the quadratic formula. Its sign predicts the outcome before you finish. Positive means the root is a real number and the plus or minus gives two distinct real solutions. Zero means the root is zero and the two solutions collapse into one repeated value. Negative means you would need the square root of a negative number, which has no real value, so there are no real solutions. Example: x squared plus x plus 1 has discriminant 1 minus 4, negative, so it never crosses zero.

segments.title: A word problem: equation first, interpretation last
segments.text: A rectangle has sides x plus 5 and x minus 2 and area 18 square units. Before solving, state the conditions the situation imposes: both sides positive, so x greater than 2. Area is length times width, so x plus 5 times x minus 2 equals 18. The product is 18, not zero, so the zero-product rule does not apply yet. Expand to x squared plus 3 x minus 10 equals 18, move the 18 across to get x squared plus 3 x minus 28 equals zero, and factor: the numbers with product negative 28 and sum 3 are 7 and negative 4, so x plus 7 times x minus 4 equals zero, giving x equals negative 7 or x equals 4. Now apply the condition. Negative 7 would give negative side lengths, so only x equals 4 is valid, and the sides are 9 and 2, whose product is indeed 18. An algebraic root that violates the situation is still a root of the polynomial; it is just not an answer to the question. State the conditions before you solve, so the rejection is a decision, not an afterthought.
segments.expand: Set up and solve a similar rectangle problem with different numbers, including the rejection step.

check.q: The rectangle equation gave x equals negative 7 or x equals 4. Why was negative 7 rejected?
options: It would give negative side lengths
It is not a root of the polynomial
check.again: Negative 7 really is a root of the polynomial; the algebra is correct. It is rejected because the situation forbids it: a side of x minus 2 would be negative 9, and a rectangle cannot have a negative side. The condition x greater than 2 was written before solving, so throwing out negative 7 is a planned decision. Only x equals 4 survives, giving sides 9 and 2 and area 18. Whenever a variable measures a length, a time, or a count, state its allowed range first and test each root against it afterwards.

segments.title: The exponent laws
segments.text: Assume positive bases for fractional exponents, and nonzero bases for denominators and negative exponents. Multiplying the same base adds exponents: a to the m times a to the n is a to the m plus n, because you are counting factors. Dividing subtracts them. A power of a power multiplies them: a to the m, all to the n, is a to the m n. A power of a product or quotient applies to each part. Any nonzero a to the zero is 1, because a cubed over a cubed is a to the zero and also 1. A negative exponent means reciprocal: 2 to the minus 3 is one eighth, and negative 2 to the minus 3 is negative one eighth. A fractional exponent uses its denominator as the root index and its numerator as a power: 8 over 27 to the two thirds is the cube root, two thirds, squared, which is four ninths. Match the operation to the rule: x cubed times x squared is x to the fifth, x cubed all squared is x to the sixth, and x cubed plus x squared has no rule at all. Simplify inside a bracket before raising it: 6 x cubed over 3 x is 2 x squared, and to the fourth that is 16 x to the 8, with x not zero.
segments.expand: Explain why a to the zero is 1 and why a negative exponent means reciprocal, both from the quotient rule.

check.q: What is the quantity 8 over 27, raised to the power two thirds?
check.again: A fractional exponent reads root first, then power: the denominator of the exponent is the root index and the numerator is the power. Two thirds means cube root, then square. The cube root of 8 over 27 is 2 over 3, because 2 cubed is 8 and 3 cubed is 27. Squaring 2 over 3 gives 4 over 9. Multiplying the base by two thirds is not what an exponent does. Another example: 16 to the three quarters is the fourth root of 16, which is 2, cubed, which is 8. Bases are assumed positive for fractional exponents.

segments.title: Mental squaring and the bridge to logarithms
segments.text: The square-of-a-difference identity is also a mental-arithmetic tool. Forty-nine squared is 50 minus 1, all squared: 2500 minus 100 plus 1, which is 2401. Thirty-seven squared is 40 minus 3, all squared: 1600 minus 240 plus 9, which is 1369. Same algebra, different job. The lecture ends with a preview. A logarithm undoes exponentiation: b to the y equals x is the same statement as log base b of x equals y, for a positive base b not equal to 1 and a positive x. The exponent laws and the log laws describe the same relationships from opposite sides. Multiplication adds exponents, so the log of a product is a sum of logs. Division subtracts exponents, so the log of a quotient is a difference. A power multiplies exponents, so the log of a power is the exponent times the log. And since b to the zero is 1, log base b of 1 is zero. The next lecture develops these in full.
segments.expand: Work 31 squared and 98 squared mentally with the same identity, then restate the four exponent-to-log correspondences.

check.q: Using 50 minus 1, all squared, what is 49 squared?
check.again: The square-of-a-difference identity does the arithmetic: a minus b, all squared, is a squared minus 2 a b plus b squared. With a equal to 50 and b equal to 1: 50 squared is 2500, 2 a b is 100, and b squared is 1. So 49 squared is 2500 minus 100 plus 1, which is 2401. Forgetting the plus 1 gives 2499; adding the middle term instead gives the wrong direction. Try 29 squared the same way: 30 minus 1, all squared, is 900 minus 60 plus 1, which is 841.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Keep these. Expand by distributing every term to every term, and know the three special products, remembering that a plus b squared has a middle term. Factor in order: common factor first, then difference of squares, then the AC method with product a c and sum b, and check by expanding. Solve by putting the equation in zero form, factoring, and applying the zero-product rule; never divide away a factor that could be zero. When factoring fails, the quadratic formula applies to every quadratic, and the discriminant tells you two, one or no real roots before you finish. In applications, state the conditions first and reject roots that violate them. The exponent laws add, subtract and multiply exponents for products, quotients and powers of powers; negative means reciprocal, fractional means root. And a logarithm is an exponent, which is where we go next.
segments.expand: Give one fresh example each of a common-factor step, a difference of squares and an AC-method factoring.

check.q: The recap says the discriminant tells you how many real roots a quadratic has before you finish solving.
check.again: That is exactly the recap's point about the quadratic formula. The discriminant, b squared minus 4 a c, is computed early, and its sign is a forecast: positive means two real roots, zero means one repeated root, negative means none. For x squared minus 6 x plus 9, the discriminant is 36 minus 36, zero, so there is a single repeated root, and factoring confirms it as x minus 3 squared. The recap also reminds you to factor in order, put equations in zero form, state conditions before solving applications, and remember that a logarithm is an exponent.

lectures.title: Logarithms and exponential functions
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 04 - Logarithms and Exponential Functions.md; Washington §13.1 to §13.5, §3.5

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: A logarithm answers one question: what exponent do I need? Exponentials and logarithms undo each other, and that single fact explains their rules, their calculator buttons and their mirror-image graphs. This lecture reads a logarithm from its definition, then builds the three rules for simplifying logs, the product, quotient and power rules, and names the traps around them. It covers the change-of-base formula for a calculator with only log and l n, and the matching-powers shortcut that sometimes makes a calculator unnecessary. Then it looks at the graphs of an exponential and its inverse log, what the base does, which bases are excluded and why, and finally how to shift any graph left, right, up or down with confidence. Keep asking the one question, what exponent do I need, and the rest follows.
segments.expand: Explain in two sentences why every log rule is an exponent law read backwards.

check.q: According to this lecture, a logarithm answers which single question?
check.again: A logarithm is an exponent in disguise. Log base 3 of 81 asks: 3 to what power gives 81? Since 3 to the fourth is 81, the answer is 4. The base is known and the result is known; the exponent is what the log finds. Because exponentials and logarithms undo each other, that one question explains the log rules, the calculator buttons, and why the two graphs mirror each other. Whenever a log looks confusing, restate it as, the base to what power gives the argument, and the rest usually follows.

segments.title: Reading a logarithm
segments.text: The definition: log base b of x equals y means exactly that b to the power y equals x. Three parts. The base b is the number being raised to a power. The argument x is the result of that power. The answer y is the exponent needed. So log base 2 of 8 reads as, two to what power gives eight? Two cubed is 8, so the answer is 3. The real-log checklist: the base must be positive and not 1, and the argument must be positive. A positive argument can still produce a negative answer. Log base 2 of one half is negative 1, because 2 to the minus 1 is one half, and log base 2 of one thirty-second is negative 5. In handwriting, keep the argument at full size on the line and put only the base as a subscript; parentheses make the argument's boundary clear when it holds a fraction or a sum. Confusing base, argument and coefficient is where most log errors begin.
segments.expand: Read log base 3 of 81 and log base 5 of one twenty-fifth aloud as questions and answer them.

check.q: What is log base 2 of one half?
check.again: Ask the defining question: 2 to what power gives one half? A negative exponent means a reciprocal, and 2 to the minus 1 is 1 over 2, so log base 2 of one half is negative 1. The argument is positive, as it must be, but the answer can still be negative whenever the argument is between 0 and 1. Similarly log base 2 of one eighth is negative 3, because 2 to the minus 3 is one eighth. Keep the three parts straight: base 2, argument one half, answer the exponent negative 1.

segments.title: Two calculator buttons, one idea
segments.text: A log with no base written means base 10, the common logarithm. The natural log, written l n, has base e, about 2.718. The calculator's inverse operations are 10 to the x and e to the x. An exact power gives an exact answer: 10 squared is 100, so log of 100 is 2, and log of 1000 is 3. An unfamiliar power needs the button: to solve 10 to the y equals 105, take the common log of both sides, and y equals log of 105, about 2.021. The exact answer is log of 105; the decimal is an approximation, and you check it by raising 10 to that exponent. Keep extra calculator digits until the very end. Why does e matter at all? The continuous-growth model N equals N nought times e to the k t describes growth when k is positive and decay when k is negative, and a doubling time T corresponds to k equals l n 2 over T. That is supporting context; the working fact for now is simply that l n means base e, so l n of e is 1.
segments.expand: Explain why log of 105 lies between 2 and 3 without a calculator, then how to check the decimal.

check.q: L n of e equals 1.
check.again: The natural log has base e, about 2.718, so l n of e asks, e to what power gives e? The answer is 1, just as log of 10 is 1 and log base 5 of 5 is 1. A log with no base written means base 10, the common log, and its inverse button is 10 to the x; the inverse of l n is e to the x. Exact powers give exact answers, like log of 1000 equals 3. Anything else needs the button: solving 10 to the y equals 50 gives y equals log 50, about 1.699.

segments.title: The three log rules
segments.text: Within a single valid base, and with positive arguments, three rules do all the simplifying. Product rule: log of u times v equals log u plus log v; multiply inside, add outside. Quotient rule: log of u over v equals log u minus log v; divide inside, subtract outside. Power rule: log of u to the r equals r times log u; exponent inside becomes a multiplier outside. Two more facts: log base b of 1 is zero, because b to the zero is 1, and log base b of b is 1. Why do the rules hold? If u is b to the p and v is b to the q, then u v is b to the p plus q, so the log of u v is p plus q, the sum of the logs. Each rule is an exponent law in disguise. Before applying a rule, name the operation inside the logarithm: multiplication, division or a power. Addition inside has no rule.
segments.expand: Derive the quotient rule from the exponent law for division, mirroring the product-rule derivation.

check.q: The product rule says log of u times v equals log u times log v.
check.again: Multiplying inside a logarithm becomes adding outside: log of u times v equals log u plus log v. Test it in base 10: log of 100 times 1000 is log of 100000, which is 5, and log 100 plus log 1000 is 2 plus 3, also 5, while 2 times 3 would be 6. The rule is an exponent law in disguise: multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents. Likewise dividing inside becomes subtracting outside, and a power inside becomes a multiplier outside. Addition inside a log has no rule at all.

segments.title: Expand and condense
segments.text: Which direction you go depends on the goal: expand to expose separate terms, condense to make one argument. Log 6 plus log 3 condenses to log 18. Log a plus 2 log b plus 3 log c condenses to log of a times b squared times c cubed. Three log 5 becomes log of 5 cubed, which is log 125. L n of 1000 is l n of 10 cubed, which is 3 l n 10. A three-rule example: 2 l n p plus l n q minus l n 4 becomes l n of p squared, plus l n q, minus l n 4, then l n of p squared q, minus l n 4, then l n of p squared q over 4. Keep the original restrictions, p and q positive. Watch the domain when you rewrite. L n of x squared is defined for every nonzero x, but 2 l n x is defined only for positive x, so the general identity is l n of x squared equals 2 l n of the absolute value of x. Two expressions can agree on positive inputs and still not be the same function. Check domains before and after a rewrite.
segments.expand: Condense 3 log x minus 2 log y plus log 5 into one logarithm, stating the restrictions on x and y.

check.q: What does log 6 plus log 3 condense to?
check.again: Condensing uses the product rule backwards: a sum of logs in one base becomes the log of a product. Log 6 plus log 3 is log of 6 times 3, which is log 18. Adding the arguments to get log 9 confuses the sum outside with a sum inside, and log 2 would come from subtracting, since log 6 minus log 3 is log of 6 over 3. Another example: log 4 plus 2 log 5 is log 4 plus log 25, which is log 100, which equals 2. Always keep the original domain restrictions when you condense.

segments.title: Three traps
segments.text: First trap: a log does not distribute over addition. Log of u plus v cannot be split into log u plus log v. Test it in base 2: log base 2 of 16 plus 16 is log base 2 of 32, which is 5, while log base 2 of 16 plus log base 2 of 16 is 4 plus 4, which is 8. Different numbers, so the rule is false. Second trap: 3 log 5 means three times a logarithm. It is not log base 3 of 5, and it is not log 15. The coefficient becomes an exponent, giving log 125. Third trap: the base is a subscript and the exponent is a superscript. Log base 3 of 7 to the fourth has base 3 and argument 7 to the fourth; read carefully which number sits where. If a rule you are about to use has no matching exponent law, it is not a rule.
segments.expand: Give a numeric test that shows log of a sum is not a sum of logs in base 10.

check.q: What does 3 log 5 mean?
check.again: A number in front of a logarithm is a multiplier, three times the log of 5, and the power rule turns that multiplier into an exponent on the argument: log of 5 cubed, which is log 125. It is not a base, so it is not log base 3 of 5, and it is not multiplied into the argument, so it is not log 15. Check in base 10 with 2 log 10: that is 2 times 1, which is 2, and log of 10 squared is log 100, also 2, while log 20 is not 2. Coefficient outside, exponent inside.

segments.title: Change of base
segments.text: If a calculator has only log and l n, either button computes any base. The change-of-base formula: log base b of x equals log base c of x, divided by log base c of b, for any valid base c. In practice, log base b of x equals l n x over l n b, or log x over log b. Why: let y be log base b of x, so b to the y is x. Take log base c of both sides and the power rule gives y times log base c of b equals log base c of x. Divide by log base c of b, which is nonzero because b is not 1. The argument goes on top and the base goes underneath, and both parts must use the same logarithm; l n on top over base-10 log underneath is not a change-of-base calculation. To find the exponent in 7 to the y equals 20, y is log base 7 of 20, which is l n 20 over l n 7, about 1.54. Reasonableness check: 7 is less than 20 is less than 49, so the answer sits between 1 and 2.
segments.expand: Estimate log base 5 of 100 between two integers, then say how the calculator would compute it exactly.

check.q: Using change of base, log base 7 of 20 equals what?
check.again: Change of base puts the log of the argument on top and the log of the base underneath, both in the same logarithm: log base b of x equals l n x over l n b, or log x over log b. So log base 7 of 20 is l n 20 over l n 7, about 1.54, and a reasonableness check says the answer sits between 1 and 2 because 20 lies between 7 and 49. Flipping the fraction gives the reciprocal, and subtracting is the quotient rule for a different problem. Example: log base 2 of 10 is l n 10 over l n 2, about 3.32.

segments.title: Matching powers
segments.text: Sometimes the base and the argument are the same power of two different numbers, and then the calculator is unnecessary. Consider log base 81 of 2401. Notice 81 is 3 to the fourth and 2401 is 7 to the fourth. Change of base gives l n of 2401 over l n of 81, which is l n of 7 to the fourth over l n of 3 to the fourth. The power rule pulls the 4 out of both: 4 l n 7 over 4 l n 3. The common multiplier cancels, leaving l n 7 over l n 3, which is log base 3 of 7. This is not permission to cancel any numbers you like inside a logarithm; it works only because both powers matched. A second check: if y is log base 3 of 7, then 3 to the y is 7, and raising both sides to the fourth gives 81 to the y equals 2401, so y is log base 81 of 2401 as well. The same idea evaluates things like log base 8 of 4: both are powers of 2, three of them and two of them, so the answer is two thirds.
segments.expand: Evaluate log base 4 of 8 and log base 27 of 9 by matching powers, without a calculator.

check.q: Log base 8 of 4 equals what?
check.again: When base and argument are powers of the same number, the exponents settle it. Eight is 2 cubed and 4 is 2 squared. Change of base gives l n of 2 squared over l n of 2 cubed, and the power rule pulls the exponents out: 2 l n 2 over 3 l n 2, and the l n 2 cancels, leaving two thirds. Check: 8 to the two thirds is the cube root of 8, which is 2, squared, which is 4. The cancelling works only because both were powers of the same 2; it is not a licence to cancel arbitrary numbers inside logs.

segments.title: The graphs tell the same story
segments.text: For a positive base a not equal to 1, y equals a to the x and y equals log base a of x are inverse functions: log base a of a to the x is x for every real x, and a to the log base a of x is x for every positive x. So 10 to the log 5 is 5 and e to the l n 3 is 3. An inverse swaps input and output, so the point 3 comma 8 on y equals 2 to the x becomes 8 comma 3 on y equals log base 2 of x, and the two graphs are reflections in the line y equals x. The exponential has domain all reals, range positive, passes through 0 comma 1 because a to the zero is 1, and hugs the horizontal axis as an asymptote. The logarithm has domain positive x, range all reals, passes through 1 comma 0, and hugs the vertical axis. Both increase when the base is greater than 1 and decrease when the base is between 0 and 1. For y equals 2 to the x, each unit step in x doubles the output: one quarter, one half, 1, 2, 4, 8.
segments.expand: Describe the graph of y equals one half to the x and its inverse, comparing them with base 2.

check.q: The point 3 comma 8 lies on y equals 2 to the x. Which point lies on y equals log base 2 of x?
check.again: An inverse function swaps input and output. Since 2 cubed is 8, the exponential contains 3 comma 8, and the logarithm answers the reverse question, 2 to what power gives 8, so it contains 8 comma 3. Swapping coordinates is a reflection in the line y equals x, which is why the two graphs mirror each other. Another pair: 0 comma 1 on the exponential becomes 1 comma 0 on the log. The exponential takes every real input and gives positive outputs; the log takes positive inputs and gives every real output.

segments.title: Which bases are excluded, and why
segments.text: Three cases are ruled out as a logarithm base. Base 1 fails because 1 to any power is 1, so the output could never identify a unique exponent; the question two to what power would have every answer and no answer. Base 0 fails because it does not define the needed positive exponential function for every real x. A negative base can produce real values at some exponents, negative 2 squared is 4, but not a real exponential function on the whole real line; think of negative 2 to the one half. Standard real logarithms therefore require a positive base other than 1. The same exclusions come from the graph: the exponential must be a smooth curve that never touches zero and passes the horizontal-line test, so that its reflection in y equals x is a function. That is the picture behind the real-log checklist, base positive and not 1, argument positive.
segments.expand: Explain the horizontal-line-test reason that base 1 cannot have an inverse function.

check.q: Base 1 is excluded as a logarithm base because 1 to any power is 1.
check.again: A logarithm has to identify a unique exponent, and base 1 cannot do that. Log base 1 of 1 would ask, 1 to what power gives 1, and every exponent works, while log base 1 of 5 has no answer at all, since 1 to any power is still 1. Base 0 and negative bases fail too, because they do not give a smooth exponential curve for every real x; think of negative 2 to the one half. So the real-log checklist is: base positive and not 1, argument positive. Base 2, base 10 and base e all qualify.

segments.title: Moving a graph with confidence
segments.text: The same translation rules apply to exponential, logarithmic and every other family. With h and k positive: y equals f of x plus h moves the graph left h; f of x minus h moves it right h; f of x plus k, with the k outside, moves it up k; and minus k outside moves it down. Why does the inside sign feel reversed? If the old input was 1, then f of x plus 2 reaches that same input when x plus 2 equals 1, so x is negative 1: the point moved left. Read which side of the equals sign changed: y plus 1 equals f of x is the same as y equals f of x minus 1, a shift down. Worked example: y equals log base 2 of the quantity x minus 2, plus 1. Start from log base 2 of x, move right 2, then up 1. Domain: x minus 2 greater than zero, so x greater than 2. Vertical asymptote at x equals 2. The anchor point 1 comma 0 becomes 3 comma 1, and 2 comma 1 becomes 4 comma 2. Check a point: at x equals 3, log base 2 of 1 plus 1 is 1.
segments.expand: Describe the domain, asymptote and two points of y equals log base 2 of the quantity x plus 3, minus 2.

check.q: Starting from y equals log base 2 of x, where does y equals log base 2 of the quantity x minus 2, plus 1, move the graph?
check.again: Changes inside the function move the graph horizontally with the opposite sign; changes outside move it vertically with the sign as written. Inside, x minus 2 moves the graph right 2, because the old input 1 is now reached when x is 3. Outside, plus 1 lifts everything up 1. So the anchor point 1 comma 0 lands on 3 comma 1, the domain becomes x greater than 2, and the vertical asymptote sits at x equals 2. Compare y equals log base 2 of the quantity x plus 4, minus 3: left 4 and down 3.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: A logarithm is an exponent: log base b of x equals y means b to the y equals x, with base positive and not 1 and argument positive. A bare log is base 10 and l n is base e. Three rules, product to sum, quotient to difference, power to multiplier, all in one base; a sum inside has no rule, and a coefficient in front is not a base. Change of base puts the argument's log over the base's log in the same logarithm, and matching powers can cancel a common exponent. Exponential and log of the same base undo each other, so 10 to the log 5 is 5, and their graphs reflect in y equals x through 0 comma 1 and 1 comma 0. Shifts: inside moves horizontally with the opposite sign, outside moves vertically, and a log's domain always comes from argument greater than zero.
segments.expand: Restate the definition of a logarithm and use it to explain one of the three rules from scratch.

check.q: The recap says a bare log is base e and l n is base 10.
check.again: It is the other way around: a log written with no base is base 10, the common logarithm, and l n is the natural logarithm with base e. So log 1000 is 3, because 10 cubed is 1000, and l n of e squared is 2. The recap's other reminders: a logarithm is an exponent; products become sums, quotients become differences, and powers become multipliers, all in one base; change of base puts the argument's log over the base's log; the exponential and log of one base undo each other; and a log's domain comes from argument greater than zero.

lectures.title: Solving logarithmic and exponential equations
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 05 - Solving Logarithmic and Exponential Equations.md; Washington §13.2, §13.3, §13.6, §6.8

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Last time we practised with the tool; this time the tool gets used. The idea that connects everything: turn the equation into one you already know how to solve. Four rewrites do that. Change the form using the definition of a log. Match the bases. Condense several logarithms into one. Or take a logarithm of both sides. The shape of the equation tells you which one to reach for, and every candidate answer then has to survive the original equation. We will start with why these equations matter, with the Richter scale, pH, growth and decay, and algorithm cost as examples, then work each method on a class example, and finish with the extraneous-root check and why rewriting can let in a value the original never allowed.
segments.expand: Name the four methods and, for each, the one-phrase description of the equation shape it suits.

check.q: This lecture says every candidate answer must survive the original equation.
check.again: The lecture's plan has two halves. First, rewrite the equation into a shape you already know how to solve, using one of four moves: apply the definition of a log, match the bases, condense several logs into one, or take a logarithm of both sides. Second, test every candidate in the original equation, not in a rewritten line, because some rewrites let in values the original never allowed. For instance, a candidate that makes a log's argument negative is thrown out even though the algebra produced it cleanly. Solve, then check, every time.

segments.title: Why these equations matter
segments.text: Logarithms and exponentials show up wherever a quantity spans many orders of magnitude. Richter magnitude is a base-10 logarithmic scale, so each whole point is a factor of ten in measured amplitude; from magnitude 5 to 7 is 10 squared, a hundred times, not twice and not twenty times. pH works the same way: one pH unit lower means ten times the hydrogen-ion concentration. Population growth, drug dosage and radioactive decay follow exponential models, and solving for the time means solving for an exponent. In computing, the cost of an algorithm is written as a function of input size n, and an exponent there matters enormously. Compare n to the 1.5 with 2 to the n at n equals 100: the first is a thousand, the second is about 1.27 times 10 to the 30. Note the difference in shape: n to the 1.5 has the variable in the base, a power function; 2 to the n has the variable in the exponent, an exponential. Exponential growth eventually overtakes every power function.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between a power function and an exponential function with a small table of values for n equals 1, 2, 3, 4.

check.q: From Richter magnitude 5 to magnitude 7, the measured amplitude grows by what factor?
check.again: Richter magnitude is a base-10 logarithmic scale, so each whole step is a factor of ten in amplitude, not an addition. Two steps, from 5 to 7, means 10 times 10, a hundred times. Magnitude 8 would be a thousand times magnitude 5. The pH scale behaves the same way: dropping one pH unit means ten times the hydrogen-ion concentration. Logs compress quantities that span many orders of magnitude into small friendly numbers, which is why these scales exist, and why reading them as ordinary linear differences goes so badly wrong.

segments.title: Method one: change the form
segments.text: The definition itself is the first tool: log base b of M equals k means b to the k equals M, for b positive and not 1 and M positive. Use it when one logarithm stands alone on one side and a number stands on the other, or when a single exponential is already isolated. One rewrite often isolates the unknown completely. Example: log base 49 of x equals negative one half. Change the form: x equals 49 to the negative one half. The negative exponent means reciprocal, so that is 1 over 49, to the one half, and the one half means principal square root, so x is one seventh. Check: 49 to the negative one half is one seventh. Where did the plus or minus go? Nowhere, because 49 to the negative one half is a symbol for the principal root, a single value. And independently, x is the argument of a logarithm, so x must be positive; negative one seventh could never qualify.
segments.expand: Solve log base 8 of x equals negative two thirds by changing the form, explaining each exponent step.

check.q: Solving log base 49 of x equals negative one half gives x equal to what?
check.again: Use the definition: log base b of M equals k means b to the k equals M. So x equals 49 to the negative one half. The negative exponent means a reciprocal, 1 over 49 to the one half, and the one half means the principal square root, so x is 1 over 7. There is no plus or minus, because a fractional exponent names the single principal root, and a log's argument must be positive anyway. Similar example: log base 8 of x equals negative one third gives x equals 8 to the negative one third, which is one half.

segments.title: Method two: make the bases common
segments.text: The rule: if b to the u equals b to the v, with b positive and not 1, then u equals v. Reach for it when both sides can be written as powers of one base. The giveaway is a number you recognise as a power: 8, 16, 32 are powers of 2; 9, 27, 81 are powers of 3; 25 and 125 are powers of 5. Example: 3 to the power of the quantity 4 x plus 1, equals 27. Since 27 is 3 cubed, the exponents match: 4 x plus 1 equals 3, so x equals one half. Check: 4 times one half plus 1 is 3, and 3 cubed is 27. Sometimes both sides need rewriting: 8 to the power of the quantity x plus 2, equals 16. Eight is 2 cubed and 16 is 2 to the fourth, so 2 cubed, all to the power of the quantity x plus 2, equals 2 to the fourth. The commonest slip in the topic: a power of a power multiplies the whole inner exponent, so the left side is 2 to the 3 x plus 6, not 2 to the 3 x plus 2. Then 3 x plus 6 equals 4 gives x equals negative two thirds. Check: 8 to the four thirds is the cube root of 8, 2, to the fourth, which is 16.
segments.expand: Solve 4 to the power of the quantity x minus 1, equals 32 by rewriting both sides as powers of 2.

check.q: In 8 to the power of the quantity x plus 2, equals 16, rewriting 8 as 2 cubed gives which left-side exponent?
check.again: A power of a power multiplies the exponents, and the multiplication applies to the whole inner exponent. Two cubed, raised to the quantity x plus 2, is 2 to the 3 times the quantity x plus 2, which is 2 to the 3 x plus 6. Multiplying only the x gives 3 x plus 2, the classic slip. With 16 written as 2 to the fourth, matching exponents gives 3 x plus 6 equals 4, so x is negative two thirds. Smaller example: 9 to the power of the quantity x plus 1 is 3 to the 2 x plus 2.

segments.title: Method three: condense, or expand
segments.text: Two hints tell you to condense before doing anything else: several log terms with one shared base, or one log of a product, quotient or power that would be easier apart. Inside one base with positive arguments, log u plus log v is log of u v, log u minus log v is log of u over v, and r log u is log of u to the r. A minus sign between logarithms becomes a division inside one logarithm, and that single translation turns the class example into a method-one problem. Solve log base 5 of the quantity x plus 1, minus log base 5 of x, equals 2. Domain first: both arguments positive, so x greater than zero. Quotient rule: log base 5 of the fraction, the quantity x plus 1 over x, equals 2. Change the form: the quantity x plus 1, over x, equals 25. Multiply by x: x plus 1 equals 25 x, so 24 x equals 1 and x is one twenty-fourth. Check: one twenty-fourth plus 1, over one twenty-fourth, is 25, and log base 5 of 25 is 2. Method three rarely finishes a problem alone; it reshapes the equation so method one or two can close it.
segments.expand: Solve 2 log base 3 of x minus log base 3 of 2 equals log base 3 of 8 for positive x, showing the condensing steps.

check.q: Log base 5 of the quantity x plus 1, minus log base 5 of x, equals 2. What is x?
check.again: A minus between two logs in the same base condenses to one log of a quotient. So the equation becomes log base 5 of the fraction, the quantity x plus 1 over x, equals 2. Apply the definition: that fraction equals 5 squared, which is 25. Multiply through by x: x plus 1 equals 25 x, so 24 x equals 1 and x is one twenty-fourth, which is positive as the domain requires. Check: one twenty-fourth plus 1 is 25 twenty-fourths, and dividing by one twenty-fourth gives 25, whose log base 5 is 2.

segments.title: Method four: take the log of both sides
segments.text: When the two bases cannot be matched, none of the first three methods closes the problem. Apply a logarithm to both sides and let the power rule pull each exponent down: log of b to the u equals u log b. Every unknown then sits in a product instead of an exponent, and ordinary algebra finishes: expand, collect the x terms, factor out x, divide. Class example: 2 to the power of the quantity x minus 3, equals 6 to the power of the quantity 1 minus 2 x. Two and 6 share no base, so take the common log of both sides: the quantity x minus 3, times log 2, equals the quantity 1 minus 2 x, times log 6. Expand both brackets, collect the x terms on one side, factor out x, and divide. Condensing the numerator and denominator tidies the answer to log 48 over log 72, which is log base 72 of 48, about 0.9052. That fraction is the exact answer and the decimal is an approximation. Sanity check: 48 is less than 72, so the quotient must be just under 1. Sign discipline matters most here; nearly every error in this method is a dropped negative, not a misunderstanding.
segments.expand: Solve 2 to the x equals 7 and 3 to the power of the quantity x plus 1, equals 5 to the power of the quantity 2 x minus 1 by logging both sides, keeping the exact form.

check.q: In method four, the exact answer log 48 over log 72 is the same as log base 72 of 48.
check.again: Change of base says log base b of x equals log x over log b, with the argument's log on top and the base's log underneath. Reading log 48 over log 72 in that pattern, the argument is 48 and the base is 72, so it is log base 72 of 48, about 0.9052. Since 48 is smaller than 72, the exponent must be a little under 1, which the decimal confirms. Method four is used when bases cannot be matched: take a log of both sides, let the power rule bring each exponent down, then solve with ordinary algebra.

segments.title: Check every candidate
segments.text: Two of the four methods can hand you a value that the algebra accepts and the original equation refuses. The pipeline is: solve, get candidates, test each one in the original equation, keep the survivors. Class example: log x plus log of the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 1, base 10. Domain first: x greater than zero and 2 x minus 1 greater than zero, so x greater than one half. Product rule: log of x times the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 1. Change the form: x times the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 10. Expand and set to zero: 2 x squared minus x minus 10 equals zero. The AC method with product negative 20 and sum negative 1 gives negative 5 and 4, so it factors as 2 x minus 5 times x plus 2. Candidates: five halves and negative 2. Negative 2 fails the domain; substituted back, it asks for the log of negative 2, which no real logarithm supplies. It is extraneous and discarded. Five halves passes: log of 2.5 plus log of 4 is log 10, which is 1. The solution is x equals five halves.
segments.expand: Solve log base 2 of the quantity x minus 1, plus log base 2 of the quantity x plus 1, equals 3, checking both candidates.

check.q: Log x plus log of the quantity 2 x minus 1 equals 1 gave candidates five halves and negative 2. Which is the solution?
check.again: Every candidate goes back into the original equation. Negative 2 would require the log of negative 2, and no real logarithm takes a negative argument, so it is extraneous and discarded even though the algebra produced it. Five halves works: log of 2.5 plus log of 4 is log of 10, which is 1. The domain written at the start, x greater than one half, already predicted that rejection. A candidate that fails the domain is not an arithmetic error; it is a value the condensing step let in, and the check is what removes it.

segments.title: Why extraneous roots appear
segments.text: Log u plus log v equals log of u v is an identity only where u and v are both positive. At x equals negative 2 in the class example, both arguments are negative, their product is positive, and the condensed equation is perfectly happy, while the original is undefined. The rewrite widened the domain. The same thing happens when you square both sides of an equation. A discarded root is not an arithmetic mistake; it is a value that the rewriting let in, and the check in the original is what removes it. This is also why the domain is written down before the algebra starts: it turns the final rejection into a decision you already planned, rather than a surprise. A useful picture of skill: at first each step is a separate action needing thought; with practice you see the whole procedure before starting; eventually the method is a tool you pick up without rehearsing. Asking which shape is this, before writing, is what moves you along.
segments.expand: Give a second example of a rewrite that widens a domain, such as squaring both sides, and how the check catches it.

check.q: An extraneous root is a value that a rewrite let in, not an arithmetic mistake.
check.again: Combining log u plus log v into log of u v is only valid when u and v are both positive. At a value where both are negative, their product is positive, so the condensed equation is satisfied while the original is undefined; the rewrite widened the domain. Squaring both sides does the same thing: x equals 3 becomes x squared equals 9, which also accepts negative 3. The cure is the same each time: write the domain before starting, then test every candidate in the original equation and keep only those that survive.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Four methods, chosen by shape. One logarithm alone equals a number: change the form with the definition. Both sides powers of one base: equate the exponents, remembering that a power of a power multiplies the whole inner exponent. Several logs in one base: condense with the product, quotient and power rules, then finish with method one or two. Bases that share nothing: take a log of both sides and let the power rule bring the exponent down. Always record the domain first, argument greater than zero for every logarithm, and test every candidate in the original equation, because condensing and squaring can widen the domain and let in an extraneous root. Keep exact answers exact, like log 48 over log 72, and label a rounded decimal as the approximation it is.
segments.expand: Pick two of the four methods and give a fresh small equation for each.

check.q: The recap says to reach for taking a log of both sides when what is true?
options: Both sides are powers of one base
check.again: Method four is the fallback when the other shapes do not appear. If both sides can be written as powers of one base, like 4 to the x equals 32 with both powers of 2, equate the exponents instead. If one logarithm stands alone equal to a number, use the definition. But 3 to the x equals 7 has no shared base, so take a logarithm of both sides and let the power rule bring the exponent down: x log 3 equals log 7, so x is log 7 over log 3. Then record the domain and check every candidate.

lectures.title: Radicals and rationalizing denominators
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 06 - Radicals and Rationalizing Denominators.md; Washington §11.3 to §11.5, §1.6

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: The one idea behind this lecture: multiplying by a cleverly chosen form of 1 changes how an expression looks without changing what it is worth. Simplifying a radical pulls perfect powers out of the root. Rationalizing pushes a root out of the denominator. Both are the same move: rewrite, never re-value. We start by pulling perfect squares out of a radicand, with divisibility shortcuts for finding factors and care about letters under the root. Then mixed form and entire form, then rationalizing a single-radical denominator, then higher roots, where you need a perfect n-th power rather than a perfect square, and finally two-term denominators, which take the conjugate. A logarithm trap that surfaced in practice gets a short visit at the end.
segments.expand: Explain in two sentences why simplifying a radical and rationalizing a denominator are the same underlying move.

check.q: This lecture says simplifying a radical and rationalizing a denominator are both the same move. Which move?
options: Dividing both sides by the root
check.again: Both jobs rewrite an expression without changing its worth, and the tool is multiplying by a cleverly chosen 1. Simplifying pulls a perfect power out from under the root; rationalizing multiplies top and bottom by the same radical so the root leaves the denominator. For example, 1 over root 2 times root 2 over root 2 is root 2 over 2, and a calculator shows both are about 0.707. Squaring top and bottom would change the value, and there are no sides to divide, since these are expressions, not equations.

segments.title: Pull perfect squares out
segments.text: The quantity under a radical is the radicand. To simplify a square root, split the radicand into a perfect-square factor times whatever is left, then take the root of the perfect square. The rule: root of a times b equals root a times root b, for a and b non-negative. That condition is not decoration; with a and b both negative 1 the left side is 1 while the right side is not even a real product. Worked example: 216 is 36 times 6, so root 216 is root 36 times root 6, which is 6 root 6. You do not have to find the biggest square first. For root of 512 k squared, take 64 k squared times 8: that gives 8 times the absolute value of k times root 8, and root 8 is 2 root 2, so the total is 16 times the absolute value of k times root 2. Where do the bars come from? The root of k squared is the absolute value of k. At k equals negative 3 the original is positive, while 16 k root 2 would be negative. Drop the bars only if the question says the variables are non-negative.
segments.expand: Simplify root 512 a second way, starting from 256 times 2, and confirm both routes agree.

check.q: Simplified, the square root of 512 k squared equals what?
options: 16 times the absolute value of k, times root 2
16 k root 2, with no absolute value bars
64 times the absolute value of k, times root 8
check.again: Split the radicand into a perfect square times what is left: 512 k squared is 64 k squared times 8. Root of 64 k squared is 8 times the absolute value of k, and root 8 is 2 root 2, so the whole thing is 16 times the absolute value of k, times root 2. The bars are there because the root of k squared is the absolute value of k: at k equals negative 1 the original is root 512, positive, while 16 k root 2 would be negative. Drop the bars only when the question says k is non-negative.

segments.title: Divisibility shortcuts and letters
segments.text: Finding the factors is the slow part, and three checks cover most classroom radicands. An even number divides by 2. A number ending in 5 or 0 divides by 5. A number whose digits sum to a multiple of 3 divides by 3. For 147, 1 plus 4 plus 7 is 12, so 147 divides by 3, giving 3 times 49, and 49 is a perfect square: root 147 is 7 root 3. With letters, split every part into perfect square times leftover. For root of 147 m cubed n cubed: 147 is 49 times 3, m cubed is m squared times m, n cubed is n squared times n. So the root is 7 m n times root of 3 m n. The expression is real only where m n is non-negative, and under that condition the absolute value of m n equals m n, which is why no bars are needed here. Multiply numbers with numbers and letters with letters, the same bookkeeping as multiplying algebraic terms; the radical sign does not change it.
segments.expand: Simplify root of 75 x to the fifth, stating what the variable must satisfy.

check.q: A number whose digits sum to a multiple of 3 divides by 3.
check.again: That is the digit-sum test, one of three quick divisibility checks: even numbers divide by 2, numbers ending in 0 or 5 divide by 5, and a digit sum that is a multiple of 3 means the number divides by 3. Try 243: 2 plus 4 plus 3 is 9, so 243 divides by 3, giving 81, which is a perfect square. Root 243 is therefore 9 root 3. With letters, split each one the same way: m to the fifth is m to the fourth times m, so root of m to the fifth is m squared root m for non-negative m.

segments.title: Mixed form and entire form
segments.text: A mixed radical has a factor outside the sign, like 7 m n root of 3 m n. An entire radical keeps everything inside, like root of 147 m cubed n cubed. Converting back is the same rule read right to left: square the outside factor and take it under the sign. So 7 m n root of 3 m n becomes root of 49 m squared n squared times 3 m n, which is root of 147 m cubed n cubed. Neither form is more correct, and there is rarely a practical advantage to one over the other; it is a manipulation exercise that trains you to move quantities across a radical sign without changing the value. Be able to go both ways and then stop agonising. One caution when going to entire form: the outside factor must be non-negative before it goes under a square root, because everything that comes out of a square root is non-negative. Negative 3 root 2 is not root 18; it is negative root 18.
segments.expand: Convert 5 root 2 and negative 2 root 7 to entire form, explaining the sign handling.

check.q: Written as an entire radical, negative 3 root 2 equals what?
check.again: To take an outside factor under the root, square it first: 3 becomes 9, and 9 times 2 is 18. But a square root only ever produces a non-negative number, so the negative sign cannot go inside; it stays out front. Negative 3 root 2 is negative root 18, about negative 4.24, whereas root 18 is positive 4.24. Compare 5 root 3, which becomes root of 25 times 3, root 75. Mixed and entire forms are two spellings of the same value; converting either way is bookkeeping, and the sign is the one thing to watch.

segments.title: Rationalize a single-radical denominator
segments.text: To rationalize a denominator is to rewrite so no radical remains below the line. The tool is a version of 1, a fraction with equal numerator and denominator. For p over root q, multiply by root q over root q to get p root q over q. Worked example: root 6 over root 5 times root 5 over root 5 is root 30 over root 25, which is root 30 over 5. The two forms look nothing alike, so check on a calculator: both are about 1.095. Same number, different clothing. Tidy the fraction before you rationalize: 6 root 14 over 12 root 22 reduces to one half times root of 7 over 11, which is root 7 over 2 root 11. Now multiply by root 11 over root 11, not by 2 root 11 over 2 root 11, because the 2 is already rational. The result is root 77 over 22. Choose the smallest multiplier that clears the root. With a two-term numerator, distribute across both terms: root 3 minus 9, over root 6, becomes root 18 minus 9 root 6, over 6, and root 18 is 3 root 2, so after cancelling a common 3 it is root 2 minus 3 root 6, over 2.
segments.expand: Rationalize 4 over root 8, reducing first, and check both forms numerically.

check.q: Rationalized, root 6 over root 5 equals what?
check.again: Multiply top and bottom by the root that sits underneath, root 5 over root 5, which is a form of 1. The numerator becomes root 6 times root 5, which is root 30. The denominator becomes root 5 times root 5, which is root 25, and that is exactly 5, not 25, because the root of a square is the number itself. So the answer is root 30 over 5, about 1.095, the same as the original. Another example: 2 over root 3 becomes 2 root 3 over 3. Tidy the fraction first so you multiply by the smallest root that clears it.

segments.title: Why rationalize at all
segments.text: Historically it mattered: when calculations were fed into room-sized machines, a radical in a denominator meant an awkward extra division, so answers were standardised with the root on top. Modern calculators do not care. What survives is the practical reason: the same value has many valid written forms, and you need to recognise your answer when a textbook, an instructor or a tool hands it back in a different one. Root 30 over 5 and root 6 over root 5 are the same number. Rationalized form is the standard way to present a final radical answer, so treat the skill as expected regardless of the history. The habit that makes it painless is the numeric check: evaluate the original and your rationalized form, and if the decimals agree you have rewritten without re-valuing.
segments.expand: Give two different-looking exact forms of the same number and show how to confirm they are equal.

check.q: The lecture says modern calculators need rationalized denominators to compute correctly.
check.again: Modern calculators do not care where the root sits; root 6 over root 5 and root 30 over 5 both evaluate to about 1.095. The historic reason was that early machines found a radical in the denominator awkward. The reason that survives is recognition: the same value has many written forms, and you need to recognise your own answer when an instructor or a textbook presents it differently. Rationalized form is the standard way to present a final radical answer, so do it, and confirm with a decimal check that the value did not change.

segments.title: Higher roots need a perfect n-th power
segments.text: The same idea extends to cube roots, fourth roots and beyond, but the target changes. For an n-th root you must build a perfect n-th power under the radical, not a perfect square, because the n-th root of a to the n is a for non-negative a. Worked example: rationalize 1 over the fourth root of 8. Since 8 is 2 cubed, the radicand is one factor of 2 short of 2 to the fourth. Supply exactly that one factor: multiply by the fourth root of 2 over itself. The denominator becomes the fourth root of 2 to the fourth, which is 2, and the answer is the fourth root of 2, over 2. The tempting wrong move is to multiply by the fourth root of 8 again; that gives the fourth root of 64, and 64 is 2 to the sixth, not a perfect fourth power, so the denominator is still irrational. The multiplier is chosen by what the radicand needs, not by copying the denominator. Count the factors: you have three, you want four, you need one more. Check numerically: both forms are about 0.5946.
segments.expand: Rationalize 1 over the cube root of 4 by counting factors of 2 to a perfect cube.

check.q: To rationalize 1 over the fourth root of 8, multiply top and bottom by what?
check.again: For an n-th root, build a perfect n-th power under the radical. Eight is 2 cubed, three factors of 2, and a fourth root needs four, so supply exactly one more: multiply by the fourth root of 2 over itself. The denominator becomes the fourth root of 16, which is 2, and the answer is the fourth root of 2, over 2. Copying the denominator and multiplying by the fourth root of 8 gives the fourth root of 64, and 64 is 2 to the sixth, not a fourth power, so the root remains. Count factors: have three, need four.

segments.title: Two-term denominators take the conjugate
segments.text: When the denominator has two terms with a plus or minus between them, no single radical clears it. Multiply by the conjugate instead: the same two terms with the sign between them flipped. The pattern is a plus b times a minus b equals a squared minus b squared; the cross products cancel and both terms get squared, which is exactly what removes a square root. Watch the middle terms die: 2 plus root 3 times 2 minus root 3 is 4, minus 2 root 3, plus 2 root 3, minus 3, which is 1. So 1 over the quantity 2 minus root 3, times the quantity 2 plus root 3 over itself, is simply 2 plus root 3, about 3.732 either way. The sign can go the other way: root 3 plus 5 times root 3 minus 5 is 3 minus 25, which is negative 22, and a negative rational denominator is still rational, so you are finished. The decision in one line: look only at the denominator. Two terms, multiply by the conjugate. One term with a square root, multiply by that root. One term with an n-th root, complete the perfect n-th power.
segments.expand: Rationalize 3 over the quantity root 7 minus 2 with the conjugate and simplify.

check.q: What is the quantity 2 plus root 3, times the quantity 2 minus root 3?
check.again: Conjugates multiply by the difference-of-squares pattern: a plus b times a minus b equals a squared minus b squared. Here a is 2 and b is root 3, so the product is 4 minus 3, which is 1. The cross terms, minus 2 root 3 and plus 2 root 3, cancel each other, and squaring root 3 removes the radical. That is why a two-term denominator is cleared by its conjugate: 1 over the quantity 2 minus root 3 becomes simply 2 plus root 3. Another pair: root 5 plus 1 times root 5 minus 1 is 5 minus 1, which is 4.

segments.title: Multiply first, then simplify
segments.text: When two radical expressions are multiplied, keep the bookkeeping from algebra: numbers with numbers, radicals with radicals. a root m times b root n is a b root of m n, for non-negative m and n. Then check the new radicand for perfect-square factors, because the product often creates one that neither factor had. Twelve root 36 is 12 times 6, which is 72, and no radical survives. Twenty-four root 28 is 24 times 2 root 7, which is 48 root 7, because 28 is 4 times 7. A worked example: 3 root 12 times 4 root 3 is 12 root 36, which is 72. The direct decimal check agrees. The order is fixed: multiply, then look for squares, then simplify. Doing it the other way round works too but usually means simplifying twice.
segments.expand: Multiply 2 root 6 by 5 root 3 and simplify, explaining why the product creates a perfect square.

check.q: When multiplying radicals, multiply numbers with numbers and radicals with radicals, then simplify.
check.again: The bookkeeping is the same as multiplying algebraic terms: a root m times b root n is a b root of m n, for non-negative m and n. So 2 root 6 times 5 root 3 is 10 root 18, and then you check the new radicand for perfect squares: 18 is 9 times 2, so the product is 10 times 3 root 2, which is 30 root 2. The product often creates a perfect square that neither factor had, so the fixed order is multiply first, look for squares second, and simplify last.

segments.title: A logarithm trap from the practice
segments.text: Splitting a number inside a logarithm uses the same find-a-convenient-factor instinct as splitting a radicand, with one rule that is easy to get backwards. Log base b of u plus log base b of v equals log base b of u times v, not log base b of u plus v. Adding logarithms multiplies the arguments. Test it: log base 2 of 16 plus log base 2 of 16 is 4 plus 4, which is 8, and log base 2 of 16 times 16 is log base 2 of 256, which is 8. Whereas log base 2 of 16 plus 16 is log base 2 of 32, which is 5, a different number. If a numeric check like this disagrees, the rule was applied in the wrong direction. Worked example from the puzzle: simplify log base 5 of 50. Write 50 as 25 times 2, so it is log base 5 of 25 plus log base 5 of 2, which is 2 plus log base 5 of 2. The split 5 times 10 is equally valid and gives 1 plus log base 5 of 10; choose the split whose perfect-power factor produces a whole number.
segments.expand: Simplify log base 3 of 45 and log base 2 of 40 by splitting off a perfect power.

check.q: Log base 2 of 16 plus log base 2 of 16 equals what?
check.again: Adding logarithms multiplies their arguments; it does not add them. Log base 2 of 16 is 4, because 2 to the fourth is 16, so the sum is 4 plus 4, which is 8. The product rule confirms it: log base 2 of 16 times 16 is log base 2 of 256, and 2 to the eighth is 256. The tempting wrong turn is log base 2 of 16 plus 16, which is log base 2 of 32, equal to 5, a different number. Same trick on log base 3 of 27 plus log base 3 of 9: 3 plus 2, which is 5.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Everything today was multiplying by a version of 1. Simplify a square root by pulling out perfect-square factors, using divisibility checks to find them, repeating passes as needed, and remembering that the root of k squared is the absolute value of k. Mixed and entire forms are two spellings of one value, and a negative outside factor stays outside. To rationalize, read the denominator: one term with a square root, multiply by that root; one term with an n-th root, supply exactly the factors that complete a perfect n-th power; two terms, multiply by the conjugate and let the difference of squares kill the cross terms. Multiply radicals number with number and root with root, then simplify. And adding logarithms multiplies their arguments; log of a sum has no rule. Check every rewrite with a decimal.
segments.expand: Give a fresh example for each of the three denominator types and name the multiplier for each.

check.q: The recap says a two-term denominator is cleared by multiplying by its conjugate.
check.again: Read the denominator and choose the multiplier. One term containing a square root: multiply by that root. One term with an n-th root: supply exactly the factors that complete a perfect n-th power. Two terms with a plus or minus between them: multiply by the conjugate, the same two terms with the sign flipped, so the difference of squares kills the cross terms. For example, 3 over the quantity root 5 plus 2 times root 5 minus 2 over itself gives 3 root 5 minus 6, over 1. Check every rewrite with a decimal.

lectures.title: Radians and the unit circle
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 07 - Radians and the Unit Circle.md; Washington §8.3, §8.4, §4.1, §8.2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: You build the unit circle by counting, not by memorising it. That is the whole lecture. Walk around the rim twice, once in steps of pi over 4 and once in steps of pi over 6, simplifying each fraction as you meet it, and every standard angle appears with its degree partner. The unit is what makes the counting honest: a radian is defined by the circle's own radius, so angle and arc length become the same arithmetic. We define the radian and derive why a full turn is 2 pi, see why degrees are a convention and why the 180-degree triangle is a flat-surface fact, do the two counting passes, attach signs to direction and meet coterminal angles, and finish with converting between radians and degrees using the single relation pi equals 180 degrees.
segments.expand: Explain in two sentences why counting around the circle beats memorising a table of angles.

check.q: This lecture builds the unit circle by counting around the rim in steps of pi over 4 and pi over 6.
check.again: The lecture's whole method is counting, not memorising. One pass steps around the circle in eighths of a turn, pi over 4 each, and a second pass in twelfths, pi over 6 each, simplifying each fraction as you go. Every standard angle appears, each with its degree partner, because a step of pi over 4 is 45 degrees and a step of pi over 6 is 30. Before the counting, the lecture defines the radian from the circle's own radius, explains why degrees are just a convention, and afterwards attaches signs to direction and converts using pi equals 180 degrees.

segments.title: A radian is built from the circle
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: Take the radius, bend it around the rim, and mark where it ends. The central angle you have just opened is one radian: the angle whose arc length equals the radius. How many fit around? The circumference is 2 pi times the radius, so exactly 2 pi radii wrap the circle, and one full turn is 2 pi radians, about 6.28. That is the whole reason the unit exists. In degrees you have to remember that a circle holds 360 of them; in radians the count falls out of the definition of a circle. The same relationship gives the arc-length formula: s equals r theta, where s is arc length, r is the radius in the same length unit, and theta is the angle in radians. Substitute 2 pi and you get the circumference, so the formula agrees with itself. Substitute 360 for a full circle and you get 360 r, which is nonsense. Convert to radians before the formula, never after. And because a radian is a ratio of two lengths, it carries no units of its own, and doubling the circle changes nothing.
segments.expand: Compute the arc length for a radius of 3 and an angle of 2 radians, then for an angle of 90 degrees, showing the conversion.

check.q: One radian is the central angle whose arc length equals what?
check.again: Bend one radius around the rim and the angle it opens is one radian. Because the circumference is 2 pi times the radius, exactly 2 pi radii fit around, so a full turn is 2 pi radians, about 6.28. That also gives the arc-length formula: arc length equals radius times angle, s equals r theta, with s and r in the same length unit and theta in radians. Example: a radius of 3 metres and an angle of 2 radians gives an arc of 6 metres. Feeding in degrees breaks the formula, so convert to radians first.

segments.title: Degrees are a convention
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: Degrees are learned so early that they feel like a property of the world. They are a choice, a useful one inherited from base-60 counting. Base 60 is all around you: 60 seconds to a minute, 60 minutes to an hour. Then the pattern changes: 24 hours to a day, 7 days to a week, 52 cards in four suits. A light switch is base 2. None of these is more natural than another. A ten-finger counter in binary makes the point: each finger is a binary digit with place values 1, 2, 4, 8, up to 512, so ten fingers give 2 to the tenth, which is 1024 patterns, and you can count from 0 to 1023. Ten fingers used one unit each reach only 10. The lesson is that a convention that has worked everywhere you have used it may still be a special case. Radians are not immune either, but at least they tie the measurement to the object being measured.
segments.expand: Explain why 2 to the tenth minus 1 is the largest number ten binary fingers can show.

check.q: Ten fingers used one unit each can count only to 10, but in binary they count to 1023.
check.again: The finger example shows that a counting convention is a choice. Treat each finger as a binary digit with place values 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on up to 512, and ten fingers give 2 to the tenth, which is 1024 patterns, so you can count from 0 to 1023. The ordinary one-unit-per-finger habit reaches only 10. Degrees are the same kind of inherited choice, from base-60 counting, like 60 seconds in a minute. Radians at least tie the angle measure to the circle's own radius rather than to a historical convention.

segments.title: The triangle that is not 180 degrees
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: You have been told all your life that a triangle's angles sum to 180 degrees. That is true on a flat surface, and only there. Picture a triangle on a sphere, on a basketball or on the Earth, with sides that are arcs of great circles, and its angles sum to more than 180 degrees. How much more depends on how big the triangle is compared with the sphere. The exact statement: for a triangle of area A on a sphere of radius R, the sum of the angles minus pi equals A over R squared, angles in radians. That excess is called the spherical excess. Let the triangle shrink toward zero area and the excess vanishes, recovering the familiar pi radians, or 180 degrees. The planar theorem is exact for flat triangles, and a small spherical triangle approaches it as the curvature effect becomes negligible. The practical reading is the same as before: check whether the rule you are using actually applies to the surface you are on.
segments.expand: Describe a triangle on the Earth with three right angles and explain why its angle sum is 270 degrees.

check.q: On a sphere, the angles of a triangle add up to what?
check.again: The 180-degree rule is a flat-surface fact. Picture a triangle on a ball with sides that are arcs of great circles and the angles add to more than 180 degrees; the extra is called the spherical excess, and it equals the triangle's area divided by the radius squared, in radians. A triangle from the north pole down to the equator, along the equator a quarter turn, and back up has three right angles, 270 degrees. Shrink the triangle and the excess fades toward zero, recovering the familiar 180. The lesson: check that a rule applies to the surface you are on.

segments.title: First pass: count in pi over 4
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: Start at zero and step around the rim, writing every step as a multiple of the same fraction, and only simplify afterwards. Step 1 is pi over 4, which is 45 degrees. Step 2 is 2 pi over 4, which simplifies to pi over 2, 90 degrees. Step 3 is 3 pi over 4, 135 degrees. Step 4 is 4 pi over 4, which is pi, 180 degrees. Step 5 is 5 pi over 4, 225 degrees. Step 6 is 6 pi over 4, which simplifies to 3 pi over 2, 270 degrees. Step 7 is 7 pi over 4, 315 degrees. Step 8 is 8 pi over 4, which is 2 pi, 360 degrees. Only four of the nine reduce, and they reduce because 4 shares a factor with the numerator. The slip to watch: 6 pi over 4 reduces by 2 to 3 pi over 2, not to pi over 2. Dividing the numerator by 2 leaves 3 pi, not pi. Reduce the fraction; do not delete the number in front of pi. Where does 5 pi over 4 sit? Five steps of 45 degrees is 225 degrees, one eighth-turn past 180, in the third quadrant. You never had to convert; the step number times 45 gives the degrees.
segments.expand: List the pi over 4 pass again, saying for each mark whether it reduces and why.

check.q: Six pi over 4 simplifies to what?
check.again: Reduce the fraction, and only the fraction. Six over 4 divides top and bottom by 2 to give 3 over 2, so 6 pi over 4 is 3 pi over 2, which is 270 degrees, six steps of 45. The slip is deleting the number in front of pi as if dividing by 2 left just pi; that would give pi over 2, which is 90 degrees, a completely different point. Same care with 2 pi over 4, which is pi over 2, and with 4 pi over 4, which is pi. Step number times 45 gives the degrees as a check.

segments.title: Second pass: count in pi over 6
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: Now walk the same rim with a smaller foot. Twelve steps of pi over 6 make a full turn, because 12 times pi over 6 is 2 pi, and each step is 30 degrees. Step 1, pi over 6, 30 degrees. Step 2, 2 pi over 6, which is pi over 3, 60 degrees. Step 3, 3 pi over 6, which is pi over 2, 90. Step 4, 4 pi over 6, which is 2 pi over 3, 120. Step 5, 5 pi over 6, 150. Step 6, pi, 180. Step 7, 7 pi over 6, 210. Step 8, 8 pi over 6, which is 4 pi over 3, 240. Step 9, 9 pi over 6, which is 3 pi over 2, 270. Step 10, 10 pi over 6, which is 5 pi over 3, 300. Step 11, 11 pi over 6, 330. Step 12, 2 pi, 360. Lay the two passes on one circle and the standard unit circle is complete. The two passes agree on the quadrantal angles, 0, pi over 2, pi, 3 pi over 2 and 2 pi, and that agreement is a free check: 2 pi over 4 and 3 pi over 6 must land on the same point. If your two passes disagree anywhere, one has a counting or simplifying error.
segments.expand: Name the quadrant of 7 pi over 6, 4 pi over 3 and 11 pi over 6 without converting, by comparing with pi and 3 pi over 2.

check.q: Counting in steps of pi over 6, step 8 is 8 pi over 6, which simplifies to what?
check.again: Divide numerator and denominator by their common factor 2: 8 over 6 becomes 4 over 3, so 8 pi over 6 is 4 pi over 3. Check with degrees: eight steps of 30 degrees is 240 degrees, and 4 pi over 3 times 180 over pi is 720 over 3, which is 240. Two pi over 3 would be 120 degrees, step 4. The pi over 6 pass and the pi over 4 pass must agree at the quadrantal angles, for instance 9 pi over 6 and 6 pi over 4 both reduce to 3 pi over 2, and that agreement is a free check on your counting.

segments.title: Direction carries the sign
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: Angles are measured from the positive horizontal axis. Counterclockwise is the positive direction; clockwise gives a negative angle, the opposite way round from a clock face. Two angles that stop at the same point on the rim are coterminal, and they differ by a whole number of full turns: theta and theta plus 2 pi k are coterminal for every integer k. Going counterclockwise to the fourth-quadrant mark takes 7 pi over 4. Going clockwise to the same mark takes only pi over 4, written negative pi over 4, and indeed 7 pi over 4 minus 2 pi is negative pi over 4. Why is coterminal not the same as equal? As positions on the circle, 7 pi over 4 and negative pi over 4 are the same place, and every trig function agrees on them. As measures of rotation they are different journeys, one most of a turn forward, the other a short turn back. If a question asks how far something rotated, the sign and the size both matter.
segments.expand: Find one positive and one negative angle coterminal with 5 pi over 3, and with negative pi over 6.

check.q: Going clockwise to the fourth-quadrant mark that 7 pi over 4 reaches gives which angle?
check.again: Counterclockwise is positive and clockwise is negative, measured from the positive horizontal axis. The mark at 7 pi over 4 is one eighth of a turn short of a full circle, so going the short way, clockwise, takes pi over 4 and is written negative pi over 4. The two are coterminal: 7 pi over 4 minus 2 pi is negative pi over 4. Similarly 11 pi over 6 and negative pi over 6 stop at the same point. As positions they are identical and every trig value agrees; as rotations, one is most of a turn forward and the other a short turn back.

segments.title: Converting between radians and degrees
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: One relation does all the work: pi radians equals 180 degrees. Divide it either way to get the multiplier you need. Going from degrees to radians, multiply by pi over 180: 210 degrees times pi over 180 is 210 pi over 180, which reduces to 7 pi over 6. Going from radians to degrees, multiply by 180 over pi: 3 pi over 5 times 180 over pi is 540 over 5, which is 108 degrees. Pick the multiplier by asking what must cancel; the old unit should disappear and the new one remain. A radian value need not contain a written pi: an angle of 3 radians is perfectly ordinary, about 172 degrees. Pi over 6 is an exact value; 0.5236 is a four-place decimal approximation of it. Keep the pi form through the algebra and approximate only at the end, if at all. Five pi over 6 is a cleaner and more precise answer than 2.618.
segments.expand: Convert 135 degrees to radians and 5 pi over 9 to degrees, choosing the multiplier by cancellation.

check.q: To convert degrees to radians, multiply by 180 over pi.
