check.again: The single relation is pi radians equals 180 degrees, and you pick the multiplier that cancels the unit you are leaving. Going from degrees to radians, multiply by pi over 180 so the degrees cancel: 90 degrees times pi over 180 is pi over 2. Going from radians to degrees, multiply by 180 over pi: pi over 3 times 180 over pi is 60 degrees. Keep the exact pi form through the algebra; 2 pi over 3 is cleaner than 2.094. A radian value can also be plain, like 3 radians, roughly 172 degrees.

segments.title: Comparing radian measures without converting
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: Which is larger, 3 pi over 4 or 2 pi over 3? You could convert to 135 and 120 degrees, but the faster habit is to compare the fractions directly. Put both over 12: 3 pi over 4 is 9 pi over 12 and 2 pi over 3 is 8 pi over 12. Since pi is positive, the comparison follows the numerators, and 3 pi over 4 is larger. That is the kind of reasoning the polygraph game from class asks for: eliminate a partner's angle card with yes-or-no questions phrased in radians, like is it greater than pi, or is it between pi over 6 and pi over 3. Each question is a fraction comparison. Naming the quadrant of a radian measure works the same way: an angle between pi over 2 and pi is in the second quadrant, between pi and 3 pi over 2 the third, and between 3 pi over 2 and 2 pi the fourth. Reasoning in radians directly is what you need when the problem never mentions degrees.
segments.expand: Compare 5 pi over 6 with 4 pi over 5 without converting to degrees.

check.q: Which is larger, 3 pi over 4 or 2 pi over 3?
check.again: Compare radian measures as fractions without converting. Put both over a common denominator of 12: 3 pi over 4 is 9 pi over 12 and 2 pi over 3 is 8 pi over 12. Pi is positive, so the larger numerator wins and 3 pi over 4 is bigger, matching 135 degrees against 120. The same habit names quadrants: 5 pi over 6 is 10 pi over 12, between 6 pi over 12 and 12 pi over 12, so it lies between pi over 2 and pi, in the second quadrant. Reasoning directly in radians is essential when a problem never mentions degrees.

segments.title: Recap
segments.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
segments.text: One radian is the central angle whose arc equals the radius, so a full turn is 2 pi radians because the circumference is 2 pi r, and arc length is s equals r theta with theta in radians only. Build the unit circle by counting: eight steps of pi over 4, each 45 degrees, and twelve steps of pi over 6, each 30 degrees, simplifying each fraction properly, so 6 pi over 4 is 3 pi over 2. Counterclockwise is positive, clockwise negative, and angles that differ by whole turns of 2 pi are coterminal, like 7 pi over 4 and negative pi over 4. Convert with pi radians equals 180 degrees, choosing the multiplier that cancels the old unit. Compare radian measures as fractions, and name quadrants by comparing with pi over 2, pi and 3 pi over 2.
segments.expand: Rebuild the pi over 6 pass from memory and give the degree partner of each mark.

check.q: The recap says clockwise angles are positive.
check.again: Counterclockwise is the positive direction and clockwise is negative, the reverse of a clock face. So pi over 3 is a third of a half turn counterclockwise, and negative pi over 3 is the same size of rotation the other way. The recap's other points: one radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius, so a full turn is 2 pi; build the circle by counting in pi over 4 and pi over 6 and reduce fractions properly; coterminal angles differ by whole turns; convert with pi equals 180 degrees; and compare or place angles by comparing fractions.

lectures.title: Special triangles, trig ratios and coterminal angles
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 08 - Special Triangles, Trig Ratios and Coterminal Angles.md; Washington §4.2 to §4.4, §8.1, §8.2, §20.6

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: Trigonometry is the unit circle and triangles saying the same thing twice. Drop a vertical from any point on the rim and you have a right triangle whose hypotenuse is 1, so the ratios collapse into the coordinates themselves, and the sign of every answer is just the sign of an x or a y. Two triangles, the 45 45 90 and the 30 60 90, give the exact values. The quadrant gives the sign. And the calculator's inverse keys hand back one of the infinitely many angles that fit, which is where the care is needed. We will name the sides correctly, work the forward direction on the calculator and explain the negative answers, go backwards with inverse trig, define coterminal angles and expose the trap hiding in inverse tangent, and finish by deriving the exact sides of both special triangles.
segments.expand: State in one sentence why the unit circle makes the trig ratios equal to coordinates.

check.q: Why does the lecture say the trig ratios collapse into coordinates on the unit circle?
check.again: Drop a vertical from any point on the rim and the radius becomes the hypotenuse of a right triangle. On the unit circle the radius is 1, so every ratio with hypotenuse underneath loses its denominator: sine is opposite over 1, which is the y coordinate, and cosine is adjacent over 1, the x coordinate. At 60 degrees, the point is one half comma root 3 over 2, so cosine is one half and sine is root 3 over 2 directly. The sign of each answer is then just the sign of x or y in that quadrant.

segments.title: The unit circle and the two triangles
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: The circle is called the unit circle because its radius is 1, and it is worth saying that out loud every time you draw one. Take any standard angle, run the radius out to the rim, and drop a vertical straight down to the horizontal axis. You now have a right triangle, and because the radius is the hypotenuse, the hypotenuse is 1 for every triangle nested in the unit circle. There are exactly two shapes worth knowing by heart. The 45 45 90 triangle comes from the pi over 4 radius; both legs are equal, since it is half a square. The 30 60 90 triangle comes from the pi over 6 radius; it is half an equilateral triangle. The tool that ties the legs together is Pythagoras: a squared plus b squared equals c squared, where a and b are interchangeable but c must be the hypotenuse. In the unit circle c is 1, so a squared plus b squared equals 1, and knowing one leg gives the other immediately.
segments.expand: Explain why the 30 60 90 triangle is half an equilateral triangle and what that says about its short leg.

check.q: Every right triangle nested in the unit circle has hypotenuse 1.
check.again: The circle is called the unit circle because its radius is 1, and the radius is the hypotenuse of every triangle you make by dropping a vertical from the rim. So Pythagoras, a squared plus b squared equals c squared with c the hypotenuse, becomes a squared plus b squared equals 1, and one leg gives the other at once. If one leg is 0.6, the other is root of 1 minus 0.36, which is 0.8. The two shapes to memorise: the 45 45 90 triangle, half a square, from pi over 4, and the 30 60 90, half an equilateral triangle, from pi over 6.

segments.title: SOH CAH TOA depends on where you stand
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent is opposite over adjacent. The names are on the calculator keys, so they are never the problem. Naming the sides is. Pick the angle first. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle and never changes. The opposite side is the one furthest from your chosen angle, not touching it. The adjacent side is the remaining leg, the one that touches your angle. Change which acute angle you stand at and opposite and adjacent swap places, though nothing about the triangle moved. Greek letters like theta, phi and alpha are just conventional names for angles; learn the symbol and its role, not the language. And tangent is not an accidental name: a tangent line touches a circle at one point, and the tangent ratio is related to that construction.
segments.expand: Label the sides of a 3 4 5 triangle from each acute angle in turn and give sine, cosine and tangent of both.

check.q: If you change which acute angle you stand at, which sides swap names?
check.again: The hypotenuse is fixed: it is always across from the right angle. The other two labels depend on where you stand. The opposite side is the leg not touching your angle; the adjacent side is the leg that does. Move to the other acute angle and those two legs trade names while the triangle itself never moves. In a 3 4 5 triangle, standing at the angle facing the 3, sine is 3 over 5; standing at the other angle, sine becomes 4 over 5. Pick the angle first, then name the sides, then read off the ratio.

segments.title: Forward on the calculator
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: The forward direction is a couple of button presses, and the only real hazard is the mode. The calculator answers in whichever mode it is in and will not warn you. Sine of 52 degrees is about 0.788, but sine of 52 radians is about 0.987; both are correct answers to different questions. Check degrees versus radians before every session. The class worked six values: sine 52 degrees, 0.788; cosine 81, 0.156; tangent 172, negative 0.141; sine 191.3, negative 0.196; cosine 2 degrees, 0.999; tangent 298, negative 1.881. These are decimal approximations with no tidy exact form, unlike the special-triangle angles. Read cosine of 2 degrees as a sanity check: a 2-degree angle is almost no rotation, so the point is almost at 1 comma 0 and its x coordinate is almost 1. A number that close to 1 is the calculator confirming the geometry.
segments.expand: Explain how to tell from a single value like sine 52 equals 0.987 that the calculator is in the wrong mode.

check.q: Sine of 52 degrees is about 0.788. What does the calculator give for sine of 52 in radian mode?
check.again: The calculator answers in whatever mode it is in and gives no warning. Sine of 52 degrees is about 0.788, but sine of 52 radians is about 0.987, a correct answer to a different question, since 52 radians is more than eight full turns. Neither is an error message, which is the danger. Check the mode before every session. Cosine of 2 degrees, about 0.999, is a good sanity check: a tiny angle barely moves the point from 1 comma 0, so the x coordinate should be almost 1. If it is not, the mode is wrong.

segments.title: The negative answers are not mistakes
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: Past 90 degrees the sides of the triangle are really the coordinates x and y of the point on the rim, and coordinates carry signs. Cosine of theta is x over 1, which is x. Sine of theta is y over 1, which is y. Tangent is y over x, for x not zero. Quadrant one, both positive: everything positive. Quadrant two, x negative and y positive: sine positive, cosine and tangent negative. Quadrant three, both negative: sine and cosine negative, tangent positive. Quadrant four, x positive and y negative: cosine positive, sine and tangent negative. Now the three negatives from class. Tangent 172 is in quadrant two: positive y over negative x is negative. Sine 191.3 is in quadrant three: y is negative, the hypotenuse is always the positive radius 1, so negative. Tangent 298 is in quadrant four: negative y over positive x is negative. And tangent is undefined where x is zero, at 90 and 270 degrees, because y over x has no value there. Sine and cosine exist for every angle; tangent does not.
segments.expand: For each quadrant, say which of sine, cosine and tangent are positive and explain it from the signs of x and y.

check.q: In quadrant three, which trig function is positive?
check.again: On the unit circle cosine is x, sine is y, and tangent is y over x. In quadrant three both coordinates are negative, so sine and cosine are both negative, but tangent is a negative divided by a negative, which is positive. Run the same reasoning elsewhere: quadrant two has negative x and positive y, so only sine is positive; quadrant four has positive x and negative y, so only cosine is positive. Tangent 200 degrees, for example, is positive, while sine 200 and cosine 200 are both negative. Tangent is undefined where x is zero, at 90 and 270.

segments.title: Backwards: inverse trig
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: Anything you can do you must be able to undo, and undoing a ratio means the inverse function, usually the second function on the key: inverse sine, inverse cosine, inverse tangent. Tangent of 298 degrees is negative 1.881. Inverse tangent of negative 1.881 gives negative 62 degrees, not 298. The calculator is not wrong, but it has not given back what you started with. Infinitely many angles share any given tangent, so the function has to choose, and it always returns the one in its principal range. Inverse tangent returns between negative 90 and 90 degrees. Inverse sine returns the same band, negative 90 to 90, with its endpoints included. Inverse cosine returns between 0 and 180. If your angle was outside that band, the key gives a different angle with the same ratio, and recovering the one you wanted is your job. Do negative 62 and 298 finish in the same place? Yes: 298 minus 360 is negative 62. One rotates 298 counterclockwise, the other 62 clockwise, and both arrive at the same point. A lazy mathematician takes the short way round.
segments.expand: Explain why inverse sine and inverse cosine need different principal ranges, using the shapes of their graphs.

check.q: Inverse tangent of negative 1.881 gives what, according to the segment?
check.again: Infinitely many angles share the same tangent, so the inverse key must pick one, and inverse tangent always picks from the band negative 90 to 90 degrees. Tangent of 298 is negative 1.881; feeding that back returns negative 62, not 298. The calculator is right, it just took the short way round: 298 minus 360 is negative 62, so the two are coterminal. Inverse sine uses the same band, and inverse cosine returns from 0 to 180. If your original angle was outside the band, recovering it is your job, not the calculator's.

segments.title: Coterminal angles
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: Co means together, as in cohabit or cooperate, and terminal means end. Two angles are coterminal when they end in the same place on the rim, which happens exactly when they differ by a whole number of full turns: theta and theta plus 360 k degrees, or theta plus 2 pi k radians, for any integer k. Direction supplies the sign. In standard position, vertex at the centre and initial side along the positive horizontal axis, counterclockwise is positive and clockwise is negative. So the angles coterminal with 298 degrees are negative 422, negative 62, 298, 658, 1018 and so on. You can go round as many times as you like in either direction, and the numbers get as large as you please without the position changing at all. That is why an equation with one trig solution has infinitely many, a point the trig-equations lecture leans on hard.
segments.expand: List three angles coterminal with 40 degrees, two positive and one negative, and three coterminal with pi over 3.

check.q: Angles that differ by 180 degrees are coterminal.
check.again: Coterminal means ending at the same point on the rim, and that needs a difference of a whole number of full turns: 360 k degrees or 2 pi k radians. A difference of 180 degrees is half a turn, landing on the opposite side of the circle, so 30 and 210 degrees are not coterminal. Angles coterminal with 30 degrees are 390, 750, negative 330 and so on. Direction supplies the sign: counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative. Because you can keep going round, one trig solution always comes with infinitely many coterminal partners.

segments.title: The trap: same tangent is not coterminal
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: This is the one place in the lesson where the shortcut breaks. Tangent of 172 degrees is negative 0.141, and inverse tangent of that gives negative 8 degrees. Are negative 8 and 172 coterminal? No. Their difference is 180 degrees, half a turn, not a whole one. They end at opposite ends of the same straight line through the centre, so both x and y flip sign, the ratio y over x is unchanged, and the tangent comes out the same. Equal tangent, different terminal point. This pairing was called coterminal in class, but by the definition given in the same breath it does not qualify; use the definition, a difference of a whole 360. The rule that makes inverse tangent safe: tangent repeats every 180 degrees, so theta equals inverse tangent of the value plus 180 k. If your angle was in quadrant one or four, the calculator's answer is coterminal with it; add 360 if you want it positive, as with 298. If your angle was in quadrant two or three, add 180 first, as with 172. Decide the quadrant before trusting an inverse-trig result.
segments.expand: Given tangent theta equals 0.75 with theta in quadrant three, recover theta from the calculator's answer.

check.q: Inverse tangent of negative 0.141 gives negative 8 degrees, but the angle was 172. What do you add?
check.again: Negative 8 and 172 differ by 180, half a turn, so they are not coterminal; they sit at opposite ends of a line through the centre. Both x and y flip sign there, so y over x is unchanged and the tangent matches while the point does not. Tangent repeats every 180 degrees, so the safe rule is theta equals inverse tangent of the value plus 180 k. Decide the quadrant first: for an angle in quadrant two or three, add 180 to the calculator's answer; for quadrant one or four, the answer is already coterminal, and adding 360 just makes it positive.

segments.title: Exact sides of the 30 60 90 triangle
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: Now run the ratios in the direction that earns exact values. The angle is known, the hypotenuse is 1, and the side is unknown. For the side adjacent to 30 degrees, known hypotenuse and adjacent means cosine: adjacent equals 1 times cosine 30, which is root 3 over 2, about 0.866. For the other leg there are two routes, and they must agree: opposite to 30 is 1 times sine 30, which is one half, and adjacent to 60 is 1 times cosine 60, which is also one half. They agree because they name the same side; standing at 30 it is opposite, standing at 60 it is adjacent. Check with Pythagoras: one half squared plus root 3 over 2 squared is one quarter plus three quarters, which is 1. The two legs are genuinely different lengths because the angles differ, and the bigger angle faces the bigger side, so the leg facing 60 is the long one. Root 3 over 2 is exact; 0.866 is a rounded approximation.
segments.expand: Give all six values, sine, cosine and tangent of both 30 and 60 degrees, from this one triangle.

check.q: In the 30 60 90 triangle with hypotenuse 1, the side adjacent to 30 degrees is what?
check.again: Known hypotenuse and wanted adjacent means cosine: adjacent equals hypotenuse times cosine of the angle, so 1 times cosine 30, which is root 3 over 2, about 0.866. The other leg is 1 times sine 30, one half, and standing at the 60-degree angle it is also 1 times cosine 60, one half; both routes name the same side. Pythagoras confirms it: one quarter plus three quarters is 1. The bigger angle faces the bigger side, so the leg opposite 60 is the long one, root 3 over 2. Root 2 over 2 belongs to the 45-degree triangle.

segments.title: Exact sides of the 45 45 90 triangle
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: The class began this triangle and broke for practice; the same method finishes it. Both acute angles are 45 degrees, so it makes no difference whether you use sine or cosine, and the legs are equal. Each leg is 1 times sine 45, which is root 2 over 2, about 0.707, and 1 times cosine 45 gives the same. Check with Pythagoras: root 2 over 2 squared is one half, and one half plus one half is 1. Now the three exact values as coordinates. Every one is just the point where the radius meets the rim, cosine theta comma sine theta. At 30 degrees, pi over 6, the point is root 3 over 2 comma one half, and tangent is 1 over root 3, which rationalizes to root 3 over 3. At 45 degrees, pi over 4, the point is root 2 over 2 comma root 2 over 2, and tangent is 1. At 60 degrees, pi over 3, the point is one half comma root 3 over 2, and tangent is root 3. Rationalizing 1 over root 3 is exactly the move from the radicals lecture, now with a reason to use it.
segments.expand: Use the three exact points and the quadrant signs to give cosine and sine of 135, 210 and 300 degrees.

check.q: At 60 degrees, or pi over 3, what is tangent?
check.again: Tangent is sine over cosine, or y over x on the unit circle. At 60 degrees the point is one half comma root 3 over 2, so tangent is root 3 over 2 divided by one half, which is root 3, about 1.732. At 30 degrees the coordinates swap, giving one half over root 3 over 2, which is 1 over root 3, rationalized to root 3 over 3. At 45 degrees both coordinates are root 2 over 2, so tangent is 1. A quick sense check: a 60-degree line is steep, so its slope should be well above 1.

segments.title: Recap
segments.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
segments.text: The unit circle has radius 1, so every nested triangle has hypotenuse 1 and the ratios become coordinates: cosine is x, sine is y, tangent is y over x, undefined where x is zero at 90 and 270 degrees. Name the sides from the angle you stand at; opposite and adjacent swap when you move. Signs come from the quadrant: all positive in one, sine in two, tangent in three, cosine in four. Inverse keys return one angle from a fixed band, negative 90 to 90 for inverse tangent, so decide the quadrant first and add 180 for quadrant two or three. Coterminal means differing by a whole 360 degrees or 2 pi; same tangent only guarantees a difference of 180. The exact values: 30 degrees gives root 3 over 2 and one half, 45 gives root 2 over 2 twice, 60 gives one half and root 3 over 2, and the bigger angle faces the bigger side.
segments.expand: Recite the exact sine and cosine of 30, 45 and 60 degrees and explain how to remember which is which.

check.q: The recap says tangent is undefined at 90 and 270 degrees because x is zero there.
check.again: Tangent is y over x, and at 90 and 270 degrees the point on the rim sits on the vertical axis where x is zero; division by zero has no value, so tangent does not exist there. Sine and cosine exist for every angle because their denominator is the hypotenuse, always 1. The recap's other reminders: name sides from the angle you stand at; signs come from the quadrant; inverse keys return from a fixed band, so decide the quadrant and add 180 for quadrants two and three; and the exact values from the two special triangles.

lectures.title: Pythagorean identities and proving identities
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 09 - Pythagorean Identities and Proving Identities.md; Washington §20.1, §4.2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Every identity in this lesson is Pythagoras wearing a different hat. Put the unit circle's own coordinates into a squared plus b squared equals c squared and you get cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta equals 1 for nothing. Divide that through by cosine squared or by sine squared and the other two identities drop out. Proving an identity then needs only two habits: turn everything into sine and cosine, and change one side only, because the destination is already printed in the question. We will derive the first identity, meet the three reciprocal ratios and the naming rule that keeps them straight, derive the two further identities with their restrictions, say exactly what a proof has to do and why working on both sides proves nothing, and then work two proofs, one that collapses to secant and one with conjugate denominators.
segments.expand: Summarise in two sentences why all three Pythagorean identities are the same fact.

check.q: This lecture says every identity in it comes from Pythagoras applied to the unit circle.
check.again: The lecture's claim is that its identities are Pythagoras in different clothes. The rim point has coordinates cosine theta and sine theta and the hypotenuse is 1, so a squared plus b squared equals c squared becomes cosine squared plus sine squared equals 1. Dividing that through by cosine squared or by sine squared produces the other two identities. Proving an identity then rests on two habits: convert everything to sine and cosine, and change one side only, since the target is already printed. Two worked proofs finish the lecture.

segments.title: The first identity, straight off the circle
segments.text: Two facts from last time are all that is needed. The coordinates of a point on the rim are x equals cosine theta and y equals sine theta, and the hypotenuse is the radius, which on the unit circle is 1. Pythagoras says a squared plus b squared equals c squared, where a and b are interchangeable and c must be the hypotenuse. Substitute a equals cosine theta, b equals sine theta and c equals 1: cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta equals 1. This is the first Pythagorean identity. It holds for every angle with no exceptions, no restriction and no quadrant condition. That unconditional truth is what makes it useful: any time sine squared and cosine squared appear added together, they can be replaced by 1 on sight. It is most often used rearranged: sine squared equals 1 minus cosine squared, and cosine squared equals 1 minus sine squared. So any 1 minus sine squared x can become cosine squared x, and both worked proofs below turn on exactly that substitution.
segments.expand: Verify the identity numerically at 30 degrees and at 120 degrees, using the exact values and the quadrant signs.

check.q: Which identity comes straight from Pythagoras on the unit circle?
options: Cosine squared plus sine squared equals 1
Cosine squared minus sine squared equals 1
check.again: Put the unit circle's own numbers into Pythagoras: legs cosine theta and sine theta, hypotenuse 1. Then a squared plus b squared equals c squared reads cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta equals 1, for every angle without exception. Check at 30 degrees: three quarters plus one quarter is 1. Cosine plus sine, unsquared, is not 1 in general; at 45 degrees it is root 2. The identity is mostly used rearranged, so 1 minus sine squared can be swapped for cosine squared on sight, which is what both worked proofs depend on.

segments.title: The square sits on the function
segments.text: Cosine squared theta means take the cosine, then square the result. It does not mean the cosine of theta squared, where the angle is squared first. Test it at 30 degrees. Cosine of 30 is root 3 over 2, and squaring that gives three quarters exactly, so cosine squared of 30 degrees is 0.75. Squaring the angle instead gives 900 degrees, which is two full turns plus 180, so its cosine is negative 1. Two completely different numbers from the same symbols read two ways. The exponent belongs to the output of the function, not to its input. The same applies to sine squared and tangent squared. When you say an identity aloud, say cosine squared of theta, and when you use one in a proof, keep the brackets in your head around the function value before it is squared.
segments.expand: Compare sine squared of 45 degrees with sine of 45 squared degrees, and explain which the identity uses.

check.q: What is cosine squared of 30 degrees?
check.again: The square sits on the output of the function, not on the angle. Take cosine of 30 first, root 3 over 2, then square it: 3 over 4, exactly 0.75. Squaring the angle instead gives cosine of 900 degrees, which is two full turns plus 180, so negative 1, a completely different number. Root 3 over 2 is cosine 30 before squaring. Same rule for sine squared: sine squared of 45 is root 2 over 2, squared, which is one half. Say cosine squared of theta out loud and picture brackets around the function value.

segments.title: Six ratios, three reciprocal pairs
segments.text: Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent is opposite over adjacent. There are three more, and they are not new ideas; each is one of the above turned upside down. Cosecant is hypotenuse over opposite, which is 1 over sine, undefined when sine is zero. Secant is hypotenuse over adjacent, which is 1 over cosine, undefined when cosine is zero. Cotangent is adjacent over opposite, which is 1 over tangent, or cosine over sine, undefined when sine is zero. The naming rule that makes these memorable: within each reciprocal pair exactly one of the two names carries the prefix co. Tangent has no co, so its reciprocal must: cotangent. Cosine already has the co, so its reciprocal drops it: secant. Sine has none, so its reciprocal takes it: cosecant. That is a naming pattern, not a derivation, but it stops you pairing the wrong two. The pairing the prefix does not give you is which side goes on top; if you are guessing, go back to the side ratios.
segments.expand: Give the six ratios for a 30 degree angle exactly, and check each reciprocal pair multiplies to 1.

check.q: Within each reciprocal pair, exactly one name carries the prefix co.
check.again: The three new ratios are the old three turned upside down: cosecant is 1 over sine, secant is 1 over cosine, cotangent is 1 over tangent. The naming pattern that stops mispairing is that each pair has exactly one co. Sine has no co, so its reciprocal takes one, cosecant. Cosine has the co, so its reciprocal drops it, secant. Tangent has none, so cotangent. It is a memory aid, not a derivation, and it does not tell you which side goes on top; for that go back to the side ratios, for instance secant is hypotenuse over adjacent.

segments.title: Every reciprocal inherits a restriction
segments.text: A reciprocal is a fraction, and a fraction with a zero denominator has no value. So secant does not exist where cosine is zero, at 90 and 270 degrees and every 180 from there. Cosecant and cotangent do not exist where sine is zero, at 0 and 180 degrees and so on. These are not technicalities; they are the reason the next two identities carry conditions. Some exact values worth having: since cosine of 60 degrees is one half, secant of 60 is 2. Since sine of 30 is one half, cosecant of 30 is 2. Since tangent of 45 is 1, cotangent of 45 is 1. Since cosine of 45 is root 2 over 2, secant of 45 is 2 over root 2, which rationalizes to root 2. Each reciprocal is the flipped fraction, sign included, so in quadrant two, where cosine is negative, secant is negative too.
segments.expand: Find secant, cosecant and cotangent of 120 degrees exactly, with signs.

check.q: Secant of 45 degrees equals what?
check.again: Secant is 1 over cosine. Cosine of 45 degrees is root 2 over 2, so secant of 45 is 2 over root 2. Rationalize by multiplying top and bottom by root 2: 2 root 2 over 2, which is root 2, about 1.414. Root 2 over 2 is the cosine itself, not its reciprocal, and 2 would be secant of 60, since cosine 60 is one half. Every reciprocal inherits a restriction: secant does not exist where cosine is zero, at 90 and 270 degrees, and it keeps cosine's sign, so it is negative in quadrant two.

segments.title: Two more identities for free
segments.text: The move is the one used throughout the radicals lecture: multiply by a well-chosen version of 1, or equivalently divide every term on both sides by the same nonzero quantity. Divide cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta equals 1 through by cosine squared theta, legitimate provided cosine theta is not zero. Cosine squared over cosine squared is 1. Sine squared over cosine squared is sine over cosine, squared, which is tangent squared. One over cosine squared is secant squared. So 1 plus tangent squared theta equals secant squared theta, provided cosine theta is not zero. Now divide the first identity through by sine squared instead, provided sine theta is not zero: cotangent squared theta plus 1 equals cosecant squared theta. Keep the restrictions with the identities. The first identity is unconditional; these two are not, because each was obtained by dividing. Conveniently, the excluded angles are exactly where the functions involved are themselves undefined, so the restriction is the same fact stated from the other end.
segments.expand: Derive cotangent squared plus 1 equals cosecant squared step by step, naming each fraction.

check.q: Dividing cosine squared plus sine squared equals 1 through by cosine squared gives which identity?
options: 1 plus tangent squared equals secant squared
Cotangent squared plus 1 equals cosecant squared
1 plus secant squared equals tangent squared
check.again: Divide each of the three terms by cosine squared theta, allowed when cosine is not zero. Cosine squared over cosine squared is 1. Sine squared over cosine squared is tangent squared, because sine over cosine is tangent. One over cosine squared is secant squared. So 1 plus tangent squared theta equals secant squared theta, with cosine theta not zero. Dividing by sine squared instead gives cotangent squared plus 1 equals cosecant squared, with sine not zero. Check the first at 45 degrees: 1 plus 1 is 2, and secant 45 squared is root 2 squared, also 2.

segments.title: What a proof has to do
segments.text: An identity claims two expressions are equal for every value of the variable where both are defined. Proving one means demonstrating that equality, not checking it at a couple of angles. Two rules. First, convert everything to sine and cosine; every other trig function is defined from those two, so it is always possible, and it puts the whole expression in one language. Second, change one side only, transforming it step by step until it reads exactly as the other side, which you leave untouched. Why is rule two not a matter of style? Operating on both sides at once, squaring both, multiplying both, cross-multiplying, assumes the two sides are already equal, because that is the only thing that licenses doing the same operation to both. But their equality is the very thing you were asked to establish. A proof that works on both sides starts from its own conclusion. Change one side, and each step is just a rewriting of a single expression into an equal one.
segments.expand: Explain with a false statement, such as 1 equals negative 1, how squaring both sides can seem to prove something untrue.

check.q: When proving an identity, why must you change one side only?
options: Working both sides assumes the conclusion
Both sides must stay in sine and cosine
The other side has no trig functions
check.again: Doing the same operation to both sides, squaring, multiplying or cross-multiplying, is only justified if the two sides are already equal. But that equality is exactly what the proof is supposed to establish, so a both-sides proof starts from its own conclusion. Instead, transform one side step by step, each step rewriting a single expression into an equal one, until it reads exactly as the untouched other side. The companion rule is to convert everything to sine and cosine, because every other trig function is built from those two.

segments.title: Which side to pick
segments.text: Pick the side that looks gnarlier: more terms, more fractions, more exotic functions. There is more to do there and more scope to simplify. Heading the other way means trying to make a simple expression complicated, which offers no guidance about the next step. And the destination is printed in the question, which is what makes these puzzles rather than searches. If the target has a single denominator of cosine x, work towards that specifically. If the target contains secant, expect 1 over cosine to appear. If it contains a product, expect to factor. Formal proofs traditionally close with Q E D, for the Latin quod erat demonstrandum, which was to be demonstrated, or with a small square in the margin. Either is optional and adds nothing mathematically; it simply marks where the argument finishes.
segments.expand: Given the identity secant x minus cosine x equals sine x tangent x, say which side to start from and what the target suggests.

check.q: Which side should you pick to work on?
check.again: Choose the side with more terms, more fractions or more exotic functions. There is more to simplify there, and simplifying gives you a direction. Starting from the simple side means trying to make something more complicated with no guide to the next step. The printed target also tells you what to aim for: a lone cosine denominator, a secant meaning 1 over cosine, a product meaning factor. If the left is secant x and the right is a messy sum of fractions, work on the right. Q E D at the end is optional decoration.

segments.title: Worked proof: a sum that collapses to secant
segments.text: Prove that tangent x sine x plus cosine x equals secant x. The left side has two terms and a tangent, so it is the gnarlier one; the right side stays as it is. Rule one: write tangent x as sine x over cosine x, so the first term becomes sine squared x over cosine x. Now the two terms have different denominators, so multiply cosine x by the version of 1 cosine x over cosine x, giving cosine squared x over cosine x. Add over the one denominator: sine squared x plus cosine squared x, all over cosine x. Identity one flattens the numerator to 1, leaving 1 over cosine x, which is secant x. Both sides now read secant x, so the identity holds for all x with cosine x not zero, which is required for tangent and secant to exist in the first place. The shape to recognise: the whole proof turns on manufacturing sine squared plus cosine squared so that identity one can collapse it. Look for a way to get those two over the same denominator and added, and the expression usually finishes in one more step.
segments.expand: Prove tangent x cosecant x equals secant x the same way, naming the rule at each step.

check.q: In proving tangent x sine x plus cosine x equals secant x, the numerator collapses to what?
check.again: Rewrite tangent as sine over cosine, so the first term is sine squared x over cosine x. Give the lone cosine x the same denominator by multiplying by cosine x over cosine x, making cosine squared x over cosine x. Adding over the shared denominator puts sine squared x plus cosine squared x on top, and the first Pythagorean identity turns that into 1. What remains is 1 over cosine x, which is secant x, valid where cosine is not zero. The whole proof is engineered to manufacture sine squared plus cosine squared so the identity can flatten it.

segments.title: Worked proof: conjugate denominators
segments.text: Prove that 1 over the quantity 1 minus sine x, minus 1 over the quantity 1 plus sine x, equals 2 tangent x secant x. Again the left is gnarlier. The two denominators are conjugates, the same two terms with opposite signs, so multiply each fraction by the other's denominator over itself. The combined numerator is 1 plus sine x, minus the bracket 1 minus sine x. Distribute the minus over the whole bracket: 1 plus sine x minus 1 plus sine x, which is 2 sine x. The combined denominator is a difference of squares: 1 minus sine squared x, which identity one turns into cosine squared x. So the left side is 2 sine x over cosine squared x, which factors as 2 times sine over cosine times 1 over cosine, that is 2 tangent x secant x. Valid where cosine x is not zero. The two places this proof is usually lost: the denominator, where the conjugate product must be recognised as a difference of squares, and the numerator, where the minus sign in front of the second bracket must flip both of its terms. Getting that wrong leaves zero on top and the proof dies.
segments.expand: Simplify 1 over the quantity 1 minus cosine x, plus 1 over the quantity 1 plus cosine x, using the same conjugate technique.

check.q: In the conjugate-denominator proof, the combined numerator simplifies to what?
check.again: Combining 1 over the quantity 1 minus sine x with 1 over the quantity 1 plus sine x over a common denominator gives numerator 1 plus sine x, minus the bracket 1 minus sine x. The minus must flip both terms in the bracket: 1 plus sine x minus 1 plus sine x, which is 2 sine x. Flipping only the first term leaves zero, and the proof dies. The denominator is a difference of squares, 1 minus sine squared x, which is cosine squared x. So the left side is 2 sine x over cosine squared x, which factors as 2 tangent x secant x.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Pythagoras with legs cosine theta and sine theta and hypotenuse 1 gives cosine squared plus sine squared equals 1, true for every angle, and its rearrangements let you swap 1 minus sine squared for cosine squared on sight. The square sits on the function, so cosine squared of 30 degrees is three quarters. The three new ratios are reciprocals: cosecant of sine, secant of cosine, cotangent of tangent, with exactly one co in each pair, and each undefined where its partner is zero. Dividing the first identity by cosine squared gives 1 plus tangent squared equals secant squared; by sine squared gives cotangent squared plus 1 equals cosecant squared, each with its restriction. To prove an identity, convert to sine and cosine and change one side only, aiming for the printed target, manufacturing sine squared plus cosine squared where you can, and treating conjugate denominators as a difference of squares.
segments.expand: State the two rules of proof and the single most common tactic, with a fresh two-line example.

check.q: According to the recap, which identity is true for every angle without restriction?
options: Cosine squared plus sine squared equals 1
1 plus tangent squared equals secant squared
Cotangent squared plus 1 equals cosecant squared
check.again: The first identity comes straight from Pythagoras with hypotenuse 1, and nothing was divided to get it, so it holds for every angle. The other two were obtained by dividing through by cosine squared or sine squared, so each carries a restriction: the tangent-secant form needs cosine not zero, ruling out 90 and 270 degrees, and the cotangent-cosecant form needs sine not zero, ruling out 0 and 180. Conveniently, those are exactly the angles where tangent, secant, cotangent and cosecant are themselves undefined. Keep the restriction attached whenever you use them.

lectures.title: Solving trigonometric equations
lectures.source: MATH 237/Lectures/MATH 237 - Lecture 10 - Solving Trigonometric Equations.md; Washington §20.5, §20.1, §7.2, §8.1, §8.2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: You already know how to solve every equation in this lesson; you just have to make it look like one of them first. Algebra, factoring and substitution reduce a messy trigonometric equation to the single familiar shape, one trig function equals one number. The unit circle then supplies the angles, and because the circle repeats forever, each angle is not an answer but the start of an infinite family: plus 2 n pi for a full turn, or plus n pi where half a turn is enough. We will contrast an equation with an identity, set out the four tactics and the shape that calls for each, then work four examples: isolate and read the circle, a squared function with both roots, a common factor to pull out, and a substitution that exposes a quadratic. One result stated in class is corrected along the way, with the disproof shown rather than asserted.
segments.expand: Explain in two sentences the difference between what an identity asks and what an equation asks.

check.q: Into what single familiar shape does this lecture reduce every trig equation?
options: One trig function equals one number
check.again: The lecture's promise is that algebra, factoring and substitution turn any messy trig equation into the one shape you can read off the unit circle: a single trig function equal to a single number, like sine x equals one half or cosine theta equals negative root 3 over 2. From there the circle supplies the angles, and each angle starts an infinite family because the circle repeats: plus 2 n pi for a full turn, or plus n pi when half a turn already works. The equation is not solved until the families are written.

segments.title: Identity versus equation
segments.text: An identity is true for every angle in its domain, and proving one means transforming one side until it matches the other. A trigonometric equation is the opposite kind of object: it is true only for particular angles, and solving it means finding those angles. That difference in purpose changes the permissions. In a proof you may not multiply both sides or move a term across, because that assumes the very thing being proved. In an equation you may; the usual algebra is back, the same operation on both sides, exactly as in the algebra lectures. The finishing condition differs too. A proof is finished when the two sides read the same. An equation is finished when the angles are listed, together with their families, which is the next point and the one that costs the most.
segments.expand: Give one example of a legal move in an equation that would be illegal in an identity proof, and say why.

check.q: In solving a trig equation, you may do the same operation to both sides.
check.again: An identity is true for every angle and proving it means transforming one side only, because acting on both sides would assume the result. An equation is true only for particular angles, and finding them is ordinary algebra: add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides just as in the algebra lectures. So from 2 sine x minus 1 equals 0 you may add 1 and divide by 2 to get sine x equals one half. The finishing conditions differ too: a proof ends when both sides match, an equation ends when the angles and their families are listed.

segments.title: Every answer is a family
segments.text: The unit circle closes on itself. An angle that satisfies the equation still satisfies it after one more full turn, after a hundred more, and after any number of turns backwards. So a trigonometric equation with any solution at all has infinitely many, and the answer must be written in a form that says so: x equals theta nought plus 2 n pi, with n an integer. The symbol for the integers is a capital Z, and n in Z reads n is an element of the integers, so n may be 0, or 1, or 15, or negative 3; each choice adds or removes that many complete circles. Here is the most expensive habit in the topic. Writing x equals 5 pi over 6 and x equals 7 pi over 6 and stopping is not a slightly incomplete answer. It is two answers out of an infinite number, and the class put it plainly: two over infinity is essentially nothing. The general term is not decoration; it is most of the answer. Only when a question restricts x to one interval, such as 0 to 2 pi, are the bare angles enough.
segments.expand: Write the general solution for an equation whose solutions in one turn are pi over 4 and 3 pi over 4, and list the n equals negative 1, 0 and 1 members.

check.q: Writing x equals 5 pi over 6 and 7 pi over 6 and stopping gives how much of the answer?
check.again: Because the circle closes on itself, any solution is still a solution after one more full turn, or a hundred, or any number of turns backwards. So a trig equation with one solution has infinitely many, and the answer must say so: x equals 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi, with n any integer, meaning n can be 0, 3, or negative 7. Two bare angles are two out of infinity, which the class called essentially nothing. Only when the question restricts x to an interval like 0 to 2 pi are the bare angles enough.

segments.title: Four ways to make it familiar
segments.text: The method the whole lesson runs on was given a name in class: lazy mathematics. Not laziness about the work, but refusing to invent a new technique when an old one can be made to fit. Four tactics, chosen by the shape of the equation. One trig function to the first power only: do the algebra until the function stands alone. A squared trig function sitting alone: take both square roots, plus and minus. Every term sharing a common factor: factor, and use the zero-product rule to split into two simpler equations. A squared function and a first power of the same function: substitute a letter, factor as a quadratic, then undo the substitution. Factor first if you can; it was called out as the move that always makes things simpler, because it splits one hard equation into two easy ones. The zero-product rule only works against zero, so getting everything onto one side is a precondition, not tidiness. A fifth move sits behind all of these: when sine squared and cosine squared are mixed, convert with the Pythagorean identity to reach one function.
segments.expand: For each of the four tactics, give a short example equation that calls for it and nothing else.

check.q: The lecture says factoring is the move that always makes a trig equation simpler.
check.again: Factoring splits one hard equation into two easy ones through the zero-product rule, which is why the lecture calls it the move that always simplifies. The rule only works against zero, so first get every term onto one side. For instance, sine x cosine x plus sine x equals 0 factors as sine x times the bracket cosine x plus 1 equals 0, giving sine x equals 0 or cosine x equals negative 1. The other tactics: isolate a first-power function, take both square roots of a squared function, and substitute a letter when a squared and a first power appear together.

segments.title: Worked example: isolate, then read the circle
segments.text: Solve 2 cosine x plus root 3 equals 0. Step one, algebra until the function stands alone: 2 cosine x equals negative root 3, so cosine x equals negative root 3 over 2. Step two, the reference angle, the acute angle between the terminal arm and the horizontal axis, comes from the size of the number with the sign set aside. From the special triangles, cosine of pi over 6 is root 3 over 2, so the reference angle is pi over 6. Step three, choose the quadrants from the sign. Cosine is the x coordinate, so a negative cosine means the left of the vertical axis, quadrants two and three. Step four, build each angle from the reference: in quadrant two, pi minus pi over 6, which is 5 pi over 6; in quadrant three, pi plus pi over 6, which is 7 pi over 6. Step five, extend to every turn: x equals 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi, or 7 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi, n an integer. The commonest wrong answer is pi over 6 and 11 pi over 6, the reference angle used as if the number were positive; those solve cosine x equals positive root 3 over 2. Check the sign before the size.
segments.expand: Solve 2 sine x minus 1 equals 0 with the same five steps, naming the reference angle and the quadrants.

check.q: Cosine x equals negative root 3 over 2. Which quadrants hold the solutions?
check.again: Cosine is the x coordinate, so a negative cosine means the point is left of the vertical axis, in quadrant two or three. The size, root 3 over 2, gives the reference angle pi over 6 from the special triangles. Build each solution from the reference: quadrant two is pi minus pi over 6, which is 5 pi over 6; quadrant three is pi plus pi over 6, which is 7 pi over 6; then add 2 n pi to each. Quadrants one and four would be right for positive root 3 over 2. Check the sign before the size.

segments.title: Why 2 n pi and not n pi
segments.text: The step size of the family is a property of the particular equation, not a rule to memorise. For cosine x equals negative root 3 over 2, a half turn from 5 pi over 6 lands at 11 pi over 6, where cosine is positive root 3 over 2, the wrong sign. The two solutions in one revolution are not half a circle apart, so nothing smaller than a full circle maps one onto the other, and each family needs the full 2 n pi. The test is always the same: add pi to a solution and check whether the original equation is still satisfied. If it is, half turns stay inside the solution set and n pi covers everything with fewer families. If it is not, use 2 n pi. The next example is the case where half a turn does work, and the reason is that the equation is blind to the sign of the function.
segments.expand: Test whether n pi works for tangent x equals 1 by adding pi to pi over 4 and checking.

check.q: How do you test whether a family can use n pi instead of 2 n pi?
options: Add pi and check the original equation
Add 2 pi and check the equation
Divide the reference angle by two
check.again: The step size is a property of the particular equation. Take one solution, add pi, which is half a turn, and substitute back. If the equation still holds, half turns stay inside the solution set and n pi covers everything with fewer families. If it fails, only full turns work and the family needs 2 n pi. For cosine x equals negative root 3 over 2, half a turn from 5 pi over 6 gives 11 pi over 6, where cosine is positive, so it fails and 2 n pi is required. For tangent x equals 1, adding pi keeps the value, so n pi suffices.

segments.title: Worked example: a squared function and both roots
segments.text: Solve 4 sine squared theta equals 3. Isolate the squared function: sine squared theta equals three quarters. Take the square root of both sides, keeping both signs, because squaring destroyed the sign information and undoing it must restore both possibilities: sine theta equals plus or minus root 3 over 2. The denominator simplifies exactly because 4 is a perfect square; the numerator does not, so root 3 stays. Dropping the negative root loses half the solutions, and no later step can recover them. Sine is the y coordinate, so plus or minus root 3 over 2 describes two heights, each reached twice: four points, one in every quadrant, all with reference angle pi over 3. In one revolution they are pi over 3, 2 pi over 3, 4 pi over 3 and 5 pi over 3. Now the shortcut: pi over 3 plus pi is 4 pi over 3, and 2 pi over 3 plus pi is 5 pi over 3. Each solution's diametrically opposite point is also a solution, so two families cover all four: theta equals pi over 3 plus n pi, or 2 pi over 3 plus n pi. Listing four families with 2 n pi describes the same set; the two-family form is just shorter.
segments.expand: Solve 2 cosine squared theta equals 1, keeping both roots and writing the shortest general solution.

check.q: Solving 4 sine squared theta equals 3, what does sine theta equal?
check.again: Isolate the squared function first: sine squared theta equals three quarters. Undoing a square means taking both square roots, plus and minus, because squaring erased the sign. The root of three quarters is root 3 over 2, since 4 is a perfect square and 3 is not. So sine theta is plus or minus root 3 over 2, two heights on the circle, each reached twice: pi over 3, 2 pi over 3, 4 pi over 3 and 5 pi over 3. Dropping the minus loses half of them. Because opposite points are also solutions, two families with n pi cover all four.

segments.title: Worked example: factor out the common factor
segments.text: Solve 2 cosine theta sine theta minus cosine theta equals 0. Everything is already on one side, so factor. Both terms carry cosine theta: cosine theta times the bracket 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0. The zero-product rule splits it: cosine theta equals 0, or 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0. The cosine branch: cosine is the x coordinate, zero where the terminal arm lies along the vertical axis, at pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2. Those are half a circle apart, so one family covers both: theta equals pi over 2 plus n pi. The sine branch: sine theta equals one half, positive y, quadrants one and two, reference angle pi over 6, so theta equals pi over 6 plus 2 n pi or 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi; here the full 2 n pi is needed, since half a turn from pi over 6 reaches 7 pi over 6 where sine is negative one half. Never divide the common factor away. Cancelling cosine theta from both sides to leave 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0 silently deletes the entire cosine branch, because you divided by something that is zero at exactly the angles you were about to lose.
segments.expand: Solve sine theta tangent theta equals sine theta by factoring, and say what dividing by sine theta would have lost.

check.q: Why never divide 2 cosine theta sine theta minus cosine theta equals 0 by cosine theta?
options: It deletes the cosine equals zero branch
check.again: Cosine theta is zero at some of the very angles you are looking for, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2. Dividing by it assumes it is not zero, so those solutions silently vanish and only 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0 remains. Factor instead: cosine theta times the bracket 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0, then set each factor to zero. The same trap appears in plain algebra with x times the quantity x minus 4 equals 0; dividing by x loses x equals 0. Never cancel a factor that could be zero.

segments.title: A correction from class
segments.text: The transcript records the cosine branch of that example as cosine theta equals 0 giving theta equals n pi, listed as 0, pi, 2 pi, 3 pi. That cannot be right, and it is worth being certain rather than taking a guide's word for it. Substitute theta equals pi into the original equation: 2 cosine pi sine pi minus cosine pi is 2 times negative 1 times 0, minus negative 1, which is 0 plus 1, which is 1, not 0. So pi is not a solution. The angles where cosine vanishes are pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2, not 0 and pi. Theta equals n pi is the answer to sine theta equals 0, the neighbouring fact and easy to reach for. Checking theta equals pi over 2 the same way gives 2 times 0 times 1, minus 0, which is 0. Whether the slip was on the board or in the recording cannot be told, so check this line against your own notes. The four solutions of the equation in one turn are pi over 6, pi over 2, 5 pi over 6 and 3 pi over 2.
segments.expand: Verify each of the four solutions in the original equation by substitution, using exact values.

check.q: The corrected cosine branch: cosine theta equals 0 at which angles?
check.again: Cosine is the x coordinate, and x is zero only where the terminal arm lies along the vertical axis: straight up at pi over 2 and straight down at 3 pi over 2, so the family is pi over 2 plus n pi. Zero and pi are where sine is zero, the neighbouring fact that the transcript reached for by mistake. Substitution settles it: at theta equals pi the original expression gives 2 times negative 1 times 0, minus negative 1, which is 1, not 0. Pi over 6 and 5 pi over 6 come from the other branch, sine theta equals one half.

segments.title: Worked example: substitute to expose a quadratic
segments.text: Solve 2 sine squared x minus 3 sine x plus 1 equals 0. Recognise the shape: a squared term, a first-power term of the same function, and a constant. That is a quadratic wearing a disguise. Let y equal sine x, and the equation becomes 2 y squared minus 3 y plus 1 equals 0. Factor: looking for numbers with product 2 and sum negative 3 gives negative 1 and negative 2, so it is 2 y minus 1 times y minus 1 equals 0, and y is one half or 1. Expand to check. Now undo the substitution; the question was never about y. Sine x equals one half, or sine x equals 1. The first is the branch from the previous example: pi over 6 plus 2 n pi or 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi. The second is the maximum sine ever reaches, attained at the single point at the top of the circle: pi over 2 plus 2 n pi. Three families, not four, and the asymmetry is the useful part. A value strictly between negative 1 and 1 is hit twice per revolution; the extremes plus and minus 1 once; a value outside that range never, so an equation reducing to sine x equals 2 has no solution rather than a hard one.
segments.expand: Solve 2 cosine squared x plus sine x minus 1 equals 0 by converting cosine squared first, then substituting.

check.q: Sine x equals 1 gives how many solutions per revolution?
check.again: Sine is the y coordinate, and the circle reaches height 1 at exactly one point, the very top, pi over 2. So sine x equals 1 has one solution per turn, the family pi over 2 plus 2 n pi. A value strictly between negative 1 and 1, like one half, is hit twice per revolution, once on each side. A value outside that range, like sine x equals 2, is never reached, so there are no solutions at all. That asymmetry is why the substitution example ended with three families rather than four.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: An equation is true for particular angles, and you may do the same thing to both sides; an identity is true for all angles and you may not. Every solution is a family: base angle plus 2 n pi, or plus n pi when a solution plus pi is still a solution, and two bare angles are two answers out of infinity. Four tactics, chosen by shape: isolate a first-power function; take both square roots of a squared function; factor out a common factor and use the zero-product rule, never dividing it away; substitute a letter for a squared-and-first-power function, factor, and undo the substitution before touching the circle. Convert mixed sine and cosine squares with the Pythagorean identity. Read the circle by reference angle for size and quadrant for sign, remembering cosine is zero at pi over 2 plus n pi and sine is zero at n pi, and count the expected solutions per turn before you finish.
segments.expand: Restate the four tactics and give the shape of equation each one is for, in one line each.

check.q: The recap says sine is zero at n pi and cosine is zero at pi over 2 plus n pi.
check.again: Sine is the y coordinate, zero where the arm lies along the horizontal axis at 0, pi, 2 pi and so on, which is n pi. Cosine is the x coordinate, zero on the vertical axis at pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2, which is pi over 2 plus n pi. In each case the two points are half a turn apart, so one family with n pi covers both. The recap also says: every solution is a family, choose the tactic by shape, never divide away a common factor, use the Pythagorean identity to reach one function, and read the circle by reference angle and quadrant.

lectures.title: Soldering fundamentals and bench setup
lectures.source: EFAB 202/Lab/EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup.md

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture walks through the first soldering lab: what the wire and the solder are made of, how the station and the tip behave, how heat actually gets into a joint, what a finished joint should look like, and how the bench and the hand tools fit around all of that. If you keep one sentence, keep this one: you do not make the solder joint, you make the conditions, and the joint forms itself. Clean metal, both parts hot, and surface tension does the rest. Almost every fault you will see on this bench traces back to heat that never arrived. So as we go, keep asking: where is the heat going, and is it reaching both pieces of metal?
segments.expand: Give a short overview of why heat arriving in both parts is the theme, with a one-sentence preview of the thermal bridge.
segments.eli5: Think of baking bread. You get the ingredients right, you get the oven hot, and the loaf rises by itself. A solder joint works the same way. Your job is not to sculpt the solder. Your job is to set the conditions: clean metal, and heat in both pieces. When both are true, surface tension pulls the molten solder into the joint on its own. Where the picture breaks: an oven heats the whole loaf from all sides, but the iron touches only one spot, so the heat has to travel into each piece, and that is where most faults begin. So: clean metal plus both parts hot, and the joint forms itself.
segments.deep: Molten solder only bonds, or wets, where the metal is both clean and hot enough to keep it liquid. The iron heats only the spot it touches, so every other part of the joint gets its heat second hand, by conduction through whatever contact exists. If one piece never reaches temperature, the solder wets the hot piece and simply lies against the cold one. That is a cold joint, and it can look finished. So the result depends on three things you control: how clean the metal and the tip are, how much clean contact area carries the heat, and how long you let the heat go in. An example from the lab: lift the iron from its sensing stand and it is back at working temperature in about five seconds. That tells you the tip is ready. It tells you nothing about whether the second wire is ready. The common misconception is that a hot iron means a hot joint. It does not, because heat has to cross into each piece, and two round wires touch at only a point. That is exactly why this lecture builds the thermal bridge and the far side feeding test, and why the second lab insists both parts be hot and clean.

check.q: According to the one sentence this lecture asks you to keep, what actually makes the solder joint form?
options: Clean hot metal and surface tension
The tip shaping the molten solder
Firm pressure from the solder wire
check.again: The point is that you do not build the joint by hand. You set up the conditions: the metal is clean, and both pieces are hot. Once that is true, surface tension pulls the molten solder into the joint on its own. Think of a drop of water on a clean glass: it spreads by itself, nobody pushes it. Pressing harder with the solder or sculpting with the tip does nothing useful, because a joint that is not hot or not clean will not bond no matter how it is pushed. That is why the lecture says nearly every fault traces back to heat that never arrived.

segments.title: Tinned copper wire
segments.text: Start with the wire in the parts kit. It looks silver, but it is copper. A thin layer of tin has been plated over it. Copper oxidises in air, and oxide is exactly what stops solder from bonding. So the tin takes the oxidation instead, and the copper surface underneath stays clean and easy to wet. That is the whole purpose of the coating: protect the copper and keep it solderable. Two cautions follow. First, a silver surface does not certify a current rating. How much current a wire can carry depends on the size of the conductor, the insulation, the temperature and how it is installed, not on the plating. Second, the coating is thin. Grip tinned wire hard with sharp serrated plier jaws and the teeth bite through the tin into the copper, opening the very path the coating exists to close. Use smooth or fine jaws on tinned wire, and keep the aggressive serrated jaws for work where the surface does not matter.
segments.expand: Explain why oxide blocks wetting and why a thin sacrificial tin layer helps, and give the plier-jaw example again.
segments.eli5: Think of a phone with a screen protector. The protector takes the scratches so the real glass underneath stays clean. The tin on the practice wire is that protector. Copper reacts with air and grows a film of oxide, and oxide is what stops solder bonding. The thin tin layer takes that oxidation instead, so the copper underneath stays protected and easy to solder. A screen protector says nothing about how powerful the phone is, and the silver surface says nothing about how much current the wire can carry. One difference: you never peel the tin off; solder bonds straight onto it. So the tin protects the copper surface and keeps it solderable.
segments.deep: Solder bonds by wetting a clean metal surface, and an oxide film on copper gets in the way of that bond. The tin plating sits on top of the copper and takes the oxidation, which keeps the surface solderable. That protection depends on one thing: the coating staying intact. It is thin, so sharp serrated plier jaws squeezed hard bite through the tin into the copper, and the exposed spot is now a place where the copper can corrode. The fix is smooth or fine jaws on tinned wire. Now the common misconception: that the silver plating is what sets how much current the wire can carry. Severe corrosion can eat away some of the conductor, so protecting it does matter, but the current a wire can carry depends on the conductor size, the insulation, the temperature and how it is installed. A worked comparison from the lab: the practice wire here is twelve gauge, and you will move to twenty two gauge. Both are silver, so colour cannot be what tells them apart in current; the conductor size is. This idea comes back in the second lab twice: smooth jawed pliers are chosen to protect this coating, and the silver pads on a circuit board use the same tin logic.

check.q: Why is the practice wire in the kit plated with a thin layer of tin?
options: To raise the current rating of the wire
To take the oxidation instead of the copper
To make the wire stiffer and easier to form
check.again: Bare copper reacts with air and grows an oxide skin, and oxide is what stops solder from bonding. The tin layer is a sacrificial coat: it oxidises instead, so the copper underneath stays clean and wets easily. That is its only purpose. It says nothing about current rating, which depends on conductor size, insulation, temperature and installation, and it does not stiffen the wire. Because the layer is very thin, sharp serrated plier jaws can bite through it and expose copper, so use smooth or fine jaws on tinned wire and save serrated jaws for surfaces that do not matter.

segments.title: Solder and what flux does
segments.text: The solder is a lead and tin alloy with flux in its core. Flux has one job, and it is worth saying precisely: flux removes oxide so the solder can wet the metal. Wetting means the molten solder bonds to the surface and spreads across it instead of sitting on top as a ball. Now the distinction that matters at the bench. On fresh, clean, tinned wire, the flux in the core may be all you need for the joint we practise, and the proof is that the solder wets properly as it heats. On a surface that is already oxidised, the core flux may not be enough. There is more oxide than that small amount of flux can clear, and the solder will sit on top instead of bonding. Then you clean the surface and use approved extra flux. Notice what flux does not do. It adds no strength and it is no substitute for heat. It only clears the way.
segments.expand: Describe what wetting looks like versus solder balling up, and why more flux cannot fix a joint that is not hot enough.
segments.eli5: Rinse a greasy plate and the water beads up in drops. Wash the grease away with soap and the water spreads across the plate in a thin, even sheet. Oxide plays the part of the grease, and flux plays the part of the soap: it clears the oxide so the solder can spread and bond instead of sitting in a ball. Where the picture breaks: a plate washes at room temperature, but solder also needs the metal hot, and no amount of flux replaces heat. So flux clears oxide so solder can wet the metal, and that is all it does.
segments.deep: Wetting means the molten solder bonds to the metal and spreads across it, rather than sitting on top as a ball. It needs two things at once: an oxide free surface, and metal hot enough to keep the solder liquid. Flux handles only the first. The solder used here carries its flux in a core, so the flux arrives in proportion to the solder you feed. For the demonstrated joint, roughly an eighth of an inch of solder wire was the cue, and on fresh, clean, tinned wire the small amount of flux inside that length may be all the joint needs; the proof is that the solder wets properly as it heats. On a surface that is already oxidised there is more oxide than that small amount can clear, so the solder sits on top without bonding. The answer is to clean the surface and use compatible, approved extra flux. The common misconception is that more flux rescues any bad joint. It cannot fix a joint that is not hot enough, and it adds no strength. The idea returns in the second lab, where a joint that was hot enough still rolled away from the metal, and the cure was to clean, reflux and rework.

check.q: True or false: flux adds strength to the joint and can make up for a joint that is not hot enough.
check.again: Flux has exactly one job: it removes oxide so the molten solder can wet the metal and spread across it instead of balling up. It contributes no strength at all, and it cannot replace heat. Picture a joint that is oxidised and lukewarm: adding a pile of flux clears some oxide, but the solder still sits on top because the metal never reached temperature. On fresh tinned wire the flux inside the solder core is usually enough, and the proof is that the solder wets as it heats. On an already oxidised surface, clean it and use approved extra flux, then still get both parts hot.

segments.title: The station and its sleep mode
segments.text: The soldering stations are temperature controlled, with a stand and a heat resistant pad for the iron. The stands are sensing stands: park the iron and after a while the station drops into a sleep mode, shown on the display. Lift the iron and it is back at working temperature in about five seconds. Sleep exists to extend tip life, so let it work; leaving the iron out of the stand to keep it hot just wears the tip for nothing. On temperature, the instruction is simple: use the approved bench setting and do not raise it on your own. Here is the reasoning. A hotter tip can move heat faster, but it also raises the risk of damaging the component, and it does not guarantee less total heat in the part. What controls the heat is good contact and short dwell time. If a joint is slow to heat, suspect contact first: a dirty tip, the wrong face, or the wrong tip size.
segments.expand: Go deeper on why dwell time and contact quality, not the number on the display, decide how much heat the component absorbs.
segments.eli5: Think of a laptop that dims its screen when you walk away and wakes up the moment you touch it. It is resting so the parts last longer. The soldering station does the same thing. Park the iron in its sensing stand and after a while the station drops into sleep. Lift the iron and it is back at working temperature in about five seconds. Keeping the iron out of the stand to stay hot is like a screen at full brightness all day: it just wears out. So let sleep mode work, because it extends tip life, and use the approved bench temperature rather than turning it up on your own.
segments.deep: The stand senses when the iron is parked, and after the iron has sat a while the station lowers into a sleep state, shown on the display. Lifting the iron brings it back to working temperature in about five seconds. The reason it exists is tip life: a tip sitting hot and unused is wearing for no benefit. The second half of this segment is about the temperature setting. The benches were described as set to four hundred, with the unit not clearly stated, so read the actual display rather than assuming. The mechanism that matters is this: a controlled station keeps supplying energy while the tip touches the work, and the tip and the joint do not simply settle at one shared temperature. A higher setting can move heat faster, but it also raises the risk of damaging the part, and it does not guarantee less total heat in the component. What decides how much heat the part absorbs is the quality of contact and how long you stay on it. The common misconception is that a hotter tip is always gentler or always better. If a joint is slow, suspect contact first: a dirty tip, the wrong face, or the wrong tip size. The next segments take exactly those three, tip cleaning and contact area.

check.q: If a joint is slow to heat, what does the lecture say to suspect first?
options: Poor contact: dirty tip, wrong face, wrong size
The approved bench temperature setting is too low
The station has dropped into sleep mode
check.again: The amount of heat that reaches a part is set by contact quality and dwell time, not by the number on the display. So when a joint heats slowly, question the contact before anything else: is the tip oxidised, is the rounded edge touching instead of the flat face, is the tip too small for the joint? Turning the temperature up on your own is not the fix; it raises the risk of damaging the component without guaranteeing less total heat in the part. Use the approved setting, and remember the station wakes from sleep in about five seconds, so sleep is not what makes a joint slow.

segments.title: Tip care: brass wool, never a file
segments.text: Oxide on the tip is a thermal barrier. Watch a freshly cleaned and tinned tip and you can see it go from bright to dark in a few seconds; that is the oxide re-forming. So the tip is cleaned immediately before every joint, not at the start of the hour. The cleaning motion matters. Wipe and roll the tip through the brass wool as you pull it out. That shears the oxide off. Stabbing the tip into the wool does not clean it and shortens its life. Never file a tip. A tip is plated, and a file goes straight through the plating. A tip that is dull, dark and will not take solder after proper cleaning is replaced, not resurfaced. And before you switch the station off, leave fresh solder on the tip; that coating protects it in storage. Bright tip, every joint.
segments.expand: Explain what the plating on a tip is for and why filing destroys it, and describe the wipe-and-roll motion in more detail.
segments.eli5: Think of oxide on the tip as an oven mitt. The mitt blocks heat, and oxide does the same between the tip and the joint. The catch is that this mitt grows back on its own within a few seconds of cleaning, so you take it off right before every joint, not once an hour. You remove it by wiping and rolling the tip through the brass wool, not stabbing it in. Where the picture breaks: a mitt comes off cleanly, but you must never file the tip to get it bare, because the file cuts through the tip's plating. So a bright, freshly wiped tip lets the heat through, and a dark one holds it back.
segments.deep: The tip of the iron is plated, and its working surface is meant to carry a bright coat of solder. On a hot tip oxide forms fast: you can watch a freshly cleaned and tinned tip go from bright to dark in a few seconds. That oxide is a thermal barrier and it stops the solder wetting, so cleaning has to happen immediately before each joint. A worked comparison: a tip wiped at the start of an hour has had many times the few seconds it needs to go dark. The motion matters. Wiping and rolling the tip through brass wool as you pull it out shears the oxide off; stabbing into the wool does not clean it and shortens the tip's life. The common misconception is that a file would make a dull tip bright again. It would make it bright for a moment by cutting through the plating, and then the tip is destroyed. A tip that stays dull, dark and will not take solder after proper cleaning is replaced, not resurfaced. Before switching off, leave fresh solder on the tip, because that coat protects it in storage. The second lab turns this into a routine every time the iron leaves the holder.

check.q: True or false: a tip that stays dull and dark and will not take solder after proper cleaning should be filed bright again.
