check.again: A soldering tip is plated, and that plating is what lets it take solder and resist wear. A file cuts straight through the plating, so filing ruins the tip rather than restoring it. The correct routine is to wipe and roll the tip through the brass wool as you pull it out, which shears the oxide off, and to do that immediately before every joint because a bright tip goes dark again in seconds. If a tip still will not take solder after a proper cleaning, it is replaced, not resurfaced. Before switching off, leave fresh solder on the tip to protect it.

segments.title: Contact area moves heat
segments.text: Here is a principle you will use on every joint: heat moves through contact area. A wedge tip has a flat face and a rounded edge. Put the flat face against the work and it touches over an area, and heat flows in. Touch the work with the rounded edge and it meets at essentially one point, and almost nothing transfers, even though the tip is exactly as hot. This is also why tip size and shape are chosen to fit the joint. A tip too small for the joint gives a poor contact area no matter how precise it looks. And it is why a clean tip matters: oxide between the tip and the work is a layer that heat has to fight through. Temperature is only one part of heat transfer. Area of clean contact is the part you control with your hands.
segments.expand: Give an everyday analogy for contact area and heat flow, and connect it to why oxide on the tip slows a joint.
segments.eli5: Think of warming cold hands on a hot mug of coffee. Wrap your whole palm around it and the warmth pours in. Touch it with one fingertip and you barely feel anything, even though the coffee is exactly as hot. A soldering tip works the same way. Lay the flat face of a wedge tip against the work and heat flows in across that whole area. Touch with the rounded edge and it meets at almost a single point, and very little gets through. Oxide on the tip is like wearing a glove. So clean contact area, not just tip temperature, decides how fast the joint heats.
segments.deep: Heat moves from the tip into the work only across the surfaces that are actually touching. How much flows depends on how hot the tip is, how much area is in clean contact, and how long the contact lasts. Temperature is only one of those, and contact area is the one you control with your hands. A wedge tip shows it clearly. Its flat face laid on the work touches over an area and heat flows in; its rounded edge meets the work at essentially one point and transfers almost nothing, at exactly the same temperature. That is why tip size and shape are chosen to fit the joint. And it is why the tip must be clean: oxide between tip and work is a layer the heat has to fight through. A semi quantitative way to hold it: same tip, same setting, same few seconds of contact, yet a flat face can get the joint there while an edge may never manage it. The common misconception is that a slow joint needs a hotter setting. Usually it needs better contact. The very next idea, two round wires touching at a point, is this same principle between the two pieces of metal.

check.q: Why does touching the work with the rounded edge of a wedge tip transfer almost no heat?
options: The rounded edge runs cooler than the flat face
It meets the work at essentially one point
The edge carries a thicker layer of oxide
check.again: Heat flows through contact area. The whole tip is at the same temperature, so the rounded edge is just as hot as the flat face. The difference is geometry: the flat face lies against the work over an area, while the rounded edge touches at nearly a single point, and almost nothing can cross a point. Think of warming your hands on a mug: wrap your palms around it and heat pours in, touch it with a fingertip and you barely feel it. The same idea explains tip size, since a tip too small gives little contact, and why oxide on the tip slows a joint.

segments.title: Two round wires and the thermal bridge
segments.text: Now the central problem of the lab. Cross two round wires so they touch, and the contact between them is essentially a single point. Almost no heat crosses from one to the other. Heat the top wire and the bottom wire stays cold. Solder then wets the hot wire and lies against the cold one without bonding. That is a cold joint, and the dangerous thing about it is that it looks finished. The fix is a deliberate technique called a thermal bridge. Clean and tin the tip, place the iron so it touches the joint, and add a small amount of solder right at the point where the iron meets the work. That molten solder spreads the contact and conducts heat into both wires at once. Then leave the iron there and let the heat go in. Location is everything: solder somewhere nearby, or solder kept only on the tip, bridges nothing. Do not confuse this with an electrical bridge, which is unwanted solder shorting two separate pads.
segments.expand: Explain step by step why a point contact conducts so little heat and how the bead of molten solder changes the geometry.
segments.eli5: Think of two buckets joined by a pinhole. Hardly any water passes. Widen it into a pipe and water flows freely. Two crossed round wires are joined by the heat equivalent of a pinhole: they touch at a single point, so heat from the iron stays in the top wire. The thermal bridge is the wide pipe. A small bead of molten solder placed right where the iron meets the work fills the space around that point and carries heat into both wires at once. Where the picture breaks: water runs downhill by gravity, while heat simply flows from hotter metal to cooler metal. So the bridge widens the contact, and both wires heat together.
segments.deep: Two round wires crossing each other touch along almost no area at all, essentially a single point. Heat crosses between metals only through contact, so almost none crosses. Heat the top wire and the bottom wire stays cold. The solder then wets the hot wire and lies against the cold one without bonding: a cold joint, and the danger is that it looks finished. The thermal bridge changes the geometry. Molten solder is liquid metal, so a small bead of it placed at the point where the iron touches the work flows into the space around the contact, spreading it out, and conducts heat into both wires at once. It depends on location: solder somewhere nearby, or kept only on the tip, bridges nothing. The lab gave a real example of what happens without enough heat: two of the bus joints on the demonstration board had pulled off, an under heated joint failing eventually. The common misconception is that metal touching metal shares heat freely. It shares heat only through what is really touching, and a point is almost nothing. Nor is it an electrical bridge, which is unwanted solder shorting two pads. Next comes feeding from the far side, which checks that the bridge worked.

check.q: Where does the small amount of solder for a thermal bridge go?
options: On the tip before the iron touches the joint
Right where the iron meets the work
On the wire a little way from the iron
check.again: Two crossed round wires touch at a point, so heat from one barely reaches the other, and solder ends up bonded to the hot wire while lying loose against the cold one: a cold joint that looks finished. The thermal bridge fixes the geometry. With a clean tinned tip resting on the joint, you add a little solder exactly at the spot where the iron touches the work. That bead of molten metal spreads the contact and carries heat into both wires at once. Then leave the iron there. Solder only on the tip, or nearby, bridges nothing. An electrical bridge is different: unwanted solder shorting two pads.

segments.title: Feed from the far side
segments.text: With the bridge in place and the iron resting on the joint, feed the solder from the side of the joint opposite the iron. This is a test as much as a technique. If solder melts when it touches the far side, the joint itself is hot enough, not just the iron. If it does not melt, the joint is not ready, so keep the iron there and wait. The work tells you when it is time; you do not count seconds. The shortcut to avoid is melting solder on the iron and wiping it across the metal. That produces a blob that looks finished and has never bonded, because the metal under it never reached temperature. When the solder has flowed around the joint, take the solder away first, then the iron. The order of the whole thing, then: clean and tin the tip, place the iron, build the bridge, leave the iron, feed from the far side, let it flow, remove solder, remove iron.
segments.expand: Walk through the full joint sequence again slowly and explain what a wipe-on blob looks like compared with a wetted joint.
segments.eli5: A hot oven does not prove a cake is baked; you poke a toothpick into its centre. Feeding solder from the far side of the joint is that toothpick. Touch the solder to the side of the joint away from the iron, and if it melts there, the joint itself is hot. If not, keep waiting. Melting solder on the iron and wiping it on is like icing a raw cake: it looks finished and it is not. Where the picture breaks: a cake needs a timer, and here you never count seconds, because the solder tells you. The work melting the solder is the signal that the joint is ready.
segments.deep: Solder melts only on metal that is hot enough. The far side of the joint is the part furthest from the iron, so for solder to melt there, heat must have travelled from the tip, through the bridge, into the work. If it melts, the joint has reached temperature, not just the iron. That turns feeding into a test, which is why you do not count seconds: the time it takes depends on wire size, contact and tip condition, and the work reports it for you. The full sequence is: clean and tin the tip, place the iron, build the bridge with a little solder at the iron contact, leave the iron there, feed from the far side, let it flow around the joint, take the solder away, then take the iron away. About an eighth of an inch of solder wire was used for the demonstrated joint. The common misconception is that melting solder on the iron and wiping it across the metal is a quicker way to the same result. It gives a blob that looks finished and has never bonded, because the metal under it never reached temperature. In the second lab the same reading returns: watching which side the solder flows toward tells you which part actually got hot.

check.q: When you feed solder from the far side of the joint and it melts, what does that tell you?
options: The iron has reached its set temperature
The joint itself is hot enough
You have left the iron on too long
check.again: Feeding from the side opposite the iron turns the solder into a thermometer for the joint. The solder wire never touches the iron, so the only thing that can melt it is the metal of the joint. If it flows, the joint is at temperature; if it does not, keep the iron in place and wait, because the work tells you when it is ready rather than a count of seconds. The shortcut of melting solder on the tip and wiping it across proves nothing, since the metal underneath may never have got hot. When the solder has flowed, remove the solder first, then the iron.

segments.title: The fillet and how much solder
segments.text: What does a finished joint look like? The solder pulls itself into a concave, feathered curve where it meets each wire. That curve is the fillet, and it is made by surface tension, the same property that shapes a water droplet. On a joint this small, surface tension dominates and gravity matters very little. You do not shape the fillet; you create the conditions and it forms itself. How much solder? Roughly an eighth of an inch of solder wire was the cue for the demonstrated joint, but that is a cue for that solder diameter and that joint, not a specification. On stranded wire there is a clear test: you should still be able to see the individual strands through the solder. The layer is thin and has wetted into the strands. If you cannot see the strands, there is too much solder, and a smooth blob hides exactly the evidence an inspector wants.
segments.expand: Describe a convex ball versus a concave fillet and what each says about wetting, and why extra solder is not extra strength.
segments.eli5: Think of water in a clean drinking glass. Where the water meets the wall it climbs a little and curves, because water clings to clean glass. Nobody shapes it. A solder fillet is the same kind of curve. Once molten solder has wetted clean, hot metal, surface tension pulls it into a smooth, concave, feathered edge where it meets each wire. Where the picture breaks: water stays liquid, while solder freezes in that shape as it cools. On stranded wire the solder layer should be thin enough that you can still see the individual strands under it. So a concave fillet is the visible sign that the solder wetted and bonded.
segments.deep: The fillet forms because of wetting and surface tension. When solder wets a clean, hot surface it spreads and clings, and surface tension pulls the liquid into a smooth concave curve where it meets the wire. On a joint this small, surface tension and wetting dominate the shape. Gravity is not literally absent, and geometry, solder quantity, cleanliness, flux and temperature all affect the result, but you do not shape the fillet by hand. So its shape is evidence: a concave, feathered edge says the solder wetted. How much solder: about an eighth of an inch of solder wire was the cue for the demonstrated joint, a cue for that solder diameter and that joint, not a universal specification. The stranded wire test applies the same idea: you should still see the individual strands through the solder, because a thin layer has wetted into them. The common misconception is that more solder means a stronger joint. Extra solder only hides the evidence. The second lab uses this directly: a sound concave fillet versus a convex ball or a rolled under edge, and the rule that if you had to add solder to make it look right, the joint is wrong.

check.q: True or false: on a stranded wire joint you should still be able to see the individual strands through the solder.
check.again: The amount of solder on a good joint is small. It wets into the strands as a thin layer, and the strands stay visible under it. That visibility is the evidence an inspector wants: it shows the solder bonded to the metal rather than covering it. A smooth blob that hides the strands is too much solder, and it also hides whether the joint ever wetted. The fillet itself is a concave, feathered curve made by surface tension, which dominates at this size while gravity hardly matters. The eighth of an inch of solder wire from the demonstration was a cue, not a specification.

segments.title: Set the bench up for your hand
segments.text: The benches are shared between classes, and the layout you sit down to was set up by someone with the other dominant hand. Resetting it is part of starting work. The iron stand goes on your dominant side and close to the work, because a long reach is a long time holding a hot iron over the joint you just made. Bring the cleaning pad forward, near the front edge; if it sits behind the work, every trip to clean the tip drags the iron across what you built. Uncoil and separate the cords. Coiling a cable twists it along its own axis, and that stored twist is what leaves cords permanently kinked; keep the power leads apart from each other and clear of the hot tip. Solder also needs the work to be stable, which is what the vise and holding fixtures are for: find an arrangement that keeps it steady and leaves both hands free.
segments.expand: Describe the right-handed and mirrored left-handed layouts in words, and why a stable workpiece matters for wetting.
segments.eli5: Think of a cook stepping into a kitchen used by someone else. Before cooking, they move the knife and cutting board to suit their own hand. The soldering bench is the same. The last person may have used the other hand, so the iron stand goes on your dominant side, close to the work, and the cleaning pad comes forward so you never drag the iron back across your joint. Cords are uncoiled, because coiling twists a cable and that twist leaves kinks. So resetting the bench is part of the work, because it keeps the hot iron's path short and clear.
segments.deep: Every rule in the bench layout comes from the path the hot iron travels. The stand goes on your dominant hand side and close to the work, because a long reach is a long time holding a hot iron over a joint you just made. Right handed means stand on the right; left handed is the same layout mirrored. The cleaning pad comes forward near the front edge, because if it sits behind the work, every trip to clean the tip drags the iron across what you built, and you clean before every joint, so that trip happens constantly. Cords are uncoiled and separated: coiling a cable twists it along its own axis, and that stored twist is what leaves cords permanently kinked. Power leads stay apart from each other and clear of the hot tip. Finally the work itself must be stable, because both hands are busy, one with the iron and one with the solder, so the vise or holding fixture has to hold the piece. The common misconception is that the bench as you found it is fine. It may suit the other hand. The second lab begins the same way: no tangled wires and nothing near the tip, and turrets need a third hand or a vise.

check.q: When you set up the shared bench, where does the iron stand go?
options: On your dominant side, close to the work
Behind the work, away from both hands
On your non-dominant side, next to the pad
check.again: The iron stand belongs on your dominant hand's side and near the work, because every trip to the stand is time spent holding a hot iron over the joint you just made. A long reach means a long time with the tip in the wrong place. The cleaning pad comes forward to the front edge so you do not drag the iron over your work to reach it. The benches are shared, and the last user may have had the other dominant hand, so resetting the layout is part of starting. Uncoil and separate the cords, and hold the work in a vise or fixture so both hands are free.

segments.title: Fumes, lead and burns
segments.text: Three physical facts about the bench. First, smoke. As flux burns and solder melts it gives off fumes, and the extraction filters pull that smoke away from your face. The switches are ganged: turning one on turns them all on, so it affects everyone in the room. If extraction seems ineffective, stop and report it rather than assuming the filter is the fault. Second, lead. The solder is a lead and tin alloy, and residue on your hands travels to your face, your food and your belongings later. Use the hand wash station after soldering. Third, heat. At working temperature the tip burns on contact, and when you do eventually touch a hot iron, it is most likely to be further down the barrel rather than the tip itself. So the iron lives in its stand whenever it is not in your hand, and you know where that stand is without needing to check.
segments.expand: Explain the exposure route for lead residue and why hand washing matters even though nobody eats in the lab.
segments.eli5: Think of handling raw chicken in a kitchen. You wash your hands before you eat, even if the chicken never touched your sandwich, because whatever is on your hands travels to the next thing you touch. Lead residue from solder works the same way: it rides on your hands to your face, your food and your belongings later, so you use the hand wash station after soldering. Where the picture breaks: lead residue gives no smell or warning, so washing has to be a habit. So wash after soldering, because the lead goes wherever your hands go.
segments.deep: Three hazards, each with a mechanism. Smoke: as flux burns and solder melts it gives off fumes, and the extraction filters draw that smoke away from your face. The switches are ganged, so one switch turns on every station's extraction, and it affects everyone in the room. If extraction seems ineffective, stop and report it; the cause could be the filter's condition, the positioning, the airflow or the power, so do not assume it is the filter. Lead: the solder is a lead and tin alloy, and residue on your hands moves later to your face, food and belongings. That is the exposure route, and it is why the hand wash station is there. The common misconception is that washing does not matter because nobody eats at the bench. The residue does not stay at the bench; it leaves on your hands. Burns: at working temperature the tip burns on contact, and when you do eventually touch a hot iron it is most likely to be further down the barrel rather than the tip itself. So the iron lives in its stand when it is not in your hand, and you know where the stand is without looking for it. These habits apply to every joint in both labs and to every session that follows.

check.q: True or false: the fume extraction switches are ganged, so turning one on turns them all on for the whole room.
check.again: The extraction filters pull the smoke from burning flux and melting solder away from your face, and their switches are linked: switch one on and every unit in the room starts. That means extraction affects everyone, so if it seems ineffective you stop and report it instead of assuming the filter is at fault. The other two bench facts sit alongside it. Lead residue from the solder travels from your hands to your face and belongings, so use the hand wash station afterwards. And the iron burns on contact, usually further down the barrel than the tip, so it lives in its stand whenever it is not in your hand.

segments.title: Hand tools and the combination tool
segments.text: Three tools carry most of the work: small needle-nose pliers, small wire cutters, and a combination crimping tool. The combination tool packs several features. Serrated jaws at the tip grab and hold, but remember what they do to tinned wire. Stripping holes are sized by wire gauge; match the hole to the gauge in your hand. A shaping hole lets you form a loop by moving the wire around it progressively. Threaded screw holes restore a damaged thread: run the screw in, cut the excess, and back it out. The crimp dies are colour coded red, yellow and blue to match the insulated terminal's colour, and each die has a flat side and a round side, so the terminal goes in the correct way round. One rule to carry: a crimp is a complete connection on its own. Crimp or solder, never both. Seat the terminal properly and squeeze fully.
segments.expand: Explain why a crimp is not soldered afterwards and what seating the terminal fully means for a hand crimper.
segments.eli5: Think of a socket wrench set. Each socket fits one size of nut, and using the wrong one slips or never grips properly, no matter how hard you pull. The combination tool's crimp dies work the same way: they are coloured red, yellow and blue, and you match the die colour to the colour of the insulated terminal, put the terminal in the right way round, and squeeze fully. Where the picture breaks: a bolt can be tightened a little more later, but a crimp is made in one full squeeze and is then a complete connection on its own, so you never solder it afterwards. So match the die to the terminal.
segments.deep: The combination tool is several tools in one body, and each feature only works when it is matched to the job. The serrated jaws at the tip grab and hold, but they are the jaws that bite through the coating on tinned wire, so not for that. The stripping holes are sized by wire gauge: the practice wire here is twelve gauge and you will move to twenty two gauge, so the hole you choose changes with the wire. The shaping hole forms a loop as you move the wire around it progressively. The threaded holes restore a thread: run the screw in, cut the excess, and back it out, and the thread is restored as the screw withdraws. The crimp dies are colour coded red, yellow and blue to match the insulated terminal, and each has a flat side and a round side, so the terminal goes in the correct way round. Production crimping uses large ratcheting tools, which is why the hand tool is a compromise: it works if you seat the terminal properly and squeeze fully. The common misconception is that a little solder makes a crimp more secure. The rule is crimp or solder, never both. The second lab moves on to pliers and cutters.

check.q: After you have made a proper crimp on an insulated terminal, what does the lecture say to do next?
options: Add solder to make it permanent
Nothing; a crimp is complete alone
Squeeze again with the next die size
check.again: A crimp is a finished connection by itself. The rule to carry is crimp or solder, never both. What makes a crimp good is choosing the right die and squeezing it fully with the terminal seated properly. The dies are colour coded red, yellow and blue to match the insulated terminal, and each die has a flat side and a round side so the terminal goes in the right way round. Going back over it with another die is not part of the process. The same combination tool also has gauge-sized stripping holes, a shaping hole for forming loops, and threaded holes for restoring a damaged screw thread.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from this lab. One: the wire is tinned copper and the solder carries flux, and both exist to fight oxide, because solder only wets clean metal. Two: heat moves through clean contact area, so wipe and roll the tip bright before every joint and put the flat face on the work. Three: two crossed round wires touch at a point, so you build a thermal bridge, a little solder at the iron contact, and leave the iron there. Four: feed from the far side; when the work melts the solder the joint is ready, and a wipe-on blob has never bonded. Five: the fillet is concave and made by surface tension, strands stay visible through the solder, and more solder is not more strength. Around all of it: stand on your side, pad forward, extraction on, hands washed.
segments.expand: Quiz the student with one mixed question that combines the thermal bridge, far-side feeding and reading the fillet.
segments.eli5: Think of buttering toast. On hot toast butter melts into a thin layer by itself. On cold bread it sits in lumps. Soldering works the same way. Hot, clean metal is the fresh toast, and that is what tinned wire, flux and a wiped tip are for. Heat has to reach both wires, so you use the flat face, build a thermal bridge, and let the far side melt the solder. A thin feathered fillet is butter that soaked in. Where the picture breaks: butter never sets into a bond. So the five ideas come down to clean metal, heat in both parts, and solder that wets.
segments.deep: The five ideas are one chain of cause and effect. Solder bonds only by wetting, and wetting needs metal that is clean and hot. Clean comes from the tin on the wire, the flux in the solder core, and a tip wiped and rolled bright in brass wool before every joint, because oxide re-forms on a hot tip in a few seconds. Hot comes from heat transfer, which travels through clean contact area: the flat face of the tip, not the edge. Two crossed round wires touch at a point, so the thermal bridge, a little solder at the iron contact, spreads that contact and heats both wires together. The far side test then proves the joint itself is hot, not just the iron: when the work melts the solder, it is ready. The fillet is the evidence at the end, concave and feathered, made by surface tension, with strands still visible on stranded wire. The misconception behind all of it: a joint is made by adding solder. A joint is made by heat and cleanliness; solder only shows whether they arrived. The second lab carries this forward into hook joints, pads, plated holes and a tip check every time the iron leaves the holder.

check.q: In the recap, what tells you the joint is ready for solder?
options: The work itself melts the solder
You have counted a few seconds
The solder on the tip turns bright
check.again: The recap's fourth idea is the far-side test. You feed solder from the side away from the iron, and only when the joint metal is hot enough does that solder melt and flow. A count of seconds proves nothing, and a bright tip only shows the tip is clean, not that the work is hot. The recap's other ideas hang together: tin and flux fight oxide, because solder only wets clean metal; heat moves through clean contact area, so the tip is wiped bright and the flat face goes on the work; crossed wires need a thermal bridge; and the fillet is concave with the strands still visible.

lectures.title: Soldering techniques and tool selection
lectures.source: EFAB 202/Lab/EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection.md

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture covers the second soldering lab: the two hand tools and what makes a good pair, how to read a fillet and diagnose a joint from it, the mechanical joints that come before any solder, the hook joint and its rules, the layers of a printed circuit board and what a plated hole changes, the three ways to form a component lead, and the tip routine you run every single time. The idea that connects all of it is that the joint is decided before the iron ever touches it. Forming, cleanliness and a tight mechanical wrap are what make solder work; the solder only fills what the forming already holds. Keep that in mind and the rest follows.
segments.expand: Preview why mechanical forming comes before solder, with the hook-joint wrap as the example.
segments.eli5: Think of a bricklayer building a wall. Each brick is set level and tight first; the mortar then fills the joints and bonds them, but no amount of mortar will straighten a wall that was stacked crooked. The forming is the bricklaying: a tight hook wrap, a wire sitting properly on its pad, a lead set over in its hole, and clean metal. The solder is the mortar. It bonds and fills what the forming already holds, and it cannot rescue loose or dirty work. So the joint is decided before the iron touches it.
segments.deep: The mechanism is that solder only wets and fills; it does not hold things in place or close gaps. The mechanical position comes from forming, and the bond needs clean, hot metal. Take the hook joint as the worked example. The wire is wrapped around the terminal with a finger inside the loop, each turn pushed hard against the last, for a minimum of six turns. If the wrap is tight, the solder bonds a structure that already holds. If there is daylight between the turns, the wire is standing off the post, and solder added afterwards does not close that gap. The same logic runs through the rest of the lab: a wire on a pad must sit within the pad with nothing overhanging, a component lead is formed in its hole before soldering, and the tip and the metal must be clean. The common misconception is that a generous amount of solder can make up for poor forming. It cannot, and needing extra solder to make a joint look right is itself a sign the joint is wrong. These ideas carry straight into the bridge exercise in sixteen gauge wire, formed straight and to length so it sits on its pads.

check.q: True or false: this lecture's connecting idea is that the joint is decided before the iron touches it, and solder only fills what the forming already holds.
check.again: The thread running through the second lab is that solder is the last step, not the main event. Forming the wire, keeping the metal clean and making a tight mechanical wrap are what make the joint work; the solder then fills a shape that is already holding. A tight hook wrap around a terminal, for example, is a sound mechanical connection before any solder arrives, and the solder just bonds it. Get the forming loose or the metal dirty and no amount of solder rescues it. The lecture builds on that idea through the tools, the fillet, the hook joint, the board, lead forming and the tip routine.

segments.title: Needle-nose pliers: the jaw surface
segments.text: The first tool is a pair of needle-nose pliers, and the jaw surface is the whole point. The jaws must be flat and smooth, never serrated. Serrated jaws cut through the coating on the wire. On tinned copper that coating is what keeps the copper from oxidising, so every serration mark is a corrosion site you built yourself. When you buy them, check the jaws by eye before you pay. After you form a hook, inspect the gripped section for nicks or exposed copper before you solder it; a good bend can still hide a broken coating. Bargain sets were described from direct experience as unusable; one good pair you can actually form wire with is worth more than two bad ones.
segments.expand: Explain why a tiny break in the tin coating matters over the life of a joint, and what to inspect after forming.
segments.eli5: Think of the paint on a car. As long as the paint is unbroken, the steel underneath stays protected. Put one deep scratch through it and that scratch is where rust starts. The tin on the practice wire is the car's paint, and serrated plier jaws are the thing that scratches it. Smooth, flat jaws grip the wire without breaking the coating. Where the picture breaks: car paint is mainly for looks and rust, while the tin also keeps the copper easy to solder. So choose pliers with smooth jaws, because every serration mark on tinned wire is a corrosion site you made yourself.
segments.deep: The jaw surface matters because of what it does to the coating. Tinned copper relies on a thin tin layer to keep the copper from oxidising. Serrated jaws grip by biting into the surface, and on tinned wire they cut through the tin into the copper. That exposed spot is a corrosion site, and it sits right where the wire was formed. Smooth, flat jaws spread the grip over an area instead of concentrating it on teeth, so the coating survives. The habit that follows: after forming a hook, inspect the gripped section for nicks or exposed copper before soldering, because a good bend can still hide a broken coating. A worked way to see why it matters: a hook joint needs a minimum of six turns, and the pliers touch the wire many times while forming those turns, so a serrated pair has many chances to break the coating on a single joint. When buying, check the jaws by eye before you pay. Bargain sets were described from direct experience as unusable. The common misconception is that jaw marks are only cosmetic. They are breaks in the protective layer. These pliers are the forming tool for everything that follows in this lab: hook joints, bus wire, turrets and lead forming.

check.q: Why must the jaws of your needle-nose pliers be smooth and flat, never serrated?
options: Serrations cut through the wire's tin coating
Serrated jaws grip too weakly to form wire
Serrations scratch the plating on the iron tip
check.again: The tin coating on the practice wire is what stops the copper underneath from oxidising. Serrated jaws bite through that coating, and every tooth mark becomes a spot where bare copper is exposed and will corrode over the life of the joint. So the jaws must be flat and smooth, and you check that by eye before buying. Grip is not the issue; the coating is. After you form a hook, inspect the section the jaws held for nicks or exposed copper before you solder, because a bend that looks good can still hide a broken coating. One good pair beats two bargain pairs.

segments.title: Cutters: flush or side, and lending
segments.text: The second tool is a cutter, and there are two designs. Flush cutters are spring loaded; the blades cross over and cut cleanly. Side cutters are the long-standing squeeze and release design, and they tend to fold the wire as they cut. Either is acceptable for this work. You do not need both; what matters is a cutter of the right size, the size that was passed around in class. Now a warning about lending. A borrowed pair of cutters came back with a perfect semicircular notch bitten out of the blades, because someone used them on tungsten, which is roughly ten times harder than the wire they are designed for. A notched blade cannot be repaired. Cutters are rated for soft wire; whether a wire fits between the jaws says nothing about whether the blade can take it. If someone genuinely needs a cut made, make the cut for them and keep the tool in your own hand.
segments.expand: Describe the difference in the cut face between flush and side cutters, and why hardness matters more than thickness for blade damage.
segments.eli5: Think of lending a good kitchen knife to a friend who uses it to chop through frozen bone. The bone fit under the blade but was far harder than the knife was made for, so it comes back chipped for good. Wire cutters are the same. They are made for soft wire. A borrowed pair came back with a semicircular notch in the blades because someone cut tungsten, roughly ten times harder than the wire they are designed for, and a notched blade cannot be repaired. So if a classmate needs a cut, make it for them. Fitting between the jaws says nothing about whether the blade survives.
segments.deep: First, the two designs. Flush cutters are spring loaded, and their blades cross over to cut cleanly. Side cutters are the long-standing squeeze and release design, and they tend to fold the wire as they cut. Either is acceptable for this work, and you do not need both; what matters is a cutter of the right size, the one passed around in class. Second, why blades get ruined. A cutter blade is rated for soft wire. What damages it is the hardness of what it cuts, not just the thickness. Tungsten was described as roughly ten times harder than the wire these cutters are designed for, so even a piece that fits easily between the jaws can bite a permanent notch out of the edge. A notched blade cannot be repaired. The common misconception is that if the wire fits in the jaws, the cutter can handle it. Fitting is about size; damage is about hardness. That is the reason behind not lending your cutters: you cannot control what someone else feeds into them, so make the cut yourself. You will use this cutter next for clipping hook joint ends and component leads, where a clean cut and a covered end both matter.

check.q: Why did the borrowed cutters come back with a semicircular notch bitten out of the blades?
options: The wire was too thick to fit between the jaws
They were used on tungsten, a much harder metal
The spring failed and the blades crossed over badly
check.again: Cutters are rated for soft wire. Tungsten is roughly ten times harder than the wire the blades are designed for, so cutting it takes a permanent bite out of the edge, and a notched blade cannot be repaired. The lesson is that fitting between the jaws says nothing about whether the blade can survive the cut; hardness matters, not thickness. Either flush cutters, spring loaded with crossing blades, or side cutters, which tend to fold the wire, are acceptable, and you need only one of the right size. If someone needs a cut, make it for them and keep the tool in your own hand.

segments.title: Reading the concave fillet
segments.text: A sound joint shows a concave fillet. The solder curves inward, meeting both the wire and the pad at a shallow angle, pulled into that shape by surface tension as it bonds to the copper. You do not make the fillet; you let the heat and the surface tension make it. So you should not have to shape it, and you should not have to add extra solder to get it. That gives you a diagnostic you can apply to your own work. If you had to keep adding solder to make the joint look right, the joint is wrong. Reheat and redo the whole thing, both parts. Never paint solder over a bad joint; you are relying on a bond that is not there. A joint that is convex, rounded or balled has not wetted. And one that looks fine on one side but rolls under itself on the other has a rolled region where nothing is stuck at all.
segments.expand: Describe the three cross sections, sound concave fillet, convex ball, and rolled-under edge, and what each says about wetting.
segments.eli5: Think of rain on two surfaces. On a clean window, water spreads into a thin film and curves smoothly where it meets the frame. On a freshly waxed car, the same water pulls up into round beads that sit on top. A concave fillet is the clean window: the solder wetted and bonded. A convex, rounded ball is the waxed car: the solder never wetted. An edge that rolls under itself is a spot where nothing is stuck. And painting more solder over a bad joint is like painting over a crack. So the fillet's shape tells you whether the solder actually bonded.
segments.deep: The shape of the fillet is a readout of wetting. When molten solder wets clean, hot copper, it spreads and clings, and surface tension pulls it into a concave curve that meets both the wire and the pad at a shallow angle. When it cannot wet, the same surface tension pulls it into a convex ball that sits on the surface. So you do not make the fillet; heat and surface tension make it, and you should not have to shape it or add extra solder to get it. Three cross sections to hold in mind. Concave fillet: wetted on both surfaces. Convex or balled: not wetted. Fine on one side but rolled under itself on the other: the rolled region is a region where nothing is bonded. If you kept adding solder until the joint looked right, the joint is wrong, so reheat and redo the whole thing, both parts. For scale, the first lab's demonstrated joint used only about an eighth of an inch of solder wire. The common misconception is that a bad looking joint can be finished by painting solder over the top. That only hides a missing bond. The next segment asks why a hot joint can still fail to wet.

check.q: If you had to keep adding solder to make a joint look right, what does the lecture say to do?
options: The joint is wrong; reheat and redo both parts
Add a little more solder and let it flow again
Leave it as long as the fillet ends up concave
check.again: A sound fillet forms on its own: surface tension pulls the molten solder into a concave curve that meets the wire and the pad at a shallow angle. You never shape it and you never top it up. So needing to add solder to make a joint look acceptable is itself the diagnosis that something failed underneath, usually wetting. The fix is to reheat and redo the whole joint, both parts, not to paint more solder over it, because painted solder relies on a bond that is not there. A convex or balled joint has not wetted, and a rolled-under edge has a region where nothing is stuck.

segments.title: Hot and clean: which one fails
segments.text: Two conditions must both hold: both parts hot, and both parts clean, free of plastic, oxide and old solder. Hot is not sufficient. The rolled-under failure is the instructive one, because it can happen on a joint that was hot enough. If the metal was not clean, the solder will not stick no matter how much heat arrives. Heat is the condition people check; cleanliness is the one that quietly fails. When heat was adequate and the solder still lifted, clean and reflux the surface, then rework. Heat also does not arrive evenly. On a joint between two different wires, one heats quickly and the other does not. Put the iron where the slow one is and let the fast one come along with it. Then read the joint: watching which side the solder flows toward tells you which side actually got hot. A fixed count of seconds tells you nothing; the solder does.
segments.expand: Explain why cleanliness is easy to overlook, and how to tell from solder flow which part of a joint reached temperature.
segments.eli5: Think of sticking tape to a dusty wall. However hard you press, it will not hold, because the tape grips the dust, not the wall. Solder needs two things at once, metal that is hot and metal that is clean of plastic, oxide and old solder. Heat is the one people check; cleanliness is the one that quietly fails. Where the picture breaks: tape never needs heat, but solder needs both conditions, so a clean joint that is cold fails too. When a light and a heavy wire meet, the iron goes on the slow, heavy one. So a joint needs both parts hot and both parts clean.
segments.deep: Wetting is a bond between molten solder and the metal surface, so it needs both an oxide free, contaminant free surface and enough heat to keep the solder liquid there. Either one missing and the solder will not stick. The rolled under failure is the instructive case because it can happen on a joint that was hot enough: the solder flowed, but on a dirty patch it had nothing to bond to and lifted away. When the heat was adequate and the solder still lifted, the cure is to clean the surface, reflux it, and rework. Heat also does not arrive evenly. A worked example: joining a light wire to a much heavier one. The light wire heats quickly and the heavy one slowly, so put the iron on the heavy wire and let the light one come along with it. Then read the result: solder flows toward whichever side is actually hot, so the direction of flow tells you where the heat really reached. The common misconception is that a joint that will not take solder needs more heat or a fixed number of seconds. A fixed count of seconds tells you nothing, and more heat cannot fix dirty metal; the solder's behaviour tells you which condition failed. The same reading matters on turrets.

check.q: True or false: a rolled-under failure can happen on a joint that was hot enough, because the metal was not clean.
check.again: Two conditions must both hold: both parts hot, and both parts clean of plastic, oxide and old solder. Heat is the one people check; cleanliness is the one that quietly fails. So a joint can reach full temperature and the solder still lifts and rolls under, because it will not stick to dirty metal however much heat arrives. When that happens, clean and reflux the surface and rework. Between two different wires, put the iron on the slow one and let the fast one come along. Then read the flow: the side the solder runs toward is the side that really got hot. Counting seconds tells you nothing.

segments.title: The pad and the butt joint
segments.text: For a wire soldered onto a board pad, the rules are short. The wire sits on the pad; nothing overhangs past it. Cut the wire a little shorter rather than letting it run past. Solder going over the pad edge does not matter. Fully covering the pad is not required. What does matter is the concave fillet where the wire meets the pad. Now the butt joint, where two wire ends meet end to end. It is tested by pulling hard on it, not lightly. But even a well-made butt joint is held only at the end of the metallic layer: the contact area is the cut face of the wire and nothing more. There is no overlap and no wrap. That is why it is discouraged for anything structural. It can pass a visual inspection and still be the weakest thing on the board, because the weakness is in the geometry, not in anything you can see.
segments.expand: Contrast the butt joint's end-face contact with a hook joint's wrap, in terms of what actually resists a pull.
segments.eli5: Think of joining two pencils by gluing their flat ends together. Only the two small end faces hold, and a sideways tug snaps it; overlapped and wrapped, far more surface carries the load. A butt joint, two wire ends meeting end to end, is the glued pencil ends. It is held only at the cut face of the metal, with no overlap and no wrap. Where the picture breaks: solder wets metal, unlike glue on wood, but the geometry problem is the same. So a butt joint can look perfect and still be weak, because the weakness is in the small contact area.
segments.deep: Two different joints, one principle: what holds a joint is the area and geometry of the bond. For a wire on a board pad, the wire sits within the pad with nothing overhanging past it. Solder going over the pad edge does not matter, and covering the whole pad is not required. What matters is the concave fillet where the wire meets the pad, because that fillet is the wetted bond. The butt joint shows the principle from the other side. Two wire ends meet end to end, so the only bonded area is the cut face of each wire, the end of the metallic layer and nothing more. There is no overlap and no wrap. As a worked comparison, a hook joint has at least six tight turns of wire against its terminal, while a butt joint has one end face. That is why a butt joint is tested by pulling hard on it, not lightly, and why it is discouraged for anything structural. The common misconception is that a joint which passes a visual inspection must be strong. A butt joint can pass and still be the weakest thing on the board. The next segment is the hook joint, where the wrap does the holding.

check.q: Why is a butt joint discouraged for anything structural?
options: It is held only at the cut end face
The solder will not wet a freshly cut end
It always fails a hard pull test
check.again: In a butt joint two wire ends meet end to end, so the only contact is the small cut face of each wire. There is no overlap and no wrap, nothing that mechanically resists a pull; only that tiny end-face bond does. That is a weakness of geometry, so the joint can look perfect and still be the weakest thing on the board. Compare a hook joint, where six tight turns hold the wire first. It is tested by pulling hard, and a well-made one can pass, but it stays discouraged for structural use. For a wire on a pad, nothing overhangs, and the concave fillet is what counts.

segments.title: The hook joint
segments.text: The hook joint is where mechanical forming does the work. Bring the wire in and hook it round the terminal. Put your finger inside the loop and wrap it tight, pushing each turn in hard against the last. Continue for a minimum of six turns. Then clip the ends so nothing pokes out, and bend the remainder in tight. The finger inside the loop is not a detail. Wrapping without it leaves the wire standing off the post, and you finish with visible gaps between the turns. Solder does not close a gap that the forming left behind. It fills a tight wrap; it does not replace one. The wrap is the mechanical hold, and the solder bonds a wrap that is already tight. If you can see daylight anywhere in the wrap, undo it and do it again before any solder goes near it. The forming takes practice, and that is where the effort belongs.
segments.expand: Explain why a gap in the wrap cannot be fixed with solder, in terms of what holds the joint mechanically.
segments.eli5: Think of tying a boat's rope around a dock post. Wrap it tight, each turn snug against the last, and the rope grips the post and holds. Wrap it loosely and the turns stand off the post with gaps, and it slips. A hook joint is the same. Hook the wire round the terminal, keep a finger inside the loop, push each turn hard against the last, and make at least six turns. Where the picture breaks: rope is untied later, but this wrap is meant to stay. So solder bonds a wrap that is already tight; it fills, and it cannot close a gap the forming left behind.
segments.deep: The hook joint separates two jobs: holding and bonding. The wrap holds. The wire is hooked round the terminal, a finger goes inside the loop, and each turn is pushed hard against the last, for a minimum of six turns. Then the ends are clipped so nothing pokes out, and the remainder is bent in tight. The finger is the mechanism: without it, the wire stands off the post and the turns spread apart, leaving visible gaps. Solder then does the bonding. It wets and fills a tight wrap, but it does not close a gap the forming left behind, because the wire that should be pressed against the post is simply not there to bond to. A worked way to see it: if only the first two of six turns sit tight and the other four stand off with daylight between them, you do not have six turns of hold, you have two. The common misconception is that a little extra solder will fill the gaps and make the joint sound. It will not; if you can see daylight anywhere in the wrap, undo it and wrap again before any solder goes near it. The next segment adds the rules around this joint: the insulation gap, bus wire, stranded wire and turrets.

check.q: What is the minimum number of turns in a hook joint wrap?
check.again: The hook joint is the case where forming does the real work. Hook the wire round the terminal, put your finger inside the loop, and wrap each turn tight against the previous one for at least six turns, then clip the ends and bend the remainder in. The finger in the loop matters: without it the wire stands off the post and gaps appear between turns. Solder fills a tight wrap, but it cannot close a gap the forming left, because the wrap is the mechanical hold and the solder only bonds what is already tight. Any daylight in the wrap means undo it and form it again before soldering.

segments.title: Insulation gap, bus wire, strands, turrets
segments.text: A few more forming rules. On a hook terminal there is a deliberate gap between where the insulation ends and where the joint begins, and its length equals the diameter of the insulation on that same wire. Measure it against the wire in your hand; that is what the specification is referenced to, not a fixed number. On a bus wire, hook around as normal, but the hook must not extend past the boundary of the bus wire. Stranded wire is prepared in a fixed order: twist, then tin, then form the loop. Tinning binds the strands so they bend as one wire, and the loop then holds its shape well; formed before tinning, loose strands keep the shape poorly. For a turret, tin the wire to the turret first, then attach it to the board, wrapping about three-quarters of the way around and cutting. Turrets cause trouble because heat travels through the post: sit on one joint too long and you reflow the joint on the other side. Get in and out quickly, and support the work with a third hand or a vise.
segments.expand: Go through the stranded-wire order again and explain why tinning before forming makes the loop hold, then the turret reflow problem.
segments.eli5: Think of threading a needle with frayed thread. Loose fibres splay and will not go through. Twist the end and wet it, and the fibres stick together and behave like one stiff strand. Stranded wire is prepared the same way, in a fixed order: twist the strands, tin them so the solder binds them into one, then form the loop. Formed before tinning, the loose strands hold the shape poorly. Where the picture breaks: water on thread dries off, but the tin stays and becomes part of the joint. Also: the insulation gap equals that wire's own insulation diameter. So twist, tin, then loop.
segments.deep: The insulation gap: on a hook terminal, the gap between the end of the insulation and the start of the joint follows a rule in words: gap length equals the diameter of the insulation, both measured on the same wire. Because the reference is the wire itself, it scales: change from the twelve gauge practice wire to twenty two gauge, and the gap follows that wire's own insulation. That is why it is measured against the wire in your hand, not to a fixed number. Bus wire: hook around as normal, but the hook must not extend past the boundary of the bus wire. Stranded wire: twist, then tin, then form the loop. Tinning binds the strands so they bend as one wire and the loop keeps its shape. Turrets: tin the wire to the turret first, then attach it to the board, wrapping about three quarters of the way around and cutting. Turrets cause trouble because heat travels through the metal post, so sitting too long on one joint reflows the joint on the other side. The common misconception is that longer heating is always safer. On a turret it damages a joint you were not working on, so get in and out quickly and support the work with a third hand or a vise.

check.q: On a hook terminal, how long is the gap between where the insulation ends and where the joint begins?
options: The diameter of the insulation on that wire
A fixed length, the same for every wire
About three-quarters of the way round the terminal
check.again: The insulation gap is specified relative to the wire in your hand: its length equals the outside diameter of that wire's insulation, so a fatter wire gets a longer gap. Measure it against the wire itself rather than remembering a number. The three-quarter figure belongs to turrets: tin the wire to the turret first, wrap about three quarters of the way round and cut, and work fast because heat down the post can reflow the joint on the other side. On a bus wire the hook must not extend past the bus wire's boundary. Stranded wire is twisted, then tinned, then formed, so the strands bend as one.

segments.title: The board: FR4, finish, mask, silkscreen
segments.text: The board in your hand is a printed circuit board, though a limited one, because it carries only pads and not the printed wiring that gives the board its name. The common material is FR4, a fibreglass substrate with copper bonded to it; the fibreglass is the structure and the copper is the conductor. Over the pads sits a tin based finish. Copper oxidises, so the tin is allowed to oxidise instead, protecting the copper without thinning it; that is why you see no bare copper on a new board, and it is the same logic as the tinned practice wire. The green layer is solder mask. It masks off everything not meant to be soldered. That is what makes machine soldering possible, and it prevents a great many bridges and shorts in hand soldering too. The white printing is silkscreen, the legend; any shape can go on it. Green and white are common here, not a universal rule.
segments.expand: Explain how solder mask prevents bridges between neighbouring pads, and why the finish over the pads is like tinned wire.
segments.eli5: Think of painting a room with masking tape. You tape over everything that must stay clean. The green solder mask on a circuit board does that job for solder. It covers everything that is not meant to be soldered, so solder only lands on the pads, and that prevents bridges and shorts between neighbours. The white printing on top is like a stencilled label: the silkscreen legend. Where the picture breaks: masking tape comes off when you finish, but solder mask stays on the board for good. So mask decides where solder can go.
segments.deep: FR4 is the common material: a fibreglass substrate that gives the structure, with copper bonded to it as the conductor. Over the pads sits a tin based finish. Copper oxidises, so the tin is allowed to oxidise instead, protecting the copper without thinning it. That is why a new board shows no bare copper, and it is the same logic as the tinned practice wire. The green layer is the solder mask. Molten solder only wets where it finds exposed, solderable metal, so a layer covering everything not meant to be soldered stops solder spreading from one pad to its neighbour. That is what makes machine soldering possible, and it prevents a great many bridges and shorts in hand soldering too. The white printing is the silkscreen legend; any shape can go on it, and the back of your practice board has none. The common misconception is that silver pads are bare copper; they are copper under a protective finish. Green and white are common colours, not a universal rule. Next comes the hole, which decides how many sides you solder.

check.q: True or false: the green solder mask covers the pads so that the solder has a surface to bond to.
check.again: Solder mask does the opposite: it covers everything that is not meant to be soldered and leaves the pads open. That is what makes machine soldering possible and it prevents many bridges and shorts in hand soldering, because solder cannot wet the masked copper between neighbouring pads. What actually sits on the pads is a tin based finish over the copper: copper oxidises, so the tin is allowed to oxidise instead, the same idea as the tinned practice wire. Under it all is FR4, fibreglass for structure with copper bonded on. The white silkscreen is just the printed legend, and green and white are common colours, not a rule.

segments.title: Holes: unplated, plated, multilayer
segments.text: How many sides you solder is decided by the hole. A single-sided board has copper on one face only. A double-sided board with unplated holes has copper on both faces but nothing inside the hole, just bare fibreglass. A lead pushed through has to be soldered on each side separately, because nothing carries between the two faces. A plated through hole is different: copper is deposited on the hole wall as well, forming a barrel that connects the layers. For the demonstrated process you heat and feed from the specified side, and wetting and capillary action carry the solder up through the barrel. Gravity is barely involved; the fill would happen much the same upside down. You still check the result: the required fill and fillet have to be there, and sometimes the solder only reaches partway up the hole. Beyond that are multilayer boards, with conducting layers buried between sheets of FR4; boards with eighteen layers exist, and space hardware goes further.
segments.expand: Describe capillary action drawing solder into a wetted copper barrel and why an unplated hole has no such path.
segments.eli5: Think of dipping the corner of a paper towel into a spill. The water climbs up the towel by itself, against gravity. A plated through hole works like that. Its wall is lined with copper, a narrow wettable barrel, so molten solder fed from one side is drawn up through it by wetting and capillary action. An unplated hole is bare fibreglass inside, with nothing for the solder to wet, so nothing climbs, and each side has to be soldered separately. Where the picture breaks: a towel soaks water into its fibres, while solder fills the open barrel. So copper in the hole decides whether solder can travel through.
segments.deep: How many sides you solder is decided by what lines the hole. A single sided board has copper on one face only. A double sided board with unplated holes has copper on both faces but bare fibreglass inside the hole, so a lead pushed through must be soldered on each side separately; nothing in the hole connects the two faces. A plated through hole has copper deposited on the hole wall, with a thickness set by the board construction, forming a barrel that connects the layers. Because that barrel is clean, wettable copper, molten solder fed from the specified side is drawn through by wetting and capillary action. Gravity is barely involved; the fill would happen much the same upside down. You still check the result, because sometimes the solder only reaches partway up the hole, and the required fill and fillet have to be there. Beyond this sit multilayer boards, with conducting layers buried between sheets of FR4; a board with eighteen layers is shown later in the course. The common misconception is that gravity carries solder down through a plated hole. It is wetting and capillary action. Feeding from one side is the procedure for this work, not a universal rule. Next, the lead that goes through the hole.

check.q: When you feed from one side of a plated through hole, what carries the solder up through the hole?
options: Gravity pulling the molten solder down the hole
Wetting and capillary action in the copper barrel
Pressure from the solder wire being pushed through
check.again: A plated through hole has copper deposited on its wall, forming a barrel that joins the two faces. Once that barrel is hot and clean, the solder wets it and capillary action draws the molten metal along the copper, the way water climbs a narrow tube. Gravity is barely involved; the fill would happen much the same with the board upside down. That is why you heat and feed from the specified side. With an unplated hole there is only bare fibreglass inside, so nothing carries between faces and each side is soldered separately. Either way you still check the fill and fillet.

segments.title: Lead forming and clipping
segments.text: A component lead can sit in its hole three ways. Straight through gives the least support; it is simple, but the part can fall out while you work. Fully clinched, bent flat along the pad, gives the most support and also lowers the part's height, but it is the hardest to remove later. Set over to one side gives enough support to hold the part and is quick to undo, and that is the everyday choice. Whichever form you use, mind the clipped end. If you cut the lead after soldering, you can be left with a bare copper end sticking out of the solder. If the lead was tinned before it went in, you are fine. If bare wire runs through, the cut end must finish covered. Check every clipped end; clipping can create a defect as easily as finish a joint.
segments.expand: Compare the three lead forms on support, height and ease of removal, and explain the bare-copper-end problem.
segments.eli5: Think of a twist tie on a bread bag. Poke it through and leave it straight and it slides out. Twist it flat and tight and it holds firmly, but it is a fight to undo. One quick bend to the side holds well enough and undoes in a second. Component leads have the same three choices. Straight through holds least, and the part can fall out. Fully clinched, bent flat along the pad, holds most and sits lowest, but is hardest to remove. Set over to one side holds enough and undoes easily, so it is the everyday choice. So pick the form by the hold you need against how easily the part must come out.
segments.deep: Lead forming is a trade between mechanical support, height and how easily the part can come out later. Straight through gives the least support; the part can fall out while you work. Fully clinched, the lead bent flat along the pad, gives the most support and also lowers the part's height, but that same grip makes it the hardest to remove. Set over to one side gives enough support to hold the part and is quick to undo, which is why it is the everyday choice. As a worked comparison: ranked by support, clinched is first, set over second and straight through third, yet clinched is also the one that is hardest to take out again. The second idea is the clipped end. If you cut the lead after soldering, the cut exposes a fresh end, and you can be left with bare copper sticking out of the solder. If the lead was tinned before it went in, that end is fine; if bare wire runs through, the cut end must finish covered. The common misconception is that clipping is just tidying up. Clipping can create a defect as easily as finish a joint, so check every clipped end. These forms come back every time a component lead goes through a hole on these boards.

check.q: Of the three ways a component lead can sit in its hole, which is the everyday choice?
options: Fully clinched flat along the pad
check.again: The everyday form is the lead set over to one side: it gives enough support to keep the part from falling out while you work, and it is quick to undo. Straight through is the simplest but gives the least support, so the part can drop out. Fully clinched, bent flat along the pad, gives the most support and lowers the part, but it is the hardest to remove later. Whatever form you choose, inspect every clipped end afterwards. Cutting a bare lead after soldering can leave exposed copper sticking out; a lead tinned first is fine, and any bare cut end must finish covered.

segments.title: Tip discipline, every single time
segments.text: Before you start, reset the bench: no tangled wires, nothing lying near the iron tip. Check the tip every time it leaves the holder, not once at the start of the session. A clean tip is bright and shiny. Oxidation impairs wetting and the heat transfer at the contact, so the routine is fixed. Lift the iron and check the tip. Wipe it, every time, without exception. If a wipe does not clean it, add a little fresh solder to the tip and wipe again. Then go to the joint with a clean, hot iron. The diagnostic for a dead tip: put solder on it and watch. If the solder pulls away into a ball instead of spreading, surface tension is not working for you; there is an oxide coating on the tip. Clean it properly with tip cleaner. If that does not recover it, the tip is replaced, never filed. And you cannot wait for a convenient moment. A tip sitting in your hand goes dark while you are deciding.
segments.expand: Explain why solder balling on the tip proves an oxide layer, and walk through the check, wipe, re-tin, wipe routine.
segments.eli5: Think of checking your mirrors while driving. You check them every time before you move, not once in the driveway, because traffic changes in seconds. The soldering tip is the same. Oxide re-forms on it within seconds, so you check the tip every time it leaves the holder, wipe it every time, and if a wipe does not clean it, add a little fresh solder and wipe again. Test it with solder: spreading means clean. If it pulls away into a ball, oxide is blocking it. So check and wipe on every lift, because a tip in your hand goes dark while you are deciding.
segments.deep: The routine exists because of how fast oxide forms on a hot tip: a freshly cleaned and tinned tip can go from bright to dark in a few seconds. Oxide impairs wetting and the heat transfer at the contact, though not literally to zero. So the steps are fixed. Lift the iron and check the tip. Wipe it, every time. If the wipe does not clean it, add a little fresh solder to the tip and wipe again. Then go to the joint with a clean, hot iron. The dead tip test reads surface tension directly. Put solder on the tip: on clean metal it wets and spreads; on an oxide coating it cannot wet, so surface tension pulls it into a ball that pulls away. That ball is the proof of oxide. Clean it properly with tip cleaner, and if that does not recover it, replace the tip, because a plated tip is never filed. A worked comparison: a check once at the start of a session against an oxide layer that returns within a few seconds means nearly every joint of the session would start with a dirty tip. The common misconception is that a clean tip stays clean. It does not; this routine runs before every joint you make from here on.

check.q: True or false: if solder placed on the tip pulls into a ball instead of spreading, the tip has an oxide coating.
check.again: A clean tip is bright and shiny, and fresh solder spreads across it because surface tension pulls solder onto clean metal. When the solder draws itself into a ball and refuses to spread, the metal it is sitting on is not clean; an oxide skin has formed and is blocking wetting and heat transfer. Clean it properly with tip cleaner, and if it will not recover, replace the tip, never file it. The routine is fixed: every time the iron leaves the holder, check the tip, wipe it, and if a wipe is not enough, add a little fresh solder and wipe again. A tip goes dark while you hesitate.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from this lab. One: smooth flat plier jaws and one good cutter of the right size; serrations cut the coating, and a cutter lent out on hard wire comes back notched. Two: a sound joint has a concave fillet you did not shape; if you had to add solder to make it look right, redo it, and never paint over a bad joint. Both parts hot, both parts clean, and cleanliness is the one that quietly fails. Three: forming comes first. Finger in the loop, six tight turns minimum, no daylight, because solder fills a tight wrap but cannot close a gap. Four: the hole decides the soldering. Unplated means each side separately; plated means capillary action carries the solder through, and you still check the fill. Five: set the lead over for everyday work, cover every clipped end, and check and wipe the tip every time it leaves the holder.
segments.expand: Quiz the student with one mixed question that combines the hook wrap, the insulation gap and reading the fillet.
segments.eli5: Think of a tailor pinning a seam before sewing. The pins hold the fabric in line and the stitches lock it in; sewing a crooked seam just stitches the mistake in place. This lab follows the same order. Good tools protect the wire. A tight hook wrap, a wire on its pad and a properly set lead are the pinning. The solder is the stitching: a concave fillet shows it bonded, and it cannot fix what the forming got wrong. Where the picture breaks: stitches need no heat, and solder needs hot, clean metal. So form it right first, then let the solder bond it.
segments.deep: The five ideas share one mechanism: solder wets and fills, it does not hold or straighten. Tools come first because they protect the metal: smooth jaws keep the tin coating intact, and a cutter used only on the wire it was made for keeps a clean edge, since tungsten, roughly ten times harder, can notch a blade for good. Reading the fillet is reading wetting: concave means bonded, convex or rolled under means not, and needing extra solder to make it look right means redo it. Both parts must be hot and clean, and cleanliness is the one that quietly fails. Forming comes before solder: finger in the loop, a minimum of six tight turns, no daylight, and an insulation gap equal to the diameter of that wire's own insulation. The hole decides the soldering: unplated means each side separately, plated means wetting and capillary action carry solder through the barrel, and you still check the fill. Finally, set the lead over for everyday work, cover every clipped end, and check and wipe the tip every time it leaves the holder. The common misconception tying them together is that solder fixes things. It only bonds what is already clean, hot and well formed, and that is what the bridge exercise and the power supply build will test.

check.q: In the recap, what does an unplated hole mean for how you solder a lead?
options: Capillary action carries solder through the hole
Only one side of the board needs solder
check.again: The recap's fourth idea is that the hole decides the soldering. An unplated hole has nothing conductive inside it, so a lead pushed through has to be soldered on each face on its own. A plated hole has a copper barrel, and capillary action carries the solder through from one side, though you still check the fill. The other recap ideas: smooth flat jaws and one good cutter; a concave fillet you did not shape, with both parts hot and clean and cleanliness the one that quietly fails; forming first, six tight turns with no daylight; set the lead over, cover every clipped end, and wipe the tip every time.

standing.why: ELTR rule-set quiz can happen at the start of any class
